en: [After 7.45, S₁ K₁.₃ Dn Ds D₁.₄ insert:]
I shall proclaim the sages of the first Manvantara, that of Merusāvarṇi; listen, O sage.
Meghātithi was of the lineage of Pulastya, Vasu was of Kaśyapa,
Jyotiṣmat was of Bhṛgu, and likewise Dyutimat was of Aṅgiras.
Savana Vāsiṣṭha, Havyavāhana Ātreya,
and Paulaha— these seven are the sages in the Rohita interval.
O lord of men, there are exactly three hosts of deities there;
they are the sons of Rohita, the Prajāpati who was the son of Dakṣa.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Dīptaketu, Pañcahotra, Nirākṛti,
Pṛthuśravas, Bhūridyumna, Ṛcīka, Bṛhat, and Gaya—
these were the nine sons of great power belonging to the first Sāvarṇi.
Now, in the tenth period, during the interval of the second Manu,
Haviṣmān the son of Pulaha, Sukṛti the son of Bhṛgu,
Āpomūrti the son of Atri, and Vasiṣṭha is recorded as the eighth.
Paulastya, Pramati, Nābhoga Kāśyapa,
Aṅgiras, Nabhas, and Satya— these seven are the supreme ṛṣis. These two groups of deities are remembered as the ṛṣi-mantras.
The sons of Manu were Uttamaujas, the heroic Nikuṣañja,
Śatānīka, Nirāmitra, Vṛṣasena, Jayadratha,
Bhūridyumna, and Suvarcas; these ten were the sons of Manu.
Now, in the eleventh period, during the interval of the third Manu,
learn from me as I proclaim his seven Ṛṣis as well.
Haviṣmān Kāśyapa, Haviṣmān Bhārgava,
Taruṇa Ātreya, and likewise Anagha Vāsiṣṭha.
Aṅgiras, Cārudhiṣṇya, Paulastya, Niścara,
Paulaha, Agnitejas, and Bhāvya— these shall be the seven great ṛṣis.
The gods are the sons of Brahmā; three groups of them are recorded:
Sarvatraga, Suśarman, Devānīka, and Purūdvaha.
Kṣemadhanvan, Dṛḍhāyu, Ādarśa, Paṇḍaka, and Manu—
these nine are recorded as the sons of the third Sāvarṇa.
Now learn from me the seven sages of the fourth Sāvarṇi:
Dyuti, the son of Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Sutapas, the son of Atri.
Aṅgiras was the embodiment of austerity, as was the ascetic Kāśyapa;
Paulastya was Tapośana, Paulaha was Tapas, and Ravi was Taporavi.
Among them, the seventh should be known as Bhārgava, who is steadfast in austerity. These five groups of gods are declared to be the mind-born sons of Brahmā.
Devavāyu, Adūra, Devaśreṣṭha, Vidūratha, Mitravān, Mitravinda, Mitrāsena, Mitrakṛt,
Mitrabāhu, and Suvarcas were the sons of the twelfth Manu.
Now, in the thirteenth period to be described, during the Manvantara of Manu,
there will be Aṅgiras, Dhṛtimat, and he who is the Paulastya Havyavat.
Paulaha was a seer of reality, and Bhārgava was free from worldly desire;
likewise Ātreya was unshakable, and Kaśyapa was free from delusion.
And Suta-pāśa Vāsiṣṭha—these seven are the great seers (maharṣis). Three groups of deities were proclaimed by the Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū).
These sons of Trayodaśa are to be known as the sons of Ruci:
Citrasena, Vicitra, Naya, Dharmabhṛt, and Dhṛta.
Sunetra, Kṣatravṛddha, Sutapas, Nirbhaya, and Dṛḍha—
these were the sons of Manu Raucya during the thirteenth interval.
Then, in the fourteenth period of the Manu Bhautya,
Agnīdhra Kāśyapa, Paulastya, and Māgadha [were the sons].
For Bhārgava, Atibāhu, Śuci Āṅgirasa, the disciplined Atri,
Śukra Vāsiṣṭha,
Ajita Paulaha, and the final ones— these are the seven ṛṣis.

[After the additional colophon following 7.47,] The *Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa* has been completed. May there be auspiciousness! May there be success! May there be well-being! May there be prosperity! May the illustrious Goddess Anasūyā, the consort of the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Lord Agastya, the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Goddess Lopāmudrā, the consort of the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Lord Kaśyapa, the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Goddess Aditi, the consort of the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Lord Dakṣa, the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Goddess Prasūti, the consort of the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Lord Manu, the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Goddess Śatarūpā, the consort of the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Lord Yama, the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Goddess Yamunā, the consort of the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Lord Varuṇa, the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Goddess Gaurī, the consort of the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Lord Vāyu, the supreme person, be pleased with me! May the illustrious Goddess Svāhā, the consort of the supreme person,
N (except S1 N1) T2-4 G insert: Janamejaya said: O you of great intelligence, [tell me] the enumeration of the Manvantaras and of the Yugas.
O twice-born one, you should also tell me the measure of a day of Brahmā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The sun divides day and night by means of worldly measurement;
taking that calculation as a basis, listen to the enumeration, O subduer of enemies.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty of those make one *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* make one *muhūrta*; so say the wise.
"O King, they say that a day and night consist of the movement of the moon and the sun; indeed,
throughout all these [periods], it is by the specific movement of the sun that [time is measured] eternally."
But especially among all [beings], day and night are constant.
Fifteen days and nights are designated as a *pakṣa* (fortnight);
two *pakṣas* are known as a *māsa* (month), and two months are called an *ṛtu* (season).
A year is said to consist of two solstices (*ayana*), and each solstice is composed of three seasons (*ṛtu*);
this is taught by those expert in calculation regarding both the southern and the northern courses.
Those who know the measurement of time understand that a month, consisting of two fortnights according to this calculation, constitutes a single day and night for the ancestors (pitṛs).
For them, the dark fortnight is the day and the bright fortnight is the night;
O King, the ancestral *śrāddha* ceremony for the ancestors takes place during the dark fortnight.
That which is known as a year by human measurement is but a single day of the gods; likewise, the arrangement of months and years is established according to that same scale.
That constitutes a day and night for the gods; the northern course [of the sun] is their day.
A divine year is one day and night; its northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) is the day,
and its southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is recorded as the night by the wise who are skilled in the meaning of reality.
Ten times a divine year is recorded as a day and night of Manu;
ten times that day and night is called a fortnight of Manu.
Ten *pakṣas* (fortnights) constitute a month; twelve months multiplied together are declared by the wise who perceive the truth of reality to be a season (*ṛtu*) for the Manus.
Three seasons constitute an *ayana*, and two such *ayanās* make a year.
Six of those years are declared to be a *vatsara*; by that reckoning, the calculation is established.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of exactly four thousand years.
O King, the twilight (saṃdhyā) and the period of twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) shall each last for three hundred years; the Tretā age shall be three thousand years in duration,
and its twilight and the subsequent period of twilight shall likewise each last for three hundred years.
Likewise, two thousand years are proclaimed as the Dvāpara age.
His twilight period was also two hundred years, and his period of twilight was likewise.
The Kali age is reckoned here by the wise as one thousand years; its dawn (saṃdhyā) is one hundred years,
and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
This number of twelve thousand years has been proclaimed as the duration of a *yuga*. Now learn from me the calculation of the *yugas* according to this divine measure.
O dear one, that all-pervading Lord again emitted this entire world;
he created the four ages: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.
O best of kings, that yuga multiplied by seventy-one is declared as a *manvantara* by those expert in calculation and its meaning.
And that is also declared to be the *ayana*; there are two *ayanās*, the southern and the northern.
O Lord, at the conclusion of the *ayana*, Manu indeed dissolves here;
a thousand cycles of four *yugas* is said to be a single day of Brahmā.
For him, the night is of the same duration; by these two [day and night], the reckoning of the fortnights and so forth is made.
Thereafter, another Manu exists for that same length of time. O King of kings, when those have passed away, that is indeed declared to be one year.
That very number, ten thousand, was declared by the sage who perceives reality;
that is said to be a day of Brahmā, and it is designated as a *kalpa*.
Those people who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas,
and that his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas— they are the ones who truly understand day and night.
That night which is said by the wise to last for a thousand yugas, during which the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, sinks into the waters; 44–45.
When that thousand yugas is completed, O best of the Bharatas,
at the end of a day of Brahmā, the kalpa is said to be entirely exhausted.
[h: HV (CE) Appendix I, No. 3, transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus, proof-read by Horst Brinkhaus, version of January 22, 2001 :h]
Thus,
these ancestors are gods, and the gods are again the ancestors.
For these ancestors are indeed both gods and ancestors to one another.
"O dear one, three of them are formless, while four possess forms;
the gods diligently perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) for them with great care."
The gods, with palms joined in reverence and their minds fixed upon him, were devoted;
as were the Viśvedevas, the Sikatas, the Pṛśnis, and likewise the Śṛṅgins.
Kṛṣṇā, the Viśvas, and the Ajās likewise worship according to the rules;
so too do the Prajās, the Vātaraśanas, and the Divākīrtyas.
The clouds and the winds, as well as the inhabitants of heaven beginning with Brahmā,
and all the ṛṣis headed by Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Atri.
Yakṣas, nāgas, suparṇas, and kinnaras, together with the cāraṇas—
all these indeed worship the ancestors, seeking their rewards.
Thus, when these great-souled ones are honored and worshipped with faith,
they bestow all desires by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Having abandoned the cycle of existence in the three worlds as well as the fear of old age and death,
the Grandfathers bestow the yoga of liberation and sovereign power.
Furthermore, these grandfathers bestow the means to liberation, sovereignty, the subtle body, bodilessness,
complete dispassion, and infinity.
Yoga ordained by sovereignty is called the sovereignty of yoga.
Without the sovereignty of yoga, liberation is in no way possible,
just as it is impossible for a wingless bird to travel through the sky.
The eternal dharma of liberation is the most excellent among all dharmas;
it is attained through the presentation of offerings to the great-souled ancestors.
Grandfathers bestow pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, horses, elephants, pairs [of oxen], and indeed jewels by the millions.
They were filled with swans and cranes, adorned with pearls and lapis lazuli,
provided with networks of small bells, and always bearing flowers and fruits.
The Grandfathers bestow thousands of celestial chariots, frequented by throngs of Apsarases and abounding in all objects of desire.
When pleased, the ancestors constantly bestow upon human beings progeny, nourishment, steadfastness, intelligence, sovereignty, and even health.
[h: HV (CE) Appendix I, No. 4, transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus, proof-read by Horst Brinkhaus, version of January 22, 2001 :h]
Sanatkumāra said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for rites according to the prescribed rule.
In the performance of the *kāmya*, *naimittika*, and *ajasra* śrāddha rites, one should always [behave] thus.
The three Aṣṭakās should occur at the end of Āgrahāyaṇa and Mūla. Of these, the first is declared to be the most excellent, belonging to Indra;
the second belongs to Prajāpati; and the third belongs to the Viśvedevas.
The first [offering] is prescribed as being with cakes; another should always be with meat;
the third should be made with vegetables—this is the rule regarding the substances.
Indeed, the Anvaṣṭakya rite for the ancestors is ordained as a constant obligation.
And whatever other fourth [rite] there may be, that too he should perform with diligence.
A wise man should constantly perform the *āyuḥ-śrāddha*, even at the cost of his entire wealth;
thus, blessings come swiftly, and he rejoices both in this world and the next.
At all times and on every lunar day, the ancestors and the deities all come toward a man, like cows to watering holes.
If they are not honored on the Aṣṭakā day, they will not grant what is beneficial;
his hopes will always be in vain, both in this world and in the next.
For those who worship, there is constant prosperity; for the nihilists, there is a downward course. Those who give gifts go to the gods, while those who do not give fall among the animals.
Bestowing nourishment, progeny, memory, intelligence, sons, and even sovereignty,
one who performs [this rite] on the full moon day attains everything in its entirety.
The first practice leads to the acquisition of wealth, and what has been acquired does not perish for him.
But he who performs it on the second day shall become a lord of bipeds.
The third [lunar day] brings fruit for those seeking results; it is the destroyer of enemies and the annihilator of evil.
One who performs [rites] on the fourth [lunar day] perceives the vulnerabilities of his enemies.
Performing [the rite] on the fifth day as well, one obtains great prosperity;
performing *śrāddha* offerings on the sixth day, one obtains the honor of the twice-born.
The man who constantly performs śrāddha rites on the seventh lunar day attains the merit of a great sacrifice and becomes a leader of hosts.
The man who performs the Śrāddha on the eighth day attains a complete livelihood;
one desiring sovereignty among men should perform the Śrāddha on the ninth day.
By performing [this rite] on the tenth day, a man shall obtain the splendor of Brahman;
he shall acquire all the Vedas and become esteemed by the brahmins.
On the eleventh day, there is supreme generosity, sovereignty, and likewise progeny;
on the twelfth day, for the sake of attaining victory, there is kingship, long life, and wealth.
For one performing the thirteenth [lunar day rite], there is an increase in progeny, pure descendants, independence, supreme nourishment,
long life, and sovereignty.
One should cause [the offering] to be given to those whose young [sons] have died in the house;
and to those who were slain by a weapon, one should give [the offering] on the fourteenth day.
On the new moon day, one who is pure should always perform the *śrāddha* with diligence;
he attains all desires and enjoys infinity in heaven.
One should give food on the new moon day; thus there shall be the nourishment of Soma.
One attains the world of Manu, and there one enjoys everything.
Thus nourished, Soma will sustain the three worlds.
The powerful one is constantly praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas with holy and pleasing hymns, accompanied by all objects of desire as offerings.
Seated upon his celestial chariot, devoted to his ancestors and firm in his vows, he was attended by thousands of Apsarases with dance, instrumental music, and song.
The gods, gandharvas, and hosts of siddhas always praise him;
moreover, one who is devoted to his father shall obtain all desires on the new moon day.
Performing *śrāddha* rites under the asterism Maghā, one shall obtain all desires;
by him the ancestors are always worshipped directly.
Since the ancestors and the gods are [present] in Maghā, therefore they know that [the merit of offerings made] under those [asterisms] is inexhaustible.
Now hear from me those optional *śrāddha* rites which Yama proclaimed to Śaśabindu, categorized individually according to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
The man who constantly performs a *śrāddha* during the conjunction with Kṛttikā,
having established the sacred fires, shall sacrifice along with his offspring, free from all distress.
The steadfast man always crosses over difficulties and shall become prosperous;
one desiring offspring should perform the rite under Rohiṇī, and through the power of Soma, he shall attain vigor.
One who performs a *śrāddha* under Ārdrā shall partake in cruel deeds;
one performing a *śrāddha* under Punarvasu shall partake in [the fruits of] fields and sons.
Under Mṛgaśīrṣa he will be renowned;
under Ārdrā he will be wise in policy and gentle; and under Punarvasu he will be prosperous.
Furthermore, a man desiring prosperity should perform a śrāddha during the Puṣya asterism.
Furthermore, by giving after the Āśleṣā asterism, one obtains heroic sons;
by performing a śrāddha during the Maghā asterism, one becomes the most excellent among one's kinsmen.
Furthermore, by performing [the rite] under the Phalgunī asterisms, a man obtains good fortune;
he who is disposed toward giving and has offspring performs it under the Uttarā-phalgunīs.
He who offers libations to the ancestors with his hand becomes preeminent in assemblies.
He who performs [the rite] under Citrā shall obtain handsome sons.
A twice-born man desiring to live by trade should perform it under Svāti.
A man should endeavor to perform a śrāddha under the asterism Viśākhā for the sake of obtaining sons.
A man performing [this rite] under Anurādhā may set the wheel in motion;
indeed, he who performs it under Jyeṣṭhā shall obtain sovereignty through faith.
Through the Mūla constellation, there shall be the attainment of health; through the Āṣāḍhās, great fame;
and likewise, through the Uttarā-Āṣāḍhās, a man shall become free from sorrow.
By hearing [this], one shall attain the supreme goal among the worlds;
under Śraviṣṭhā, one shall obtain royal enjoyments and abundant wealth.
Performing a *śrāddha* under the asterism Abhijit, one obtains the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*);
performing it under the asterism of Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), one obtains success as a physician.
Performing [the rite] under Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā, one obtains a long life;
performing it again under Uttarā-proṣṭhapadā, one acquires cattle by the thousands.
The man who performs [the rite] under Revatī obtains much silver;
under Aśvinī, he obtains excellent horses; and under Bharaṇī, he obtains the highest longevity.
Performing this ritual for the ancestors, Śaśabindu obtained this entire earth without effort,
and having acquired it, he ruled over it.
A vessel made of silver, or one coated with silver, is said to be the vessel for the ancestors.
Even a conversation about silver, the sight of it, or the gift of it [is beneficial].
The gift of silver is said to lead to infinity, imperishability, and heaven.
By that gift, good sons indeed deliver their ancestors;
this [text] is always recited at a *śrāddha* by those disciplined in the exposition of the Veda.
For in ancient times, the *svadhā* was milked by the ancestors into this vessel;
since the earth is for the sake of imperishability, what is given therein is therefore inexhaustible.
The proximity to, the sight of, and the gift of a black antelope skin destroy demons,
increase Vedic splendor, and rescue one's cattle and sons.
A golden vessel, a silver vessel, a daughter’s son, a woolen blanket, sesame seeds,
a goat, and likewise a triple-staffed ascetic and a yogin are purifying.
O Brahmin, this is the supreme and eternal rule for the ancestral rites (śrāddha);
it increases lifespan, nourishment, glory, fame, wisdom, and progeny.
In the south-eastern direction, one should establish the site for the altar;
it should be square, measuring one cubit on all sides, and well-enclosed.
In accordance with the scriptures, I shall duly describe the place for the ancestors,
which brings wealth, long life, health, and increases nourishment and fame.
In that place, three pits should be prepared and three staffs made of khadira wood;
they should be one cubit (aratni) in length and adorned with silver.
Those pits, one span in length and four finger-breadths wide on all sides,
should be made extending toward the east and south, stable and without holes.
Being pure, one should constantly bathe with water purified by a strainer;
or one may perform purification with milk and ghee from a cow, as well as with sacred utterances.
For this is indeed a constant libation; it brings eternal satisfaction.
In this world and in the next, one becomes glorious and endowed with all desires.
Thus, he who, having bathed at the three sessions of the day, always worships with self-restraint according to the rule and with the mantra,
shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
For those [mantras] are known as the "twenty-one," since by them the triple world is indeed sustained.
For him there is nourishment, as well as sovereignty, long life, and indeed progeny;
he shines with splendor in heaven and attains liberation in due course.
One shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice, which removes evil and purifies;
therefore, I shall declare this mantra, which is like nectar and equal to the Veda.
Salutation to the deities and to the ancestors, and likewise to the great yogis; salutation always to Svadhā and to Svāhā—salutation, salutation!
One should always recite this three times at the beginning and the end of a *śrāddha* ceremony;
for this has been honored and praised by Brahmins as yielding the fruit of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
And during the offering of the funeral ball (piṇḍa), one should likewise recite with a concentrated mind;
thus the ancestors arrive quickly and the Rākṣasas flee.
This mantra pertaining to the ancestors saves one in the three worlds when it is constantly recited during a śrāddha by self-controlled exponents of the Veda.
One who desires sovereignty should thus constantly recite this mantra without weariness;
it increases vigor, heroism, wealth, intelligence, prosperity, long life, and fame.
I shall now fully declare the auspicious seven-verse hymn, which grants all desires and by means of which the ancestors are gratified through recitation and observance.
I always pay homage to those ancestors who are formless and those who possess form, who are of blazing splendor, who are meditative, and who possess the eye of yoga.
I bow to the ancestors of Indra and the other gods, as well as those of Dakṣa and Mārīca; I pay homage to the ancestors of the seven ṛṣis, who grant all desires.
Having paid homage to all those ancestors of Manu and the others, who are honored by all the worlds, as well as those of the waters and the ocean; HV_App.I,4.129–130.
With palms joined in reverence, I always pay homage to the constellations and the planets, to Vāyu, Agni, and the Pitṛs, and to Heaven and Earth.
To those who give birth to the divine sages and are honored by all the worlds.
And endowed with this ritual procedure, O illustrious lord of men, one should perform it:
"I pay homage to the grandfathers, the sustainers of all the worlds. (HV App. I, 4.133–134)
With palms joined in reverence, I always pay homage to Prajāpati, to the cows, to Agni, to Soma, to Yama, and to the Lords of Yoga.
Salutations to the seven groups of ancestors who have been proclaimed;
I bow to the self-existent Brahmā, whose eye is yoga.
And this seven-verse hymn, worshiped by the hosts of gods and sages, has been spoken;
for it is supremely purifying, glorious, and indeed a destroyer of demons.
A man who is endowed with this method obtains three boons,
provided he is possessed of supreme devotion, full of faith, and has conquered his senses.
Whoever, being constantly composed, should recite this hymn of seven verses,
shall become the sole sovereign of the earth with its seven islands and oceans.
Homage to that Self-Existent One by whom this ritual manual was proclaimed;
and to the great lords of yoga, I am forever bowed down in reverence.
The ancestors, O dear one, exist as deities among the gods in heaven;
these imperishable ancestors are eternally established in seven stations.
These are all the sons of Prajāpati; indeed, they constitute the first host of all those great-souled ones, the eternal group of yogis that increases through yoga.
The second belongs to the gods, while the third belongs to the Dānavas and others;
having reached the condition of the age (yuga-dharma), they follow the path of yoga.
But the remaining ones are to be known as belonging to the social classes; thus they have all been proclaimed.
He who gratifies the ancestors with devotion, the ancestors gratify him in turn. Being pleased, the ancestors bestow progeny as well as nourishment,
heaven, long life, health, and whatever else is desired.
O Sage, the rite for the ancestors is praised even more than the rite for the gods;
for the ancestors are traditionally held to be the primary abode of the deities.
They are exceedingly gracious, well-pleased, and the supreme nourishment for the world;
their favor is ever-stable—bow down to them, O Bhārgava.
[h: HV (CE) Appendix I, No. 5, transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus, proof-read by Horst Brinkhaus, version of March 1, 2001 :h]
[Yudhiṣṭhira said:]
O Lord, for what reason was the venerable little bird of Brahmadatta made blind by you in the past, O son of Gaṅgā, toward his eldest son?
Having resided in his house for so long, for what reason did she do this unpleasant thing to that high-souled king?
She paid him homage; what kind of friendship did she have with him?
Tell me all of this doubt exactly as it is.
Bhīṣma said:
Listen, O great king, to everything as it happened in the past;
learn of that which took place in the palace of Brahmadatta, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
O King, there was a certain bird that was the friend of Brahmadatta;
it had white wings, a red head, a white back, and a white belly.
That friend of Brahmadatta was bound by very firm affection;
O best of men, she made her nest within his house.
Every day, having emerged from that king’s excellent palace,
she wandered along the shores of the ocean, by the ponds, and at the lakes.
In rivers, mountain groves, and various forests,
and in blossoming ponds fragrant with white lotuses.
In places where the wind was made fragrant by the filaments of white and blue lotuses,
and which resounded with the cries of swans and cranes and the calls of water-fowls;
Having performed her duties among them, O King, she arrived at night in Kāmpilya,
at the palace of the wise King Brahmadatta, O Pārtha.
O King, she constantly engaged in conversation with that king.
And whatever wonders had occurred during her travels through various lands, she recounted them all that night.
O descendant of Kuru, O tiger among kings, at one time that monarch Brahmadatta had a son known as Sarvasena.
She was worthy of worship, and moreover, she had given birth to an egg there;
for long ago, a single [egg] had burst forth from that shell within that nest.
But the mass of flesh burst open, joined with arms, feet, and a mouth;
O lord of the earth, it became tawny-faced and eyeless.
Later, however, it came to possess eyes and rose slightly upon its wings.
Then that venerable lady, out of equal affection for both the prince and her own son, was filled with joy day after day.
O King, every evening she would bring two fruits with her beak for the two sons of Sarvasena,
which were like the taste of nectar.
That boy was indeed the worshipful son of Brahmadatta.
Having eaten those fruits, the two of them became broad-chested and filled with joy;
moreover, those fruits remained delicious for them here forever.
When that venerable woman had departed on the day of the full moon,
O King, the nurse then constantly amused that infant— the son of Brahmadatta— with a young sparrow.
When Pūjanī had departed, having then dragged [the bird] from its nest,
that sparrow was once seized by the playing prince.
Seized by the neck with a firm fist by the child,
O King, he whose fist was difficult to break immediately gave up his life.
But seeing him who had met his death, with his mouth wide open, having been slain by the child— though he had somehow been rescued— the king became sorrowful.
Then the king, his eyes overflowing with tears, rebuked the nurse;
filled with grief, the monarch stood there lamenting for that sparrow.
At that time, the forest-dweller, though herself worthy of worship, took two fruits and went to the palace of Brahmadatta.
Then, O lord of men, having arrived at that house, he beheld his own son,
a corpse abandoned by the five elements.
Seeing her own son, she fainted, but then she regained consciousness;
and having regained consciousness, O King, that poor woman lamented.
"O son, do you not indeed approach Vāsantī when she has arrived, offering thousands of endearments with a voice of indistinct modulations? (HV App. I, 5.55–56)
With mouth wide open and afflicted by hunger, O dear son,
why do you not slither today with your yellowish-red mouth and palate, my son?
Having embraced me with both your wings,
why indeed do I not hear you even now calling out "cī-cī-kū-cī" with your beak?

But this was my heart’s desire: that I might see my little son before me, with his mouth agape, begging for water, and flapping his wings. That hope of mine has been shattered now that you have met your death.
Having lamented thus in many ways, she then said to the king:
"Are you not indeed one who has been consecrated with the royal aspersion; do you not know the eternal laws of dharma?"
"How is it that you have had my son killed by this nurse? O lowest of Kṣatriyas, tell me how you had him dragged away by your own son!"
Surely you must have heard this Vedic tradition of the descendant of Aṅgiras:
one who has come for refuge, one afflicted by hunger, or one oppressed by enemies—
even if he has lived in one's own house for a long time— should be protected in every way.
A man who fails to protect [his dependents] goes undoubtedly to Kumbhīpāka;
how then can the gods accept his sacrificial offering, and the ancestors his *svadhā*?
Having spoken thus, O Great King, she who was devoted to the ten dharmas,
afflicted with grief, pierced out the eyes of that boy.
Then, having rendered the prince's eye blurred with his two hands and leaving the king’s son blind, he flew up from there into the sky.
Then the king, seeing his daughter worthy of worship, said:
"Be free from grief, O auspicious one; you have done well, O timid lady."
Your grief has passed; turn back. Let there be with you an undecaying friendship. O friend, as before—blessings upon you—turn back and rejoice.
"Even though this suffering has come upon my son, O friend, I have no anger toward you; may you be blessed, for you have done what was required of you."
Pūjanī said:
"By means of comparison with myself, I understand your affection for your son as well.
Yet, I do not wish to live with your son who is sightless."
Having indeed committed an offense in your house, O tiger among kings, she has been placed there.
And hear also these verses sung by Uśanas, as they are recited by me.
One should avoid from afar a bad friend, a bad country, a bad king, a bad companion, a bad son, and a bad wife.
There is no friendship with a bad friend; how can there be delight in a bad wife?
How can there be sustenance from a bad son? And there is no truth in a bad king.
Where is trust to be placed in a bad friend? One does not live in a bad country.
There is constant fear under a bad king; with a bad son, there is unhappiness on all sides.
That lowest of men who places his trust in one who has done him harm does not live long, just like one who is helpless and weak.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one even trust the trustworthy. Danger arising from misplaced trust cuts down even the very roots.
That foolish man who places his trust in royal servants or in those born of mixed lineage does not live for long.
"Having attained great elevation, a king may perish without a doubt—just as a small insect [is destroyed] by its own cocoon; thus Uśanas spoke, O King. (HV App. I, 5.99–100)
Moreover, by means of gentleness, a wise man always destroys his enemy by causing him to shrink away from his body,
just as a creeper destroys a great tree.
Becoming mild, fierce, and emaciated, the enemy gradually withdraws;
like an anthill at the base of a tree, he cuts away the root from behind.
O King, having made a covenant of non-injury in the presence of the sages,
Hari subsequently slew Namuci with the foam of the waters.
Men slay an enemy while he is asleep, intoxicated, or heedless,
either by means of poison, fire, a weapon, or even through illusion.
Out of fear of their enmity, men do not leave even a remnant;
for having heard this simile, O King, they cause [the enemy] to be destroyed root and branch.
O King, the remnant of an enemy, the remnant of a debt, and the remnant of a fire will grow again when they meet;
therefore, one should leave no remnant.
The enemy laughs and talks with him, and they eat from the same vessel;
he even sits upon the same seat, yet he remembers that sin.
One should not place trust even in an enemy after having established a bond;
for Śatakratu, though he was his son-in-law, slew Puloman in battle.
That man who, harboring enmity in his mind, speaks pleasant words here—
no wise person should approach him, just as a deer does not approach a hunter.
One should not dwell near an enemy whose enmity has increased;
for he will surely cause one to fall, root and all, like a tree on a riverbank.
Having attained elevation from an enemy, one should not trust that "I am exalted.
Therefore, having attained such elevation, one may perish just like the *prāvārakīṭaka* insect.
Thus, O lord of the earth, these verses sung by Uśanas should be retained by a wise man who desires to protect himself. (HV App. I, 5.123–124)
"And a most terrible offense was committed by me against you, in that I made your son blind; therefore, do not trust us. Having spoken thus, she then flew away into the sky like a female moth.

Thus, O King, I have related to you this ancient account concerning Brahmadatta, O Indra among kings, and what occurred with that venerable lady; and as for the *śrāddha* rites which you, O high-minded Yudhiṣṭhira, asked me about.

Janamejaya said:
"How did the celestial Gandharvī Urvaśī come to reach a mortal king, having abandoned the gods? Tell me that, O one of great learning."
Having heard Urvaśī being sung of by the celestial sage in Indra’s abode,
the goddess, afflicted by the arrows of Love, approached his presence.
Beholding her, the king’s eyes blossomed with joy;
his hair standing on end, he spoke to the queen in gentle words.
"Welcome to you, O lady of excellent hips; please be seated. What may we do for you?
Delight yourself with me; may our pleasure endure for eternal years.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Overcome by the curse of Brahmā, she approached a human being;
that woman of beautiful limbs arrived there in accordance with the agreement.
Thus she dwelt there, desiring an end to the curse;
for the sake of her own release from the curse, she made a solemn agreement.
Beholding the naked and sexual intercourse with a woman who desires it.
"O King, O giver of honor, protect these two lambs as a trust.
I shall sport with you; for you are considered the most praiseworthy among men and the best of women."
Two rams always remained tied near his bed;
O King, his food consisted of nothing but a single drop of ghee.
"O King, if this is your resolve and it remains firm for as long as you wish,
then your union with me shall come to pass."
"I shall remain for as long as you act in this manner.
O King, this is the agreement made for your dwelling in my house:
I shall dwell there for that duration; such is the compact we have established."
The king observed all those conditions of hers.
The King said:
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what presence, which deludes the world of men!
What mortal would not serve you, O Goddess, who have come of your own accord?
Thus did that beautiful woman dwell there with Purūravas.
Then, deluded by that curse, she remained devoted to him for sixty-one years.
While Urvaśī was dwelling among mortals, the Gandharvas were filled with anxiety;
Indra saw Urvaśī and then spoke to the Gandharvas.
"Without Urvaśī, this assembly hall does not shine for me.
The Gandharvas said:
"O highly fortunate ones, consider how that excellent woman may be found."
Urvashi, the ornament of heaven, shall once again come together with the gods.
Then Viśvāvasu, the best among speakers, said there:
"I previously heard the agreement being made by me with those two."
Indeed, having transgressed her agreement, she will surely abandon the king;
I know that entirely, how this monarch will break his word.
"I shall go accompanied by my companions for the sake of accomplishing your purpose.
Having spoken thus, the highly illustrious one departed for Pratiṣṭhāna.
Then, having arrived at night, he carried off one of the rams;
yet that woman of lovely smiles behaved toward the two rams as if they were her own mother.
Having learned of the Gandharva's arrival and the end of the curse, the illustrious lady said to the king there, "My son has been carried off."
Thus addressed, having reflected, he did not rise at all while naked:
"The Goddess will see me naked; my vow would be rendered false."
Then the Gandharvas took away a second ram from me.
When the second ram had been taken, the goddess spoke these words to Ela: *HV_App.I,6.29–30*
"O King, O Lord, my two sons are being carried away like one who is helpless.
Hearing the lamentation of the queen as her two sons were being led away, [she cried out].
I have been ruined by this wretched protector, a eunuch who fancies himself a hero.
"Because of my confidence in him, I was lost to the bandits and deprived of my children—
he who sleeps at night as terrified as a woman, though he is a man by day. Having been addressed thus, the king then rose up naked and ran away.
Then, seeking the tracks of the two rams, the Gandharvas produced a great flash of lightning by which that vast palace was suddenly illuminated; thereupon, he beheld them naked.
Seeing him naked, the Gandharvī vanished and indeed went to heaven.
But seeing her vanished from sight, the Gandharvas indeed went to heaven.
Seeing that she had vanished, the Gandharvas there quickly abandoned the two rams and departed from that place as they pleased. Seeing the two rams abandoned,
the king took them and returned home.
Not seeing Urvaśī there, he lamented, deeply afflicted by grief;
he wandered the earth, searching for her here and there.
Then that mighty king beheld her at Kurukṣetra;
having seen her at Kurukṣetra, he also saw her companions by the Sarasvatī.
With a joyful countenance, Purūravas spoke these well-spoken words: **HV App. I, 6.40** 10:2: "Five..."
"Alas, my wife! Alas, my wife! Stay, O terrible one; you ought not to abandon me.
Without having attained me, you shall find no rest; such are the words we shall utter."
"O Goddess, let this fair-bodied one, who has gone far away with you, fall today;
let the wolves and vultures devour him, for he is no longer a fit recipient of your grace. [She replied:
'I have bathed at the Plakṣatīrtha, at Puṣkariṇī, and on the Himavat.'"
Seeing that beautiful woman playing with five celestial nymphs, he then lamented, overcome with great sorrow.
And she too, seeing the king there not far away, said to her friends: "This is that best of men, with whom I indeed dwelt; show me that king. (HV App. I, 6.44–6.46)
But all of them, being greatly agitated, O lord of men, spoke such auspicious words to one another as follows: "O wife, stay! Stay in my mind, O terrible one; stay in my speech! (HV App. I, 6.47–49).
And Urvaśī said to Aila: "O Lord, I am pregnant by you; after one year, a son shall be born to you, of this there is no doubt. And for one night, O King, you shall dwell with me."
The king, possessed of great fame, departed for his own city in high spirits;
when a year had passed, Urvaśī returned once more.
And the highly illustrious one dwelt with her for a single night.
Then Urvaśī said to Aila: "The Gandharvas are granters of boons to you;
choose them, O great king, and speak to them yourself."
"O King, choose equality with the high-souled Gandharvas.
Having said, "So be it," he chose that boon, and the Gandharvas replied, "So shall it be."
Having set down the vessel and gone into the forest, he returned home at night;
when the Tretā age had fully commenced, the three Vedas appeared within his mind.
Having filled the vessel with fire, the Gandharvas said to him:
"O lord of men, by sacrificing with this, you shall attain our worlds."
Taking those boys, he prepared to depart;
having placed the fire in the forest, he went home with his sons.
Having approached the fire, however, he did not see it; he saw an *aśvattha* tree there. Seeing that *aśvattha* tree grown from a *śamī* tree, he was then struck with wonder.
Then he informed the Gandharvas of the destruction of Agni;
having heard that entire matter, they commanded the fire-drills (araṇī).
Having made a fire-drill from an aśvattha tree and having churned out the fire according to the prescribed rite,
that lord of men divided the churned fire into three parts and performed sacrifice. Having sacrificed with various kinds of offerings, he attained the same world as those [deities].
Having sacrificed there, that lord of men attained those worlds;
having obtained a boon from the Gandharvas, he established the three sacred fires.
In the beginning there was but one fire; Aila established it as three.
Such was the power of King Aila, O best of men.

Janamejaya said:
I have heard that the highly wise and great-minded grandson of Budha was born of Urvaśī;
how did he attain the status of a Kṣatriya?

O high-minded one, tell me how in this world Ātreya was purified after violating another's wife; what kind of expiation was seen for him? And what is the nature of a Brāhmaṇa in this world—tell me that as well.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Behold, I shall tell you; listen, O best of kings!
From his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the Lord created the Brahmins and the other [castes]."
Because he was born from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and likewise because of his teaching of the Veda,
the Brāhmaṇa is, according to dharma, the lord of this entire creation.
That whose mouth the gods of the triple heaven always consume as sacrificial offerings (havya),
and the ancestors as offerings to the manes (kavya)— what being could be greater than that?
One born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a consecrated Brāhmaṇa;
it should be known that Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are likewise to be recognized as such when they are born from their own respective mothers.
Teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these are the six duties of those born of the first caste.
The best of the twice-born should always practice the study of the Veda as his austerity;
for the study of the Veda is said to be the supreme austerity for a brahmin in this world.
One who knows the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, who understands words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge,
and who is cognizant of the auxiliary sciences, is fit to know the meaning of the Veda.
For one has studied in every way the systems of grammar such as those of Pāṇini and all the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas),
as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and the Vedas at all times.
The speaker who understands words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge enjoys the fruit;
likewise the listener, but if it were otherwise, it leads only to hell.
The best of the twice-born should not be satisfied with the mere recitation of the Vedas;
for one who rests content with mere recitation sinks like a cow in the mud.
Immediately after birth, the birth-rite (jātakarman) should be performed according to the rules;
then, on the tenth or twelfth day, one should have the naming ceremony (nāmadheya) performed.
In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) should take place, and the tonsure (cūḍā) should be performed according to family custom;
when the fifth year has arrived, however, the practice of learning the alphabet (akṣarābhyāsa) is prescribed.
One should perform the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
one should provide him with the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) made of a cord of nine strands.
That Brāhmaṇa should carry a staff made of either Bilva or Palāśa wood;
having worshipped his guru and the sun, he should beg for alms, self-restrained and pure.
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules,
and supports him with food, is called his guru.
But he who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda and explains its meaning— that one they call an Ācārya.
But he who teaches a single portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas,
for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya.
Ten preceptors (ācāryas) are equal to one teacher (upādhyāya), and a hundred teachers are equal to a father;
a thousand fathers, however, are less than a mother, who is the most venerable of them all.
Having duly obtained knowledge through service to his teacher, the twice-born man,
with the teacher’s permission, should perform the ceremonial bath after giving him a cow as a sacrificial fee.
Permitted by his teacher and having performed the ceremonial bath according to the rules,
the twice-born man, upon returning home, should marry a wife who possesses auspicious marks and noble kin.
And one should abandon a maiden who is bereft of kinsmen and one who is diseased.
Regarding the instruction of mantras, officiating at sacrifices, marriage, and the eating at a *śrāddha*,
the teaching of Manu and others is that these should be performed only among one's own kinsmen;
thereafter, one should establish the sacred fires in every respect according to the prescribed rule.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and meditated with a concentrated mind upon the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, he should thereafter discharge his feces and urine.
Then, having covered the ground with grass on the southern side toward the southwest,
and having applied a coating of clay and performed purification according to the prescribed rule;
Having cleansed the anus, feet, and hands with earth, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa).
Having sipped water and become pure, one should then perform the bath.
Having immersed oneself in water and meditated upon the stainless Nārāyaṇa within the heart,
one should then rise and offer the *arghya* oblation to the Sun, O protector of the earth.
Having recited the supreme mantra a thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having worshipped the Sun, one should perform the second oblation.
Having taught the Veda according to the rules and the Vedāṅgas on the third lunar day,
one should take flowers and other offerings at the auspicious hour and go to that Lord.
Having bathed for the sake of attaining security and prosperity, and having performed the midday rites with the *Puruṣasūktas* and the eight-syllable mantra, he worshipped Hari.
Then, having worshipped and gratified [the deities], and having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite according to the rules,
as well as the hospitality for guests and the meal in due order;

During the sixth and seventh watches of the night, the wise man should pass the time with the study of *itihāsa* and *purāṇa*. While chewing betel, the wise man should do so again. Having performed the evening twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), he should diligently perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
Among Brahmins, those who are learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are refined;

among those of refined intellect, those who perform their duties; and among those who perform their duties, those who discourse on the Brahman—these are the most excellent Brahmins in the world, always considered worthy recipients of gifts.
First, one should always give the best portion as a gift to the guru;
likewise, whatever is given to mother and father, and to brothers, sisters, and sons [is likewise meritorious].
A gift given to a sister, a nephew, maternal uncles, a father’s sister,
and to poor kinsmen, is inexhaustible for one who knows the Vedas. A gift to a father is said to yield a hundredfold merit, while that to a mother is said to yield a thousandfold.
The twice-born man who passes by a fellow student who is nearby while he is giving gifts or offering food for the ancestors burns his family down to the seventh generation.
One should give double to a Brāhmaṇa, but an equal amount to one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa;
a hundred-thousandfold to one who has studied extensively, and an infinite reward to one who has mastered the Vedas.
The scriptures prescribe expiations for mortal sins and minor offenses;
they provide the authority for those born in the lands of action (karmabhūmi).
O King, the gods who dwell in heaven have no authority over these matters.
Born from Budha to the daughter of Vairāja, he is known as Ila;
through the power of his maternal grandfather, he attained the status of a Kṣatriya.
Nevertheless, purified by an expiation through the power of Atri,
Śaśāṅka was released from his waning and became highly honored by all the worlds.

Vaiśampāyana said:
They were all born as the sons of Elā, resembling the sons of gods;
high-souled ones born in heaven: Āyu, Dhīmat, and Amāvasu.
Viśvāyu, the righteous-souled Śrutāyu, and another,
Dṛḍhāyu, Vanāyu, and Śatāyu were the sons of Urvaśī.
The heir of Amāvasu was King Bhīma, a sovereign among kings; the illustrious Bhīma’s heir was King Kāñcanaprabha. The learned and mighty Suhotra was the son of Kāñcana as well.
Sauhotri was Jahnu, born from the womb of Keśinī;
he who performed the great sacrificial session, the Sarpamedha, the great sacrifice.
Because she had pursued him out of desire for his favor,
the Gaṅgā flooded that assembly hall of his even though he did not wish it.
Seeing the sacrificial enclosure inundated on all sides by her,
O best of the Bharatas, the son of Suhotra spoke to Gaṅgā in anger.
"This water of the three worlds I now drink up for you in brief;
O Gaṅgā, receive immediately the fruit of this arrogance."
Then, seeing that Gaṅgā had been drunk by the royal seer,
the highly fortunate great seers offered Jāhnavī to him as a daughter.
Jahnu, however, took Kāverī, the daughter of Yuvanāśva, as his own.
By the curse of Gaṅgā, half of her body was later turned into a river;
by the curse of Yuvanāśva, she was fashioned from half of Gaṅgā.
The Kāverī, the best of rivers, the blameless wife of Jahnu.
Jahnu, however, begot upon Kāverī a beloved and most righteous son named Sumahat;
and Ajaka was his son.
The heir of Ajaka was the lord of the earth Balākāśva, who was devoted to hunting;
his son was Kuśa.
Indeed, Kuśa had four sons of divine splendor:
Kuśika, Kuśanābha, Kuśāmba, and Mūrtimat.
The king was raised among the Pahlavas and with forest-dwellers.
The powerful Kuśika performed austerities, thinking, "May I obtain a son equal to Indra. Out of fear, Śakra approached him and was born as that son.
When a full thousand years had indeed passed, Śakra beheld him;
seeing him engaged in most intense austerity, the thousand-eyed Purandara appeared.
Being capable of fathering a son himself,
that lord of the gods, the best of deities, undertook the matter personally and resolved to become his son.
He became King Gādhi, Maghavan Kauśika himself;
Paurukutsī was his wife, and Gādhi was born of her.
And Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi; King Viśvaratha;
as well as Viśvakṛt, Viśvajit, and Satyavatī, O King.
Formerly, there was a highly fortunate and auspicious maiden named Satyavatī;
the twice-born Ṛcīka requested her daughter Satyavatī from him.
Considering it an unsuitable boon, Gādhi spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
{Gādhi said:} [I desire] horses with the luster of the moon, each having one ear black.
"Let a dowry of a thousand be given for the maiden; we are the Kuśikas."
Having been addressed thus, he accepted their proposal and went to the destroyer of Varuṇa (Yama).
Having brought those horses and given them [to him], he married the lovely-faced woman.
The lord Gādhi gave her to Ṛcīka, the son of Kāvya.
The husband of that woman, the descendant of Bhṛgu and joy of the Bhṛgus, became pleased;
that ṛṣi was entreated by his wife and by his mother out of a desire for offspring.
Having cooked the *caru* with both sets of mantras, the sage went to bathe;
he then prepared a *caru* for Gādhi as well, for the sake of obtaining sons.
Then Ṛcīka, the descendant of Bhṛgu, called his wife and said:
"This sacrificial porridge is to be consumed by you, and this other one is for your mother."
In her shall be born a son, radiant, a bull among Kṣatriyas,
invincible by the Kṣatriyas in this world, and a slayer of the foremost of Kṣatriyas.
O auspicious lady, this sacrificial oblation shall likewise produce for you a son who is steadfast, rich in asceticism,
composed in spirit, and the best among the twice-born.
Having spoken thus to his wife, Ṛcīka, the joy of the Bhṛgus,
entered the forest, ever devoted to ascetic penance.
Then Gādhi, the lord of men, accompanied by his wife, went to the hermitage of Ṛcīka on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, in order to see his daughter.
Then Satyavatī took those two sacrificial offerings;
having taken one offering with care, she presented it to her mother.
The mother, having made an exchange by fate, gave her own sacrificial oblation to her daughter;
then, out of ignorance, she took the daughter's oblation for herself.
Then Satyavatī conceived a fetus that was to be the ender of the Kṣatriyas;
she bore it with a radiant body, though its appearance was terrible.
Then Ṛcīka, having perceived her through his yogic power and followed after her,
spoke to that woman of excellent complexion, his own wife, O best of the twice-born.
"O blessed lady, you have been deceived by the exchange of the sacrificial oblations;
for a son will be born to you who is a performer of cruel deeds and exceedingly terrible."
A brother shall also be born to you, one who has become Brahman and whose wealth is asceticism;
for by means of my ascetic power, the entire universe has been entrusted to him as Brahman.

Thus addressed by her husband, the highly fortunate Satyavatī then sought to appease him, saying, "Let my son not be such; let there be no outcaste among the Brahmins born from you. When she had spoken thus, the sage replied:
"O blessed lady, this desire was not so intended by me that 'let it be thus':
that a son should be of fierce deeds because of his father and mother."
Having spoken these words, Satyavatī further said this:
"O Sage, if you so desired, you could create even the worlds; how much more so a son?
You ought to grant me here a son who is peaceful in nature and upright."
"O Lord, O best of the twice-born, let such a grandson be mine and yours as well,
if it is indeed impossible to do otherwise."
Then, by the power of her asceticism, he showed her favor:
"O lady of excellent complexion, there is no distinction for me between a son and a grandson;
O blessed one, the word spoken by you shall come to pass exactly as it was said."
Then Satyavatī gave birth to a son of the Bhṛgu lineage,
Jamadagni, who was devoted to austerity, self-controlled, and composed in spirit.
Long ago, due to a reversal of the sacrificial oblations (caru) between the rites of Rudra and Viṣṇu performed by Bhṛgu,
the portion of Viṣṇu was born on earth as Jamadagni.
For she is the meritorious Satyavatī, devoted to truth and righteousness;
this great river has set forth, renowned as Kauśikī.
There was a lord of men named Reṇu, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage;
his daughter was the highly fortunate Kāmalī, known as Reṇukā.
Endowed with ascetic power and knowledge, the son of Ṛcīka begot upon Reṇukā,
the daughter of Kamaṭha, the exceedingly fierce Jāmadagnya.
The foremost among all those who have mastered the sciences, one who has reached the further shore of the art of archery,
Rāma— the slayer of Kṣatriyas— who was like a blazing fire.
Thus, from Aurva’s son Ṛcīka,
through the power of his asceticism, Jamadagni— the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman— was born of Satyavatī and attained great fame.
Śunaḥśepha was the middle one, and Śunaḥpuccha was the youngest.
Gādhi, the son of Kuśika, begot as his heir a son named Viśvāmitra, whose very nature was asceticism, sacred knowledge,
and self-restraint; he who attained equality with the Brahman-sages and became one of the Seven Sages.
But the righteous-souled Viśvāmitra, known by the name Viśvaratha,
was born through the grace of Bhṛgu from the Kauśika lineage as the increaser of his race.
From Gādhi was born one of great splendor, like a kindled fire, who,
having renounced the power of the *kṣatriya* through asceticism, attained the luster of the *brahman*.
O King, Viśvāmitra had one hundred and one sons; Madhucchandas was the middlemost, and they were all known as the Madhucchandāsas. The others were Aṣṭaka, Hārīta, Jayakratu, Mada, and so forth.

Thus, the Kauśika lineage and the Viśvāmitra lineage, though distinct, have entered into different *pravara* groups and are thus conceived as being twofold. The sons of Viśvāmitra are recorded as Devarāta and others.
They are renowned throughout the three worlds; hear their names from me.
Devashravas and Kati—because of him, they are known as the Katyayanas.
From Hiran yaksha, born of Shalavati, was born Renu; from Renu was born Renumat.
Sāṃkṛti, Gālava, and the renowned Mudgala;
Madhucchandas and the others, as well as Devala and Aṣṭaka.
Kacchapa and Hārita were indeed the sons of Viśvāmitra;
the lineages of those high-souled Kauśikas are well known.
Pālita and Babhru, as well as Karajapya;
likewise the Pārthivas, Devarātas, Śālaṅkāyanas, and Bāṣkalas.
The Lohityas, the Yamadūtas, and likewise the Kārīṣayas are recorded;
O King, the Sauśrutas, the Kauśikas, and others such as the Saindhavāyanas.
The Devalas, the Reṇus, the Yājñavalkyas, the Aghamarṣaṇas,
the Audumbaras, the Abhiṣṇātas, the Tārakāyaṇas, and the Cañcalas.
The Śālāvatyas, Hiraṇyākṣas, Sāṃkṛtyas, and Gālavas,
as well as Nārāyaṇi and Nara, and others— many Kauśikas who intermarried with other lineages of seers— are recorded as the descendants of the wise Viśvāmitra.
O great king, even within this lineage of his, the connection between the Brahmanical seer Kauśika and the Paurava lineages of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas is renowned.
Among the sons of Viśvāmitra, Śunaḥśepa is remembered as the eldest;
that best of sages, though born of Bhṛgu’s lineage, attained the status of a Kauśika.
It is said that Viśvāmitra’s son was Śunaḥśepa;
he was indeed assigned to the state of a sacrificial animal at the sacrifice of Hariścandra.
The man who was sold as a sacrificial animal at Hariścandra’s sacrifice was released from his bonds after he had praised the gods, beginning with Prajāpati.
He who was known as Devarāta, the ascetic among the Gādhis,
was Śunaḥśepha of the Bhṛgu lineage;
indeed, Śunaḥśepha was given back to Viśvāmitra by the gods.
Having made Śunaḥśepha his son, as well as Devarāta Bhārgava,
he said to his sons: "Ājīgarta, let this eldest one be appointed as the substitute."
Those Madhucchandasas, who were the eldest, did not consider that to be well;
the enraged sage cursed them: "Become Mlecchas, you wicked men!"
Then Maducchandas spoke together with fifty others:
"O sir, we shall abide by whatever you know to be our duty."
They made you the eldest among the seers of mantras; we are your followers.
Viśvāmitra said to his sons: "You shall be possessed of heroes.
Because he was indeed given by the gods, he therefore became Devarāta.
Devarāta and the others were the seven sons of Viśvāmitra;
likewise, Aṣṭaka was the son of Viśvāmitra by Dṛṣadvatī.
I have described to you the group of Jahnu’s descendants, beginning with Lauhi, the son of Aṣṭaka.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the lineage of the high-souled Āyu.

for this matter, which was previously foreseen by the Lotus-born One, is destined to come to pass.

"I shall take refuge in that deity who will grant me a son.

But the royal sage Divodāsa, O King, having reached the city,

instead, she smiled and then approached Bhava’s side.

With perfumes, incense, garlands, and likewise with sprinkled waters,

thereafter, he bestows thousands of boons upon the Nāgas—
sons, gold, long life, and likewise all their desires.

There is a place called Prabhāsa, O King, which is the most excellent of all holy sites (*tīrtha*). It is there that the Lord of the World, the Self-born One, dwells together with Umā. Having gone there, O King, you shall attain the fruit of your deed. There, O King, you shall behold the Lord of the World, the Self-born One, who is accompanied by Umā and surrounded by hosts of gods. Having beheld him, you shall attain the highest state. Thus addressed by the sage, the king, filled with joy, set out for Prabhāsa with his wife and his ministers. Having reached Prabhāsa, he bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī and beheld the Lord of the World, the Self-born One, who was accompanied by Umā and surrounded by hosts of gods. Having beheld him, the king, together with his wife, attained the highest state. While Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa were frequently engaged in excessive play,
they would sometimes go out from the house and seize fresh butter.
Having repeatedly stirred up buttermilk with other boys,
O King, those two youths then broke water-jars;
having drunk the curd, the two lords of gods crushed those jars as well.
And Kṛṣṇa, appearing in the guise of a young boy, took up the sling;
having pierced and split [the vessel], Govinda drank the milk entirely.
Then the Lord of Gods cast what remained upon the earth.
Having brought the milk-rice from the house and scattering it elsewhere,
Kṛṣṇa then gave it to the children, acting according to his own nature.
And the best of children, taking a jar of curds from the hanging shelf, [gave it to them].
Having pierced and torn through the earth, Keśava then crushed him to pieces.
Then those two boys, O scorcher of foes,
suddenly released the calves from their ropes and drove the cows away. At that time, they caused distress in every house.
Seeing that the two of them were wandering through the entire settlement with excessive restlessness,
Nanda Gopa was unable to restrain those two who were exceedingly difficult to control. Then Kṛṣṇa, together with the other boys, fixed his gaze upon them.
But then, O lord of the earth, Kṛṣṇa quickly concealed one boy and spoke to another boy:
"Go, child, just as you have seen with the other boys elsewhere."
"If you have been seen by others, you shall be defeated and punished by me," having said this,
the powerful one sent Balabhadra to see him.
Balabhadra, having gone there, seized the boy by force.
He gave him to Keśava; but you were defeated, and Keśava said:
"Having brought the *kīlaka* and scattered it, hidden within the earth, the Lord of the World summoned all the children and said this: (HV App. I, 9.25–27).
"If any among you is capable, let him take the stake while watching;
having come to my side, he shall indeed be given a staff.
Hearing that, all the boys made an effort to see it.
And when they were all unable [to defeat him], he spoke to those who had been conquered. Thus Govinda, the wise Kṛṣṇa, performed such childhood sports together with the boys in Gokula.

In one house, having gathered together and taken all the jars of milk placed on hanging scales,
they drank the milk all at once with great joy.
Then, having struck them all, he laughed aloud and crushed them outside;
tearing away the carrying-sling, he threw the jars of curd elsewhere,
and having drunk as much as he desired, he gave some to the children.
Then, with joy, Kṛ� jars hidden elsewhere in some other room; taking them, he quickly broke them there. In another room, taking many jars filled with clarified butter, he likewise shattered them.
He distributed [the curds] among the children, eating some himself and giving some away;
filling jars with buttermilk from another room,
he took them, shook them repeatedly in many ways, and threw them back into that very same place.
That boy laughed variously and laughed aloud, and he danced;
throwing milk into buttermilk and buttermilk into milk,
and mixing milk with water, he offered clarified butter into the fire.
In this way, the two of them constantly engaged in that battle for the cattle there;
the cows were well-nourished, free from disease, affectionate toward their calves, and yielded milk at will.
Having arrived, they were delighted and clung to his tail and other parts.
Well-bathed with cow-urine from the tail, with horns and ears adorned with ornaments, they mounted the calves;
while the young calves frothed at the mouth as they drank.
Then, having repeatedly broken and cut the ropes with which the calves were tied to the stakes,
he led the calves away from their mothers;
tearing the cords everywhere and driving the calves in all directions.
Dragging the boys by their hair, they bound them together; being restrained by the cowherd girls, he repeatedly filled the empty vessel with clarified butter, milk, curds, and buttermilk.
Accompanied by his elder brother, he generally frequented the cow-pen;
and while the cowherd girls were looking on, Kṛṣṇa always acted with playful agitation.
And drinking various kinds of milk, he thus committed that slaughter.
Then, crying out repeatedly, the cowherd women went to Yaśodā’s side and reported all of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds to her.
"Ten jars of mine have been destroyed by this wicked-minded son!
Not even a trace of milk, buttermilk, ghee, or curd remains.
What can be done now, O fool? My livelihood is perishing!"
"Taking fifty other jars of mine, filled with ghee and well-sealed, from the shelf, your son kills me as I look on."
"Furthermore, all the jars within the inner apartments were indeed full of ghee;
I had them emptied of it, yet there was no ghee remaining for me."
Then another, being exceedingly enraged, tore at her hair on all sides and said:
"Kṛṣṇa has shaken, lifted up, whirled around, and crushed thirty-five jars filled with ghee and milk upon the surface of the earth!"
"O foolish woman, not even a single morsel remains in my house;
and the cows have been drunk by their calves, who were released by this Kṛṣṇa."
"O blessed lady, he has indeed eaten much of my well-cooked milk-rice; furthermore,
rice with curds and rich flavors was given to the children."
Many cakes were eaten by me while protecting them for the sake of my husband;
many prepared parched grains mixed with sugar and other ingredients were drunk.
"What need have I for a house? What need for cowherd settlements or cattle and the like?
O dull-witted woman, you fool who gives birth to wicked sons, I shall depart!"
"O foolish woman, ten other cows of mine, along with their calves, must have been lost today;
they have been driven away by this wicked-hearted son of yours."
The fresh butter I ate was like an anthill;
my livelihood has been destroyed, so I shall go to another country.
Thus the cowherd women, who were to be strictly concealed, cried out loudly and discordantly;
then all the cowherd women said, "Tell us, O blessed one, what will our fate be?"
Then Yaśodā gave them back their lost child;
having thus consoled them all, she sent each of them to her own home.

Vasudeva, however, was already restrained by Nandagopa, who said:
"Your residence in Vṛndāvana must also be avoided."
Perceiving his son’s great dignity and seeing that the forest was inhabited by asuras,
the high-minded Nandagopa then reflected upon it with his intellect.
Having observed the great abundance of cattle in the forest of Vṛndāvana, the cowherds desired to enter it; and there was an asura named Pralamba present therein.
I see no other forest nearby endowed with such abundance;
what indeed should be done so that it may be for the welfare of my two sons?
While he was reflecting in this manner, the sage Nārada approached him in private,
having been dispatched by Brahmā and the high-souled Indra, O Brahmin.
By chance, the great yogi, who was constantly devoted to the welfare of the world,
had his feet saluted by Nanda the cowherd, O sage.
The Brahmin spoke with a smile to him, whose mind was agitated by distress:
"Knowing that there is sorrow in your heart, I have come here out of affection for you."
This secret of the gods must never be disclosed;
O highly wise one, you shall indeed understand it at that time.
O Lord of Ghoṣa, O All-pervading One, you shall indeed understand that which I shall tell you:
these two sons of yours, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who have been born as humans, are not merely mortals; they are gods descended to earth for the purpose of uprooting the Daityas.
Knowing that Janārdana was being born to uproot the faction of the Asuras,
the Daitya, an Asura, took refuge with you in the guise of a cart;
he was determined to kill the infant while you were sleeping beneath the cart.
Then, seeing that Dāmodara was bereft of protection and separated from you two— and indeed, seeing him released from you two— the Dānava [acted].
And having found an opening, he was killed by the child at that very moment so that he could be crushed.
Struck by my left foot, he fell over and died;
meanwhile, the boy woke up and yawned for a moment.
And on that very night, he took away the life of a Rākṣasī named Pūtanā, who was giving him her own poisoned breast-milk to drink.
Then those two Daityas, having assumed the forms of Arjuna and having spotted that vulnerability, desired to kill him; however, the boy himself slew them.
"Your son shall thus slay the Daityas who assume various forms;
O cowherd, do not enter the forest of Vṛndāvana, for it is a place of fear for you."
Even there, this Kṛṣṇa will perform such a very great task;
these deeds have been performed here before your very eyes.
Rāma, the crusher of enemy forces, will slay Pralamba, and Kṛṣṇa will destroy the host of Asuras; let no fear approach you.
Having spoken thus to Nandagopa, Nārada praised Kṛṣṇa:
"Salutations to you, the sustainer of the world; salutations again and again to the creator of the universe."
Salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa, who possesses strength and many forms;
salutations to him whose color is like a dark cloud, who plays the flute as a cowherd.
Homage to you, O son of Devakī; homage to you, O Lord of the Yādavas!
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; homage to the creator of *māyā*. Homage again and again to the author of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the three worlds.
Enter Vṛndāvana, O Lord, and sport there as you please;
being diligent, slay the Daityas of great prowess who dwell therein.
When Nārada had departed after saying this, the high-minded cowherd Nanda,
freed from fear and trembling, experienced great joy for his two sons.
