Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached Vṛndāvana, both those sons of Vasudeva wandered about in their own forms,
tending the herds of calves.

And having entered that great forest, the woods of Vṛndāvana, they then took delight for a very long time as they pleased together with Keśava. The cows were rich in milk, and the buffaloes were perfectly contented.
At that time, they then wandered about with their calves as they pleased.
And when Kṛṣṇa was wandering in the forest of Vṛndāvana, [the following occurred].
Then, as the thirteenth year was passing and Keśava was growing in strength,
the summer season arrived while Kṛṣṇa remained in Vṛndāvana.
When the sun of piercing rays had reached the northern quarter,
its beams of sharp luster spread in all directions,
constantly enticing the deer while the sun possessed its fierce heat.
Emerging from the kīcaka reeds split by the forest fire,
the seven-flamed fires rose up here and there over the scorched mountain; likewise,
hyenas and jackals, their bodies consumed by the forest fires, let out their cries.
The elephants, trumpeting with gurgling sounds,
agitated by the heat of the season and assailed by hot winds, let out discordant cries.
Split open by the heat of the fire and torn asunder by the forest winds, the *kṛṣṇala* fruits fell everywhere upon the earth like showers of blood upon mountains.
The abundant dust of the earth, obstructing the path of their eyes,
repeatedly covered the vision of the cowherds like darkness.
When the sun had reached the meridian, the cowherds, scorched by the heat,
gathered the cows at the roots of trees in the forests and stood there.
Taking up jars filled with water on all sides,
the cowherd women stood in the shade, tormented by the rays of the hot-rayed sun;
they constantly fanned their broad breasts with garments wet with water.
On the road, the cowherds, repeatedly taking cool and pure drops of water contained in their leather bags, dispelled the dryness of their mouths.
The birds dwelling in their nests, distressed by the heat, cried out with harsh, gurgling sounds as they sought refuge among dry leaves;
struck by the fierce flames of the forest fire, they shrieked in intense torment. Their bodies were parched by the lotus stalks, and they remained huddled within their nests.
They were covered with *vaibhītaka* flowers that simultaneously destroyed the lives of living beings;
rich with the scent of *kiṃpāka* fruit, they drove away the deer and birds.
From here to somewhere, then immediately from there to another place, and again from there—
winds of great velocity blew, driving the dust toward every quarter.
This is indeed the fiery splendor of Mādhava that has spread forth,
while the great heat increases as the cause of the world's desiccation.
While Keśava, the protector of the worlds, was staying in the forest of Vṛndāvana,
a great and tumultuous disease broke out there among the community of cowherds.
When the hot season had arrived, many diseases of various forms appeared among the cows and the cowherds.
And the buffaloes, severely tormented, fainting from fever and dysentery,
suddenly fell down like mountains split by thunderbolts.
With their body hair and eyelashes stiffened, their ears and necks hanging down,
with fluid trickling from their eyes, mouths, and nostrils, and their teeth grinding together.
With their muzzles lowered and their snouts and teeth protruding, they lay down;
the animals, of an unprecedented color, did not desire even the grass or fodder.
They were constantly restless in limb, and their eye-sockets were deeply sunken.
They stood crying out by the thousands, and they lay prostrate;
they rolled upon the ground, even voiding excrement.
In this manner, after five or six such days had passed,
there occurred a terrible threat of death for both the buffaloes and the cows.
Thus, an unprecedented fear suddenly arose among the cowherds while Govinda was tending the herd of cattle together with the cowherds.
In this way, various kinds of diseases among cows with their calves were observed,
though they remained undiagnosed by the elderly cowherds and even by the learned.
And though the cowherds exerted themselves with mantras, principal medicines, and the methods prescribed in the medical treatises, they were unable to ward them off.
Having applied cauterization to their limbs and performed bloodletting through venesection,
those experts exerted themselves in many ways, yet they could not overcome the diseases.
Then that family of cowherds, including the elderly and children, along with the women, became despondent; they themselves cried out in distress due to the affliction.
It became intensely distressed and terrified, afflicted by a fever born of the humors' conjunction,
and possessed by great agony that pierced all its vital organs.
Afflicted with pustules and covered all over their bodies with boils,
[the worms] emerged through the veins, bones, and flesh, accompanied by agonizing pain.
Severely afflicted by other diseases that leave them motionless,
the aged cowherds, having perished, fell down along with their herds of cattle.
The cowherds, as well as others who dwelt in that forest,
all ran about drinking the water of the Yamunā.
And all were quickly touched by the wind born on the banks of the Yamunā.
Then that disease overcame all the hosts of cowherds.
Some fell ill with fever, others became afflicted by consumption;
still others were stricken with dysentery, fanned by the winds of the Yamunā.
In this way, many kinds of diseases afflicted the cows;
some died, while others were on the verge of dying.
At that time, they became intensely afflicted by many kinds of diseases in various forms.
Reptiles, predatory beasts, all wild animals, and birds—
creatures of diverse forms who had taken refuge in the forest on the Yamunā.
All those cowherds, resolved upon death, died by the thousands;
together with their cattle, they fled in all ten directions.
O King, with their eyes rolling and utterly motionless, all those forest-dwellers fell down in a deep swoon; though still alive, they were as if dead.
From the passages of the anus and urine, from the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears,
and from the pores of the skin, living creatures emitted much blood.
It is impossible for all living beings to carry water from within [the ocean] through their wounded mouths on every side; how much more so, then, food and other such things?
The teeth of some are shattered, O Brahmin, yet they are unable to speak;
their tongues are forced out from their throats, which are completely covered in wounds.
An especially unbearable stench arose there;
in all those gatherings, it was difficult to look upon from any direction.
And on all sides along the bank of the Yamunā, there was a great deal of shouting.
Of the herds of men, cattle, and deer, distressed in every direction.
The cows did not eat fodder, nor medicine, nor any solid food;
the entire cow-pen was filled with nothing but the sound of their breathing as they lay down together with the herds of cattle.
When Vraja had thus departed and remained there with only its breath, O King,
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma then, together with some other cowherds,
decided from the very beginning to dwell separately elsewhere.
Even as a child, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, having reflected with his intellect, the Lord determined: "This is what must be done here."
Having traveled for the distance of a *krośa*, he was separated by a mountain;
yet, accompanied by more than a hundred of his own friends, he became free from illness.
Having observed the configuration of the earth through its clay, stones, pebbles, trees, grass, wood, creepers, and fibers, he caused the ground to be excavated.
Having produced water together with his companions and the herds of cows,
Kṛṣṇa drank that water and became free from disease.
Seeing that, other cowherds, though endowed with much less strength, followed his lead; for them, Kṛṣṇa became their refuge.
Having seen their two sons free from distress, Nanda the cowherd and Yaśodā were both intensely filled with grief, even as they were inwardly filled with joy.
Nandagopa also had a very large circle of kinsmen;
seeing him, they were not greatly distressed in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
"Together with this circle of kinsmen and my wealth of cattle," [he said].
And the thought arose in me: "I too might die right here."
Then Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, having heard that their parents were afflicted with fever, became extremely anxious; indeed, they remained there deeply distressed.
Seeing their entire circle of kinsmen and their wealth of cattle likewise fallen, Balarāma and Keśava were seized by the utmost terror.
Now,
at that moment, during that tumult, a certain man who had passed his youth, having come from Videha, arrived among the cowherds.
Having looked upon his circle of kinsmen and his wealth of cattle, the wise man, having approached the assembly, spoke these words whose intent was nectar-like to the Tathāgata.
We live free from anxiety, depending entirely upon our cattle;
and the Lord whose banner is the bull is in every way the master of these cattle.
"Quickly perform the ritual of worship for him and for the bull,
by which we shall attain peace— not through mantras, medicinal herbs, or nourishing rites."
"Having summoned Brahmins endowed with Vedic learning according to the prescribed rite,
let us properly worship Śaṅkara in this sacred place where he is present. Thus addressed by the family elder, those cowherds took refuge in Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, those experts in ritual worship summoned the foremost of the twice-born and performed the rites.
With various offerings, prostrations, and modes of worship,
the brahmins, their minds well-pleased, performed [the rites] in due order.
Satisfying Viśveśa with oblations of milk-rice, ghee, milk, and water,
and having offered into the fire to the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva),
as well as to the Goddess, the hosts of Skanda, the bull, and Nandikeśvara.
Having fully worshipped Vināyaka, they praised Hara with hymns of praise.
Thus, the best of Brahmins, his devotees, worshipped that one who is affectionate toward his devotees with Maheśvara mantras joined with rites for peace and auspiciousness.
With flowers, perfumes, incense, and lamps on all sides,
the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas worshipped [him] individually.
For seven nights, they continuously performed three types of worship upon his head.
Furthermore, streams of cow's ghee were offered separately, prepared according to the prescribed rites.
On those very days, O best of Brahmins, they who were devoted to the study of the *saṃhitās* likewise performed [the rites] with the three Vedas for the sake of propitiating Mahādeva.
Some sing songs of praise to Śaṅkara, whose banner is the bull;
and others, exerting themselves for the sake of pleasing Rudra, dance with particular fervor.
By the knitting of eyebrows, by the casting of glances from the eyes, by gestures of the face and hints from the eyes,
by the application of hand movements, and by the striking of the feet in their respective parts.
Then, on the seventh day at midday, while the Brahmins were performing a dance before Śiva, a great marvel appeared.
Among them, one eminent brahmin, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
became like a madman, laughing out loud again and again.
He engaged in divine dancing and likewise in divine singing;
possessed and deluded by the being of Maheśvara.
Everyone present in that assembly was struck with wonder;
and at the conclusion of that divine dance, the one possessed by the god spoke these words.
At this very moment, he has arrived from Kailāsa,
having received upon his head the command of the Supreme Lord, the Teacher of the entire world.
Having perceived the present distress of the cattle and the cowherds,
as well as the great fear of living beings dwelling in the forest, [he acted].
On account of your specific worship, the excellence of this ritual act,
and your devotion to the Bull among the Gods, the Lord of Creatures spoke these words.
"O Śaṅkukarṇa, go quickly and, having entered the body of an excellent brahmin, speak my words to those distressed inhabitants of the Yamunā bank."
At the end of the Dvāpara age, that great asura, having seen his numerous kinsmen in the world of men for the sake of enjoyment, [was born] everywhere among all living beings.

The time known as Kali was born, the powerful son of Virocana. Formerly, the mighty lord of the asuras was born as the son of Bali. On the southern bank of the Kālindī, there grew a poisonous tree, a wood-apple (kapittha).
With its abundant trunks and branches, it was frequented by birds.
Depending upon him, his many attendants and those who took refuge in him were born as trees with poisonous thorns, as well as creepers and climbing vines.
His wives, along with their wings and thousands of sons,
having become cows and calves, roam upon the banks of the Yamunā.
Those cows, accompanied by their calves and filled with pride, wandered through the forest without their cowherds;
likewise, the cattle along with their calves were everywhere in the forest, deprived of their keepers.
And they partake of the fruit of the poison-tree with complete satisfaction.
And at the end of twelve years, that tree becomes laden with flowers and fruit;
then diseases arise, overcome by its fragrance and taste.
But that tree might become laden with fruit as soon as it has blossomed;
yet, repeatedly emitting a pungent odor, it remains a constant source of maladies.
Formerly, living beings fled from that forest out of fear;
moreover, a disease arising from the possession of trees would afflict the trees themselves. At this time, cowherds generally go to that forest.
They wandered together with their cows not far from that tree.
When the twelfth cycle of the ages had arrived in due order,
a kapittha tree, laden with flowers and fruit, grew up there.
And diseases such as fevers arose in many forms;
due to their extreme proximity, it became a source of great suffering for those dwelling there.
Moreover, Mahādeva said: "Both sons of Nandagopa are capable of quickly removing poison and even a poisonous tree."
From this point forward, diseases shall no longer arise here as they did before;
for both the poison-tree and its attendant shall indeed be destroyed by these two.
Once he was cut down, diseases no longer arose as they had before.
May the cows and the cowherds live by the grace of the Supreme Lord.
"I shall go there where the Supreme Lord resides,
whose chest is marked by the musk-paste from Ambikā’s breasts.
Having said this, the brahmin was possessed [by the deity] and then regained his own consciousness.
Having spoken thus, the mighty Śaṅkukarṇa vanished.
Then all the cowherds looked at one another.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, filled with joy, gazed upon them especially.
Having perceived their gestures and facial expressions, the wise Kṛṣṇa, who possessed a sweet appearance, spoke these sweet words to his kinsmen.
Not a child, yet appearing in the form of a child, he deludes all human beings;
by the command of the God of gods, we have all [cut down] the poison-tree.
"We shall go; let the elder cowherds remain here together with the children."
Having spoken thus, the wise Kṛṣṇa, having quickly circumambulated the brahmins and that temple,
proceeded to the forest of the Yamunā.
Accompanied by Saṃkarṣaṇa, those young bulls among cowherds went before Kṛṣṇa, uttering lion-like roars.
Freed from disease by the arrival of Hari behind Gaṇapati,
all the cowherds and Brahmins followed him from behind.
Searching everywhere along the banks of the Yamunā as directed,
they caught a scent that was bitter, harsh, foul-smelling, and unbearable to the nose.
Not seeing him on the riverbank, they saw a massive, towering tree from afar, rising high in the sky above the forest like a banner.

Having cut down that terrible forest— which was exceedingly difficult to penetrate and guarded by Dānavas in the form of trees, creepers, and vines— with axes, spears, hatchets, and other firm iron spades, they [proceeded].
Having cut down those poison trees, both Rāma and Keśava went to the vicinity of that tree which was hostile to living beings.
The two of them saw that Daitya standing there, transformed into a tree,
with shoulders thirty *vyāmas* in length and a girth half as much;
it was exceedingly tall, possessed great branches, and provided no refuge for any living beings.
Except for his sons and wives, those who lived depending on him [perished].
Having quickly seen them in the pen together with their calves, they were intoxicated with pride.
Previously, cows that had never seen humans stood there out of curiosity.
Beholding both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, [he saw] that poisonous tree covered on all sides with fruits, both ripe and unripe, and with tender shoots.
Then those two bulls among men, intent on cutting down the poisonous fruit,
became enraged and began to strike the fruit with pieces of wood and stones.
Raising his two massive arms and biting his lip, he stood there.
They scattered fragments of wood and even stones;
though these were indestructible by archers due to their distance, they were intercepted by those who move through the sky.
Kṛṣṇa struck down the fruits with his two hands using wooden stakes.
The cowherds quickly presented many pieces of wood graspable by the hand and heaps of stones into their hands from all sides.
Having raised and struck them in this manner, both of them, with their trunks turned upwards,
caused fruits as large as jars to fall upon the earth.
Striking with great force in many ways upon the numerous branches,
they produced a tumultuous sound with the falling fruits.
The cowherds cried out in great joy, and those two roared like lions;
and there arose a single, immense clamor born from the gathering of fruits.
And those cows, becoming greatly agitated and assuming a demonic state,
saw and heard in the forest things never before seen or heard.
Terrible and fearsome cows, accompanied by their calves, rushed toward them;
having resolved to kill them, they fell upon the cowherds.
Striking them with their tusks, horns, feet, tails, heads, and hooves,
they trampled those who had Kṛṣṇa as their mace-weaponed protector.
Thus were the cowherds in the forest slaughtered by the beasts of terrible prowess.
Unable to do so, they fled from there in the ten directions.
The lowing sounds, the cries, the various movements,
and the qualities that belong to the offspring of Surabhi do not exist in these [cows] anywhere.
Kṛṣṇa, who was accustomed to the nature of cows, observed all of that;
for he himself was a cowherd, intelligent, and though a child, always skillful.
Then, having recognized the host of Dānavas through their outward forms, gestures, and reasoning, that wise one became certain that they were assuming the form of cows.
Having seized the *sāla* tree, he of exceeding strength then remained right there.
At that very moment, the four sons of Kali, who had become calves, appeared.
They suddenly struck Kṛṣṇa with their foreheads, feet, and hooves.
Struck by those sharp [arrows], Kṛṣṇa, free from agitation,
seized with both his hands those arrows, which were compacted together and possessed the speed of the wind.
Having understood through their strength that they had fallen into his hands, Hari reached this certain conclusion: "The Daityas are beyond doubt [defeated]."
At that very moment, without even reflecting,
Kṛṣṇa, remaining unperturbed, did not cut down his own task that had already begun, even though it was within his grasp.
He playfully seized one of them by the foot and threw him, and likewise he took hold of the others with his right hand alone.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa thus attacking the poison-tree with his calves, all the other calves ran toward him, abandoning their companions, in order to crush it.
Supporting all of them with one hand, that immensely radiant and powerful one raised up a tree and struck [them] with its branches.
Then, having gathered together, those calves rushed from all sides;
enraged, they struck one another with their hooves, teeth, and heads.
Having slain them with his feet, knees, shoulders, and elbows, the powerful Kṛṣṇa shook them off and cast them to the ground, remaining steadfast in his purpose.
The lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa shone as if dancing, performing the gestures of dramatic expression with his entire body.
Then, by those sturdy calves released in many ways,
they broke the branches of the trees as they were being struck down by the powerful one.
Then, upon the meeting of the calf and the tree, there arose once more an exceedingly loud, fierce, and most terrible roar, harsh as that of a thunderbolt.
With their limbs mangled by the branches of the tree, those great Asuras, the Kāleyas,
fell to the earth with their own bodies turned into corpses;
the branches were accompanied by fruits, and the corpses were accompanied by branches.
There, in a brief moment, the ground became drenched with blood.

When that clamor had arisen, all those cows, along with their calves, being greatly agitated, rushed toward the place where they stood. As they were first charging forward, the powerful son of Rohiṇī [Balarāma] [restrained them].
Threatening him with blows of wood and whirling him about in every direction.
Seeing his sons being slain, and because of what he had previously seen and heard,
that one of immense strength joined them all together with a single hand.
On another day,
[the demons] were greatly agitated by the calves, and they themselves were also severely struck by Mahārevaṇa.
With their tails raised high and their ears and necks stiffened,
their hair standing on end from fear, they entered the forest from all sides.
The Asuras were their offspring; their lineage on earth was fruitless.
Even today they still roam in the great forest, which is crowded with people.
[Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Dāmodara quickly [reached] the range of his hand.
He threw the calves in all directions and broke the tree.
With both hands, simultaneously and separately,
he struck the tree with those many calves, each seizing it with a single grip.
Then, as they were being hurled, the tree was broken by Viṣṇu with the calves;
the sturdy trees were struck down, and the calves were likewise slain.
Having brought about the complete destruction of the calves,
Kṛṣṇa, the consumer of men, together with Saṃkarṣaṇa as his companion, roared like a lion.
Those Dānavas, their bodies closely pressed together and having become corpses,
lay everywhere upon the surface of the earth around the poison tree.
With those terrible bodies and their limbs broken in many ways,
they appeared wonderful as they shone, drenched in a flood of blood.
Having witnessed that deed of Kṛṣṇa, those who stood there were struck with amazement;
having accomplished this most great and impossible task, Kṛṣṇa remained standing.
Then, having taken leave of his elder brother, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa uprooted the remaining tree and burned it along with the cowherds;
he likewise destroyed all those trees there that were poisonous and thorny.
Then, having cut down the numerous creepers and the shrubs that depended upon them,
and having gathered them all together where the poison-tree stood broken,
he made a heap like a mountain and brought fire to it.
He completely burned the poisonous tree, together with its roots, trunk, and branches,
along with the fallen fruits, flowers, and corpses.
It burned that entire forest, along with its mountains and great trees;
for it was mostly dry leaves, grass, and reeds, as it was the height of summer.
Janārdana reduced to ashes that place filled with flowers, leaves, and grass;
having completely consumed it until only ashes remained, that fire was extinguished. (HV App. I, 11.302–303)
And a rain of flowers fell from the sky onto the surface of the earth.
A breeze blew with a pleasant touch, and the dust became stilled;
the celestial drums resounded, and the forest became free from disease.
Then Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, being honored and filled with joy,
returned from the great forest together with the cowherds and the Brahmins.
Having completely consumed that great tree, root and all,
the cowherds, their purpose accomplished and their task finished, repeatedly let out a lion’s roar.
Having entered the Yamunā, the cowherds and the leaders of the cowherds, who sported constantly, performed many water-sports together with Kṛṣṇa.
Playing many kinds of water-instruments against one another,
they displayed their specialized skills and performed various aquatic exercises.
Dancing and striking one another, singing, embracing, and leaping over each other in great delight, the cowherd boys— *Hari-vamśa App. I, 11.315–316*
Having mastered the path of combat, they repeatedly practiced their martial maneuvers;
with their bodies concealed by water, they moved about in the river, going beneath its surface.
And on the surface of the water, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, filled with joy and being praised by the cowherds, attained the status of lords.
Then, at the time of afternoon, having performed their special water-rites,
those two lords emerged together like two leaders of elephant herds with their respective herds.
Indeed, by the direction of Nandagopa,
food and provisions had already been prepared there previously for the festival of his two sons.
Then, by his command, the cowherd women, together with their children, brought pure food and presented it there to them.
There, having put on two spotless garments and being well-adorned,
they brought forth pure food, like the immortals bringing nectar.
Food to be chewed, food to be swallowed, and food to be drunk, served according to rule with various condiments;
and foods to be chewed, swallowed, sucked, and licked, combined with diverse side dishes.
Having brought [the water] and sipped it, they rested there for a short while.
There, on the banks of the Yamunā, auspicious birds appeared,
and for the sake of the world’s success, jackals uttered auspicious cries.
Then Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, intent on their play with the cowherds,
rose up from there and the cowherds set out toward their own country.
Endowed with joy and freed from all taints, they entered their dwellings at the close of day.
Dancing, laughing, and running about one another,
they embraced in great joy, while others leaped over them.
Likewise, others played the lute with playful movements of their eyebrows.
(HV App. I, 11.337) [For line 337, D3 substitutes:]
Playing the flute, the horn, the cane-pipe, and the lute,
the cowherds— possessing beautiful necks and sweet voices— returned happily.
And the sound of kettledrums, mingled with the notes of flutes and lutes,
arose from all sides, produced by the cowherds filled with joy.
Making such an incomparable sound as they were thus assembled, the young princes,
having attained incomparable joy, returned to their very quarters.
After that god had departed, a great time for dharma arrived;
it was a period of scanty water, most terrible, and one in which all living beings were without refuge.
[Colophon] [HV (CE) Appendix I No. 12, transliterated by Peter Schreiner; version of March 5, 2002.]
Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, the brother-in-law of Nandagopa, a master of cattle, lived among the Mithilās.
Skilled and possessing abundant cattle, he was known by the name Kumbhaka;
he was a giver of milk, buttermilk, and ghee to all people,
and as the youngest son of Yaśodā, he was always dear to them.
Dharmadā was his wife, and she was indeed named Dharmadā;
she gave birth to a pair of beautiful children who were adorned like cowherds.
From those two, a son was born there, renowned by the name Śrīdāmā;
he was endowed with all excellent qualities and was pleasing to the hearts of all living beings.
There was a maiden named Nīlā, endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue;
she would laugh as she walked, her feet repeatedly touching the ground while overtaking the swans.
Her feet resemble lotus petals; her shanks are rounded and long; the joints of her knees are hidden within bone; and her two thighs are fleshy and soft.
Her hips were as broad as a chariot, her neck was soft and well-proportioned;
she possessed broad thighs and a beautiful navel like the hub of a wheel.
Gradually, her upper folds of skin became sunken, the hair on her slender waist grew thin,
and her breasts— firm, full, and soft— became like golden jars.
Possessing a soft touch, she was the mother of desire for men;
with a neck like a conch shell, a beautiful nose, and lovely, well-formed cheeks, she was enchanting.
Her lips were like two auspicious coral beads; she possessed beautiful teeth and a lovely nose. Her face was like a lotus free from sleep, and her eyes resembled blue water-lilies.
The playful woman possessed two very glossy eyebrows, reaching as far as her ears and resembling the bow of Smara;
she bore a half-moon mark upon her forehead.
Abounding with long, curled hair and endowed with all auspicious marks,
she was a jewel of the three worlds, agitating the minds of the universe. Standing in the prime of youth, her limbs were most beautiful, and she captivated both gods and mortals.
O lord of the people, all the kings sought her again and again;
yet she was not given to any one of them by her father, due to his reliance on the power of destiny.
At that very time, however, there were seven great Asuras in the form of bulls, the sons of Kālanemi, who were valiant and possessed of mighty arms.
Then, during the war between the gods and asuras, after many battles had been fought by the powerful Viṣṇu, they were defeated by him in that conflict;
bewildered regarding the directions, they fled, intent on slaying Viṣṇu.
O best of Daityas, as soon as they learned that Kṛṣṇa had been born in the Yadu clan,
they rose up with great effort, knowing him to be Viṣṇu.
Seven bulls, assuming the forms of boars, lived in the cow-pen of Kumbhaka;
they were powerful, with great horns and massive bellies and necks.
With long dewlaps, large necks, and great humps upon their backs,
these donkeys had broad and long manes and wide, sharp hooves.
Long-faced, long-toothed, with eyes like pots and beautiful ears,
they were eternally arrogant, possessing great roars that terrified the remaining herds of cattle.
Those bulls, intoxicated with pride, struck the cows and calves on all sides;
they caused all the cows' embryos to miscarry and devoured the crops.
Having repeatedly devoured the crops grown by the Videhas,
they rushed in every direction toward all the guardians of the grain.
At night, they dwelt joyfully in the cow-pen of Kumbhaka.
Then all the farmers reported to King Mithilavarman the entire destruction of the crops by the bulls.
"O King, all the crops that were produced throughout your kingdom have been entirely devoured by the bulls of Kumbhaka— those seven who are exceedingly powerful and devoid of self-restraint."
They must be restrained, O protector of the earth, if you would have the three worlds;
for if they prevail, O King, all your subjects will repeatedly be destroyed.
Having heard these words of theirs, King Janaka summoned Kumbhaka by means of messengers and spoke these words:
"O cowherd, you have seven bulls that are difficult to subdue and destroy the crops;
let all those bulls be tamed today by every possible effort."
"Otherwise, you, along with your kinsmen and your offspring, would surely be subject to punishment. Go together with cowherds who are wise and skilled in taming;
let those seven bulls be subdued by you, for no danger shall befall you."
Then, at night, he began to subdue certain arrogant Dānavas in the form of bulls,
together with other cowherds;
holding ropes in their hands, they all then approached very slowly.
Then, seeing those cowherds on all sides with ropes in their hands, the bulls,
uttering lowing sounds, rushed toward the cowherds;
they attacked them from every direction with their hooves and the tips of their horns.
Those chief cowherds were struck down by them; deprived of life, they fell together upon the earth and lay prostrate on the ground like mountains shattered by a thunderbolt.
Boys, girls, and calves were struck down by them and fell to the ground;
in Kumbhaka’s cow-pen, they lay there for the most part as if dead.
The entire Vraja became motionless, its young men struck down;
they were unable to restrain the bulls, despite their efforts with strong ropes.
All these [bulls] were rendered powerless and broken by those who had taken the form of bulls.
When Vraja had been slain and likewise that other one was killed, O protector of the earth,
Kumbhaka became unconscious and fell motionless.
Then, after reflecting, those cowherds resolved their minds thus:
"To him who shall become the subduer of the heated bull-fighters on this earth,
I shall give my daughter Nīlā, whose eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus."
"Let all the cowherds come, those cowherds who live by their cattle;
or let those Śūdras who are capable also go from every side.
Thus, it is said, Kumbhaka made this proclamation throughout Vraja.
[Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the entire host of cowherds followed after Mithilā.
"Having struck down the seven bulls, let us seize Nīlā with effort!"—
thus the cowherds gathered together, each desiring to capture her.
That capital city of Mithilā was nowhere without cowherds;
indeed, this very kingdom of Mithilavarman belonged to the gopas.
Those cowherds, however, with their long arms and endowed with extensive strength,
followed each bull individually, intoxicated and slapping their arms.
Then, summoned by the messengers of Kumbhaka,
Nanda, the son of Gopa, arrived together with other cowherds.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, it is said, went together to the cow-pen of Kumbhaka,
accompanied by other boys of their own age who were filled with joy.
Mayūrāṅgada and Caitrāṅga had dark, curly hair;
they wore yellow garments and were anointed with yellow sandalwood.
With forest garlands adorning their chests and wearing bark as sacred threads,
they held water-pots suspended from carrying-frames and amused themselves with the music of leaf-instruments.
Resounding with the tinkling of networks of small bells, adorned with peacock feathers,
making music with flutes and lutes, and filled with the sound of horns,
those two high-minded ones were followed by gods and gandharvas dwelling in the heavens.
Having crossed the Yamunā, which is garlanded with waves, by means of boats, those cowherds,
accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, proceeded toward the Gaṅgā and reached Mithilā.
And Kumbhaka, possessed of great intelligence and filled with joy,
seeing Nanda the cowherd then arrived together with his son— HV_App.I,12.101–102.
Rising up, he approached them first and embraced them with joy; then, full of delight, he urged Yaśodā and Dharmadā to take their seats upon the grass mats.
Śrīdāmā gave a seat to Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa; then, filled with joy, he offered to Nanda the cowherd and his sons plenty of *kṛsara*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and curd-rice (*dadhyodana*).
Cakes, flour-meal, and parched grains mixed with sugar and milk were given to Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Nanda, and his kinsmen.
Thus delighted and joyful, with Nanda the cowherd at their head,
all those cowherds then dwelt happily during that night.
Then, during that night, those seven Mallas, who were like bulls in form, repeatedly slaughtered the cattle; each one individually killed the calves and the cows, and further demolished the huts.
Then, they struck with their horns and hooves those guest cowherds who had gone out to fight at night;
the remaining cowherds fled in all directions.
Letting out lowing cries, they stood firm like the elephants of the quarters.
Having cut the ropes, broken the jars, and likewise the pegs and the hanging-baskets, [he departed].
O King, they drove the calves and the cows away in the ten directions.
Then, when the night had indeed passed and the clear dawn broke,
the bulls, emitting great roars, stood within that potter’s dwelling.
Like the elephants of the quarters, mountain-like in stature and resembling Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time, they let out a roar preceded by the sound of their trumpeting.
[Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, in that state, Kumbhaka was indeed motionless.
Having seen such bulls, who were causing the destruction of the cow-pen, he summoned all the cowherds and spoke these words: *HV_App.I,12.125–126*
"Listen to my words, O cowherds headed by Nanda!
Seven bulls have appeared in this Vraja, intoxicated with rut."
Like lions seized by planets, like world-elephants armored for battle,
they were inconceivable and unassailable, having transgressed the bounds of both cows and cowherds.
We have repeatedly made many efforts to restrain them;
yet, having gathered together, we said, "We are not able to fight even one of them by force. Terrified of them, O cowherds, we wander about repeatedly, deprived of our senses.
Moreover, we are repeatedly punished by King Mithilavarman;
we know neither their destination nor their origin, nor even what they intend.
Neither are those bulls, nor Rākṣasas in the form of bulls,
nor Daityas, nor Dānavas, nor even Yakṣas or Gandharvas,
who have arrived here in this cow-pen for the purpose of destroying us.
"But among you who have arrived, he who shall subdue the bulls—
to him this all-auspicious, wise Nīlā shall be given;
to him this lotus-eyed Nīlā of slender waist shall be bestowed."
Having spoken thus, he summoned that maiden who was standing with her hands folded among the cowherds;
the hearts and eyes of the youths were fixed upon her alone.
They came to rest upon the breasts of some, in the lotus-eyes of others,
on the lips of yet others, and on the slender waists of still others;
thus the cowherds, their minds utterly agitated, stood as if fixed in a painting.
There, a certain son of Nanda, the eldest and highly esteemed by Kṛṣṇa,
then proclaimed with his voice, "I shall subdue those bulls," and set out to slay those Daityas in the form of bulls.
Then, though restrained by his father who exerted himself, that dull-witted one slapped his arms and desired to fight those whom Mādhava was unable to overcome.
He who was the slayer of Rāvaṇa in battle and the slayer of Sumālin—
standing in their midst, he then let out a roar of "humbha."
At that sound, those seven roaring bulls raised their hooves and horns and stood up, prepared for action.
While they were standing there, Ghoṣavān struck one of them on the head;
then the cowherds gathered together and let out a lion’s roar.
Then that bull was struck on the head by Ghoṣavān;
seizing him by the forefeet with his hooves, he bit Ghoṣavān.
Striking him again with his horn, he flung him a great distance with his two hooves;
then, bellowing suddenly, he put the cowherds to flight.
Then those young cowherds, eager to seize the dark one,
repeatedly clenching their fists and intent on slapping their arms,
placed themselves before them while performing the sports of cowherds.
While the cowherd heroes stood their ground,
those bull-killers struck them all from every side with the tips of their horns; and,
being greatly delighted, they struck them down with their heads and hooves.
Those cowherds were struck down by the bull-demons and cast to the ground;
having slain those who came toward them, the great bulls stood firm.
Terrifying the herds of cattle with their thundering roars,
they forcibly scattered the cowherds and the chief herdsmen, even though they were clad in armor;
devouring the anthills, they indeed began to batter the riverbanks.
Kumbhaka, Nandagopa, and those elders who lived by their cattle—
bewildered as to what should be done and well-composed— they then stood at the head of the cowherds,
terrified of the king and resolved that "we are to be punished."
[Vaiśampāyana said: Then, when the slaughter had occurred, Kṛṣṇa spoke to Rāma.
O mighty-armed one, these seven Daityas who have arisen are not bulls.
"O Noble One, the sons of Kālanemi have assembled here to kill me;
they were previously slain by me in battle during the Tārāmaya conflict, O Lord."
These are exceedingly powerful and are constantly intent on showing me hostility.
O Rāma, they must be slain by me while protecting the cows and cowherds together.
"The cowherds have been struck by these [weapons] again and again, yet they are intent on striking back;
we, along with the cowherds, shall engage in play with them as is appropriate."
Both Nanda and Kumbhaka became despondent:
"O Lord, these two cowherds, who are my kinsmen, must be protected by me with all my strength."
"I shall seize this Nīlā after killing these seven bulls;
I shall accept Śrīdāmā as my friend, of this there is no doubt."
Having thus resolved, Rāma placed the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa at the front of those bulls who were endowed with great strength.
Those bulls, leaping up in anger upon seeing Viṣṇu standing before them,
resorted to their former enmity and set about to strike him down.
Those Dānavas fell suddenly and all together upon Kṛṣṇa;
then a battle took place between them and the Lord Kṛṣṇa.
Then all the herds of cows took refuge in Kṛṣṇa alone;
desiring to kill him, they suddenly struck Kṛṣṇa with their horns.
The Vṛṣa-dānavas struck Keśava individually and separately, some with kicks to the feet and others with blows from their tails;
some bit Janārdana with their tusks, while others did so with their hooves.
Then Kṛṣṇa, clenching his fist in rage, struck them;
having slain one of them in an instant, he struck another again.
Having slain all those lords of the Daityas with his fist in succession,
Kṛṣṇa then took Nīlā by the hand and shone resplendent in her presence.
Kumbhaka spoke to Nandagopa in the assembly of Vraja:
"By the grace of your son, we live free from all distress,
together with our sons, the cowherds, and our cattle along with their calves."

"O Nanda, by seven bulls, thousands of cows have been killed; likewise, as many embryos have been brought forth as there were calves. Since they have been slain, O Nanda, we shall obtain happiness from that."
"O Lord, I shall give you a thousand buffaloes and a hundred buffalocows;
or whatever else you desire, O Nanda, that much indeed I shall give to you."
I shall give a hundred thousand or ten thousand [cows] of blue color, along with much wealth in cattle.
Nandagopa said:
"Enough for me, O Lord, with cows, calves, or even wealth!
Let your cows remain here today; I consider my own cows to be many."
From the birth of my son, the cows became rich in ghee and rich in milk;
and ever since Kṛṣṇa appeared, they have been so in my Vraja.
As soon as the milk has appeared, it shall become ghee;
in every cluster there shall be honey, sweet and exceedingly delicious.
When Kṛṣṇa was born in my cow-pen, the cows and calves became free from disease;
moreover, in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, I would have no small amount of property in my home.
"Then, O cowherd, I shall go home with your permission. Having said this, Nanda departed together with the settlement and the herd of cows.
And Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Nīlā and joined by Śrīdāmā,
as well as with Balabhadra, went to the Vṛndāvana forest.
Having reached Vṛndāvana, the cowherds rejoiced together with Keśava.
[Colophon] Janamejaya said:
"Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how wonderful is the power of Mādhava, the Lord of the World!"

This is the play of Vāsudeva as he performs his pastimes among the cowherds. Blessed indeed are those who have beheld the Lord of Gods, the Divine Master, adorned in the guise of a cowherd and decorated with peacock-feather armlets.
The god whose hand rests upon a spiked chain, whose armlets jingle with tiny bells, who delights in rhythmic singing, and who seeks the internal resonance of leaf-instruments; HV_App.I,12.229–230.
They behold the god Hari, the Lord of lords, whose head is blossoming with *bāṇa* flowers and who resembles a dark blue cloud; to them, I bow again and again.

Having slain the seven bulls, Hari, the descendant of Madhu, returned once more to Vṛndāvana together with Rāma and the cowherds, O great sage. Tell me, O ascetic rich in penance, what that Lord of the World did there.
Vaiśampāyana said: In that autumn, Govinda, who increases the joy of the worlds, wandered happily with his wealth of cattle in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
[h: HV (CE) App. I, No. 13, transliterated and collated with ViP and BrP by Utz Podzeit, extracted and edited by Peter Schreiner;
version of March 5, 2002:h]
While Janārdana was sitting comfortably and sporting at Bhāṇḍīra,
Vāmadeva and Bharadvāja arrived there by chance.
Wearing black antelope skins, self-controlled, and emaciated by their observances and vows,
they set out for the Ganges tirtha like two suns that had descended.
With their necks encircled by massive, tawny masses of matted hair,
they were the authority for all the worlds and had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
clad in bark garments and deerskins, those two sages were ever devoted to self-restraint.
Then, O hero, [he went] to pay homage to Bhāṇḍīra, which is frequented by yakṣas.
The two great sages, intent on performing a circumambulation,
saw the calves and the herds of cows belonging to Kālī being tended by the cowherd boys.
Then they asked the inhabitants of the Bhāṇḍīra tree:
"O dear ones, where is our path for visiting the sacred sites on the Yamunā?
And where is the bathing place with excellent steps, free from fish and crocodiles?"
Having heard these words of the boy, the two bulls among sages laughed and said:
"We are but children; let us be praised by those who possess knowledge.
How can the bright Yamunā be here? Where is the path, and where are we?"
In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa, having heard their words as well as those of the two [others], approached them and proceeded to speak as follows.
He is indeed the guide for you both upon this path, like one well-restrained driving cattle;
I am the son of Nanda, renowned as Kṛṣṇa.
"This elder brother of mine, Rāma, shines like the moon;
let all our herds of cattle and our words be heard."
If it pleases you, let this curd-rice be properly accepted;
as well as the delicious milk-porridge, the milk, and the roasted grains mixed with jaggery.
When the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus,
those two sages then entered into a state of meditative absorption, wondering, "Who are these two?
Having opened their eyes, they joyfully beheld the Lord of the World.
The two sages spoke thus concerning the inner self, in accordance with the opinion of Kṛṣṇa.
You are the beginning of all beings, as well as their middle and their end;
O Janārdana, you are the creator, the protector, and the enjoyer of the entire world.
O Hari, you are the creator of the Veda, of sacrifice, of oblations, and of the officiating priests;
you are the enjoyer of the fruits of actions and the bestower of fruits upon those who perform deeds.
You are the restrainer of wicked beings and the supreme destroyer of darkness;
the sun and moon are your two eyes, and the wind is your nose.
The goddess Sarasvatī is proclaimed to be speech, and the tongue is celebrated as the cloud;
the teeth are to be known as mountains, and the ear is the domain of the netherworld (pātāla).
Lakṣmī is to be known as the chest, while Śaṅkara is the left arm;
the right shoulder and arm are remembered as the oceans, and the fingers are the [seven] seas.
The belly is said to be the sky, and the cavities are remembered as the directions;
heaven and earth are your two feet, and the gods are remembered as the hair of Hari.
O All-pervading Lord, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas are your body hairs.
O Mādhava, O Puruṣottama, whatever kinds of things are seen in the world, we see those very same things upon your limbs, O Hari.
O Blessed One, we shall behold you from below with our whole being;
we shall see you above, and then you from behind;
having beheld you from the sides and from the front as well, we shall be at peace.
At first, you placed the earth, together with its mountains, upon the tip of your boar’s tusk;
then, having established him in his proper place, you slew Hiraṇyākṣa.
O Viṣῃu, having assumed the body of a man-lion, you slew the lord of the Daityas, who was a thorn to gods and men,
after restoring the kingdom to Indra.
Having become the son of Jamadagni, he slew the slayer of his father,
the high-souled Kārtavīrya, who was a thorn to the entire warrior class.
O Lord of the worlds, you alone have entered the lineage of Raghu;
O Viṣṇu, having gone by bridge across the ocean to Laṅkā, which was ruled by Rāvaṇa.
O Lord, O Supreme Person, having slain Rāvaṇa along with his sons, his younger brothers, and his army,
you have made this world free from thorns.
Having assumed the form of a dwarf by means of your illusory power (māyā), you took the earth from Bali and gave it to the Lord of the Thirty-three; you established it in the netherworld (pātāla).
Assuming various forms, O Mādhava, you protect the worlds;
even now, O Lord of Gods, God of gods, you have appeared in the lineage of Yadu.
Having descended, O Hari Viṣṇu, you who oppose the faction of the gods,
you are Kṛṣṇa, assuming the guise of a cowherd and wearing an auspicious appearance.
"O Mādhava, having slain the long-armed Keśin, you shall slay Kaṃsa.
Oh, how beautiful is this body of Viṣṇu, with the luster of a blue lotus,
enriched by dark, curly hair, and possessing eyes like blossoming lotuses!"
His chest was adorned with a forest garland, and he wore a sacrificial cord made of rope as his upper garment.
With a water-pot hanging from a sling at its side, its interior sprinkled with dried cow-dung,
covered by a network of tiny bells, it was radiant and beautiful at the waist.

Adorned with two arms bound by the *dāma-kīla*, producing the sounds of flutes and lutes and the charming resonance of leaf-instruments—O Mādhava, oh, we behold your most enchanting form! (HV App. I, 13.69–71)
Those cowherds are blessed for a long time who constantly behold such a form as this, O Viṣṇu; salutations to you, O Supreme Person.
Salutation to you who assume a dark form, who sport in the guise of a cowherd;
salutation again and again to you of inconceivable power, who are all-pervading.
Homage to the source of all auspiciousness, homage again and again;
homage to the supreme reality, homage to the supreme yogin.
O God of gods, O Abode of the universe, O Cause of all causes!
Once again we bow to you, O Hari; [we seek] your state of yoga.
May we attain success; salutations be to you, the sacred ford of the worlds, O Lord of the universe!
Having thus addressed Hari, the Lord of lords, the two bulls among sages departed for the sacred ford; meanwhile,
Rāma and Keśava remained there at Bhāṇḍīra and played with the cowherds as was fitting.

The minister said:
O King, how was it previously spoken by the celestial sage Nārada?
"O subduer of enemies, this wonderful thing has been told by you and heard by me."
"How were you born by another, O Ugrasena, without a father?
O King, how was such a deed as this committed by your mother?"
"Even an ordinary woman would not commit such a loathsome act;
for I wish to hear the details of this, as I have a great curiosity."
Kaṃsa said:
"Just as the lordly great seer, the brahmin Nārada, has spoken,
so shall I relate it to you, if your mind is set upon hearing it."
That sage, the friend of Śakra, has indeed come from the abode of Śakra;
wearing garments as white as moonbeams, he bears a mass of matted locks.
With a black antelope skin as an upper garment, wearing a golden sacrificial thread,
carrying a staff and a water-pot, he was like another Prajāpati.
He was a master of the four Vedas, a learned scholar, and a knower of the Gandharva-veda;
he was that imperishable celestial sage Nārada, who wanders through the world of Brahmā.
Seeing that the seer had arrived, he honored him according to the prescribed rites;
having offered water for his feet, the guest-offering, and a seat, he ushered him inside and seated him.
Then the sage, seated at the entrance, having seen my well-being,
spoke with a joyful mind, that celestial seer of purified soul.
I have been honored by you, O hero, through this rite performed according to the prescribed rules.
Now, listen to these words of mine alone and accept them.
I went to the golden abode of the gods on Mount Meru;
there, at one time, I was in the assembly of the gods upon the summit of Meru.
There, while the gods were indeed deliberating, I heard a most terrible means for the slaughter of you and your followers here.
There, this Devakī who is your paternal aunt in Mathurā—
therein is this child of Devakī’s womb, Viṣṇu, who is honored by the worlds.
O Kaṃsa, that which is her eighth embryo shall be your death.
He is indeed the entire possession of the gods and the refuge of the triple heaven;
he is the supreme secret of the gods, and he shall become your death.
O Kaṃsa, let effort be made toward the destruction of the embryos;
one must not show contempt for an enemy, whether they be strong or weak.
And this Ugrasena here is not your father, O mighty one;
he is the radiant and powerful lord of Saubha named Drumila.
"O Kaṃsa, you were born from him, not from the powerful Ugrasena.
Having heard those words of his, I was somewhat filled with anger. (HV App. I, 14.32–33)
I asked again: "O Brahmin, how was the Dānava named Drumila?"
"O Brahmin, tell me how my mother met with him;
O one rich in asceticism, I wish to hear this in detail."
Nārada said:
"Behold! O King, I shall relate to you exactly as it happened the conversation and the meeting between Drumila and your mother; listen to it according to the truth."

The hero ascended his divine chariot, which moved at will, traveled swiftly, and possessed the splendor of the rising sun; and desiring to see Suyāmuna, he went to that region.
He arrived there by chance, desiring to see the daughter of the Yamunā,
traveling through the air with a speed swifter than thought, moving according to his will.
He arrived at the excellent mountain frequented by sages and perfected beings.
Having seen that forest, which resembled the Nandana grove, his heart was filled with joy.
Having descended from his chariot, King Drumila walked forth boldly. Wandering through the forest interior, he reached that delightful mountain with divine peaks;
having arrived at that lord of mountains, he alighted from his excellent chariot.
Having stationed the chariot, which crushes the chariots of enemies, in the mountain grove,
both of them, accompanied by their charioteers, moved about upon the mountain peak.
Then they beheld many groves and forests,
endowed with the excellences of all seasons, like the groves of Nandana.
He wandered upon the peaks of the Naga mountains, in the caves, and by the rivers;
[he beheld] many lofty peaks covered with various minerals.
[He saw] trees of gold, emerald, and silver, variegated with many colors; rich with the scents of various flowers, inhabited by various throngs of creatures,
resounded by various flocks of birds, and laden with various flowers and fruits.
[They were] endowed with various medicinal herbs and frequented by sages and perfected beings (siddhas).
The Vidyādharas,
Kiṃpuruṣas, bears, monkeys, and Rākṣasas;
lions, tigers, boars, buffaloes, deer, and hares.
Sṛmaras, camaras, nyaṅkus, mātaṅgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
Seeing many such sights while wandering upon that best of mountains,
the king beheld from afar the queen, who resembled the daughter of a god,
playing with her companions and gathering flowers.
Then, seeing that woman of beautiful hips walking along, surrounded by her companions,
the lord of the earth observed her from afar and, filled with wonder, spoke to his charioteer:
Whose is this girl with eyes like a young fawn, wandering within the depths of the forest,
endowed with the qualities of beauty and nobility, like Rati herself to the God of Love?

Is she Śacī, the wife of Indra, or perhaps Tilottamā? Or is this woman of excellent complexion born from the split thigh of Nārāyaṇa? Is it the goddess Urvaśī, the beloved of Aila and a jewel among women?
We have heard that while the Ocean of Milk was being churned by the hosts of gods and asuras together,
they made Mount Mandara the churning-stick for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
Then, from that nectar, the goddess Śrī, the creator of the world, rose up;
she who sports upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa—could this beautiful woman be Śrī herself?
Like a flash of lightning illuminating the midst of dark clouds,
so did she illuminate her form in the midst of the throng of women;
her limbs were exceedingly delicate, and her face resembled the radiance of the moon.
Having seen that form, whose limbs were composed of ignorance, I became bewildered with my senses agitated;
fallen under the power of desire, my mind seems to reel.
The arrows of the flower-weaponed god cut my limbs deeply.
Having pierced my heart with five arrows, they seem to consume my mind as it were;
Kāma, as if burning my heart with his five shafts.
The fire of his heart increases like a flame sprinkled with clarified butter.
"How might the task for today be accomplished for the sake of pacifying the flame of Manmatha?
By what means and what shall we do so that this woman of intoxicating beauty may favor me?"
Having reflected thus at great length and finding no [solution], the Dānava said to the charioteer:
"Wait here for a moment, O sinless one."
"I shall go to see that woman—to whom she belongs.
Wait for me until my return."
Having heard these words, the Sūta replied, "So be it."
Having spoken thus, the lord of the Dānavas set his mind upon departing.
His heart possessed by desire upon seeing that dark-eyed woman,
the powerful one touched water for purification and fell into deep reflection.
Then, having perceived her through the power of knowledge by means of mere meditation for a moment,
he recognized her as the wife of Ugrasena and attained great joy.
Having assumed the form of Ugrasena and transformed his own appearance, that mighty-armed lord of the Dānavas approached him laughing; and smiling gently, he of immeasurable prowess seized him.

[The following passage is inserted by D6, T2, G1, 3, 5, and M4 after the reference to Adhyāya 81; by T1, M1–3 after 81.3; and by G2 after line 14 of Appendix I (No. 18): "O King, you have heard from me the entire account of the lineage of the Kurus, as well as the history of the sons of Pāṇḍu. Now listen further to this ancient narrative concerning the origin of the Kuru race. Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O grandfather, I wish to hear in detail the account of the birth of the Kuru dynasty, which is filled with many wonders and possesses great merit. Bhīṣma said: "Listen, O King, to this ancient history that bestows longevity, fame, and progeny. It is a sacred narrative that destroys all sins and increases merit. In the beginning, there was a king named Kuru, who was a performer of sacrifices and a protector of his subjects. He ruled over the earth bounded by the four oceans. That king, devoted to righteousness, performed many horse-sacrifices and other rites accompanied by abundant gifts. Having ruled for a long time, he eventually ascended to heaven. His son, Avikṣita, likewise protected the earth according to dharma. From Avikṣita was born Suvīra, and from Suvīra came Aṅga. From Aṅga was born Vṛhatkṣatra, and from Vṛhatkṣatra came Bṛhadratha. From Bṛhadratha was born Pratiśravas, and from Pratiśravas came the famous Pratīpa. Pratīpa begot three sons: Devāpi, Śāntanu, and the youngest, Bāhlīka. Devāpi, though possessed of every auspicious mark, was afflicted with leprosy. Therefore, the people did not accept him as their king. Then Śāntanu became the ruler of the earth. He was a man of great splendor, devoted to truth, and skilled in the Vedas. He protected the world righteously, and through his power, he subdued all enemies. From Śāntanu was born the illustrious Bhīṣma, who was born of the river Gaṅgā. He was a knower of the Vedas, a master of weapons, and a performer of great deeds. After Śāntanu’s passing, Bhīṣma installed Citrāṅgada on the throne. When Citrāṅgada was slain in battle by the Gandharva of the same name, Bhīṣma installed Vicitravīrya as king. Vicitravīrya married two daughters of the King of Kāśī—Ambikā and Ambālikā—and begot two sons upon them: Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu. Since Vicitravīrya died childless, Satyavatī, the daughter of Śūrasena, urged Bhīṣma to raise offspring for the sake of the lineage. Thus, through Niyoga, Dhṛtarāṣṭra begot one hundred sons through Gāndhārī, and Pāṇḍu begot five sons through Kuntī and Mādrī. These were the sons of Pāṇḍu: Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva. After the death of Pāṇḍu, these five brothers, along with their mother Kuntī, lived in the forest. There they encountered the sage Vyāsa, who granted them divine vision. Later, when the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra plotted against them, the Pāṇḍavas were forced to go into exile. After many trials and the burning of the lacquer house, they escaped and lived in disguise. Eventually, they revealed themselves at the Swayamvara of Draupadī and won her hand. Then the great war of the Mahābhārata took place at Kurukṣetra, where millions of warriors perished. Finally, the Pāṇḍavas, having conquered their enemies, ruled the earth.
This is the history of the Kuru dynasty,
Having arrived at the bank of the Yamunā, the powerful son of Jarā commissioned Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti to act as his envoys.
Having gone to Mathurā, those two heroes were lodged by Dvārṣṭi.
Then, O King, [he saw] Ugrasena, his lord, seated upon his throne, O monarch,
and Kṛṣṇa standing by his side together with Balabhadra.
Having seen the highly heroic Vasudeva, the immensely wise Sātyaki, and other Yādavas standing near the lord of the earth, [he spoke].
Having addressed all those present, including Kaṃsa’s father, the two of them,
sitting comfortably, then spoke to Vāsudeva and his elder brother.
He said: "The powerful Jarāsaṃdha, possessed of great heroism, addresses you.
Listen to my words, for I am distressed and weak."
"O Great King, I wish to see my two sons, who are distressed,
helpless, tormented by grief, and submerged in an ocean of suffering."
As for the fact that Kaṃsa was slain in battle by the more powerful Kṛṣṇa,
O King, I am likewise incapable of counteracting what has been done.
As for the fact that the battle was fought by the powerful Kṛṣṇa,
I should not feel any astonishment at this, for he is powerful along with his elder brother.
But a great suffering has arisen within me that is difficult to endure;
I consider that suffering unbearable, and even to speak of it is unbearable for me.
O Lord of Magadha, O giver of honor, while I am present here with my army and great prowess,
this which has been done against me is truly strange, O Great King, as long as I am alive.
"Thinking even this: 'Kṛṣṇa has done a good deed, regarding me as a beast,' and likewise, 'But Kṛṣṇa has done an evil deed, regarding you as a beast.'"
"What difficult deed must Kṛṣṇa have performed that he continues to live?"
"O best of the Yadus, do not despise me while Jarāsandha’s son still lives;
yet my life is now at an end, O Kṛṣṇa, while he lives."
Having spoken thus, with his face wide open in rage, he spoke again:
"If Kṛṣṇa stands in battle, I shall slay him; if he stands before me, I shall slay him."
"I am neither Kaṃsa, nor Keśin, nor Ariṣṭa, nor Pūtanā;
O lord of the earth, do not despise King Jarāsaṃdha."
O King Keśava, hear this other vow as well:
if you should stand before me, then I shall slay you along with your kinsmen.
"Prepare yourself for battle; I stand here, eager for combat.
Wherever you go, there I shall follow."
"As long as you live, O Govinda, Jarāsaṃdha does not live.
Come for battle together with the wise Balabhadra."
"What is the use of these many elders led by Ugrasena?
May you come quickly, accompanied by Balabhadra."
"O Satyaki, this which has been done by Kṛṣṇa is indeed appropriate; O Lord, what is improper?
O Vasudeva, best of the Yadus, what is improper for your son?
O Akrūra, tell me truly whether this is right or otherwise."
O Kṛṣṇa, best of the Yadus, remain firm in battle and do not waver. What is the use of saying more here? Your life is not secure.
"Tomorrow I shall besiege your city; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. O Kṛṣṇa, who indeed would commit such a rash act as this now, were it not for you?"
Having spoken thus, those two of great heroism then took their rest.
Thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa, his eyes copper-red with rage, then spoke these words:
"O Great King, Kaṃsa has been slain; what rash act has been done beyond this?
O Indra among kings, tell me, what is so wonderful here that Kaṃsa has been killed by us?"
And this must be said to him by you two, O best of kings:
"I stand here, impassioned for battle, and I shall conquer my enemies in combat."
"Having slain you along with your army in battle, I shall now take the kingdom and give it to Ugrasena; I swear this by the truth."
Having spoken thus, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, ceased speaking;
then those two went and reported everything to him, O Lord.
[Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, when the two messengers had departed from the lord of Magadha, the ruler of men—
Having heard that the king of kings was desirous of combat and impatient with wrath, [he set out].

The Yadavas, who were well-acquainted with the prowess of the great-souled Magadhan king Jarāsandha, feared him; for they knew that the Lord of the World and Balabhadra desired to slay him. (HV App. I, 16.57–59)
For while this Lord of the World remains— the one who robs all of their strength—
that powerful majesty of the Lord of Magadha prevails everywhere.

Vāsudeva struck Rukmin with twenty-five arrows;
then the enhancer of the Bhojas struck Keśava with those two shafts.
Rukmī, however, proceeded to cut the string of Vāsudeva’s bow;
but Vāsudeva, perceiving this, cut his own bow as well.
His bow having been severed, the self-controlled Bhoja took up a spear;
with that, the hero struck Hari, who in turn cut it down with his arrows.
Again, O Great King, the monarch dispatched another mace;
while all the kṣatriyas looked on, the Lord of the World shattered it as well.
That king struck Vāsudeva with an iron club,
but the bull among the Yadus split that weapon in two with his own blows.
Taking up the chariot wheel, the king pierced Viṣṇu;
and likewise, O God, he cut that wheel into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his arrows.
Whatever weapon Rukmin, the son of Bhīṣmaka, took up,
the joy of the Yadus split each one of them in two and laughed.
The joy of the Yadus fashioned a chariot without strings and without wheels;
Madhusūdana rendered it weaponless and devoid of a bow.
While all the kṣatriyas looked on, Kṛṣṇa restored [the prince] to life;
having glanced at Rukmiṇī, Kṛṣṇa did not cause Rukmin to perish.
Āhuka struck Bhīṣmaka with twenty-five [arrows].
Then Bhīṣmaka, O king of kings, being an expert in the vital points, struck Ugrasena with more than a hundred arrows capable of piercing the vitals.
But Āhuka, that bull among the Yadus, having severed the bow of the high-souled Bhīṣmaka,
also cut down his chariot and his banner.
The joy of the Yadus struck his charioteer and his horses;
then Bhīṣmaka, overcome with fatigue, withdrew from that battle.
But Vasudeva, O king of kings, pierced Kratha with feathered shafts;
and Kratha, O king, pierced him in return with seven swift-flying arrows.
Vāsudeva also pierced the four horses with four arrows;
he quickly struck down the charioteer as well as both the outrider-guards.
Then Vasudeva, enraged, cut his bow with feathered arrows and swiftly deprived him of his chariot while Jarāsandha looked on.
Deprived of his chariot and his bow, he proceeded toward Māgadha.
Babhru pierced that king of the Kauśikas with various arrows;
then Babhru struck the high-souled one with sharpened shafts.
And Kauśika, knowing the vital spots, pierced Babhru deeply in battle with arrows that strike the vitals; it was like a marvel.
While Jarāsaṃdha looked on, the mighty-armed one cut off his head, adorned with blazing earrings, using a razor-sharp arrow.
Then, having slain the high-souled one, the exceedingly powerful Babhru,
who possessed a massive form, quickly let out a lion’s roar in the midst of the army.
And Gada struck the King of Cedi with sharpened arrows;
the King of Cedi also, O Indra among kings, pierced Gada with swift-flying shafts.
O Great King, the King of Cedi suddenly [attacked] the joy of the Yadus;
[the variant reads:
but the King of Cedi suddenly [attacked] Gada, the best of the Yadus, in battle.
The King of Cedi, however, suddenly deprived Nandana, the joy of the Yadus, of his chariot and his bow; indeed, the lord of Cedi rendered him both carless and weaponless.
Then that best of the Yādavas went into the presence of Vasudeva.
O great king, Śambhu then repeatedly pierced Dantavaktra with arrows as sharp as iron weapons, O joy of the Yadus.
He violently oppressed more than a hundred thousand in battle;
and Sātyaki, O great king, pierced the two sons of Avanti.
And those two high-souled ones, O King, afflicted Satyaki of true prowess with feathered shafts in all his vital parts.
Having turned back those two mighty warriors, O King, Sātyaki pierced them with sharp arrows while they stood in the midst of all the kings.
And those two kings, Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, struck that hero Sātyaki with sharp arrows,
O delighter of the Yadus.
O King, O Indra among kings, while all the kshatriyas looked on, Sātyaki struck that high-minded one with twenty-five [arrows].
O King, while Vāsudeva looked on, both of them pierced Sātyaki’s bow, his arrow, his chariot, and even his charioteer.
Then, O King, the enraged Sātyaki struck them both with his mace;
he then dealt blows to their chests, arms,
and torsos, and likewise crushed their chariot as well as both the outriders and the charioteer.
And the Yādava crushed all his weapons as well.
And again,
O great king, Satyaki, the joy of the Yadus and one whose prowess is truth, desiring to slay him,
quickly struck with his mace; and while Vāsudeva looked on, he hurled that mace at the two of them.
Beholding her approaching, they then became intent on flight;
they went before Jarāsaṃdha and into his presence.
Ekalavya pierced this Vārṣṇeya with seven arrows.
Then Ekalavya struck Pradyumna with five arrows and with seven;
the Vārṣṇeya struck Ekalavya with thirty-seven, and Ekalavya struck him with twenty.
But those two great heroes, O King, each desiring to slay the other—
heroes preeminent in the worlds, the foremost of archers in battle.
Having severed each other's bows and likewise each other's standards,
O King, they both struck each other's chariots with swift arrows.
And the two heroes cut down the two banners and the two mighty charioteers.
Having descended to the ground and swiftly seizing their maces,
the two of them struck one another with their maces in that great battle;
eager for combat, they let out lion-like roars in that great conflict.
Then Pradyumna, the wielder of the mace, struck Ekalavya;
the mighty-armed Ekalavya, in turn, crushed the Yadu with his mace.
The lord Pradyumna struck Ekalavya with his mace;
however, that Yādava again shattered the king's mace.
Having released him, O Great King, he struck the Lord of the Yādavas with his fist;
and that expert in combat engaged in such a struggle, using his knees, palms, feet, and the tops of his knees with great effort.
Furthermore, O King, having struck the scion of the Yadu clan with his fist,
he bit him with his teeth in the assembly of kings.
Then all the soldiers were filled with the utmost wonder.
A wrestling match then took place between those two heroic men;
they both advanced from every side to fight in that great battle.
Then the mighty-armed Pradyumna, the lord of the Yādavas, becoming enraged,
struck him with his fist while Jarāsaṃdha looked on.
Then Pradyumna, filled with rage, struck him with his fist;
vomiting blood from his mouth, he gasped like one whose life had departed.
Then, tormented by Pradyumna, he desired to depart from the battle.
To him who was intent on flight, the high-minded Jarāsaṃdha said:
"O hero, you must not go; you are a Kṣatriya."
And for the other warriors, there was a great and terrible battle.
HV App.I,18.1: There Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by and joined with the son of Rohiṇī, was present.
He dwelt happily in that city of Mathurā, which was under the dominion of the Yādavas.
But when his body had reached youth, the powerful lord, endowed with royal splendor,
wandered joyfully through Mathurā, which was adorned with groves and mines. Then, after some time, the king who was the lord of Rājagṛha—
The powerful Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of the earth, who had been urged again by his two daughters to go to war, remembered the slain Kaṃsa.
Having suffered humiliation in battle, that king, the lord of Magadha,
entered his own city with his head bowed down in shame.
Then he entered the city like a serpent trodden upon by a foot;
tormented by grief, he found no peace by night nor by day.
Deliberating with all those kings, he who was skilled in secret counsel said:
"Alas! Shame upon the prowess of all these monarchs, O kings, for they, along with their armies and followers, have been utterly defeated by Gopa and Vanakṛṣṭa."
"Let us go back there to Mathurā with our fourfold army,
joined by a great force, to where those two wretched cowherds are;
otherwise, our infamy will endure as long as the worlds exist."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of his, the kings from various lands spoke these words and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Let us all go together to crush Mathurā;
having struck down all the Yādavas and cleared the earth on every side,
we shall return once more together, resounding with shouts of victory."
Then those kings, having made their resolve firm for battle,
set forth with their banners in the fray, making the earth tremble.
The Yādavas fought seventeen battles against Jarāsaṃdha,

Then,
