That powerful King Jarāsaṃdha quickly marched forth against him.
The king, the Great Being of great splendor, equipped with his vehicle,
set forth with chariots whose rims thundered, with elephants trumpeting with the sound of rut,
with neighing horses, and with foot-soldiers making fierce war-cries.
Making all the directions resound, as well as all those dwelling in caves,
that king, who resembled the ocean, appeared together with his army.
The commander of the forces, the highly heroic Ekalavya, the lord of the earth—
bow in hand, with a quiver of arrows, armed with a sword, equipped with a scabbard, and full of strength.
The lord of Magadha, charioteer, sword-bearer, arrow-wielder, bowman, quiver-carrier, and adorned with golden earrings, let out lion-like roars.
He was seen at the head of all the armies like a second Antaka;
I alone rose up against those two sons of cowherds.
"What is the use of these lions among men? said the mighty one.
That army of the lords of the earth, crowded with arrogant warriors, resounded with the noise of roars and the slapping of arms, appearing like an army of clouds.
With chariots that moved like the wind, with elephants resembling clouds,
with horses the color of white clouds, and with armored foot soldiers,
that mixed army shone, crowded with rutting elephants and chariots.
Just as a mass of clouds at the end of the summer heat dissolves into the ocean.
Those powerful rulers of the earth, having arrived at the city of Jarāsaṃdha,
all surrounded the mountain and proceeded to take up residence there.
As he sat there, the splendor of his camp shone forth,
like the appearance of the great ocean when it is full during the bright fortnight.
Then, at the end of the night, those kings, having performed the auspicious rites and longing for battle, assembled for the purpose of ascending the mountain.
All those kings, having gathered together on the mountain plateaus,
settled down and held counsel, eager for the time of battle.
A tumultuous sound was heard from those rulers of the earth,
like the roar of oceans bursting asunder at the end of an eon.
For them, elder attendants wearing tunics and turbans and holding canes in their hands moved about by the king's command, saying, "Make no noise!"
The appearance of that army, which was indeed silent and still,
was like that of the great ocean when its fish and crocodiles have withdrawn and it is hushed.
In that still and silent assembly, which resembled the great ocean in its state of yoga,
Jarāsaṃdha took up these weighty words, just as Bṛhaspati might do.
Let the armies of the rulers of the earth assemble quickly;
let the mountain as well be surrounded on all sides by floods of troops.
Let stone-engines be set in place, and let the slings and mallets be prepared;
let javelins and iron clubs also be hurled upward.
"Let artisans quickly construct strong yet light structures for the purpose of looking upward, which will ward off the falling of weapons."
"Let it be carried out quickly, exactly as the lord of men has commanded, regarding these heroes who are fighting, yet distracted with one another."
Let this best of mountains be split apart with multitudes of axes and excavated by pits;
and let kings skilled in siege warfare be stationed nearby.
"From this day forward, let the siege of my mountain be undertaken by my armies,
so that we may strike down both these sons of Vasudeva."
"Let this mountain, whose source is stone, be made motionless; let the birds be rendered still. Let even the sky be made impassable by the floods of your arrows."
"Instructed by me, let the lords of the earth remain upon the mountain slopes;
having quickly ascended the mountain, take your positions in those various locations."
Bhadra, the lord of Kaliṅga, Cekitāna along with the Bāhlīkas,
Gonarda the king of Kaśmīra, and likewise the lord of Karūṣa.
Let Druma, Kimpuruṣa, and the mountain-dwelling men quickly cause these people to ascend the other side of the mountain.
Paurava, Veṇudāri, Vaidarbha, and Somaka;
as well as Rukmī, the lord of the Bhojas, and Sūryākṣa the Yavana.
Drupada, the lord of the Pañcālas and king of men;
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti; and the heroic Dantavaktra.
Chāgali, Purumitra, and Virāṭa the lord of the earth;
Kauśāmbya, Mālava, Śatadhanvan, and Vidūratha.
Bhūriśravas, Trigarta, Bāṇa, and likewise Pañcanada—
let these kings, who are capable of enduring difficult terrain and possess a majesty like that of the thunderbolt, ascend the northern mountain slope while trampling their enemies.
Ulūka, Kaitaveya, and Vīra, the son of Aṃśumat; Ekalavya, Dṛḍhākṣa, Rathavarman, and Jayadratha.
Uttamaujas, as well as Śālva, Kairaleya, Kaiśika,
Vaidiśa, Vāmadeva, and the heroic Suketu.
"Let our front line be dependent upon these mountain peaks;
let them charge forward, rending [the enemy] like winds tearing through the clouds."
I, along with Darada and the King of Cedi,
having united and donned our armor, shall shatter the southern mountain range.
Thus, may this mountain, quickly surrounded on all sides by the forces,
encounter a tumultuous terror resembling the falling of a thunderbolt.
Let those who possess maces strike with maces, and those whose weapon is the iron club with iron clubs;
let others tear apart the best of mountains with various kinds of weapons.
This mountain, filled with uneven and lofty crags, must this very day be made entirely level with the ground by you,
the lords of the earth.
Having heard the words of Jarāsaṃdha and his command over the kings,
they surrounded Mount Gomanta just as the oceans encompass the earth.
The king of the Cedis spoke, like Maghavan among the gods.
"What is the use of war for us here in this Durgā mountain, this best of peaks,
whose lofty summits are difficult to climb and crowded with towering trees?"
"Surrounding him on all sides with many pieces of wood and grass, let him be set ablaze this very day, quickly; enough with any other course of action."
For these Kṣatriyas, delicate though they be as warriors who fight with arrows in battle,
are not suited to be employed on a mountain fortress as foot-soldiers.
"O dear one, this mountain cannot be crushed even by the gods, neither by means of obstruction nor by a sudden assault."
O King, a siege-warfare is superior to a blockade-warfare;
those who have taken refuge in mountains are brought down once their provisions of food, water, fuel, and fodder are exhausted.
"Thinking 'we are many'—this is not a clever strategy either.
These two Yādavas, both standing ready for battle, must not be disregarded."
These two are heard of as being like gods, possessing the power of the unknown;
yet we know them to be immortal through their deeds—two children endowed with exceeding strength.
But by their incomparable deeds, both heroes were exceedingly powerful.
These two best of the Yadus have performed deeds here that are difficult to accomplish.
Having wrapped that best of mountains on all sides with dry wood and grass, we shall set it ablaze with fire; let them burn, deprived of consciousness.
If they should attempt to escape from here while being burned, we shall surround them and strike them down; then they will lose their lives.
This speech, uttered by the King of Cedi out of a desire for the welfare of the kings, was pleasing to those powerful rulers of the earth.
Then, with wood, grass, bamboos, and the dry branches of trees,
that lord of mountains was set ablaze like a cloud by the rays of the sun.
Those kings, swift in their movements, quickly set fire to the mountain on all sides, according to the location and the direction of the wind.
Fanned by the wind, that fire leapt up on all sides,
as if beautifying the sky with its radiant garlands of smoke and flames.
Driven by the wind and rooted in a mass of wood,
that fire burned the glorious Mount Gomanta, with its lovely trees.
Being scorched, that lord of mountains released massive boulders by the hundreds;
appearing like great meteors, they split into hundreds of fragments.
The lord of mountains, possessing variegated splendor, like the sun with its rays upon a cloud,
seemed to anoint it on all sides in due manner with masses of radiance.
With the elements being cooked and the trees set ablaze,
the king of mountains, like one being tormented, roared as wild beasts ran about in confusion.
Being continuously consumed by the black-pathed fire,
that mountain produced streams of gold, antimony, and silver.
And with its limbs ablaze by fire, the mountain did not shine brightly;
its body darkened by smoke, it resembled a cloud sinking down.
With its masses crushed by rocks and raining down harsh coals,
the mountain shines with outbursts of fire like a cloud pouring down a shower of meteors.
Sprinkled by waterfalls and cascades, its interior perfumed by incense, that mountain was reduced to ashes like one consumed by the fire at the end of an eon.
From his sides, agitated serpents with half their bodies burnt,
panting and possessing large heads and inauspicious eyes, issued forth.
Leaping up again and again from the sky, they fell once more with their faces turned downward;
and the lions, agitated and terrified, as well as the tigers, roared, their eyes inflamed by fire.
And the trees released water produced from their burning resin.
The wind blows with an upward motion, turning the ashes and embers a tawny-brown;
and in the sky, the shadow of smoke appears like a mass of proud clouds.
Even as its great peaks were being abandoned by birds and even by beasts of prey,
the mountain fell into a state of distress due to the audacity of the fire.
He released boulders from the mountain with its shifting and lofty masses of rock,
so that it was as if it were being split apart by the thunderbolt of Indra.
And great sounds arose from the high mountains being split asunder, O King;
then the Man of the Black Path (Agni), having bowed, appeared before the two of them.
He paid homage to Hari, and that best of speakers said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, my offense must be forgiven."
Yet, being under the control of another, I am burning this best of mountains.
But you,
O Lord of the World, accept this armor joined with Rāma; having donned it, wander at your pleasure.
O highly fortunate one, this fierce fire shall not overcome you;
O Rāma, choose one of these two armors that ward off the flames.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the Fire-god gave him two excellent armors.
Then, O King,
Hari and Saṃkarṣaṇa both put on their respective armor, one for each of the two brothers, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and vanished from sight.
On the delightful Gomanta peak, those two, who were honored by the fire-god, moved about;
yet, O lord of the earth, the heat of the fire did not cause them any distress.
Having set that lord of mountains ablaze, those kṣatriyas, armored and drawn up in battle array,
retreated half a krośa, scorched by the fire.
While that best of mountains was burning and its great trees were withering,
its base became indistinguishable due to masses of smoke and grew slack.
Then Rāma, with eyes like lotus petals, spoke these words in anger to the slayer of Keśin, Madhusūdana himself.
"O dear one, this mountain, along with its plateaus, peaks, and trees, is being consumed by fire because of our enmity with Kṛṣṇa and the hostile lords of the earth."
Behold, O mountain-like one, these forests on this mountain, heated by the fire of Kṛṣṇa and filled with smoke on all sides, as if they are crying out in lamentation.
If this cow-pasture, dear father, is burned for our sake,
it will result in infamy in the world and bring reproach upon our lineage.
Therefore, O best of warriors, for the sake of discharging my debt to this mountain, I shall slay the kṣatriyas with my two arms in battle, just as that mountain-like being [did].
All these Kṣatriyas, O dear one, having set the mountain on fire and donned their armor,
are seen with their chariots, eager for battle according to their assigned positions.
"I shall slay Jarāsaṃdha along with his army and his mounts;
O best of the Yadus, I shall rid the surface of the earth of all other kings."
Having spoken thus,

the glorious youth Bala, wearing a forest garland, blue garments, and a bright face, descended from the mountain peak like the moon-king from the summit of Mount Meru, intoxicated by the wine of the *kādambarī* flower.
Resembling the autumn moon, his chest adorned with a forest garland,
wearing a single beautiful earring and a lovely crown, the elder brother of Keśava fell with his face turned downward into the midst of the lords of men.
When Rāma had thus leaped down, the illustrious Kṛṣṇa,
who possesses immeasurable prowess and resembles a dark rain-cloud, leaped down from the peak of Mount Gomanta.
Then Hari pressed down upon that best of mountains with his two feet.
Afflicted by that mountain, he sank down on all sides;
with his stones submerged in water, he was like an elephant emerging from a stream.
By that water, the fire was extinguished at that very moment,
just as the sun is quenched by the masses of clouds with their torrents of rain at the end of a kalpa.
With a roar like the sound of a lion’s laugh, clad in yellow garments, and possessing the form of a cloud;
with a crown upon his head, a gentle face, and eyes resembling white lotuses.
With the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, handsome-faced, and possessing a splendor equal to that of the thousand-eyed Indra, the illustrious younger brother of Haladhara—
**[After line 775a, D6 T1-3 G M2.4 G(ed.
insert:]** The glorious one, the younger brother of the wielder of the plow.
Resembling the flax flower,
Kṛṣṇa leaped after Rāma, following immediately behind him.
And by those two who had leaped down, the mountain was so pressed with their feet that it released violent gushes of water streaming upwards.
Seeing the surging of the waters, fear entered the kings.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen those two sons of Vasudeva leaping down from the mountain, [the people were amazed].
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and supreme ṛṣis,
praised the Lord Īśāna with Bhāgavata mantras at that time.
The entire army of the best of men was agitated, and all their mounts were utterly bewildered.
Those two Yādavas, using their arms as weapons,
moved about there like two enraged crocodiles submerged within the ocean.
When those two Yādavas had entered into the fray,
their minds became intent upon seizing ancient weapons.
Then,
from the expanse of the sky, they fell once more upon the two great-souled ones in the midst of a thousand kings who were longing for battle.
Indeed, those [weapons] which were obtained by the two who grace the battlefield in the battle at Mathurā.
Then,
as those enemies of the gods were intent on the wine of blood in that tumultuous battle,
divine [garlands] fell from the sky during the carnage of the fray.
They were divine, flickering, and truly resembled blazing fires.
Having deposited those very things right there, the two Yādavas reached them—
those large, embodied objects that were being pursued by flesh-eating demons.
They were thirsty to devour the king's flesh entirely in battle.
Wearing celestial garlands, they struck terror into the sky-dwellers;
shining with splendor, these armored beings pervaded the ten directions.
The plow named Saṃvartaka, as well as the club named Saujanya;
the discus named Sudarśana, and likewise the mace Kaumodakī.
These four are indeed the fiery weapons of Viṣṇu:
the conch and the discus, which destroy enemies and possess a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun.
A sword and a shield, as well as two quivers with inexhaustible arrows.
They were brought down by those two Yādavas in the great battle.
Rāma first took up his peerless plow in battle—
that divine plow, adorned with garlands, which resembled the king of serpents as it glided along.
With his left hand, the best of the Sātvatas grasped the excellent club named Saunanda,
which brings joylessness to men.
Delighted, Keśava took up that discus, which was beautiful to behold in all the worlds and radiant as the sun, and named it Sudarśana.
Beautiful to behold among all the worlds and sounding like a rain-cloud,
the heroic one joyfully took up that bow renowned by the name Śārṅga.
In his upper hand, a mace was placed for that lotus-eyed one whose purpose had been proclaimed by the gods; it is known by the name Kaumodakī.
Then,
upon the upper hand of that god Viṣṇu,
those two heroes appeared, bearing weapons and resembling the very personification of Viṣṇu’s own body.
In the battle, Rāma and Govinda fought back against those enemies.
Those two heroes, grasping their weapons, both exerted themselves against one another;
they were known as the elder and the younger brother, characterized by the names Rāma and Govinda.
In battle, those two were like his own image; they were as if Viṣṇu himself had been divided in two.
Displaying great prowess against their enemies, they acted like two sovereign lords.
Raising his mace like an enraged king of serpents,
the heroic Rāma moved about in battle like the Destroyer of his enemies.
Dragging away the multitudes of chariots belonging to the high-souled Kṣatriyas,
he made his wrath bear fruit against both the elephants and the horses.
In that battle, the delightful Rāma crushed the elephants— uprooted by his plow and struck by the hurling of his mace— as if they were mountains.
Being slaughtered by Rāma in battle, those bulls among Kṣatriyas,
terrified and deprived of their chariots, fled back toward Jarāsaṃdha.
Jarāsaṃdha, established in the duty of a Kṣatriya, said to them:
"Fie upon this conduct of yours as Kṣatriyas, you who are so cowardly in battle!"
The wise declare that for one who has exerted his prowess in battle, yet flees while deprived of his chariot, there is an unbearable sin equal to the killing of an embryo.
"Terrified by a single cowherd on the ground who possesses but little strength, why do you turn back? Fie upon this conduct of the Kshatriyas!"
"Come forth quickly, urged by my command;
or else remain with your chariots as spectators, stationed here."
I shall dispatch these two cowherds to the abode of Yama in battle.
Then all those Kṣatriyas, urged by Jarāsaṃdha,
stood ready to fight with joy, discharging nets of arrows.
They [advanced] with horses adorned with golden crests, with chariots possessing the luster of the moon,
and with elephants resembling clouds, urged on by their mahouts.
Wearing armor, carrying swords, and equipped with weapons, ornaments, and garments;
they had strung their bows and were provided with quivers and arrows.
All those lords of the earth, standing upon their chariots on the field of battle, shone resplendent, holding white umbrellas aloft and being fanned with beautiful yak-tail whisks.
Having entered the arena of battle, those two best of warriors,
the heroic sons of Vasudeva, were seen eager for combat as they rushed forward.
Then that battle took place there between those two and their [allies] in the encounter;
it was characterized by the frequent discharge of arrows and was terrible with the blows of maces.
Then, receiving thousands of arrows,
those two leaders of the Yadus, seeking battle, stood firm like mountains drenched by rain.
By those best of warriors, their eyes reddened with the passion for battle, as they shouted,
with heavy maces and missiles such as mallets, [the earth was covered].
Though being tormented, those two great archers of the Yadava clan did not tremble.
Then Kṛṣṇa, possessing great splendor and bearing the conch, discus, and mace, grew like a cloud, resembling a fire fanned by a favorable wind.
With his wheel, blazing with a splendor equal to the sun,
that hero cut down the men, elephants, horses, and great chariots into pieces.
Struck down by the falling mace and dragged by the plow,
those kings, their minds lost, were unable to stand in battle.
The diverse chariot-divisions of the kings, mangled by the wheels and eyes [of the weapon],
were shattered and unable to move in battle.
And sixty-year-old elephants, their hopes shattered by the hurling of pestles,
cried out with broken tusks like clouds at the end of the rainy season.
Struck by the flames of the fire of the discus, the riders along with the foot soldiers fell there, their life-breaths departed,
just as if they had been struck by thunderbolts.
Burnt by the discus and the plow, that army was shattered;
appearing like everything destroyed at the end of an eon, it lay fallen in its entirety.
But those kings, being weak, were not even able to behold that playground of the divine, embodied Vaiṣṇava weapons.
Some chariots were crushed, some had their kings slain,
and others had a single wheel broken, scattered upon the surface of the earth.
In that terrible slaughter, overwhelmed by the discus and the plow, dreadful and portentous omens involving the *rākṣasas* began to manifest.
Headless trunks rose up,
and shaven heads began to roll about.
And thousands of *rakṣasas* and *piśācas* were seen there,
crying out in pain as they were being split like pieces of wood.
The end of the men, elephants, chariots, and horses cannot be found.
That battlefield, drenched with the blood of fallen kings,
appeared truly terrifying, like a woman whose limbs are moistened with sandalwood paste.
There, a river of blood from the tuskers— whose heads had been severed by the hair, bones, and marrow of the hell-beings— covered the earth.
In that most terrifying destruction of those who ride upon men,
which was dreadful to behold and resounded with the inauspicious howls of jackals;
Resounding with the cries of the distressed, crowded with clouds of blood, resembling the sport of Death himself, and filled with the bodies of elephants; HV App I, 18.869–870.
It resounded with the echoes of many slain warriors and horses torn asunder,
as well as the cries of herons and vultures.
While the *rākṣasas* were active and the *piśācas* were roaming about,
as well as among the packs of jackals and on all sides among the *rākṣasas*, [the following occurred].
In that battle where the fall of lords of the earth was common to all,
Kṛṣṇa, appearing like the God of Death himself, moved about to effect the slaughter of his enemies.
He [wielded] a discus resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, an iron mace like Kālī herself,
the great bow Śārṅga, and various kinds of arrows.
Having taken hold of his army and entered the field, Keśava spoke to the kings.
"Why indeed do these heroes, joined by elephants, horses, and chariots, fight? Why do these heroes, bulls among kings skilled in weapons, proceed in this manner?"
Together with my elder brothers, I stood at the front in the battle as a foot soldier.
Why does Jarāsaṃdha not now advance, he by whom you were protected in battle through his unseen merit?
Seeing him, the plow-bearer, his eyes copper-red with rage, took up his mace.
He spoke to the copper-eyed one:
"Come, come, O Rāma, subduer of enemies; fight with me like a bull with a goad."
When this had been said, the valiant king named Darada advanced toward Rāma, whose arms were formidable with the tips of his plow, as he stood in the midst of the army.
Then that battle took place between those two, Rāma and Darada,
like two elephants, the best in the world, contending with their might in combat.
Then, having placed Darada upon his shoulder in the battle, Rāma,
the best among the strong, crushed him with his plow as if with a mace.
Falling with his knees upon the ground, he rolled about on the surface of the earth; indeed,
with his head pressed against his body, he was crushed by the mace.
Darada fell to the ground like a mountain split in half.
When that best of kings, the Darada, had been slain by Rāma,
King Jarāsaṃdha then came into conflict with Rāma.
Like the terrible and hair-raising encounter between Mahendra and Vṛtra,
the two valiant warriors, seizing their maces, rushed at one another.
Making the earth tremble, those two great-souled heroes, with their massive maces raised aloft,
appeared like two mountains with their peaks.
Seeing those two bulls among men rushing forward as if enraged, renowned for their skill in mace-fighting, the battles ceased.
Those two supreme teachers, renowned in the world and possessed of great strength,
rushed at one another like two elephants in rut.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis,
as well as the Yakṣas and Apsarases, arrived there by the thousands.
O King, adorned by gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and great ṛṣis, that place shone exceedingly,
like the sky filled with hosts of luminaries.
King Jarāsaṃdha rushed toward Rāma,
while Baladeva took his position on the left and [the other] on the right.
Those two, experts in mace-fighting, struck one another,
making the ten directions resound like two elephants with their tusks.
The fall of Rāma’s mace was heard like the roar of a thunderbolt,
as it struck Jarāsaṃdha’s foot like a splitting mountain.
The mace, hurled from the hand of Jarāsaṃdha, could not shake Rāma,
the best of mace-wielders, just as fire cannot shake the Vindhya mountain.
But that king, the lord of Magadha, endured the force of Rāma’s mace with great fortitude and warded it off through his skill.
Then a sweet-sounding voice, a witness to the world, arose in the sky:
"O Rāma, this one must not be slain by you; enough with this exertion, O giver of honor!"
His death has been ordained by me; therefore, desist from this well.
In no long time at all, the King of Magadha shall cast off his life-breaths.
But Jarāsaṃdha, having heard that, became despondent;
therefore, the plow-wielder did not strike him again.
Those two ceased from the fight, as did the Vṛṣṇis and those kings;
for a long time, O great king, they had struck one another down.
When King Jarāsaṃdha had been defeated and had fled,
the army became isolated, for its great chariot-warriors had turned back.
The imperishable Viṣṇu swiftly slew Jarāsaṃdha with his mace;
striking the king once more, he also struck him with his fist.
Striking with his strength, he repeatedly assailed him with his mace with great force.
Though unconscious, the valiant Jarāsaṃdha cast aside his mace and then desisted from the battle,
along with his bow and arrows.
The king became a foot-soldier, terrified and moving with swift strides;
as he saw his enemy fighting, he quickly vanished from sight.
Driven by those goaded elephants, chariots, and horses,
those kings fled with terrified minds, like deer scenting a tiger.
Abandoned by the kings and the great car-warriors whose pride was shattered,
that terrible, fierce battlefield, teeming with flesh-eating creatures, shone forth.
Then Viṣṇu blew the Pāñcajanya conch, which strikes fear into his enemies.
Then the great conch was blown by the god of gods, the hero, the wielder of the discus and the bow Śārṅga; it filled the heaven and earth.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas,
being delighted by that sound, let out lion-like roars.
Because of that, O King, all the monarchs fled in fear to every direction;
then the Blessed Viṣṇu comforted the king of conchs.
Then, having won the battle, Mahāviṣṇu, the upholder of the Yadu lineage,
rested for some time on the great mountain Gomanta;
O Bhārata, at that time, Kṛṣṇa was exhausted by the fight with his elder brother.
While the foremost chariot-warriors were fleeing, the highly resplendent King of Cedi,
remembering his kinship with the Yādavas, followed after Kṛṣṇa alone.
When King Jarāsaṃdha had departed, terrified of Kṛṣṇa and the festival of battle,
O sinless one, he was surrounded by the armies of Karūṣa and Cedi.
Desiring a matrimonial alliance, the King of Cedi spoke this very thing to Govinda.
"I am the husband of your father's sister, O delight of the Yādavas;
I have returned with my army, for you, O Lord, are dear to me."
"I am Damaghoṣa; may you be blessed. I am your devoted companion.
And I have already spoken to this King Jarāsaṃdha, who is of little intelligence.
Desist from Kṛṣṇa, O evil-minded one, from this conflict in the act of battle!
Thus, this Jarāsaṃdha, who reviled my words, has been abandoned; broken in battle by you, he flees along with his followers.
This lord of the earth does not return to his own city without having been free from enmity;
for when the powerful one is intent on hostility and engaged in combat at the front of the battle.
Indeed, he will display yet another offense against you once again.
"O Vārṣṇeya, he has departed in a great rage along with his army and vehicles. Therefore,
quickly abandon this earth, which is now crowded with slain men."
It was crowded with throngs of flesh-eating spirits and frequented by non-human beings;
there, piśācas and flesh-consuming rākṣasas were seen.
The ḍākinīs dance here, having drunk the flood of blood.
"O Kṛṣṇa, let us go to Karavīrapura with our army and followers;
there we shall indeed see King Sṛgāla Vāsudeva."
These two preeminent, excellent chariots have been fashioned for you by me;
they are yoked with swift horses and equipped with swords, wheels, axles, and poles.
"Ascend quickly—blessings be upon you—accompanied by Baladeva as your companion;
we must hasten to see that lord of the earth seated at Karavīra."
Let the Yādavas, exalted by their own strength, great-bodied and possessed of great power—
those tigers among kings, mighty and exceedingly vigilant— stand firm.
On a resplendent chariot yoked with all its horses,
Śauri was seen with the discus raised in one hand and the mace held in the other.
Let alone all those followers of Jarāsaṃdha who were not intimidated;
all the kings and lords of men had incurred the enmity of this one man alone.
Those kings, with wicked minds, will strike at our hearts filled with apprehension,
even though this land is generally pleasant.
Therefore, O hero, go together with Rāma, joined by your companions;
protect this Mathurā, the ancestral source of the Yādava clan.
Having heard the words of his father-in-law, the lord of Cedi,
Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world, then spoke with a joyful mind.
Ah! While you were intent on your own battle, you have been sprinkled with the water of these words by one who, though appearing as a kinsman, has mastered both place and time.
O best of the Cedis, speakers of words that are appropriate to the place and time, beneficial, and sweet are indeed rare to find in this world.
"O Lord of Cedi, by the sight of you we have become truly well-protected;
for us, there is nothing unattainable when one such as you is our kinsman."
O upholder of the Kuru lineage, with you as our protector, we are fully capable of accomplishing the destruction of Jarāsaṃdha and whatever other kings are his equals.
Know, O great king, that an incomparable battle then took place between me and that Jarāsaṃdha in the field of war.
O King of Cedi, a truly great battle has taken place right before your very eyes.
For you are the foremost kinsman of the Yadus and indeed of all the rulers of the earth;
from this time forward, O best of the Cedis, you shall witness battles.
Those kings who shall endure in this world will speak of this battle as "The Cakramausala," for such is the conduct of warriors in war.
By hearing and by retaining this account of the defeat of kings in battle on Mount Gomanta, the best of mountains, people indeed go to the heavenly world.
Therefore, O great hero, let us go to Karavīra, the best of cities,
by the path you have indicated, for the welfare of the King of Cedi.
Mounted upon their chariots with horses that leaped as if driven by the wind, they all traversed the long distance like personified fires.
Having stayed there for three nights, those who resembled the gods arrived at Karavīra, the most excellent city; and they settled in that auspicious region for the sake of Śiva.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
having learned that they had arrived, the jackal, fierce in battle, [prepared for them].
Having entered its gate in the morning, he spoke these words to the doorkeeper.
Then the mighty-armed Keśava said, "Inform us, O lord of men."
"The two heroes, sons of Vasudeva, have encountered the King of Cedi.
Having said "So be it," the gatekeeper then reported everything to him.
Considering it an insult to the city, he who possessed the prowess of Indra went forth.
With a chariot the color of the sun, radiant, destined for battle, filled with weapons, and resounding with the roar of its rims; HV App I, 18.968–969.
Resembling Mount Mandara, adorned with variegated ornaments,
he was equipped with inexhaustible arrows and quivers that resounded like the ocean.
With its swift-moving, bay-colored horses, though they were clinging even to the mountain peaks;
with its golden interior pole, its firm axle, and its brilliant appearance.
With its brilliantly shining seat and moving with the speed of the best of birds,
it was like Indra’s mountain-chariot, the Haryaśva, traveling through the sky.
When the Savitṛ vow was completed, Savitṛ himself bestowed [a boon] upon him;
he who is restrained by rays, as if by the rays of the sun.
With that preeminent chariot, which was the destroyer of the chariots of his enemies,
that jackal rushed toward Kṛṣṇa like a moth toward a fire.
Bow in hand, with very sharp arrows, clad in armor and wearing a golden garland;
a chariot-warrior, armed with a sword, arrows, and a bow, equipped with quivers, wearing earrings, and full of strength.
He possessed a mace, necklaces, armor, hand-guards, and a diadem.
Clad in white garments and wearing a turban, his eyes were shaped like fire.
Repeatedly drawing his unbearable bow with its string flickering,
he exhaled the wind born of his wrath, which was encircled by a wreath of flaming fire.
Blazing with the radiance of rows of ornaments like the immovable Mount Meru,
Sṛgāla appeared like the lord of mountains standing upon his chariot.
By the sound of his roar and the clatter of his chariot wheels,
and by his weight as he bent it down, the earth trembled just as it did in ancient times.
Seeing that glorious jackal approaching, resembling a world-protector and like fire incarnate, Kṛṣṇa was not disturbed.
Then both the King of Cedi and Bala were somewhat distressed;
and Sṛgāla, becoming enraged, drove that well-guided chariot forward.
Desirous of battle, he appeared in the presence of Vāsudeva.
Seeing Vāsudeva standing there, the jackal, eager for battle,
rushed forward with speed like a mass of clouds toward a mountain;
Vāsudeva, having smiled, stood ready to fight back.
Seeing his astonishment, he stood ready to fight back;
that battle between the two of them in the encounter was terrible to behold.
It was as if two rutting elephants were contending with one another in the forest.
Then Vāsudeva struck him with a thousand arrows.
He pierced the high-souled Vāsudeva again with eight arrows;
Vāsudeva, for his part, struck Sṛgāla, who was intoxicated with the pride of battle, with seventy-three shafts.
Then, O Indra among kings, the hero of the Vṛṣṇis struck the highly effulgent Vāsudeva,
as well as Sṛgālābha and Sṛgāla, with nine arrows. Thereafter, Sṛgāla indeed struck Viṣṇu with five hundred [arrows].
Vāsudeva struck Sṛgāla with twenty-five [arrows].
Then Śṛgāla,
O King, struck Vāsudeva with fifty arrows while Baladeva looked on.
O Great King, the two Vāsudevas,
renowned as great archers and mighty heroes, fought with each other, each desiring the other's death.
Then the jackal took up the missiles of Vāyu and Varuṇa;
thereafter, Vāsudeva took up those of Agni and Parjanya.
O Indra among kings, with those weapons, the two Vāsudevas, eager for battle and filled with wrath,
then fought in the fray with their lips bitten in anger.
O Indra among kings, having struck those supreme missiles one after another,
they fell to the earth and thus became fruitless.
The jackal discharged the Māheśvara weapon, and Janārdana discharged the Raudra; then the jackal discharged the Yāmya, and Janārdana discharged the Kāla weapon.

O King, when their weapons proved fruitless, they both fell upon the afflicted earth. Then the jackal, his anger kindled, desired to cut the bowstring of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with a razor-sharp arrow, even as that god looked on.
Knowing that, the Blessed Viṣṇu cut his bow with arrows;
having cast aside that bow along with the arrow, he took up another.
The Blessed Viṣṇu cut that bow as well and let out a roar;
O King, he then took up another bow capable of bearing a great burden.
With that bow, he struck Govinda with hundreds of sharp arrows;
then again, O King, Viṣṇu struck him with ninety, and the king struck him again with nine.
Furthermore, he struck the god with eighty supreme arrows;
then, in a rage, he struck Hari with hundreds of thousands of arrows.
Then the Blessed One, enraged, shattered that excellent bow;
having slain his charioteer, he then struck down the driver of the side-carriage.
Then Viṣṇu, of powerful prowess, let out a lion’s roar.
Then the courageous jackal, having taken up a great bow capable of bearing a heavy strain,
fixed a sharp arrow and made that bow ready.
But the jackal, radiant with the passion for battle and his dignity shaken by delusion, spoke to Kṛṣṇa as he stood ready for combat.
Rudhirākṣa was exceedingly fierce, with his lips bitten together;
O Kṛṣṇa, that which was performed by you on the path of battle at Gomanta— **HV_App.I,18.998–999**.

O Kṛṣṇa, this defeat of the Kṣatriyas— those who are leaderless, deluded, and possess weak forces— is well known to me; it is the lot of those who are wretched, lacking in spirit, and unwise in the festival of battle.
Now stay as you please; I am established in my kingly station.
A great serpent does not tolerate a wild beast in the ocean.
"Where will you go, having been blocked by me, you who have not yet reached the end in battles?"
It is not fitting for me, together with my army, to fight you alone in battle;
rather, let us two stand in the fray and fight as equals, I alone against you alone.
What is the use of this rejected crowd? You and I shall stand in battle;
let one of us meet his end in the fray through a righteous war.
"If you are slain, I shall become Vāsudeva in this world;
if I am slain, you alone shall become Vāsudeva."
Having heard the words of the jackal, Vāsudeva, who is devoted to forgiveness,
said to him, "Strike as you please," and took up his discus.
Then the jackal, frantic with rage and swift in his prowess, hurled terrible nets of arrows at Kṛṣṇa for the sake of battle.
Skilled in the application of weapons in battle, he hurled it at the chest of Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever other weapons there were in the battle, such as maces and the like,
that powerful jackal hurled them at Govinda.
Struck mercilessly by the weapons discharged by the jackal, which were garlanded with flames of fire,
Kṛṣṇa stood firm like an immovable mountain.
Struck by that blow from the weapon and somewhat incited to anger,
Govinda raised his discus and brought it down upon the chest of Sṛgāla.
He spoke these words to the jackal:
"O king of kings, if you are able, carry this uplifted wheel."
What is the use of this idle chatter? You shall behold my prowess.
"O King, with this discus I shall sever your head from your body!
Having spoken thus, his eyes copper-red with rage,
he [aimed] at that jackal who stood upon his chariot, possessed of great stature, and intoxicated by the pride of battle.
In battle, he struck down the mighty Cakra,
who was filled with pride; having slain the heroic Sṛgāla, who was eager for combat, in that same fray.
Then the Sudarśana discus returned once more to the hand of the Guru.
Pierced in the chest by the discus, he fell down, his life departed and his joy gone,
streaming with blood like a mountain struck down by a wild beast.
Having seen him fallen like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt,
his armies retreated dejected once the king had been slain.
Some, having entered the city, were deeply overcome by dejection;
tormented by grief and oppressed by sorrow for their husband, they wept.
Some, grieving right there and remembering his good deeds,
remained distressed and would not abandon the fallen lord of the earth as he lay upon the ground.
Then, with a voice like the roar of a thundercloud,
Kṛṣṇa, the crusher of enemies and lotus-petal-eyed one, granted fearlessness to the people.
With a hand worthy of a king, its fingers and joints adorned with silver, he addressed them, saying:
"Do not fear! Do not fear!"
I shall not slay in battle a person who is free from harm on account of this evil man's fault; this is not considered the vow of a hero.
Then, with faces filled with tears, wretched and crying out piteously,
he who was known as Sṛgāla fell down, fallen and dejected in mind.
They beheld the lord of the earth fallen upon the ground,
his chest mangled by the discus like a mountain with its peak shattered.
All those ministers, together with the subjects, lamented intensely;
their eyes filled with falling tears, they were dejected and fallen under the power of grief.
At the sound of their weeping,
with voices full of lamentation, his queens emerged along with their sons, their faces bathed in tears.
Seeing that praiseworthy lord of the earth fallen there, they,
deeply afflicted, tore at their breasts with their fingernails and lamented aloud.
Beating their chests, their breasts, and even their disheveled hair mercilessly, those women wailed in discordant tones.
Afflicted by intense grief, with their eyes bathed in tears,
they all fell upon his chest with their arms upraised, like creepers severed at their roots.
The eyes of those royal women, filled with tears,
shone like lotuses struck by raindrops.
Beating their breasts with their hearts, those women wept and lamented piteously as they mourned for their husband fallen upon the ground.
And placing his young son before him, whose eyes were streaming with tears, he set forth,
leading the child who was like a young jackal.
The women wept twice as much at the side of their father as they had for Śakra-deva.
Behold this boy, your son, who is undisciplined and lacking in wisdom;
bereft of you, how shall he stand firm in his father’s station?
How is it that, having abandoned [me] in a single moment, you have gone to the inner apartments?
Unsatisfied with your happiness, what can we do? We are widows.
His queen, named Padmāvatī, the most excellent of women,
took that son and approached Vāsudeva there.
O hero, this son of the one whom you struck down by the deed spoken in battle has come to you for refuge after he has passed into the state of a ghost.
If he should bow down to you, or if he should again carry out your command—
if you are the praiseworthy kinsman of my son who bows before you— then [act accordingly].
"O Lord, let life be granted to this kinsman just as it is to yourself."
This person would not suffer such terrible pain from a single blow.
If this fool were to perform toward you the rites due to a kinsman, this wretched man,
so overwhelmed by grief, would not lie upon the surface of the earth in such a state.
O sinless one, O hero, let the lineage of this deceased kinsman be protected by you, just like your own son, O son.
Having heard those words of the queen, the delighter of the Yadus,
the best among speakers, spoke these words preceded by gentleness.
"O Queen, my anger toward this evil-minded man has passed;
we have returned to our natural state, O Goddess, and here I am, your kinsman."
O virtuous lady, my anger has vanished through your faultless words;
this son of the jackal is undoubtedly mine as well.
"I grant him both fearlessness and consecration for his well-being.
Let the subjects, the family priest, and the ministers be summoned;
let your son be consecrated in the kingdom of his father and grandfather."
Then all the subjects, as well as the family priest and the ministers,
came for the sake of the consecration to where Rāma and Keśava were.
Then the heroic Janārdana joined that prince, who was seated upon the throne, with a divine consecration.
Having consecrated Sṛgāla’s son in Karavīrapura,
Kṛṣṇa immediately resolved to depart on that very day.
With that chariot yoked with bay horses, which had indeed been won in battle,
Keśava set out upon the road, just as Indra proceeds to the third heaven.
Accompanied and following one another, the two of them went toward Mathurā.
The righteous Damaghoṣa also, together with his army and his circle of friends,
took leave of Keśava and returned to his own city.
Śakradeva, whose soul was devoted to dharma and who was a scorcher of his enemies, together with his mother,
as well as the principal subjects— including children, the elderly, and young women— [remained there].
Then, having placed the jackal— who was fierce in battle— upon a palanquin,
they traveled together along a distant path toward the west.
They performed his funeral rites according to the prescribed ordinances;
they caused the post-mortem honors for the ancestors to be performed,
offering *śrāddha* ceremonies by the thousands, dedicating each one specifically to the king.

Then, having offered water for his father who had passed away in that terrible state, and having performed the water-libation while reciting his name, lineage, and other particulars, the king, his mind agitated by grief, entered the supreme city.
His chest was adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark and illuminated by the brilliance of excellent jewels; his divine body was radiant with unguents,
and he was captivating with his shining discus and conch, his great crown shimmering, and his necklaces and armlets.

O heart, always worship the tall-bodied form of the Victorious One— resembling a cloud, clad in yellow garments, adorned with jeweled makara-earrings, moon-faced, with eyes like blooming lotuses of rising splendor. [Colophon]
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having stayed for five nights on the road, those two, after a short time—
They met with Damaghoṣa;
then, according to the rules for guests, the two of them— [K:
After line 1073, K1 (marg.), 2 Ñ2.3 V B Dn Ds D1.4.6 T1.3 G2.3.5 M insert:]
Having met with Damaghoṣa, as if they had stayed together for a single night,
the two heroes went forth together, filled with supreme joy.
Both sons of Vasudeva reached the city of Mathurā.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the Yādava, the world-renowned Supreme Person, blew his great conch, Pāñcajanya, with a beautiful sound.
Then all the Yādavas, led by Ugrasena and accompanied by their armies, went out with joyful hearts to welcome the two delights of the Yadu clan.
The guilds, the subjects, and the ministers together with the family priests,
along with the children and the elderly, all flocked toward that city.
Joyful musical instruments were played, and let the two Supreme Men be praised;
the streets, garlanded with banners, shone brilliantly on all sides.
The entire city was thrilled and delighted, appearing most magnificent;
Akrūra, Sātyaki, and the ministers likewise were as befittingly joyful.
Upon the arrival of those two brothers, it was just as at the festival of Indra.
There, on the royal highways, joyful singers sang songs consisting of hymns and blessings that brought delight to the Yādavas.
"The two world-renowned brothers, Govinda and Rāma, have arrived.
All of you Yādavas, being free from fear in your own city, may you sport in happiness."
In that Mathurā, upon the meeting of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, there was no one who was dejected, nor filthy, nor deprived of consciousness.
The birds sang auspicious songs, and the cows, horses, and elephants were overjoyed;
likewise, the throngs of men and women experienced mental bliss.
Auspicious winds blew, and the ten directions were free from dust;
and all the deities in their abodes were filled with joy.
All those signs that appear in the world during the Kṛta Yuga were seen here, portending the arrival of the two brothers.
Then, at an auspicious and holy time,
those two heroes, the crushers of enemies, entered the city of Mathurā in a chariot yoked with bay horses.
As Govinda and Rāma entered the beautiful city,
the hosts of Yadus followed them, just as the hosts of gods follow Śakra.
Those two delights of the Yadu clan entered the palace of their father Vasudeva with joyful countenances, like the sun and the moon entering a mountain.
Having laid aside their weapons in their own home,
those two best of the Yadus, both sons of Vasudeva, wandered at will and rejoiced.
Then, having both pressed the feet of Vasudeva,
they [honored] King Ugrasena there, as well as the other leaders of the Yadu clan.
Having honored them according to the prescribed rule and being greeted by all with blessings,
they departed with joyful hearts for their mother’s very abode.
Thus, those two of auspicious countenance, having become two emanations accompanied by Ugrasena, rejoiced in Mathurā for some time.
Rāma and Ugrasena were both valiant and adorned by Viṣṇu.
Having set out from Mount Gomanta, that king, the lord of Magadha,
entered his own city with his head bowed down in shame.
[Colophon] [h: HV (CE) App.I No. 18A, transliterated by Renate Söhnen-Thieme, 22.06.2003, version of June 2003. :h]
Accompanied by his army and his forces, he indeed followed behind him.
Having spoken thus to all the kings, Kṛṣṇa, who resembles a dark rain-cloud,
stood at the head of the battle with his elder brother as his companion.
Upon hearing this, Jarāsaṃdha’s eyes widened with rage;
and the king was thus addressed by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Armed with a bow, arrows, a chariot, a sword, earrings, and armor,
the powerful king was the foremost of heroes, truly peerless and alone.
Standing before Keśava, he addressed the slayer of Keśin.
What is the use of these trivial words? Stay now before me!
Show whatever strength and whatever heroism you possess, if you so desire.
"I shall strike you; stay then for a moment in this battle."
"O cowherd, these kings who have been slain were deluded by their own strength;
O cowherd, these wretches, who were mere mockers of kings, have now brought this about."
"I shall indeed show you King Yama himself," having said this,
Jarāsaṃdha rushed toward Kṛṣṇa in battle.
Seeing him with eyes copper-red with rage, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words:
"Strike as you wish, O king, if you are able!"
"O King, here I stand before you; why do you boast?
O King, it is not by such [words] that the best of monarchs are considered heroes in battle."
"Show your prowess either with arrows or with weapons!
Having spoken thus, Hari, the Lord of the World and leader of all,
Kṛṣṇa, mounted his excellent chariot bearing the banner of Suparṇa.
He approached Jarāsaṃdha and pierced him with eight arrows.
The valiant one pierced his charioteer with five sharp arrows and slew the horses in battle as he strove against him.
And Baladeva cut his bow with a straight-knotted arrow.
Perceiving him to be in distress, the mighty Citrasena,
the commander-in-chief, and Kauśika both pierced Kṛṣṇa with five arrows.
Enraged, Kauśika pierced Kāmapāla with three arrows;
then Baladeva split his bow in two in the battle with a broad-headed shaft.
And the blessed Janārdana, having assailed those enemies with showers of arrows, also struck the King of Magadha with great speed.
The great car-warrior Jarāsaṃdha, a mighty hero, also swiftly strung another bow and struck Keśava’s body— which had the luster of the petals of a blue lotus— with sharpened arrows.
The Blessed One Govinda, the conqueror, also struck Jarāsaṃdha on the forehead with a straight-knotted arrow.
Furthermore, he pierced him with sharpened arrows resembling mountains,
and struck his gold-adorned banner with a razor-headed shaft.
The enraged Citrasena pierced him with sharpened arrows;
Kauśika struck him with twenty-five, and Jarāsaṃdha with seven.
Janārdana pierced them with three iron arrows each,
while Baladeva struck those enemies with five arrows each.
The heroic Kṛṣṇa cut through Citrasena’s chariot horses,
and Baladeva split his bow in two with a broad-headed arrow in the battle.
With his bow severed and deprived of his chariot, the valiant one took up a mace and,
filled with great rage and desiring to kill him, rushed toward the wielder of the club.
But as he was desiring to discharge iron arrows in his wish to slay Citrasena,
the mighty Jarāsaṃdha cut through the bow of Rāma.
And Citrasena quickly struck Halāyudha with a mace;
meanwhile, the powerful Jarāsaṃdha struck Keśava with five arrows.
Again Jarāsaṃdha pierced Kṛṣṇa, who had the luster of a blue lotus, with ninety arrows, and again with seven, and then with eighty.
The Blessed One severed the bow of the wise Jarāputra;
casting aside his bow along with its arrow, the valiant one took up a mace.
Then the powerful one struck Viṣṇu on the region of his arm,
and Govinda likewise struck him on the chest with his mace.
The King of Magadha fell to the earth on his knees; rising once more, he then struck Hara violently in the chest with his mace.
And Hari, O King, struck the impatient Jarāsaṃdha with his mace.
Jarāsandha could not endure Janārdana approaching with his mace;
while Baladeva looked on, he struck him in the middle of the chest.
Then, with all his limbs tormented, Kṛṣṇa fell to the ground. Thereupon the king of Magadha, the best of monarchs, let out a lion’s roar and cried out the words, "Kṛṣṇa is slain! Kṛṣṇa is slain!"
Seeing Kṛṣṇa fallen, Rāma’s prowess redoubled with rage;
seizing his mace, he rushed toward Jarāsaṃdha.
The joy of the Yadus struck him between the breasts with his two arms;
then Rāma struck him again on the forehead with his mace. Deprived of consciousness, the son of Jarā fell to the ground upon his knees.
Then the powerful Jarāsaṃdha, the king of Magadha, suddenly rising from the ground,
quickly struck Balabhadra with a loud roar.
Then the heroic Haladhara, with his club Sarvapuṣṭā,
shattered that club of Kṛṣṇa right before him.
But the powerful Jarāsaṃdha, having hurled his great mace,
again released another one that was exceedingly fierce and equipped with all kinds of weapons.
Taking up that sharp and terrible [weapon], he struck Halāyudha;
and again, the powerful one struck him on the forehead with his mace.
Then, while Vāsudeva looked on, he struck him violently with his fist and his mace, and quickly struck him again with his palm.
Then the powerful Balabhadra fell into a swoon;
thereupon, that king, the lord of Magadha, let out a lion’s roar.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu, having regained consciousness, struck the son of Jarā with his mace, which was drenched in the blood of the Dānavas. Then the son of Jarā hurled an excellent spear at him.
Beholding it as it came rushing toward him, the imperishable hero Viṣṇu seized it and hurled it back right at him,
just as Viṣṇu himself had done to Bala.
Struck by her, the king fell down and lost consciousness;
having regained his senses, the king then struck him with an iron club.
Between those two, who were each seeking the other's death,
there occurred a battle equal to that between the gods and the asuras; it was like the first encounter between Namuci and Śakra, or between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
Both of them were world-renowned, celebrated for their strength and their mastery of weapons;
both heroes were equally renowned for their prowess in battle and combat.
In the meantime, the heroic Viṣṇu, taking up his Śārṅga bow,
pierced the Lord of Magadha with an arrow resembling a thunderbolt.
Afflicted by that blow, the lord of kings struck Hari with his mace;
casting aside his Śārṅga bow, Hari then struck him back with his own mace.
The righteous Balabhadra was also determined to strike him;
in the meantime, the heroic king named Darada spoke:
"O Lord Rāma, it is not fitting to cry out 'Rāma, Rāma' against one who is intent on harming another."
Seeing him, the wielder of the plow, his eyes copper-red with rage, took up his mace;
the king [saw] Rāma, the wielder of the plow, who was intoxicated by battle.
Between those two, that battle took place like one between two leaders of elephant herds.
[h: HV (CE) App.I No. 19, transliterated by Renate Söhnen-Thieme, 22.06.2003, version of June 2003. :h] [k: T1.3 G3 M cont. after App.I No. 18: :k]
Janamejaya said: O best of the twice-born, having been defeated by Kṛṣṇa along with his army and followers, what did Jarāsaṃdha think as he went to his own home?
"Alas, O best of the twice-born, Jarāsaṃdha, who was equal to them in strength, has committed this grievous act: the flight of those two lions of the Yādavas."
O Brahmin, it does not seem right to me that you have placed him at the front;
for Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of kings, stands as the leader of them all.
"O best of the twice-born, I consider this a cause for shame for that king:
having approached from behind, he passed in front while they were looking on."
O best of the twice-born, O ascetic rich in penance, tell me in detail what answer the powerful King Jarāsaṃdha gave to that lion of the Yadus, Mādhava.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having burned [the city] and departed from Gomanta, that king, the lord of Magadha,
entered his own city, bowing down with shame.
Then, having entered his own city like a serpent trodden upon by a foot, he,
emaciated by grief, found no peace by night nor by day.
Then, on one occasion, the king, overcome with pain and grief,
summoned all the monarchs and spoke these words:
"O best of kings, we shall deliberate upon a great matter that has arisen.
O lords of kings, I have been defeated by the two cowherds in the assembly of monarchs."
He, the knower of counsel, deliberated together with all the kings:
"Alas! I consider our human prowess to be pitiable, since these kings are directed against us."
"Those kings who were defeated by Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa along with their armies and followers— we shall besiege the beautiful city of Mathurā, which is now occupied by the Yādavas."
"O Blessed Ones, let us go there with a great fourfold army to slay those two, Gopa and Kilbiṣa, in the city of Madhurā."
Otherwise, there would be infamy for us among all those of beautiful form in the world;
O best of kings, hear also this vow of mine.
"Indeed, having slain those two heroic cowherds, I shall go to my own city accompanied by many forces; this is the truth."
"O best of kings, I possess many powerful forces;
those two Yādavas are without resources, for their weapons are unsheathed and they are weak."

"Then the entire city of Sādhyā shall be [conquered]; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. Therefore, O kings, having fixed your minds upon battle, let all you monarchs set forth, making the earth tremble."
The city protected by the Yādavas must be besieged on all sides;
it must be utterly uprooted by you, whose fame is renowned.
[Colophon] [h:
HV (CE) App. I, No. 20, transliterated by François Painchaud, proof-read by André Couture]

Vaiśampāyana said:
In the meantime, men who followed worldly customs arrived at the residence of the one whose weapon is the discus, which resembled the abode of the world-protectors.
Regarding those matters which were urgent and relevant to worldly affairs here,
the best of the Yadus, perceiving their significance, assembled in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
When all the leaders of the Yadus had assembled in the council,
the men from Prāvṛtti spoke words concerning the urgent crisis facing the king.
"O Janārdana, there will be a very great assembly of kings, lords of men,
and rulers of the earth," he said many times.
The lords of various realms are hastening there.
O lotus-eyed one, [he went] to Kuṇḍina by the command of the son of the Bhojas.
There, conversations spoken by men were heard openly:
"It is said that there was a woman named Rukmiṇī, the renowned sister of Rukmin."
"O Janārdana, it is said that her svayaṃvara will take place there."
For this purpose, these best of men go forth with their armies and followers.
O Yādava, on the third day from now, the svayaṃvara of that woman, the most beautiful in the three worlds, who is adorned with golden ornaments, shall take place.
There we shall see the hundreds of camps of the high-souled kings who have assembled there, traveling by elephant, horse, and chariot.
Possessing the pride of lions and tigers, moving with the gait of elephants in rut,
they were always fond of battle and intolerant toward one another.
"Let us go quickly for victory, united and accompanied by a flood of troops!
Why should we, who were once lords of the earth, now remain restricted and wander in solitude?
O best of the Yadus, shall we become devoid of spirit? Let us depart!"
Having heard these words, which were like a thorn driven into his heart, Keśava,
the best of the Yadus, departed from among the Yadus accompanied by his forces.
Those Yādavas, all exalted by their strength and eager for battle,
set forth on divine chariots like proud gods.
Commissioned by the commander-in-chief, Hari, who was equal to Īśāna, shone forth with Kṛṣṇa at his side;
Kṛṣṇa, with discus raised in hand and mace in grasp, gleamed brilliantly.

For Kṛṣṇa too, mace in hand, bearing the Śārṅga bow, the conch, the mace, and the sword, as well as the other Yādavas there who followed Vāsudeva— **HV App. I, 20.29–30**1:2: [Note: For the second occurrence of line 29, Ñ₂ V₃ substitute: Kṛṣṇa too, mace in hand, bearing the Śārṅga bow, the conch, the mace, and the sword; and the other Yādavas there who were followers of Vāsudeva.
With chariots resembling the sun, resounding with the tinkling of small bells.
They followed the lotus-eyed one, who was surrounded by his own followers bearing various weapons empowered by *śakti*; he then spoke to the lord of the Yadus.
Then Govinda, whose vision was certain, spoke to Ugrasena: [HV App. I, 20.32]
"Stay here, O tiger among kings, together with my brother, O sinless one."
"O hero, these base Kṣatriyas— deceitful in intellect, though learned in the scriptures, and experts at spotting vulnerabilities— are afflicting us in this empty city."
All those who were once our enemies, now followers under the power of Jarāsaṃdha,
rejoice there in happiness like the immortals in the world of the gods.
Having heard those words of his, the highly illustrious King of the Bhojas,
transformed by his affection for Kṛṣṇa, spoke these nectar-like words.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who increase the joy of the Yadus!
Listen, O slayer of enemies, to that which I shall now speak.
Deprived of you, we are all unable to dwell in happiness,
whether in this city or in the countryside, like women who have lost their husbands.
"O dear one, with you as our protector and relying on the strength of your arms,
we have no fear even of the lords of men, including Indra himself, O giver of honor.
O best of the Yadus, wherever you go, it shall lead to victory."
Therefore, O bull among the Yādavas, you should go there accompanied by us.
Having heard the words of that king, the son of Devakī smiled and said:
"Without a doubt, I shall do exactly as you desire today."
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa indeed departed swiftly on his chariot.
He arrived at the house of Bhīṣmaka while the sun was turning red.
When the royal assembly had arrived and the ground was crowded with tents,
he beheld the vast arena and entered the body of a Rākṣasa.
For the purpose of terrifying kings and for the sake of making [his power] manifest,
he meditated in his mind upon the mighty Vainateya, the ancient one.
Then, having perceived his mere thought, the son of Vinatā assumed a form easily discernible and hid himself near Keśava.
By the falling of his wings, which caused the wind to swirl,
all men were shaken; they fell prostrate upon the earth,
and with their heads bowed, they all trembled like serpents.
Seeing them gathered together, Kṛṣṇa, immovable like a mountain,
then considered that best of birds by the wind from his wings.
He saw Garuḍa arrive, adorned with divine garlands and unguents,
repeatedly shaking the earth with the wind from his wings.
With weapons fastened to his back like hissing serpents,
he bent down the Vaishnava embrace as it was being applied face-downward.
Dragging with his two feet the foremost of serpents,
which was white and adorned with golden leaf-patterns, like a mountain rich in minerals.
The bringer of the commencement of nectar, the destroyer of the lord of the double-tongued serpents,
the terrifier of the hosts of Daityas, the vehicle, and the emblem upon the banner.
Seeing that the minister Dhṛtimat had arrived at the banner,
Madhusūdana spoke to Garuḍa, who was prepared for the encounter.
Seeing him standing there like another body, he was exceedingly delighted.
With words of equal power, he addressed Garuḍa who had approached him.
He went to the great inner apartments of the Bhoja king, the most excellent of the triple heaven.
"Welcome, O best of sky-goers, crusher of the enemies of the divine army! [he said].
O delighter of Vinatā’s heart, welcome, O beloved of Keśava!
"O best among the foremost of birds, go to the residence of Kaiśika;
having gone there ourselves today, we shall await the svayaṃvara."
There we shall behold hundreds of great-souled kings assembled together, traveling by means of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having spoken thus to the mighty Vainateya,
the long-armed Kṛṣṇa then went to the city of the high-souled Kaiśika,
accompanied by his friend Vainateya and the illustrious Yādava great-chariot warriors.

When Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, had arrived at the city of Vidarbha, everyone was thrilled and exceedingly joyful; they began the preparations for his reception. All the powerful kings, bearing weapons and arms, [prepared themselves].
At that very time, however, King Kaiśika, who was skilled in statesmanship,
rose up with a joyful heart.
Having offered the guest-water and water for sipping, King Kaiśika himself,
having honored Kṛṣṇa according to the prescribed rites, led him into his own city.
But a divine palace had already been prepared for Kṛṣṇa;
the glorious one entered it with his army, just as Śaṅkara enters Kailāsa.
Honored with floods of jewels such as food and drink, the younger brother of Vāsava took his place.
Kṛṣṇa dwelt in great comfort in the residence of that king,
honored with high esteem and with a heart full of affection.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen that highly resplendent son of Vinatā, Kṛṣṇa, arrive, they...
All those best of kings became possessed by anxiety.
Having assembled, O King, those monarchs of terrible prowess— skilled in counsel and most proficient in the meaning of the treatises on policy— proceeded for consultation.
Having gone to Bhīṣmaka’s beautiful assembly hall, which was adorned with gold,
those best of kings sat upon variegated thrones with wonderful coverings, like gods in the assembly hall of the gods.
With their minds agitated by fear, they became overwhelmed with anxiety.
Then Jarāsaṃdha, the best of speakers, spoke these words;
in their midst, the mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful Jarāsaṃdha,
possessed of great splendor, addressed them like the Lord of the Gods himself.
"Listen, O best of kings, as I speak according to my understanding; Bhīṣmaka is indeed highly intelligent, O best among speakers. (HV App. I, 20.105–106)
He who is known as Kṛṣṇa, the powerful son of Vasudeva,
has arrived here at Kuṇḍina with Vainateya as his companion.
For the sake of the maiden, the one of great splendor, surrounded by the Yādavas,
will certainly exert effort so that the acquisition of the maiden may come to pass.
O tigers among kings, having determined the relative strength and weakness of the situation, perform here that which is beneficial, whether it be a cause or an effect, endowed with sound policy.
Those two sons of Vasudeva, both of great heroism,
were on foot upon that best of mountains, Gomanta, without Vainateya;
you all know indeed what very great and terrible deed was performed by them there.
When Kṛṣṇa encounters and fights with the Yādavas, the Bhojas, and the great chariot-warriors of the Andhakas, what kind of conflict will there be?
When Viṣṇu, mounted upon Garuḍa, strives for the sake of the maiden,
who will stand in that battle— even Śakra together with the gods?
And when she is never given to him as a daughter,
then he will be able to take her away by force, even with the gods.
In ancient times, it is heard that when this earth was submerged at the bottom of the netherworld (pātāla) during the terrible period of the single vast ocean,
she was lifted up by the powerful Viṣṇu,
the originator of the world, who had assumed the form of a boar.
And Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the Daityas, was struck down by the Boar.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu, possessed of great strength and prowess,
was of great heroism and was the great grandfather of all the Daityas.
He is invulnerable to the immortals and the Daityas, as well as to the ṛṣis, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras.
Neither for Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, nor Nāgas is there [a place] in the sky or on the surface of the earth;
nor during the night or the day, nor with anything dry or moist.
The lord of the Daityas, who was indeed unconquerable and invincible throughout the three worlds,
was slain in ancient times by Viṣṇu in his Man-Lion form.
In the form of a dwarf, the powerful son of Kaśyapa,
born as the embryo of Aditi, bound Bali, the best of the Asuras,
with ropes made of the cord of truth and established him in the refuge of Pātāla.
Kārtavīrya, of great heroism and possessing a body with a thousand arms,
[arose] through the grace of Dattātreya and from my own intoxication with royal power.
The son of Jamadagni, possessed of great splendor and born from the womb of Reṇukā,
was Rāma, the best among those who uphold the sacred scriptures, appearing at the junction of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages.
The king who was the lord of the seven continents was slain by Viṣṇu with an axe like a thunderbolt;
furthermore, the Haihaya was slain by Viṣṇu in a disguised form.
In former times, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
struck down the heroic Rāvaṇa, the conqueror of the three worlds.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, during the Tārakāmaya war, the heroic Viṣṇu,
having become eight-armed and mounted upon Garuḍa,
slew in battle the Asuras who were arrogant due to the granting of boons.
And the Daitya Kālanemi, who indeed struck fear into the gods,
was slain in battle by a discus possessing the brilliance of a thousand rays.
By the power of great yoga, Viṣṇu, assuming his universal form (viśvarūpa),
struck down many asuras in battle after finding an opening in the course of time.
In the forest dwell the Daityas, possessed of great strength and prowess.
In his childhood, he slew Pralamba, Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka,
as well as Śakuni, Keśin, and the two Arjuna trees.
Having slain the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, as well as Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika,
and Kaṃsa— the best among the strong— along with his followers, Keśava, the son of Devakī,
sported while disguised as a cowherd.
Such divine disguises were created by the powerful Viṣṇu in various places;
therefore, out of a desire for your welfare, I shall relate them to you.
I consider him to be Keśava, Viṣṇu, the foremost of the gods, the destroyer of the Asuras;
Nārāyaṇa, the source of the world, the ancient, eternal Puruṣa.
The creator of all beings, both manifest and unmanifest, eternal,
invincible to all worlds, and worshipped by all creatures.
Without beginning, middle, or end; perishable yet imperishable and eternal;
self-existent, unborn, and firm; unconquerable by all things moving and unmoving;
the one who took the three strides, the Lord of the three worlds, and the destroyer of the enemies of the lords of the thirty gods.

Thus my mind has reached this certainty: this lord of Mathurā has been born into a great and vast lineage of kings who were universal monarchs (cakravartins). How could Garuḍa become the vehicle for any other mortal?
Especially since Janārdana is currently in the sign of Leo for the sake of the maiden,
what powerful man would stand today before Garuḍa?
"Because of the *svayaṃvara*, Viṣṇu himself has come here.
It is proclaimed that there is great danger in the arrival of Viṣṇu.
Having reflected upon this, you must decide what should be done next."
To the king who was speaking thus, the lord of the Magadhas,
the highly wise Sunītha then spoke these words:

The mighty-armed king, the lord of Magadha, has spoken correctly regarding what occurred in the great battle in the presence of these lords of men— the exceedingly difficult deeds performed by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa on Mount Gomanta.
That vast army, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and teeming with infantry and banners,
was utterly consumed by the fire of the discus and the plough.
Therefore, this glorious lord of Magadha reflected upon the future; and remembering that most terrible event, he spoke thus within the royal army: (HV App. I, 20.181–182).
As Balarāma and Keśava fought there on foot in battle,
the terrible destruction of the army became truly difficult to restrain.
O best of kings, it is known to you that Suparṇa has arrived.
Stirred up by the wind from the force of their wings, the sky-dwellers wandered about.
All the oceans were agitated, and the mountain and the earth trembled repeatedly.
We were all utterly terrified, bewildered as to what omen had arisen.
When he, mounted by Keśava, fights while clad in armor,
how could one such as I be able to stand firm on the field of battle?
The so-called *svayaṃvara* of kings is a truly great increaser of joy;
it was established by the ancient best of men as a treasure-house of fame and dharma.
"But now that these lords of men have reached this city of Kuṇḍina,
the form of the Great Being will surely not be seen as it was before."
If that princess should choose another from among the kings,
what man would dare to withstand the prowess of Kṛṣṇa’s arms?
This fault has been made public at the great festival of the *svayaṃvara*;
for that reason, Kṛṣṇa, we ourselves, and these lords of men have come here.
And the arrival of Kṛṣṇa, which is utterly contemptible for kings—
just as the Magadhan speaks regarding the lords of men on account of the maiden.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
When these words had been thus spoken by the high-souled Sunītha, HV App. I, 20.201.
The heroic Dantavakra, the lord of Karūṣa, addressed him.
O lords of men, that which was spoken by Sunītha, the lord of Māgadha,
I consider to have been previously appropriate, as it was beneficial advice for us.
Neither out of malice, nor as one who speaks with egoism,
nor out of a desire for self-aggrandizement do I defile these immortal words;
they are an ocean of speech, profoundly deep and augmented by the meaning of the treatises on ethics.
Who indeed is capable of telling all this in the assembly of kings?
However, listen to what I say for the sake of remembrance:
O lords of men, what wonder is there in saying that Vāsudeva has arrived? (HV App. I, 20.209–210)
Just as we have all come here, so too has Kṛṣṇa come;
what fault or even minor transgression is there in our having assembled for the sake of the maiden?
Since we have come together to perform this enclosure of the cows,
how can you possibly attribute the fault for the battle committed therein to us?
O King, those two heroes remained in forest exile due to the delusion caused by Kaṃsa;
at the word of the celestial sage, they stayed on the banks of Vṛndāvana.
Having summoned both those heroes, Rāma and Janārdana, for the purpose of their slaughter, [Akrūra] urged them on with the serpent;
having killed the serpent, the two entered [the city].
Then, relying on his own prowess, he was struck down in the ocean of the arena;
and like one whose life-force had departed, the Lord of Mathurā sat there with his followers.
"What fault has been committed here,
O King, because of which we, though superior in age, have all assembled together intent on obstructing you?"
Beholding that immense army, Rāma and Keśava became terrified;
abandoning the city and their forces, they fled to Mount Gomanta. We too, as warriors skilled in combat, went there to slay them.
And on that field of battle, a conflict was waged by two foot soldiers who had not yet reached their youth against chariots, horses, men,
and elephants; having laid siege to him, that mountain was set ablaze in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya.
If those two ascetics enter the mouth of a forest fire and die,
we all consider them to have been truly disciplined, O bulls among the Kṣatriyas.
But if we act thus in every battle, we shall bring reproach upon Janārdana.
"Wherever we shall go, there let there be strife;
O lords of the earth, we shall strive for the sake of friendship with Kṛṣṇa."
"Kṛṣṇa has not come to this Kuṇḍipura because of the influence of the Kali age;
for whose sake will he give battle when he comes for the sake of the maiden?"
In this mortal world, he is no ordinary man, but a lord among men;
and in the world of the gods, he is the sovereign of the gods, the most excellent Puruṣottama.
He is the creator even of the gods, and especially of the worlds.
O God, his intellect is not that of a fool; he possesses neither envy nor avarice.
Neither arrogant, nor emaciated, nor afflicted, he is the eternal remover of the suffering of those who bow before him;
this Viṣṇu is the Lord, the God, the deity even of the gods.
Kṛṣṇa has come here with Garuḍa for the purpose of revealing his disguise;
he does not go forth to destroy the enemy accompanied by an army.
Understand this journey: Hari has indeed come here for the sake of joy, accompanied by the lords of the Yādavas—the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas.
"O lords of men, having offered the guest-offering of water for honor and water for sipping,
we shall all perform hospitality for the high-souled Keśava."
Having thus formed an alliance with Kṛṣṇa,
we dwell free from anxiety, fearless, and devoid of all distress.
Having heard those words of the wise Dantavaktra,
Śālva, the best among eloquent speakers, addressed those lords of men.
Why, out of fear of him, have we all laid down our weapons,
trembling with dread at Kṛṣṇa for the sake of making peace?
"What need is there for praise by others when one has disparaged one's own strength? This is not the dharma of kings; it is inconsistent with the duty of a Kṣatriya."
Born into great royal lineages and increasing their families,
how could the intellect of such men be that of a coward?
I truly know Kṛṣṇa as the eternal primordial god,
the lord of all kings of men, who is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
I conquered Vaikuṇṭha in this world, where Hari, the teacher of all things moving and stationary,
had appeared in the womb of Devakī as Viṣṇu, who is honored by the worlds.
For the purpose of slaying King Kaṃsa, for the removal of the earth's burden,
for our own destruction, and for the protection of the world—
I know all the activities of Viṣṇu regarding his descent with partial incarnations.

"O lords of the earth, having waged an incomparable battle with Viṣṇu, we shall go to the abode of Yama, consumed by the fire of his discus. And I know this, O best of kings: that the exhaustion of life must come through Time."
No one dies before their time, nor does anyone live when their time has come;
having understood this certainty, one should not feel fear for anyone.
That very Lord Viṣṇu, the knower of yoga, having observed the exhaustion of their ascetic penance,
became at the proper time the slayer of the lords of the Daityas.
Having perceived that Bali, the son of Virocana, was invincible and possessed of great strength,
the Lord of the Gods made him a dweller in the depths of Pātāla.
O kings, these and other deeds of Viṣṇu are indeed well-known;
therefore, your deliberation regarding war is improper.
Therefore, it is appropriate for us that your minds are set upon war;
for Kṛṣṇa’s arrival here was certainly not for the sake of battle.
