Whichever king’s daughter she chooses, she shall belong to him; what cause for conflict among the kings is there? Indeed, there will surely be joy.
While those wise kings were speaking thus,
King Bhīṣmaka said nothing at all on account of his son.
Reflecting in his mind upon his son— a great hero, intoxicated with pride, protected by the weapon of Bhārgava, and a fierce *atiratha* in battle— [he was filled with joy].
"My son, ever arrogant in his strength, cannot endure Kṛṣṇa;
he is constantly full of self-conceit and fears no one in battle."
"He will be carried away by the strength of Kṛṣṇa’s arms; there is no doubt in this.
Thereafter, a battle will take place, a confrontation between two great men."
"Full of hatred and full of pride, how can my son live?
I see no life for my son here, because of Keśava."
"For the sake of a maiden, how can I cause my eldest son, who increases the joy of his ancestors, to wage war against Keśava? How can I make him fight with his own son?"
Rukmin did not seek a boon from the god Nārāyaṇa,
nor was a boon granted to Rukmin by the god Nārāyaṇa.
Intoxicated by the pride of delusion and never retreating from battles,
he is surely reduced to ashes like a heap of cotton in a fire.
The heroic Karavīreśvara, who fought with diverse maneuvers like a jackal,
was reduced to ashes in an instant by the mighty Keśava.
While dwelling in Vṛndāvana, the glorious Keśava, the best among the strong,
lifted up the mountain with a single hand and held it for seven days.
Recalling that difficult feat, my mind sinks deeply in distress.
Having suddenly approached the Lord of Nagas together with the gods, the slayer of Vṛtra,
the husband of Śacī, consecrated Kṛṣṇa and addressed him as Upendra.
Just as the serpent Kāliya was subdued in the pool of the Yamunā—
terrible, blazing with the fire of poison, and possessing a splendor like that of Death at the end of time.
And the Dānava Keśin, possessed of great heroism and having the form of a horse,
who was difficult even for the gods to approach, was slain by Vāsudeva.
And the son of Sāndīpani, who had long been lost in the ocean,
was recovered after [Balarāma] slew the Daitya Pañcajana and brought him back from the abode of Yama.
Both of them, possessing great strength, engaged in a massive battle with many [combatants],
causing terror and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
With his elephant he struck down hosts of elephants, with his chariot he struck down chariot-warriors;
with his horse he struck down horsemen, and with his feet he struck down the infantry—
those two sons of Vasudeva, possessed of great heroism, thus assailed their foes.
Neither gods, asuras, nor gandharvas; neither yakṣas, uragas, nor rākṣasas;
neither nāgas nor lords of the daityas; neither piśācas nor guhyakas [could prevail].
Recalling that battle, in which they wrought such terrible destruction of elephants, horses, and chariots, my mind sinks deeply in despondency.
Having made Govardhana his dwelling, he protected the cows along with the men;
yet, overwhelmed by wind and rain, my mind suffers because of that.
Never before have I heard of or seen such a thing anywhere on this earth among mortals as that which has come from Vāsudeva, the best of gods.
"The mighty-armed king Dantavaktra has spoken rightly.
Having conciliated that one of great heroism, we shall provide whatever is appropriate."
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the determination of strengths and weaknesses,
he set his heart on going to propitiate the Infallible One.
While being reflected upon by many powerful kings,
he was awakened by bards, panegyrists, and female heralds with auspicious hymns of praise.
When the night had turned to dawn, all the kings, having performed their morning rites, sat down in their respective chambers of rest.
Those distinguished kings who were among the lords of men in Vidarbha arrived and, having gone into private with their own sovereigns, reported [the matter].
Upon hearing of Kṛṣṇa’s consecration, some kings were emboldened;
some became even more dejected and terrified, while others remained indifferent.
That army, consisting of men, elephants, and horses, was divided into three parts;
agitated like a great ocean, it was set in motion by the consecration.
Observing the dissension among the kings and the inconceivable transgression committed by the king himself, Bhīṣmaka, the best of monarchs, [reflected].
Having reflected thus in his mind, O King, with a burning heart,
he went to the assembly of the lords of men to awaken them.
In the meantime, messengers arrived from the presence of Kaiśika;
taking a letter upon their heads, they entered the ocean that was the king.
[Colophon] Janamejaya said:
Having slain Kaṃsa, who was possessed of great heroism and difficult even for the gods to approach, HV App. I, 20.338.
He was not consecrated in the kingdom, nor did he sit upon the royal throne.
Kṛṣṇa came there for the sake of a maiden, yet he was not treated as a guest;
having encountered such incomparable insult, for what reason did he remain patient?
And the son of Vinatā, possessed of great strength and prowess—he too was endowed with forgiveness; what cause did he have in view? Tell me this, O Blessed One, for my curiosity is great.
Vaiśampāyana said: When the son of Vinatā, together with Acyuta, had arrived at the city of Vidarbha,
the King of Keśin reflected in his mind upon Vāsudeva.
For by seeing this wonder, all of us shall surely experience the destruction of our sins.
I shall proclaim the royal lineage:
when the son of Vasudeva is seen,
our nature becomes purified through the true perception of Kṛṣṇa’s reality.
Therefore, who else in the three worlds exists as a more worthy recipient than Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-eyed Janārdana, the God of gods?
"O King, what shall we two give as hospitality to him who has arrived as a worthy recipient, O monarch, so that our duty is not violated? (HV App. I, 20.351–352)
Having thus deliberated with one another, the two brothers Kratha and Kaiśika,
desiring to give their own kingdom [to Kṛṣṇa], went into the presence of Keśava.
Having approached the God, those two heroes, the lords of the city of Vidarbha,
bowed their heads to Hari and spoke to those two high-souled ones.
Today our birth has become fruitful; today our fame has become fruitful.
Today our ancestors have been satisfied, O God, now that you have come to our home.
The yak-tail whisk, the fan, the parasol, the banner, the lion-throne, and the army;
as well as the city with its abundant treasury, filled with elephants, horses, and chariots.
"O mighty-armed Upendra, you have been consecrated by Devendra;
indeed, O Lord, we two shall now consecrate you here in this kingdom."
The task that has been accomplished by us could not have been performed otherwise even by many kings,
nor by Jarāsaṃdha himself.
Your enemy is the king of Magadha, Jarāsaṃdha, of great splendor;
he who grants fearlessness to kings constantly recounts your story.
Since he does not occupy the lion-throne and his city is no longer found,
why does the son of Devakī not sit here in this assembly of kings?
Kṛṣṇa, who is indeed of great heroism, full of self-confidence, and of great splendor,
will not come to this *svayaṃvara* for the sake of the maiden.
While the kings were seated upon their own thrones,
how could that one of great splendor sit upon low seats?
Thus urged, King Bhīṣmaka, having heard all that Jarāsaṃdha intended to do, related it in the presence of Vāsudeva.
Then he announced this very desire of his.
Having consulted with us together, he desires the cessation of hostilities.
Indeed, this excellent house was built for the sake of your rest;
for you are the primordial god of the gods, honored by all the worlds.
Exercise the sovereignty of a king of kings in this mortal world of men,
so that there may be no overcrowding on the seats within the assembly of the lords of men.
"O great-splendored one, exercise this sovereignty in the city of Vidarbha;
sit upon this auspicious throne tomorrow at dawn."
Having composed myself through rites prescribed by rule,
I shall act according to the command of the god so that the kings will arrive.
Having spoken thus to the best of the gods and prostrating with palms joined in reverence,
he sent those two heroes into the midst of the arena, which was surrounded by kings.
Having written down the words of the divine messenger exactly as spoken by Vajrapāṇi, Kaiśika, possessed of great splendor, did so out of fear arising from the curse.
"O all you kings, it is known to you that Acyuta Hari, accompanied by Vainateya,
arrived at the city of Vidarbha in the guise of a guest."
Perceiving that he had arrived and reflecting, "This man is a worthy recipient," the king,
for the sake of dharma, bestowed his own kingdom upon Vāsudeva.
"O sinless ones, sit upon this seat together with my brother"—
thus spoke a certain bodiless voice moving through the sky.
"O lord of men, it is not proper for you to give a seat while you remain seated;
here is a divine seat for him, adorned with every kind of jewel."
Divine, made of Jāmbūnada gold, and fashioned by Viśvakarman;
it was sent by the King of the Gods, marked with the characteristics of a lion.
"Consecrate the Lord of Gods, who is saluted by all that is moving and unmoving, as the king of kings while he is seated here together with many monarchs."
"O lords of men, you have come to the city of Kuṇḍina for the sake of the maiden;
whoever does not come shall be put to death by him."
And these eight jars, born from portions of the treasures,
are inexhaustible for the high-souled Dhaneśa, the king of kings.
Divine beings, rich in gold and jewels, sources of celestial ornaments,
arrived for the sake of the consecration of the lord of kings, escorted by other monarchs.
"O lords of men, this message from Śakra has been told to you;
having summoned them all by letter, let them consecrate Keśava."
Kaiśika said:
Having thus exhorted him, that messenger of the gods, composed in mind,
departed for heaven after offering a seat to Kṛṣṇa that possessed a radiance like the rising sun.
Therefore, I shall urge you, O assembled ones,
against this terrible [weapon] which, once discharged by Śakra himself, is most difficult to ward off.
It was fitting for you to behold this marvel, so difficult to find on earth:
him being consecrated by water-pots falling of their own accord from the vault of heaven.
"Indeed, by seeing this wonder, the destruction of all our sins will surely occur;
and for the sake of bathing Kṛṣṇa, the God of gods, Viṣṇu."
"Come, O best of kings; you ought not to fear.
Janārdana has made a pact with us for your sake."
Hari grants fearlessness to all the lords of men;
the pure nature of Kṛṣṇa has been seen by us in its true essence.
No enmity toward the King of Magadha is seen in his heart;
you must consider what the cause and purpose here may be.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O king of kings, while they were thus reflecting, all those monarchs, tormented by the fear of the curse, heard [the following] once again.
Filling the sky with a voice as deep-sounding as a thundercloud,
an incorporeal speech spoke by the command of the King of the Gods.
Citrāṅgada said: Śakra, the lord of the three worlds, by reason of protecting his subjects and out of a desire for your welfare, O kings, issues this command to you.
"It is not right for you, O lords of men, to speak thus to one another as enemies with Kṛṣṇa; rather, generate affection and dwell within your own kingdoms."
Kṛṣṇa, who removes the suffering of those who bow before him, is like a fire that destroys opposing armies;
rejoice with him in friendship, free from all distress.
Among men, kings are gods; among kings, the deities are gods;
among the gods, Śakra is the deity; and even for Śakra, Janārdana is the deity.
To him also, that god Śiva is superior; and to Śiva, Janārdana is superior. This Viṣṇu is the Lord, the god who is the deity even of the gods.
This Keśava has been born in the world of men in human form.
He is invincible in all the worlds by gods, dānavas, and humans—
even for the wielder of the trident himself, even when accompanied by Kārttikeya.
Having consecrated that high-souled Keśava, the god beyond all gods, together with the deities, what do you desire further than this?
Furthermore, the gods have no authority over the consecration of the king of kings;
therefore, I do not consecrate him who is honored by all the worlds.
This is the prerogative of kings for the consecration of a lord of kings.
"Having gone to Vidarbha together with the Krathakaishikas,
O best of kings, deliberate and act according to the prescribed rule."
"Thinking, 'This is the time for reconciliation,' Vāsava has been sent by me for the purpose of awakening you, O lords of men."
In the city of Vidarbha, Kṛṣṇa caused the two kings, Kratha and Kaiśika, to hear of her consecration for the purpose of her installation as queen of the lords of kings.
O best of kings, having celebrated a very great festival with those two,
and having honored them with the consecration and accepted their sacrificial fee,
you shall return full of joy to the svayaṃvara once again.
Jarāsaṃdha, Sunītha, and Rukmin the great chariot-warrior,
as well as Śālva, the lord of Saubha— these four best of kings, O monarchs,
shall remain so that the arena is not left empty.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus heard the command of the Lord of the Gods as uttered by Citrāṅgada,
all those best of kings set their minds upon departing.
Permitted by the wise King Jarāsaṃdha,
they set out, surrounded by their own forces, placing Bhiṣmaka at their head.
And the mighty-armed Bhiṣmaka, accompanied by his own forces,
went along with other kings with a burning heart to where the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa was in the residence of Kaiśika.
From afar, the radiant and beautiful assembly hall of the gods, adorned with garlands of flags and banners, has come here for the purpose of bathing.
It was strewn with the radiance of divine jewels, crowded with celestial banners,
enriched with divine garments and flags, and adorned with divine ornaments.
Intertwined with divine garlands and perfumed with celestial fragrances,
she was surrounded on all sides by magnificent celestial chariots.
And hosts of divine apsarases, as well as groups of vidyādharas,
gandharvas, sages, and kinnaras from all sides,
having taken their place within the expanse of the sky, sang praises to the Lord of the Gods.
All the sages, the Siddhas, and the supreme seers offered praise;
and the celestial drums themselves resounded spontaneously in the sky.
Camphor, agallochum, musk, kaṅkola, and sandalwoods—
these numerous aromatic powders produced from five sources.
They were being cast down from all sides by the gods dwelling in the sky.
The lord of kings, the husband of Śacī, having come in person together with the gods and mounted his excellent celestial chariot, stood resplendent in the sky.
And by the eight world-protectors stationed in their respective directions,
who were singing, dancing, and offering praise on all sides.
The eight guardians of the world, stationed in their respective directions,
sing, dance, and offer praise all around him.
Hearing that tumultuous roar, all those lords of men,
their eyes wide with wonder, entered the auspicious assembly hall.
And the mighty Kaiśika, possessed of great splendor, approached the lords of men and, having honored them according to the prescribed rites, caused them to enter.
When it had been announced that the assembly of kings was gathered,
the glorious Hari, the best of gods, honored with every auspicious rite, went forth.
Then those divine jars, situated in the sky and adorned with cloths around their necks,
rained down together with mango blossoms like clouds.
With floods of divine gold and jewels, accompanied by celestial flowers,
and mixed with fragrant powders, [the consecration] of the lord of kings was performed.
Having consecrated Janārdana according to the previously stated rites,
and having initiated the lords of men with divine and auspicious ornaments, [he performed the ceremony].
Having honored the kings according to the prescribed rites with divine garments of various kinds, celestial garlands, and ointments, Janārdana sat down.
When he had arrived here for the sake of bathing in the auspicious and delightful assembly hall of the gods,
he shone forth while being attended by the Yadus and the lords of men.
And the powerful Vainateya, who can assume any form at will, took human shape;
taking his place on the right side, he sat down.
And those two heroes, Kratha and Kaiśika, the high-souled kings, sat upon their own seats on the left side with the permission of the god.
In the same way, on the left side sat the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas,
heroic and mighty men led by Sātyaki.
Seated comfortably upon a divine throne resembling the sun, covered with celestial rugs, he was glorious like the god Śacīpati himself.
Having been previously announced by their ministers, those lords of men entered;
and after all those kings had been honored according to their rank,
the sovereigns sat comfortably upon their respective seats.
But Kaiśika, who was highly wise and the best among those who know the meaning of all scriptures,
honored him according to tradition and spoke, being the foremost of eloquent men.
"O Lord, all these kings, not recognizing you as a mere mortal, have obstructed you; O God, you ought to forgive them."
Kṛṣṇa said: "O Kaiśika, no enmity dwells within me even for a single day;
especially so toward kings who are established in the duty of the Kṣatriya."
"Since it is by dharma that they must fight, and adharma is utterly turned away from them— O lords of the earth, for what reason should anger be directed toward them?"
That which has passed away is gone beyond; those who have died have gone to heaven.
This is the law in this world of men: they are born and they die.
Therefore, O lords of men, there is no cause for grief for you regarding those who have died;
you should forgive us, and let us indeed be free from enmity.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to those lords of men and having comforted them, the slayer of Madhu,
possessed of great splendor, looked toward Kaiśika and fell silent.
At that very time, Bhīṣmaka, skilled in statecraft and the best among speakers, having honored them according to custom, spoke.
[Colophon] Bhīṣmaka said:
"Out of childishness, my son wishes to give away his sister."
Nor do I venture to give her at a svayaṃvara of the lords of men.
Because of my extreme youth, my mind desires to give;
however, my mind will choose one after gazing upon each one individually.
Therefore, I shall propitiate you because of my son’s misconduct;
O Lord of Gods, grant me your favor; O Master, you ought to forgive me.
Kṛṣṇa said:
When the circle of kings was agitated by the boyhood of a son,
what kind of insolence would there be once he had indeed reached maturity?
[He saw] kings in this world who were like the sun and moon, whose splendor was acquired through asceticism,
and who were born of great lineages.
He who, out of delusion, speaks falsely even before a single king shall not remain in this world; he shall be consumed by the fire of punishment.
"O Lord, it is known to you that this is the duty of kings;
having placed worldly custom foremost, it was sung of old by the Self-born One."
O lord of men, O Indra among kings, how can your son, in the presence of those [elders],
utter such falsehood in this assembly of kings?
How is it that such an incomparable arena was constructed by your son without your knowledge? This is a great doubt of mine.
Having arrived, you have honored the lords of men, who possess the splendor of fire, the sun, and the moon,
by performing hospitality according to their merit.
O King, how was it that you did not know of the incomparable carnage of chariots, horses, men, and elephants here, nor of the deeds of your son?
There should be no despondency here upon the arrival of the fourfold army;
"O King, why is it not known?"—this is the doubt in my mind.
"O lord of men, my arrival here was generally not for your benefit; therefore, hospitality was not extended to me, who am unworthy."
"O mighty-armed one, let the maiden be given to the suitors;
setting me aside, why will you not give away the maiden because of the fault of my arrival?"
"One who creates obstacles for a maiden is cooked in hell"—
thus has it been sung by Manu and others, the best of men and knowers of dharma.
For this reason, O lord of the people, I did not enter the midst of the assembly;
having learned, O god among men, that hospitality had not been prepared in your abode.
Overcome by shame, O Indra among kings, I was entreated by you, O lord of men,
in the city of Vidarbha, O King, for the purpose of resting from your fatigue.
Kaiśika, who is so fond of guests, offered hospitality to us both;
we dwelt there as Garuḍa and Keśava once did long ago in heaven.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To Kṛṣṇa, who was speaking in this manner and was impelled by the thunderbolt of his speech, [he replied].
The best of speakers addressed Keśava, the slayer of Kaṃsa,
sprinkling him with the water of his gentle words like one who has extinguished the sacrificial fire at a ritual.
Bhīṣmaka said:
Be gracious, O Lord of the world of the gods; O Lord of the world of mortals, protect me!
You who possess the eye of knowledge, become the bestower of that eye upon me, who am enveloped by the darkness of ignorance.
Because we possess only the fleshly eye of humanity, we have not understood correctly;
thus, our undertakings do not succeed when performed without careful deliberation.
Having come for refuge to you, the deity even of the gods,
may my vision become perfect and may my ritual actions be successfully accomplished.
For the wise, even an action that is not yet completed, if it is endowed with proper method,
bring forth fruit, just like a great general.
Having obtained you as my refuge, fear no longer oppresses me greatly;
you ought to hear that task which has been contemplated by me.
"I do not wish to give my daughter to the kings in a *svayaṃvara*.
O Lord of Gods, show me favor; you ought not to be angry."
For this was indeed told previously by Nārada, O Govinda:
"This young girl is your younger sister; she is Śrī herself, come down in an incarnation."
Having attained birth for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, she was born once again by her own will.
In former times, she was indeed Janakī, brought down for the sake of Rāma;
now she has been born again on the surface of the earth by the name of Rukmiṇī.
"Afflicted by affection for his son, this wretched man has killed him; O Lord of Gods, you whose prowess remains unvanquished in battle, you ought to forgive him."
O Janārdana, that which is destined must indeed come to pass;
the word of the Veda, as spoken by Nārada, a twice-born man would never speak falsely.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O King of great intelligence, what is the use of speaking further words?
Will you not give your daughter to the sky? O sinless one, who here is to prevent you?"
"Do not say 'do not give' nor 'give,' for such words are not mine;
because of Rukmiṇī’s divine form, she is a worthy cause for this alliance."
Long ago, on Mount Meru, the gods performed the descent of their portions; at that time, she was first released with these words: "Go now, together with your husband."
"O lady of broad hips, may you be born in the human world in the city of Kuṇḍina from the womb of Bhīṣmaka's wife; look favorably upon Keśava."
Therefore, O King, I shall speak to you words that are not fabricated;
having heard them and deliberated for yourself, you shall do what is appropriate.
That maiden named Rukmiṇī is not an ordinary human being;
she is Śrī herself, born for some specific purpose according to the word of Brahmā.
Nor was she fit for the ritual of a *svayaṃvara* among the lords of men;
for the established law is that a single woman must be given to a single man.
And you are not able, O King, to bestow that fortune [of your daughter] at a *svayaṃvara*;
rather, having looked for a suitable groom, you ought to give her away in accordance with the Dharma.
For this reason, this son of Vinatā has come to the city of Kuṇḍina, urged by the King of the Gods for the purpose of creating an obstacle.
"And I myself have come, desiring to see the great festival of the kings,
and that maiden of beautiful limbs, who is like the goddess Śrī bereft of her lotus."
"O King, that which was spoken by you out of a desire for me— that 'it must be forgiven'—
I consider it to have been previously appropriate, O Ruler of the Earth, and not for the sake of impurity."
"I have already forgiven you, which is why I remain within your domain."
He arrived in a gentle form, and for that reason, O Lord, you were patient with him.
In those who practice forbearance, there is an abundance of virtues and the removal of faults;
O King, how could such impurity dwell in the heart of one like me?
O King, how can such defilement dwell in the heart of one like you— one born of noble lineage, endowed with goodness, a knower of dharma, and a speaker of truth?
Protect the city properly; if anyone should behave with impurity,
you must consider yourself as having been patient toward him, even though you have come with an army.
Nor will I go against the enemy's host accompanied by an army.
Unable to endure the enemy host, I shall go mounted upon my bird-vehicle,
standing firm and bearing weapons as radiant as the sun in my hands.
O King, you are worthy of our respect; in age, you are equal to our father. Protect the city properly and dwell among your sons like a father.
O Indra among kings, it is said that impurity dwells among base men;
how could impurity dwell among heroes who are pure in nature?
"Know this to be my way of life toward my sons, for he is indeed like a father to them;
likewise, the two kings who rule over the city of Vidarbha are fathers to us both."
In performing hospitality, those two auspicious ones gave their own kingdom to us;
by the fruit of that gift, ten ancestors of theirs have gone to heaven.
O Indra among kings, your future sons and grandsons, numbering at least ten,
those lords of men shall likewise go from that very place to the world of the gods.
Having enjoyed the kingdom free from all thorns for a very long time,
when their desire for enjoyment has ceased, they will attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
And the highly fortunate lords of men who had come to consecrate him.
In due time, they too shall go to the celestial world, Triviṣṭapa.
May it be well with you; I shall depart, accompanied by Vainateya, to the beautiful city of Mathurā, which is protected by the King of the Bhojas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus spoken to King Bhīṣmaka,
that bull among the Yadus took leave of the kings, and especially of the two princesses of Vidarbha.
Having emerged from the assembly hall, the Lord of Gods went near his chariot.
Then, having seen Keśava, that royal sage Bhīṣmaka was indeed [delighted],
while all those lords of the earth became dejected of countenance.
The primordial form of Svayambhū, saluted by gods and asuras,
possessed a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, and a body with a thousand arms.
The god with a thousand heads, blazing with a thousand crowns,
wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes.
Adorned with divine ornaments and brandishing many divine weapons,
Kṛṣṇa has eyes like red lotuses and eyes that are the moon, the sun, and fire.
Having seen him with the Kaustubha gem adorning his neck and decorated with a forest garland, that king of kings, bowing down with palms joined in reverence, [spoke]. (HV App. I, 20.628–630)
Then, joined by speech, mind, and body, he began to offer praise.
Bhīṣmaka said:
"O God of gods, salutations to you, who are indeed without beginning or end;
to the eternal primordial deity, O Nārāyaṇa, the supreme refuge!"
To the self-existent, to the universal, to the immovable pillar, and to the ordainer;
to the lotus-navelled one, to the one with matted hair, to the staff-bearer, and to the tawny-hued one.
Salutation indeed to Haṃsa-prabha, to Haṃsa who possesses the form of the swan;
salutation to that Vaikuṇṭha, the unborn Supreme Self.
Salutations be to you, the Ancient Person, who is endowed with both existence and non-existence; salutations to Puruṣottama, who is disciplined and devoid of qualities.
O best of gods, be forever a granter of boons to me, your devotee;
you are the Lord of the worlds, you are the Protector, and you are Viṣṇu for those who have realized the Self.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus praised Mahādeva in the presence of the kings, O King,
[the monarch] [offered a garland] shining with precious gems and pearls, and gleaming with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
The king presented a heap of gold to Kṛṣṇa,
and again he paid homage to the mighty Vainateya.
Bhīṣmaka said:
Salutations to that Lord of Birds, who possesses the speed of mind and wind;
salutations indeed to the divine son of Kaśyapa, who can assume any form at will.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus praised him in brief and honored him with excellent ornaments,
he then bid farewell to the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa.
And the kings followed as the younger brother of Vāsava set forth.
Having accepted the hospitality and taken leave of the kings,
the heroic Kṛṣṇa departed for Mathurā, illuminating the ten directions,
preceded by Vainateya, the best of birds, who appeared in a gentle form.
Surrounded on all sides by a great multitude of chariots,
with the sounding of kettledrums and tabors, and the blasts of conchs and dundubhi drums;
With the trumpeting of elephants, the neighing of horses,
the lion-roars of heroes, and the sound of chariot rims;
A tumultuous and very great noise arose, resembling the roar of massive clouds,
when the highly heroic Kṛṣṇa had departed, taking with him the supreme seat.
Taking the assembly with them, the gods departed for the abode of the thirty-three.
Surrounded by a great fourfold army,
and having followed Janārdana for the distance of one *krośa*, all those kings took their leave and departed once again toward the *svayaṃvara*.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, when the son of Vasudeva had set out...
The lords of men, their limbs adorned with ornaments and resembling the lords of the gods, went to one another,
eager to go for the sake of awakening.
Having observed those who were of equal status, radiant as the moon and silver, seated comfortably upon beautiful thrones, the king, who spoke words of righteous policy, [addressed them].
The lion among kings spoke these words.
"O lords of men, the fault committed during the *svayaṃvara* is known to you;
let this ripening of the fruit of my misconduct as an old man be forgiven."
Having addressed them all in this manner and honored them according to the prescribed rites,
he then dismissed those kings born in the Middle Country,
as well as those from the East and West, and even those from the Northern Region.
All those kings, great archers with joyful minds,
having honored that bull among men as was fitting, departed.
Jarāsaṃdha, Sunītha, and the heroic Dantavakra;
Sālva, the lord of Saubha, and King Mahākūrma.
And the kings who were the leaders of the Krathakaishikas, born of a preeminent lineage,
as well as the royal seer Venu-dari and the sovereign of Kashmir.
These and many other kings from the southern region,
desiring to hear his words in private, stood indeed near Bhīṣmaka.
Having observed those lords of the earth standing there with hearts full of affection, that king Bhīṣmaka, the lord of the people and a powerful ruler, spoke to them.
He spoke with a voice that was smooth, affectionate, and deep, words endowed with policy, auspicious, consistent with the three aims of life, and adorned with the six political measures.
Having observed the speech uttered by you, the lords of the earth, which was full of wisdom,
and having heard it, I have accomplished such a task as this;
you virtuous ones must forgive us, for we are constantly at fault.
Having spoken thus, King Bhīṣmaka, who was skilled in statecraft,
addressed these words regarding his son in the assembly of kings,
his eyes agitated with fear upon beholding his son’s conduct.
I consider these worlds to be fools; he is that very Lord, the Puruṣa. He is the preeminent among the famous, the glory of the glorious, the powerful one who shares in fame.
Upon this mortal earth, he has established the might of his own arms.
Blessed indeed is the highly fortunate Devakī, the best among women,
who has borne Keśava, the most excellent in the three worlds, within her womb.
He gazed with eyes full of affection at Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were like lotus petals, who was a mass of splendor, and who was worshipped by the immortals,
as he looked upon his own lotus-face.
To the king who was thus lamenting in the royal assembly,
the highly effulgent King of Śālva spoke with gentle words.
Enough with this grief, O Indra among kings, for the sake of your son, the crusher of enemies;
O King, victory and defeat in battle are certain for a Kṣatriya.
The destiny of mortals is fixed; this is the eternal law.
Who else here besides Bala and Keśava could be a third man?
He alone among the hosts of chariot-warriors and great car-fighters is capable of fighting your mighty son in battle on the field of war;
that long-armed one, grasping his bow, is able to repel the enemy.
Who among men will be able to withstand the most terrible Bhārgava weapon, difficult even for the gods to approach, when it is released through the power of his arms?
But this person Kṛṣṇa is indeed without beginning or end, and immutable;
even the wielder of the trident himself could not conquer him in this world.
Your son, O man of great wisdom, who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures,
having recognized the Lord Īśāna, does not fight Keśava.
There is a king, the lord of the Yavanas, who is his conqueror in battle;
that Kālayavana, O Namuci, is indeed incapable of being slain by Keśava.
Having performed most terrible and formidable asceticism that was exceedingly difficult to practice,
Ayośana propitiated Rudra for twelve years.
Twelve years ago, that sage was propitiated by him;
desiring a son, the sage pleased Rudra and chose a son from him.
"And so that he might be unslayable by the people of Mathurā," Rudra likewise granted the son to the sage, saying to Śaṅkara, "So be it."
Thus the illustrious Bhava, the son of Garga and born from a portion of Rudra,
was incapable of being slain by the people of Mathurā, especially within the city of Mathurā itself.
"This Kṛṣṇa is indeed powerful, and he was born in Mathurā;
having encountered him in battle at Mathurā, he will defeat Kṛṣṇa."
"If you consider the words spoken by me to be appropriate, O kings,
then dispatch a messenger there toward the city of the Yavana lord."
Having heard the words of the lord of Saubha, all those best of kings, filled with joy, said to the mighty king of Śālva, "We shall do so."
Having heard their words, O King, Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of the earth,
became despondent as he recalled the words of Brahmā.
Jarāsaṃdha said:
"Relying upon me in this world, kings who have been afflicted by the fear of other monarchs shall regain their lost kingdoms, along with their servants, armies, and vehicles."
In this world, I am not spoken of by kings as one who has taken refuge with another for the sake of a cause,
like a maiden devoted to pleasure who, out of hatred for her husband, seeks another.
"Ah! Fate is exceedingly powerful and impossible to turn back, since for the sake of Kṛṣṇa I must take refuge with one who possesses superior strength."
"Surely I am bereft of yoga; I shall seek refuge with another.
O kings, death is indeed better for me than to take refuge with another."
Whether it be Kṛṣṇa, or Baladeva, or whatever other man he may be,
I shall slay him and strike him down, as I am impelled by Brahmā.
This is my firm resolve; this is the vow of a noble man.
For this reason, I am unable to act otherwise by relying on another.
He causes no affliction to you who are of virtuous conduct;
therefore, I shall indeed grant him as a messenger for the protection of kings.
"You must travel by way of the sky so that Kṛṣṇa does not obstruct you. O best of kings, dispatch him while reflecting thus as he departs.
This glorious lord of Saubha possesses the prowess of fire, the sun, and the moon."
Let the powerful one proceed to that city in a chariot with the color of the sun.
Just as the Yavana king approaches the assembly of kings,
and just as he spoke these words to us in our mission as envoys in the conflict with Kṛṣṇa.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Once again the king spoke to the powerful lord of Saubha:
"Go, O giver of honor, and provide assistance to all the lords of men."
Let such a policy be ordained so that the Yavana king approaches us, so that he shall be defeated by Kṛṣṇa,
and so that we ourselves may be satisfied.
Having thus instructed them all and honored Bhīṣmaka according to dharma,
the king, surrounded by his own army, departed for his own city.
The powerful Sālva, the best of kings, having honored them,
departed by way of the sky in his chariot that moved with the speed of the wind.
All those rulers of the earth dwelling in the southern region,
having followed Jarāsaṃdha, indeed returned to their own cities.
Having reflected upon that wicked deed, Bhīṣmaka and his son,
both dejected, entered their home while thinking only of Kṛṣṇa.
The virtuous Rukmiṇī understood the reasons for the withdrawal from the *svayaṃvara* and the arrival of Kṛṣṇa, as well as the perception of faults in the other kings.
Having gone into the midst of her friends, she spoke with a bashful face:
"I do not wish to become the wife of any other kings;
this word of mine is true regarding Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals."
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, that Kālayavana was a ruler of the Yavanas, formidable in his military strength.
She became the protector of the city-dwellers according to the duty of a queen.
One whose wisdom is known through the three goals of life, who subsists upon the six political measures,
who is not deluded by the seven vices, and who is always devoted to virtuous qualities.
One who is learned in the scriptures, virtuous in character, truthful, and has conquered his senses;
one who knows the rules of warfare and the methods for seizing and pursuing fortresses;
one who is brave, possesses peerless strength, and serves the most eminent ministers.
Seated comfortably in a delightful assembly hall, he was surrounded by his ministers.
He was being worshipped by wise Yavanas who were knowers of the Self,
as they recounted various divine stories among themselves.
At that very time, however, a wind carrying divine fragrances blew forth,
pleasantly cool and awakening his passion.
"Why is it that all those who were gathered in the assembly, as well as the king himself, look on with their eyes wide open?"— thus [he asked] the mindless one.
He beheld a divine chariot approaching, resembling the sun,
adorned with divine parts made of gold.
Strewn with the luster of divine jewels and adorned with celestial banners and flags,
it was carried by divine horses possessing the speed of thought and the wind;
having fashioned auspicious orbs of Jāmbūnada gold into the forms of the sun and the moon.
It was indeed fashioned by the Creator of the Universe and adorned with a choice tiger-skin covering.
Causing terror to enemies and increasing the joy of friends,
that chariot— which crushes the chariots of foes— came from the southern direction.
Seeing the illustrious lord of Saubha, the conqueror of thighs, seated there,
he was exceedingly delighted and repeatedly offered him water for the feet and the guest-offering.
The lord of the Yavanas, the best among eloquent speakers, spoke;
then the mighty-armed one rose there from his royal throne himself,
and having offered the guest-offering (*argha*), he stood ready as [the king] descended from the chariot.
Sālva too, possessed of great majesty, seeing the king arrive—
whose splendor was equal to that of Śakra— was filled with supreme joy.
Having descended from his excellent chariot alone and with full confidence,
he entered, supremely delighted and longing for the sight of his friend.
Seeing that the guest-offering had been extended by the king, Sālva, the best of kings, spoke in gentle words: "O one of great splendor, I am not worthy of such an offering."
"I am a messenger from the presence of the lords of men,
sent to you along with many others by the wise Jarāsaṃdha.
Therefore, O Great King, I consider that you are not worthy [of this]."
Thus [it was said] among kings.
Kālayavana said:
"O mighty-armed one, I know that you have come here on a mission as an envoy,
sent indeed by the King of Magadha to this assembly of lords of men."
Therefore, O King, O high-minded one, I shall honor you especially with the rites of guest-hospitality,
such as the offering of water for the feet and the respectful seat, according to the prescribed rule.
When you are honored by kings, it is as if all have been honored;
O Indra among kings, when you are respected, it is as if all have been respected.
"O lord of men, please sit upon this divine seat together with me."
Having embraced each other by the hand and inquired after one another's welfare,
the two kings sat together comfortably upon a beautiful throne.
Kālayavana said:
Relying upon the strength of our arms, we all, as lords of men,
dwell free from anxiety, just as the gods dwell under the lord of Śacī.
"What might be impossible for him, that he has sent you to me?
Speak the truth; what does that lord command?
I shall carry out his word, even if the task be exceedingly difficult."
Śālva said:
"O Indra among kings, O lord of the Yavanas, listen as I shall explain exactly what the sovereign of Magadha has told you."
Jarāsaṃdha said:
"I was born as an oppressor of the worlds, and Kṛṣṇa is supremely difficult to conquer;
having learned of his wicked conduct, I am prepared to slay him."
Together with many sons of Pṛthu and their complete forces and vehicles,
the great army besieged Gomanta, the best of mountains.
Having heard the highly significant words of the King of Cedi,
I employed the fire for the destruction of the two foot-soldiers.
Seeing that [mountain] rich with hundreds of thousands of flames and possessing a radiance like the fire at the end of an eon,
Rāma, bearing a golden palm tree, leaped from the mountain peak.
Having emerged from the midst of that great army, which resembled the ocean,
the invincible one struck down men, horses, chariots, and elephants.
Dragging his plow again and again like the king of serpents gliding along,
he crushed the multitudes of men, elephants, and horses with his mace.
An elephant having struck down an elephant, a chariot-warrior by a chariot,
a horseman by a horse, and a foot-soldier by a foot-soldier.
In that battle crowded with hundreds of kings like suns, he of great splendor moved through various paths, like the sun in the summer heat.
Immediately after Rāma, Kṛṣṇa— the best among those who wield the discus— seized the discus, which possessed a radiance equal to the sun, just as a lion seizes a small deer.
And that one of great splendor [took] the discus and the iron mace Kālī.
The wielder of the discus, Cakrin, possessed of the Sudarśana; and the elder brother of Gada,
the great hero of immense prowess, having shaken that mountain with the force of his feet,
the majestic hero of the Yadu clan fell high upon the enemy host.
Being sprinkled by the streams of water, that mountain seemed to dance;
whirling about, it entered the earth after extinguishing the fire.
Leaping down from the blazing peak,
O King, Janārdana struck the army with his hand, which was gripped by the discus.
Having hurled his vast discus immediately after the strike of his mace,
he pulverized the multitudes of men, elephants, and horses with his club.
The great army, already scorched by the sun-like king, was utterly consumed by the fire of the discus and the plow, which had arisen from the fire of his wrath.
The chariot division, thick with men, serpents, and horses, and crowded with foot soldiers and banners,
was in an instant thinned out by the two foot soldiers.
Seeing the army broken and afflicted by the fear of the fire of the discus,
I surrounded it on all sides with a great multitude of chariots;
there I fought, while his powerful and mighty brother [stood by].
The heroic Halāyudha stands before me, mace in hand.
Having destroyed twelve akṣauhiṇīs like a lion with its mane disheveled,
he raised his Saunanda plow and struck me with a mace.
Having brought down with great force a blow resembling a thunderbolt upon me,
he stood upon the earth in the month of Vaiśākha, desiring to strike me once more.
Occupying the Vaiśākha stance, as Guha formerly did against Krauñca,
he gazes at me with his long eyes as if consuming me.
Having beheld Baladeva in such a form upon the field of battle,
what man in this world who desires life would dare to stand?
Having seen that terrifying great mace, raised like the staff of Death and brandished by Kālāṅkuśa, standing right before me, [he said: HV_App.I,20.864–865.
Then, filling the sky with a voice as deep as a rain-cloud, the Grandfather of the Worlds himself spoke with an incorporeal voice:
"This king must not be struck; he is not to be slain by you, O sinless one."
His slaughter has been ordained by another; desist, O Halāyudha!
Having heard those words spoken by him, I was overcome with anxiety and turned back;
for that terrible speech, which would take away the lives of all beings, had been uttered by Brahmā himself.
Therefore, out of a desire for the welfare of kings, I shall declare it to you;
having heard it, O Indra among kings, you yourself ought to act according to my words.
Having propitiated Śaṅkara with great and fierce austerity for the sake of a son,
he obtained from the God of gods you, who are unslayable by the people of Mathurā.
And the Great Sage, consuming iron filings,
undertook a twelve-year vow,
he whose lotus-feet were praised by gods and asuras.
Having obtained the fulfillment of his desired wishes.
By the power of the asceticism of the great-souled sage Gārgya,
and by the influence of the boon granted by the moon-crested Lord Śiva,
Janārdana encountered the snow in battle.
It dissolves just as [ice] does by the rays of the sun.
Urged by the words of the kings, prepare yourself; set out on an expedition for victory against Keśava. Having entered the kingdom of Mathurā, bring it under your control.
Having slain Kṛṣṇa, indeed spread your fame!
"This Vāsudeva is from Mathurā, and Baladeva is his kinsman;
you will conquer them in battle once you have gone to that city of Mathurā."
Śālva said:
Thus has this speech, sung by the sun among kings, been told to you— this which is for the welfare of monarchs.
Having deliberated upon all that with your ministers through your intellect,
O lord of men, do what is fitting for yourself and desired by you.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
While the king of the Sālvas was speaking thus, by the command of the monarch...
The king, the lord of the Yavanas, spoke, being exceedingly pleased.
I am blessed, I am favored, and my life has become fruitful,
since I have been appointed by many kings for the purpose of subduing Kṛṣṇa.
He is difficult to conquer even by the hosts of gods and asuras in the three worlds;
therefore, regarding me as the means for his subjugation, bestow upon me the blessing of victory.
When those lions among kings, being greatly delighted, perceive victory as mine,
my triumph will come through the rain of their words.
"O best of kings, I shall carry out the words urged by them;
O Indra among kings, even defeat is equal to victory for me."
"O King, this very day the lunar date, the asterism, the hour, and the astrological configuration are auspicious;
I shall go to Mathurā to conquer Keśava in battle."
Having thus addressed the king, the lord of Saubha,
who was victorious in battle, he honored him according to custom with highly precious and excellent ornaments.
The king set his mind upon bestowing gifts upon the Brahmins for the sake of the prophecy of success;
O Indra among kings, he gave abundant wealth to his domestic priest.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules and performed the auspicious rites for his departure,
the king set out properly, desiring to conquer Janārdana.
O best of the Bharatas, King Śālva also, having achieved his purpose and with a joyful mind,
embraced the lord of the Yavanas and departed for his own city.
[Colophon] Janamejaya said:
When he whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra had gone to the city of Vidarbha...
For what purpose was Garuḍa led away, and what deed did he perform?
And the Blessed One did not mount the mighty Vainateya;
O Brahmin, O great sage, explain the truth to me regarding this doubt of mine.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen, O King, to the superhuman deed performed by Suparṇa;
when the immensely radiant son of Vinatā had gone to the city of Vidarbha.
And when Madhusūdana had not yet reached the city of Mathurā,
the high-minded Vainateya reflected thus in his mind:
O Lord, that which was spoken by the God of gods in the presence of the kings:
"I shall go to the beautiful Mathurā, protected by the King of the Bhojas."
At the conclusion of those words, reflecting that he was about to depart,
the illustrious one, with palms joined in reverence, prostrated himself and spoke this:
"O King, I shall go to the city of Kuśasthalī belonging to Raivata;
to the delightful Mount Raivata and the forest resembling the Nandana grove—
delightful, inhabited by Rākṣasas, and situated on the shore of the ocean."
It was overgrown with trees, shrubs, and creepers, and adorned with the pollen of flowers.
It was crowded with lordly elephants and serpents, frequented by bears and monkeys,
trodden upon by boars and buffaloes, and filled with numerous herds of deer.
Having surveyed it on all sides, if it should be found suitable for habitation and capable of accommodating you,
and if this city should be pleasing and praiseworthy to you,
I shall remove the thorns [of opposition] and then come into your presence.
Having thus informed the Lord of the Gods and having prostrated before Janārdana,
the powerful lord of birds indeed departed facing the west;
Kṛṣṇa, too, entered the city of Mathurā together with the Yadus.
Ugrasena and all the citizens,
with great enthusiasm, went out in a throng of people to meet the arriving Kṛṣṇa and paid him their respects.
Janamejaya said:
Having heard that the lord of the earth, Ugrasena, the mighty-armed king of kings, had been consecrated by many rulers of the land, what did he do?
And by that very report,
Ugrasena and all the citizens were informed.
{Vaiśampāyana said:}
Having heard that the lord of kings had been consecrated by many rulers of the earth,
and that Citrāṅgada had been made his envoy to establish an alliance with Indra;
Each individual portion of the king was measured at one hundred thousand;
each circle of kings was likewise measured at one hundred thousand.
An arbuda was given to the lords of kings, and ten were indeed given to human beings.
Having honored the lord of men with the arghya offering,
those lords of men who had arrived there departed for their own homes.
Śaṅkha, in the form of a Yādava, bestowed that which was desired by Hari.
Thus did the glorious Lord of Treasures, cheered by the gods,
hear from the people nearby regarding the events of the world.
He indeed performed great worship in the temples of the gods,
and in the palace of Vasudeva on both sides of the archway.
He caused actors' dances, songs, and instrumental music to be performed on all sides,
and had the area everywhere adorned with garlands of flags and banners.
[He entered] the assembly hall of King Kaṃsa, which was radiant with variegated garments.
The King of the Bhojas caused various kinds of banners to be presented.
O Indra among kings, he caused to be constructed an archway and a gateway, plastered with a paste of lime, as a dwelling for the throne of that Indra among kings.
On all sides were the dances, songs, and instrumental music of actors;
here and there were full water-jars adorned with banners and garlands of forest flowers.
O Indra among kings, on the royal highways sprinkled with sandalwood water,
the king had carpets of cloth spread upon the ground.
Beside them stood incense burners filled with sandalwood, agallochum,
and guggulu, as well as molasses and resin, all burning on every side.
And groups of elderly women, singing auspicious hymns of praise,
waited in their respective places after having adorned themselves.
Having thus brought joy to the city, King Ugrasena went to the house of Vasudeva and, having delivered the pleasant news,
consulted with Rāma and departed for his chariot.
In that very interval, O King, there arose a great sound of conch shells.
Hearing the roar of the Pāñcajanya, the inhabitants of Mathurā— the women, the elderly, and the children, as well as the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards— [were struck with wonder].
O King, placing Rāma at their head, those great armies marched forth;
Ugrasena, the lord of the earth, preceded them, offering the guest-water and water for the feet.
Having come upon the path of vision, King Ugrasena descended from his bright chariot and proceeded ahead on foot along the footpath.
He saw him seated upon a divine chariot, adorned with celestial jewels.
He wore ornaments upon his limbs endowed with the luster of divine jewels,
and a celestial forest-garland upon his chest, shining like the scorching sun.
She was attended by yak-tail fans, a parasol, and the raised banner of the king of birds;
endowed with the marks of royalty, she was as radiant as the sun near its zenith.
Seeing Hari, the Lord of gods, overwhelmed by splendor and exceedingly difficult to behold,
that king, O Indra among kings, addressed the lotus-eyed Rāma, the slayer of Bala, with a voice faltering with joy.
"O illustrious one, having reflected that it was never before fitting for me to go by chariot, I have descended; you, however, may proceed by means of the chariot."
Having gone to this city of Mathurā in a disguised form,
Viṣṇu revealed his true self here in the ocean of kings as the lordship of the gods;
him, Keśava, I desire to praise with my whole being.
The highly effulgent elder brother of Kṛṣṇa replied to the king:
"O King, it is not fitting to praise the best of gods as he departs.
O King, Janārdana is satisfied with you even without praise."
What need have you for praises when you are already satisfied? Your very sight is praise unto me.
"Having attained the status of a lord of kings, he has come to your residence;
why then have you praised that king with divine and superhuman hymns?
As they were speaking thus, the two of them arrived in the presence of Keśava.
Seeing his arm raised to offer the guest-water (arghya), and having halted his excellent chariot,
the best of speakers addressed King Ugrasena.
"O Lord of Mathurā, it is not right for me myself to act otherwise than that I have consecrated you, saying: 'May you become the Lord of Mathurā.'"
"O King, you ought not to offer us the guest-water, the water for sipping, the water for washing the feet, and this food; this is what my heart desires."
"Having understood your intention, O King, I speak these words:
you alone are King Māthura; you ought not to act otherwise."
"O King, I shall grant you a place and a share on your right side;
just as it has been established for all other kings, so shall it be placed before you."
A hundred-thousandth part [of that merit] remains, excluding the garments and ornaments.
Ascend the bright chariot adorned with gold,
O lord of men, along with the yak-tail fans, the parasol, and the banner;
and [take] the crown endowed with divine ornaments, radiant as the sun.
"O highly fortunate one, uphold [this] and protect this city!
Surrounded by your sons and grandsons, govern Mathurā."
Having conquered the hosts of enemy forces, cause the lineage of the Bhojas to flourish.
To the infinite Śrī, the god of gods and others, the divine ornaments and celestial garment were sent by Vajrapāṇi, the king of the gods.
All the Māthuras received ten dīnāras each as their share;
for each of the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards, there was one thousand;
and for the groups of elderly women and the courtesans, there were one hundred each.
Those led by Vikadru who remained with the king—
the Creator ordained a share for them amounting to ten thousand.
The Creator ordained that they should receive a share consisting of ten thousand portions.
Having thus honored the king at the head of the Mathuran army,
Madhusūdana brought great joy to Mathurā.
Shining on all sides with divine ornaments, garlands, and excellent celestial unguents, he was like the gods in the third heaven.
With the sound of kettledrums and tabors, the resonances of conchs and dundubhi drums,
and with the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses.
With the lion-roars of the heroes and the sound of chariot rims,
there arose a tumultuous and immense noise, resembling the roar of clouds.
And even as he was being praised by bards, the subjects bowed down to him;
yet Hari, though Ananta (the Infinite), felt no astonishment after giving the gift.
Because his nature was inherently exalted, because he had previously seen [the gods],
and because he was free from the sense of "I," he did not experience any astonishment at that which surpassed it.
Seeing him approaching, blazing with his own body and possessing the radiance of the sun,
the inhabitants of Mathurā paid homage at every step.
This glorious Nārāyaṇa, whose abode is the Ocean of Milk,
has risen from his serpent-couch and gone to the city of Mathurā.
Having bound the immensely powerful Bali, who was invincible even to the thirty gods,
he bestowed the sovereignty of the three worlds upon Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Having slain all the hosts of Daityas and Kaṃsa, the foremost among the strong,
the slayer of Keśin gave Mathurā back to the King of the Bhojas.
Neither having been consecrated himself in the kingdom nor having sat upon the royal throne,
he then entered Mathurā, desiring indeed the status of a lord of kings.
Having thus heard the mutual conversation of the city-dwellers,
the crowds spoke these words to the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, and bards:
Or rather, O ocean of virtues, what shall we be able to say with this single tongue of ours regarding the qualities arising from your power and energy?
At some time, the lord of serpents Vāsuki, possessing a thousand enjoyments and endowed with divine intelligence,
will extend himself with two thousand tongues.
But this is a marvel in the world among the lords of men upon the earth:
that no one other than Śakra has ever attained, nor will ever attain, his seat.
That he himself arrived at the entrance of the assembly hall with water-jars—neither has such a thing been heard nor seen; therefore, we consider it a marvel.
Blessed is the illustrious Queen Devakī, the best among women,
who has borne you, O Keśava, foremost of the thirty gods, within her womb.
[With eyes like lotus petals, a mass of splendor, and worshipped by the immortals, Kṛṣṇa gazes with eyes full of affection at his own lotus-like face.]
Hearing these various utterances of those who were thus conversing,
the two brothers Rāma and Keśava placed Ugrasena at their head.
Having arrived at the city gate, she then paid her respects;
having offered water for the hands, water for sipping, and water for the feet, she said, "Water for the feet! (pādya).
Then the wise and heroic Ugrasena, having bowed his head to Kṛṣṇa at the front of Keśava’s chariot, ascended the chariot.
With thick torrents of water, he rained down hailstones;
raining down floods of wealth, they arrived at the father’s house.
The illustrious lord of Mathurā spoke to Madhusūdana:
"O Lord, having attained the status of a king of kings, it is not fitting for you to remain in your father's house;
this lion-throne has been established and given by the King of the Gods."
"I shall lead [him] to the assembly of the Lord of Mathurā, which was acquired by the strength of my arms.
O Blessed One, I shall propitiate him; you ought not to be angry."
O lord of the people, Devakī, Vasudeva, and Rohiṇī were not capable of doing anything, being utterly bewildered by joy and exhaustion.
Then, O King, Kaṃsa’s mother, taking the guest-offering (*argha*)—
wealth acquired by Kaṃsa from various regions and countries—
and having considered the place and time, presented it at the pair of Keśava’s feet.
Having summoned Ugrasena, he spoke with gentle words:
[Kṛṣṇa said:
"I do not desire Mathurā, nor have I come out of a desire for wealth."
Those two sons of yours have been slain; they have met their end through the power of Time.
Perform various sacrifices, bestow abundant wealth,
and conquer the enemy armies by relying on the strength of my arms.
Abandon the distress of your mind and the fear arising from the destruction of Kaṃsa;
take back the collection of wealth that was given by me to you once again.
Having thus consoled the king, the illustrious Kṛṣṇa,
together with Balarāma, then entered the inner apartments of his mother and father.
With their hearts full of joy, the two mighty ones,
bowing low, paid homage at the feet of their father and mother.
At that moment, the city of Mathurā became like Amarāvatī descended from the heavenly realm;
having beheld the palace of Vasudeva, the city-dwellers [were filled with wonder].
They reflected in their minds upon the world of the gods, not the surface of the earth.
Then, having bid farewell to the Lord of Mathurā together with his queen,
Balarāma and Keśava entered the palace of Vasudeva.
Having laid down their weapons, both heroes remained there, moving at their own will;
then, having performed their daily rites, they sat comfortably in the course of conversation.
At that very time, however, a great portent occurred:
the clouds wandered in the sky, and the earth and mountains shook.
All the oceans were agitated, and the foremost of the serpent-king Bhoga was bewildered;
all the Yādavas trembled and fell prostrate upon the earth.
Seeing them fallen and observing that Rāma and Kṛṣṇa remained motionless, [the people were struck with wonder].
The best of birds was recognized by the great wind from his wings.
Having arrived, adorned with divine garlands and unguents, he beheld them;
bowing his head to the two of them, he of gentle appearance took his seat.
Seeing that minister of the hereafter had arrived,
Madhusūdana spoke to the steadfast Garuḍa.
Welcome, O best of sky-travelers, crusher of the enemy of the divine armies!
Welcome, O delighter of Vinatā’s heart, beloved of Keśava!
Then Kṛṣṇa spoke to the son of Vinatā, who was seated like another embodied being,
with words of equal power.
"O best of birds, we shall go to the great inner apartments of Bhoja. Having gone there and being comfortably seated, we shall deliberate upon what is in our minds."
Having entered, those two of great heroism, Baladeva and Janārdana,
together with Vainateya as the third, deliberated upon a secret counsel.
"He has been made invincible by us, and the enemy's force is exceedingly great;
furthermore, a vast destruction of our army has been wrought," so it was said by the lords of men.
"Even in hundreds of years, we shall not be able to destroy Jarāsaṃdha’s army or bring his forces to ruin, for he possesses powerful troops along with their legions."
For this reason, O Vainateya, I tell you regarding the city of Mathurā:
it is my conviction that no good will come of our two dwelling there.
Garuḍa said:
Having paid homage to the God of gods, I departed from your presence, O Lord,
to seek a place for my dwelling upon your earth, Kuśasthalī.
Having gone and stationed myself in the sky, O best of the gods, I looked all around and beheld that city, which was honored with auspicious marks.
It was as vast as the coastal plains of the ocean, cool and sloping toward the east and north,
situated between mountains and the sea, and impenetrable even by the gods.
Possessing mines of every kind of jewel, with trees that bear the fruits of all desires,
strewn with flowers of every season, it was enchanting from every side.
It was inhabited by those belonging to all stages of life, endowed with all objects of desire,
crowded with throngs of men and women, and ever-increasing in fragrance.
It was equipped with walls and moats, adorned with a garland of gate-towers and watchtowers,
featuring various courtyards and roads, and possessed broad gates and archways.
[It was] richly adorned with various mechanical bolts, beautified by golden ramparts,
crowded with men, serpents, and horses, and filled with chariot armies.
It was crowded with trees bearing divine flowers and fruits from various directions and lands;
it was richly adorned with rows of banners and flags, and graced with magnificent palaces.
Terrifying to the hosts of enemies and increasing the joy of friends,
it was the best of cities, superior to the dwellings of lords of men.
And, O God, make Raivata, the best of mountains, a divine abode for the gods,
resembling the Nandana grove and serving as an ornament for the city gate.
O best of gods, having caused that consecration (adhivāsa) to be performed and having gone there,
the conduct of the princes will become honored by the gods.
By name it shall be called Dvāravatī, renowned throughout the three worlds;
it will be a beautiful city, like Amarāvatī belonging to Śakra.
If the great ocean should provide a level ground,
Viśvakarman will perform various tasks as desired.
With gems, pearls, and corals, radiant with the luster of diamonds and lapis lazuli—
with divine jewels born in the three worlds that fulfilled every desire.
[He saw palaces] filled with divine pillars, resembling the assembly halls of the gods in heaven,
made of bright Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with every kind of jewel.
O Lord, have palaces constructed that are made of Jāmbūnada gold, radiant, adorned with every kind of jewel,
rich with divine banners and flags, protected by gods and kinnaras,
and resplendent like the moon and the sun.

Nārada said:
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, to Hari, to the Creator, the sustainer of all beings;

salutations to you, the Lord of all, who are beyond qualities yet the very soul of the qualities.
Homage to you who took the form of a dwarf and dwelt in the world of illusion;
homage to you in the form of a boar, supporting the earth with your tusk.
Homage to you, O horse-headed one, whose form was that of the bringer of the Vedas;
homage to you, O Trivikrama, O Janārdana, whose nature is the triple Veda.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, who consists of the syllable *oṃ*, whose form is the three Vedas,
whose nature is stainless knowledge, and who is the abode of supreme consciousness.
Homage to you, O Udgītha; let there be homage to you, O Rathantara, whom those who know the essence of the Vedas—Brahmā and the others, Sanaka and the rest—recognize.
Searching with the lamp called consciousness, O Keśava,
you are that very one, O God, Lord of the World, who has been seen by the exponents of Brahman.
Having reached which the yogins of restrained mind do not return—that art thou, O God, the Ancient Self; to thee, O God, salutations again and again!
In the certainty of knowledge, all the Vedas declare you to be Brahman;
you alone are this entire universe, and everything is established in you.

For all living beings are indeed covered by the veil of your *māyā*; fallen through the pride of thinking "I am," they fall into the hells. And those who call you Viṣṇu, they too reach you through diligent effort.
But those mortals who possess knowledge, strengthened by the wisdom of the Vedānta,
they enter you, O Lord of the gods of gods, the Ancient One.

"O Blessed One, this is Your illusion (māyā), relying upon which all living beings constantly breathe out that which consists of the world; for it is indeed difficult to endure. Indeed, this entire sport (vihāra) is for the sake of the arising of all living beings."

O Lord of the World, formerly you were known by the name Vārāha; indeed, for the benefit of living beings, you upheld the Earth. Furthermore, having become Aśvaśiras, you remain after having recovered the Vedas.
In the form of a dwarf, you bound Bali at the sacrifice;
having taken back the kingdom from him, O Lord, you restored it to Indra.
And you became Nārasiṃha and slew the preeminent Daitya.

O Lord of the World, best among those who possess noble lineages, you were born in the lineage of Raghu; O All-pervading One, you were known by the name Rāma and slew Rāvaṇa. O Supreme among Gods, you made this world free from thorns.

And you were once the son of Jamadagni, O Lord; having taken up your axe, O mighty one, you slew the son of Kṛtavīrya in battle. You indeed delivered this world, rendered devoid of Kṣatriyas, to Kaśyapa.
Even now, O Govinda, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
you remain established in Dvāravatī, having assumed a human form.
O Lord, while sporting in Gokula during his childhood, he killed Pūtanā;

Furthermore, you indeed lifted up Mount Govardhana,
that great mountain, for the protection of the cows while all the cowherds looked on.
The Blessed One danced again in the pool of the Yamunā at Hare; O Viṣṇu, you rendered Kāliya devoid of pride on the bank of the Yamunā.
O Viṣṇu, having slain Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika in the midst of the arena,
you have by your might killed Kaṃsa, who was unbearable and hated by the world.
Ugrasena has been consecrated in the kingdom with all thorns removed;
he now stands established in his sovereignty, relying upon you as Indra relies upon heaven.
O Lord of the World, why [say more]? The entire world is subject to your will.
O Soul of All, Lord of All Beings, Creator of All, Source of All! Homage to you, O Lord of the Gods of Gods; homage again and again, homage!
Having thus praised the Lord of the World, Nārada ceased;
hearing that, all the Yādavas were struck with great wonder.

"O Blessed Viṣṇu, hear the reason for my coming."

For King Śiśupāla, the lord of the Cedis,
and Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva, O Lord, always hate you.

Having heard that, O god, best of the Vṛṣṇis, I have come to you in haste;
therefore, go together with the Vṛṣṇis to the city of that wise one.
"O Kṛṣṇa, having conquered the foremost of kings, take Rukmiṇī as your bride."
Then King Śiśupāla stood there, arrayed in the attire of a bridegroom.
O Lord of the World, if that king were to marry Rukmiṇī, it would be an improper act and bring you dishonor; of this there is no doubt.
Although she was requested by you, Bhīṣmaka indeed did not give her.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, Jarāsaṃdha the protector, Pauṇḍra the best of kings, Ekalavya, and Rukmin will give [their daughters] to him.
O Lord, he who always hates you does not challenge you.
"Jarāsaṃdha, however, is always an enemy of the Vṛṣṇis, without a doubt;
therefore, may you depart quickly by means of chariots, horses, and even elephants."
Placing Ugrasena and the mighty Sātyaki at the front,
O Lord of the World, take her and go without delay.
And she, O Hṛṣīkeśa, having been seen with her consciousness stricken by grief,
fixes her mind on you alone and constantly remembers you, O Lord.
If the King of Cedi were to become her husband, O Hari, Rukmiṇī would have died.
O Hari, O Viṣṇu, restore to life Rukmiṇī, who is adorned with golden ornaments!
"Thus, O Lord, I have arrived; let what remains to be done be considered.
O Hari, wielder of the discus, nothing whatsoever is difficult for you to accomplish."
"O King, let us accomplish our purpose"; having yoked [the chariot], he departed.

She was endowed with a radiant body and possessed great strength.
Then Kṛṣṇa beheld her standing near the temple of the deity, endowed with such beauty that she was like Lakṣmī herself manifest before his eyes.
Like a blazing flame of fire, like an illusion descended to the earth,
or like the profound earth itself risen from the surface of the ground.
Like a ray of the moon, yet embodied in a lovely female form;
like the goddess Śrī without her lotus, accompanied only by handmaidens.
Beheld by Kṛṣṇa with his mind, she was difficult to look upon even for the gods.
For she was dark-complexioned yet radiant, with large and beautifully arched eyes;
her lips, eyes, and outer corners were copper-hued, and her thighs, hips, and breasts were full.
She was tall, with all her limbs beautiful, slender, and with a face like the moon;
she had copper-colored, elevated nails, lovely eyebrows, and dark, curly hair.
She was adorned with teeth that had sharp, white nails and were radiant with luster.
There is no other woman in the world equal to Rukmiṇī in beauty, fame, and splendor— the goddess-like lady of exquisite form, clad in white silk garments.
Upon seeing her, who was so pleasing to behold, Kṛṣṇa’s desire increased;
his mind became fixed upon her, just as the flame of a fire fed with oblations is directed toward the sacrificial butter.
And likewise the queen Rukmiṇī beheld the Lord Kṛṣṇa;
and having seen Kṛṣṇa standing there, that queen reflected:
"This is indeed Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, the virtuous younger brother of Rāma, manifest in person."
His discus and conch shell shall always adorn both his arms;
may those two, the destroyers of Daityas and Dānavas, forever grace him.
The Śārṅga bow, which strikes terror into the Daityas and Dānavas, rests in his hand;
that great bow of Hari always shines, renowned throughout the world.
Relying upon that god, O Lord, there is always that mace called Kaumodakī,
the slayer of Daityas and Dānavas, which pierces through their very marrow.
Relying upon this permission, the sword named Nandaka slays enemies of great prowess who are unbearable even for the gods.
Viṣṇu’s vehicle was Garuḍa, the foremost of birds;
he, having conquered the gods beginning with Śakra, carried off the supreme nectar of immortality.
Thus this all-pervading Viṣṇu himself, adorned with the dress of a cowherd,
sported at his pleasure among the cowherd women in those pastures.
This is Hari, who at that time danced in the waters of that Yamunā;
therefore, he [subdued] Kāliya, who was garlanded with the blazing flames of poison.
This Lord of the World held up Mount Govardhana with a single hand,
as easily as a child holds a ball.
This is that lotus-eyed one who indeed struck down the elephant.
And Govinda, having slain Aṇūra and the mighty Kaṃsa in battle,
danced upon the stage together with the cowherds and the Yādavas.
This is that best of the Yādavas, whose eyes are like the filaments of a lotus; dark yet radiant, glorious, the successful younger brother of Indra in person;
the youthful Hari, the ancient Self, lotus-eyed and possessing the splendor of a lotus.
Today this Yādava, the Lord of the World, has arrived here before me;
I shall bear the pair of his feet—of this there is no doubt.
"I shall offer service at her lotus-like feet.

Having deliberated with Rāma, the mighty Keśava,

Having suddenly overpowered him, Kṛṣṇa led him away on his own excellent chariot.

and upon learning this, all the Daśārhas fully prepared themselves for battle.

Having taken Rukmiṇī with him, the heroic Kṛṣṇa departed quickly toward his city,
having entrusted that burden to Rāma and Yuyudhāna.
In Akrūra, Vipṛthu, Gada, and Kṛtavarman;
in Vasudeva, Sudeva, and the mighty Sāraṇa.
Keśava [was present] at Nikṛttaśatru, Vikrānta, Bhaṅgakāra, Vidūratha, Ugrasena’s son Kahva, and Śatadyumna.
In Rājādhideva, Mṛdara, Prasena, Citraka,
as well as Agnidatta, Bṛhaddurga, Śvaphalka, Satyaka, and Pṛthu.

To Rukmī and Bhīṣmaka, to the high-souled Pauṇḍra,
