I shall give him to the wolves; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
When that Jarāsaṃdha, my protector, has been slain, I alone shall become Vāsudeva upon the surface of the earth.
Having spoken thus, he took up his bow and roared in the assembly of kings.

Then, O great king, while all the kṣatriyas looked on, the ruler of the Cedis—disguised in excellent attire and overcome with shame—took up a terrible iron club and spoke these words to the best of kings: HV_App.I,22A.37–39: caidyo æpy atha mahārāja sarvakṣatrasya paśyataḥ / varaveṣapraticchanno lajjayā ca samanvitaḥ / ādāya parighaṃ ghoraṃ idam āha nṛpottamān // 39 //
"O bulls among kings, having slain the Yādavas along with their armies in battle by this very [means], I shall deliver them to King Yama. Stay here, O kings; this defeat is mine alone."
"O best of kings, O bulls among monarchs, this violation of another's wife is not fitting for kings born into the Kṣatriya lineage."
But that is appropriate, O Lord, since they are Kṣatriyas born in the lineage of Yadu;
especially so when they have grown up among cowherds and herdsmen.
Just as cowherds always maintain the livelihood of cattle,
so too Kṛṣṇa grew up in Gokula, indeed moving about together with the cowherds.
"O Lord, Keśava is indeed constantly intent upon the wives of others;
I shall by all means slay that evil-souled one along with his followers in battle.
And I shall bring her back, O kings; remain here, O rulers of the earth!"
Where indeed are those kinsmen of yours, depending upon whom the Yādavas have shown contempt for us? Let this be considered by you here.
Having spoken thus, the King of Cedi then advanced for battle;
and all those kings, enraged and clad in armor for combat,
stood with their bows strung, equipped with finger-guards and yak-tail fans.
Then King Jarāsaṃdha, having mounted his chariot and donned his armor, O great king,
set his mind upon battle, that lord of the earth.
Then, O great king, the mighty Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva,
having mounted his chariot, suddenly set his mind on battle alone.
Dantavaktra, Jarāsaṃdha, and the heroic Śiśupāla set forth, armored and enraged, desiring to slay Janārdana.
The heroic king of Cedi went forth together with the kings of Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and Aiśa, along with Pauṇḍra, and accompanied by his brothers and kinsmen.
Where is Vāsudeva, and where is the cowherd? Where indeed is the king of those born in the Yadu lineage? And where is Rāma, who is arrogant and intoxicated with pride?
Whence indeed has the hero Sātyaki come in battle? So it is said.
Speaking thus, those best of kings, joined with their forces and accompanied by the Magadhas, then prepared for battle,
striking down [the enemy] in combat with arrows and swords.
Great chariot-warriors of fierce valor went forth.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, O great king, in the army of the high-souled lord of Magadha...
Conch shells and kettledrums resounded, foreboding battle;
and then, O great king, Mādhava also blew his conch shell separately.
The sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and cymbals arose everywhere there in the assembly of the Yadu forces.
Then a battle broke out between the two armies;
at that time, the Vṛṣṇis set forth with Jarāsaṃdha at their head.
King Jarāsaṃdha, together with his army and his powerful followers, encountered those enraged Vṛṣṇi heroes, who were great chariot-warriors.
The mighty Vṛṣṇi heroes, filled with zeal, received him,
placing Saṃkarṣaṇa at their head, just as the immortals receive Vāsava.
As the mighty Jarāsaṃdha was rushing forward with speed,
Yuyudhāna pierced him with six iron arrows in that great battle.
Akrūra, however, pierced Dantavakra with nine arrows;
Kārūṣa, in turn, struck him back with ten swift-flying shafts.
Vipṛthu pierced Śiśupāla with seven arrows,
and the powerful Śiśupāla pierced him back with eight.
Gaveṣaṇa, however, pierced the king of Cedi with six arrows;
Aniruddha likewise with eight, and Bṛhaddurga with five.
The King of Cedi pierced them back with five arrows each,
and with four arrows he slew the four horses of Vipṛthu.
Then that slayer of foes cut off the head of Bṛhaddurga with a broad-headed shaft.
And he dispatched Vipṛthu’s charioteer as well to the abode of Yama.
Abandoning his chariot whose horses had been slain, the exceedingly powerful and heroic Vipṛthu quickly mounted the chariot of Bṛhaddurga; having ascended,
he proceeded to control the swift horses.
Enraged, they overwhelmed Sunītha with a rain of arrows as he fearlessly danced along the paths of his chariot, bow in hand.
The god Śakra pierced Dantavaktra in the chest with a barbed arrow (karṇin),
and he also struck him in battle with five sharp shafts.
Pierced by those two with ten sharp arrows that struck his vital organs,
the powerful one then, in his wrath, pierced Śakradeva with ten shafts.
And from no great distance, he also pierced Vidūratha with five arrows.
Vidūratha also pierced him in battle with six sharp arrows.
The powerful Kṛtavarman pierced that great car-warrior with thirty arrows;
he, in turn, quickly struck the prince with three shafts.
He struck his charioteer and cut down his lofty banner;
then Pauṇḍra, enraged, pierced him in return with six feathered arrows.
And with a straight-knotted broad-headed arrow, he cut off his bow;
having severed the enemy's weapon, he pierced the Kalinga king’s body with shafts.
The king born of Kaliṅga pierced him with a lance in the same place;
meanwhile, the valiant Kahva, having encountered the elephant of Aṅga, struck that elephant with his own elephant.
The valiant one quickly struck with a lance and pierced the body;
Citraka, Śvaphalka, and the mighty Sātyaki pierced the chariot-force of Kaliṅga with sharp iron arrows.
Enraged in battle, Rāma struck down the elephant of the Vaṅga king with a released plowshare, and he also slew the Vaṅga king himself in the fray.
Having slain him and mounted his elephant,
the heroic Saṃkarṣaṇa took up his bow and struck down many of the Kāśikas with fierce iron arrows.
Having struck down the Kārūṣas with six arrows, the heroic and mighty archer,
that great chariot-warrior, furiously slew a hundred Māgadhas.
Having slain them, O great king, he then marched against Jarāsaṃdha.
As he was attacking, the King of Magadha pierced him with three iron arrows;
enraged, the club-wielder (Balarāma) struck him back with eight iron shafts.

And with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), Halāyudha cut down his gold-adorned banner; with arrows alone, he also severed his greatly drawn bow. O great king, he then shattered his chariot into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
With his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, that Māgadha took up a mace and struck Balabhadra again and again; furthermore,
that Māgadha pulverized the other's chariot with his mace.
As he was being struck down from that chariot,
Halāyudha leaped down and proceeded toward the chariot of Sātyaki while all the kṣatriyas looked on;
then, O great king, Sātyaki pierced the ruler of Magadha with arrows.
O great king, Baladeva, quickly seizing his mace,
struck the King of Magadha in battle, just as Hari struck a mountain with his thunderbolt.
Then a terrible battle took place between them, resembling that of the gods and the asuras,
as they discharged showers of arrows and struck one another.
Enraged elephants by the thousands clashed with elephants;
chariots furiously encountered chariots, and horsemen likewise met horsemen.
Likewise, the foot soldiers, with spears, shields, and swords in hand,
severed the heads of other infantrymen and shouted individually in the battle.
The great roar of arrows falling upon armor—
whether already fixed or being discharged in the battle— was heard like the sound of birds alighting.
In that battle, there arose the sound of kettledrums, conchs, clay drums, and flutes,
as well as the clashing of weapons and the twang of the bowstrings of the great-souled warriors.
In the meantime, the heroic and highly illustrious Balabhadra struck the hero Jarāsaṃdha with his mace in that great battle;
the king fell unconscious and collapsed upon the earth.
Sātyaki, however, struck the King of Vaṅga with sharpened arrows;
and when Jarāsaṃdha had been struck down, that army turned its back in retreat.
Having defeated thousands of warriors, Sātyaki and Balabhadra stood at the forefront of all and blew their conchs, O King. Then the army fled and Jarāsaṃdha was defeated.
Hearing the sound of those two conchs while still on his way,
Janārdana perceived that the army of the King of Magadha, which was supported by many kings, had already been defeated.
Having reflected thus, the powerful Vāsudeva,
born of the Yadu clan, blew his great conch shell, Pāñcajanya.

On August 23, 2002:
The Yādavas proclaimed the wedding of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
"Let the streets be adorned on all sides with banners! they declared.
"Let the kings and thousands of brahmins be summoned,
as well as the sūtas, the māgadhas, the bards, and others."
Let the jars be filled even with waters from the great ocean;
let all the banners be raised high, and let courtesans be brought here.
Let the family priests be summoned, and let the princes likewise be gathered from all sides;
let the great kettledrums be beaten, and let the clay drums resound everywhere upon the earth.
Let all the dancers dance, and likewise let the singers sing;
let all the Brahmins be fed, and let wealth be distributed.
"Let palaces be constructed everywhere; indeed, let them all be built!
Thus did the Yādavas, eager for the festival, issue their commands.
And they all, by the thousands, did exactly as they were commanded.

In some places, singers then performed songs in beautiful melodies; in other places, kettledrums were struck, filling the air with a great roar. They filled both heaven and earth, and the netherworld (pātāla) was also filled.
In some places, O Great King, conchs were blown by the lords of the Yādavas,
shaking the earth and causing the oceans to swell.
In some places, during that great festival, elephants and horses let out their cries,
while the youths of the Yadu chiefs raised a lion’s roar.
While Keśava was intent on the festival, Sātyaki served as the overseer;
he moved here and there, directing him to various tasks.
And he appointed each person to that specific task which was appropriate for them.
The righteous and steadfast Baladeva also, together with the kings,
bestowed honors upon them as was fitting and appropriate.
While that clamor was thus occurring, O great king, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
[addressed] the Brahmins who had assembled from various directions.
O king of kings, having paid homage to the elders led by Ugrasena, Hṛṣīkeśa set his mind upon the marriage.
And having been granted permission by them, O King, the Lord Keśava— clad in washed garments and well-adorned— formally took the hand of Rukmiṇī according to the prescribed rites.
The word "Victory! was uttered by the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas;
and the bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists praised the Lord of the World.
Then the sounds of conchs and kettledrums arose in the sky;
a rain of flowers fell, and a pleasant breeze blew.
Then Janārdana, having given jewels to the Brahmins,
Hṛṣīkeśa bestowed eight thousand horses upon each of those preeminent Brahmins, along with various garments.
More than a hundred elephants, ten thousand cows,
and hundreds of thousands of millions of loads of gold.
And this, O Indra among kings, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, said:
"Let whatever beautiful object there is, designated as a jewel, be given away;
and let those who come with requests be honored, O King, during this great festival."
Having thus given his command, Govinda, together with Rukmiṇī, paid homage to the Yādavas,
and immediately thereafter to his own father and Devakī.
And Ugrasena, the lord of kings, and the other elders along with the Yādavas—
all those best of the Yadus shed tears born of joy.
But when the wedding of Keśava had been completed, O King,
all those kings and brahmins who had assembled there from every direction,
having witnessed the marriage ceremony, departed as they had come.

Vaiśampāyana said:
O best of those who recite prayers, here is a wondrous and marvelous mantra for daily recitation.
When Pradyumna had returned to Dvārakā after slaying that Kālaśambara,
Baladeva spoke for the sake of protection; his daily observance (*āhnika*) is now being told.
O best of kings, by reciting this morning and evening, one shall obtain auspiciousness.
It was proclaimed by Balabhadra and likewise proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa;
it has also been proclaimed by sages and ṛṣis who desire righteousness.
And it has been proclaimed by great sages and by seers as well.
Once, the son of Rukmiṇī was together with Balarāma in his home.
Having sat down and bowed to him, he then spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Pradyumna said:
"O elder brother of Kṛṣṇa, O highly fortunate one, O son of Rohiṇī, O Lord!
Recite some hymn for me, by the recitation of which I may become free from fear."
May Brahmā, the preceptor of the gods and asuras and the lord of the world, protect me;
likewise may the syllable *oṃ*, the *vaṣaṭ* call, the *Sāvitrī*, and various ritual acts [protect me].
The *ṛg*-verses, the *yajus*-formulas, the *sāman*-chants, and the *Atharvan* hymns—
the four complete Vedas in their entirety, along with the *Rahasyas* and the detailed expositions.
May the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, the Khilas and Upakhilas,
as well as the Aṅgas and Upāṅgas together with their commentaries, protect me.
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth;
the senses, mind, and intellect; as well as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Vyāna, udāna, samāna, prāṇa, and apāna as the fifth—
these, along with seven other winds, upon which this entire world depends.
Āvaha, Pravaha, Udvaha, Saṃvaha,
Vivaha, Parāvaha, and likewise Parivaha are the winds.
May Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Bhṛgu, and the venerable Vasiṣṭha— may these great ṛṣis protect me.
May Kaśyapa and the other sages, the fourteen [protectors] of the ten directions,
and the two gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa together with their hosts, always protect me.
The Rudras are said to be eleven, and the Ādityas are indeed twelve.
And the eight Vasu gods and the two Aśvins are proclaimed.
Hrī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Svadhā, Medhā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Smṛti, and Dhṛti;
Aditi, Diti, Danu, and Siṃhikā are the mothers of the Daityas.
Himavān, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Śvetaparvata, Ṛṣabha, Pāriyātra, Vindhya, and Vaidūryaparvata; HV_App.I,24.23 / HV_App.I,24.24
May the Sahya and other mountains, Malaya, Meru, Mandara, Dardura, Krauñca, Kailāsa, and Maināka— these upholders of the earth— protect me.
And Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Viśālākṣa, and Takṣaka;
Elāpatra, Śuktikarṇa, and both Kambala and Aśvatara.
Hastibhadra, Piṭharaka, Karkoṭaka, Dhanañjaya,
as well as Pūraṇaka, Nāga, and Karavīraka.
Sumanāsyas, Dadhimukha, as well as Śṛṅgārapiṇḍaka,
and the blessed Maṇināga, who is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Dadhikarṇa, the king of serpents, as well as Hāridraka and others—
these and many others, and those who have not been mentioned, [all came].
May the mountain-dwellers who uphold truth and righteousness protect me; may the lords of the serpents protect me.
May the four oceans and Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, protect me.
The Sarasvatī, Candrabhāgā, Śatadrū, and the auspicious Devikā;
the Irāvatī, Vipāśā, Śarayū, and likewise the Yamunā.
The Kauśikī, the Devikā, and the holy, divine Dṛṣadvatī;
the Kulmāṣī, the Rathavāmā, the Bāhudā, and the Hiraṇyadā.
The Plakṣā, the Ikṣumatī, the Tāpanī, the Bṛhadrathā, the famous Carmaṇvatī, and the holy Vadhūsara; HV App I, 24.40–41.
May these rivers, and others not mentioned here,
which flow toward the northern region, bathe me with their waters.
The Veṇṇā, Godāvarī, Sītā, Kāverī, and Kāñcanāvatī.
The Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Śuktimatī, Tamasā, and Puṣpavāhinī; the Tāmraparṇī, Jyotimatī, and the Utpalodumbarāvatī.
The holy river Vaitaraṇī, the auspicious Vidarbhā and Narmadā;
the Vitastā, the Bhīmarathī, and the great river Elā;
the Kālindī, the holy Gomatī, and the famous river Śoṇa.
May these and other rivers, as well as those others that have not been mentioned,
which flow toward the southern region, purify me with their waters.
The Siprā, Carmaṇvatī, the holy Mahī, and likewise the Sābhramatī;
the Sindhu, Vetravatī, as well as the Bhojā and Vanamālikā.
Pūrvabhadrā, Aparabhadrā, Ūrmilā, and Varadrumā;
she who is known as Vetravatī and is celebrated as Cāpadāsī.
The Prasthāvatī, the meritorious river, the holy Sarasvatī,
the Mitraghnī, the Indumālā, and likewise the river Madhumatī.
Umā, Gurunadī, and the Tāpī with its pure waters; Vimalā, Vimalodā, Mattagaṅgā, and Payasvinī.
May these and other rivers, as well as those others not mentioned here,
who dwell in the western quarter, consecrate me.
The Bhāgīrathī, whose waters are meritorious, is situated in the eastern direction; may she,
praised by Śambhu and upheld by him, burn away my sin when her name is invoked.
Prabhāsa, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes;
the Ganges-tīrtha, Kurukṣetra, Śrīkṣetra, and Gautama’s hermitage;
Rāma’s lake, Vinaśana, and likewise Rāmatīrtha.
Gaṅgādvāra, Kanakhala, and where indeed Soma arose.
The holy ford Kapālamocana, the renowned Jambūmārga,
the celebrated Suvarṇabindu, and likewise Kanakapiṅgala.
And also Daśāśvamedhika, adorned with holy hermitages;
and the famous Badarī, the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
The famous Phālgunītīrtha, as well as the Bhadravaṭa tīrtha;
Kokāmukha, the Puṇyanada, and the Gaṅgāsāgara;
and in Magadha, the renowned Tapoda and Gaṅgodbheda.
Reva, Arisaṃgama, and likewise Śūlabheda—
these are sacred fords (tīrthas) frequented by the great seers;
may they, both those named and those unnamed, purify me with their waters.

Rudrāṇī, Bhadrakālī, Bhadraṣaṣṭhā, Vāruṇī,

The noble Kuhū, Sinīvālī, Bhīmā, Citravatī, Rati,

May Lohityāyanamātā and those who are remembered as the celestial maidens (devakanyās),
as well as Gonandā, the wife of a god, protect me along with my kinsmen.
With various ornaments and gestures, their faces marked with diverse forms,
they wandered through many lands, adorned with various weapons.
They were fond of fat and marrow, and likewise fond of wine, meat, and marrow-fat;
they had the faces of cats and leopards, and countenances resembling elephants and lions.
Some had faces like those of herons, crows, vultures, and cranes;
some wore serpents as sacred threads, and others were clad in skins.
With faces smeared with blood, their voices sounding like the harsh rattle of a kettle-drum,
they are envious and wrathful, yet they find pleasure in beautiful palaces.
Intoxicated, frenzied, and heedless, they stood ready to strike;
some had tawny eyes and tawny hair, while others had their hair cut short.
Those with upward-pointing hair, those with black hair, and likewise those with white hair;
those possessing the strength of ten thousand nāgas, and those possessing the speed and strength of the wind.
Some had one hand, some one foot, and some one eye; their faces were trembling;
some had many sons, some few sons, and some had two sons; they were fond of ornaments.
Mukhamandī, Biḍālī, Pūtanā, Gandhapūtanā,
Śītavātā, Uṣṇavetālī, and those known as Revatī and Graha.
They were fond of laughter, fond of anger, fond of dress, and fond of speaking;
they were easy to please, givers of happiness, and always beloved by the twice-born.
May the night-walkers, who are always fierce on the sacred festival days but bring happiness as their ultimate result,
protect my son constantly like mothers protect their own children.
The fierce fevers born from the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā), those produced from the limbs of Rudra,
those born from Kumāra and Skanda, and indeed the Vaiṣṇava and other fevers.
They were most terrifying, possessed of great heroism, puffed up with pride, and endowed with mighty strength;
they were wrathful, yet capable of suppressing anger, cruel, and makers of conflict with the gods.
Night-roaming lions with fangs, fond of conflict,
pot-bellied, thick-hipped, tawny-eyed, and possessing every form.
Holding in their hands spears, double-edged swords, tridents, iron clubs, darts, shields, and scimitars.
They are fond of weapons such as the Pināka bow, the thunderbolt, the club, and the Brahma-staff.
The Daṇḍins and Kuṇḍins were heroes who wore matted hair and crowns;
they were skilled in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and they always wore the sacred sacrificial thread.
Afflicted by serpents, those heroes wore earrings and armlets;
they were clothed in various garments and adorned with variegated garlands and unguents.
Some had faces resembling elephants, horses, camels, bears, cats, lions, and tigers;
others had the faces of boars, owls, jackals, deer, mice, and buffaloes.
Some were dwarfish, some misshapen, some hunchbacked, some formidable, and others with shorn hair;
and yet others by the hundreds of thousands wore a thousand matted locks.
Some resembled white Kailāsa, others possessed the radiance of the sun;
some had the hue of clouds, and others were like heaps of blue collyrium.
Some had one foot, some two feet, and others had two heads;
they were fleshless, with shanks as thick as palm trees, with gaping mouths, and terrifying.
In ponds, wells, and tanks, in oceans and lakes,
and dwelling in cremation grounds, mountains, trees, and empty houses—
may these grahas constantly protect me on all sides.
Mahāgaṇapati, Nandin, Mahākāla, and Mahābala;
and the two fevers, Māheśvara and Vaiṣṇava, who bring fear to the world.
Grāmaṇī, Gopāla, Bhṛṅgarīṭi, Gaṇeśvara,
Deva, Vāmadeva, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and Karaṃdhama.
Śvetamoda, Kapālī, Jambhaka, Śatrutāpana,
both Majjana and Unmajjana, as well as Saṃtāpana and Vilāpana.
Nijaghāsa and Ghasa, Sthūṇākarṇa and Praśoṣaṇa; Ulkāmālī, Dhamadhamas, Jvālājihva, and Pramardana.
Saṃghaṭṭana, Saṃkucana, Kāṣṭhabhūta, Śivaṃkara,
Kūṣmāṇḍa, Kumbhamūrdhan, Rocana, and the Graha Vaikṛta.
He is homeless, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, auspiciousness itself and yet the inauspicious;
he is Kṣemaka, the eater of flesh, the enemy of the gods, and the yellow-eyed one.
Bhīmaka and Grāhaka, as well as Ugra and Mahāgraha; Upagraha and Aryaka, and likewise the other, Skandagraha.
Vetāla, Asamavetāla, Tāmasa, Sumahākapi,
Hṛdayodvartana, Caṇḍa, Kuṇḍāśin, and Kaṅkaṇapriya.
With tawny beards, possessing the speed of Garuḍas and the mind and wind,
hundreds and thousands [of them] were born from the wrath of Pārvatī.
They were powerful, radiant, devoted to Brahman, and true to their word;
they were providers of all desires and slayers of enemies in battle.
Praised for all their virtues during the night, by day, and in difficult places— may the lords of those hosts, together with their attendants, protect me always.
Nārada and Parvata, the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
the ancestors, as well as causes and effects, mental anxieties, and physical ailments.
Agastya, Gālava, Gārgya, Śakti, Dhaumya, Parāśara,
the venerable Kṛṣṇātreya, Asita, and the stainless Devala.
Bṛhaspati, Utathya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Śrutaśravas,
Dvaipāyana, Vidarbha, Jaimini, Māṭhara, and Kaṭha.
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and the great seer Lomaśa;
Uttaṅka, Raibhya, Pauloma, Dvita, and Trita.
The seer Vaikālavṛkṣīya, the sage Medhātithi,
as well as Sārasvata, Yavakrīta, Kuśika, and Gautama.
Bṛhaspati, Dīrghatamas, and likewise Śunaḥśepa.
Saṃvarta, Ṛśyaśṛṅga, Svastyātreyo, Vibhāṇḍaka, Ṛcīka, Jamadagni, and likewise Aurva, the treasury of ascetic power.
Bharadvāja, Sthūlaśiras, Kaśyapa, Pulaha, Kratu,
Bṛhadagni, Hariśmaśru, Vijaya, and Kaṇva.
Śamīka, Śunaḥśepa, Cyavana, Bhārgava, and Aṅgiras; [HV App. I, 24.171] 10:1.
Vaitaṇḍī, Dīrghatapas, Veda, Aṃśumān, and Śiva.
Śunaḥśepha, Śunaḥpuccha, and Śunolāṅgūla;
as well as Aṣṭāvakra, Dadhīci, and likewise Śvetaketu.
Uddālaka, Kṣārapāṇi, Śṛṅgin, Gauramukha,
as well as Agniveśya, Śamīka, Pramucu, and Mumucu;
These and many other sages of firm vows,
the seers of disciplined soul, and others who have not been mentioned—
may they, being upright, praiseworthy, and tranquil, always grant me peace.
The three fires, the three Vedas, the triple knowledge, the Kaustubha jewel,
the glorious horse Uccaiḥśravas, and the physician Dhanvantari— these are Hari.
Nectar, a cow, gold, curdled milk, cows, mustard seeds,
white maidens of uniform mind, a white umbrella, barley, and unbroken grains.
Dūrvā grass, gold, perfumes, and a yak-tail whisk; likewise, the unassailable discus, a great bull, sandalwood, and poison.
A white bull, an elephant in rut, a lion, a tiger, a horse, and arrows;
the earth being lifted up, parched grain, and honey-milk for the Brahmins.
The svastika, the vardhamāna, the nandyāvarta, the priyaṅgu,
the śrīphala, cow dung, fish, the dundubhi drum, and the sound of the paṭaha drum.
The wives of the sages and maidens, the glorious Bhadrāsana bow,
Rocanā and Rucaka, and the water from the confluence of rivers.
Suparṇas, śatapatras, cakoras, and jīvañjīvakas;
the Nandīmukha, the peacock, and those with banners of diamonds, pearls, and gems.
These verses, which bestow long life, are highly praised and bring about the accomplishment of one's goals;
they are meritorious, free from affliction, glorious, and endowed with auspiciousness.
They were previously recited by Rāma, who desired longevity, prosperity, and victory.
The wise man who should cause this to be heard, and the person who should likewise hear it—
having bathed, he should recite these One Hundred and Eight Auspicious Verses at every sacred festival.
He does not encounter slaughter, bondage, affliction, disease, grief, or humiliation; nor does he suffer any deficiency, but rejoices both in this world and the next.
It is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, purifying, and equal to the Vedas.
It is glorious, leading to heaven, ever meritorious, the source of offspring, and auspicious.
It is auspicious, bringing security to men, and the supreme generator of intelligence;
it pacifies all diseases and increases one's good reputation and lineage.
A man who is faithful, compassionate, and self-possessed should recite this;
with his soul purified of all sins, he attains the supreme goal.

Having obtained boons from the four-faced Brahmā, that best of Dānavas oppressed the foremost of the gods;
at times, that most excellent of Dānavas caused wonder throughout the quarters of the world.
Accompanied by many hundreds of thousands of Dānavas,
he quickly went to the world of the gods, repeatedly uttering a lion’s roar.
Having gone to the abode of Indra and rattling the door-panel, Danu said:
"Either fight, or let victory be granted [to us]."
Having heard that, the king of the gods also, accompanied by all the gods,
mounted Airāvata and was protected by the divine armies.
For the sake of battle with the great-souled Narakā,
the lord of the Dānavas, he emerged from that city into the presence of the Dānavas.
Mounting Airāvata, the husband of Śacī stood there.
Then a battle took place between the evil-minded Dānavas and the gods,
with Śakra as their ally, as they struck one another down.
The gods struck down the Dānavas, who resembled mountains,
with their arrows; and the Dānavas, O great king, struck down the gods led by Indra in that battle with swords, spears, and axes.
The mighty Daityas let out a great lion’s roar in battle;
they oppressed the gods even before the very eyes of the Lord of Śacī.
Afflicted and exhausted by battle, the gods fled in the ten directions;
yet even when restrained by Śakra, those deities were unable to stand their ground.
Seeing them thus routed, the great lord Vṛtrahā, the slayer of Bala, said to the immortals, "You must stand firm."
Taking up his bow according to the prescribed rite, he released the twang of the bowstring;
then Vāsava loosed thousands of arrows in the battle.
Likewise, O King, the world-protectors assembled from all directions,
as did Vaiśravaṇa together with the Yakṣas and Guhyakas.
Varuṇa, the king of aquatic creatures, accompanied by his Varuṇa-hosts and followed by hundreds of thousands of nāgas, was there as the lord of the quarter.
O Indra among kings, even King Yama, accompanied by Time and Death,
went forth to fight Naraka, the foremost of the Dānavas, O great king.
Together with them, the high-minded king of the gods also waged war;
O great king, Naraka too waged a most terrible battle.
Hayagrīva, Niśumbha, and Mura, the crusher of enemies, O Lord,
waged a most terrible battle with Naraka.
O Great King, the world-protectors are intent on engaging in battle.
The great king Hayagrīva encountered Varuṇa and waged a most terrible battle, just as in the past during the slaying of Vṛtra.
Nisumbha joined with Yama, who held a staff in his hand;
and Mura also, O King, being valiant, joined with the king of kings (Kubera).
Even Naraka, O Great King, was joined by the king of the gods;
and those gods, O Great King, were joined together with the Dānavas.
Those gods and dānavas, each desiring victory over the other,
waged a most terrible battle with spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and lances.
O great king, Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, struck Hayagrīva with sharp,
swift arrows that pierce the vital organs.
In that battle, the Dānava, resembling a mountain, pierced Varuṇa, the lord of the world-protectors,
with more than a hundred arrows.
In that battle, the Lord of the Gods released thousands of arrows; as he was shooting those sharp shafts, the Lord of Nooses discharged his own weapons at him.
Again, O Great King, the enraged Dānava, who resembled a mountain,
shattered Varuṇa’s great bow at the grip with an exceedingly sharp razor-edged arrow, even as the King of the Gods looked on.
Casting aside his bow and arrow, the wielder of the noose took up a lasso and struck the mighty Hayagrīva with it.
As it came flying with great speed, the Dānava seized the noose;
with that very same weapon, he struck Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures.
But that noose, rendered powerless there, did not afflict its master.
Then, O King, the enraged Hayagrīva struck the mighty Varuṇa, lord of aquatic creatures,
on the crown of his head with a mace.
Struck on the head by him, vomiting copious blood,
he then quickly lost consciousness and departed from that battle difficult to cross;
thus was he defeated by those foremost Dānavas, who were endowed with the powers of Varuṇa.
The mighty Nisumbha struck Yama with twenty-five arrows; Yama,
too, taking up his bow,
struck the Dānava in battle with a straight-knotted shaft while the Lord of Śacī looked on.
Nisumbha, his eyes copper-red with rage, cut that bow of his.
Having cast aside his jewel-like bow and raising his staff against the Dānava,
O King, the mighty Yama rushed forward, desiring to kill him.
But having cast aside his excellent bow, O great king,
the Dānava then took up a sharpened sword and advanced toward the Lord of the Dead.
Then a great battle took place between those two with those two weapons,
like that between Bali and Vāsava in the ancient war of the gods and asuras.
He struck the head of the evil-minded Nisumbha with a staff,
as he was being beaten by the great-souled Yama, the wielder of the staff.
With his eyes somewhat strained, Nisumbha, the best of the Dānavas,
struck Yama, the son of Vivasvat, with a sword in that battle.
With his armor shattered, Yama, the lord of the gods, accompanied by his followers from the southern quarter,
became unconscious; his senses and vital self failing him as he gasped in the peril of his life, he fled swiftly from the battle to his city, terrified of that best of Dānavas.
Likewise, Rājarāja was there together with the Guhyakas who resemble gods,
along with the Yakṣas and Vidyādharas led by Māṇibhadra.
The high-minded king of kings struck Mura, along with more than a hundred Mauryas, with sharp-edged arrows.
Mura, with seventy thousand Māuravas skilled in combat,
struck the king of kings with exceedingly sharp arrows;
having pierced that king of kings, he then assailed the Guhyakas as well.
Then the enemy of the gods struck the yakṣas with swords and nooses;
the yakṣas and guhyakas, filled with fear, fled from the battle,
casting aside their principal weapons, led by Māṇibhadra.
Having defeated the Yakṣa army,
the Dānava then pierced Vaiśravaṇa in battle with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
The Dānava, intoxicated by battle, assailed him at will upon his breasts, his chest, and within the sockets of his eyes; then,
afflicted and despondent, he departed from the field of battle.
And then, O King, those Yakṣas and Guhyakas from all sides gathered at Alakā,
terrified and turning their backs on the battle.
Then Yama, Varuṇa, and the high-minded Kubera—
having been defeated by the lord of the Dānavas— returned each to his own city.
All the gods were utterly defeated by the Dānavas, who resembled mountains;
terrified, with eyes rolling, they all fled in the ten directions.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen his own army defeated, the king of the gods, the husband of Śacī, [reflected].
Then, having mounted the tall elephant Airāvata, which resembled the moon, he departed.
Then, having strung his most formidable bow, the Māhendra,
he engaged in a most terrible battle with the evil-minded Naraka.
O Great King, even Naraka, upon seeing Śakra, the lord of Śacī,
let out various roars like a lion at a lordly elephant.
"Come! he said, and he made the twang of his bowstring;
then a battle took place between the two of them, like that in the slaying of Vṛtra of old.
Taking up a sharpened arrow, the evil-minded Naraka drew it back to his ear and struck the enemy of Vṛtra once more.
Struck by him, the lord of the gods became overwhelmed;
Śakra bled profusely and then lost consciousness.
Then Śakra, having recovered his composure, pierced him with eight arrows;
he pierced the chariot with seventy and the charioteer with nine arrows.
Then, O King, with a razor-sharp arrow he cut down his excellent banner,
and with sharpened shafts he dispatched his charioteer to Yama.
With four well-sharpened arrows he struck the horses,
and with a broad-headed shaft he cut through the bow of the evil-minded Naraka.
With his bow broken, his chariot destroyed, his arrows spent, and his charioteer slain,
he took up a sharpened sword and leapt toward the Lord of Śacī;
mounting Airāvata, he struck the King of the Gods upon the frontal globe.
But the Daitya, having brandished it again, struck the chest of the king of the gods with his sword in the assembly of the gods and Gandharvas.
Senseless and utterly overwhelmed, Śatakratu, the king of the gods,
abandoned the elephant Airāvata and departed like one in deep distress.
That Dānava struck the nāga on the region of its frontal globes;
and that nāga, O great king, then fled away in fear.
Then, having defeated the slayer of Vṛtra in battle, Narakasūnu, the son of the Earth,
uttered various roars, making both heaven and earth resound.
Having conquered Akhaṇḍala Śakra as well as the guardians of the worlds,
Naraka, the best of the Dānavas, proclaimed his victory.
Then the Daitya, having entered Amarāvatī with the great Asuras, summoned Urvaśī and spoke these words: *Note: The first pāda of this verse contains one syllable in excess.*
"Devote yourself to me here, O fair-thighed one; Śakra has been defeated by me in battle.
I am Indra, I am King Yama, I am Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures;
I alone, O auspicious and radiant lady, am eternally the king of kings."
Urvaśī said:
"O King, O Lord of the Daityas, if the sages always worship you with sacrifices, then I shall accept you; there is no need for hesitation in this matter."
Thus addressed, the Daitya then replied with the words, "So be it."
Having crushed the ladders to heaven along with the sons of Diti, O Great King,
they seized the celestial trees as well as other divine maidens.
O King, having taken eight thousand [followers], that best of Dānavas,
the king of the Daityas, went wherever he pleased together with the Dānavas.

D6 S (except G2) insert: Vaiśampāyana said: Having reached the world of mortals, Naraka, the best of the Dānavas—
While that Lord of the World was protecting the earth in Dvāravatī,
the Dānavas oppressed all humans, sages, and brahmins.
While the Lord of the World was indeed protecting the brahmins as well as the hosts of sages,
that Daitya then began to harass those brahmins and the hosts of sages.
Then once, O great king, the lord of the Daityas, remembering the words of Urvaśī,
went to Badarī to perform a sacrificial session (*satra*) for the sake of worshipping Śakra,
the lord of the gods, as well as the hosts of sages and the other celestial hosts.
Having seen those heroic sages, Naraka, the best of the Dānavas, spoke these words at that time: "O lords of sages, I am to be sacrificed."
"At this time, O Brahmins, I am Indra, the Lord of the World and sovereign of the gods;
yet Śakra, along with the world-protectors and the immortals, has been defeated in battle.
Therefore, he must indeed be worshipped, saluted, and honored for the welfare of the world."
Having heard these words of the evil-minded Naraka,
all those sages, who were devoted to their residence at Badarī, spoke.
"We shall not sacrifice, O Daitya; you are a Dānava of evil soul.
Free from all anxiety, we shall sacrifice to Indra together with the hosts of gods."
Hearing that, his eyes copper-red with rage, he spoke this to the Dānavas:
"Let all the sages be slain; let the sacrificial grounds be destroyed!"
"O Daitya, we shall not sacrifice you," the ascetics said, so it is told.
And all those Dānavas of wicked intent did exactly as they were told.
Having trampled the sacrificial ground and completely destroyed all the sacrificial burdens,
they mixed the sacred fires together and burned the heaps of *darbha* grass.
Having split their water-pots in two and having cut off their matted locks,
all the Dānavas were cast far away along with Naraka.
Having trampled the sacrificial enclosure, O King, they then reduced it to ashes;

meanwhile, by their sheer power, they devoured the oblations brought there for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice at that assembly of rites. They also consumed the animals that had been brought to the sacrificial gathering.
And having been burned in those very fires, with Agni at their head, those foremost of Dānavas [perished].
Thus all those Dānavas then created obstacles;
and all those excellent sages fled in the ten directions.
Thereupon, Naraka then abducted those daughters of the sages;
accompanied by those very maidens, the Dānava quickly went to Prāgjyotiṣa and rejoiced there at will with his beloveds.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
When the Daitya armies had departed, the sages were oppressed by dejection.
Having consulted with one another in that very delightful hermitage, they [departed].
To the god, the protector of the world, and to the high-souled Kṛṣṇa,
we report once again what has been done by the sinful Dānava.
"We shall report what has been done by that sinful Dānava;
for if he should retaliate, that will lead to our welfare."
If that wicked Naraka, the best of Dānavas, were to live,
the world would not remain in order and people would be utterly destroyed.
Having thus deliberated, the sages dwelling in Badarī then took up the burden of the sacrifice that had been seized by the evil-minded Naraka;
all those sages, their veins standing out, were accompanied by their disciples.
And to that Keśava they gave a cluster of jujube fruits which had been enjoyed by Keśava within that enclosure of the hermitage; then,
having traveled a long distance, they set out upon the southern path.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and Kāśyapa; Kaṇva, Dhūmra, Bṛhaddurga, Bharadvāja, and Gālava;
Kavaṣa, Dhūmraketu, Kāśya, and likewise Kāpilaka.
These and other sages, ascetics oppressed by the evil-minded Naraka,
desired to see the lotus-eyed Lord.
Accompanied by her disciples, she arrived distressed by the sinful Dānava;
being knowers of the true meaning of the Vedas, she desired to see Janārdana.
Having reached the Gaṅgā, they stood upon its bank;
there, the sages of rigid vows began to bathe, saying:
"Having bathed here, we shall go to see the one who desires the welfare of the world."
The Lord of the World, eternally pure, dwelling in the city of Dvārakā.
Having reflected thus, the sages performed their ablutions according to the prescribed rites,
so that those best of sages might become worthy to behold the imperishable Keśava.
Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, all those ascetics rich in penance became pure.
Then, having descended into the Gaṅgā by means of boats, those best of sages gradually reached Dvārakā, which was protected by Kṛṣṇa.
Having entered Dvārakā, those lords of sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others,
passed by thousands of the residences of the leaders of the Yadus.
Standing at the gate of that assembly hall which is world-renowned and celebrated as Sudharmā, the great seers spoke to the doorkeeper.
"O gatekeeper, let it be announced to the high-souled Keśava:
'The sages of rigid vows, who dwell indeed at Badarī,
have arrived to see you, being oppressed by the foremost of the Dānavas.'"
Having heard that, the gatekeeper then reported to the high-souled Keśava everything that had been said by the best of sages.
Having heard this, the Lord of the gods of gods, who is honored by the best of the Yadus, said to the sages,
"Let them be ushered in," and then he urged Pradyumna.
"Let water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), vessels, and seats be brought from all sides as is appropriate"; and he did all of that.
Those best of sages entered that assembly hall, which was honored by its members.

After 91.24, D₆ S (except G₂) ins. :k] The king said: "O best of brahmins, tell me truly how this great wonder occurred. How did the son of the sage come to be born from a human womb? And how did he, having been born from a human womb, attain the status of a brahmin? I wish to hear all this exactly as it happened. Vyāsa said: "Listen, O king, to the ancient account of how this great wonder occurred. In the past, there was a king named Pratīpa, who was devoted to dharma and truthful in speech. He had a son named Śāntanu, who was wise and possessed of great splendor. That king, having obtained that son, ruled the earth according to dharma. Now, O descendant of Bharata, there was a certain brahmin who was a master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, well-versed in the Purāṇas, and skilled in the science of grammar. He was a knower of the meaning of the scriptures and a performer of sacrifices. He was pure and always intent on the welfare of all beings. He was a reciter of the *Bhārata*, a speaker of truth, and one who delighted in the company of the virtuous. He was a worshiper of the gods and ancestors, and he was always devoted to his father. His name was Māṇḍavya, and he was highly honored by the king. Once, while wandering about, that best of brahmins arrived at the hermitage of the sage Vasiṣṭha. Having paid his respects to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, he sat down near him. Then, O best of the Bharatas, the sage Vasiṣṭha, having offered him hospitality, spoke these words to that best of brahmins: 'Welcome, O best of brahmins! I hope you are well, O sinless one. I hope you have come here without fatigue. What can I do for you today? Māṇḍavya said: 'O illustrious one, I am well in every respect, O best of sages. But I have come to you with a certain purpose; listen to it, O lord. Vasiṣṭha said: 'Tell me what is in your mind, O best of brahmins. I shall do whatever you desire. Māṇḍavya said: 'O illustrious one, I wish to dwell in your hermitage, free from fear, for the sake of practicing penance. Vasiṣṭha said: 'You may stay here, O best of brahmins, as long as you wish. I shall provide for all your needs. Having said this, the great ascetic Vasiṣṭha gave him a place to stay and provided him with everything necessary for his comfort. There, Māṇḍavya lived, performing severe austerities, subsisting on air and water, and remaining silent. Now, once, while the king Śāntanu was out hunting, he entered the forest and came upon that hermitage. Having seen the sage Vasiṣṭha, he paid his respects to him and sat down nearby. Then, O descendant of Bharata, the king asked the great-souled Vasiṣṭha about the welfare of the inhabitants of the hermitage. Vasiṣṭha said: 'All is well here, O king, with our disciples and our attendants. But there is one thing that causes me anxiety; listen to it, O lord of men. There is a young brahmin here who has taken up residence in my hermitage. He is a man of great ascetic power, but he is very harsh and prone to anger. He does not speak to anyone, nor does he show respect to the elders. He wanders about the hermitage at will, disturbing the animals and the birds. Because of his conduct, the other residents of the hermitage are troubled. I fear that some misfortune might befall us because of him. The king said: 'O illustrious one, I shall look after him myself. You

Having taken their seats, the sages of rigid vows were offered water for honor, as well as water for the feet and water for rinsing the mouth.
Having released the cow, the Lord of the World again offered the honey-mixture;
then the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis paid homage to the sages.
Permitted by those best of sages, all those Yādavas,
world-renowned, each took his own respective seat.

O great king, Keśava also returned to his own abode. *[Note: The line counter for verse 10 is erroneously printed after verse 9; consequently, the automatically inserted line counters for the remainder of this appendix differ from those in the printed edition.]*

While those heroic sages were seated there, the Lord of the World [spoke].
At that time, Hari spoke these words, which were full of courtesy.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, it is well that you have come to me in all my undertakings and austerities; your arrival constantly and exceedingly gladdens me."
The Yādavas and the best of sages have attained supreme joy, O brahmins; what more need be said here regarding your arrival?
O Brahmins, the family is always purified in which Brahmins have assembled;
therefore, it is not appropriate for us to ask about the purpose of your arrival here.
Nevertheless, O best of sages, our minds here are forcibly drawn toward curiosity when we are in the presence of hearing your questions. Therefore,
O brahmins, you should explain the cause exactly as it is.
Thus questioned then by the high-souled Keśava, all those brahmins spoke with palms joined in reverence to Keśava, the slayer of Keśin.
Listen, O God, Lord of the World, you who are the cause and the essence of all causes.
"O Lord of the Gods, that one named Naraka, the son of the Earth and the most excellent of Dānavas,
O Lord of the World, oppresses us along with the other Dānavas, he who is the lowest of Dānavas."
O God, those Dānavas struck down the oblation already offered and that which was yet to be offered;

And this the evil-minded one said: "I am to be worshipped," O Mādhava.
Those wicked-souled Dānavas, who fought from mountain peaks, shattered his water-pots, matted locks, and thousands of huts.
O Lord of Gods, we shall never obtain his skin as long as he remains alive.
O Lord of the World, since he has become wicked, we have gone to hell; fie upon us!
O Lord of the Gods, slay that evil-minded Dānava.
Having slain all the Dānavas of wicked prowess, protect us all.
Danu brought the wives of the sages together and led them to his own city.
"For protection, O Govinda, Lord of the World, is ever established in you."
O Hari, abiding by the conduct of a kṣatriya while dwelling in Dvāravatī,
restrain the wicked and protect the virtuous, for you are indeed beloved by the righteous.
O Lord of the World, we are distressed and have been ruined by that evil-minded one.
And this cluster of jujube fruits, O Lord Acyuta, has been brought by us for you;
it was previously enjoyed by you, O all-pervading Lord.

Having spoken thus, O great king, those sages presented before the Lord of the Universe all the burdens of the sacrifice— which had been gathered by their circle of disciples and scattered by the foremost of the Dānavas— straightway and in their entirety.
Having seen and heard this, the Lord of the Gods, his eyes clouded and copper-red with rage, thought:
"Alas, alas! A great calamity has befallen the sages of purified souls.

When the Lord of the World was overcome by anxiety, he thought of protection for himself.
Then the sages, free from envy, bowed down to the Lord, the lotus-eyed one,

Salutations to the primordial deity who removes the suffering of those who have sought refuge; salutations to the Lord of the World, the cause of all causes,

To him who is worthy of the virtues of the gracious Govinda.
Salutations, salutations to the God who is the eternal Self!
Salutations, salutations; O God, you are Janārdana! Salutations, salutations; O Mādhava, you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Homage, homage to you, O Dwarf, you who have the form of a dwarf!
Homage to you, O Lord, whose power originates from your own nature, O Hari! Victory to you, O Acyuta, O Ananta, O Abode of the World!
Victory to you, O Lord of the Immortals, who removes the suffering of those who have sought refuge!
Victory to you, O Lord of the Immortals; you are the eternal one.
O primordial god of the world, when you have awakened, everything has likewise always been awakened; O god, abode of the world, it is as if the world has risen from sleep.
How indeed does the world attain awakening?
This power of yours is peerless and incomparable;
its form is difficult to comprehend even for all the gods.
Even now, with undistracted mind, one seeks to know it.
O Janārdana, Brahmā is certainly devoted to you.
O Lord of the World, how are we able to know you,
O Hari, for we are submerged in the great ocean of saṃsāra and are constantly contemplating you?
O Lord, O Teacher, we strive to understand this.
Nevertheless, O Lord of all, Sovereign of the universe, and eternal regulator of the worlds, Your subtle form is constant,

We worship him, the primordial god.
O Blessed One, those virtuous ones such as Janaka and others constantly worship that very [Lord];
O Ancient One, we too perpetually honor him.
O Lord, O Primordial God, who removes the suffering of those who have sought refuge!
We bow eternally to that supreme and eternal station of yours, O abode of the worlds; we bow,
O Govinda, who are worthy of praise for your virtues.
O Lord of the world, O Cause, whose very self is the Cause!
Salutations to you, salutations to you, O God of gods, Hare, Hare!
Homage to Govinda, whose lotus feet are difficult to know and are meditated upon by yogis.

We bow to that supreme, eternal state of yours, O Viṣṇu, O Hara, which is yours alone and which yogis behold, O Lord of the World. Salutations, salutations to you, Hara, Viṣṇu; salutations to Mādhava, Keśava!
We bow to that state of yours which yogis of restrained mind constantly behold, and having attained which, they do not return.

O Govinda, we bow to that Māyā of yours which is difficult to comprehend even for those who contemplate Yoga; O Lord of the World, we bow to her depending upon whom you remain established. O Viṣṇu, O Hari, we always pay homage to her who protects the world.
O Hari, he who constantly praises you with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas— O Lord of the World, you are praised by the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
By two, by two, by three, and indeed by five, O Janārdana.
And again, O Lord of the World, O Master of the Universe, he praises You with two verses:
"We bow to You, O Lord of Gods, who have the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas."
O Lord of the World, you are the syllable *A*; likewise, you are designated as the syllable *U*.
O Viṣṇu, you are the syllable *M*; salutations to you, whose essence is the *praṇava*.
Homage ever to the Udgātṛ, homage to the Hotṛ, O Janārdana;
homage to you as the Adhvaryu, and homage to you in the form of the Sacrificer.
O Cāturhotra, salutations to you, the manifestor of the fourfold social order!
You alone are the entire world, and the world rests within you.
O Lord of the World, you are likewise the destroyer and the protector of the worlds;
and so too, O God, best among those who abide, you are the creator for the sake of their preservation.
O Lord Vāsudeva, O Viṣṇu, O Master of the World, within you is the creation;
salutations to you, the Soul of All, who abide in the hearts of all beings.
O you who are the self of all, the creator of all, the one who brings all beings into existence;
salutations to you, the self of all—again and again, salutations, salutations!
Having thus praised the Lord of the World, they prostrated themselves before Hari.
Then all the Vṛṣṇis, led by the heroes of the Śini clan,
rose from their seats and all offered salutations to Hari.
All those Yādavas there became serene in mind:
"This very Lord of the World, dwelling here, always protects us;
relying upon him, we shall all dwell happily in the city of the Yādavas."
Thinking thus, all the Yādavas then [honored] the imperishable Kṛṣṇa.
The highly fortunate ones paid homage to the Imperishable One, who had been praised by the sages.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus was the Lord of the World praised by the sages of meritorious fame.
The best of the Yādavas considered himself to have been strengthened.
Keśava, though remaining in his natural state, was filled with inner joy;
he then made a promise to those sages in the assembly of the Yadus.
"O lords of sages, having slain this wicked man along with his followers, I shall make this world free of thorns; here I am."
"Both the stationary and the moving shall soon sleep in peace;

"O Brahmins, I shall slay Mura the Dānava, and the Dānava Hatagrīva;

When the Lord of the World had thus pledged himself, the Yādavas then shouted for joy;

Then the brahmins offered their blessings to that high-souled one.

O Lord of Gods, O scorcher of enemies, may your vow be free from obstacles for the sake of the welfare of all beings; we shall depart from here. May it be well with you; we shall go to your beautiful Badarī.
Having spoken thus and having prostrated before Keśava, O great king, all those sages,
whose wealth is their austerity, departed for that Badarī with their disciples.

D6 S insert after 91.52, D3 after 91.52cd :k] The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard that their father had been slain in battle by Bhīmasena, were overcome with grief and spoke these words to one another. "Alas, O King! Alas, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra! You have been slain by Bhīmasena, who acted contrary to dharma. Having obtained sovereignty over the earth through unrighteous means, you have now met your end. O Lord of men, you who were the refuge of all kings, you have been struck down by one who was not your equal in strength or in weapons. How could he, relying on his own power, slay you who were like a god? O King, we have been deprived of our protector and our lord. Bereft of you, we shall surely perish. We have no other refuge than you, O best of men. Thus lamenting, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, their voices choked with tears, surrounded their fallen father and sat down upon the ground. Then Vidura, filled with sorrow, approached them and spoke these words: "Do not grieve, O princes, for this is the way of the world. All beings must depart according to their karma. Rise up, O lords of men, and perform the funeral rites for your father, for he has gone to the abode of Yama. Having spoken thus, Vidura assisted the king’s sons in performing the cremation of Dhṛtarāṣṭra according to the prescribed rites. Then, having offered water libations and performed the final ceremonies, they departed from the battlefield. Meanwhile, Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by his brothers and the Pāñcāla army, entered the city of Hāstinapura, which was filled with joy and adorned with banners. There, the righteous king, having established his rule, governed the earth with justice, honoring the elders and protecting his subjects. Thus ends the narrative of the fall of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the entry of the Pāṇḍavas into the capital. May there be peace. insert after 91.55, M1-3 after 91.53 :k] The king said: "O best of Brahmins, tell me truly how this great wonder occurred. How did the son of the sage become a horse? And how did he come to be born from a mare? Vyāsa said: "O King, listen with an attentive mind as I relate this ancient account, exactly as it happened, concerning the birth of that horse. In former times, O King, there was a great sage named Cyavana, the son of Bhṛgu, who was devoted to truth and self-restraint. He performed a long-term sacrifice on the banks of the Sarasvatī, accompanied by his wife and sons. While he was performing that sacrifice, O King, the gods led by Indra came there to see him. Then, O King, the Aśvins, seeing that great sage engaged in the sacrifice, approached him and spoke these words: 'O Brahmin, we two have come here to receive our sacrificial portion. Grant us our share of the oblation. Cyavana said: 'You two are excluded from the sacrifice of the gods. You are not worthy of a share in the sacrificial offerings. The Aśvins said: 'We are the physicians of the gods. We restore youth to those who have grown old and cure the sick. Cyavana said: 'Even if you were the physicians of the three worlds, you would still not be entitled to a share in the sacrifice. The Aśvins said: 'We are the physicians of the gods, and we are also the lords of the world. Therefore, O best of Brahmins, grant us a share in the sacrifice. Cyavana said: 'If you two wish to drink Soma at my sacrifice, then take up the form of horses and enter the sacrificial ground. Vyāsa said: Having been addressed thus by the sage, O King, the two gods took the form of horses and entered the sacrificial ground. Then the gods, led by Indra, struck the two with their weapons as they stood there in the form of horses. Struck by the gods, the two fell down on the earth, their bodies covered in blood, looking like two crimson lotuses. Seeing them fallen, the sage Cyavana, filled with anger, created a terrible army of Rākṣasas. Then the gods, seeing that army of Rākṣasas, fled in all directions, terrified by the power of the sage's wrath. Indra himself, seeing that army of Rākṣasas, went to the abode of Brahmā and reported everything to the Grandfather. Brahmā, having heard the words of the gods, went to the hermitage of Cyavana and spoke these words to the sage: 'O best of Brahmins, do not be angry. Be pacified. Spare the gods. For the gods are your guests. Cyavana said: 'O Lord of the World, if you are pleased with me, then let these two drink Soma at my sacrifice. This is my firm resolve. Brahmā said: 'O best of Brahmins, I am pleased with you. Let these two drink Soma at your sacrifice. I grant your wish. Vyāsa said: Having obtained that boon from the Grandfather, the sage Cyavana, O King, joyfully allowed the two to drink the Soma. Then, O King, the two gods, having drunk the Soma, rose up and shone with splendor, their forms restored to their original state. The two gods, having regained their own forms, were delighted and spoke these words to the great sage Cyavana: 'O best of Brahmins, we are satisfied with your conduct and your self-restraint. Choose a boon from us according to your heart's desire. Cyavana said: 'Let my wealth be inexhaustible, and let me be able to summon the Aśvins whenever I wish. Furthermore, let my body be free from old age and disease. The Aśvins said: 'O Brahmin, your wealth shall be inexhaustible, and you shall summon us at will. Your body shall be free from old age and disease for
With many thousands of arrows he struck Puruṣottama;

He pierced the joy of the Yadus with a thousand iron arrows.

The son of Devakī pierced the Dānava with six iron arrows (nārācas),
and the Dānava also pierced the Lord of the World with seven shafts.
Those two, eager for battle, waged a most terrible war,
just as Śambara and Vāsava did of old in the battle between the gods and the asuras,
and like the most dreadful combat between Rāma and Rāvaṇa on earth.

then Garuḍa was struck by that evil-minded Naraka.

while Vāsudeva looked on, he bled profusely and horribly. Struck on his wing, the bird trembled again and again.

and the Lord of the World trembled like an elephant struck by a goad.

then began a battle with the evil-minded Naraka.
With iron shafts, crescent-headed arrows, and well-sharpened bhallas,

cut through the bow of that evil-minded Naraka as well with a sharp arrow.

Then, O King, Naraka took up a club and brandished it;
he hurled it at her, but she struck it down mid-air.

"Stay here for now, O Goddess; you are weary from fatigue, O fair-faced one.

An weapon world-renowned and worshipped by the hosts of celestial sages,

he struck with that blazing, whirled, and sharpened wheel.
The mighty-armed Lord of the World, honored by all the worlds, cut Narakāsura’s heart in two while everyone in the world looked on.
