Janamejaya said:
O best of sages, [tell me] the auspicious account of the manifestation in Mathurā.
[M4 omits the reference; T1–3 G1.3–5 M4 insert after the reference;
M4 before line 1; G after line 4: [The text to be translated follows here.]
How did the divine son of Devakī seize the celestial tree?
O Teacher, tell me that quickly; how was Hari tireless in this?
Indeed, even while listening, I do not attain satiety regarding the wise Kṛṣṇa.
Tell me all the virtuous deeds and conduct of Kṛṣṇa while he was living in Dvārakā after taking a wife, for everything is known to you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Janamejaya, descendant of Bharata, listen now to the wonderful life-story of Kṛṣṇa after he had taken a wife— a story worthy of that very Lord.
Having taken a wife, the highly energetic and majestic Vāsudeva went to Mount Raivataka,
O King, accompanied by Queen Rukmiṇī.
Honoring Rukmiṇī at the conclusion of her fast,
Madhusūdana himself went forth, desiring to gratify the brahmins.
The princes, his sons and brothers, set out for that place,
dispatched by Vāsudeva with the permission of Nārada.
And sixteen thousand women followed that wise one,
O King, by means of a supreme supernatural power that was truly worthy of Viṣṇu himself.
Then, there, Adhokṣaja granted the desires of the twice-born who were seekers,
ever devoted to dharma, and bards who spoke pleasing words.
O joy of the Kurus, [they were born] from those of auspicious names and lineages, great performers of meritorious deeds, and pure through their ancestral, Vedic, and sacrificial rites.
Having gratified the twice-born with their desired objects, Hari,
who is beloved by the virtuous and devoted to dharma, satisfied his kinsmen according to their merit.
And at the conclusion of the fast, the Blessed One spoke with particular emphasis.
{Vaiśampāyana said:}
Once, while Janārdana was dwelling in the house of Rukmiṇī,
he held his beloved wife Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, in high esteem.
While that Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable luster was dwelling there with his wife,
seated together with Rukmiṇī, the sage Nārada approached him.
Then Keśava, the one whose self is immeasurable, having arrived, honored the Sage according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures, like the younger brother of Indra.
O Bhārata, that sage, the most worthy of worship among the virtuous, being thus honored by Vāsudeva,
gave a flower from the Pārijāta tree to Kṛṣṇa.
Hari gave that flower from the king of trees to Rukmiṇī;
for she, standing by the side of Kṛṣṇa, became the wife of that best of men.
Having accepted that flower, the blameless one,
who was the source of desire and followed Kṛṣṇa’s hint, placed it upon her head, which was adorned with stainless leaves.
Rukmiṇī, who was as enchanting as Nārāyaṇa— the very essence of beauty in the three worlds—
then shone all the more with that flower.
Then the sage Nārada, the son of Brahmā, spoke thus to her:
"O Goddess, O devoted wife, this single flower is indeed suitable for you."
This flower is adorned in every way by its association with you;
and you, O lady of firm vows, are considered by me to be worthy of this flower.
O lovely woman, for one who is endowed with auspicious virtues and is ever devoted to her husband,
this flower remains perpetually unfading.
For a period of one year, that best of speakers, who knows the proper time and is esteemed for his virtues,
gave even desired perfumes.
O Goddess, this flower bestows both cold and heat as desired;
O Goddess, it also flows with the excellent juices wished for by the mind.
O woman of excellent complexion, when it is used, it bestows good fortune;
likewise, it causes desired fragrances that promote growth to flow forth.
"And whatever flowers you desire, O Queen,
the king of trees will provide those very blossoms for you."

This very [practice] is the installation of fortune; likewise, it bestows righteousness upon the righteous, and when constantly maintained in what is auspicious, it does not place the mind in what is inauspicious.
Whatever complexion you desire, it shall all maintain for you;
whether it be very slight or even gross, it shall be according to your will.
O lotus-eyed one, this [ointment] removes unpleasant odors, increases excellent fragrances,
and performs the function of a lamp at night.
He will offer garlands of *saṃtānaka* flowers, wreaths, or unfading garments and the like; he will provide excellent flower-pavilions and other such things by mere thought.
Whether it be hunger, thirst, exhaustion, or even old age,
O Goddess, these shall be subject to your own will while you maintain this [vow].
And he will also provide for you, as you think of them, songs that are like the Anugītā,
along with very sweet musical instruments that are pleasing to you.
O Goddess, when a full year has passed, this flower shall return from your presence; by that agreement, the best of trees will depart.
This is indeed the work of Pārijāta; may you be blessed, O radiant one!
It was created by the Creator himself for the sake of honoring the enemies of the asuras.
Umā, the beloved of the best of gods, the virtuous daughter of Himācala,
that sovereign lady, O radiant one, should always wear these flowers.
Aditi, along with Paulomī, Mahendrāṇī, Surasā, Tāraṇī, Sāvitrī the mother of the Vedas, and Śrī, who is exalted by all virtues; HV App I, 29.67–68.
Likewise, the wives of the gods, other gods, and the Vasu deities—the year is the supreme time for all of them; of this there is no doubt.
"You indeed abide in the midst of sixteen thousand women;
O Bhoja-nandinī, I know you to be the beloved of Vāsudeva."
O beloved of the Lord of All, all your co-wives are endowed with every virtue;
yet today, O beautiful lady, you have been drenched by them with the sprinkling of contempt.
Today your good fortune has become manifest, and your glory is now irresistible,
since the slayer of Madhu has bestowed upon you this mandāraka flower.
Today the goddess Sātrājitī, of excellent complexion, will come to know herself;
for though she is truly fortunate, she always considered herself richly endowed with good fortune.
Then Sāmba’s mother Gāndhārī and the other wives of that great-souled one,
their desires having been fulfilled, shall today become free from longing, having attained the excellence of good fortune.
"O Queen, today your victorious chariot, the sole vehicle of good fortune, has set forth;
it is one that cannot be conquered even by thousands of chariots of desire."
Today I understand, O most beautiful one,
that in every way you are the second self of Kṛṣṇa among the Bhojas, O noble lady.
O beloved of Hari, because Acyuta gave you the entire treasure of the three worlds, you have attained this supreme gift of life.
O lord of men, when Nārada had thus spoken these truthful words,
the servants stationed there, who had been sent by Satyabhāmā, heard them.
O Lord of the People, having seen her and those other queens and co-wives, Nārada spoke with particular distinction regarding her.
And having heard that entirely from the female servants, it was then made public within Viṣṇu’s inner apartments due to the nature of women.
Then, from ear to ear, the goddesses everywhere joyfully discussed, as if it were a popular rumor, the extraordinary excellence arising from Rukmiṇī’s virtues.
"Is this the mother of a son? and "Is this the eldest?"—thus did the women of Damodara generally exclaim with joy as they gathered together.
But she could not endure that manifestation of her co-wife’s good fortune and virtues;
"Alas! How great is the arrogance of this son of the Yadavas!"—thus she thought, having come before him.
Satyabhāmā was the constant beloved of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor.
Endowed with beauty and youth, the queen, proud of her own good fortune and full of self-conceit,
fell under the sway of jealousy as soon as she heard [the news].
Casting aside her beautiful saffron-colored garment, she of the pure smile took up two white robes dyed with great silver-gold.
Casting off her saffron-scented garment,
she of the pure smile took up a single, most white silk cloth with a mind agitated by rage.
Like the flame of a fire, she increased as her fuel was augmented.
Burning with the increasing fire born of envy, as if her radiance had departed,
she was filled with wrath and entered the secluded chamber of anger.
She entered him like a star entering a cloud laden with rain.
Having tied upon her forehead a silk cloth as white as the snowy moon— a mark of her anger toward her beloved— the queen moistened its border with saffron.
Having smeared herself with red sandalwood paste.
Remembering [it] again and again with her head trembling in anger,
she sat down according to the rule upon a bed with a long pillow, having removed [her ornaments].
Her ornaments were fastened upon her single braid of hair.
Being obstructed by her noble lineage— which was incompatible with the status of a servant— and being entreated [by him],
she crushed that lotus.
Sighing again and again with her curved eyebrows, she scratched herself with her fingernails.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Knowing that the sage was seated, Keśava, together with Rukmiṇī, [approached him].
He of immeasurable self, the doer of all, emerged by means of a designation.
He went quickly indeed to the great residence of Satyabhāmā,
which had been constructed by Viśvakarman on the lovely site of Raivataka.
Knowing that the daughter of Satrājit was full of pride, beloved, and dearer to him than his own life, Viṣṇu entered her presence as if with great slowness.
As if imagining that the queen was angry out of affection,
the joy of the Yadus, trembling with fear, entered very slowly.
Having told Dāruka, "Stay at the gateway," and having appointed Pradyumna for the purpose of attending to Nārada, he entered.
Then he saw his beloved from afar, situated in the chamber of anger,
standing in the midst of her maidservants, sighing repeatedly out of wrath.
Having pressed a lotus, licked by the tips of her claws, against the lotus of her face,
she sighed and dallied with it again and again.
With her foot slightly contracted at the toes, she pressed against the earth;
then, placing her face upon her back, she laughed again and again.
Furthermore, having placed her lotus-face perpetually upon his lotus-hand,
he gazed at Vinatā, whose every limb was beautiful, who was meditating, and whose eyes were like lotuses.
Dejected, with all her limbs beautiful, the lotus-eyed woman remained lost in thought.
Taking fresh sandalwood paste from the hand of her maidservant,
the blameless woman applied it to her heart, striking it mercilessly once again.
Rising again from her bed and falling down again and again—
Hari beheld those various gestures of his beloved and others as well.
When she covered her face and laid her head upon the pillow,
Janārdana, thinking "this is the opportunity," [acted accordingly].
Having commanded his servants, "I am one who must not be named," he followed her with hurried steps and cautious movement.
Standing by his side, he took up a fan;
he fanned him gently with a breeze and laughed softly, as it were.
Perfumed by contact with that tree whose flowers were fully blossomed,
the Blessed One bore a divine fragrance, difficult for mortals to obtain.
Having smelled that most wonderful fragrance, Satyā was filled with amazement; she uncovered her face and asked, "What is this? (HV App. I, 29.151–152).
Having safely emerged from behind and seeing no god, she was greatly amazed;
then she questioned her maidservants regarding the source of that fragrance.
When questioned, they remained silent; falling to the ground on their knees, they then stood with their faces cast downward and their palms joined in reverence.
Having never before seen such a thing, it releases its fragrance to the earth;
how indeed has this particular scent of hers arisen?
Thinking, "What could this be?", she looked all around;
then the goddess suddenly beheld Keśava, the creator of the worlds.
"It is fitting," she said then, her eyes suddenly clouded with tears;
drenched as if by wrath, she became filled with affection.
Then that beautiful woman, her lovely lips quivering, sighed with her face cast downward;
for a moment, the auspicious one with dark-cornered eyes stood with her gaze fixed elsewhere.
Knitting his left eyebrow and properly raising his eyes,
he placed his face in his hand and said to Hari, "You shine."
From her eyes flowed water born of the anger of love,
like dew-drops from the petals of two lotuses.
Having leaped up, the water that had fallen from his lotus-like mouth,
the lotus-eyed one quickly caught with both hands.
Then, as the water fell upon his chest, the lotus-eyed god, marked with the Śrīvatsa, wiped away the tears born from the eyes of his beloved and spoke these words:
"O dark-eyed one, O beautiful woman, for what reason does water flow from your eyes,
O lovely lady, like water from two lotuses?"
Does your face bear the beauty of the full moon at dawn and of the lotus at midday? Your form is truly enchanting to my mind.
"For what reason, O lady of beautiful hips, do you not accept this saffron-colored garment and this great gold, but instead accept only a white garment?"
These two garments of yours, O beloved, are made of great silver and saffron; for since your arrival among the gods, white clothing is no longer desired by you, my dear.
Moreover, O fair-limbed one, tell me why your body is without ornaments;
and why, O woman of excellent complexion, has the place for painting been covered?
O lady of lovely appearance, why is your forehead adorned with a white silken cloth and served by fragrant sandalwood paste?

"O lady with long-cornered eyes and full breasts, beloved of my heart! For what reason, O dear one, do you suppress my luster and the radiance of my face, and why do you cause my mind such extreme distress?"
The sandalwood paste spread across your cheeks,
having attained the status of a rival to the decorative leaf-designs (*patralekhā*), does not shine very brightly.
Your neck, though adorned with jewels and pearls, does not shine;
it is like the indistinct autumnal sky when devoid of planets and stars.
Why do you not speak to me today with a smile like the full moon,
speaking little, happily, and fragrant as a blue lotus?
Why indeed do you not look at me even with the corner of your eye?
You are merely shedding tears like a rain-cloud of collyrium, accompanied by sighs.
Enough with weeping, O high-minded lady, you who are dark as a blue lotus! Do not let water, stained by collyrium, release its enemy from your face.
"O Goddess, since I am known in the world as your servant,
why do you not command me as before, O lady of excellent complexion?"
"What unpleasant thing have I done to you, O goddess, O passionate lady,
by which you distress yourself so excessively, O beautiful one?"
"In thought, in deed, or in word, I do not transgress against you;
O lady with every limb beautiful, I tell you this truth in every way."
"Indeed, O citizen, I have not said anything a second time regarding what is mine."
O beautiful one, I have great respect for all other women;
however, except for you, I have neither affection nor respect for any others.
"O you who resemble the daughter of a god, know that this is my firm resolve: 'May Madana, who is mine, never abandon me while I am alive.'"
Know for certain that my mind is eternally and perfectly steadfast in you.
Patience and the other virtues exist in the earth, while sound and the others are qualities in the ether;
fragrance is a quality of the earth, and sound is likewise a quality of the sky.
Surely my affection for you, who possess the luster of the interior of a lotus, is likewise firm.
As splendor is in fire, as divine radiance is in the sun,
and as eternal beauty is in the moon, so is my affection for you.
To Janārdana, who was speaking thus and was dear to her, the fortunate Satyabhāmā spoke softly, wiping the tears from her eyes.
"O Lord, my mind has always been that 'you are mine';
today, however, I have realized that you are indeed common to all in your affection."
Previously, I did not understand that the passage of time is impermanent;
today I comprehend the entire course of the world to be unstable.
Having observed the entire course of events today, I either perceive it thus, or perhaps I know it for certain.
"This second birth of mine is, in every respect, for the sake of immortality;
what is the use of much speaking here? O Acyuta, your heart knows [my intent]."
I perceive that your sweetness is like mere words;
your affection for me is feigned, while it is not so toward another.
"O Supreme Person, you who have adopted a deceitful course of conduct despise me, though you know me to be upright in nature and devoted to you in every way."
Indeed, this much is sufficient: that which was to be seen has been seen today, or likewise that which was to be heard has been heard; the fruit of affection has now been witnessed.
But if I am worthy of your favor, you ought to grant me permission;
O Supreme Person, having made this firm resolve, I shall practice supreme austerity.
For women, austerity or vows performed according to the will of their husband indeed bear fruit;
however, whatever is performed against the husband's will is truly fruitless.
Having spoken thus, the beautiful Satī once again shed tears born from her eyes; the auspicious woman took them up and drank them from the one clad in yellow garments.
Placing the edge of her garment over her mouth, she of the pure smile [spoke].
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: O Bhārata, Nārāyaṇa then spoke again to Satyabhāmā.
Out of affection, he spoke to the angry and proud Satī.
"O lotus-eyed one, this grief seems to burn my very limbs;
what is the cause by which you are so exceedingly distressed?"
"I adjure you by my life:
tell me if there is no transgression, O lady beautiful in every limb, if there is anything to be heard by a devoted husband."
Then Satyā, remaining with her face cast downward, spoke to her husband— who was steadfast in his vow of truth— with a voice faltering with tears.
O giver of honor, O slayer of Keśin, that auspiciousness which was formerly established by you alone for me in this world, O you of stainless-petal eyes, is now renowned.
"O God, because you move [within me], I bear your head;
proud as I am, I am in every way desirable among all women."
"Thus today I shall become an object of ridicule for my co-wives and for the people," she thought,
having heard from various attendants here and there that this was indeed the truth.
That *pārijāta* flower which Nārada gave to you, it is said, was given by you to a beloved person; I have been cast aside by you.
Indeed, by the gift of such an extraordinary jewel,
you have made manifest your excessive affection and great esteem for her.
It is said that Nārada praised your beloved in your very presence;
and you, indeed, heard that eulogy of your beloved with great joy.
If she was indeed to be praised by Nārada in your presence,
why was this unfortunate person made to repeat her words?
O Lord, if there is to be regret after having given the essence of my affection, then grant me permission; be gracious to me so that I may perform ascetic penance.
O lotus-eyed one, I would not have believed it even in a dream had I not heard of this other event that has occurred while you were looking on.
"O God, let his desire indeed be fulfilled for that sage of incomparable splendor; however, my indignation lies in this: that you were present there."
"You have said that in this world the virtuous live for the sake of honor;
since that is so, I do not wish to live, deprived of honor."
Since my protection lay with him, fear has come upon me today;
he who protected me from all sides does not protect me now.
"Alas! To what destiny shall I go, O Lord, having been abandoned by you, O All-pervading One?
Bereft of you, I shall surely go the way of the night-lily."
"What have I done out of delusion, both pleasing and displeasing to the lords,
that I, who was once dear to you, O giver of honor, have now become unwelcome?"
How shall I, who was once beloved, behold again that mountain Raivataka, ever variegated with spring blossoms, now that I have become unloved?
How indeed could I, being unfortunate, endure this pure wind, mingled with the songs of cuckoos and carrying the fragrance of flowers? How could I, an ill-fated woman, endure it?
"O Lord, having enjoyed water-sports with you in my lap upon the great ocean,
how have I come to such misfortune that I can no longer even behold the sea?"
"Know me to be Sātrājit’s beloved wife; there is no other woman dear to me besides you.
"Where has that gone? you said, or rather, who will remember it?
"You have spoken the truth to me; I certainly think it cannot be otherwise. **HV App. I, 29.277**10:1
For my mother-in-law looked upon me, Nandinī, with great respect;
surely the queen has been treated with contempt by you and proclaimed as unfortunate.
O giver of honor, why does the god not look upon me constantly, even though my love for him is hidden yet so very tender, and I am equal to other women?
O subduer of enemies, I did not know you to be a gambler or a rogue;
today you are known for what you are—a fickle partisan and a deceiver of people.
"O King, you have been discovered with effort through your voice, complexion, gestures, and appearance.
You thief, you are known; you are a rogue whose side is sweet only in words."
Then the god Hari spoke with conciliatory words to the queen Sātrājitī, who was thus under the sway of jealousy and full of resentment.
"Do not speak thus, O lotus-petal-eyed one; tell me, my mistress, my beloved.
What is the use of much speaking here? Know me to be yours."
O Goddess, that *pārijāta* flower was placed by me before her;
the sage Nārada, performing deeds without weariness, acted thus to please me.
Out of courtesy and consideration, he gave it; of this there is no doubt.
Be gracious, O lady of pure smiles, and forgive me for this one transgression.
"O highly irascible one, if you desire the flowers of the *pārijāta* tree, then I shall give them to you, O fair-hipped lady; I tell you this truly."
Having brought the Pārijāta, the lord of trees, from the abode of heaven,
I shall establish it in your home for as long as you desire.
Having been addressed thus by Hari, the beloved of Hari replied:
"If that tree can indeed be brought here, O Acyuta..."
For this anger, once wiped away, would be of great benefit to me;
O Adhokṣaja, I would become superior to all women.
"So be it; let this be the first option," said the peerless god Madhusūdana, the inexhaustible source of the world.
When Kṛṣṇa had said "So be it," Satyabhāmā— the beloved of the slayer of Kaṃsa and the one desired by the virtuous— rejoiced, O conqueror of assemblies.
Then the Lord of the World, the Master of All, the Creator of All Beings, who grants all desires to the virtuous, bathed and performed all his necessary duties.
And having bathed, O King, the god meditated upon the divine sage Nārada;
at the conclusion of his bath, that best of sages arrived at the great ocean.
O lord of men, when he had arrived, Adhokṣaja, whose nature is dharma and who is the refuge of the virtuous,
honored him according to the prescribed rites along with Satyabhāmā.
Sātrājitī herself washed the feet of the sage,
while Lord Kṛṣṇa himself then poured the water from a golden pitcher.
Then Keśava,
the teacher of the world, being self-restrained, prepared supreme food for the sage who was seated comfortably.
The sage of noble intellect,
the best among speakers, partook of that which was respectfully offered by the Creator of the World, being filled with supreme faith.
Having sipped water and being thus satisfied, he then bestowed blessings upon the Lord;
and Keśava accepted them with a joyful heart.
Then Nārada, extending his right hand which was wet with water, spoke to the lotus-eyed queen, the daughter of Satrājit, as she stood bowed before him.
O Goddess, remain a devoted wife just as you are now;
and by the power of your asceticism, may you become even more exceptionally fortunate.
Having been addressed thus by the chief of sages, Satyabhāmā, the beloved of Hari,
rose up filled with great joy, O lord of men.
Having then received permission from that best of sages, the wise Kṛṣṇa,
whose prowess is immeasurable, partook of the remains of the sacrificial food.
Then, O Bhārata, having performed her necessary duties and with her husband’s permission, Satyabhāmā also entered the inner apartments with joy.
Then, having emerged with the very permission of Kṛṣṇa,
the goddess stood by the side of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa after having paid him homage.
Then, having sat for a moment, Nārada said to Kṛṣṇa:
"I take my leave of you, O Adhokṣaja; I shall go to the world of Śakra."
Having paid homage there to the first god, Īśāna Maheśvara, the celestial Gandharvas and the foremost of the Apsarases shall sing.
For this is the custom, O Lord, month after month in the abode of Mahendra:
the dance of the Gandharvas for the sake of worshipping the God of gods.
The omnipresent Lord of gods, Soma, together with his excellent attendants, vanished;
yet he beheld what was performed with devotion by the chief of the immortals, the destroyer of mountains.
O one of great splendor, may you be blessed; yesterday I was invited to give a flower from the Pārijāta, the king of trees and high-souled sovereign.
"O Lord, that which has been brought from heaven for your sake by me is indeed fit for the enjoyment of a god,
for it originates from the king of trees."
O lotus-eyed one, that tree is constantly beloved by Śacī;
when it is worshipped perpetually, it indeed brings about good fortune.
"Therefore, I gathered these flowers specifically for the sake of your good fortune."
Then, for the sake of performing meritorious deeds, the great tree Pārijāta was created by the high-souled Kaśyapa, who is ever devoted to righteousness, for Aditi.
It is said that Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci and a treasure-house of asceticism, having been gratified by the immensely radiant Āditya, invited him to choose a boon.
She said, "O best of sages, tell me how I may become fortunate,
well-adorned according to my desire with all ornaments."
O one whose wealth is asceticism, may singing and dancing be to my liking;
O treasure of austerities, may I always remain a maiden through my penance.
May I always be free from passion and devoid of sorrow;
may I likewise be devoted to my husband and possessed of a virtuous character.
Then, out of a desire to please Aditi, he created the *pārijāta* tree,
which was covered with flowers that grant all desires and emit divine fragrances.
Always visible with its three branches, it captivates the minds of all beings;
all kinds of flowers are seen upon that very great tree.
One woman of extraordinary beauty wears such flowers as these;
another wears many-colored ones, and yet another likewise wears lotuses.
And having extracted the *sāra* (essence) even from the *mandāra* tree, Kaśyapa [did so];
therefore, this best of trees has attained preeminence over all others.
The illustrious one gave the great Pārijāta tree to Aditi;
then, having fastened it there, the auspicious lady presented Kaśyapa.
Aditi [acted] for the sake of my merit and likewise for the sake of my good fortune.
Then, for the sake of merit, Aditya gave Kaśyapa to me;
the self-possessed one, having wound a garland of flowers around his neck, did so for the sake of merit.
"Kaśyapa, whose wealth is his asceticism, was released by me through a ransom;
likewise, Indra was given to Indrāṇī by me for the sake of her good fortune."
Soma belongs to Rohiṇī, and likewise Dhanada belongs to Ṛddhi;
thus, the Pārijāta tree bestows good fortune—of this there is no doubt.
Because it is situated on the Viṣṇupadī river, it is called Pārijāta;
and because it is joined with Mandāra flowers, it is therefore called Mandāra.
Because people, not knowing what it was, said, "What kind of wood is this?",
that great tree has ever since been known as the Kovidāra.
By these names— Mandāra, Kovidāra, and Pārijāta—
that divine tree is known, from which this most excellent flower comes.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then, as Nārada, the best of sages, was desiring to depart from there—
The Blessed Viṣṇu, whose prowess is immeasurable, said:
"O great ṛṣi, knower of the essence of dharma, O sinless one, having gone to heaven and seen the members of the assembly of the wise god, the slayer of Tripura, you [spoke thus]."
With my permission,
O Sage, you should inform Indra (Pākaśāsana) after praising our ancient brotherhood, since you know it.
O best knower of dharma, that tree Pārijāta which the blessed Kaśyapa, the foremost of sages, formerly created for the sake of pleasing the Ādityas— 382–383.
That best of trees bestows merit and great good fortune;
you previously gave that gift of the best of trees during your vow.
"O best of immortals, having heard that what was given for the sake of Dharma by the goddesses who are ever-devoted to Dharma [is inexhaustible], my wives, O Lord, desire to give as well."
For the sake of merit, for the sake of the duty of giving, and indeed for my own pleasure,
he brought the great Pārijāta tree from Dvāravatī.
"Furthermore, you shall lead him to heaven for that gift;
thus indeed should the Blessed One, the slayer of Bala, be addressed by you."
O best of sages, you must exert such effort that the Lord of the Gods might grant you the Pārijāta, the finest of trees.
In this matter, O ascetic, let us first consider the qualities of a messenger;
for I believe that the perfection of all tasks rests upon you.

Thus addressed by Nārāyaṇa, the venerable seer Nārada, whose wealth is his asceticism, laughed and spoke these words to the slayer of Keśin: Thus addressed by Nārāyaṇa, the venerable seer Nārada, whose wealth is his asceticism, laughed and spoke these words to the slayer of Keśin.
"Very well, I shall speak thus to the lord of the gods, the chief of the Yadus;
yet the lord of the deities will by no means give up the Pārijāta tree."
Having first cast Mount Mandara, the best of mountains, into the ocean by the Dānavas and the gods, the Pārijāta tree was then brought forth.
O Janārdana, in the past, even Hara, the creator of the worlds, sent you to bring Mandara, the best of mountains, as well as the Pārijāta tree.

"So be it," O sinless one, was the boon granted by Mahādeva;
yet Pārijāta was not taken to Mandara, the mountain of variegated caves.
O mighty-armed one, in former times that Pārijāta tree was spared by Mahendra under the pretext that it was Śacī’s pleasure-grove.
For the sake of Umā, Hara created the Pārijāta grove,
one *gavyūti* in extent, within a single cave of Mount Mandara.
O Kṛṣṇa, the rays of the sun do not enter that best of mountains;
nor do the cool rays of the moon, nor indeed the wind, O Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, in that place, cold and heat occur according to one's will for the daughter of the mountain;
for that forest is self-luminous through the splendor of Mahādeva.
O enhancer of the Yadu clan, with the exception of Mahādeva together with his attendants and myself,
no one else ever enters that divine forest by any means whatsoever.
There, O Vārṣṇeya, pārijāta trees flow forth on all sides,
as do all the most excellent jewels that one has indeed desired in one's mind.
The Gaṇas enjoy those [offerings] belonging to the most excellent great-souled ones,
O Keśava, by the command of the God of gods, the Lord of the world.
Their fruit is many times greater than that of the *pārijāta* tree, as is their wealth;
likewise their self-confidence, their splendor, and their qualities are of manifold excellence.
And those trees, O Keśava, together with their preeminent [attendants], constantly attend upon the embodied god Soma, whose banner bears the bull.
Endowed with fierce splendor, freed from sorrows and filled with happiness,
those trees on Mount Mandara were indeed beloved by the Daughter of the Mountain.
There entered the terrible and mighty Daitya named Andhaka, who,
arrogant due to the granting of a boon, was fixed in his evil resolve.
He was slain by Hara, the God of gods and slayer of enemies;
though he was invincible to all beings, he was ten times stronger than Vṛtra.
"Thus, O lotus-eyed one, the thousand-eyed god will give you the Pārijāta tree with difficulty; I tell you this as the truth."
O Kṛṣṇa, that tree of boons was always accompanied by the goddess Śacī; it granted all desires to Indra, who possesses immeasurable power.
Vāsudeva said:
O sage, that was rightly done by the wise Mahādeva,
in that he did not take away that tree long ago, making Śacī the cause.
He is the eldest of all beings, the creator of the worlds, the source, and the imperishable; it is my conviction that he has established what is appropriate for both the higher and the lower realms.
"I am the youngest of the god who destroys all forces with his might; O Blessed One, I am to be cherished by you in every way, like Jayanta, O best of beings."
In every way, O Lord, you who are rich in asceticism and are indeed capable, should exert yourself through many extensive means for the sake of my pleasure.
"O Sage, for the sake of merit, I have made a vow in the presence of Satyabhāmā:
'O Lord, I shall bring the Pārijāta tree here from heaven.'"
"How could I possibly utter that falsehood, O ascetic?
For never before, O sinless Brahmin, have I spoken an untruthful word.
If my vow were broken, there would indeed be a dissolution of the worlds."
O best of sages, since all the worlds endowed with the qualities of dharma must be protected by me in their stability, how indeed could I speak an untruth?
Neither the hosts of gods and gandharvas, nor the rākṣasas,
nor the asuras, nor indeed the yakṣas and pannagas [could do so].
Neither the hosts of gods nor Gandharvas, nor indeed Rākṣasas or Asuras;
neither Yakṣas nor Piśācas, nor even all the Pannagas [could do so].
O great sage, those who strive to subvert my vow live for a long time in happiness.
If that Lord of the Immortals, when being entreated by you, does not grant the Pārijāta tree,
then [the earth] will have its ointments crushed by Śacī.
I shall hurl my mace at the chest of Purandara.
If, after being thus addressed with conciliation,
he does not yield the tree when entreated, then,
having understood me to be entirely resolute in every way—
Indeed, you too must certainly reach a decision in this matter.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the powerful sage Nārada, having gone to the abode of Mahendra...
He stayed there that night and witnessed a great festival.
There dwell the high-souled Ādityas and the Vasus, the best of gods,
as well as wise royal sages who have gone to heaven by means of their auspicious deeds.
Nāgas, yakṣas, siddhas, cāraṇas, and those whose wealth is asceticism;
and brahman-sages by the hundreds, as well as celestial rishis and manavas.
The high-souled Suparṇas and the mighty Maruts,
as well as hundreds of other hosts of celestial beings, have assembled there.
Above all of them stood the god Soma, the Great Lord (Maheśvara),
of immeasurable prowess, surrounded by his own hosts.
Surrounded by divine sages and the best of munis, he is the creator of all beings;
for thousands of other kalpas, there is no end to them.
Those who constantly worship [them]— the gods who resemble the lords of the gods,
those who know the self yet are blinded by pride, and those who stand upon the path of dharma.
And the Rudras and Kāśyapas worshipped the god, O Bhārata;
as did the blessed Skanda, son of Rudra, and Gaṅgā, the best of rivers.
Arciṣmān, Tumburu, and Bhāri, the best among speakers—
these leaders of the gods of gods are indeed endowed with ascetic power.
O King, all the hosts of gods follow these [sages],
who are constant in dharma, constant in austerity, and who have taken refuge in the path of the virtuous.
But those human beings who, seeking merit, worship the gods— O King, the immortals likewise worship them, seeking merit in return.
O descendant of Kuru, those who have performed renunciation for the sake of the ancestral rites of the gods, who are devoted to sacred study, and who always observe their religious vows;
There, O King, the illustrious Citraratha, the lord of the Gandharvas,
joyfully played divine musical instruments together with his sons—
namely Ūrṇāyu, Citrasena, Hāhā, and likewise Hūhū.
Ḍambara, Tumburu, and other members of his host sang as well.
Urvaśī, Pūrvacitti, Hemā, and Rambhā, O Bhārata;
Hemadantā, Ghṛtācī, and likewise Sahajanyā.

The self-possessed Lord, the God, the Master of the World, graciously accepted that worship; satisfied with Śakra’s conduct, he departed. When the Lord of Beings had gone, all the kings returned as they had come.
The gods, honored by Mahendra, returned to their own abodes.
Then, after everyone had departed, the sage Nārada approached Purandara as he sat at ease together with his own assembly members.
Indra rose up and honored that ascetic rich in penance;
he offered him a seat made of kuśa grass, which was equal to his own throne.
Then Nārada, possessed of great splendor, spoke thus to Mahendra:
"O best of immortals, I am a messenger of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable majesty."
Having been sent by that high-souled one for a certain purpose, I have come from Ānarta to remove the distress of him whose splendor is sinless.
Having then addressed the sage with pleasing and heart-pleasing words,
the blessed Lord Pākaśāsana, being greatly delighted, spoke.
"O Sage, tell me quickly what that best of men said;
indeed, it has been a long time since we were remembered by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
Speak those words, O best of the upholders of dharma, which are pleasant and heart-pleasing."
Nārada said:
"O best of men, I went to Dvārakā to see your brother, the younger sibling of Indra, the lord of the great gods, who brings glory to the descendants of Kaśyapa."
I then beheld that subduer of enemies,
the hero, seated upon Mount Raivataka together with Rukmiṇī, like the bull-bannered Śiva with Umā.
O sinless one, O Lord of the Gods, I gave him a flower from the Pārijāta tree for the purpose of astonishing his wives of great splendor.
Seeing that flower, which fulfills many desires and grows upon the king of trees, his wives were filled with the utmost wonder.
O giver of honor, I have described to you the qualities of those flowers;
and the creation of the *pārijāta* tree was performed by Kaśyapa of exceeding splendor.
Just as Kaśyapa was given by Āditya for the sake of my merit, so too did that self-possessed man,
having wound a garland of flowers around his neck, [bestow it] for the sake of merit.
And you, O Lord of the Gods, were given by Śacī as well as by the other gods;
and how the ransom was paid by the high-souled ones, beginning with Kaśyapa.
Having heard that, his wife, one renowned as Satyabhāmā,
set her mind upon performing meritorious deeds for the sake of your younger brother, whom she held dear.
And entreated by the goddess, her husband, the lord of the hosts of gods, that righteous-souled one, O giver of honor, promised: "He shall be your younger brother."
Then the hero Viṣṇu, the best among the strong, spoke to me:
"O Lord of the chief of gods, O Creator, listen as I speak to you exactly as it is."
But the younger brother, who was to be cherished, prostrated himself and Acyuta said:
"O best of gods, cause the Pārijāta, that tree of boons, to be brought here."
O slayer of asuras, may the desire of your daughter-in-law be fruitful;
O best of the immortals, this is especially so regarding the religious duty of your daughter-in-law.
This rare auspicious one, the lord of the hosts of the world,
let mortals behold him— this auspicious being of the immortals— through my power.
Vaiśampāyana said: O descendant of Kuru, having heard the words of Vāsudeva, Mahendra then spoke these words to Nārada, the best among speakers.
"O best of the twice-born, attend to your seat; O twice-born one, you have spoken what was heard [by me].
I shall deliver a message from Viṣṇu, whose splendor is incomparable."
Then, after Nārada had sat down, Śakra, having received permission from Nārada,
took his own seat, O Lord, which was equal to that very one.
Having sat down and surveyed his own army, its prowess, and his attendants, the Lord of the Gods, the slayer of Vṛtra, then spoke to the one whose wealth is asceticism.
O great seer, having inquired after his welfare, you should speak to Janārdana on my behalf,
O knower of dharma, words that bring happiness to all beings.
After Madana, you are the Lord of the world; there is no doubt in this.
O Acyuta, the Pārijāta tree and other jewels are yours.
But you, O God, have come to the earth to remove its burden;
you, O God, have descended to the world for the sake of relieving the earth's weight.
Having assumed a human form among all beings for the sake of accomplishing his purpose.
For when you have fulfilled your vow and returned again to heaven,
O Adhokṣaja, I shall fulfill the desired wishes of your daughter-in-law.
"O Keśava, celestial jewels must not be taken to the human world for a trivial purpose; such was the rule established of old."
"O mighty one, if I were to overstep the divine order and act otherwise,
O Lord, what would the hosts of Prajāpatis say of me?"
Together with his sons and grandsons, the high-souled Brahmā established the eternal rules for all duties in the world.
"If I depart, having abandoned the path created by Prajāpati,
the wise and powerful Lord Prajāpati might even cast a curse upon me."
"For if this bridge of the boundary is broken by us,
the Daityas and others who side with the Daityas will break it without hesitation."
O giver of honor, when the Pārijāta, the lord of trees, has been led away from here on account of a woman,
the inhabitants of heaven will become dejected in mind.
Whatever enjoyments have been ordained for human beings by the Self-Existent One— may my brother be satisfied with them, seeing the revolution of time.
Even here, whatever possessions I may have in the third heaven—
O Kṛṣṇa, though staying in the third heaven, he deserves to enjoy all of that here.
Is Janārdana not cognizant of the states of being eldest or youngest? For Janārdana is indeed satiated with the enjoyment of meat and food due to his pride.
Then, having utterly abandoned the Dharma, he follows only after evil.
It is my opinion that the subjection of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa to women, if it were made public, would bring about a connection with infamy in the world.
O Nārada, that Madhusūdana has attained this human state among men and acts in such a way as to be constrained by his eldest brother.
O sinless one, there would be an insult to me by the plundering of the jewels of heaven;
indeed, an insult from one’s own kinsmen is especially contemptible.
May Madhusūdana practice virtue, wealth, and pleasure in due order,
following the duties of the virtuous established by the Lotus-born One.
"If I were to bestow the Pārijāta tree upon you from the surface of the earth,
who indeed would think much of me, starting with Paulomī?"
Having seen and touched the *pārijāta* tree upon the surface of the earth,
humans will no longer exert themselves for the sake of heaven, having seen the fruit of heaven here on the ground.
O Nārada, if mortals were to enjoy the qualities of the Pārijāta tree,
there would be no distinction between gods and humans.
Whatever action is performed there, that is experienced by men here;
those endowed with the virtues of the Pārijāta tree will not strive for the sake of heaven.
O ascetic, if the Pārijāta tree— the best of all jewels in heaven—
were always present for mortals who are equal to the gods, the world would be so at all times.
Having obtained the fruit of heaven on earth, mortals will no longer perform sacrifices;
having attained equality with the immortals, they will no longer bestow charitable gifts. It is through sacrifices, recitations, and daily rites that they constantly nourish us.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, human beings who desire heaven are full of faith.
Endowed with the virtues of the Pārijāta tree, they will not perform all of that;
we shall become devoid of splendor once they have attained that state of excellence.
From here, by means of good rain and crops, those men on earth shall live.
May they, in turn, cause us to swell with prosperity through their gifts and likewise through their sacrifices.
O knower of dharma, neither hunger nor thirst afflicts human beings there, nor do disease,
old age, death, or even passion.
Whether it be foul odors or most terrible calamities arising from karma—
what effort can they exert against one who is endowed with the virtues of the Pārijāta tree?
"In every way, O Brahmin, it is not fitting for the Pārijāta tree to be brought there";
thus should you speak to Viṣṇu, the performer of effortless deeds.
"In whatever way my brother finds satisfaction while reflecting on this,
in that very way you must act, if you desire my pleasure."
Take the necklaces, the gems, the sandalwood, the aloe-wood,
and the variegated garments, and carry them to Dvārakā for the bride.
Whatever is appropriate for mortals, Keśava desires as much as he wishes;
however, Keśava ought not to plunder heaven.
I shall give you jewels according to your desire, many and variegated ornaments; but I will by no means give the Pārijāta tree.
O Sage, I shall grant what is pleasing to the dwellers of heaven.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: O descendant of Kuru, having heard the words of the king of the gods, Nārada—
The great-souled one, skilled in speech and the foremost knower of dharma, spoke these words.
"O slayer of Bala, O mighty-armed one, I must certainly speak what is beneficial for you; I have great respect for you."
Knowing your intention, I spoke to Vāsudeva:
"Indeed, you did not previously give the Pārijāta tree even to Hara."
And I have shown him the reasons for this in brief, O sir;
yet the god did not understand them—this I tell you truly.
"The Lord God said to me: 'I am Upendra, who must always be cherished by Mahendra.
I tell you this as the truth."
Then the lotus-eyed one spoke those various replies.
Again and again, O Lord, I pointed out the reasons to him;
yet, O slayer of Vṛtra, his resolve did not turn away.
Moreover, O Madhusūdana, that god, the best of men, spoke these words to you while laughing, like Vāsava when he is as if filled with wrath.
Neither the hosts of gods and gandharvas, nor the rākṣasas,
nor the asuras, nor even the best of the pannagas,
are capable of subverting my vow.
O Sage, you are indeed capable; may it be well with you!
If that Lord of the Immortals, being thus entreated by you, does not grant the *pārijāta* tree,
then [the earth] will be stripped of its ointments by Śacī.
I shall hurl my mace at the chest of Purandara.
This is the firm resolve of your brother Upendra regarding Mahendra:
having deliberated upon what you deem to be just in this matter, do that.
O Lord of Gods, listen as I speak that which is both the truth and beneficial:
it pleases me that the *pārijāta* tree be brought to Dvārakā.
O lord of men, having been addressed thus by Nārada, the thousand-eyed Indra, overcome with rage, spoke these words clearly to Baladeva.
O ascetic, if Keśava has behaved in this manner toward me, his eldest brother and uterine sibling who am innocent, what can possibly be done now?
"O sinless Nārada, in the past he committed many hostile acts against me; yet, O blameless one, I endured them because he was my brother."
In the past, while driving Arjuna’s chariot at Khāṇḍava,
I restrained my clouds as they were extinguishing the fierce fire.
By supporting Govardhana, he has done what is displeasing to me.
Likewise, when the slaying of Vṛtra was at hand, he was chosen by me for assistance;
and having declared, "I am equal toward all beings," Vṛtra was slain by me relying upon the strength of my own arms.
O Nārada, when the gods and asuras have engaged in battles, Kṛṣṇa fights according to his own will; this is well known to you, O sage.
What is the use of saying more here? Therefore, let it proceed according to your wish.
I must not cause a division among my kinsmen; you, Nārada, are my witness.
If Keśava were prepared to hurl his mace at my chest, then Paulomī would be pitied;
what virtue, then, would be seen here?
"Our wise father, the lord Kaśyapa, has gone to dwell in the waters;
this must be told to him and to my mother Aditi."

My brother Ajita, overcome by great passion and moved by his desire for a woman, spoke thus to me, his elder: *HV_App.I,29.658–659* My brother Ajita, overwhelmed by great passion and driven by his longing for a woman, addressed these words to me, his superior.
In every way, fie on women, O Brahmin! Fie on passion (rajas) and likewise on darkness (tamas)!
Everything that is censurable should be attributed to women; fie on women, whatever they may be!
"O twice-born one, it was there that Viṣṇu reviled me thus: 'You are a slave to women.'"
O Great Sage, the lineage of Kaśyapa has not been seen by me;
nor indeed has the lineage of Dakṣa been seen, from which my mother’s birth occurred.
Neither seniority nor kingship was respected by the gods,
O Nārada, because Kṛṣṇa was indeed overcome by lustful passion.
"O sinless one, a brother is indeed superior to thousands of sons and wives;
for he who is of good conduct and endowed with knowledge—so Brahmā declared in the past."
"There is no kinsman equal to a brother; all others are merely acquired persons"—thus did my mother, my father, and Prajāpati himself say to me.
My father Kaśyapa spoke specifically regarding my brothers:
"The Dānavas, whose resolve is evil, oppose me with arrogance."
Granted, this should not be said by me, as it involves self-praise;
yet, O Brahmin, the occasion has arrived for what I shall now say here.
O best of sages, O sinless one, in former times the bowstrings of the archers among the immortals were indeed severed by the granting of boons, O high-minded one.
O great sage, in ancient times, when Viṣṇu’s head was severed by the bows of the Asuras and Dānavas, his body was supported by me.
And his head, though joined together, was severed with effort by means of fierce energy.
Having said, "I am the most distinguished among the gods," Keśava, the infallible one, O Nārada, once again strung his bow and stood there in pride.
"O Sage, O best of sages, out of affection for Viṣṇu, I held onto his body, thinking, 'What will my father or my mother say to me? (HV App. I, 29.680–681)
O Sage Nārada, I gave a portion of this very [sacrifice] to Indra and Viṣṇu;
out of affection, I look upon Kṛṣṇa, my younger brother, with love.
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, one must strike first in battles;
for I am indeed a king, and I certainly strike at the front in combat."
O sinless one, O knower of dharma, in all my manifestations I strive to protect Keśava, who has taken refuge in devotion, as if he were my own body.
"O Blessed One, having destroyed this world of mine, Viṣṇu has created,
O Sage, a superior abode above all the worlds."
"And that insult, O sage, was overlooked by me;
out of respect for my brother, I thought, 'This boy must be cherished by me.'"
"O Nārada, Govinda was not excessively scolded by his father or mother, who said, 'This boy is my son,' and 'He is the youngest.'"
There, Keśava was especially dear to his mother; we were objects of her dislike, there is no doubt, for her affection for him exceeded all else.
"He is omniscient, powerful, heroic, a worthy recipient, and likewise one who honors [others]"—
and even the meditation on him as "Keśava" has thus become false.
"Go, Nārada, and speak these words of mine to Keśava:
'Once summoned by my enemies to battle, I shall not turn back.'"
"If you so desire, then come; whatever you wish for Sahya, let it be yours.
And you, who have conquered your wife, strike first as you please!"
Then, O Janārdana, having mounted Garuḍa and become firm, strike with the discus, the Śārṅga bow, the mace, or the Nandaka sword.
"O Keśava, when struck, I shall strike back according to my strength;
alas, fie! if affection does not make me falter."
"O best of sages, as long as I have not been defeated by the wielder of the discus while engaged in battle, I shall not give up the Pārijāta tree."
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, my younger brother is challenging me, his elder.
Why should I tolerate that Hari, who is conquered by a woman?"
"O Blessed One, go this very day to Dvārakā, which is protected by Kṛṣṇa;
you must say to Acyuta: 'That dispute has been settled today.'"
"O Acyuta, you should say: 'I stand ready with all my limbs. Even if you were defeated by him by as much as half a *palāśa* leaf, [you must still say this]."
"He will not give you the Pārijāta tree," O ascetic,
this is what Madhusūdana must be told by you,
remembering my words.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, you should speak again to Acyuta for my sake, so that he may act without hesitation:
"You ought not to take away this tree here by means of illusion."
Let there be only fair combat; fie upon deceit!
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Mahendra, Nārada, the best among speakers, spoke.
In that secluded place, he spoke these words to the king of the gods.
"O Acyuta, it is certainly true that kings should be told what is pleasing; there is no doubt in this. However, when the time is right, one must speak what is beneficial even if it is unpleasant."
For they say that one who is not appointed should not have a forward-looking bias;
he indeed knows the truth regarding the courses of the world and is skilled in the knowledge of policy.
"Since you have approached me to inquire about what ought to be done and what ought not to be done when such matters arise, I shall explain them; let it be accepted if it pleases you."

Even by a friend who has not been asked, that which is beneficial should be spoken if he knows it; likewise, that which is just and timely should be said by one who does not wish for the other's downfall.
The virtuous must speak that which is beneficial even if it is unpleasant in every way;
this is the fulfillment of affection, as esteemed by the virtuous of old.

When there is falsehood, when dharma has been destroyed, or when one does not wish to listen to what is unpleasant, neither what is pleasant nor what is beneficial should be spoken; these [situations] are censured by the virtuous.
O Lord, best among those who hear, you must speak in every way; let it be heard.
And having heard it, O All-Knowing One, act upon my words which bring about one's welfare.
O Lord, the mutual dissension of brothers or friends brings about an end to their strength;
it causes them no joy, O God, and there is no doubt in this matter.

O Lord of the Gods, O best among the wise, one should understand that an action is beneficial when it is accompanied by a beneficial consequence; and having understood it as the opposite, one should avoid it.
A wise man should never undertake such an action as would cause him suffering later; this is the rule for the intelligent.
I do not perceive any auspicious result from this deed;
however, O God, Lord of the Immortals, learn what the cause of it is.
Hari is that one who dwells within the entire universe as its primary source;
he whom the wise know as the supreme Kṣetrajña beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Of that Unmanifest, the manifest portion which is the source of all existences—
of that wise one, the first deity is the Self, Viṣṇu.
The first portion of Prakṛti is the illustrious goddess Umā;
Viṣṇu, the creator of the world, who is manifest and consists of all things, is designated as female.
Rukmiṇī and his other wives are the first quality when he is manifest;
the Goddess Prakṛti is the imperishable, and Maheśvara is the god of the qualities.
O best of immortals, there is no distinction between Rudra and Viṣṇu;
for he who possesses the qualities is eternal, constant, and forever the primordial quality.
Nārāyaṇa, of great splendor, the creator of all, the nourisher of the worlds,
the enjoyer, the supreme lord, the god, the maker, Viṣṇu, the one who is beyond the senses.
O Lord of Gods, Brahmā and the other hosts of gods were created later by the Great-Souled One,
as were Mahādeva and the hosts of Prajāpatis.
Thus Viṣṇu is recited among the gods as the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa),
inconceivable, immeasurable, and likewise beyond all qualities.
In ancient times, Viṣṇu, the Great-Souled One, was propitiated by Aditi through her ascetic penance;
and she, being satisfied, was invited by him to choose a boon.
O best of gods, having been told by her, "I desire you as my son," and having recognized that the god Nārāyaṇa, Adhokṣaja, was bowing before him— 762–763.
He said to her: "In this world there is no other man equal to me;
indeed, I myself shall become your son through a portion of my own being."
This very one is the God of gods, who, out of a desire for the welfare of the world,
is Keśava— the primordial source, the lord of the universe, the creator, and the sustainer.
He has been born as the all-creating god, your brother, O Lord of the Gods;
he is Nārāyaṇa of great splendor, whom they call Upendra.
Desiring it indeed, the divine Lord Hari assumed the state of Kaśyapa;
the imperishable source of past and future beings transforms himself through various states of being.
The Lord has manifested out of a desire for the welfare of the world;
Keśava, the protector of the world, is both its creator and its destroyer in Mathurā.
And just as a sesame pod, O giver of honor, is pervaded by oil,
so too is this world pervaded by the powerful Viṣṇu.
The God who is devoted to Brahman, the Self of all, transforms himself through various states of being;
in this world, the Lord Vaikuṇṭha is beyond the qualities (guṇas) and is the creator of all beings.
Therefore, Keśava alone is worthy of worship among all the gods;
so too is the Lord Padmanābha, the omnipresent one who brings forth the creation of beings.
Ananta bears [the world] for the sake of upholding it and possesses great glory;
he is also called "Sacrifice" (Yajña) by the virtuous who proclaim the Vedas.
In the Kṛta age the Lord is white, and likewise red in the Tretā age;
in the Dvāpara he is yellow, and in the Kali age the omnipresent one is black.
"In the morning, the Kṛta Yuga belongs to me; likewise, the Tretā is in the midday period;
in the third watch it is the Dvāpara, and at twilight it is indeed the Kali."
In the course of the four ages (*caturyuga*), for the purpose of a day,
there is likewise the attainment of the four ages at every single day.
Hari, assuming a divine form, slew Hiraṇyākṣa;
Hari, in the body of a man-lion (nārasiṃha), struck down Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Having assumed the form of a boar out of a desire for the welfare of the world, this God supported the Earth as she was sinking into the waters.
Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a dwarf, conquered the entire world;
and the glorious god bound Bali with the bonds of serpents.
The highly illustrious one desired even the prosperity arising from the gods and the *dānavas*,
as well as other varieties of jewels, such as elephants and the like.
In former times, Viṣṇu, who possesses noble and supreme valor, was dependent upon you.
Janārdana slays him whose ascetic merit (*tapas*) is still incomplete;
this is the vow of the Great-Souled One, which applies even to those who behave falsely.
And for the sake of your pleasure, Govinda— the constant upholder of dharma and the refuge of the virtuous— slew the chief Dānavas who were the enemies of the gods.
Having attained the state of Rāma as well, the self-possessed one slew Rāvaṇa;
and having become a lion endowed with the power of his will, Hari slew the elephant.
For the welfare of the world, Upendra— the lord of the universe and the highest of all beings— dwells even today in human form within this world.
I have previously seen Hari with matted hair, clad in a black antelope skin, and carrying a staff;
that god, moving among the Daityas, was like a fire rising up amidst blades of grass.
I also beheld Govinda making this world— a single ocean of Dānavas—
devoid of those demons, out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
"O best of immortals, Janārdana will certainly carry the Pārijāta tree to Dvārakā; I do not speak untruth."
"Overcome by brotherly affection, O Kṛṣṇa, you will not strike;
nor, O Vāsava, will Kṛṣṇa strike you, O elder brother."
If you do not listen at all to what has been spoken by me, O Lord,
then ask those ministers of yours who are well-wishers and know the principles of policy.
O Janamejaya, having been addressed thus by Nārada,
the lord Mahendra then replied with this answer to the Teacher of the World.
"O twice-born one, you speak of Kṛṣṇa as having such power;
O sage, this has indeed been heard by me many times."
And since Kṛṣṇa is such as this, therefore, remembering the duty of the virtuous, I shall not give him that tree, even though it ought to be given.
Thinking, "One of great power should not be angry for the sake of a trivial matter," I remain established [in this state]— blessings be upon you, O Sage, endowed with all virtues.
For those who constantly listen to the elders who possess the eye of knowledge are indeed always of great power and patient endurance.
The high-souled Kṛṣṇa, the best among the upholders of dharma and a knower of righteousness, would not enter into conflict with his eldest brother for a trivial reason.
Just as Adhokṣaja granted that boon to my mother,
even so he ought to endure it for her eldest sons.
Just as Janārdana himself, desiring it, attained the status of Upendra,
so too should he show honor to his brother Indra.
Was this primacy not already established by that god in the past? Or does he desire it even now? Let Madhusūdana be the eldest.
Having observed that Balaripu was firmly resolved, Nārada,
the knower of dharma, being dismissed by the best of the gods,
departed for the city protected by the bull of the Yadus.
The ascetic Dhṛtimat went to Kuśasthalī.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having arrived at the beautiful Dvārakā, Nārada, the best of sages—
He beheld Nārāyaṇa, the best of men and the subduer of enemies.
Seated comfortably in his own home together with Satyabhāmā,
he was resplendent with a form that surpassed all other splendors.
He saw that high-souled one of firm vows contemplating that very same matter,
engaging the beautiful woman with nothing more than his words alone.
Upon seeing Nārada, the god Adhokṣaja rose from his seat and then honored him with the rites prescribed by rule.
When he was comfortably seated and rested, Madhusūdana smiled and inquired about the account concerning the Pārijāta tree.
Then the sage, whose wealth was his asceticism, related everything in detail to the younger brother of Indra,
O Janamejaya, recounting the entire speech of Indra.
Having heard all those words, Kṛṣṇa spoke to Nārada:
"O best of the upholders of dharma, I shall go to the city of Amarāvatī."
Having spoken thus, he went to the ocean accompanied by Nārada;
then, in a secluded place there, Hari gave instructions to Nārada.
"O ascetic, having gone today to the palace of Mahendra,
salute that high-souled one, the best of the immortals, and speak my words."
"O Śakra, O Lord, you ought not to stand before me in battle;
know that I am resolved upon the taking away of the Pārijāta tree."
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, Nārada went to heaven and reported what Kṛṣṇa had said to the lord of the gods, who possesses immeasurable power.
Then Śakra, the destroyer of Bala, reported this to Bṛhaspati;
having heard it, O joy of the Kurus, Bṛhaspati spoke to the god.
"Alas! Woe to the abode of Brahmā now that I have departed, O Śatakratu!
This ill-conceived plan has been undertaken; for the resulting division here will be terrible."
"O Lord of the World, O God, how indeed could you have undertaken this task of mine without having explained it first, and for what reason?"
Or rather, O slayer of Vṛtra, the world is deluded by that which must come to pass, born of karma; no ordinance can transcend destiny.
The hasty commencement of undertakings is not praised; this very work, begun with such haste, will bring about insignificance.
Mahendra spoke these words to the high-souled Bṛhaspati:
"Since things have come to this pass today, you ought to say what must be done."
Then the righteous-souled Bṛhaspati, whose intellect was noble and who knew the truth of the past and the future, spoke to him after reflecting with his face cast downward.
"Exert yourself together with your son and fight Janārdana;
O Śakra, I shall act in such a way that it will be right."
Having spoken thus, Bṛhaspati went to the ocean Kṣīroda and related everything to the high-souled sage Kaśyapa.
Having heard that, Kaśyapa became enraged and spoke to Bṛhaspati: "O sir, this must necessarily come to pass; there is no doubt about it in any way."
Because he desired a wife worthy of the great seer Devaśarman,
this fault arising from ill-will has fallen upon Śatakratu.
O Sage, this dwelling in the water was undertaken by me for the sake of pacifying that fault;
yet that very fault has now become truly terrible.
Therefore, O ascetic, I shall go with his mother and Āditya;
I will restrain them both, provided that fate permits it.
But Bṛhaspati, whose soul was righteous, said this to Mārīca:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, you must go there when the time has arrived."
Having said, "So be it," Kaśyapa dismissed Bṛhaspati and went to worship the god Rudra, the lord of the hosts of spirits.
There, for the sake of obtaining a boon, the wise and powerful Kaśyapa, accompanied by Aditi, worshipped the high-souled Soma, whose emblem is the bull.
Then Kaśyapa Mārīca praised that Lord,
the teacher of the world who is worthy of praise, with hymns from the Vedas and those composed by himself.
To the wide-striding one, the architect of all,
the Lord, the creator of the world, visible through dharma, the Supreme Ruler.
I bow to you, the Lord of All, the divine abode of steadfastness, the Blessed One, the Sovereign of the Universe,
who is the overlord of the gods and the remover of sin.
By whom the entire universe is pervaded because it consists of the world;
he whose embryo is the waters and whose auspicious ones are the earths.
I take refuge in that Lord of All.
He who, in the form of an ascetic, slew the Śālāvṛkas;
he who repelled the enemies sent by Indra;
Virūpākṣa, Sudarśana, and Puṇyayoni.
I go to Viśveśvara; I seek refuge with my head bowed.
May He who alone, as the all-pervading Lord, enjoys the entire universe— the foremost of all abodes— being unassailable due to His state of perfect virtue,
nourish me with His eternal splendor.
He is the most excellent among the drinkers of Soma and the drinkers of Marīci.
Atharvan, who has a beautiful head, the source of all beings, skillful, heroic, and the subduer of the Dānavas; he is honored by Viyat,
refined, and subject to transformation.
I go for refuge to the god Viśveśvara.
I bow to the God who brings joy to those who prostrate themselves, the Soul of the universe, upon whom the entire web of the world is spread,
and who, mounting his upward-moving chariot, traverses it.
May that Lord of All be ever well-disposed toward me.
Moving within, radiant, with beautiful branches, possessed of great strength, the leader of dharma, the primordial one;
thousand-eyed, having a hundred paths, the formidable one.
I bow down to Mahādeva, the creator of the universe.
To Śociṣkeśa, the pacifier who has quelled all evil;
to Śarva, Śambhu, Śaṅkara, the Lord of Beings;
to Dhuraṃdhara, Gopati, and the one marked by the moon.
I go to that which is the refuge of the senses with my head bowed.
The swift one [saw] the moon, the bellowing bull;
he made the established Dharma false and did not leave any remainder.
He [saw] the supporter of the earth, the prosperous and capable one.
I take refuge in the wielder of the trident, whose vows are steadfast.
He of infinite vigor, who maintains his actions, the primordial one, the impulse of sacrifice, and the supreme sacrificer among those who offer sacrifice.
I take refuge in the consumer of oblations, the eldest of all beings, the twice-born one among those who uphold dharma.
Beyond all qualities, he is the very form of Pṛśnigarbha;
he is the pinnacle of glory, the manifestation of beautiful form,
the Person who pervades the sky, and the abode of truth.
I pay homage to that which deludes the evildoers.
He was disciplined, possessed of a noble head and beautiful deeds, firm in his vows and firm with his bow in battle;
he was a hero, a master of the bow, and unsurpassed in the use of missiles.
I bow down to the Lord of cattle, the pacifier.
He who is alone, yet possesses both the past and the future;
he who is a guest to all, for he delights [in all]; he who is a slayer of enemies; he who inflicts wounds; he who is unsurpassed; and he who shares [with others].
May the Lord God, the distributor, protect me.
He who alone goes as the Lord of the entire universe;
he who formerly gave the foremost vital breath to the Maruts;
by whom, out of compassion, the eternal Sāman was cherished.
May that virtuous one favor me for my ultimate welfare.
Brahmā created him who is the highest of the high among the worlds;
Rudra is the destroyer, and Viṣṇu alone is the protector.
The wise Brāhmaṇa, being satisfied with the sixfold [qualities],
beholds that creator who abides in the sacred utterances (vyāhṛti), complete in every respect.
And he is the destroyer of the world for those who commit evil deeds.
May he protect me here with his many-formed limbs.
He is the manifest, the unmanifest, and the wise; he is complete, the toucher, Śambhu, the giver of life, and the one clothed in animal skins.
He is the essence, the eternal, and the sustainer of that which purifies.
May Śiva— the purifier, the renowned wielder of the trident, praised by hosts of gods,
the auspicious one, the moon, and the unborn— protect you.
Śaṅkara is the lord of his wife; he is the creator of the essence.
Tryambaka, who bestows prosperity upon you, who proclaims the dharma for brahmins and grants boons to sacrificers— the Lord,
the bestower of boons, the victor in battle.
I go for refuge to Rudra, the god of gods.
The mouth of the gods, the ender of evildoers, the threefold Soma, the destroyer of trees, the witness of actions,
the refuge of beings, the lord of beings, and the knower of qualities.
I go for refuge to Rudra, whose form consists of qualities.
The Lord, who is unperturbed, the performer of sacrifice, the end,
the middle, and the beginning of this world, whose nature is incomparable,
is praised in many ways among the divine vows.
I go for refuge to Rudra at the triple-heavened abode.
The great conqueror, the observer of vows, adorned with a girdle, the one who is easily satisfied, whose wealth is his wrath, the sinless one;
the existent, the knower of the field, the possessor of qualities, or the one with matted hair.
I am born, O Lord, as the highest among those worthy of worship.
The god of gods, the purifier of purifiers,
the creator among creators, the greatest of the great;
the hundred-fold self, praised as the lord of the guardians of the earth.
I go for refuge to the Lord Rudra, the husband of the gods.
The inner-moving Person known as the Secret,
the radiant Praṇava, the lamp of the intellect,
the supreme cause of the highest Imperishable.
I bow down to the auspicious god who is endowed with all virtues.
The progenitor of both, yet not a progenitor; subtle, neither separate from the elements nor identical with them;
self-existent, may he who is the essence of all protect me.
May the giver, the one who tastes, the one who rejoices, protect the jewel.
He is near and even closer to those practitioners who possess faith; he is the inspirer of the faithful way of life,
the lord of the great and honored hosts.
May the ram, the fulfiller of the six qualities, protect me.
The destroyer of inner and outer evils, the self-acting creator of all beings, manifesting through transformation;
bearing weapons, he is the one of supreme power among the doers of good.
May the God of gods drive away my sin.
By whom the deceptive inhabitants of Tripura were indeed uprooted and,
having committed great offenses against the gods, were burnt with a terrible arrow that brought their ends to naught.
May that Lord, the creator of the universe, protect me.
Desiring the end through the portion of those who possess a share, the sacrifice performed by Dakṣa was cut asunder;
yet that God, knowing both the beginning and the end of the sacrifice, pursued it.
May the Lord, the cause of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, protect me.
He who is another, the blessed, the well-fashioned, and the supreme,
who having created the world devours it as the most profound secret— may he always protect me at the very beginning of my speech.
He was the foremost among those who investigate the six qualities of statecraft.
The God whose three qualities are eternal, from whose being the predominance of *sattva* is produced,
the protector of protectors, the destroyer of evildoers.
The first [is] enraged at the universe as it runs about.
In whose abode Hari is foremost, and then Viśva,
O twice-born ones, as well as Brahmā together with his sons;
and in whose world Soma was utterly defeated— 1002–1004.
May he, the protector of the virtuous, be pleased for the sake of our highest good.
Because he is the origin, the end, and the middle of all beings;
he is steadfastness, prosperity, the cave, and sacred revelation;
and he resides within the cave-like hearts of all beings as the Lord of Men.
He belongs to that Great-Souled One, who is to be known as Mṛḍa.
May that high-souled God of gods protect me—
he who is the Lord Tryambaka, marked by whose *liṅga* all things exist.
That which is marked with the vulva is indeed Umā, the sustainer of all;
and that which is marked with the linga, and whatever in the world is marked with the vulva— [is she].
O Soma, you are everything; O Tryambaka, you are all, O Lord. There is nothing else whatsoever here in this world that is third apart from Mahādeva—he is the Lord of all and everything.
Thus being praised, the Blessed One whose banner bears the bull,
the righteous-souled one, revealed himself to Kaśyapa, the best among the upholders of dharma.
And the Lord of Gods, with a serene inner soul, said to him:
"O Prajāpati, I know the purpose for which you offer this praise."
The two high-souled gods, Indra and Upendra, shall return to their natural state;
however, the righteous Janārdana will take away the Pārijāta tree.
For in former times, Mahendra was cursed by the sage Devaśarman, O Kaśyapa; he desired the wife of that one blazing with ascetic power.
O knower of dharma, go there together with you and Dākṣāyaṇī to the abode of Śakra; for Āditi, it will certainly be for the welfare of your two sons.
Having heard these words of Hara, the immeasurable son of the grandson of the lotus-born Brahmā, the wise one,
bowed down to Rudra, the teacher of the hosts of the thirty gods.
With a joyful mind, he then went to his own home.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, when the sun had risen for a short while, HV App. I, 29.1028.
Under the pretext of hunting, he went to Mount Raivataka.
O best of the Kuru lineage, having placed Sātyaki, that bull among men, upon a single chariot with himself, the god said, "Follow Pradyumna."
Having gone to Mount Raivata, the god said to Dāruka:
"Dāruka, take this chariot of mine and remain right here."
"Wait for me, O gentle one, for half a day while you tend the horses;
I myself shall enter Dvārakā by chariot, O best of charioteers."
Having thus given his instructions,
the wise Lord of immeasurable prowess, intent on victory, ascended Tārkṣya along with Sātyaki.
O descendant of Kuru, O King, Pradyumna, the slayer of enemies,
followed behind Kṛṣṇa on a chariot that travels through the sky.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, the wise Hari went to the Nandana grove,
the celestial garden, with the desire to seize the Pārijāta tree.
There, the Blessed One Adhokṣaja beheld the gods' warriors, difficult to approach,
those heroes bearing various weapons who stood like those in the Nandana grove.
While they were looking on, the one of great strength [seized] the Pārijāta tree.
Having uprooted it, he who follows the path of the virtuous offered the *pārijāta* tree to her.
O Bhārata, Garuḍa, the king of birds, appeared without any effort,
and the Pārijāta tree itself, taking embodied form, presented itself before Keśava.
O Bhārata, the Pārijāta tree was consoled by Vāsudeva, and it was said to the tree by the high-souled Keśava: "Do not fear."
Seeing that tree, the Pārijāta, set forth, Adhokṣaja then performed a circumambulation of Amarāvatī, the most excellent city.
O King, those guardians of the Nandana grove went and reported to the great Indra that the Pārijāta, the best of trees, was being carried away.
Then the Lord, the subduer of Pāka, mounted Airāvata and went forth,
followed from behind by Jayanta standing in his chariot.
First, Keśava, the slayer of enemies, arrived at the gate;
thereafter, all the hosts of Viṣṇu and the warriors prepared for the assault.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the inhabitants of heaven, for it was certain.
Having seen it, he said: "O Madhusūdana, what is this that has begun?"
Then Keśava, mounted upon Garuḍa, bowed down and said to Śakra:
"This excellent tree is being led away for the sake of performing a meritorious act for your daughter-in-law."
Then Śakra said to him, "O lotus-eyed one, do not say such a thing!
O Acyuta, you must not take this tree away without having fought."
Strike me first, O mighty-armed Keśava!
Let your vow bear fruit, even if you must set aside the Kaumodakī mace.
Then, O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa, as if laughing, pierced the excellent elephant of the king of the gods with sharp arrows resembling thunderbolts.
The wielder of the thunderbolt likewise pierced Garuḍa with divine showers of arrows,
and he also cut down the shafts of the swift Keśava.
Whatever weapons the Lord of the Gods released, Mādhava cut them all to pieces; and the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra cut down those that were hurled by Mādhava.
O descendant of Kuru, by the sound of Mahendra’s bow and by the roar of the Śārṅga,
the inhabitants of heaven were bewildered.
As their battle raged on, the mighty Jayanta, mounted upon Garuḍa,
rose up with great strength to seize the Pārijāta tree.
Then the slayer of Kaṃsa said to him,
"Restrain Pradyumna," and thereupon the powerful son of Rukmiṇī restrained him.
Then Jayanta, the best among victors,
standing upon his chariot, laughing, struck the son of Rukmiṇī with arrows in all his limbs.
While still standing upon his chariot, the lotus-eyed Kāma tormented the son of Indra, that charioteer,
with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
O descendant of Kuru, that tumultuous encounter took place;
then Jayanta, the slayer of all heroes, held him back.
And [the chariot] of both the hero Jayanta and the son of Rukmiṇī.
Those two of great strength,
the sons of Mahendra and Upendra, the best among weapon-wielders on earth, engaged in a battle of mutual retaliation.
The gods and the sages, as well as the Siddhas and the Cāraṇas, beheld that most terrible battle filled with wonder.
Then, O joy of the Kurus, a mighty celestial messenger named Pravara desired to seize the Pārijāta tree once again.
