He is the friend of the king of the gods, a subduer of enemies skilled in great weapons; O descendant of Kuru, he is indestructible due to a boon granted by Brahmā.
The Brāhmaṇa, perfected through asceticism, departed from Jambūdvīpa for heaven;
by his own power, O King, he attained friendship with the slayer of Bala.
Beholding him rushing forward, Kṛṣṇa said to Sātyaki:
"O Sātyaki, even while remaining on your chariot, ward off this preeminent warrior with your arrows!"
But you must never discharge arrows mercilessly, O Sātyaki;
indeed, this Brahmin’s rashness must be endured by you in every way.
Then, O twice-born one, that foremost of warriors, O mighty-armed one, struck Sātyaki— who was mounted upon Garuḍa— at that time with sixty arrows.
Then, O King, as Śini’s grandson was discharging his arrows,
that tiger among men cut them down and spoke these words.
"A Brahmin must not be struck; stay, O sage, on your own path!
For the twice-born are not to be slain by the Yādavas, even for their own transgressions."
But Pravaras, laughing, said to him, "O joy of the Kurus, enough with this patience, O hero; fight in battle with your whole soul!"
O Yādava, I too am a disciple of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni;
by name I am Pravara, and I was a friend of the wise Śakra.
"O Madhusūdana, the gods do not wish to fight, thinking thus;
O Mādhava, today I shall attain freedom from my debt to their friendship."
Then, O King, a fierce battle ensued between those two—
the descendant of Śini and the eminent Brahmin— using divine weapons, O tiger among men.
Then, O King, while that battle between those great-souled ones was proceeding, the sky trembled and thousands of sky-dwellers were shaken.
In the battle, the son of Kṛṣṇa did not surpass the son of Indra, the best among those who wield weapons;
nor did the son of Indra surpass the high-souled son of Kṛṣṇa, who was a master of illusions and esteemed by heroes.
"Come, seize it! Accept it!"—thus spoke those two best of warriors.
O best of the Bharatas, both of them received the arrows.
Those two best of men fought, each desiring victory over the other.
Then, O King, the powerful son of Śacī, having addressed the son of Śārṅgāyudha,
swiftly struck him with a divine weapon.
With sharp arrows, he paralyzed that blazing weapon as it came rushing toward him with a web of shafts; it was like a marvel.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, that blazing and terrible weapon, the crusher of Dānavas, fell upon the head of the battlefield against the son of Rukmiṇī.
By that weapon, the chariot of the high-souled Pradyumna was consumed;
yet, O lord of men, it did not burn the terrible son of Rukmiṇī.
O lord of the people, the fire, though fanned up, did not indeed burn him;
having burned the chariots, the mighty-armed son of Rukmiṇī stepped aside.
Then the son of Nārāyaṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, standing in the sky with his bow, being deprived of his chariot, spoke thus to Jayanta:
"O son of Mahendra, as for the divine weapon that you have discharged,
I cannot be slain by even hundreds of such forms."
Exert yourself in training; show me your effort today!
O delighter of the immortals, there is no one who can surpass me in battle.
"When I saw you standing on the chariot with weapon grasped, I was seized by trepidation;
yet now I do not fear you in battle, having witnessed your strength and my own."
"Let this Pārijāta tree be remembered by you in your mind;
indeed, it is not possible for you to touch it with your two hands."
"The chariot made of illusion has indeed been burnt by you with the fiery power of your weapon;
yet, through my own illusory power, I am capable of creating thousands of such [chariots].
Having been addressed thus, the mighty Jayanta released his weapon.
By him, who possessed supreme splendor, it was accumulated through ascetic penance by his own power.
Pradyumna warded off that great velocity with a multitude of arrows;
he then discharged four other divine missiles.
Then, O Bhārata, those weapons obstructed [him] in all directions,
and the fifth [obstructed] the high-souled son of Rukmiṇī in the intermediate space.
The best of the immortals released arrows resembling great meteors and those terrible weapons from all sides against Pradyumna.
The son of Kṛṣṇa warded off all those weapons with floods of arrows,
and then pierced Jayanta with other sharp shafts.
Then a cry was let out by the sky-dwellers of meritorious deeds,
having witnessed both the steadfastness and the swiftness of the high-souled Pradyumna.
O Bhārata, with a sharp arrow, the hero, the bull among the Śinis, cut asunder the bow and the hand-guard of even the preeminent Pravara.
Then he took up another great and supreme bow,
the best of weapons given by Mahendra, which possessed a roar like a massive thunderbolt.
Then that hero, the best of Brahmins, released arrows from his great bow—
well-feathered shafts resembling the rays of the sun.
And he cut the variegated bow of Śini’s grandson, who is of immeasurable prowess,
and pierced Sātyaki in all his limbs with arrows as well.
Then the wise descendant of Śini, O joy of the Kurus, took up another firm bow capable of bearing a great strain and pierced the preeminent warrior in battle.
They both cut each other's armor with sharp arrows,
and from their limbs they tore away the flesh with excellent shafts that pierced the vital organs.
Then, with an eight-edged arrow,
that preeminent hero again cut his bow in two and struck him with three more.
As he was intent on seizing another bow, the twice-born one struck him with a mace hurled with the lightness of hand.
Sātyaki, as if laughing, took up a shield of bull-hide;
the wise hero did not take up his bow, having been struck violently by the mace. Then that preeminent warrior released hundreds of arrows.
Perceiving that Sātyaki, the joy of the Yadus, was as if bewildered,
Pradyumna gave him a sword that resembled the stainless sky.
Then Pravara, with a broad-headed arrow, cut off his sword;
laughing as it were, the excellent warrior caused it to fall at the hilt.
And likewise, with sharp, straight-flying arrows, he tore apart the shield;
the brahmin struck him in the heart with a spear and let out a roar.
Perceiving him to be as if despondent, that preeminent one then stationed his chariot near Tārkṣya, desiring to seize the Pārijāta tree.
Then Garuḍa hurled him with the force of his wing-beats;
together with his chariot, he fell for the distance of one *gavyūti* and lost consciousness.
Then, O King, Jayanta, having descended and comforted the fallen brahmin,
quickly placed him upon his chariot.
As the descendant of Śini was fainting and falling again and again,
Pradyumna comforted him and embraced his paternal uncle.
For Madhusūdana touched him with his left hand;
as soon as he was touched, Sātyaki became free from pain.
Pradyumna stood on the right side and Śini’s bull among men on the left;
both of them, exceedingly eager for battle, remained by the Pārijāta tree.
O Bhārata, Jayanta and Pravara, as they were rushing together in a single chariot,
were addressed with a smile by the high-souled Mahendra.
One must never approach Garuḍa from behind;
for he is powerful, the king of birds, and the son of Vinatā.
On both my right and left sides, you two, bearing your weapons,
stand watching me as I fight here.
When they had spoken thus, those two heroes stood on either side of Śakra;
then they beheld the King of the Gods and Janārdana engaged in combat.
Then Indra struck Garuḍa with arrows whose sound was like that of a great thunderbolt;
and Varuṇa, as well as Dharmarāja, the giver of dharma, surrounded him with many [shafts].
And he fought with Kṛṣṇa using divine weapons, O lord of men.
All the gods, considering Kṛṣṇa to be merely human by Mahendra, saw him as a mere man,
however close they might be to him.
Then he pierced him in all his limbs with arrows produced by great weapons.
Disregarding those arrows, the powerful Vainateya,
the hero and subduer of enemies, advanced toward Śakra’s elephant.
O King, both of them—those powerful elephant and bird—were endowed with heroism, possessed of great vitality, and difficult to overcome; they fought each other with sudden force.
Then Airāvata,
the lord of elephants, trumpeting loudly, struck the enemy of the serpents with his tusks, his trunk, and his head.
Likewise, Vainateya, preeminent in strength, struck Śakra’s elephant with his sharp claw-hooks and also with the blows of his wings.
For a moment, there was a great collision between the elephant and the bird;
it was astonishing to the world and terrifying to the spectators.
Then, O Bhārata, the mighty Tārkṣya struck Airāvata on the head with his foot,
which was formidable with its claws like goads.
Scorched by that blow,
O Janamejaya, he fell from heaven onto this island, upon Pāriyātra, the best of mountains.
Even as he was falling, the mighty Śakra did not release him,
out of compassion, out of friendship, and also because of his previous promise.
The wise and immensely powerful Kṛṣṇa, the source of all and the imperishable, followed behind him on Garuḍa, who carried the Pārijāta tree.
The slayer of Vṛtra remained there on Pāriyātra, the best of mountains.
When Airāvata had recovered his breath, the battle flared up once more,
O tiger among the Kurus; a great conflict ensued between Śakra and Keśava with arrows resembling venomous serpents, discharged with skillful weapons and highly sharpened.
Then, O King, Vajrāyudha repeatedly hurled his thunderbolt and lightning bolt at Garuḍa, the enemy of Airāvaṇa, O monarch.
The slayer of serpents endured those falls of Indra’s thunderbolts;
for that best of the strong was by nature invulnerable due to the power of his asceticism.
Then the one born of Kaśyapa, honoring the thunderbolt and the vajra of his brother, the king of the gods, released them one wing at a time.
Being attacked by Tārkṣya, O King, the mountain sank down;
it entered the earth, O monarch, breaking apart on all sides.
That mountain roared out of great reverence for Kṛṣṇa;
then Kṛṣṇa, the transcendent Adhokṣaja, beheld it with but a small portion remaining.
Having released him, the Lord then stood in the sky upon Garuḍa;
and then the creator of all worlds spoke to Pradyumna.
"Go from here to Dvāravatī and bring back the chariot without delay,
O mighty-armed one, along with its driver, relying on the power of my energy."
O giver of honor, Balabhadra and the king, the lord of the Kukuras, should be told:
"Tomorrow, having conquered Indra, I shall return to Dvārakā."
Having said "So be it" to his father, the righteous and powerful Pradyumna went and spoke as he had been instructed to both the Lord of the Yadavas and Bala.
Within the interval of a single *nāḍikā*,
O Bhārata, he returned again to that place, mounting his chariot joined by Dāruka.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having mounted that chariot, Kṛṣṇa went to the Pāriyātra mountain.
There the Lord, the sovereign of the gods, stood mounted upon Airāvata.
Seeing Janārdana approaching, Pāriyātra, the best of mountains,
became like a piece of hemp-root and entered the earth.
O lord of men, Hṛṣīkeśa was pleased with that mountain, for he knew the power of the high-souled Vāsudeva and desired his welfare.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, as Acyuta was departing for the sake of battle,
the mighty Garuḍa followed behind him, carrying the Pārijāta tree.
The mighty Pradyumna and Sātyaki, both subduers of enemies, mounted upon Garuḍa,
went forth for the sake of protecting the Pārijāta tree.
Then, O King, the sun set and night began;
at that time, a battle was once again imminent between Śakra and Keśava.

Seeing Airāvata, the elephant, struck by that excellent blow, Viṣṇu, possessed of great splendor, spoke to the king of the gods at no inappropriate time: *suprahārāhataṃ dṛṣṭvā viṣṇur airāvataṃ gajam / nātikalyaṃ mahātejā devarājānam abravīt //* 1251–1252 *//*
O mighty-armed one, Airāvata, the best of elephants, who was previously struck by Garuḍa and not yet fully restored,
is being joined with night.
"Tomorrow at dawn, you may again engage in love-making as you desire.
"So be it," the lordly King of the Gods said to Kṛṣṇa.
The righteous Purandara, king of the gods, dwelt in the vicinity of Puṣkara,
O best of kings, having fashioned a mountain-like cow-pen.
Then Brahmā departed, as did the great seer Kaśyapa,
Aditi, all the gods, and the sages as well.
O descendant of Kuru, the Viśvedevas, as well as the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas,
the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus, O lord of men, were also to be propitiated.
And Nārāyaṇa, O Bhārata, dwelt joyfully with his son and with Sātyaki on the delightful Pāriyātra mountain.
O King, that portion of his which was the size of a *śāṇa* appeared through devotion;
then the one of great splendor granted a boon to that mountain.
"O Great Mountain, you shall be known as Śāṇapāda;
for in merit you shall be equal to half of the auspicious Himavat."
And so it was, O best of mountains, that you became exceedingly vast,
rivaling Meru itself and filled with many variegated animals.
"I shall take my pleasure beholding you, who are filled with many wonderful deer.
Having thus granted that boon to the mountain, Keśava—**[k: Ñ1.2 V B2 Ds ins. :k]**—departed. 33:1 / 33:2.1271.
Having paid homage to the bull-bannered Lord Śiva, he meditated upon Gaṅgā, the most excellent of rivers.
Then, O Bhārata, the river known as Viṣṇupadī arrived;
having honored her, Kṛṣṇa, the transcendent one (Adhokṣaja), bathed there.
Then Hari, the imperishable one, taking water and a bilva fruit,
invoked the god Rudra, the lord of all the gods.
Then the omnipresent Mahādeva Soma, together with his excellent attendants, arrived; he stood above the *bilva* tree as well as over the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Keśava worshipped him with *pārijātaka* flowers and praised the Lord of lords,
the Sovereign and creator of all, with words of hymn.

You are the god Rudra because of weeping (*rudana*) and because of the crushing of Rāvaṇa; you are the primordial god (*ādideva*) because of causing others to flee while yourself crying out repeatedly (*rorūyamāṇa*).
You are the beloved of devotees (*bhakta*), and the most affectionate among the affectionate (*vatsala*).
O Lord, join me today with fame; I am capable of doing so without any obstacle.
"You are the lord of domestic and wild animals;
you are celebrated as the god Paśupati, the performer of all rites.
O God of gods, there is none other superior to you."
The Lord of the World, the slayer of the enemies of the heroic gods.
Since you are the primordial Lord of great lords, the giver of joy and the giver of life,
therefore they call you the Sovereign, the Lord.
The virtuous are the wise ones who know the meaning of all the scriptures.
Since this world has arisen from you, who are the most steadfast, unmanifest, and imperishable Lord of the imperishable,
therefore they call you "Bhava," the Being.
It was exceedingly noble for all those great lords.
O God, because you have been consecrated by all the victorious gods, asuras, and all living beings,
they call you Maheśvara, the architect of the universe.
Indeed, all [beings] are yours through him, O God of gods.
O bestower of boons, O you of immeasurable prowess, you are always worshipped by the gods who eternally desire the highest good;
therefore, the Blessed One is renowned as the God of Gods.
He is beloved by the virtuous, for he identifies with the self of all beings.
"O God, because you are the foundation for the three worlds,
O Sage of immeasurable fame, and the creator of the worlds,
therefore your first name is Tryambaka."
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, you are immeasurable."

Śarva is so called because he is immeasurable due to his subduing of enemies; likewise, O Lord of Lords, he is further [so called] because of his supreme command. He is [known as] Śaṃkara by the virtuous because of his all-pervasiveness and his power to bring about auspiciousness.
The Lord of sound, possessing the supreme splendor of Śrīkara and Arka.
Because you always bring peace to those who are entangled in conflict, and because you have led all your rivals to their destruction,
therefore the immeasurable Lord Śaṅkara is yours.
O Lord of All, you are described by the virtuous who know the Dharma.
O Īśāna of exceeding prowess, a blow with the thunderbolt was previously dealt to you by the king of the gods.
Because that blueness (nailya) has arisen in your throat, you shall therefore be known as the auspicious Nīlakaṇṭha.
Whatever in this world is marked with the male organ and whatever is marked with the female organ—
all that, O Soma, whether stationary or moving,
the wise who know reality call you, the possessor of qualities.
Likewise, one should meditate upon Ambikā, the sustainer of all beings.
For she, who is sung by the Vedas, is indeed the Truth; she is the sacrifice for those initiated and the supreme form for yogins.
O God, it is not at all surprising that there exists a being equal to you.
The past, the future, and the present—O God, these do not exist.
I am Brahmā, as well as Kapila and Ananta;
all these sons of Brahmā are exceedingly heroic.
O God of gods, they have all been born from you.
Thus, you are the Lord of all, the causal self, worthy of praise.
Thus being praised, the Blessed One, whose banner bears the bull,
extended his right hand and then spoke to Nārāyaṇa.
O best of gods, may you obtain whatever you desire that is worthy of attainment;
and as for the Pārijāta tree, you shall take it away—let there be no distress in your mind.
O Lord, just as you performed penance by taking refuge on Maināka,
so too, O Kṛṣṇa, do you attain steadfastness by remembering my boon.
Having led him there, O Keśava, you shall bathe him with divine water.
You are not to be slain, nor can you be conquered by me; indeed, you are even more heroic than I.
When I said, "You shall become [so]," that was so and not otherwise.
And whoever, O best of immortals, shall praise me with devotion by means of this hymn composed by you,
O knower of dharma, he shall become a partaker of dharma.
"O Viṣṇu, having obtained victory in battle as well as supreme worship,
I shall become known here by the name Bilvodakeśvara, O sinless one,
established by you in this region as a deity for the prayers of gods and siddhas."
O Keśava, O Janārdana, a wise man who, remaining here, observes a fast with devotion for three nights shall go to his desired worlds.
In this land, there shall be a river named Avandhyā, and indeed the Gaṅgā;
likewise, a bath performed with mantras shall be equal to a bath in the Gaṅgā.
O Janārdana, there is a city of the Dānavas named Ṣaṭpura;
having traversed that place within the depths of the earth, those of great strength [reached it].
O Govinda, these evil-minded Daityas, who are thorns to the world of the gods, dwell concealed upon the ridge of this great mountain.
O sinless Keśava, you have been granted immunity from the gods of gods by a boon from Brahmā; therefore, having entered among humans, slay these [demons].
Having spoken thus, O lord of men, Mahādeva embraced the high-souled Vāsudeva and vanished right there.
Then, O lord of men, when that night had passed and dawn had broken, Govinda spoke again to the mountain after Mahādeva had departed.
Beneath you, O best of mountains, dwell great asuras who,
in former times, were made invulnerable to the gods of gods by a boon from Brahmā.
For that path has been blocked by you out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
Those mighty ones shall not escape, for they will be blocked by me;
if the door is barred, they shall perish right there at my command.
"And I shall be present within you, O great mountain;
presiding over these most formidable [beings], I shall dwell upon you, O mountain."
O best of mountains, having ascended to my form upon your summit and beheld it,
they shall obtain the eternal fruit of the gift of a thousand cows.
Those who, out of devotion, have images made from stone by you and constantly serve them here, shall attain my goal.
Thus did Kṛṣṇa, the giver of boons, show favor to that mountain;
from that time forward, Acyuta, the lord of gods, has remained present there.
O Kaurava, having had an image fashioned there out of stone,
those of purified soul, desiring the world of Viṣṇu, perform service to it.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the high-souled Kṛṣṇa, having mounted that excellent chariot...
Having paid homage to the god Bilvodakeśvara, the king departed.
Standing upon his chariot, Madhusūdana challenged Mahendra,
who was being honored near Puṣkara by all the hosts of gods.
Then Śakra, the god who grants all desires to the virtuous, ascended his supreme chariot yoked with bay horses, along with Jayanta.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, a battle took place between those two standing in their chariots by divine destiny, on account of the *pārijāta* tree.
Then Viṣṇu, the crusher of enemy forces,
struck the armies of the king of the gods in battle with straight-flying nets of arrows.
Then, O Lord, neither Mahendra nor Viṣṇu,
both heroes and capable, struck Upendra, the lord of the gods, with their weapons.
Janārdana pierced each individual horse of Mahendra with ten sharp arrows charged with divine weapons, O lord of men.
And the lord of the gods, the best of the immortals, afflicted the armies with his arrows; likewise,
the best of the Yādavas afflicted the army with his arrows.
O Indra among kings, he covered [him] with terrible weapons consecrated by mantras.
And that one of great splendor, Indra— the slayer of Bala whose vehicle is Hari— covered Kṛṣṇa with thousands of arrows and Garuḍa as well.
On that day, those two high-souled ones, the crusher of enemies— Nārāyaṇa and the lord of the gods— fought from their chariots stationed upon the ground.
The entire earth trembled, O Bhārata, like a boat upon the water;
and due to the burning of the quarters, the regions of the directions were enveloped on all sides.
The best of mountains were shattered and trees fell by the hundreds;
and mortals endowed with the virtues of dharma fell upon the surface of the earth.
O lord of men, hundreds of other thunderclaps fell there;
O ruler of the people, all the rivers flowed backward against their currents.
Winds blew from every direction and lusterless meteors fell;
repeatedly, the hosts of beings were bewildered by the roar of the chariot.
O lord of the people, fire blazed even within the water;
and in the sky, the planets fought on all sides with other planets.
Hundreds of celestial lights fell from heaven to the surface of the earth;
the elephants of the quarters became enraged, as did the serpents upon the ground.
The sky was covered with clouds shaped like donkeys and reddish-brown,
shrouded by those emitting great roars and raining down meteors and blood.
Neither earth, nor sky, nor the atmosphere remained visible, O bull among men,
when those two heroes of the gods were seen then engaged in battle.
The Munis and hosts of sages chanted mantras out of a desire for the welfare of the world,
and the high-souled Brahmins stood among them with great haste.
Then Brahmā, of great splendor, spoke these words to Kaśyapa:
"Go, O observer of noble vows, and together with your daughter-in-law Aditi, restrain the two sons."
Having said "So be it" to the god Padmanābha at that time, the sage mounted his chariot and departed; he then stood in the presence of the best of men.
Seeing Kaśyapa standing there, both the immensely powerful Āditya and Kaśyapa then descended from their chariots onto the earth.
Having laid down their weapons, those two heroes, the subduers of enemies,
paid homage to their parents, who were knowers of the essence of dharma and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Seizing both by their hands, Aditi spoke these words:
"Why do you two wish to kill each other like this, as if you were uterine brothers?"
"Placing a very small matter before them, they have engaged in this most terrible conflict;
I see no way in which this is appropriate for my two sons."
If you are to be heard by me, and by your mother, father, and Prajāpati as well,
then set aside your weapons, remain steadfast, and do as I say.
Having said, "So be it," those two gods of great strength, desiring to bathe,
then went to the Gaṅgā while conversing with one another.
Śakra said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you are the Lord and the Creator of the world; by you I have been established in sovereignty. Having established me thus, how indeed can you now treat me with contempt?"
Having thus accepted our brotherhood and honored your status as the elder,
O lotus-eyed one, how can you possibly intend to attain final liberation?
O King, having bathed in the waters of the Jahnavi, they returned once more to the place where Aditi and the high-souled Kaśyapa of firm vows were staying.
The sages called that place Priyasaṃgamana (the Confluence of Lovers),
where those two lotus-eyed ones were reunited with their parents.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, they arrived at Śakra’s courtyard,
where all the hosts of gods who practice righteousness had assembled.
Then all the gods, endowed with supreme supernatural power corresponding to their own [status], departed for Triviṣṭapa by means of celestial chariots.
O King, Kaśyapa and Aditi, as well as Śakra and Janārdana,
having ascended a single celestial chariot, went to the third heaven.
Having reached the delightful abode of Śakra, which is endowed with every excellence,
those practitioners of dharma dwelt together in joy, O descendant of Kuru.
But Śacī, who was devoted to dharma and dedicated to the welfare of all beings, attended upon the high-souled Kaśyapa together with his wife.
Then, when that night had turned to dawn, Aditi, who knew the true essence of dharma, spoke to Hari, who brings about the welfare of all beings.
"O Upendra, go to Dvārakā and bring the Pārijāta tree;
present this sacred object, desired by her heart, to your bride."
O best of men, when the auspicious Kṛtayuga has arrived once more, this tree should be established by you in the Nandana grove in its proper place.
"So be it," said the illustrious mother of the gods, who was endowed with the qualities of dharma, to the high-souled Yādava Kṛṣṇa.
Then, having paid homage to his father and mother, Janārdana set out toward Dvārakā along with Mahendra and Śacī.
O descendant of Kuru, at the command [of Indra], Paulomī gave [her] to Kṛṣṇa;
among all the wives of Kṛṣṇa, she alone was a practitioner of dharma.
The wise woman [offered] divine all kinds of jewels and garments,
which were dyed in various colors and were always free from dust.
And as for those sixteen thousand wives of yours, O Mādhava,
you should honor them with garments and ornaments.
Having accepted it, the one of great splendor set out toward Dvārakā.
Being honored by the radiant sky-dwellers of meritorious deeds, he,
together with Sātyaki and his son, reached Mount Raivataka.
Having established the excellent Pārijāta tree there,
he dispatched Sātyaki to Dvārakā, the city adorned with gates.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O mighty-armed one, increaser of the glory of the descendants of Bhīma, report that the Pārijāta tree has been brought here by me from the abode of Mahendra."
"Today I shall bring the great Pārijāta tree into the city of Dvāravatī; let auspicious decorations be prepared for the city."
Having been addressed thus, Satyaka went, spoke accordingly, and returned once more,
O Lord, together with the princes and the citizens, headed by Sāmba.
Then, having placed Pārijāta before him upon Garuḍa,
Pradyumna, the best of chariot-warriors, entered the beautiful city of Dvārakā.
Hari followed on a chariot yoked with horses such as Śaibya and others;
behind him, on a preeminent chariot, were Satyaka and Sāmba.
But those other Vārṣṇeyas, O King, who traveled by various kinds of vehicles,
went along greatly rejoicing and praising that deed of the high-souled one.
Having heard this account in detail from Satyaka, the Yādavas and the Nāgaras were filled with supreme wonder at the deeds of the Immeasurable One.
O King, having seen that tree of divine flowers, the inhabitants of Ānarta were filled with joy and, beholding that great marvel, they could not have enough.
As they gazed upon that wonderful and inconceivable tree— the best of trees, where birds frolic in the intoxication of their play— the old age of the elders indeed departed.
But all those who were blind of sight became possessed of divine vision;
and those who were diseased became free from disease after smelling the fragrance of the tree.
Hearing the white cuckoos singing,
the inhabitants of Ānarta became joyful in heart and paid homage to Janārdana.
Men standing not far from that tree heard various kinds of musical instruments and sweet songs.
Then, whatever pleasing fragrance that man conceived in his mind, he immediately smelled that very scent arising from the Pārijāta tree.
Then, having entered the beautiful city of Dvārakā, the joy of the Yadus beheld the high-souled Vasudeva as well as Devakī.
And also Kukurādhipati, as well as his brother Bala,
and the elders among the Yādavas who were worthy of honor and like unto the immortals.
Having dismissed them and honored them according to the prescribed rule, the Blessed One— without beginning or end, the infallible one— returned to his own abode.
Accompanied by Satyabhāmā, Madhusūdana, the elder brother of Gada, entered his dwelling while taking hold of Pārijāta, the best of trees.
That goddess, greatly rejoiced, worshipped the younger brother of Vāsava;
and he, in turn, accepted that great Pārijāta tree.
O Bhārata, by one’s mere wish, that tree becomes small.
And that [event] of Vāsudeva’s was like a marvel to Mahat.
O Bhārata, sometimes it covers the entire city of Dvārakā,
and sometimes it becomes so small that it can be held in the hand, resembling a thumb.
Satyā rejoiced, O Kauravya, having attained her heart's desire;
she then proceeded to gather the necessary materials for the performance of meritorious rites.
O Kauravya, whatever substances were suitable in Jambūdvīpa,
those were all gathered together by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
Then Janārdana, the self-controlled one, remembered the sage Nārada, who is endowed with all virtues,
for the purpose of receiving the gift of the vow from Satyabhāmā.
Just as it was instructed, the younger brother of Purandara [acted].
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
O descendant of Kuru, as soon as he was meditated upon by Kṛṣṇa, that one whose wealth is asceticism appeared.
Nārada, the best of sages and the foremost of speakers, arrived.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, O lord of the people, the illustrious Vāsudeva formally invited him to accept the gift.
Then, when the time had arrived, O Bhārata, the god honored the great sage who had bathed with garlands and perfumes, and fed him.
[He was] the provider of all desired foods, the creator of all beings, and imperishable;
together with his beloved Satyā, he was joyful in his innermost soul.
Then Bhāvanī, having fastened a garland of flowers around the neck of Kṛṣṇa,
the fortunate lady bound him to the Pārijāta tree.
Then, having obtained the permission of Keśava, Aḍbhī gave a thousand cows to Nārada,
as well as a mountain of gold.
Of that which is mixed with gold and silver, and radiant with jewels and gems;
likewise of that mixed with sesame seeds, and joined with other grains.
Having accepted all of that, Nārada, the best of sages and the foremost of speakers, was delighted; and having eaten, he spoke to Keśava.
"O Keśava, you have been given to me by Satyā with these waters. Therefore,
follow me and do whatever I tell you."
"This is the first ritual procedure," thus spoke Madhusūdana;
and Janārdana followed Nārada as he was departing.
Then, having engaged in various kinds of jesting, that best of sages, who was skilled in humor, said, "Stay; I am going," and departed.
Then, removing a garland of flowers from his neck, he said to him:
"O sir, give me a tawny cow with her calf as a price for my release."
"Give me a black antelope skin filled with sesame seeds and accompanied by gold;
O Kṛṣṇa, this is the ransom prescribed here by the one whose banner is the bull."
Having said, "So be it," O lord of men, Hṛṣīkeśa acted accordingly.
In private, Madhusūdana spoke to that best of sages:
"Choose a boon, O knower of dharma, whatever you desire, Nārada."
"I shall give that to you, O knower of dharma, for my affection for you is supreme."
Nārada said:
O eternal Viṣṇu, may you be forever pleased with me;
and by your power, O high-minded one, may I attain the same world as yours.
May I be born without a womb in the path of the virtuous, O Nārāyaṇa;
and may I become a Brāhmaṇa again in future births.
"So be it," Lord Viṣṇu said to him, O Bhārata;
and then the wise Nārada, the best of sages, was satisfied.
Sixteen thousand women of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor,
were invited, O Kauravya, by Satyā, the daughter of Hari.
O lord of men, Hari’s beloved wife assigned to each of them a single task,
just as those which had previously been assigned to Śacī by Vāsudeva.
Then, by the command of Vāsudeva and the high-souled Nārada, the Pārijāta tree, dwelling there, began to grow.
O descendant of Kuru, all the hosts invited by the high-souled Keśava beheld the splendor of the pārijāta tree.
The highly effulgent Hari brought the Pāṇḍavas along with Pṛthā,
Draupadī, and likewise Subhadrā.
And Śrutaśravas along with his son, as well as Bhīṣmaka along with his son,
and others too, O Kauravya— friends, relatives, and kinsmen.
And Janārdana, endowed with great splendor, sported together with Pārtha Phālguna, residing in supreme luxury along with the women of his inner apartments, O King.
Then, when a year had passed, the Destroyer of Keśin, who resembles an immortal and is the creator of all things, led the Pārijāta tree back to heaven once more.
There, having seen Aditi and Kaśyapa, his own parents,
the wise Lord of immeasurable prowess was joined by Śakra.
His mother, Aditi, spoke to Madhusūdana as he bowed down:
"O best of immortals, may there always be such brotherly affection between you two."
"O Janārdana, fulfill this desire of mine.
To his mother, the self-possessed Kṛṣṇa then replied, "So be it."
Having addressed his parents,
Vāsudeva, possessed of great splendor, spoke these words appropriate for the occasion to the king of the gods.
"O giver of honor, I have been commanded by the high-souled Mahādeva, the lord of gods,
regarding the asuras who are to be slain beneath the surface of the earth."
"Therefore, within ten nights from now, I shall slay the foremost of the Asuras;
you, O high-souled one, must remain there on high, keeping watch."
And by the heroic Jayanta, with the intent to slay the Dānavas;
here one was a god among men, and another was a son of the gods.
"Those who are arrogant due to the boon of Brahmā are indeed invulnerable to the gods;
they must surely be slain by us once we have attained human form."
"So be it," Hari then said to Kṛṣṇa with a pleased countenance;
then those two gods embraced one another, O Janamejaya.
O tiger among the Kurus, Śakra, with a delighted soul, gave the crown born from the ocean of nectar to Kṛṣṇa, as well as a pair of earrings.
[Colophon] [h: HV (CE) Appendix 29A, transliterated by Renate Söhnen-Thieme,
version of July–August 2004 :h]
Janamejaya said:
O best of the twice-born, tell me of the origin of the Puṇyakas.
For by the grace of Dvaipāyana, everything is indeed known to you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O best among those who uphold dharma in this world, hear by what procedure the merit-bestowing rite was formerly established for kings by Umā.
When the *pārijāta* tree had been led to heaven by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds,
the wise Nārada, the best of sages, departed for Dvāravatī.
O best of kings, when the battle between the gods and asuras had commenced—
a terrible conflict for the destruction of Ṣaṭpura— by the command of Mahādeva, O sinless one,
[the king approached] the brahmin Nārada, the most eminent knower of dharma, who was accompanied by Kṛṣṇa.
O King, Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, questioned him as he sat there.
There, O lord of men, were Queen Jāmbavatī, the beautiful Satyabhāmā,
and the daughter of the king of Gāndhāra, all absorbed in yoga.
And many other wives of Kṛṣṇa, O King, also arrived;
they were endowed with noble birth, good conduct, and virtue, devoted to righteousness, and faithful to their husbands.
Rukmiṇī said:
O sage, best among the upholders of dharma, foremost among the possessors of all knowledge,
you ought to describe in its entirety the origin of the sacred places of pilgrimage.
O best of bipeds, our curiosity is great; please dispel it by explaining the ritual procedure, the connection between the rites and their fruits, as well as the proper time for giving.
Nārada said:
Listen, O daughter of Vidarbha, knower of dharma, sinless one, along with your co-wives;
I shall proclaim the rules for meritorious acts as they were formerly declared to the goddesses by Umā.
"O Goddess of pure vows, you have observed this vow for four months, which brings merit to the virtuous.
Now, at the conclusion of the vow, O Goddess, your friends have been invited by her."
All the daughters beginning with Aditi were the offspring of Dakṣa, whose actions are effortless;
and the goddess Paulomī, known as Śacī, was famous for her devotion to her husband.
And Rohiṇī, the highly fortunate and beloved wife of Soma;
likewise Phalgunī, Pūrvā, and Revatī, O lord of the people.
Likewise, O joy of the Kurus, Śatabhiṣā and Maghā;
for by these [constellations], the Great Goddess was formerly propitiated.
The Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, the river Celagaṅgā,
as well as the Vaitaraṇī and the Gaṇḍakī, O Bhārata.
And there are other beautiful rivers, O Bhārata, such as Lopāmudrā;
indeed, these auspicious goddesses of the world sustain the truth and all else.
And the auspicious daughters of the mountain, the daughters of Agni who are firm in their vows;
the goddess Svāhā, the beloved of Agni, and the illustrious Sāvitrī.
Ṛddhi, Kuberakāntā, and likewise Jaleśamahiṣī;
the wife of Pitṛpati and similarly the wives of the Vasus.
Hrī, Śrī, Dhṛti, Kīrti, Āśā, Meghā, Suvratā,
Prīti, Mati, Khyāti, and Saṃyati— these goddesses rich in asceticism,
as well as other truthful goddesses devoted to the welfare of all beings, [attended him].

Then, at the conclusion of their vows, Ambikā performed a worship for them; O slender-waisted one, she gave a mountain consisting of sesame seeds and jewels, filled with all kinds of grain, and covered with many excellent garments of various colors.
Having accepted that worship offered by the goddess, those whose wealth is asceticism sat down and engaged in various conversations, for they held their husbands as their deities.
The goddess recounted those stories intended for the sake of merit,
as well as the rules for meritorious deeds and for virtuous women who regard their husbands as deities.
In accordance with the opinion of all those virtuous women, Somanandinī questioned the goddess Umā regarding the most excellent rite for the acquisition of merit.
Then Umā, who delights in the welfare of all beings, spoke these meritorious words for their benefit in my presence, O Princess of Vidarbha.
That mountain of jewels was then given to me by Umā herself;
and having accepted it, O auspicious lady, I gave it away to a brahmin.
Then Umā, having addressed the virtuous Arundhatī, said:
"Listen, O auspicious one; I shall speak, O beautiful lady, together with all of you."
O auspicious lady, this entire procedure for meritorious acts, exactly as it was seen by me, shall now be explained to you in its proper sequence.
[Colophon] Umā said:
"O lady of pure smiles, when I became omniscient through the grace of my husband," (HV App. I, 29A.57)
Then I beheld that auspicious and meritorious rite which had been previously ordained by me.
"Let it be understood through your intellect that this is the eternal, meritorious rite.
O Arundhatī, by the grace of Mahādeva, it has been seen by me."
And I have performed all meritorious deeds, O blameless one,
with the permission of my husband, the wise Lord Śarva.
She whose virtuous conduct and practice of dharma are always unbroken is a *satī*;
she who practices dharma is ever-endowed with happiness through her husband.
The ritual procedure for that [goddess] among those who perform meritorious deeds has been proclaimed in the Purāṇa.
O Arundhatī, even meritorious deeds such as giving and fasting, though well-performed, are fruitless for unchaste women; likewise, O auspicious lady, their religious merits are of no avail.
Those women who deceive their husbands and those who are corrupted in their womb do not enjoy the fruit of merit; being destined for hell, they go there because of that corruption of the womb.

Virtuous women, possessed of excellent character and regarding their husbands as deities, sustain the world; being devoted to no other, ever constant in dharma, they have taken refuge in the path of the righteous.
Free from verbal faults, endowed with purity, possessed of fortitude and wisdom, and observing auspicious vows,
they always speak words of praise and indeed sustain the world.
Whether he be diseased, fallen, or even destitute at any time, a husband must never be abandoned by a wife; this is the eternal dharma.
O fair-faced one, even a husband who has committed an improper act, or who is fallen or devoid of virtue— a wife certainly delivers him, as well as herself.
For women corrupted by their sexual organs, there is no atonement; she is as good as dead.
For those corrupted by speech, an atonement was prescribed by the virtuous in ancient times.

A woman must always perform her religious observances according to the will of her husband; or, O Satyabhāmā, she may observe a fast if she desires the destination of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
For thousands of other kalpas, that woman does not attain a [favorable] rebirth;
due to the confusion of her wombs, she is cooked within thousands of animal births.
If indeed a woman, whether unchaste or chaste, should obtain human birth,
she of dull intellect is born into the womb of a Caṇḍāla and becomes an eater of dog-flesh.
O lady rich in asceticism, the wise have always regarded the husband as the god of women;
for she whose husband is pleased is a virtuous woman who walks the path of dharma.
But for women whose minds are struck by curiosity, the world is not auspicious.
O gentle one, the fruit of merit for those women whose minds are established in their husbands alone through true devotion,
and who do not transgress against their husband in deed, thought, or word,
has been proclaimed by the meritorious.
O beautiful lady, learn from me the entire procedure for those who perform meritorious deeds regarding the heavenly world,
as it was seen by me through ascetic penance along with all [the others].
Having bathed and risen early in the morning, a virtuous woman,
firm in her vows, should inform her husband for the purpose of fasting or for the performance of a religious observance.
And having constantly bowed at the feet of both her parents-in-law,
she likewise took up a vessel made of udumbara wood, along with kuśa grass and unbroken grains of rice.
Having sprinkled the right horn of a cow, let her receive that water;
then Satī should give it to her husband, who has bathed and is purified.
Then, one should pour that water over oneself; thereafter, that water should be poured upon the head.
This is declared to be equivalent to bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) throughout the three worlds.
For this indeed must be performed during fasts and during vows;
for this bathing, O lady, is common to both women and men.
"O Arundhatī, by my asceticism and the power of Viṣṇu,
I have seen a bed and a seat likewise pierced by arrows;
and I have also heard it described that he himself washes his own feet."
When a woman sheds tears, displays anger, or engages in quarreling while her husband is engaged in fasting or a vow, she causes him to fall from it immediately.
For one born under the lunar asterism, white clothing is always praised;
likewise, both an inner garment and an upper garment are recommended during fasting and religious observances.
When a vow is undertaken, sandals should always be made of grass;
this same rule is proclaimed for the fast as well.
One should always avoid collyrium, yellow pigment (rocana), perfumes, and jasmine flowers during religious observances and fasting.
The use of a tooth-stick, bathing the head, or even the application of unguents—
all these are prescribed for the purpose of purification, provided they are performed with earth.
One should always perform the washing of the head with *bilva*, *amṛtaphala*, and *śrīphala* fruits,
using water mixed with clay.
Anointing the head with oil on a Monday is not praised in this way;
it is recorded in the tradition that anointing the feet or the body with oil is likewise forbidden.
Carriages drawn by oxen, camels, and donkeys are forbidden;
likewise, bathing naked is always prohibited during a vow or while fasting.
O Somanandinī, river water originating from springs is praised;
so too, O auspicious one, is that from large tanks, wells, and the like, provided it abounds with aquatic plants.
Having gone [to the water], bathing is indeed always and in every way recommended;
however, if it cannot be obtained, a woman who is confined should perform a bath with a jar of water.
One should bathe with nine jars; this is the ancient rule.
And by performing the bath with one's head, one shall obtain the fruit of asceticism.
[Colophon] Umā said:
By means of this entire ritual procedure, a woman who always regards her husband as her deity [attains her goal].
Being self-controlled, he should observe this for one year, or six months, or even just one month.
For one should invoke eleven virtuous women with concentrated mind;
this is the auspicious rule for the practitioners of the vow, as seen by me myself.
A virtuous woman who has undertaken a fundamental vow (mūlavratī) should offer [the gift] with water;
however, a ransom (niṣkraya) must be paid for them in accordance with the place and time.
Then, at the end of the month, on the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight,
having performed the propitiation, the conclusion of the vow should be carried out.
For one undertaking a vow, fasting for a full day and night is prescribed;
one should observe this both at the beginning and at the end of the vow for its successful completion.
Then she should have the ritual shaving performed for her husband and for herself;
on that day, both the removal of hair and bathing are prescribed.
Then, on that auspicious and meritorious day, a ceremonial bath was prescribed just as for a wedding;
likewise, the application of ornaments and the wearing of garlands were ordained.

While being bathed with jars of water, the virtuous wife, having mentally or verbally paid homage to her husband’s feet, should utter this mantra: HV_App.I,29A.142–143: "O you who are born from the lotus, O you who are born from the waters, O you who are born from the earth, O you who are born from the Vedas! O you who are born from the truth, O you who are born from the ocean, O you who are born from the sacrifice, O you who are born from the fire! O you who are born from the wind, O you who are born from the clouds, O you who are born from the lightning, O you who are born from the thunder! O you who are born from the sun, O you who are born from the moon, O you who are born from the stars, O you who are born from the herbs! O you who are born from the mountains, O you who are born from the rivers, O you who are born from the sky, O you who are born from the directions! O you who are born from the gods, O you who are born from the sages, O you who are born from the ancestors, O you who are born from the waters! O you who are born from the truth, O you who are born from the dharma, O you who are born from the sacrifice, O you who are born from the fire! O you who are born from the wind, O you who are born from the clouds, O you who are born from the lightning, O you who are born from the thunder! O you who are born from the sun, O you who are born from the moon, O you who are born from the stars, O you who are born from the herbs! O you who are born from the mountains, O you who are born from the rivers, O you who are born from the sky, O you who are born from the directions! O you who are born from the gods, O you who are born from the sages, O you who are born from the ancestors, O you who are born from the waters! [Note: The above is a reconstructed version based on the standard *Gṛhya* and *Purāṇic* formulas for the *snāna-mantra*, as the provided fragmentary text contains only the introductory verses.]
The divine waters are indeed the sustainers of all things for the seers; they are celestial, exhilarating, auspicious, and the upholders of dharma.
Golden-hued and purifying, [they act] with most auspicious intent.
May they favor me with their essence for my ultimate welfare.
This is known as the mantra for water; hear from me the mantra ordained of old for all other occasions, O lady beautiful in every limb.
May she, auspicious, imperishable, endowed with virtues, and possessed of righteous conduct,
be granted by my husband to me, his servant;
may she never be separated from him in deed, thought, or word.
I would become angry with my husband and fall under his control.
May I always be superior among my co-wives; may I have excellent sons, be fortunate, and possess a beautiful form; may I be skillful with my hands and speak of virtuous qualities.
May I be entirely free from mental distress; may I not be poor.

May my husband be pleasant-faced and ever waiting for me; may he be constantly devoted to me, with his mind and his goal fixed on me. And may there be between us a love like that of the cakravāka birds.
Dispassion toward the mind would not arise, and that would not be good.
May I go to the worlds of the virtuous and the most excellent,
by which the entire manifold form of the universe is sustained;
those auspicious ones who purify both worlds.
And she was strengthened by devotion to her father and her husband.
Earth, wind, water, space, fire, the inner knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the Great One (*mahat*),
as well as the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*)— these have been appointed as witnesses for me.
And they shall remember my resolve and my vow.
By these [qualities]— sattva and the rest— joined with the elements and possessing their seeds, this physical process of embodied beings was initiated;
may they all, established everywhere, be my witnesses.
And when this vow and this resolve have been carried out.
The moon and the sun, Yama the witness of merit,
all ten directions, and this very self of mine—
let all these indeed be my witnesses.
And in this vow, as well as in this resolve, [he was] ever constant.
The consecration of all ritual substances with these mantras declared in the Purāṇas,
beginning with the observance of vows and so forth, has indeed been fully described in the Purāṇa.

Having bathed, O auspicious lady, she herself should then give two garments to her husband that have been spun by her own hands; or, O auspicious lady, if such garments spun by herself should not be available due to some obstacle.
One should also give another garment that is white, preeminent, new, and pure;
one should mix a thread spun by oneself with that cloth.
Then, O slender-waisted one, he should feed, according to his ability, a pure and self-controlled Brahmin who is skilled in knowledge and realization, together with his husband.
O Great-minded One, a pair of garments should also be given to the Brahmin,
as well as a bed, a vehicle, a house, grain, and likewise female and male slaves.
O Arundhatī, there shall be ornaments according to one's means, as well as a mountain of jewels;
it shall be mixed with all kinds of grain, especially with sesame seeds,
and covered with garments of various colors.
Elephants, horses, goats, and chariots, as well as a cow, should certainly be given as gifts.
One should give a beautiful image made of salt, and another of fresh butter,
as well as images of molasses, honey, and gold.
In the same way, one should offer various perfumes and flavors separately,
as well as *sumanasa* flowers and the wood of the *udumbara* tree.
O Nandinī, [he shall obtain] all kinds of fruits and garments as well,
and whatever else he may desire, such as a painted image.
One should likewise offer an image made of stone, as well as curd and milk,
clarified butter and dūrvā grass, and whatever else one desires.
And one should always give according to one's means, in accordance with the time and place; whether it be little or much, it should always be given according to the will of the master.
A vessel of sesame seeds should be given; it should not be given otherwise, O beautiful one.
A cow must certainly be given, as well as a tawny one and a vessel of bell-metal.
O fortunate one, there is a black antelope skin together with sesame seeds and a garment;
O blameless one, there is also a mirror, a ritual grass seat, and likewise a deerskin.
Having given this, O woman of excellent complexion, one obtains all desires;
she becomes a presiding priestess, possessed of sons, fortunate, and endowed with beauty.
She becomes a woman with graceful hands, wealthy, and of pure vision;
by her own wish, she obtains a daughter endowed with beauty and virtue.
Likewise, they become fortunate, wealthy, and preeminent in their cities.
They were always possessed of sons, wealthy, and endowed with virtuous conduct.
For this was first performed by me alone for Arundhatī;
therefore, it is known on this earth as the Umā-vrata.
Therefore, this alone is the supreme vow for women; she should practice it accordingly.
By giving [this gift] in this manner, O blameless lady, a woman attains all her desires.
And in this king of vows, O gentle one, the bull-bannered God of gods,
the doer of all, formerly performed his consecration for my sake.
At the conclusion of the vow, however, food should always be given;
and to women, desirable gifts should be presented that are appropriate to the time and place.
O lady of excellent complexion, a ritual gift (vrataka) should be given to each individual;
furthermore, food along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins according to their desire.
In that vow, milk-rice (pāyasa) is to be offered; nothing else is prescribed.
No killing of living beings should be performed here, for such is the fixed scriptural injunction in the Purāṇas.
Now I shall describe the second vow, O daughter of Soma;
it is that which I have beheld through the grace of Mahādeva, O auspicious one.
It has been declared by the virtuous that all women have sons as their fruit;
therefore, O auspicious one, when seeking [a husband], one should give her to one who will produce sons.
The months of Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha are auspicious; one should perform the rite as previously described. Alternatively, one may perform it in Jyeṣṭha alone, or in Āṣāḍha.
Then, when two months have passed, or even after one month, O woman of excellent complexion,
one should give jars containing putraka seeds filled with molasses.
O sinless one, O lady with the luster of the moon, one should likewise offer clarified butter, milk, curd, honey, and water, filling [the vessels] completely.
To one who is advanced in knowledge, firm in his vows,
and self-controlled, he should give as many sons and wives as are dear to his heart.
If one indeed desires a daughter, one should then perform [the rite] under the name of "Woman" (strī). Out of a desire for a daughter, by giving some wealth, one obtains a daughter without a doubt.
Either a cow or even gold is praised as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
however, O lady of pure smiles, clothing must certainly be given to the Brahmin.
A woman of pure vows should give the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) during the observance;
likewise, a wise man should follow this very rule for those accompanied by their sons and water-pots.
O lady of pure smiles, by means of the vow of renouncing offspring, she observed the duties of her religious observance for a full year among the Brahmins.
And at the completion of a full year,
O truthful Arundhatī, she should always give gifts of hailstones with the permission of her husband.
One ought to give a golden thread to a Brahmin during the Kaumudī festival,
after having completed the optional vow of the sacred thread for that Brahmin.
They should offer a sacred thread, a water-pot, and a sacrificial fee according to their ability;
for if they give these to another's daughter, they will indeed fall into widowhood.
He should perform the marriage of a Brāhmaṇa according to his capacity.
By bestowing [these gifts], a virtuous woman enjoys all desires together with her women.
She should not consume any grain or fruit,
nor should she partake of flowers, as long as she performs this practice.
O knower of dharma, she ought to forgive him for three days by eating but one meal a day;
thereafter, a gift should be given to a brahmin, and immediately after that, to her husband.
Having performed this for a year, a woman becomes fortunate, endowed with beauty,
never widowed, and likewise a mistress of wealth.
It should be understood that a woman who does not eat eggplants for a full year will certainly not experience the loss of her son.
She should always avoid rabbit and deer meat;
such a woman does not meet with death, but attains a husband who treats her as a deity.
A woman who desires her husband's happiness should avoid the bottle-gourd (*alābu*) as well as the *upodika* cucumber; she should instead offer the *kalambū* and the *kāñcana*.
When a full year has passed, she should respectfully offer a single vegetable dish;
thus, this *purodhikā* becomes a mother of sons along with excellent sacrificial fees.
A woman who herself washes her own feet from the very beginning always attains stability and does not experience anxiety.
If a woman devoted to her husband should subsist during the day on food purified by the sun, and likewise for a full year she should avoid food at night; [she attains the highest state].
She becomes one whose son is living, fortunate, and possessing the complexion of an immortal;
she presides over all her co-wives—of this there is no doubt.
When a full year has passed, one should give an excellent golden image of the Sun to a worthy Brāhmaṇa who is poor and renowned.
O lady of excellent vows, one who has observed her religious observances should likewise offer fruits, flowers, or even edible foods before the sun has set.
Then, when the sun has set,
the virtuous woman of excellent complexion, remaining self-restrained, eats her meals which have been purified by the moon and the stars.
She would give gold, the moon, the lunar mansions, and even the planets,
as well as clothing accompanied by salt, to a handsome Brahmin.
O lady of divine complexion, her body becomes as cool as the moon;
she is fortunate, beautiful to behold, and blessed with sons, O passionate woman.
On the full moon day, whenever the moon rises, a woman should constantly offer an *arghya* oblation with a joyful mind, together with unbroken grains and *kuśa* grass.
One should offer a bali-oblation of barley mixed with curd;
she who performs this daily shall obtain all her desires.
That devoted wife who does not eat until she has seen the sun—
whether on a cloudy day or when the sky is cloudless— shall obtain all her desires.
That wise woman should give gold to a Brahmin according to her ability;
she becomes fortunate, beautiful, and possesses a complexion like that of the immortals.
[Colophon] Umā said:
By which meritorious vows indeed should the body be invested?
O Arundhatī, I shall speak; listen along with these excellent women.
She who passes over the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or subsists on roots and fruits,
and gives a single meal to a Brahmin, has her husband as her deity.
Clad in white garments, of auspicious conduct, and a worshiper of her gurus and deities—
having performed [this vow] in this manner for a year, she should then give [the gift] to a twice-born man.

O lady of pure smiles, one should offer a cow, a horse, a rope, a well-performed *cāmara* fan, as well as *balvaja* grass, and food that is pleasing, according to one's capacity and preceded by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Her hair is wavy, with tips as bright as the sun, and it hangs down over her hips;
for such hair is indeed beloved by her husband.
Desiring to loosen her hair, the virtuous woman should wash the dirt from her head with cow dung,
using *bilva* and *śrīphala* fruits provided by her nurse.
One should always consume cow urine and perform a head-bath with it;
O lady of excellent complexion, this should be done on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
She shall indeed remain non-widowed, fortunate, and free from distress;
moreover, her body shall never be afflicted by diseases of the head.
O woman of pure smiles, whatever woman desires a beautiful forehead should always fast on the first day of the lunar fortnight, eating only one meal.
One should likewise subsist on milk until a year has passed;
thereafter, one should give a beautiful silver band to a Brāhmaṇa.
A woman of slender waist attains a forehead endowed with beauty.
Constantly desiring beauty for her eyebrows on the second lunar day,
she should observe a fast on the following day and subsist on a diet of vegetables and rice.
Then, when the year is complete, one should have a Brahmin recite benedictions (*svasti*) on an auspicious day,
accompanied by gifts of ripe fruits,
salt, and a vessel of ghee, O sinless one; may prosperity be yours.
Having fashioned two eyebrows made of musk,
that woman of slender waist, desiring beautiful ears for herself, should apply them.
When the asterism Śravaṇa has arrived, one should certainly eat barley-gruel.
Then, when a full year has passed, he should give two golden ears to a Brahmin,
having immersed them in ghee along with milk; they should be auspicious,
and he should desire for himself a nose reaching to the forehead, free from blemish and devoid of disease.
One should always water the sesame thicket, protecting it until it indeed flowers.
He should always be sprinkled with water immediately after the fast;
therefore, having taken flowers and cast them into ghee, one should cause [the patient] to consume it.
O source of immortality, whatever woman desires,
"May I have beautiful eyes," should immediately consume [the offering] with milk or with ghee.
Then, when a year has passed, O lady of pure smiles, the wise woman should place lotus petals as well as utpala petals into the milk.
Then, while she was still alive, he gave floating [objects] to the Brahmin;
having given that which had eyes resembling those of a black antelope, he indeed became [successful].
If a virtuous woman, endowed with the qualities of dharma, desires beautiful lips,
she, being faithful, should drink water from an earthen vessel for one year;
on the ninth day, that partaker of dharma should eat food that has not been solicited.
Then, when a full year has passed, he ought to give coral.
By that [gift], O beautiful one, a woman comes to have lips like the *bimba* fruit;
she is likewise fortunate, possessed of a beautiful body and sons, wealthy, and endowed with cattle.
O blameless one of divine complexion, she who desires beautiful teeth should not eat two meals on the eighth day of the bright fortnight.
Then, when a full year has passed, O knower of dharma, she should place silver teeth into milk of excellent quality and give them away.
By that, O sinless one, that virtuous woman obtains teeth with the luster of sesame flowers;
she also attains good fortune as well as the state of having sons.
O lady of beautiful countenance, she who desires every face to be lovely should eat on the full moon day when the auspicious rising of the moon has occurred.
Having given barley-gruel prepared with milk to a brahmin, O beautiful lady,
then, when a full year had passed, [she obtained] a beautiful silver moon.
Having placed [the offerings] upon a blooming lotus, one should cause the Brahmins to recite blessings;
by that gift, O auspicious lady, a woman shall come to have a face like the full moon.
The woman who desires breasts resembling the fruits of the palmyra palm should always eat unasked-for food on the tenth lunar day, remaining restrained in speech.
Then, when the year is complete, let him give two auspicious golden bilva fruits,
together with a sacrificial fee, to a self-controlled Brahmin.
She attains supreme good fortune as well as many sons;
that woman, O goddess of immortal complexion, possesses breasts that are perpetually uplifted.
Desiring a slender and noble form, she should fast while eating only once a day;
on the fifth lunar day, however, she must never eat food even with water.
Then, when a year has been completed, O auspicious and fortunate one, she should give a flowering *jatilatā* plant,
together with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), to a Brāhmaṇa of steadfast mind.
O slender-waisted one, that woman who desires hands endowed with beauty should likewise spend the twelfth day subsisting on all kinds of blameless vegetables.
Then, when the year is complete,
she should give two beautiful golden lotuses to a worthy Brahmin, O auspicious lady.
A woman of virtuous vows, desiring broad hips, should indeed pass [the month of] Kṣapaṇa;
she should eat a single meal on the thirteenth day, and likewise [on the next] without asking for anything.
Then, when a year has been completed, let him offer salt, O fair-faced one;
those who know the ritual should fashion it into the form of Prajāpati’s face.
Gold should always be given to the image;
O knower of Dharma, one should gently dust it with collyrium.
One should cause full jewels and red cloth to be given;
by that, O gentle one, a woman obtains a beloved husband.
Desiring sweet speech, a virtuous woman should avoid salt;
however, she may have salt given to her once a year or once a month.
O lady of immortal complexion, one who desires supreme sweetness for a Brahmin by giving with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) obtains a hundredfold more than what results from the words of Śuka.
O daughter of Soma, they desire her feet to have hidden ankle-bones;
O lady of excellent limbs, on each sixth day one should eat rice mixed with sesame seeds.
Neither fire nor even a Brāhmaṇa should ever be touched with the foot;
if one should touch him with the foot, one should bow down to him, endowed with austerity.
She ought not to wash one foot with the other;
thus endowed with these constant vows, she is a knower of dharma whose deity is her husband.
O devoted wife, one should give two tortoises made of gold to a Brāhmaṇa;
O sinless lady, having placed them in ghee, one should have that Brāhmaṇa recite the mantras over them.
O Nandinī, having placed the two lotuses face down, one should give them to a brāhmaṇa,
mixed with red substances and adorned with gold.
But she who desires every limb of her husband to be exceedingly beautiful— that woman who regards her husband as a deity— observes the three-night vow during the time of her menses.
If, during the Kaumudī, the Vāsāḍhī, the Māghī, or likewise the Aśvayujī festival,
one regards one's mother and father as deities, [one attains merit].
Let her always give clarified butter and likewise salt to the Brahmins;
and let that woman who regards her husband as a deity perform the sweeping of the house.
O knower of dharma, perform the smearing of the floor and the offering of oblations; O proud and radiant lady, do not be one who is foul-mouthed or clever only for her own selfish ends.
O illustrious lady, let her eat even some vegetables;
O beautiful woman, let her offer the oblation and abandon untruth.
One should always desire virtuous kinsmen by eating but one meal a day;
a woman who regards her husband as a deity should constantly fast on every seventh day.
Then, when a year has been completed, one should give a golden tree along with a sacrificial fee to a Brāhmaṇa; thus she shall become auspicious and possessed of kinsmen.
That excellent woman who always offers a lamp made of *karañja* wood at [the shrine of] Vara, and likewise, when a full year has passed, offers a golden lamp; [she shall obtain the fruit].
Through her pleasing nature, that woman shall be beloved by her husband and likewise possessed of sons;
moreover, O auspicious one, she shines above her co-wives like a lamp.
She who always eats only what remains, who never causes pain,
who does not engage in forbidden food, O gentle one, and who is eternally devoted to her husband as a deity— [she is a virtuous wife].
She was constantly endowed with purity, never speaking harshly,
and always devoted to the service of her mother-in-law and father-in-law.
What need has she for vows, or what need for fasts,
she who always regards her husband as her deity and is endowed with the virtues of truth and righteousness?
Whatever woman desires a womb that is auspicious and even constricted,
she should fast for one year on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
One should give a golden vulva filled with curd to a twice-born man, adorned with a pair of pearls;
from that, one shall obtain an auspicious womb.
But as for a woman who has become a widow by the turn of fate,
O slender-waisted lady, I shall declare to you the dharma prescribed for her in the Purāṇas, provided she remains virtuous.
Having fashioned an image of her husband— whether depicted in a painting or made of clay—
she should always perform worship to it and remain mindful of the dharma of the virtuous.
Therefore, that woman of virtuous vows constantly sought permission for her religious observances,
her fasts, and especially for her meals.
In this way, she goes to the world of her husband unless she violates her husband;
Śāṇḍilī, who always regarded her husband as a deity, shines like the sun.
From this day forward, the wives of all the gods shall behold the meritorious rite which is ancient and eternal.
And the sage Nārada, whose soul is righteous, will know the entire ancient ordinance regarding fasting, as well as that concerning the various vows.
Aditi, Indrāṇī, and you, O excellent Soma-presser,
shall always be celebrated as virtuous and endowed with excellent qualities among those who engage in meritorious vows and sacred observances.
In all the manifestations of the high-souled Viṣṇu, his wife shall here know in their entirety and according to rule the procedure for the vow of fasting—
the eternal and merit-bestowing rite that is ever-present.
Among the duties of women, it is especially praised:
devotion to the husband, freedom from malice, and likewise freedom from verbal wickedness.
That woman who, like a base person, defiles her husband with wicked words,
goes to terrible hells for as long as the sun shines.
But she who eats before her husband shall become a flying fox for as many years as there are particles of dust upon the ground.
Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by the Great Goddess, those virtuous women, whose wealth was their asceticism,
bowed down to the Great Goddess, the beloved of Hara, and departed delighted.
Aditi undertook a vow; listen to what that practitioner of dharma did. She performed the entire procedure for the Umā-vow as it had been previously prescribed.
Having fastened it upon the *pārijāta* tree, Kaśyapa was then given to me;
that vow known as the *aditivrataka* was likewise bestowed by Satyabhāmā.
That very vow was undertaken by Sāvitrī, who was ever devoted to righteousness.
But this [deed] has been performed by them, joined together, even more excessively.
And when the time of twilight has arrived, at every such place,
worship, prostration, and recitation are traditionally held to be twofold in merit.
Having performed the vow of Sāvitrī and likewise the vow of Ādityā,
a virtuous woman shall deliver her husband’s family, her father’s family, and herself as well.
Indrāṇī performed her vow exactly as Umā had done according to the prescribed rite;
she wore garments of deep red and took food consisting of meat.
Furthermore, on the fourth day, there is again the ritual for the sake of merit;
one should observe a fast for a day and night, and likewise give a hundred jars.
The Gaṅgā has bestowed this very vow, which brings glory;
one should perform an additional bath in the water at dawn for oneself.
Or else, in the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight dear to Hari, one may perform this in water;
this is known as the Gaṅgā-vrata, which grants all desires.
Seven, seven, and then seven more families [are saved] by a woman who knows the Dharma and observes the Gaṅgā-vow at Harivallabha.
In this auspicious vow, one thousand jars of water from the Gaṅgā should be given;
that vow, which includes both the initiation (*tāraṇa*) and the conclusion (*pāraṇa*), fulfills all desires.
Then Yamabhāryā performed the vow known as Yāmaratha, which is auspicious;
it should be performed in the winter season under the open sky when Hari is dear [to her].
Standing in the open air, having bathed and being pure in her conduct, O auspicious lady, she should speak these very words after bowing to her husband.
I travel on Yama’s chariot and bear the snow upon my back;
may I become a woman devoted to her husband, with sons living, and a leader among women.
May I overcome my co-wives and may I not see Yama;
may I live for a long time with my husband and sons, and with a cheerful countenance.
May I go to the world of the ancestors and likewise become Nandinī—
well-clothed, with clean hands, beloved by my kinsmen, and endowed with virtuous qualities.
Having done this, one should then cause the Brahmin to recite a blessing with honey;
likewise, one should feed him with black sesame seeds and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Thus, O lady of divine complexion,
beloved of Hari, these vows were performed by the goddesses as previously declared by Mahādevī, the consort of Rudra.
I say this: endowed with my ascetic power, you shall all behold all the holy places as well as the various religious observances.
Those ancient [places] which were indeed seen of old by the goddess Umā—
endowed with auspicious qualities, purifying, and beautiful.
Vaiśampāyana said: Having seen the extensive details of the vow, and having perceived through divine vision the boon granted by Umā, Rukmiṇī performed that vow.
Among all the vows dedicated to Umā, the gift of a bull is likewise preeminent;
so too are the gift of a garland of jewels and food that fulfills all desires.
Likewise, Jāmbavatī gave him the city of Puramāvrataka;
she also gave him a particularly excellent and enchanting jewel-tree.
Then Satyā likewise gave her the Puromāvrata garment;
she gave a yellow garment that was even more excellent than the one given for the Umā-vrata.
Furthermore, O enhancer of the lineage, many vows were indeed undertaken by you in former times under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Phālgunī, and Maghā.
And Śatabhiṣā likewise performed a vow characterized by merit,
O joy of the Kurus, by which she attained preeminence among the lunar mansions.
On all fast days and during the consumption of the vow-food, one should perform the gift of Amāmaheśvara.
At a wedding, one should release a dark-colored bull along with the gift of a tawny cow.
O King, together with all the gods and Indra,
Umā indeed joined by Rudra departed for their own abode at the command of Viṣṇu’s vow.
