{Janamejaya said:}
O Vaiśampāyana, knower of dharma, disciple of Vyāsa, rich in asceticism!
In the account of the seizing of the Pārijāta tree, the city of Ṣaṭpura has been fully described.
O ascetic rich in penance, that was the dwelling place of the fierce leaders of the asuras;
O best of sages, recount their slaughter and that of Andhaka.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the heroic Tripura had been destroyed by Rudra of unwearied deeds,
many of the foremost among the best of the Asuras remained there.
Those inhabitants of Tripura were not consumed by the fire of Śiva’s arrows—
sixty hundred thousand in number, neither fewer nor more.
Tormented by the slaughter of their kinsmen, those heroes performed austerities in ancient times at Jambumārga, a place beloved by the virtuous and frequented by hosts of great seers.
Facing the sun, O best of kings, those heroes subsisted on air for a hundred thousand years, praising the Lotus-born One.
O King, one group among them took refuge in an udumbara tree;
there, O hero, they dwelt performing great austerities.
In the past, some dwelt there taking refuge at a kapittha tree,
while others performed fierce ascetic penance at Sṛgālavāṭī.
O descendant of Kuru, having gone to the banyan tree, those sons of the Asuras practiced austerities at the foot of the vaṭa tree,
studying the supreme Brahman.
O King, the Grandfather, the creator of beings, the best of gods and the foremost among the upholders of dharma, being pleased with them, arrived there to grant a boon.
"Choose a boon," they were told by the lotus-born Brahmā, O King; yet,
out of malice toward the omnipresent Tryambaka, they did not choose a boon,
desiring instead to go to their kinsmen' destruction, O joy of the Kurus.
Then Brahmā, the omniscient creator and destroyer of the entire universe, that great-souled one, said to them, "O descendant of Kuru:
Who is capable of repaying the debt of such a being? Let there be no fruitless labor for you."
Soma, the god Maheśvara, is without beginning, middle, or end;
those Asuras who desire to dwell happily in heaven praise him.
Some of those wicked-minded great Asuras desired to go there;
however, O King, other Asuras possessed auspicious dispositions.
When those very evil-minded ones sought to depart, Tāmasa said to them:
"O heroes, O Asuras, choose a boon for the sake of provoking Rudra's wrath."
They said, "O Lord, may we be unslayable by all the gods;
O God, may we have six cities within the surface of the earth."
"O Lord, may there be a city of six gates for us for the sake of fulfilling all our desires;
and O All-pervading One, may we dwell happily, having gone to that city of six gates."
"May we have no fear of Rudra, by whom our kinsmen were slain;
having seen Tripura destroyed, O treasure of asceticism, we are terrified."
The Grandfather said:
"Asuras, you are incapable of being slain by the gods or by Śaṅkara,
provided that you do not harass the brahmins who stand upon the path of the righteous and are dear to the virtuous."
If you should ever, out of delusion, cause injury to a Brahmin, you will go to destruction; for Brahmins are the supreme refuge of the world.
One should indeed fear Nārāyaṇa for performing what is harmful to Brahmins;
for the Blessed Janārdana bestows welfare upon all beings.
O King, those Asuras who were dismissed by Brahmā departed;
having established their six cities within the sacrificial arena, they were freed from their anger.
Even those Asuras who were devotees of Mahādeva and practitioners of dharma,
The Destroyer of Tripura gave them his own vision;
the Lord Soma, the most excellent master and the refuge of the virtuous, mounted his white bull and spoke these words to the Asuras.
Having abandoned enmity, hypocrisy, and violence, O best of asuras, you have taken refuge in me alone; therefore, I grant you an excellent boon.
"Go to heaven together with those sages and twice-born ones who are devoted to virtuous conduct and by whom you have been initiated; I am pleased with your good deed."
"Whatever ascetics who discourse on Brahman shall dwell here,
even beneath the *kāpitthika* tree, their worlds shall be just like mine."
In this world, whatever man at the end of a month or the end of a fortnight,
rich in austerity, shall worship me according to the forest-dweller's (vānaprastha) rite;
By performing this according to the prescribed rule for three nights, one shall obtain the fruit of a thousand years of asceticism and attain the desired goal.
For one dwelling on the island of Arka, that [result] shall be twofold;
and for one in a low-lying region—blessings be upon you—I grant this boon to you.
And whoever shall worship me by the name Śvetavāhana,
even if his mind is filled with fear on all sides, he shall attain my state.
The twice-born of Audumbara, Vāṭamūla, and Kāpitthika,
as well as those of Sṛgālavāṭī— all of whom were righteous and firm in their vows.
And those men who will constantly worship the sages of the Brahmavāṭī with special devotion, they shall go to their desired destination.
Having spoken thus, the blessed Mahādeva, whose vehicle is white,
departed for the world of Rudra together with all of them.
"I shall go to Jambūmārga; I dwell in Jambūmārga"—even by forming such a resolve, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time, however, there was one who was a knower of the four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga).
There was a Brāhmaṇa, a disciple of Yājñavalkya, endowed with the qualities of righteousness.
A Brahmin renowned as Brahmadatta, a follower of the Vājasaneya school,
performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice for the wise Vasudeva.
Having been initiated for the year-long consecration (dīkṣā), that dweller of the six cities [resided] on the auspicious bank of the river Āvartā, a beautiful stream frequented by sages.
The best of the twice-born, who was Vasudeva’s friend and fellow student,
O Kauravya, was the preceptor and the milk-offerer to that high-souled one.
O Lord, Vasudeva went there together with Devakī,
like Śakra approaching Bṛhaspati when he was performing a sacrifice in Ṣaṭpura.
That sacrificial session of Brahmadatta, abounding in food and abundant in sacrificial fees,
was attended by the best of sages— high-souled ones firm in their vows.
By means of reasoning consistent with my intellect, while officiating at the sacrifice for Vasudeva,
I was Vyāsa, as were Yājñavalkya, Sumantu, and likewise Jaimini.
Dhṛtimān, Jājali, and Devala and others, O Bhārata.
It was endowed with a supernatural power befitting the wise Vasudeva,
wherein the virtuous Devakī obtained all her desired wishes;
and by the power of Vāsudeva, O lord of the earth, she was able to create the world.
While that sacrifice was underway, the Daityas residing in Ṣaṭpura—
Nikumbha and the others— having assembled together, spoke to him, arrogant because of the boons they had received.
"Let a sacrificial portion be assigned to us; we shall drink the Soma.
And let the sacrificer Brahmadatta bestow maidens upon us."
"That high-souled one has many daughters who are beautiful;
we have heard it said that they must certainly be invited and given to us."
"May Brahmadatta grant us distinguished jewels;
otherwise, we command that no sacrifice be performed."
Having heard this, Brahmadatta said to those great Asuras:
"O best of Asuras, no sacrificial portion was ordained for you in the past."
"How can the drinking of Soma be provided by me at the sacrifice?
For you have questioned me here, O best of sages, who are experts in the meaning of the Vedic commentaries."
For those daughters of mine who are to be given away have already been designated by me;
they are undoubtedly to be bestowed within the sacrificial altar upon suitably matched husbands.
"I shall indeed bestow the jewels with conciliation after due reflection;
however, relying on the son of Devakī, I will by no means give them by force."
But the wicked Nikumbha and others, inhabitants of Ṣaṭpura, became enraged;
they plundered the sacrificial enclosure and likewise carried off those maidens.
Seeing that [host] advancing,
Ānakadundubhi reflected upon the high-souled Vāsudeva, as well as Balabhadra and Gada.

Having understood the situation, Kṛṣṇa then said this to Pradyumna: "Go, my son; rescue the maiden quickly by means of your illusory power (māyā), O Lord, until I arrive at Ṣaṭpura with the army of the Yādavas."
Then that hero, obedient to his father’s command, went to Ṣaṭpura.
Having gone there in merely the blink of an eye, the wise and mighty Kāma,
possessed of great strength, carried off those maidens by means of his illusory power.
The son of Rukmiṇī, having fashioned other [images] made of illusion, placed them [there];

Vaiśampāyana said:
While those Yādavas of meritorious deeds were thus engaged in their sports, [the following occurred].
Having found a vulnerability, the evil-minded enemy of the gods, who is difficult to overcome, [attacked].
O King, a Dānava named Nikumbha, desiring his own destruction, carried off the maiden named Bhānumatī, the daughter of Bhānu.
O King, having vanished after deluding the women of the Yadus,
the master of illusion, remembering his former enmity, employed his magic power.
O hero, Prabhāvatī, the daughter of that Vajranābha, his brother, was carried off by Pradyumna; likewise, Vajranābha was slain.
For the sun indeed dwells in the forest at its own appointed time;
thus, O lowest of Dānavas, you who know one's vulnerabilities dwell in that which is not under your control and is difficult to assail.
A great cry suddenly arose in the maidens' quarters when that maiden had been carried off while she was weeping, O conqueror of assemblies.
Then, having heard the cry of distress from the daughter’s quarters, both the heroes Vasudeva and Āhuka, clad in armor, went forth.
But those two did not see their assailant within the range of their vision;
likewise, clad in armor, they went to where the mighty Kṛṣṇa was.
Having heard this matter, Janārdana, the subduer of enemies, ascended his own celestial chariot;
accompanied by Pārtha, he mounted Tārkṣya, the enemy of serpents.
Having instructed the dolphin-bannered god (Kāma) to follow after the chariot,
the hero also commanded Garuḍa, the son of Kaśyapa, saying, "Hurry!"

As Vajra approached the city, the great-souled Pārtha and Kṛṣṇa, both subduers of enemies, encountered Nikumbha, who was difficult to conquer in battle; and Pradyumna, O King, possessed of great splendor and the foremost among masters of illusion, also joined them.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, and Pārtha, he split himself in two;
then Nikumbha, seeing him, likewise split himself into three.
Nikumbha, who resembled an immortal, fought them all while laughing,
using heavy maces bristling with many spikes.
O King, having grasped the maiden Bhānumatī with his left hand,
he then struck her with a mace using his right hand.
Neither for the sake of a maiden, nor out of anger, nor out of desire, O best of kings,
did they strike mercilessly at Nikumbha and the great asura Kṛṣṇa.
Those high-souled ones, difficult to approach, were capable of slaying the enemy;
yet, O lord of men, they sighed, oppressed by the weight of compassion.
Pārtha, the best among archers and skilled in every way in battle,
struck the Daitya with iron arrows, spears, and shafts according to the prescribed method.
But they pierced the Dānava in battle with arrows a span long,
O lord of the earth, yet not even by a hair’s breadth through skill or training did they strike the maiden.
Then, together with the maiden, he vanished right there;
for having resorted to the illusion of an Asura, no one indeed perceived him.
Then Kṛṣṇa and the son of Rukmiṇī followed behind him;
then that great asura stood there, having become a bird of the Hārīta species.
Then the hero Dhanañjaya, protecting the maiden, struck him once again with arrows a span long that pierced his vital organs.
That great asura, the crusher of enemies, wandered over this entire earth with its seven islands,
followed by those heroes.
Above Mount Gokarṇa, the great asura fell upon the sandy bank of the river Celagaṅgā together with his daughter.
Neither the gods nor the asuras,
O Bharata, can transgress Gokarṇa, which is protected by the splendor of Mahādeva and rich in ascetic merit.
Having reached this opportunity, Pradyumna, the son of Bhīma, who was swift in prowess and invincible in battle, seized the maiden Bhānumatī.
Afflicted by the two Kṛṣṇas with sharpened arrows, O King,
that Asura Nikumbha then abandoned Uttaragokarṇa and fled toward the southern direction,
while the two Kṛṣṇas, mounted upon Tārkṣya, followed behind him.
Then he entered Ṣaṭpura, the abode of his kinsmen;
there, the two heroes, the Kṛṣṇas, spent that night at the entrance of a cave.
Instructed by Kṛṣṇa, the son of Rukmiṇī also led the daughter of the Sun to the city of Dvārakā with a joyful heart.
Having led them away, the hero went to Ṣaṭpura, which was teeming with Dānavas;
and at the entrance of the cave, he beheld the two Kṛṣṇas of terrible prowess.
The two of great strength, Kṛṣṇa and Pradyumna, having reached the gate of Ṣaṭpura together with Pradyumna, stayed there, desiring the slaughter of Nikumbha.
Immediately after that, from this cave,
the exceedingly powerful and mighty Nikumbha, of terrifying prowess, then emerged to fight.
As he was emerging from that hole, O lord of the people, Pārtha blocked his path on all sides with arrows discharged from the Gāṇḍīva.
Rushing forward and raising his terrible mace, which was covered in many spikes,
Nikumbha, the best among the strong, struck Pārtha on the head.
When Pārtha was struck by the mace and was vomiting blood and fainting,
that arrogant asura laughed and struck the son of Rukmiṇī.
Then that hero, facing eastward— the foremost of illusionists among those skilled in illusion—
was struck on the head by an unseen assailant and fell into a swoon.
Seeing those two Tathāgatas bewildered and severely beaten,
Govinda, overcome with rage, rushed toward Nikumbha.
Raising the Kaumodakī mace, the one born of the Gadā lineage hurled his club;
then those two, invincible to one another, rushed at each other while roaring.
Then Śakra, mounted upon Airāvata together with all the hosts of gods,
beheld that great and terrible battle between the gods and the asuras.
Having seen the gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, the subduer of enemies, desiring the welfare of the deities, sought to slay the Dānava through various battles.
Keśava, the mighty-armed one skilled in battle, displayed various wonderful mandalas while fondling the Kaumodakī mace.
In the same way, the chief of the Asuras, whirling that mace which was full of many spikes through his training, then moved in circular patterns.
Roaring like two bulls and trumpeting like two elephants,
they were like two enraged jackals that had come upon a doe.
But Nikumbha,
O hero, having let out a most dreadful roar, struck the elder brother of Gada with his mace, which was adorned with eight clearly ringing bells.
At that very moment, O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa also whirled his great mace and brought it down upon the head of Nikumbha.
Having gripped the mace Kaumodakī for a moment, the wise Hari, the teacher of the world, stood firm; yet he fainted and fell upon the earth.
At that time, when the high-souled Vāsudeva, the god among men, had thus departed, the entire world became filled with cries of "Alas! Alas! (hāhābhūta).
The Lord of Gods himself sprinkled Kṛṣṇa with the cool and fragrant water of the celestial Gaṅgā, which was mixed with nectar.
Surely Kṛṣṇa, the best of gods, acted in that way by his own will;
for who indeed is capable of deluding the high-souled Hari in battle?
O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa,
the destroyer of enemies, having regained his strength, raised his discus and said to the evil-minded one, "Receive [this blow]!"
Nikumbha too, a master of supreme illusion and difficult to approach, leapt up;
having abandoned that body, Keśava did not perceive him.
Thinking, "He is about to die or is already dead," Janārdana,
the hero, O Lord, protected him while remembering his own heroic vow.
Then Pradyumna and the son of Kuntī, having regained their senses,
arrived and stood near Nārāyaṇa, resolved upon the slaughter of Nikumbha.
Then Pradyumna, who was skilled in illusion, spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"Father, Nikumbha is not here; that evil-minded one has gone somewhere."
When that body was released by Pradyumna alone, it perished;
then the Lord, the Master, laughed together with Arjuna.
Likewise, O lord of men, those heroes then beheld thousands upon thousands of Nikumbhas everywhere on the earth and in the sky.
Thousands [of arrows] were indeed aimed at Kṛṣṇa, as well as at Pārtha, the subduer of enemies, and likewise at the heroic son of Rukmiṇī; it was like a marvel.
Some seized the bow of the Pāṇḍava, some his great arrows;
other great Asuras grasped his hands, and others his feet.
Having thus seized that hero, they ascended into the sky;
meanwhile, there were tens of millions of Pārthas who had also been captured at that time.
Kṛṣṇa and the son of Kṛṣṇa, those two destroyers of enemies, could see no end [to the shower of arrows];
having severed Nikumbha with their shafts, those two heroes were spared by Pārtha.
O Bhārata, each one was split in two, becoming divided;
at that time, the blessed Kṛṣṇa beheld this through his divine knowledge.
And Madhusūdana beheld Nikumbha in his true form—
the creator of all illusions and the one who had taken away the life of Phalguna.

While all beings were looking on, Hari, the slayer of asuras and the source of the past, present, and future, severed his head with his discus. O King, descendant of Bharata, once the head was cut off, he released Phalguna.
Then the chief of the Asuras fell down like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Then,
O giver of honor, at the word of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna) caught Pārtha as he was falling from the sky while traversing the air.
When Nikumbha had fallen to the ground, the god consoled Dhanañjaya and,
filled with a desire for Pārtha’s welfare, departed for Dvārakā.
Then the powerful lord, the joy of the Yadus, having reached Dvārakā, was filled with delight;
he paid homage to the high-souled Nārada.
Then the highly effulgent Nārada spoke to Bhānu, the Yādava:
"Bhānu, do not harbor resentment; listen, O son of Bhīma."
While she was playing in the Raivata garden, Durvāsas was provoked to anger by her;
thereupon, out of wrath, that sage cursed your daughter.
"Because of those who are excessively indulgent, the maiden will fall into the hands of the enemy;
for the sake of your son, I, together with the sages, have entreated him."

O Sage, O knower of dharma, O best among the upholders of dharma, how is it that you have cursed this innocent girl, a young maiden observing a vow? Immediately provide a remedy for this; we beg you to do so.
O descendant of Bhīma, having been addressed by us in this manner, Durvāsas,
filled with compassion, looked downcast for a moment and spoke.
The word that I have spoken is so and not otherwise;
for it will certainly fall into the hands of the enemy, of this there is no doubt.
But she, being blameless according to dharma, will obtain a husband.
She will have many sons, great wealth, and good fortune.
And that maiden, always fragrant with sweet scent,
shall again and again bear this terrible grief of yours, O Vaṅgī.
"O hero, let Bhānumatī be given thus to Sahadeva;
for that Pāṇḍava is faithful, brave, and virtuous in character."
Then the righteous-souled Bhānu, remembering the words of Nārada, gave Bhānumatī to Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī.
And Sahadeva was brought back when the wielder of the discus sent him;
then, once the marriage had been performed, he returned to his own city together with his wife.
The man who, full of faith, reads or hears this *Vijaya* of Kṛṣṇa shall obtain victory in all his undertakings.

Version of March 2005:
Janamejaya said:
The abduction of Bhānumatī, the victory of Keśava,
and likewise the bringing of Chālikya from the world of the gods, O great sage.
O sage, best among the upholders of dharma, I have heard of the most wonderful divine play of the Kṛṣṇas, who possess supreme splendor, upon the ocean.
"For the slaying of Vajranābha was indeed mentioned during the narration of Nikumbha’s death;
O Sage, I have a great curiosity to hear about that through your grace."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Behold, O King, I shall proclaim to you the slaying of Vajranābha,
as well as the victory of Kāma and the high-souled Sāmba."
On a peak of Mount Meru, O lord of men, the great asura known as Vajranābha— resolute and victorious in battle— performed austerities.
The immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, being pleased with him and gratified by his ascetic penance, invited him to choose a boon.
That best of Dānavas chose invincibility from the gods,
as well as a city called Vajrapura, which was auspicious and composed entirely of all kinds of jewels.
And there is entry at will even for Vāyu, O Bhārata;
and the attainment of desires occurs unexpectedly, O lord of men.
And there were hundreds of market-towns belonging to the principal branch-cities all around that immeasurable city, O Janamejaya.
Thus it came to pass for him through that granting of a boon, O Bhārata:
the great Asura Vajranābha dwelt in the city of Vajra.
O King, having surrounded him who had obtained excellent boons by the millions, those Asuras dwelt in Vajrapura as well as in the Saṃvāhas.
O lord of men, in the delightful principal branch-cities,
O King, the enemies of the god were joyful, well-fed, and delighted.
Then Vajranābha, evil-minded and arrogant because of the boon he had received,
set about to harass both his own city and the entire world.
Having gone to the world of the gods, O lord of the people, he said to Mahendra:
"O chastiser of Pāka, I wish to rule over the three worlds."
Or else, O Lord of the hosts of gods, grant me battle;
for the entire world is common property to the high-souled descendants of Kaśyapa.
Having consulted with Bṛhaspati, that lord of the gods,
the best of deities born of the Kuru lineage, spoke to Vajranābha.
"O gentle one, our father, the sage Kaśyapa, is consecrated for a sacrificial session (*satra*).
When that is concluded, he will certainly act according to what is right."
Then that Dānava went to his father Kaśyapa and spoke as he had been told by the king of the gods; Kaśyapa then replied to him.
"When the sacrificial session is completed, I shall do what is right;
but you, my son, go and dwell in Vajrapura, taking up your residence there."
When this had been said, Vajranābha went to his own city,
and the god Mahendra also departed for Dvārakā, which is garlanded with gates.
Having gone there and vanished, the god then spoke to Vāsudeva;
Janārdana related that account of Vajranābha.
"O God, the great sacrifice of the horse (vājimedha) has been undertaken by Śauri.
When that is completed, O Vāsava, I shall cause Vajranābha to fall."
Therefore, let us consider a means for entering there, as that is the path of the virtuous;
for no one can enter there against their will, O Lord, not even the wind.
Then the king of the gods departed, having been honored by Vāsudeva;
and when the horse sacrifice of Vasudeva had arrived, O Bhārata.
While that sacrifice was underway, both heroes— the best of gods, the king of the gods and Acyuta— reflected upon how they might enter.
While that sacrifice was underway, a certain actor named Bhadranāman then delighted the great seers with his excellent dancing.
The best of sages invited that self-controlled man to choose a boon;
he, a noble dancer who resembled the Lord of the Gods, chose a boon.
Urged by Sarasvatī at the command of Devendra-Kṛṣṇacchanda,
he prostrated before the best of sages who had assembled for the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
"O best of sages, may I become one who is to be fed by all the twice-born;
and may I wander throughout this earth with its seven continents."
Renowned for his power of traveling through the sky and showing special honor [to the gods],
he was unslayable by all beings, whether they be stationary or moving.
"In whatever guise I should enter—
whether that of one who is dead, or one who is living, or even one produced through a supernatural state."
May I indeed become such once again, forever free from old age and disease;
may the sages and all others always be well-pleased with me.
"Let it be so," the actor was told by the Brahmins, O King;
like an immortal, he wandered throughout the earth with its seven continents.
The cities of the lords of the Dānavas, as well as the Northern Kurus,
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and Kālāpada-dvīpa.
On all festival days, O hero of the world, that great dancer who has been granted boons comes to Dvārakā, which is adorned by the Yadus.
Then the blessed Śakra, the lord of the gods, having consoled the swans of the Dhārtarāṣṭra race who dwell in the world of the gods, spoke to them.
"O brothers, we Kāśyapas are the birds of the gods;
likewise, we are the carriers of the celestial chariots of the virtuous deities."
The gods have a duty to perform, a task involving the slaying of their enemies; that must be done, and your counsel must not be disclosed under any circumstances.
If you fail to carry out the command of the deity, a terrible punishment shall fall upon you;
O best of swans, your movement is everywhere unrestricted.
"Having gone to Vajranābha’s supreme city, which is inaccessible to others,
you should roam here among the ponds of the inner apartments, for that is indeed appropriate for you."
He indeed possesses a jewel of a daughter, auspicious and surpassing all in the three worlds;
by name she is called Prabhāvatī, radiant like the moon.
It is heard by us that this fair-faced woman was indeed obtained by her mother through the granting of a boon from the great goddess Haimavatī.
And that beautiful maiden, having been established by her kinsmen in a *svayaṃvara*,
will choose a husband according to her own desire, O swans.
Therefore, you must speak of the true virtues of the high-souled Pradyumna—
his noble lineage, his beauty, his character, and likewise his youth.
When she, being of a passionate nature, is the daughter of Vajranābha,
a message must be conveyed to her through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, you must bring Pradyumna back from there in that very same manner;
and by your own intelligence, you must arrange whatever is beneficial for me according to the exigency of the time.
In every way, you must ensure that there is serenity in his eyes and countenance.
In such and such a manner should the virtues of the high-souled Pradyumna be recounted,
so that the mind of Prabhāvatī may become firmly fixed upon him.
And news of all kinds must be sent to me every day,
as well as to my younger brother Kṛṣṇa in Dvāravatī.
One should exert effort as long as Pradyumna has not yet become self-knowing;
for the Lord must win over the beautiful-limbed daughter of Vajranābha.
Proud because of the boons granted by Brahmā, those [demons] were indeed invulnerable to the gods;
therefore, they must be slain in battle by the sons of the gods, headed by Pradyumna.
Having been granted a boon, the Yādavas— Pradyumna and the others— will go there disguised as actors to bring about the destruction of Vajranābha.
All this must be done, as well as whatever else is appropriate for the occasion; indeed, you yourself should ordain it out of a desire to do what is pleasing to us.
O swans, there is no entry for the gods there by any means;
indeed, entry is granted in every way only to one desired by Vajranābha.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Vāsava, those swans went to Vajrapura.
For their departure there, O lord of men, was indeed previously ordained for them.
O hero, those birds alighted upon the delightful oblong ponds,
which were covered with golden lotuses and water-lilies that were pleasant to the touch.
Uttering sweet cries and speaking a refined language never heard before,
they indeed produce wonder even though they have arrived here previously.
O King, they roamed through the ponds within the inner apartments that were enjoyed by the inhabitants of Triviṣṭapa; those [ponds] were dear to Vajranābha.
O lord of men, as the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were conversing very sweetly,
that son of Diti spoke these words to them, the Dhārtarāṣṭras.
"You who are always delighted in Triviṣṭapa and are so eloquent in speech,
whenever our festival here is perceived by you..."
"O Jālapādas, you must come; this is your own home.
And you who dwell in Triviṣṭapa must enter with full confidence."
O Bhārata, having been addressed thus by Vajranābha, those birds,
saying "So be it," entered the abode of the lord of the Dānavas.
Out of regard for the task of the gods, they cultivated familiarity [with humans];
speaking in human tongues, they engaged in various kinds of conversation.
The wives of the Kāśyapas, who were endowed with every excellence, took special delight in listening together to these narrations composed in verse.
Then the swans beheld Prabhāvatī, the daughter of Vajranābha, as she wandered about with her lovely smile; she was of beautiful form and possessed a radiant countenance.
Thereupon, the swans became acquainted with that sweet-smiling maiden.
Then the female swan made the princess her companion, Śucimukhī.
Once, she questioned that excellent friend, the daughter of Vajranābha,
who was confident in her and had been won over by hundreds of various tales.
"O powerful one, I indeed know you as Trailokyasundarī;
O Goddess, with your beauty, character, and virtues, I venture to say something to you."
O timid one, O lady of lovely smiles, your youth is passing away;
that which has passed does not return, like the current of a flowing stream.
"O Goddess, O auspicious one, there exists no pleasure in this world equal to the enjoyment of desires among women; I tell you this truth."
"O you who are beautiful in every limb, your father has placed you in a *svayaṃvara*,
yet you do not choose anyone born of the lineage of gods or asuras."
"O lady of beautiful hips, O auspicious one, those endowed with beauty, heroism, and virtues, and who are indeed worthy of your family, depart in shame when they are rejected by you."
O Goddess, you do not wish to accept suitors who have arrived and are equal to you in lineage and beauty;
for what purpose then would Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī, come here to you?
O lady of beautiful limbs, O auspicious one, is there anyone in the three worlds who is his equal in form, or in lineage,
or in virtues, or even in valor?
Among the gods he is a god, O fair-hipped one, and among the Dānavas he is a Dānava;
even among humans he is a human, that righteous and mighty one.
O Goddess, for upon seeing him, the hips of women indeed overflow,
like the full udders of cows or the currents of rivers.
Indeed, I am not able to compare her face to the full moon, nor her eyes to lotuses,
nor her gait to that of the king of beasts.
O auspicious lady, having brought the bodiless one under his control along with his body, the powerful Viṣṇu created that son by extracting the very essence of the world.
By him, while still a child, the wicked Śambara was destroyed;
all his illusions were mastered, yet his character was not corrupted.
O lady of broad hips, whatever qualities you may conceive of in your mind as desirable within the three worlds, all of those shall belong to Pradyumna.
In brilliance he was like fire; in patience he was equal to the earth;
in splendor he resembled the sun; and in depth he was like a lake.
The noble lady Prabhāvatī said to Śucimukhī:
"I have heard many times that Viṣṇu resides in the world of men."
O gentle one, as my father and the wise Nārada were speaking, they said:
"O sinless one, he is indeed the enemy of the Daityas and must certainly be avoided."
O proud lady, it is said that by him the families of the Daityas were consumed with his blazing discus,
as well as with his Śārṅga bow and his mace.
"Those asuras who indeed dwell in the provinces and branch cities— these are being commanded by the lord of the Dānavas with respect to him."
For this is indeed the desire of all women, O lady of pure smiles:
"May my husband's family be more excellent than my father's family."
If indeed there were a means for him to come here,
it would be a great favor to me, and my lineage would be purified.
"O you of pure speech, being asked by me, give me an answer as to how Pradyumna,
born of the Vṛṣṇi clan, may become my husband."
I have heard from the elderly women of the asuras as they were speaking: Hari is the eternal enemy of the Daityas and a source of terror to them.
Likewise, I have previously heard of the birth of Pradyumna,
and how by him the powerful Kālaśambara was slain.
"O most virtuous lady, Pradyumna indeed dwells eternally within my heart;
there is no reason for him to come to me as there has been for my own union with you."
I am your slave; worthy of your friendship, I shall send you as a messenger.
"You are wise; tell me the means for our union with him."
Then, having consoled her, she spoke this with a smile:
"O lady of lovely smiles, I shall go there as your messenger;
O girl of pure radiance, I will proclaim this noble devotion of yours."
"And I shall act in such a way that he will come into your presence;
O fair-hipped one, you shall become possessed of your desire through Kāma himself."
"Thus has this truth been spoken by me; remember it, O lady of pure eyes.
O large-eyed one, report my skill in storytelling to your father."
"O large-eyed goddess, tell your father that this story is favorable to him;
thus, O goddess, you will properly accomplish what is for my benefit in this matter."
Having said this, she did exactly so; then she spoke to her as follows.
Then the lord of the Dānavas asked that female swan in the inner apartments:
"Prabhāvatī has told me that you are skilled in storytelling."
"O pure-faced one, tell the truth according to what is fitting for this excellent man:
O supreme bird of the world, what wonder have you seen?"
"O blameless one, you who have never before seen what is fit or unfit for others," the female swan said to Vajranābha, "O best among the foremost of men."
"Listen," he said, addressing the immensely radiant lord of the Dānavas:
"O best of Dānavas, I have seen a virtuous woman named Śāṇḍilī,
a high-minded lady performing a wondrous feat on the side of Mount Meru."
And Sumanā Kausalyā, who delights in the welfare of all beings,
likewise had a beautiful friend, Śāṇḍilī, the daughter of a mountain, not far away.
And I beheld the auspicious actor, who had been granted a boon by the sage; he was able to assume any form at will, was worthy of enjoyment, and was ever-honored throughout the three worlds.
O hero, O sinless one, he goes to the Northern Kurus and indeed to the island of Kālāmra,
as well as to Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and other islands.
He knows the songs sung by the gods and *gandharvas*, as well as various kinds of dances; through his dancing, he constantly causes the gods to marvel.
Vajranābha said:
"I have heard this in detail from the Cāraṇas and the high-souled Siddhas as they were speaking; it seems you will soon slay him."
"I too have curiosity in every respect, O daughter of the bird-king;
however, since that actor has been granted a boon, there is no intimacy with him."
The female swan said:
"O best of the sons of Diti, that dancer wanders through the seven islands;
having heard of people possessed of virtues, he is entirely captivated by their virtues."
O hero, O great Asura, if he should hear the true and extensive account of your virtues,
know then that the actor has arrived at your city.
Vajranābha said:
"O auspicious one, devise a means by which you may slay that dancer here;
O daughter of the birds, may it be well with you, so that he may come into my domain."
Those swans, dispatched by Vajranābha for the sake of his mission,
then reported all of that to Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the gods.
Pradyumna was appointed by Adhokṣaja to that task,
as well as to the killing of Vajranābha in connection with his union with Prabhāvatī.
Resorting to divine illusion and assuming the role of an actor,
Hari sent a messenger to the sons of Bhima in the guise of an actor, O Bharata.
Making Pradyumna the leader, Sāmba the jester,
the heroic Gada his attendant, and likewise the other sons of Bhīma;
At the side of Vīramatī was Gadā, and likewise for the Bhaimas; having appointed courtesans and actresses,
that [performance] then resembled a musical concert.
In the same way, [he saw] Bhadra’s auspicious companions, who were likewise of such a kind.
Having ascended that beautiful celestial chariot fashioned by Pradyumna, those great car-warriors departed for the sake of the mission of the gods of immeasurable splendor.
O lord of men, for each one of them there were male attendants equal in form to themselves,
and all of them had female attendants who were similar to them in voice and appearance.
Then they went from Vajranagara to an excellent branch-city, known by the name Supura, which was crowded with Dānavas.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O lord of men, [the battle took place] with the Asuras who dwelt in Supura.
Vajranābha gave his command: "Let an excellent house be provided;
let hospitality be shown to them with an offering of many jewels."
Having received their husband’s command, they all acted accordingly, providing most variegated garments for his pleasure and for the delight of the people.
A dancer heard of previously arrived, and he aroused a sense of curiosity.
Then the Daityas, with supreme joy, offered hospitality to the actor;
and for the sake of his confidence, they also gave him a great many jewels.
Then the actor Varadatta danced there at that time,
bringing supreme joy to the citizens of Supura.
The *Rāmāyaṇa*, a great epic poem, has been adapted into a dramatic outline,
describing the birth of the immeasurable Viṣṇu out of his desire to slay the lord of the Rākṣasas.
O sinless one, Lomapāda Daśaratha caused the great sage Ṛśyaśṛṅga to be brought there along with courtesans.
O Bharata, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata,
as well as Ṛśyaśṛṅga and Śāntā, were all portrayed by actors in their respective forms.
The elder Dānavas, who had lived at that time, were struck with wonder;
O Acyuta, they indeed described the identity of their forms.
Seeing their gestures, their dramatic representations, their mastery of those introductory preludes,
and their entrance, all the Dānavas were filled with wonder.
Those Asuras, filled with passion, were struck with wonder by the highest joy;
rising again and again, they performed various special dances.
Delighted, they gave garments, necklaces,
and bracelets, as well as captivating neck-ornaments adorned with gold and lapis lazuli.
When gifts had been bestowed for various purposes, those actors praised them with verses,
[extolling] both the Asuras and the sages by their lineages and ancestral origins.
Then, the arrival of the king was announced by the inhabitants of the branch cities to the divine-looking actor Vajranābha.
O Bharata, in former times, the lord of the Daityas, having heard of this matter, sent [messengers] with joyful excitement, saying:
"Let that actor be brought to Vajrapura."
Having heard the words of the lord of the Dānavas, the Yādavas were led by the inhabitants of Śākhānagara to the beautiful city of Vajrapura in the guise of actors.
Then a well-constructed dwelling was granted by Viśvakarman;
and whatever else was desired, all that was given back a hundredfold more.
Then the great asura Vajranābha celebrated the festival of Kāla;
with great joy, he had a beautiful arena constructed.
Then, after giving them many jewels, the great asura Vajranābha urged them to proceed for the sake of the spectacle once they were fully rested.
And having seated himself with his kinsmen to see them,
that self-possessed lord of men placed the umbrella over the inner apartments and fixed his gaze upon what was visible.
The sons of Bhīma, having donned their costumes and assumed the attire of actors,
those performers of formidable deeds began to dance for the sake of their mission.
Then they played various musical instruments— some solid,
some hollow, adorned with drums and cymbals, and others pierced with the qualities of stringed notes.
Then the women of Nala’s household sang the Devagāndhāra, the Śālikya, the Śravaṇa, and the Ṛta melodies, which brought pleasure to the mind and the ear.
Then, with a wealth of musical notes, they sang the delightful Āgāndhāra rāga in the Gaṅgāvataraṇa mode, performed with *viddha* and *āsārita* ornaments.
O Bhārata, having heard the auspicious account of the descent of the Gaṅgā, which was set to a rhythmic tempo, the Asuras rose up again and again to express their delight.
Pradyumna and Gada played the *nāndī* drum,
and Sāmba, endowed with great heroism, assumed the role of a dancer for the sake of the mission.
Then, at the conclusion of the *nāndī*, the son of Rukmiṇī recited a verse concerning the descent of the Gaṅgā, performing it with perfect dramatic gestures.
Then they danced the *Kauvera* drama, "The Secret Rendezvous with Rambhā";
there, Śūra took the form of Rāvaṇa, while Manovatī assumed the guise of Rambhā.
Nalakūbara was Pradyumna, Sāmba was his Vidūṣaka,
and even Kailāsa was fashioned through their illusory power by the joy of the Yadus.
Then, the wicked-minded Rāvaṇa was cursed by the enraged Nalakūbara; subsequently, Rambhā was also consoled by him.
Thus is the life-story of Rāma, consisting of six sections and its supplement;
it brings wealth, fame, and long life, and it bestows victory upon kings.

Singing with sweet voices, they performed that work previously proclaimed by Vālmīki, which is imbued with the sentiments of love and the rest, and is accompanied by the musical notes of *niṣāda* and the others.
O heroes, the delighters of the Yadu clan danced at this episode concerning the glory of the sage Nārada, the omniscient and high-souled one.
With the stamping of their feet, with dancing, and likewise with dramatic gestures,
the heroic Dānavas praised the sons of Bhīma, who possessed immeasurable splendor.
They gave them excellent garments, jewels, and ornaments;
as well as necklaces with dangling beads, adorned with lapis lazuli gems.
Variegated celestial chariots and sky-faring vehicles,
as well as elephants born of divine lineages that travel through the air.
And divine sandalwoods, cool and flavorful, O Bhārata; and heavy aloe-woods of the finest kind, rich in fragrance;
and noble *cintāmaṇi* gems that grant every desire as soon as they are thought of.
While they were giving those many gifts at the spectacles,
O best of men, the Dānavas were deprived of their wealth and jewels;
likewise, O lord of people, the wives of the chief Dānavas were taken away.
Then Haṃsī, the friend of Prabhāvatī, said to Prabhāvatī:
"O blameless one, I have gone to the beautiful Dvārakā, which is protected by the son of Bhīma."
And Pradyumna was seen by me in a secluded place, O lovely-eyed one;
and his devotion to you, O lady of pure smiles, was described by me.
Delighted by that, O lotus-eyed one, he set a time:
"Today, at the hour of evening twilight, there shall be a union with you."
Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, today there shall be a reunion with your beloved;
for those born of the Bhima lineage, being self-possessed, do not speak falsely.
Then Prabhāvatī, delighted, said this to that female swan:
"O beautiful one, you have stayed in my dwelling; you ought to sleep here."
"I wish to see the son of Kaśyapa while staying together with you;
O bird, in your company I shall be free from fear."
The female swan said "So be it" to her lotus-eyed friend,
and that bird then ascended the righteous vehicle of Prabhāvatī.
On that palace roof constructed by Viśvakarman,
Prabhāvatī quickly made preparations suitable for the arrival of Pradyumna.
When those arrangements had been made, she departed to bring Kāma, having obtained the permission of Prabhāvatī; she was like a female swan in her grace and equal to the wind in speed.
Having approached Kāma, who was wearing the dress of an actor, she of the pure smile said:
"O Blessed One, the time has now arrived in the night.
"So be it," Kāma replied to her; then that bird departed.
Having gone and returned, the female swan then said to Prabhāvatī:
"O large-eyed one, that son of Rukmiṇī is approaching; take heart."
The self-possessed hero Pradyumna,
the crusher of enemies, saw a fragrant garland being carried away, covered by bees.
Then, having become a bee, he hid himself there in that garland;
and as Prabhāvatī was leading him away, the powerful one understood the situation.
And that garland, filled with bees, was brought in by the women;
it was presented to Prabhāvatī by the women, covered all over with those humming insects.
And not far away, O lord of men, was the dwelling of Prabhāvatī;
those bees went there, O gentle one, when the time of twilight had arrived.
That hero, the foremost of Bhima’s sons, being deprived of those companions,
slowly sank, as it were, into the ear-lotus of Prabhāvatī.
Then Prabhāvatī, the best among speakers, said to the female swan:
"O friend, beholding the exceedingly beautiful full moon as it rises,
my limbs burn and my mouth dries up."
There is an exceeding eagerness in my heart; what is this incurable disease?
That full moon,
with its cool rays newly risen, doubled the longing of him who was accustomed to spending his nights in the company of his beloved.
"Indeed, such a thing as this has never been seen by me before; it was only craved through mere hearsay.
Alas, my limbs are smoking! Shame indeed upon the very nature of womanhood!"
If my beloved does not come to me according to what I imagine in my mind, alas,
I shall go the way of the night-lotus, destitute and wretched; alas,
I, the high-minded one, have been bitten by the serpent of passion!
The rays of the moon, which by their very nature possess a cooling potency and are pleasant and gladdening to the world,
why do they burn my limbs?
The wind, naturally cool and carrying the pollen of various flowers,
today burns my beautiful body as if it were a forest fire.
Therefore, one should indeed resolve that stability is to be achieved by oneself;
for the mind, when overcome by its own volitions, remains inactive and devoid of vigor.

and he, skilled in the arts of love, gradually embraced that woman of beautiful hips.

He delighted her in secret and did not cause her distress at that time; skilled in the arts of love, he accomplished his entire purpose. Thus the lordly son of Kṛṣṇa dwelt together with her, taking his pleasure.

Seeing the humility, discipline, virtue, grace, skill, elegance,

The women of the asuras long for the beauty, grace, fragrance, cleanliness, speech, and nobility of those Yādava women.
The brother of Vajranābha was the renowned Sunābha;
and that king had two daughters endowed with beauty and virtue.
One is named Candravatī and the other is Guṇavatī;
they both indeed go constantly to the abode of Prabhāvatī.
There they both beheld Prabhāvatī, intent upon her pleasure; and having approached her with confidence, they questioned her as she sat there.
She said: "I possess a lore which, once studied, brings a desired husband quickly for the sake of pleasure and bestows good fortune;
it indeed renders even a god or a *dānava* instantly helpless."
"I take my delight with that wise son of a god, my beloved;
behold Pradyumna, who is so dear to me, by means of my power. Having seen the perfection of his beauty and youth, they were filled with wonder.
Then those two sisters of lovely smiles,

The gods are always devoted to righteousness, while the great asuras are of a deceitful nature;
for the gods are indeed attached to austerity, whereas the great asuras are attached to pleasure.
The gods are always devoted to truth, while the great asuras are devoted to falsehood;
where there is righteousness, austerity, and truth, there victory is certain.
"O two sons of gods, choose the science of husbandry; I shall grant it to you.

The two sisters, delighted, said "So be it" to the lovely-eyed lady;
then that proud woman questioned the son of Bhīma regarding his purpose.
Then he spoke to his paternal uncle Gada and also to Sāmba—
both of whom were endowed with beauty, well-behaved, and heroic in the art of battle.
Prabhāvatī said:
"In the past, Durvāsas, being well-pleased with me, granted me a *vidyā*;
being well-pleased, he also granted me perpetual good fortune and maidenhood itself."
"Among gods, dānavas, and yakṣas, whomever you shall meditate upon, he shall become your husband"—
it was with this very thought that I desired this hero.
"I shall come to Pradyumna, and you two shall likewise attain him.
Accept this *vidyā*, and your reunion with your beloved shall be immediate."
Then, being delighted, they both received that lore from the mouth of their sister.
Having mastered that auspicious science, Gada and Sāmba remained there;
then those two sons of Bhīma’s daughter entered together with Pradyumna.
O King, those two heroes were concealed by the illusory power of the sorcerer Kārṣṇi.
Then Prabhāvatī, seeing these men headed by Pradyumna—
whom she had been pointed out by the mouth of the female swan— became her heart overflowing with joy.
Rising up in a state of agitation and embracing Pradyumna,
she who was skilled in speech spoke these words, drenching him with tears from her eyes.
I am blessed; I am favored, since you have been embraced by me. O giver of honor, favor me today with the status of a husband.
Thus addressed by Prabhāvatī, Pradyumna, with a joyful mind,
then accepted her according to the Gāndharva rite of marriage.
By the Gāndharva rite of marriage, those two heroes, the destroyers of enemy forces and beloved by the virtuous, took each other's hands according to the sacred mantras:
Gada with Candravatī, and Sāmba, the son of Keśin, with Guṇavatī.
Then those heroes, the bulls among the Yadus, being sought out by the celestial maidens,
waited for the permission of Śakra and Keśava.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
in the month of Nabhasya, having observed that the sky was overcast...
Then Kāma,
whose face resembled the full moon, spoke to Prabhāvatī, who possessed beautiful and wide eyes, as she was surrounded by a multitude of clouds.
O lady of excellent limbs, O beautiful one, the moon with its lovely orb is not seen,
for it is obscured by that which resembles your mass of hair.
And with clouds that were beautiful, dense, and vast.
O fair-browed one, lightning is seen amidst the clouds;
you appear as if adorned with beautiful golden ornaments.
And the thundering clouds release torrents of rain.
O fair-limbed one, they are like the staffs of your own arms.
In the dense regions, rows of cranes shine like rows of your teeth,
O fair-browed one; and in the lakes, lotuses with submerged stalks appear like your smiles.
The waters, agitated by the currents, do not shine.
These clouds, driven by the force of the wind,
with their beautiful, pure white teeth in the form of rows of cranes,
have begun to strike one another.
Like elephants with white tusks in the forests.
O lady of excellent limbs, behold this three-colored bow standing before your face like the corner of your eye,
adorning both the sky and the clouds.
It brings great joy to those filled with desire for their beloved.

O fair-hipped lady, beholding the joyful peacocks gathered together with their heavy loads of tail-feathers raised high, crying out in response to the thundering clouds, they were filled with delight.
who were dancing along with their beloveds for their delight; // HV_App.I,29F.484 //
And on other palaces, O lady of beautiful hips, flocks of peacocks shine amidst those white as the moon,
displaying for a moment a beauty of exceeding loveliness.
Having given [these], they fell upon the tops of the roof-ridges.
With their wings moistened as they have made themselves the crest-jewels for a moment upon the treetops,
they descend to the ground of fresh grassy meadows.
They, possessing beautiful bodies, were filled with apprehension.
And a pleasant breeze, cooled by sandalwood paste, blows forth from another stream;
it is filled with the fragrance of *kadamba*, *sarja*, and *arjuna* flowers.
He brought forth the fragrance of the Naga-bandhu.

O lady of lovely limbs, if the wind did not exist, it would be the cause for removing the sweat born of the exhaustion of love-making, and it would also be the cause for bringing in fresh loads of water.
The rainy season would not be dear to me.
When such pleasant unions have concluded at the end of their dalliance, the fragrant breeze arrives, removing the sweat born of the fatigue of passion.
What happiness greater than that exists in the world?
O fair-limbed one, seeing the great rivers flooded with water, the swans— eager for their residence at Lake Mānasa and weary from their journey— have not ventured onto the sandbanks.
They were filled with cranes and intermingled with flocks of *krauñca* birds.
The rivers and the lakes do not shine today, O lady with long and beautiful eyes;
their luster is destroyed now that the swans and the cranes have departed.
And likewise in those called rathāṅga and tulya.
With a portion of their wealth, they— knowing the proper time and intent on auspiciousness— lay down to sleep before the Lord of the World, Upendra, the Sovereign Druva.
Having bowed to Śrī, who possesses most excellent and beautiful form.
O lotus-eyed one, while the Blessed Upendra sleeps,
today the moon is eclipsed by the garment of clouds,
appearing like a lotus obscured by mud.
It imitates the appearance of Kṛṣṇa’s mouth.
Surely the seasons, all together, bring garlands of kadamba, nīpa, arjuna, and ketakī flowers, as well as other blossoms, to Kṛṣṇa.
They were longing for grace from Kṛṣṇa.
Nagas with mouths smeared with poison move about,
touching the flowers of the trees while the bees are greedily drinking from them.
They produce in you an exceeding sense of wonder.
Beholding the sky, obstructed by masses of clouds heavy with water as if about to fall,
he entered deeply into that place which was profound with the sound of falling rain.
Captivating, with beautiful face, breasts, and thighs.
Beholding this lovely mass of clouds, garlanded with rows of cranes,
raining down grain upon the earth.
With a stainless body, for the sake of the welfare of the world.
The wind, drawing away the masses of clouds that hang over the water,
seems to make the thick clouds fight with one another;
so too does a king who has set his wheel in motion [drive] those dwelling in the forest.
Like elephants proud of their own prowess, they [encountered] elephants as if with their own kind.
The clouds release water that does not originate from the earth—
pure, purified by the winds, fragrant,
and bringing joy to the cātaka birds and peacocks.
Of those born from eggs who delight in the clouds.
The monkey, who sleeps on the sixteenth lunar day,
cries out in the cow-pen together with his beloveds; likewise,
the twice-born man, who holds truth and dharma dear, recites the *ṛc* verses.
Just as he was being attended by his excellent disciples.
This is a great virtue arising from the time of the rainy season,
in that these women, though terrified by the roar of the swelling clouds,
embrace [their husbands] and cause them to flourish.
Even without the time for bed, [the company] of beloved ones.
This is the sole fault of the arrival of the waters:
that no one is seen who is equal to your face, O you of noble appearance and character.
The moon, its body seized by a dense eclipse, [was eclipsed].
O timid one, when the moon, the lamp of the world, is seen situated within the clouds,
then indeed people behold it with great joy.
Like one returning from exile to embrace his kinsman.
There, where the nectar-moon is clearly visible, the festival of the union of desires is seen.
O timid one, when the moon— the witness to the lamentations of women separated from their beloveds, and the festival for the eyes of those longing lovers who have gone abroad— is seen.
I know that this happens simply upon seeing my beloved.
It was a festival for the eyes of those reunited with their beloveds, yet like a forest fire for those separated from their dear ones;
by that very same body, it was [both] for the excellent women.
Even the moon, moreover, is both dear and disagreeable.
Even without the moon, there is a radiance in your father’s city as bright as the rays of the moon;
yet you do not perceive the virtues and faults of the moon.
Therefore, from that [point], I shall offer praise.
He who attained the kingdom of Brahmā—
which is difficult for others to reach through other meritorious deeds or austerities—
is celebrated by the wise as Pavamāna.
And that noble [song] which the Sāma-singers chant on the festival day.
Budha’s father was Purūravas, whose deeds were of supreme heroism; he was a god among men,
the vital fire who generated the venerable Agni.
The self of Bhava [perceived] that which had been lost, born from the womb of the Śamī tree.

O lady of excellent limbs, by the formidable and preeminent sages.
The king who [performed sacrifice] again with the tips of *kuśa* grass, and that wise one whose fire went to heaven and is honored there,

The Blessed One, the god beyond gods, Hari, the leader of the world, was born in his lineage as the preeminent hero of Bhīma for the sake of the mission of the gods.
He who, O fair-browed one, was chosen by the daughters of Dakṣa.
And there was a king named Vasu, in whose lineage arose the high-souled Śāśivamśaketu,
a hero who attained the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
By his own deeds, he attained a splendor equal to that of Śakra.
And King Yadu, the foremost of the Śāśi lineage,
who attained the status of sovereign over the earth;
in whose family were the Bhojas, that lord of men.
Brave heroes have been born, equal to the king of the gods.
He whose lineage possesses no king who is contemptible— neither an atheist, nor a deceitful man, nor one lacking faith, nor even a miser.
Or perhaps, O lotus-eyed one, he is deficient in valor.
O lotus-eyed bride, you are worthy of this lineage and a fit vessel for its virtues;
O lady with tusks like mountain peaks, offer your salutation.
Of that Lord, who is beloved by the virtuous.

To the one whose self is Nārāyaṇa, to the refuge, to the goal of the worlds, to the goal of the thirty gods,

O Queen, offer salutations to your father-in-law.

At the conclusion of the sacrificial session of the sage Kaśyapa, who was possessed of exceeding splendor...
The gods and asuras, possessed of immeasurable prowess, departed for their own abodes.
When the sacrifice was completed, Vajranābha also approached Kaśyapa;
then Kaśyapa spoke to him, who was desirous of conquering the three worlds.
O Vajranābha, listen if you wish to hear me:
dwell, my son, in Vajrapura, surrounded by your own kinsmen.
Śakra is superior in ascetic power and is naturally capable;
he is devoted to Brahman, grateful, the eldest, and the most excellent among all qualities.
The king was a worthy recipient for the entire world and the refuge of the virtuous;
having attained sovereignty over the world, he was devoted to the welfare of all beings.
O Vajranābha, you cannot conquer me; you are being struck down. Like one who steps upon a snake with his foot, you will surely perish before long.
But Vajranābha did not welcome those words, O Bharata,
like one whose limbs are ensnared by the noose of Time and who desires death refuses medicine.
That evil-minded man, having saluted Kaśyapa, the creator of the world, [departed].
The one difficult to overcome set his mind upon the commencement of the conquest of the three worlds.
Having assembled his kinsmen-warriors and very many friends,
O lord of the people, he set out first toward heaven, desiring victory.
In the meantime, the two gods Kṛṣṇa and Indra, possessed of great strength,
dispatched swans toward the slaying of Vajranābha.
Having heard those words of theirs, the swans went to Vajrapura and then spoke these words to Śakra and Keśava.
Having heard that, the mighty and high-souled leaders of the Yadus assembled; after deliberating, they then fell into anxiety, thinking:
"Without a doubt, Vajranābha must be slain today by Pradyumna."
Their daughters were their wives; through devotion, they possessed all [divine] natures.
All of them were indeed pregnant; however, what must be done next? For the time for their delivery has arrived, and it will not be long before it occurs.
Having deliberated upon this matter, those of great strength spoke thus to the swans:
"Then, the entire purpose must be related meaningfully to Śakra and Keśava."
The swans went and reported that matter to the two gods exactly as it had occurred.
O Lord, those two sent word to the swans, saying, "You must not fear."
"From you shall be born blameless sons, praiseworthy for their virtues and able to assume any form at will;
while still in the womb, they shall know all the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches."
Likewise, all future weapons of various kinds shall immediately become manifest,
and they shall all become young men, highly learned.
Having spoken thus, O Lord, the swans departed once more for Vajrapura and reported to the sons of Bhīma what Śakra and Keśava had said.
Then Prabhāvatī gave birth to a son who resembled his father,
O Bhārata— one who had attained full youth immediately at birth and was indeed omniscient.
O King, after just one month, Queen Candravatī gave birth to a son known as Candraprabha,
who was the very image of his father.
And she immediately attained youth and omniscience, O Bhārata;
and though she was herself faultless, she bore a son who was likewise virtuous and blameless.
Then, by the grace of Indra and Upendra, those two youths, the delights of the Yadu clan, instantly became experts in the meaning of all the scriptures.
O hero, it should be understood that those descendants of Yadu, growing up on the roof of the palace, were joyful by the will of Indra and Upendra, and not otherwise.
And they were announced by the agitated messengers who guarded the sky to the heroic Vajranābha, who was desirous of conquering the triple heaven.
"Having deliberated, let all these violators of my home be seized," so spoke the lord of the asuras, the unassailable Vajranābha.
Then, O scion of the Kuru lineage, the army commanded by the wise lord of the Asuras blocked all directions.
"Let them be seized! Let them be slain quickly!"—such words were raised here and there from the command of the lord of the Asuras, O crusher of enemies.
Hearing that, their mothers, who were devoted to their sons, were deeply distressed;
they wept, and as they were weeping, Pradyumna suddenly spoke.
"Do not fear; as long as we remain alive, [the Daityas] will be unable to harm you in any way. What can the Daityas do to us? May all good fortune be yours."
Then Pradyumna spoke to Prabhāvatī, who stood there distressed:
"Your father stands before you with mace in hand, and your paternal uncle also stands by your side."
O Goddess, your brothers, as well as your kinsmen and others—
these indeed must all be honored and respected by you for my sake in every way.
"Ask the two sisters—blessings be upon you—for this is indeed a terrible time;
for those who fight while enduring death, victory is certain."
"For these lords of the Dānavas and others will fight, desiring our destruction;
what is to be done here by all of us who remain within the interior of the disc?"
But Prabhāvatī, weeping, spoke thus to Pradyumna;
placing her joined palms upon her head, she fell to the ground on her knees.
Take up a weapon and protect yourself, O destroyer of enemies;
you shall see your sons and your wife alive, O delight of the Yadus.
O best of men, O giver of honor, O crusher of enemies, remember the noble Vaidarbhī and Aniruddha,
and liberate yourself from this calamity.
A boon was granted to me by the wise sage Durvāsas:
"You shall be free from widowhood, lovely, and the mother of living sons."
O son of Indra’s younger brother, this word of the sage, possessing the splendor of the sun and fire, shall be my heart’s consolation; it cannot be otherwise.
Having spoken thus, that wise and excellent woman, having sipped water and taken up her sword,
granted this boon to the son of Rukmiṇī, saying, "Be victorious!"
The righteous-souled one accepted it with a joyful inner heart,
having bowed his head to that which had been offered by his beloved wife, who was filled with devotion.
Candravatī also joyfully gave a sword to Gadāya,
and likewise Guṇavatī gave a sword to the high-souled Sāmba.
Then the Lord Pradyumna spoke to Haṃsaketu, who was bowing before him:
"Stay right here together with Sāmba and fight against the Dānavas."
"O subduer of enemies, I shall fight in the sky and in all directions," having said this,
that best of illusionists then fashioned a chariot by means of his magic power.

O descendant of Kuru, having made the self-controlled one the charioteer, he took as his mount the serpent Ananta, who has a thousand heads, possesses infinite coils, and is the most excellent among all serpents.
Delighting Prabhāvatī with that preeminent chariot,
he moved through the armies of the asuras like a fire among blades of grass.
With arrows resembling venomous serpents and shaped like crescent moons— both piercing and deeply penetrating—
he tore into the sons of Diti.
And the Asuras, intoxicated in battle and resolved upon their supreme purpose, struck the lotus-eyed son of Kṛṣṇa with weapons here and there.
He severed the arms of some, which were radiant with armlets and bracelets;
and he also cut off the heads of others, which were adorned with beautiful earrings.
With those heads severed by razors and those bodies likewise cut into pieces, [the earth was covered].
The earth of the Asuras was strewn by Pradyumna of exceeding splendor.
The lord of the gods, accompanied by the hosts of deities and victorious in battle,
joyfully beheld the conflict between the sons of Bhīma and the sons of Diti.
Those Daityas who rushed against Gada and Sāmba all met their destruction, like sea-monsters in the great ocean.
Then, seeing that the battle was becoming uneven, Hari,
the lord of the gods whose vehicle is green horses, hurled his own chariot at the mace.
The Lord commanded Mātali’s son, the resplendent charioteer,
and sent the elephant Airāvaṇa to Sāmba.
The Lord gave Jayanta as an assistant to the son of Rukmiṇī,
and he appointed him to mount Airāvaṇa, the preeminent elephant.
The two heroic sons of the gods, of immeasurable prowess,
having taken leave of Brahmā, the lord of boons and creator of the worlds, [departed].
Having been thus authorized by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt himself, they were skilled in the arts of battle;
at that time, both Mātali’s son and the elephant Airāvata [were likewise prepared].
The god Śakra, who knows the rules for excellent rites, has sent me.
His ascetic power is exhausted; this evil-minded one is to be slain by the Yadus.
Indeed, living beings enter everywhere according to their desire.

Pradyumna and Jayanta, both of great strength, reached the palace; displaying their prowess with floods of arrow-nets, they put the asuras to flight. Striding forward and fighting with iron clubs on the field of battle, they prevailed.
Then Gada, who was difficult to restrain and invincible in battle, said to the son of Kṛṣṇa:
"O younger brother of Upendra, this chariot has been sent for you by Śakra."
This chariot is yoked with tawny horses, and this driver is the mighty son of Mātali;
moreover, this elephant Airāvaṇa belongs to Sāmba and is presided over by the most excellent [deities].
"O mighty one, today there is an offering for Rudra in Dvārakā;
tomorrow Hṛṣīkeśa will arrive, O younger brother of Acyuta, once that ceremony has been concluded."
"By his command, we shall slay Vajranābha along with his kinsmen;
the evil committed by him in his rise against us for the sake of conquering heaven."
"I shall indeed perform the ritual rites; he will not conquer Śakra along with his sons. However, one must remain vigilant—this is my conviction."
Men must protect their wives by every possible means in battle;
in this world, the violation of one's wife is worse than death.
Having thus instructed the mighty Gada and Sāmba,
the son of Bhīma created ten million Pradyumnas through his divine illusory power.
And he destroyed the difficult-to-overcome darkness created by the Daitya;
and the king of the gods rejoiced upon seeing that crusher of his enemies.
All beings beheld the son of Kṛṣṇa abiding within the inner self of all his enemies; they knew him as the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña). Thus did the night pass for the son of Rukmiṇī as he fought.
And having assembled according to the proper rite in the presence of Vāsava, Kṛṣṇa struck down one-third of the Asuras, who were not possessed of excessive splendor.
For as long as the son of Kṛṣṇa fought the Daityas on the field of battle,
for that long Jayanta performed his twilight devotions in the waters of the Viṣṇupadī.
While the mighty Jayanta was fighting the Daityas,
the son of Bhīma performed his twilight devotions in the celestial Gaṅgā.

when the sun— the eye of the world— had risen for three *muhūrtas*, HV_App.I,29F.754.
The divine Hari appeared together with Tārkṣya, the enemy of serpents.
Moving with a speed far swifter than that of a swan, the wind, or the mind,
O joy of the Kurus, that bird remained in the sky near Śakra.

Having assembled there according to custom in the presence of Vāsava, the powerful Kṛṣṇa blew the Pāñcajanya conch, which increases the fear of the Daityas. Hearing that sound, Pradyumna, the slayer of enemy heroes, arrived at that place.
"Abandon Vajranābha! he was told by Keśava, and "Hurry! as well.
Being thus exhorted once more, "Mount Tārkṣya and go," that hero,
having prostrated before the two supreme gods, did exactly so.
O King, O Bhārata, that hero went swiftly with the speed of Manas and Tārkṣya toward the vicinity of Vajranābha’s great duel.
Then that hero, mounted upon Tārkṣya,
firm and irreproachable, skilled in all weapons, pierced Vajranābha at the head of the battle.
Mounted upon Tārkṣya, the son of Kṛṣṇa struck that high-souled hero Vajranābha on the chest with his mace.
Struck by him, that heroic Daitya fell under the power of delusion;
he vomited copious blood and wandered about like one whose life had departed.
"Take heart," said Kṛṣṇa’s son, who is invincible in battle;
and having regained consciousness, that hero spoke thus to Pradyumna:
"Excellent, O Yadava! By your prowess you have become a praiseworthy enemy of mine.
This is the time for a counter-strike; stand firm, O one of great strength!"
Having spoken thus and let out a great roar resembling a hundred clouds,
he hurled with force his mace, which was equipped with bells and many spikes.
Struck on the forehead by her with the mace, O King, Pradyumna,
that bull among the Yadus, vomited profuse blood and fell unconscious.
Seeing him, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of enemies, blew his water-born conch, Pāñcajanya, which brought comfort to his son.
Seeing that mighty one restored by the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, all the worlds were filled with joy, Indra and Keśava especially so.
O Bhārata, by the will of Kṛṣṇa, a discus was born in his hand—
one with a razor-sharp rim and a thousand spokes, which brought an end to the hosts and clans of the Daityas.
O Bhārata, the son of Acyuta released it for the destruction of his enemies,
having paid homage to the Lord of the Gods and having paid homage to the Great-Souled One.
Then, while the Daityas looked on, he severed the head from the body of Vajranābha with a blow released by Nārāyaṇa’s son.
Gada slew Sunābha as he was striving on the field of battle—
that terrifying one, arrogant in war, who had sought to kill him from the roof of his palace.
Sāmba, the crusher of enemies, dispatched with his sharp arrows the asuras standing in the midst of the battle to the domain of the Lord of the Dead.
When the heroic great asura Vajranābha had been slain, the hero Nikumbha,
tormented by fear of Nārāyaṇa, fled to Ṣaṭpura.
When the invincible Vajranābha, the enemy of the gods,
had been slain, the two high-souled monkeys then descended upon that city of Vajra.
The two best of gods brought about both the pacification of what had been obtained and the subduing of the adversaries of the kingdom they had recently acquired.
And at that time, he brought about the delight of the subjects and the pacification of those who had been acquired.
And they both consoled those who were terrified by fear, including the young and the old.
The two great-souled ones, Indra and Upendra, both possessed of great strength, having consulted together regarding both the future and the present, followed the counsel of Bṛhaspati.
O King, they divided that kingdom of Vajranābha into four parts:
one quarter was given to Vijaya, and indeed another quarter to the son of Jayanta.
A fourth part was for Pradyumna, and a fourth part for the son of Rukmiṇī’s son; indeed,
a fourth part was for the virtuous son of Guṇavatī.
O Lord of Men, they gave a fourth part to Candraprabha.
And at that time, O lord of men, a fourth part [of the kingdom] belonged to Sāmbaputra.
And they gave a fourth part to the wise son of Sāmba—
four crores of villages in addition to those, O lord of the people,
as well as a thousand prosperous branch-towns resembling the city of Vajrapura.
There, Śakra and Keśava, greatly rejoicing, divided it into four parts.
Blankets, skins, garments, and various kinds of jewels—
the two heroes, Vāsava and Keśava, divided these fourfold, O hero.
Then, O King, those heroes were consecrated as kings by the command of Vāsava with the sounding of celestial drums and the waters of the Viṣṇupadī.
By the god Śakra himself and by the wise Keśava,
these high-souled ones were born into the lineage of sages as the delighters of Śakra and Mādhava.
The path of the wise Vijaya through the sky was well known even to his maternal kin,
as well as to the high-souled Mādhavas, because of his own virtues.
Having consecrated Jayanta, the blessed Vāsava said to him:
"O hero, conqueror in assembly, these kings must be protected by you."
O sinless one, there shall be one here who continues my lineage and three for Keśava;
by my command, they shall be invulnerable to all beings.
Traveling to and fro in the heavens will indeed be accomplished;
[you shall go] to Triviṣṭapa and to the delightful Dvārakā, which is protected by the son of Bhīma.
Grant them at their will the elephants that are the offspring of the world-elephants, the horses of the lineage of Uccaiḥśravas,
and even the chariots fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ.
O hero, bestow upon Sāmba and Gada two elephants that travel through the sky, the sons of Airāvaṇa, named Śatruñjaya and Ripuñjaya.
"Let them travel through the sky to the city of Dvārakā, which is protected by Bhīma;
and let the two sons of Bhīma come as they please to see their son."
Having thus given these instructions, the blessed Purandara, king of the gods, departed for heaven;
and the blessed Keśava likewise went to Dvārakā.
Having stayed there for six months, Gada, Pradyumna,
and Sāmba, those mighty warriors, set out for Dvārakā mounted upon their vehicles.
Even today, those kingdoms remain on the northern side of Mount Meru;
as long as the world endures, they shall remain there like immortals.
When the battle with the clubs had ceased and the Vṛṣṇis had gone to heaven,
O Lord, Gada, Pradyumna, and Sāmba went to Vajrapura.
Then, having departed, they go again to heaven by means of their own auspicious deeds and through the grace of Kṛṣṇa, the creator of the world, O lord of men.
O god among men, this account concerning Pradyumna has been narrated by me to you;
it is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, and indeed destructive of enemies.
Sons and grandsons increase, as do health and the abundance of wealth;
one attains vast fame, just as were the words of Dvaipāyana.

Citrasena, Atisena, Viṣvaksena, and likewise Ajita;

Resembling eight *nalva*s in size, moving at will, with a luster that shatters all desires,

Accompanied by four ministers and surrounded by a vast army— Durdhara, Ketumālin, Śatruhan, and Pramardana—

Ten thousand chariots, two hundred likewise,

"Cī-cī-kū-cī! they shrieked atop Śambara’s chariot;
