That serpent-māyā she had created was filled with flames of poison;
with that serpent-made [māyā], she bound Pradyumna— along with his chariot, his horses, and his charioteer— by means of bonds of arrows.
Then, seeing himself being bound, the scion of the Vṛṣṇi clan reflected upon the Suparṇī illusion, which destroys serpents.
When Mahāmāyā was thus thought of by the high-souled Pradyumna,
she approached him; he too released her as she emerged from his mouth.
The Suparṇas roamed about, while the highly venomous serpents perished.
When the serpent-māyā was shattered, the gods and asuras offered their praise.
"Excellent, O hero, O mighty-armed one! Excellent, O son of Rukmiṇī!
Since the illusion was overcome by you, we are thoroughly satisfied."
When the serpent-illusion was destroyed, Śambara thought again:
"I have a mallet, adorned with gold and resembling the staff of Death."
Unassailable in battle by gods, dānavas, or humans,
this was created by me from my own body after performing most difficult austerities.
"O Śambara, take this golden-adorned mallet which was given to me long ago by Pārvatī when she was supremely pleased."
It is named "The Destroyer of Illusion," the annihilator of all asuras.
By this [weapon], the two fierce and powerful Dānavas who roam the mountains,
Śumbha and Niśumbha, along with their hosts, were slain by me.
"When he has fallen into a life-threatening danger, you must release him to his enemy.
Having said this, the goddess Pārvatī vanished right there.
Therefore, I shall release that most excellent mallet against the enemy.
Having understood his thought, the king of the gods spoke:
"Go quickly, Nārada, toward Pradyumna’s chariot."
Awaken the mighty-armed one and cause him to remember his former births;
bestow upon him the Vaiṣṇava weapon for the sake of slaying Śambara,
and grant him the impenetrable armor that destroys the asuras.
Thus addressed by Maghavan, Nārada departed in haste;
stationed in the sky, he spoke to the one whose banner bears the makara.
"O Prince, behold me, Nārada, the Gandharva of the gods, who has arrived;
I have been sent by the King of the Gods indeed to awaken you."
Remember your former state; you are Kāmadeva, O giver of honor!
Having been consumed by the fire of Hara’s wrath, you are therefore called Anaṅga here on earth.
You were born in the Vṛṣṇi lineage, produced from the womb of Rukmiṇī;
you were born by Keśava and are celebrated as Pradyumna.
O giver of honor, you were brought here by Śambara after being snatched from the midst of the maternity chamber on the seventh night before it was completed.
O mighty-armed one, you were indeed sought out by Keśava while being carried away for the purpose of slaying Śambara, so that the goal of the gods' mission might be accomplished.
Know that this wife of Śambara, named Māyāvatī,
is your auspicious and ancient wife Rati;
she dwelt in the house of Śambara for the sake of protecting you.
Having cast aside the illusion born of his body for the purpose of deluding the evil-minded one.
Then, for the sake of producing offspring, he sends her forth incessantly;
thus, O Pradyumna, your wife is indeed established by means of your intelligence.
"O hero, having slain Śambara in battle with the Vaiṣṇava weapon,
you should take his illusory wife Māyāvatī and go to Dvārakā."
"Accept this Vaiṣṇava weapon and the armor of great splendor, O destroyer of enemies; these were taken up by Śakra and sent to you."
Listen further to my words, and let them be carried out without hesitation:
O dear one, this mallet of the enemy of the gods has been constantly worshipped.
Bestowed by the gratified Pārvatī, it is the destroyer of all enemies;
and in battle, it is indeed unfailing against gods, Dānavas, and humans.
Therefore, for the sake of neutralizing that weapon, you ought to call the Goddess to mind;
take up the Vaiṣṇava weapon and pay homage to the Goddess.
And the Great Goddess herself is to be praised and saluted by those eager for battle.
"Therefore, indeed, let effort be made in battle against the enemy.
Having spoken these words, Nārada departed for where Vāsava was.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Śambara, filled with rage, took up that mallet.
But as the mallet was being seized, twelve suns rose up.
All the mountains shook, and the surface of the earth trembled;
the oceans overflowed their courses, and even the gods were thrown into agitation.
The sky became filled with vultures and circles of crows, and there was a falling of meteors.
The god rained down blood, and a wind blew that carried away men.
Having thus seen these great portents, the hero Pradyumna, filled with haste,
descended from his chariot and stood with his palms joined in reverence.
He remembered the goddess Pārvatī, the beloved of Śaṅkara, in his mind;
having bowed his head to the goddess, he began to offer praise.
Pradyumna said:
Oṃ, salutations to Kātyāyanī, the mother of Guha;
salutations! Salutations to Kātyāyanī, the illusion of the three worlds; salutations again and again!
Homage to the destroyer of enemies! Homage to Gārgī, the dweller on the mountain!
I bow to the slayer of Śumbha and the rending of Niśumbha’s heart.
I bow down to Kālarātri, and I also constantly pay homage to Kumārī;
with palms joined in reverence, I bow to the Goddess who dwells in the wilderness.
I bow to Vindhyavāsinī, the destroyer of difficulties, Durgā of battle, and she who loves combat; I likewise pay homage to the Great Goddess, Jayā, and Vijayā.
I bow to Aparājitā, the unconquered one who scorches her enemies;
likewise, I bow to her who holds a bell in her hand and is adorned with garlands of bells.
I bow to the wielder of the trident, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
I bow to her who is borne by a lion, whose preeminent banner is the lion.
I bow to Ekānaṃśā, to Gāyatrī, the perfection of sacrifice;
and I also bow with joined palms to Sāvitrī, the [mother] of the Brahmins.
O Goddess, protect me always and grant me victory in battle.
Having heard these words of Kāma, Durgā, her mind well-pleased,
the goddess spoke these words with a joyful inner soul.
Behold, behold, O mighty-armed one, increaser of Rukmiṇī’s joy!
Choose a boon, my child; the sight of me is never in vain.
Having heard the words of the goddess, his heart bristling with horripilation,
he bowed his head to the goddess and began to address her.
"If you are pleased with me, O Goddess, let that which I desire be granted;
and as a boon, O Giver of Boons, I beg for victory over all my enemies."
This mallet given by you, born from the self of Śambara—
having touched my body, may it become a garland made of lotuses.
Having said, "So be it," she vanished right there;
then Pradyumna, possessed of great splendor, ascended his chariot, filled with joy.
Then the powerful Śambara, seized by rage, took up a mallet,
whirled it around, and hurled it at Pradyumna’s chest.
Having gone into the presence of Madana, she then became a lotus garland;
placed upon the neck of Pradyumna, it shone brilliantly,
like the moon surrounded by a wreath of stars.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis, honored the son of Keśava, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! in their voices.
Seeing the mallet transformed into a flower in the presence of Pradyumna,
he drew his bow and fixed that supreme Vaiṣṇava weapon which had been brought by Nārada, and spoke these words:
"If I am the son of Rukmiṇī, if I am indeed the son of Keśava,
by that truth, O Bāṇa, slay this Śambara in battle!"
Having spoken thus, the high-minded one drew his bow, fixed an arrow,
and then discharged it at Śambara, burning the three worlds with its brilliance.
That arrow, which bewilders flesh-eating beasts, was discharged by the lion of the Vṛṣṇis;
having then pierced the heart of Śambara, it entered the earth.
Neither its flesh, nor its sinews, nor its bones, nor its skin, nor its blood remained;
all of it was reduced to ashes by the splendor of the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
When the great-bodied Daitya, the base Dānava Śambara,
was slain, the gods and Gandharvas rejoiced and the hosts of Apsarases danced.
Ūrvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Vipracitti, and Tilottamā danced with joyful hearts,
[causing] the world of both the stationary and the moving to rejoice.
But the king of the gods, together with all the hosts of deities, being well-pleased,
joyfully honored Pradyumna with a rain of flowers.
Then, when the king of the Daityas had been slain in battle by the son of Madhumathana with the Vaiṣṇava weapons, the gods, freed from the fear of their enemy, departed.
Praising him whose banner is adorned with a sea-monster.
Bearing the fatigue of battle,
that son of Rukmiṇī entered the gateway of the city,
as joyful as a lover with his beloved.
She made a hurried display of passion.
[Colophon] [h:

Janamejaya said: For what purpose did the Blessed One Viṣṇu, the god of gods, Janārdana,
go to the peak of Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara?
There, Mahādeva Śaṅkara Nīlalohita was beheld by those sages who had grown old in asceticism and were seers of reality, through [the grace of] Nārada.
O Brahmin, in former times, while Keśava was performing supreme austerity,
he was honored by that god who is renowned as Śaṅkara.
There the gods beheld the ancient Lord of the World;
Śakra and the others directly worshipped that Hari and Hara.
Those two gods, the Great Gods, though one, have been made twofold;
they are of a single essence, the source of the world, and the agents of its creation and destruction.
Regarding the protection and maintenance of the world through their mutual union,
[the sage related] what had occurred there on Kailāsa, the best of mountains, concerning those two.
"What did the sages do upon seeing those two supreme persons?
O best of beings, you ought to tell all of this in its entirety."
Just as Hari, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Jiṣṇu, the Ancient One came,
and how Śaṅkara himself, adorned with serpents, acted—
O best of Brahmins, tell me all this in truth with diligence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen attentively, O King, to how Kṛṣṇa went to the mountain,
and how he beheld Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, whose vehicle is the bull.
O best of kings, listen to how they practiced austerity, how those sages departed, and likewise how those two attained oneness.
Now, just as the blessed Dvaipāyana spoke to me,
so shall I proclaim Keśava, whose vehicle is the bird; having offered my salutations,
listen with care according to my power and according to my wisdom, O observer of noble vows.
For this merit of the meritorious should never be spoken to one who does not wish to listen, nor to a cruel person, nor to one who lacks austerity,
nor to one who has not studied.
Leading to heaven, bringing fame, and bestowing fortune, it always purifies the intellect;
this, which is determined by the meaning of the Vedas, should be constantly meditated upon by those of virtuous soul.
Sages such as Nārada and others, whose wealth is their austerity and who delight in the Vedas, constantly frequent such places as these, which are joined with many forests.
An exceedingly wonderful and highly meritorious event occurred there on Mount Kailāsa,
involving the two divine deities Śiva and Pārvatī, as well as Hari and Bhava.
O lord of the earth, when the hosts of Asuras had been slain,
and likewise when the kings and enemies were slain with only a few remaining, [the gods spoke].
At that time, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person,
the Lord of the World, and the Sovereign, was ruling the earth while dwelling at Dvāravatī together with the Vṛṣṇis.
The Lord Hari, dwelling there in that city in the company of Rukmiṇī,
once lay down with her at night; and the Lord of the World,
being delighted, sported with her as was fitting, she who was likewise filled with love.
Then the goddess Rukmiṇī, adorned with golden ornaments, said:
"O Lord of Gods, O son of Devakī, I desire a son from you."
O Lord, he will be powerful, endowed with beauty, and your very equal;
he will be the leader even of the Vṛṣṇis, possessed of heroism and devoted to austerity.
O best of beings, you ought to give one who is skilled in the meaning of all scriptures, honored for his knowledge of royal science, and endowed with such qualities as these.
The quality of being the giver of all things is eternally established in you alone.
For you, O Lord of the World, are the creator, the giver, and the enjoyer of all;
this is especially true for those servants whose souls are disciplined by their devotion to service.
"O Lord of Gods, O Keśava, if I am indeed your devotee, it must be told [to me].
O God of gods, O Lord of the world, if there is to be grace toward me,
you ought to grant me a son endowed with prowess, O Janārdana."
Vaiśampāyana said: Thus addressed by his beloved and gratified queen Rukmiṇī, the lord of the gods, the enemy of Rukmin and upholder of the Yadu lineage, [replied].
At that time, the Lord of the Yādavas spoke these words to Rukmiṇī:
"O beautiful lady, I shall give you such a son as you desire."
"O Goddess, you have been my constant devotee; there is no need for deliberation here.
I shall certainly grant you a son who will be the destroyer of enemies."
Through a son, one conquers those worlds which are the cow of plenty for the virtuous;
for "pu" is the name of hell, and they know hell to be suffering.
Because he protects from calamity, they desire a son both in this world and in the next.
O beloved, for a man who has a son, there are endless auspicious worlds.
The husband enters his wife, becoming an embryo within her;
having become new once more in her, he is born in the tenth month.
She is called "jāyā" (wife) because that which is born again from her becomes his "jāyā.
Indra fears those who possess sons; what, then, could there be for you that has not been conquered?
One who has no son does not attain the worlds; barrenness is better than a bad son.
Since a bad son leads to hell and a good son indeed leads to heaven,
therefore one should [rely upon] a virtuous son who is disciplined, learned, and supremely compassionate.
For humility is indeed knowledge; therefore, a daughter who desires a son, and a wise man who strives for it, should always desire a son who is endowed with knowledge and is highly righteous.
"Therefore, I shall give you a son who is learned and very righteous.
Now, for the sake of a son, I am going to Kailāsa, the best of mountains."
Having worshipped there Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the blue-and-red one,
I shall then obtain a son for you from Bhava, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Having gratified the three-eyed Virūpākṣa— the primordial god, the unborn, the all-pervading, the imperishable Lord Śaṅkara— by means of austerity and celibacy.
"I shall go this very day to see the imperishable Śaṅkara;
and he, being gratified by my ascetic penance, will grant me a son."
Having gone there and paid homage to Mahādeva together with Umā,
he entered the holy Badarī, frequented by sages and consisting of asceticism.
It was a divine land, filled with those devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and constantly bathed by the waters of the Gaṅgā;
it was frequented by beasts and birds, and crowded with hundreds of lions and leopards.
It was filled with jujube fruits, its trees shaken by monkeys,
with great trees climbing upon canes, and adorned with groves of plantain trees.
It was composed by sages who were always skilled in investigating the true meaning of the Vedas,
who had ascertained the reality of things through reasoning, and who were proficient in the means of valid knowledge.
With minds resolved that "this alone is the one, this is the truth," they worship elsewhere, being perfected beings (*siddhas*) intent upon the goal of perfection.
It was being attended by great sages learned in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas,
who were proceeding toward the abode of heaven after casting off their physical bodies.
"O Goddess, I shall go to that great, well-known abode of the meritorious," having said this,
Janārdana, the God of gods, became silent.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
When the night had turned to dawn, Janārdana desired to depart.
Having offered oblations into the fire, performed auspicious rites, and completed the distribution of excellent sacrificial fees.
Then, having given cows to the Brahmins and paid homage to those best of the twice-born,
Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World, entered the pavilion hall.
Having taken his seat upon a great throne, he summoned all the Vṛṣṇis:
Balabhadra, the son of Śini, the son of Hṛdika, as well as Śaṭha and Sāraṇa.
To Ugrasena of great intelligence and to Uddhava, who is most skilled in statesmanship—
that policy relying upon which the Yadavas live in happiness.
And he was the leader of the Yadus and Vṛṣṇis, always devoted to righteousness;
even the gods were afraid of that high-souled one because of his statesmanship.
And that Uddhava, the best of the Vṛṣṇis, a hero whose power of intellect caused Viṣṇu to rule the earth forever— he who was equal in splendor to a god.
The Blessed Lord Hari spoke also to all the other Yādavas:
"Let all the Yādavas indeed hear my words;
and you too, O father Uddhava, my friend, listen to my speech."
O kings, you have personally witnessed my efforts since childhood in the destruction of the wicked, beginning with the slaying of Pūtanā.
And Keśin was slain by me while still a child, O Yādavas;
Govardhana Hill was held up by me, and the cows were protected.
"I have been consecrated by Śakra while standing before the gods;
Kaṃsa has also been brought to his destruction by me, as has the wrestler Cāṇūra."
Ugrasena was consecrated, and Dvāravatī was established by me;
furthermore, O King, other powerful monarchs were also slain by me.
O King, even that hero Jarāsaṃdha, who was forcibly subdued by me,
was captured by the powerful Bhīma through my strategic counsel, O Yādavas.
A jackal was slain in battle by me while returning from Gomanta;
furthermore, that wicked-souled Dānava hero Naraka has been killed.
O best of kings, I have thus made this world free of thorns.
However, O Yādavas, a heroic king was born who was a friend of Bhauma;
he was Pauṇḍra, the leader of the valiant, and he has always been my enemy.

The king of kings was a disciple of Droṇa, powerful, skilled, and a knower of the Brahmāstra; he was learned in the scriptures, possessed of statesmanship, a leader of the army in person, and diligent. A warrior who delighted in battle, he was like a second son of Jamadagni.
This one, our absolute enemy, is always seeking my weaknesses;
as a warrior, he will harass the city if he should find a vulnerability.
"O best of kings, the lord of Puṇḍra is powerful and not one who can be easily subdued.
Therefore, remain on your guard with bows drawn;
act so that the king does not afflict this city which is protected by the Yadu clan."
"But as for me, O kings, I am going to Kailāsa for some reason;
I wish to see Śaṅkara, the creator of all beings. Until my return, you must remain vigilant here."
If Pauṇḍraka learns of this separation from me,
that lord of kings will come and besiege this city;
it is my conviction that he will be able to rid it of all Yādavas.
"Be on your guard, O lords of kings, with your swords, nooses, and battle-axes!"
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the Vṛṣṇis, those bulls among the Yadus, [prepared themselves]. In their midst, the mighty-armed Uddhava spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"Arm yourselves with your own stones and the plows stationed there."
And having carefully closed the great doors with their panels.
There is but one great gate for constant coming and going;
let kings who desire to go depart together with their insignia.
And no one without a seal must enter while the gatekeeper is on guard;
this shall remain so until my return.
Hunting must not be practiced here, nor should there be play outside the city;
one must always keep watch over both enemies and one's own people, as well as over all comings and goings.
Those marked with the discus-sign must be allowed to enter until my return;
those not sealed with the mark must not be allowed to enter until my return.
"Such duties as these must be performed until my return," having said this to all the Yādavas, he spoke again to Sātyaki.
[Colophon] The Blessed One said: "O Sātyaki, best among warriors, listen to my words and be vigilant."
But you, becoming armed with a sword and a mace, and equipped with a bow, arrows, and finger-guards,
stay here and protect the city with diligence, which is the refuge of many kings.
O Lord, bull of the Yadus, you must not sleep at night;
O you who are devoted to the scriptures, you must not engage in the exposition of the treatises;
and O Vṛṣṇi, you must not enter into debates with disputants.
For you are a warrior, powerful, victorious, and a knower of the science of archery;
therefore, O hero, act in such a way that we do not become objects of ridicule.
Sātyaki said:
"O Janārdana, I shall carry out your word to the best of my ability;
O Lord of the World, your command must always be observed by me with diligence."
"O Mādhava, I shall conduct myself like a servant to Kāmapāla;
I will remain here with diligence until your return."
O Govinda, O Mādhava, if you have grace toward me,
O Hari, what indeed would be difficult for me to accomplish in the subduing of my enemies?
"If I shall conquer even Śakra, Yama, Kubera, or Varuṇa—all these—how much more so Pauṇḍra, that best of kings?
Go, O Hari, and accomplish this task; I am constantly vigilant."
Then Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes resemble lotuses, spoke again to Uddhava:
"Listen, O Uddhava, to my words; you should carry them out with diligent effort."
"O Indra among kings, the city of Dvāravatī must be protected by you through prudent policy.
Be ever vigilant, my dear, and provide us with assistance here;
shame has come upon me as I speak these words to you now."
For you are the leader of this entire ocean of knowledge in every respect;
what wise man indeed would be able to speak before one so possessed of learning?
"You know what ought to be done and likewise what ought not to be done in every respect;
therefore, O dear Vṛṣṇi, I shall now desist from speaking."
Uddhava said:
O Lord Govinda, what is this that is happening toward me?
Ah, it is such great favor shown to me; yet, what is this affection of Yours?
I know, O Lord of the World, that this is the extent of your grace;
for him with whom you are pleased, O Keśava, what is there that he does not possess?
For you are the creator and destroyer of the entire world, the primary agent;
you are the source of all effects, the speaker, the listener, and the knower of the means of valid knowledge.
"Those who know Brahman understand that the meditator, the act of meditation, and the object of meditation are one;
you are the conqueror of the enemies of the gods and the protector of the inhabitants of heaven."
"Thinking 'We have you as our lord,' we live with our enemies destroyed;
this, I believe, is the policy, since you are the leader of that policy."
Tell me now, who indeed does not know you?
It is my firm conviction that you are the policy for all undertakings.
"Those who know the truth say that this path of policy is difficult to traverse," O Janārdana; "this policy is said to be fourfold: conciliation and bribery."
Punishment and dissension among men are always employed for the purpose of restraint and suppression.
O Hari, they desire punishment upon those deserving of it, but conciliation is the means for leading them.
Furthermore, if three powerful enemies are within one's range,
it is the opinion of those who possess political wisdom that a "great breach" (mahābheda) should be employed as a stratagem.
"Among all those various matters, the wise know you alone to be the authority.
What is the use of much speaking here? Everything has been entrusted to you.
Having said this, Uddhava, the most prudent of men, fell silent.
Then, O best of kings, the Blessed Viṣṇu spoke in this very manner to the mighty-armed Kāmapāla in the assembly of the Yadus,
as well as to King Ugrasena and Hārdikya, O monarch.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu spoke thus to Kāmapāla, whom he had previously known:
"You must not be negligent; always remain diligent."
But while you, O mighty-armed one, remain, what suffering could there be for the world?
O Noble One, always remain steadfast; let there never be playfulness.
"O Lord, always protect the city of Dvāravatī with diligence;
act in such a way that we do not become objects of ridicule, and take up your mace."
"Effort must be made in every way; one who lacks effort does not succeed despite his exertion.
"So be it," Rāma said to Kṛṣṇa, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
All these Vṛṣṇis returned each to his own abode;
the Lord of the World desired to go to Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then he thought of Garuḍa, the preeminent among birds.
"Come quickly, O Tārkṣya! said Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World.
Then that Blessed One, Tārkṣya, who is known as Vedarāśi,
was powerful, valorous, a yogin, and a leader of the scriptures, O best of the Kurus.
The embodiment of sacrifice, the ancient self, with the Sāman as his head and the purifier;
the bird with the Ṛgveda as his wings, tawny-hued and matted-haired in form.
Copper-beaked, the taker of Soma, the conqueror of Śakra, great-headed;
the enemy of serpents, lotus-eyed, he was like another Indra in person.
The vehicle of the God of gods, the destroyer of the wombs of Dānavīs,
he who is the conqueror of the hosts of Rākṣasas and Asuras by the strength of his wings.
Then, the one of great heroism appeared before Keśava;
he fell upon his knees on the ground and said, "Salutations to Viṣṇu, Lord of the World!"
Saying, "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Hari, O Master," Kṛṣṇa touched [him] with his hand, saying, "Welcome, O best of the Tārkṣyas."
Thus he spoke then to Tārkṣya: "I shall go to Mount Kailāsa;
I desire to see the trident-wielder, Śaṅkara, the eternal Śiva."
"So be it," Tārkṣya replied; then Janārdana, having mounted him, said to the Yādavas standing at his side, "Stay here!"
Then Hari, the Lord of the World, went toward the northeast;
with a great roar, Tārkṣya made the three worlds tremble.
Then, as the bird flew along carrying the god Janārdana on his wing, he agitated the ocean with his feet and bore all the mountains upon his wings.
Then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, stationed in the sky,
praised the lotus-eyed Lord with pleasing words.
Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World; lead us, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the Universe! Victory to the Unconquerable! Homage to you, O God, the creator of the creator of all beings!
Homage to the Supreme Lion, the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas! Victory to you, O invincible Hari, O God, the object of meditation for yogis, the remover of fear!

O Nārāyaṇa, homage to you, O God! Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare! O Original Creator, O Ancient Self, O Eternal One born from Brahman! Homage to you, the Lord of all, who are beyond qualities yet the essence of all qualities.
Salutations to the one dear to his devotees, to the devotee himself, O destroyer of the Dānavas!
"Salutations to you of inconceivable form; salutations to you, O Lord of all!"—

who was seeking his own Self in solitude, and who was self-restrained—
the cause of his accumulation of merit.
Having meditated for a very long time on the cause of his meritorious deeds, Viṣṇu,
by the instruction of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), recited my names many times upon the earth: "Vāsudeva," "Kṛṣṇa," and "Mādhava."
O Janārdana, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, O creator of the creator of beings!
O enemy of Naraka, O Lord of the world, O Nārāyaṇa, O supreme refuge!
Thus he constantly recites my names day and night—
whether sleeping, waking, standing, eating, walking, or speaking.
Devouring lumps of flesh and drinking blood as well,
he tormented him for a very long time even after killing many deer.
In killing and in eating, as well as in waking and likewise in sleeping,
and in all activities whatsoever, he thinks, "I am the doer."
"This is the ripening of that terrible deed in every respect";
having thus resolved, the Lord of the World became truly pleased with him.
Then, O lord of the earth, the Lord of the World revealed his own self to that Piśāca, whose internal organ was pure and who was none other than himself.
And that terrible Piśāca also beheld Keśava within himself—
Hari, dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotuses, dressed in yellow silk garments.
[He saw] Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord, bearing the conch and the discus, adorned with garlands and wielding the mace;
he wore a diadem, possessed the Kaustubha gem, and his chest was marked by the Śrīvatsa.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, lovely, mounted upon Garuḍa, the Wind-god—
four-armed, of auspicious speech, motionless, all-pervading, and beautiful.
Without beginning, undecaying, eternal, possessing illusory power yet free from illusion;
ever united with truth, eternally pure, accessible to the intellect, and forever stainless.
Having seen Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, in his manifold forms by means of the mind alone, he thought,
"I have achieved my purpose," even without closing his eyes.
Today Hari Viṣṇu has been seen directly, he who is all-pervading and auspicious;
for Hari was gracious toward me, and by that grace I have beheld Hari.
The purpose of my birth has been accomplished; what further duty remains for me?
My knots have been severed, and my senses are indeed under my control.
"I believe that as soon as Hari was remembered, my mind was for the most part already conquered;
all my worldly desires were cast aside, and I became thus serene."
Now, having likewise been liberated from these Piśācas,
that one who was my own younger brother— who was himself a direct devotee of Hari—
shall, through time, be freed and attain union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu.
Having reflected thus, he tore through the coils of his entrails,
gradually released his vital breath, and likewise surveyed the quarters; then,
having made his body perfectly still, he departed in peace.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
The flesh-eater beheld the Lord of the World, the Master of the worlds.
And as he was seen in meditative absorption, so too on the ground was the Lord of the World.
"This is Viṣṇu! This is Viṣṇu! cried the flesh-eater. "Just as he was seen in meditative absorption, so too is he seen here," he said again, speaking as if dancing and laughing.

This is that wielder of the discus, the one with arrows, the bow Śārṅga, the mace, and the chariot; he who possesses a banner, a quiver, and holds them in his hands; the thousand-headed lord of all the immortals.
The progenitor of the worlds and the abode of the worlds.
Viṣṇu, the Victorious, Lord of the World, the Ancient, the Supreme Person;
he who is the Soul of the Universe and the Maker of the Universe—this is that Eternal One.
Within the chest of this very god Hari,
the lamp of the Kaustubha jewel shines resplendently;
by whose grace this entire world was [created] at the beginning.
The night shines like the moon itself.
He who swiftly supported the earth from the mass of waters with his tusk—
this very one is Hari himself, who has assumed the form of a boar.
Having thus bound the Dānava of fierce prowess and having then bestowed the kingdom upon Śakra,
that Vāmana Hari forcibly took Bali as his tribute.
And he was praised with devotion by the ancient sages.
Having slain the Dānava in battle with his formidable fangs,
that great Janārdana made the entire world free from sorrow.
In the beginning, having conquered all the asuras in the great ocean, he held Mount Mandara with a single arm and bestowed upon Śakra the great vessel filled with nectar.
He himself stands here before me in person.
Having slain those two terrible Dānavas known as Madhu and Kaiṭabha, he who lies upon the serpent in the ocean, bringing happiness to the goddess Lakṣmī; [to him I bow].
Whom the wise call the primordial Lord of the world, the sustainer of all, the unborn source of birth,
subtler than the subtle and of infinite magnitude.
From the gross, [he perceives] the grossest, namely Hari himself, Viṣṇu.
He in whom all this is situated when the destruction of the world has arrived,
from whom it was produced in the beginning— he is this very Viṣṇu who stands here.
By whose will all this proceeds and by whom it also ceases—
that Janārdana is this very Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, Śiva.
The Lord of the Yadavas takes refuge in me here.
Born in the lineage of Bhṛgu, he was known as Jāmadagnya;
having attained the status of a disciple, he remained under the guidance of Mṛgavyādha.
In that great battle,
the disciple of Giriśa struck down by force with his axe-weapon the powerful Sahasrabāhu, the son of Kṛtavīrya.
And they went forth on swift horses, elephants, and chariots.
Having reached Kurukṣetra, he who performed the ancestral rites made this world devoid of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times.
Then, born in the lineage of Raghu, there was one named Rāma, who was Janārdana himself;
he was endowed with Sītā as his Śrī and had Lakṣmaṇa as his follower, being a man of virtuous deeds.
Having built a bridge across the ocean, Janārdana slew the lord of the Rākṣasas with swift-flying arrows and bestowed the kingdom upon Vibhīṣaṇa.
And he who performed ten horse-sacrifices.
Born in the family of Vasudeva, he is called Vāsudeva;
he who sports in Gokula together with Saṃkarṣaṇa as his companion.
Lying on his back and assuming the form of an infant,
Janārdana drank from the breast offered by Pūtanikā and then quickly deprived her of life.
There Hari dwelt happily with that daughter of Danu.
While drinking milk and eating lumps of curd,
Viṣṇu’s belly was firmly bound with a rope by his enraged mother.
And then, Hari— who dwells in Gokula— while playing, bound him with a very firm rope and struck down those two *yamalārjuna* trees.
The gopīs tasted his mouth and his breast.
Dwelling in Vṛndāvana with the cowherds who reside in Gokula,
Viṣṇu shone there like the sun after having slain that terrible horse.
Janārdana,
the Lord of the World, while being attended by the cowherd boys, sports upon the hood of the serpent in that great lake with the lord of snakes.
He crushed him, displaying his extraordinary prowess.
He who, having slain that fierce Dānava, struck Dhenuka down in the palm grove with its own fruits as if leveling him, thus astonishing the cowherds.
He of fierce prowess and great intelligence, who supported the mountain that holds cattle,
emulating the power of Śakra and bringing joy when the clouds gathered.
And Hari [protected] the cowherds and the cowherdesses, along with the community of cows.
The Lord sports at will among the breasts of the gopīs;
he who possesses a body of illusory human form drinks from their lips.
Having tasted his mouth, Keśava lay down comfortably that night in a secluded place,
while they [the gopīs] rested upon the space between his breasts.
Like a lover drinking from the sprout-like lower lip of his beloved.
Indeed, summoned by Akrūra, while traveling along the Yamunā, he was worshipped by him in the water;
for it was that very same deity who was worshipped by him in the world of the Nāgas.
Then, as he was proceeding along the road, the powerful Janārdana forcibly slew that fierce washerman and took the clothes as he pleased, for he is the Lord.
Accompanied by Rāma, Hari went to the city of Mathurā.
Having received many garlands and having granted a great boon to Mālyaketu,
the Yādava obtained fragrant unguents.
He quickly made the hunchbacked woman possess a most precious form.
Having taken up that great bow and broken it in the middle,
he let out a mighty lion’s roar, like a rain-cloud at the end of an eon.
Having slain the terrible elephant of fearsome form, Keśava then took its tusk; the Lord, assuming many forms, danced upon the stage.
Having instilled fear in Kaṃsa, he of fierce prowess—
Having slain the great wrestler Cāṇūra,
he who had struck down his enemy bestowed joy upon the Yādavas while Kaṃsa himself looked on.
Hari slew Kaṃsa, the slayer of his enemies' faction,
the hater of his father, who bore the name of a Yādava;
having thus established Ugrasena in the kingdom.
He approached Sāndīpani, the descendant of Kaśya.
Having acquired all the knowledge and having given his son to the great sage, he then, together with his elder brother,
quickly went to Mathurā, the city of the Yādavas.
Having slain Niśumbha and Naraka,
the high-minded Janārdana, after inflicting a most terrible slaughter,
protected the brahmins and the hosts of heroic sages.
And the Lord of the World [honored] all the gods of the world.
This very Lord Viṣṇu, Janārdana, has been seen by me today;
I have become one who has accomplished his purpose, and may I attain union with him.
Liberation stands in the palm of the hand of him by whom Hari has been seen directly;
this very Hari himself is present here before one's eyes.
What dharma must have been accumulated by me in a previous birth,
the fruition of which has now arisen, so that he is seen by me?
"In every way I am fortunate, for the bonds of saṃsāra have been destroyed. What object can be given to him? But what shall I say now?
O Viṣṇu, tell me today what I should do according to your desire."
Having spoken thus, the flesh-eater then uttered a discordant roar many times; he laughed hideously and danced again.
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Hare Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Yādavas, Keśava! And there, O King, Hari appeared visibly before them and danced in various ways.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having laughed again with a distorted expression and having danced according to his strength...
Then, having quickly taken the corpse of the slain brahmin, they departed.
Having divided that most terrible flesh, which was overgrown with hair, into two parts,
he then took a piece and carefully sprinkled it with water.
Having placed [the offering] in a beautiful vessel and having paid homage to Janārdana,
he stood with palms joined in reverence and, bowing low, spoke thus to the Lord of Gods.
"Accept this, O Lord of the World, for it is suitable food for you, O Master.
O Hari, Lord of the World, one such as you should accept this with all your being."
O Viṣṇu, we are bowed down by devotion; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
O Hari, whatever has been given by one who is bowed in devotion must be accepted by the Master.
Freshly prepared food is the best for a Brāhmaṇa, and a corpse is the best for a Brāhmaṇa;
among all the social classes, the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent.
"For in our scripture, for us who subsist on flesh, this is indeed a fixed rule.
Therefore, O Blessed One, accept it if no fault is found."
Having spoken thus, he laughed again with a distorted expression out of desire,
and then wished to give him a piece of an untouchable corpse.
Then Hari, being pleased, honored him in his mind:
"Oh, how great is his affection and compassion; it is present toward me in every way."
Having reflected thus in his mind, the bull among the Yadus spoke:
"Enough of this, O Piśāca with a flesh-eating face!
This supreme corpse of a Brāhmaṇa is untouchable for those such as me."
A Brahmin is to be honored in every way by living beings who desire the Dharma;
even Piśācas of terrible deeds strive to harm a Brahmin.
Brahmins must never be killed, for their injury leads to hell;
therefore, they are untouchable by us—of this there is no need for deliberation.
Therefore I am pleased; may it be well with you, for such is the purity of your mind.
O son of Māṣa, since your mind has attained this state of purification, I am delighted.
"Indeed, through our constant glorification, your instrument [the senses] shall be purified";
having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Hari was exceedingly pleased in his mind.

Then the god Viṣṇu, Hari, touched every limb of the piśāca with his gentle hand; he liberated him from his sins. Thereupon his form shone forth, possessing a splendor equal to that of one who can assume any form at will.
Rich with long, curled hair, long-armed and fair-eyed;
with even fingers, even nails, an even face, and a straight nose;
lotus-eyed, with the luster of a lotus, and adorned with lotus filaments.
Then, adorned with armlets and bracelets, dressed in silken garments,
he was wise and endowed with goodness, like a second Indra in person;
singing like a Gandharva, he was himself like a perfected Siddha.
Then it was touched directly by Viṣṇu’s hand with gentle care;
surely such a form had never existed even in other kalpas.
Even today, the sages do not obtain such a body,
despite performing many times over terrible austerities that are exceedingly difficult to practice.
And whatever was obtained by that Piśāca at that time, O best of kings— indeed,
O King, who that has taken refuge in the Lord of the World would ever suffer?
For indeed, O King, what is there that is not auspicious for one who constantly meditates upon, recites, or chants the praises of Janārdana?
Then the Blessed One spoke to him, who stood there like another god of love:
"Your residence in heaven shall be imperishable for as long as Indra exists."
"Let you remain in heaven for that long by my command and no other;
when Śakra has perished, let him then attain union with me from heaven."

"O brother, since this one who has gone to heaven shall become Indra, choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your mind. I shall grant everything in every way; there is no need for hesitation in this matter."
Ghaṇṭākarṇa said:
O Lord Janārdana, may he who, with self-restraint, remembers this meeting of ours have unwavering devotion toward you.
"O Hari, may his mind be pure; let there be no turbidity.
May there be no defilement of his mind—this is my boon."
"So be it," said Keśava; "go to heaven, O Lord of the Gods.
May you be the guest of Indra, for Hari has remained here waiting for you."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu departed from that place;
the Lord of the World, being praised by him, honored that twice-born man and withdrew.
Then, having dismissed him, Govinda departed from that place.
Where those perfected sages attend upon the *agnihotra* sacrifice, he,
being a dweller of heaven, went from there to heaven by the command of Keśava.
Therefore, O King, always recite this if you desire purity of mind;
for as you recite it, O Lord of the World, your mind shall become pure.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then that Blessed Viṣṇu [expounded] the truth to the sages from the beginning.
He related what had happened concerning the high-souled Piśāca.
Hearing that, all the sages were filled with supreme wonder, saying,
"Oh, how the fruit of this deed has been manifested through your appearance!"
Honored by all the sages, the beloved of those who possess love was pleased;
then, when the dawn had become clear and the sun had risen, [he departed].
Having mounted Garuḍa, Viṣṇu went to the supreme Kailāsa;
having said to those best of sages, "You must go there," he departed.
There, the lords of all beings, perfected ones who observe their vows, practice austerities;
there, Vaiśravaṇa himself always worships Śaṅkara;
and there is the great lake named Mānasa, the abode of swans.
There, having attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas, Bhṛṅgin and Riṭin constantly attend upon the god Śiva, the auspicious Śaṃkara, as his personal attendants.
There, lions and boars, together with elephants, leopards,
and deer, sported, delighting in the forest and devoted to one another's welfare.
There the rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, which flow to the ocean, have their source;
there Śambhu, the Lord of the Universe, severed the head of Brahmā;
and there the great reeds were produced, which became the staffs for all living beings.
Where Śaṅkara Nīlalohita was accompanied by Umā,
and where, previously requested by the ṛṣis, the Mountain gave his daughter to Śiva, the benefactor of the world and the source of auspiciousness, O lord of the earth.
There Hari obtained the discus after worshipping the Lord of the World for many days with lotuses,
hundred-petaled flowers, and his own eyes.
There, having taken refuge in a cave, the Siddhas and Kinnaras sport;
they rejoice together with their beloveds and drink the finest honey.
Having lifted it with all his arms, the descendant of Pulastya indeed desisted;
then Hari, the son of Devakī and joy of the Yadus, having ascended that great mountain,
went to the northern shore of Lake Mānasa.
It is said that Hari Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, Śiva,
the Master of the World, having assumed a human form with matted hair and bark garments,
sat down upon the pure ground with his mind fixed on performing ascetic penance.
Then, having descended from that vehicle, Garuda, which was equal to the Vedas,
the Lord of the World resolved to perform austerities for twelve years.
In the month of Phālguna, Janārdana began [his observance],
subsisting on vegetables, performing his recitations, and being intent upon the study of the Vedas.
"O giver of honor, for what purpose does the Lord of the World perform this penance? We do not know that, for the intentions of the Lord are difficult to comprehend."
While Viṣṇu was thus performing austerities on the mountain frequented by spirits,
Garuḍa, the son of Tārkṣya,
gathered fuel for the sake of the oblation of Vāsudeva as he practiced supreme penance.
Then, as the Cakrarāja gathered flowers for Hari,
that lotus protected him everywhere in all directions.
Then, having diligently gathered many blades of kuśa grass with his sword,
he performed service with the mace Kaumodakī as well.
The most excellent and exceedingly fierce bow, the Śārṅga, which terrifies the Dānavas,
stands before him like a servant at his own command; indeed,
the Blessed Viṣṇu always offers many kinds of fuel into it as an oblation.
Then Mādhava, having worshipped the seven-flamed fire with oblations such as clarified butter, completed all his duties and withdrew from that ritual.
In one month, he ate at one [fixed] time, being self-restrained;
then, in the second turn, he ate with whatever [food] was available.
Eating in this manner for one year with each [person] in turn,
the Lord of the World completed the entire year in this very way.
When twelve years were thus completed, and one month remained,
Janārdana, the Lord of the World, offered oblations into the fire, meditated with concentration, and recited mantras.
Reciting the Āraṇyaka, Viṣṇu himself, the Lord of All, Hari,
remains there intent on meditation, reciting the supreme *praṇava*.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Indra himself, having mounted that excellent elephant there, [proceeded].
He arrived to behold Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, who was engaged in ascetic penance.
Then the blessed Yama, having mounted his excellent buffalo,
came in person with his own servants to that supreme mountain.
Pracetas, mounted upon a swan and accompanied by the attendants of Varuṇa,
went directly to the peak of Kailāsa to see Keśava, attended by a white parasol and fanned with white whisks.
Moreover, O King, other gods as well— the Ādityas, the Vasus,
and likewise the Rudras— came to behold Keśava.
O King, there were also Siddhas and sages, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Kiṃnaras,
as well as all the Apsarases, who were experts in dance and song.
Then the entire host of gods went to Kailāsa,
as did the mountain, Nārada, and other excellent sages; likewise,
all the hosts of gods stood there with eyes wide in wonder.
"What wonder could possibly exist in this?"—thus those hosts reflected.
"Behold this marvel indeed; it has never occurred before, nor will it ever happen again."
"Kṛṣṇa himself is the object of meditation for yogis; since the Guru himself is performing penance, what could possibly be the purpose here?"—thus did those hosts reflect.
Then, when the vow of the Lord of the Universe had been completed in its entirety along with its ancillaries, Śiva, the Lord of all,
[appeared] for Hari to behold the Master who desires the welfare of the world.
He went together with Bhavānī and the hosts of spirits.
The Lord, the Sovereign Śiva, together with Kubera and his Guhyaka, accompanied by his beloved friend, himself wearing matted hair and surrounded by spirits and Piśācas; ||| 946–948 ||
Śiva, the moon-crested one, is armed with arrows and a sword.
In one hand he bore a water-pot made of *darbha* grass, in another hand he bore a lamp directly,
and with yet another he bore a great drum together with its cymbals.
And he bore a trident with his other arm.
Wearing rosaries made of rudrākṣa beads that represent his virtues,
the Lord whose crest is the moon shines forth with matted locks that are tawny and copper-colored.
Śaṅkara was yoked to a very white bull.
With his face pressed against the pair of Umā’s breasts,
he embraced her and bit her lower lip;
his crest-jewel, the moon, was washed by the waters of the Gaṅgā.
And Śiva, gazing at her many times then, said:
With his face anointed with ashes as body-unguents,
the eternal one had his matted locks bound by great serpents;
he was then further adorned with human skulls upon his head.
Śiva went forth to see Hari Keśava.
Those whose vision is bound by the Sāṃkhya system speak of him as the foremost, great, and ancient Person;
they [praise] even the complete qualities of that deity.
Some say that there are twenty-four principles (tattvas).
They call him the one ancient Person,
the unborn Maheśvara named Kaṇāda,
who indeed was born from Dakṣa after having struck down [his father].
In ancient times, the Primal One destroyed even the gods.

Those who know the truth of beings call him Vāmadeva and Virūpākṣa—he who knows the reality of all beings and whose nature is the contemplation of the Lord of Beings; so say the people who possess true knowledge.
They call Mahādeva— the thousand-eyed one, whose form is Time, the four-armed Rudra,
who is named Rodana— the Lord of the Universe, Śiva.
People devoted to Maheśvara say that he is immeasurable and without support;
they call him the Lord of All, the peaceful Śiva, the primordial and eternal one— naked, surrounded by the naked, the lord of serpents, and possessing the splendor of the naked.
O King, all these elements, beginning with the earth, are his entire manifest form.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the sun, the moon,
and fire, along with the sacrificer and primordial nature (prakṛti)— thus it is eightfold.
Mahādeva, the great yogin, lord of the mountains, Nīlalohita,
the primordial creator, the sustainer of the earth, the wielder of the trident, and the husband of Umā,
arrived together with hosts of beings to behold Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Before him, hosts of beings appeared by the thousands.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Virūpākṣa, Kuṇḍabhānu, and Kumudvaha.
Long-haired, with a long crest and long arms, he was stainless;
he had a wide face, a hundred mouths, a hundred necks, and a hundred bellies.
Kuṇḍodara, Mahāgrīva, Sthūlajihva, Dvibāhuka;
Pārśvavaktra, Siṃhamukha, Unnatāṃsa, Mahāhanu;
Tribāhu, Pañcabāhu, Vyāghravaktra, and Sitānana.
These and many others, with long faces and long eyes,
were dancing, laughing, and slapping one another.
Likewise, others were of terrible form, and others had distorted faces;
they were devourers of *pretas*, carriers of *pretas*, and consumers of flesh and blood.
Devouring very many corpses here and there with great speed, drinking terrible blood, and tearing apart many carcasses; HV App. I, 31.998–999.
Terrible, widespread, and long, they were covered with veins and sinews;
some were naked, others wore rags, and human beings were impaled on the tips of their spears.
Some were adorned with garlands of heads and bound with nooses of entrails;
they made the earth resound with their *ḍiṇḍibha* and *aṭṭahāsa* laughter.
There were those bearing skulls (*kapālins*), the terrifying ones (*bhairavas*), as well as those with matted hair and those with shaven heads.
In this way, there were many kinds of terrible piśācas with distorted faces.
Likewise, other heroic sages were meditating upon the Supreme Lord,
reciting the various Vedic scriptures along with their auxiliary branches.
Some held water-pots in their hands; some wore tawny-colored bark garments;
some were clad only in loincloths; and some were covered in rags.
Praising Śaṅkara with devotion through hymns dedicated to Maheśvara,
those hosts of sages gathered on one side, and likewise the Gaṇas on the other.
Elsewhere, perfected beings and gandharvas, united with their beloveds,
were dancing— skilled as they were in dance— and maidens were singing.
Likewise, the Vidyādharas praised Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara, elsewhere;
and hosts of Apsarases danced before him as they proceeded.
Thus Śarva arrived together with these most terrible piśācas, bhūtas, kiṃnaras,
sages, and apsarases.
Where Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, performed most rigorous penance;
where those guardians of the world stood with a desire to behold him; and where the moon-crested Lord was with Umā, the mother of the worlds, and Gaṅgā.
He is Hari, the source of all worlds, Śiva, with matted hair, manifest as the *praṇava*, and accomplished; he,
of noble prowess, came to behold Hari Viṣṇu.
Surrounded by flesh-eaters, he went wherever he desired.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus, together with many kinds of beings, Piśācas, and serpents...
The blessed Lord Rudra, Śaṅkara, whose vehicle is the bull, arrived.
He beheld Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, performing supreme austerity; he saw the Lord of the World offering oblations according to the rules into the fire with pure sacrificial offerings.
He had wood brought by Garuḍa, matted hair, and garments of bark;
likewise, he had flowers brought by the discus and kuśa grass brought by the sword.
To Janārdana, the god of gods, who had performed his customary rites with the mace.
Surrounded by hosts of gods led by Indra and by throngs of sages,
he meditated upon some inconceivable Lord who is beyond the reach of all beings.
Having descended from his bull, the blessed Lord Śarva, the creator of all beings,
the three-eyed husband of Umā, was then pleased and serene in soul.
Then the bhūtas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and likewise the guhyakas [approached].
The sages and the best of brahmins raised shouts of victory.
Victory, O God, Lord of the World! Victory, O Rudra, Janārdana!
Victory, O Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Refuge!
Victory to you, O Rudra, the soul of the Purāṇas! Victory to you, O God, the Lord of Hari!
O primordial God, Lord of the world, victory to you, O Śaṅkara, the creator!
Victory to you, whose limbs shine with the Kaustubha gem; victory to you, resplendent with sacred ashes!
Victory to you, who hold the discus and mace in hand; victory to you, the wielder of the trident, the three-eyed one!
"Victory to you, O Lord whose limbs shine with the luster of pearls! Victory to you, O Adorned with Serpents!"—thus all those sages offered salutation to Hari.
Then, having risen and seeing the god standing there—
the bull-bannered, three-eyed Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita—
Viṣṇu, with a joyful mind, praised Hara, the Lord.
The Blessed One said:
Homage to you, the blue-throated one, the dark-necked creator;
homage be to you, the radiant one; homage to you, the fasting one.
Homage be to you, the bountiful one; homage to you, O Hara, who wields the mace!
Homage to you, whose form is the universe, the bull, who possesses the form of a bull!
Having approached him, he said: "Homage to the Bull, who has the form of a bull;
homage be to you, the formless god, the wielder of the Pināka bow."
Homage to the Terrible One, to the Terrible One, and to him who is dear to the most terrible of the terrible.
Salutation to Kubja, to Kūpa, to Śiva, who possesses the form of Śiva.
Homage to Tuṇḍa, to the Contented One; homage to Tuṭi and Tuṭā as well.
Homage to Śiva, to the Peaceful One, and homage to you, O Giriśa.
Homage to Hara, the one who transcends the senses; homage to Hari and Hara as well.
Homage to the non-terrible and to the terrible, and to the one who is dear to those both terrible and most terrible.
Homage to Aghaṇṭā and to Ghaṇṭā, and homage to Ghaṭighaṭā;
homage to Śarva, the peaceful one, and homage to the Lord of Beings.
Homage, homage to the one of diverse forms, the ancient one, the destroyer of cities! Homage to the primordial seed, the pure one whose form is ash!
Homage to the one who holds the *pināka* bow in his hand; homage to the bearer of the trident and sword.
Homage to you who hold the staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) in your hand; homage to you who are clothed in a skin (*kṛttivāsas*).
Salutations to you, Vāmadeva; salutations to you whose form is space.
Salutations to Hara, who takes the form of Hari; salutations to you of piercing splendor.
Salutations to the one dear to his devotees, to the devotee, to the bestower of boons upon his devotees;
salutations, O God, to you who possess a cloud-like form and who bear the form of water.
Homage to the divine Moon and to the Sun, homage again and again;
homage to the primordial deity, homage to the Lord of all beings.
Homage to Karālamuṇḍa, to the deformed one, to the one with matted hair;
and homage to you, O Unborn One, the creator of beings, O Creator!
Homage be to Harikeśa; homage, homage to Piṅgala!
Homage to you who hold the reins in your hand, and to you who strike fear into the fearful!
Salutations to Hara, who is the embodiment of fear, the giver of terror to the terrible ones;
salutations to the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and the one who took away the eyes of Bhaga.
O Lord of Umā, salutations to you, who dwell on Kailāsa;
to the primordial god, the divine one, to Bhava, whose form is existence.
Homage to the one who holds a skull in his hand, and homage to the slayer of Aja;
homage to you, O Tryambaka, to the three-eyed Śiva.
Salutations to you, the giver of boons, the most excellent one, O moon-crested Lord! Homage to the sacrificial fuel, to the oblation, to the *dhruva* ladle, and to the *kuśa* grass.
Salutations to you, the hundredfold resplendent one, who delights in the serpent-noose;
to the one of diverse forms and beautiful form, who is fond of auspicious drinking.
To him who eternally delights in the cremation ground, who is fond of shouts of victory,
who is dear to the harsh, who is short, who is harsh, and who has a harsh form.
Homage to you, who are beloved by the auspicious, who are auspicious, who assume auspicious forms,
who are deformed, who are beautiful, and who are most terrible.
To the one with the bell, to the one whose sound is like the ringing of a bell, to the one adorned with ornaments of bells;
to the intense one, to the one of intense form, and to the one who delights in forms of intense character.
To the naked one, to the one whose form is naked, and to the one who delights in the form of the naked;
O abode of beings, homage to you! O abode of all, homage, homage!
Salutations to you, the soul of all; salutations to you, the bestower of prosperity. Salutations to you, Vāmadeva; salutations to you, Mahādeva.
What form of speech could possibly praise you? Who indeed would be able to offer praise?
Or whose tongue could even quiver in praise of you, O best among those worthy of praise?
Forgive me, O Blessed One, O God; I am your devotee, so remember me, O Hara!
O Soul of All, Lord of All Beings, remember me constantly, O Hara!
O God, Lord of the World, protect the worlds with your whole being, O Hara! Meditate always upon your devotees, O God; you who are ever dear to your devotees, O Hara!
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the god whose banner is the bull, the wielder of the trident, the manifest Lord of Umā—
Having touched his hand with his own hand, he [honored] Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus.
The Blessed Lord Rudra spoke to Keśava, whose banner bears Garuḍa,
while all the gods and the sages of purified souls were listening.
"What is this, O Lord of the gods of gods, Cakrapāṇi, Janārdana?
For what purpose is this practice of austerity for you, and what is your prayer, O All-pervading Lord?
You are Viṣṇu yourself, eternal; you are the very essence of austerity among all austerities, O Hari."
"O Lord Janārdana, if your ascetic practice is for the sake of a son,
O God, a son has already been granted by me previously, O Lord of the World."
Listen, O Blessed One, who are yourself the essence of all causes, to the reason for that as well.
O Hari, for some reason,
I formerly engaged in most terrible asceticism for ten thousand years during that Kṛta Yuga.
"O God, Bhavānī was then there to attend upon me;
O Lord of Gods, this Umā of excellent complexion had been appointed by my father.
Then Indra, being afraid, O God, dispatched Māra against me."
Then Māra, joined with Madhu, approached me;
he made me the target for an arrow that was about to be discharged.
"O Hari, she serves me there by offering flowers and other gifts."
Then, O Lord of Gods, upon seeing Māra in such a state, I became enraged;
from my eye as I was angry, fire indeed fell forth.
O Viṣṇu, at that time this very fire reduced Māra to ashes; then I thought, "This is what Śakra intends to do."
From that time forward, O Lord of Gods, compassion has been directed toward him;
and I have been appointed by Brahmā for this purpose, O Janārdana, being well-pleased therein.
O God, Lord of the World, he has been appointed by you in the form of a son;
O God, your eldest son is renowned as Pradyumna.
"Know him to be Smara, O Lord of Gods; no deliberation is required here.
Having said this, O best of beings, he spoke again as if demonstrating the true nature of things to the sages who were desirous of hearing that true nature.
Having joined his palms in reverence toward Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, the Lord,
together with Umā, desired to speak of the true nature [of reality].
While Hari was acting thus, O best of the Kurus,
the sages, gods, gandharvas, siddhas, along with the kinnaras,
offered their joined palms in reverence to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the lords of gods, Hara.
Maheśvara said:
That which the Sāṃkhyas call the cause, designated as *prakṛti*,
is the triple-natured source of the world, the *pradhāna* whose essence is causality.

O Viṣṇu, O Janārdana, the Sāṃkhya knowers of reality declare you to be the cause of the cosmic egg— the world— which consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. O Viṣṇu, you preside over it by transforming yourself into its very form.
From that, the Great One (Mahat) arose, for which primordial nature (prakṛti) is the cause;
from that formidable Mahat, indeed, the Great Ego (ahaṃkāra) came into being.
O Lord of the World, you are that very one at the beginning, for such is its transformation.
From ego-consciousness, O Lord, O God, the great causes arise;
likewise, the five subtle elements and the gross elements come into being.
They call you the Lord of all beings, O Master of the World;
[namely] earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
The eye, the nose, as well as touch, the tongue, and the ear—
O God, the mind is the sixth, acting as the impeller therein in each respective case.
And they say that the organs of action are the feet and so forth, O Janārdana;
yet you alone, with self-restraint, perform all of those functions.
O Lord of the World, O Hari, O Lord of Gods, you likewise direct each respective faculty of the senses toward its own appropriate objects.
When you were joined with *rajas*, then you created all beings;
and when you were joined with *sattva*, then you became the protector of the three worlds.
When that supreme darkness prevails, you then withdraw the universe;
endowed with the three qualities alone, you are engaged in creation, preservation, and destruction.
O Mādhava, you who possess a self-restrained mind, you abide having taken up various forms of prosperity; you employ the senses upon the objects of the senses.
O Teacher of the World, by abiding within for the sake of the enjoyment of living beings, you therefore exist in all creatures; you are omnipresent.
At the time of creation you are Brahmā; at the time of maintenance, O Lord, you are Viṣṇu;
at the time of dissolution you bear the name Rudra; thus, O Lord, you possess three abodes.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect—
O Lord Hari, these are the distinct primal natures (prakṛtis) that exist everywhere within you.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
he has a thousand bellies, possesses a thousandfold power, and is the soul of a thousand, the Lord of Heaven.
Having reached this entire earth with its seven continents and oceans,
he became a subtle atom that is omnipresent and stood ten finger-breadths above it.
You alone are this entire universe, whatever has been and whatever will be;
from you, O Janārdana, the Virāj and the Samrāj have manifested.
O Lord of the World, O Ancient Self, from your mouth there appeared in the past a Brāhmaṇa, the protector of the world, who is ever devoted to the six duties.

The Rājanya, O Viṣṇu, was likewise intent on protecting the arms; the Vaiśya came from the thighs, and the Śūdra is said to have arisen from the feet. Thus, O Lord of the World, did the castes emerge from your eternal body.
From your mind, O Lord of Gods, the moon was produced—
brought happiness to all beings, possessing cool rays and the luster of nectar.
From his two eyes the Sun was born, the eye of all living beings;
by his light the entire world shines, for he is the radiant one.
From your mouth Indra and Agni were born, and from your breath Vāyu arose;
from your navel, O Lord Janārdana, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) was produced.
O Lord of Cows, the sky was born from your head;
O Lord of the World, the earth arose from your feet and the quarters from your ears.
Having thus created the entire world, you remain pervading everything.
Pervading all these worlds, O Keśava, you abide everywhere;
therefore, because of the root *vi-āp* meaning "to pervade," you are named Viṣṇu.
The waters are designated as *nārāḥ*; since you are their primordial source (*ayana*), O Lord of the past and the future, you are therefore called *Nārāyaṇa*.
O God, because you clothe yourself and because you cause [the world] to shine, you are called Vāsudeva;
O God, because you take away the life-breaths of living beings, you are therefore remembered as Hari.

O God, you always bring about welfare (*śam*); therefore, you bear the name Śaṅkara. Because of your greatness (*bṛhat*) and because of your power to nourish (*bṛṃhaṇa*), you are designated by the word Brahman.
Since "Madhu" is a name for the senses, you are therefore the slayer of Madhu (*madhunisūdana*).
They say that the senses are the *hṛṣīkas*; since you are their lord (*īśa*), O Viṣṇu, you are therefore celebrated in the Vedas as Hṛṣīkeśa.
"I am the Lord proclaimed as Brahmā within all embodied beings;
therefore, we two have arisen within your body, and thus I bear the name Keśava."
Knowledge is called "mā" by Hari, and since you are its lord, therefore you bear the name Mādhava; you are designated as "dhava," meaning master or lord.
Since this speech is *gauḥ* (the cow), and since you know it,
O Lord, you are therefore called *Govinda* by the sages.
The three Vedas have been proclaimed as "tri" by the best of sages;
because he strides across all of them in that manner, he is remembered as Trivikrama.

You are the subtle one (aṇu) and you are named Vāmana; because you are called Vāmana, you strive [for the welfare of others]. Because of your power of reflection (manana), you are indeed a sage (muni); because of your self-restraint (yamana), you are called a yogi (yati).
Since you move about unseen and are called "the ascetic" (tapasvin),
and since all beings dwell within you, O Hari, you are therefore known as Bhūtāvāsa.
You are the Lord of all beings; therefore, O Hari, you are the Sovereign. You are the *praṇava* of all the Vedas, O Lord, and the *gāyatrī* among the meters.
Among letters you are the letter *a*, and you are the *sphoṭa* residing in phonemes;
among the Rudras I am indeed one, and among the Vasus you are Pāvaka;
among the Ādityas you are Viṣṇu, and you are Indra, the lord of the gods.
Among species of trees you are the aśvattha; you are Brahmā, the teacher of the world.
Among the lords of mountains you are Meru; and among the divine seers you are Nārada.
Among the Dānavas you are the Daitya Prahlāda, who is affectionate toward his devotees;
among all serpents you are the one known as Vāsuki.
Among all the Guhyakas, you are indeed the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada);
Varuṇa is the king of the aquatic creatures, and you are Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths.
You are the beginning of all beings, as well as their middle and their end;
from you the universe arose, and into you everything is dissolved.
I am you, O omnipresent God; you alone am I, O Janārdana. There is no difference between us, O Lord of the World, whether in words or in their meanings.
O Govinda, whatever great names you have in the world, those very same names are mine; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Lord of the World, O Lord of the Cowherds, let that very devotion to you be mine;
and whoever hates you, O Lord of Gods, he hates me as well—of this there is no doubt.
O God, since I am the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati), my expansion is yours;
O Hari, there is nothing, O God, that is devoid of you.
O Lord of the World, whatever existed, whatever exists, and whatever will exist—O Lord of Gods, all that is you alone; indeed, nothing exists apart from you.
The gods constantly praise you with their own virtues, O Lord;
you are the Ṛgveda, you are indeed the Yajurveda, and you are the Sāmaveda eternally, O All-pervading One.
"What is being said by me, O Lord? You are the creator of all beings.
"Salutations to the Soul of All," the Lord Śiva spoke again to the sages.
"Know this, O brahmins, you who have come here as devotees to see [him]:
this alone is the supreme reality; there is nothing higher than this for you."
Salutations to you, O God Viṣṇu, the soul of all, Mādhava, Keśava!
I bow with my whole being; O Hari, may there always be homage to you!
Homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; I worship you, O Lord.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus spoken to the Lord of the Gods of gods, Śiva spoke again to the sages.
"Know this, O brahmins, you who have come as devotees to behold him."
This alone is the supreme reality; there is nothing beyond this for you.
Understand this very thing; this is your highest austerity.
This alone should always be meditated upon by Brahmins with expanded minds;
this is your supreme good, this is your supreme austerity.
This is the purpose of your birth; this is the fruit of your asceticism.
This is your accumulation of merit; this is the eternal dharma.
This one is subject to liberation for you; this path has been proclaimed. This is the direct bestower of merit; this is the fruit of your actions.
The wise who discourse on Brahman praise this very thing;
O Brahmins, this threefold path is always to be sought by those who know Brahman.
Those who rely upon Sāṃkhya and Yoga praise this very path;
this is the way of the knowers of Brahman described by the exponents of the Vedas.
Know it to be thus; there is no need for further deliberation here:
Hari alone is always to be meditated upon by you who are established in goodness (sattva).
There is no other god in the world superior to Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa.
O Brahmins, always recite "Om" and meditate upon Keśava.
From that, the attainment of the supreme good will come; of this there is no doubt.
When Hari is meditated upon in this way, he will become manifest and gracious to you;
this god will bring about the destruction of existence, of this there is no doubt.
O Brahmins, if you desire to attain the Lord, always meditate upon Hari;
this Teacher of the World will destroy the power of this cycle of existence.
Always remember Viṣṇu; recite the three-bodied one.
"O Brahmins, always restrain the mind with effort;
O you whose wealth is austerity, when the internal organ is purified, Viṣṇu becomes pleased."
Having meditated upon me with all your effort, you shall then know Keśava. O Brahmins, I am always to be worshipped; I am the means for the remembrance of Hari.
"This is the means proclaimed by me; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Brahmins, since he is always a master of illusion, you must strive for the destruction of his illusion."
O best of Brahmins, act with such effort that your intellect may become entirely pure,
so that the God may be propitiated.
O King, having been addressed thus, all those meritorious ascetics, accepting his words as they were, had their doubts dispelled.
"So be it," those brahmins said to Hara with palms joined;
"all our doubt is severed, and the matter has been grasped exactly as it is."
For this purpose we have come today to your abode;
through the meeting of you two, all our great delusion here has vanished.
O Lord of Gods, as you speak, so it shall be for our supreme welfare.
As the Blessed Lord Rudra said, "One should always strive for Hari," those sages, being delighted, bowed down to Keśava Hari.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then that blessed Lord Rudra, as if causing everyone to marvel, [spoke].
Then, while the sages were listening, he began to praise Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, Hari, with meaningful words consistent with the Vedas.
Homage to you, O Blessed One, to the wise Vāsudeva;
by whose light the entire world shines eternally, O Acyuta.
Homage to the Blessed Lord, O God; eternal homage to the one whose self is the Sun.
O Lord, you who cool all these worlds as the cool-rayed moon;
salutations to you, O God Viṣṇu, salutations to you in your form as Soma.
Salutations to the god who alone impels all creatures, the soul of the universe, the creator of beings; salutations to you, O Hara, whose self is the universal soul and whose self is the wind.
Salutation to you, the Brahman-self, who always held in his hand the kuśa grass, bark garments, and other such items, and who upheld all the Vedas.
Salutations to you, whose nature is Rudra, who always withdraws all things during the dissolution, who is the all-seeing, whose essence is wrath, and who is the universal form.
Salutations to you, Viṣṇu, the unborn, the creator of all beings, the giver of life to all living creatures, the maker and the creator of the universe.
First, salutations to you, the root of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the source of all beings; O Lord of the gods of gods, salutations again and again to you, the Pradhāna.
O Hari, you who abide on earth in the form of fragrance;
salutations to you, the essence of scent, who are firm and possess a firm form.

Salutations to you, the essence of the waters, who everywhere brings about the happiness of all living beings; salutations to you, whose form is the universe, and salutations again and again to the Essence.
O God, Lord of the World, salutations to You who possess a radiant form, whose splendor is luminous, and whose quality is always devoted to the welfare of living beings.
Where touch is the quality of wind, which bestows cold, heat, pleasure, and pain—to you who take the form of wind, salutations; to Hari, whose essence is touch, salutations!
Sound abides in space and enters into all ears;
homage to you, O Blessed Viṣṇu, homage to you whose self is sound.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the World, the master of illusion, who sustains the entire universe while possessing a body that is both illusory and human, and who bestows freedom from illusion.
Salutation to the primordial seed, who is beyond qualities yet the soul of all qualities;
salutation to him, the inconceivable, the well-conceivable, whose very nature is the object of thought.
Salutation to you who are Hara, who have the form of Hari, who are Brahman, and who discourse upon Brahman;
salutation to you, the knower of Brahman, whose self is both Brahman and the Supreme Spirit.
Salutations to the one with a thousand heads and a thousand feet;
salutations to the one with a thousand faces and a thousand eyes.
Salutations again and again to the All, to the one of universal form, to the creator of all;
salutations eternally to the destroyer of all, O abode of beings, salutations again and again.

Salutations to you, Indra among the senses, whose form is that of Indra; salutations to you, O Hare, who are the eternal object of perception; salutations to you, the horse-headed one (*aśvaśiras*), whose nature is the bringing forth of the Vedas.
Salutation to Agni, O Lord of Fire; salutation to you, the Lord of lights. Salutation to Sūrya, the auspicious one; salutation to you, the Lord of splendors.
Salutations to Soma, the gentle one; salutations to Hari, whose nature is coolness.
Salutations to Rudra, who possesses the form of Rudra; salutations always to Hari, the object of the senses.
Homage to you who are invoked with the *vaṣaṭ* call, whose very nature is *svadhā* and *svāhā*.

Homage to the sacrifice, to the one worthy of worship, to the oblation, and to that which prepares the offering; homage to the sacrificial ladle, to the vessel, to the limb of the sacrifice, and to the supreme.
Salutations to the one whose body is the *praṇava*, who is both perishable and imperishable;
to the Veda, who is the form of the Veda, who is both indestructible and subject to decay.
To the Veda, who is the embodiment of the Veda; to the wielder of weapons, who is the very form of the weapon.
Salutations to you who bear the mace, the sword, the conch, and the discus; salutations ever to the wielder of the trident and the shield, the bestower of boons. Salutations, salutations!
Salutations to you, O Guru, the soul of all, who are dear to the Buddhas, who are the Buddha, the fully awakened one, and the source of happiness; salutations to you, Hari, Viṣṇu.
Homage to you, Lord of all worlds, creator of all; homage, repeated homage! Homage to you who are pure by nature; homage to you, O Sacrificial Boar!
Homage to Viṣṇu, homage to Viṣṇu, homage to Viṣṇu, homage to Hara! Homage to you, Vāsudeva, to the wise Vāsudeva!
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, to Kṛṣṇa, the abode of all; salutations, salutations! Salutations again and again to you; protect the worlds, O Janārdana!
Having thus praised the Lord of the World, he spoke to the best of sages:
"Those who constantly study this hymn should go to Keśava, the refuge of all beings; there he will ordain their welfare."
And those who shall maintain this hymn that liberates from evil—
whether reciting it or hearing it— Hari, the soul of all, being pleased and with a serene mind, will bestow the highest good upon them; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
If you, who are firm in your vows, desire to attain the highest good, you must certainly meditate in your minds upon Keśava, who is compassionate toward his devotees.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra, the creator of beings, Śaṅkara himself, together with Umā and his attendants, vanished on the spot.
Then all those sages attained supreme bliss,
having realized that very Nārāyaṇa, Hari, to be the highest reality.
Having reached a state of supreme wonder, they considered themselves to have achieved their purpose.
Then, O best of kings, the world-protectors, having paid homage to Viṣṇu Hari,
departed for their own abodes along with all their hosts.
Having mounted Garuḍa, the bull among birds, the Blessed Viṣṇu appeared equipped with the conch,
the discus, the mace, the sword, the Śārṅga bow, and quivers and finger-guards.
The Lord of the World, the lotus-eyed one, returned as he had come along the path to Badarī,
which is constantly frequented by sages, at the hour of evening.
Having gone there and rested as was appropriate, Hari,
the Lord, being honored by all the sages, sat down upon a comfortable seat.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time, O King, there was a preeminent ruler of Pauṇḍra.
