He was powerful, endowed with courage, a warrior of vast prowess.
Then that king, the enemy of the Vṛṣṇis and a hater of Kṛṣṇa,
having summoned all the kings by force, spoke in the assembly of monarchs.
"The entire earth has been conquered, and the best of kings have been subdued;
yet those Vṛṣṇis, intoxicated by their own strength, remain arrogant, relying upon Kṛṣṇa."
"Because they have taken refuge with Kṛṣṇa, none of them will pay me tribute;
moreover, that powerful Kṛṣṇa remains there, treating me with contempt."
That cowherd always possessed the pride of thinking, "I am the wielder of the discus.
He was proud of being the bearer of the conch, the discus, the mace, and the Śārṅga bow, accompanied by his quivers and arrows;
such great pride as this currently persists within him.
And whatever name is constantly applied to me in the world as "Vāsudeva," the cowherd,
endowed with pride and strength, seized that very name of mine.
Of that wheel, my own great and sharpened wheel named Sudarśana is always the subduer of his pride; it is indeed powerful.
The destruction of that thousand-spoked,
most terrible wheel was accomplished by this great discus, O best of kings, against the cowherd.
This divine bow of mine, the great and excellent one named Śārṅga,
destroys it— of that there is no doubt— as does his wondrous discus.
The great conch Pāñcajanya always resounded with a mighty roar;
behold him, O best of kings—he is the conqueror of that very conch.
This great and firm mace of mine, named Kaumodakī,
has been well-fashioned by me with the weight of a thousand units of black iron.
This sword of mine, named Nandaka, is vast and firm;
it is a terrible destroyer that brings about the end even of Antaka (the God of Death). But who is the destroyer of that sword?
Therefore, armed with a mace, a sword, the Śārṅga bow, and a discus, and wearing hand-guards, I shall be the victor over Kṛṣṇa in battle; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
And speak thus to me, O kings, as I am the wielder of the mace and likewise the wielder of the discus;
speak always to me, O best of kings, as the hero who bears the conch and the Śārṅga bow. Address me as Vāsudeva, but not as a cowherd, nor as the foremost of the Yadus.
Indeed, I alone am Vāsudeva; having slain that cowherd boy, the slayer of my friend, the great-souled Naraka.
"If you do not speak to me in such a manner, you shall be punished with a fine of a hundred niṣkas of gold each,
and likewise a great quantity of grain."
While the lord of kings was speaking thus, which was then difficult for the mind to endure,
some of the most heroic kings remained filled with shame;
for those monarchs always knew the taste of the strength and prowess of Keśava.
But other kings, O King, cried out, "It is even so! while others, arrogant with the pride of their strength, said, "We shall conquer Keśava in battle."
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then that best of sages emerged from the peak of Kailāsa.
Nārada, who knows all the worlds, [went] toward the city of Pauṇḍra.
Descending from the path of the sky and returning to the best of kings,
he was directed by the gatekeeper and entered the excellent palace.
Having received from the king the customary honors beginning with the *arghya* offering, the great sage sat down upon a bright seat well-spread with a white cloth.
The best of sages again inquired after the king's welfare;
then Pauṇḍraka, arrogant in his strength, spoke further to Nārada.
"You are skilled in all things and wise in every undertaking;
you are renowned among the great-souled gods, Siddhas, and Gandharvas."
All-pervading, free from affliction, you go everywhere at all times;
O best of Brahmins, there is nothing in this universe that is inaccessible to you.
O Nārada, speak thus: for wherever you have always gone, there you have been one perfected by austerity, renowned in the world for your prowess.
The powerful Pauṇḍra himself was renowned as Vāsudeva;
he bore the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the sword, and carried quivers and finger-guards.
A conqueror of lions among kings, a giver of gifts at all times;
an enjoyer of the entire kingdom, a teacher of kings, and more powerful than the powerful;
invincible by the armies of enemies, he is indeed the protector of his own kin.
That other one named Gopaka, who is called by the name Vāsudeva,
possesses neither the heroism nor the strength to uphold my name.
For that cowherd, out of childishness, maintains my name in vain;
O best of Brahmins, understand this: I alone am he.
Having conquered the powerful Yadu in this world,
Vāsudeva will defeat all the Vṛṣṇis by force and utterly consume that city.
O high-minded one, I am a warrior, and Dvārakā is the abode of the Vṛṣṇis;
moreover, all these powerful kings have assembled here with me.
I have swift horses and chariots with the speed of the wind; I also have a thousand, a hundred, and even a million rutting elephants.
"With this very strength, I shall slay Keśava in battle on the field;
therefore, O Brahmin, always speak thus before me."
O Brahmin Nārada, speak now even to Indra;
this is my request, O Lord. I bow to you, O one whose wealth is asceticism.
Nārada said:
"O King, I am always omnipresent as long as the cosmic egg endures;
I am unimpeded by anyone in my movement throughout all the worlds."
However, O King, best of monarchs, I do not dare to speak thus while Janārdana,
the Lord of Gods and wielder of the discus, rules the earth.

When the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu has slain the wicked along with their kinsmen, who would dare say, "Who is this Vāsudeva? regarding this Hari? Indeed, who could even speak thus while Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the cowherds, rules?
If you say this out of ignorance, then even an ordinary person would be capable of it;
however, Hari, the omnipresent Viṣṇu, will destroy your pride.
Viṣṇu, of inconceivable power, wielder of the Śārṅga bow and the mace,
the primordial god and ancient self, will remove your pride.
"O Great King, this wheel that stands before you is a source of laughter;
likewise, O King, are your Śārṅga bow, your conch, and your most terrible mace.
This present moment has arrived as a time for extreme derision for you."
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O great king, Pauṇḍra, filled with the pride of his own strength, became enraged.
He spoke to that best of brahmins, Nārada, in the assembly of kings.
"Do not speak thus, O celestial sage; I am a king who is ever victorious.
Go now as you wish; you are but a sage who always dispenses curses.
Fearing you, O one of great intelligence, go wherever you desire."
Thus addressed by the king’s hero, Nārada departed in silence;
traveling through the sky, he went to where Keśava was staying. Having approached Viṣṇu, he related everything concerning Viṣṇu.
Having heard that, the Blessed Viṣṇu said, "O best of sages, tomorrow I shall remove his pride; speak as you wish. Having said this, he became silent right there in that Badarikāśrama.
Then Pauṇḍra, the lord of great heroism, accompanied by numerous forces,
was followed by many thousands of horses and many elephants.
The Lord, true to his promise, was joined by seven crores of chariots and accompanied by many hundreds of thousands of foot soldiers,
as well as by kings headed by Ekalavya.
Eight thousand horses, a hundred thousand elephants,
and a million foot soldiers— that was the force that assembled.
O best of kings, O great monarch, with this strength he shone forth in battle like the sun standing at its rising.
In the middle of the night, during that great and terrible darkness, the infantrymen with torches in their hands proceeded toward the city of Dvārakā.
Those mighty and most excellent of kings, endowed with great heroism, advanced toward the formidable Dvārakā, raining down a torrent of various weapons as they converged.
Having mounted a great chariot equipped with a flood of weapons,
it was strewn with swords and scimitars and crowded with maces and iron clubs.
It was strewn with spears and javelins, covered with rows of banners,
equipped with networks of small bells, and adorned with arrows, swords, and darts.
Extremely terrible and most fierce, resembling the clouds at the end of an eon,
strewn with bows and maces, and possessing a speed like that of a great wind,
he whose form was like fire and the sun proceeded toward Dvāravatī.
Having seized the torches, O powerful and mighty king,
the monarch desired to slay the Lord of the World and the Vṛṣṇis on all sides.
Drawing those leading military commanders of the king toward him, the one of great splendor approached the eastern gate and, having carefully stationed his forces,
the king spoke these words to all the kings standing there:
"Let the drum be beaten here, proclaiming my name: 'Fight!
Fight! Here, let what is due be given, or let it be returned!'"
This King of Pauṇḍra, most heroic and seeking battle, has arrived;
he desires to slay all of you who rely on the strength of Kṛṣṇa’s arms.
Thus, having been sent forth, they all struck many musical instruments;
and hundreds of thousands of lamps were lit.
From here and there, kings eager for battle were stationed;
likewise, armed Kṣatriyas stood surrounding your city.
Uttering lion-like roars and bristling with streams of weapons, they cried out:
"Whence has the best of the Vṛṣṇis come? Whence has the king, the lord of the world, come?"
"Whence has the hero Sātyaki come? Whence indeed has Hārdikya come?
And whence has Balabhadra, the best of all the Yādavas, come?"—thus did all the kings speak.
Taking up many weapons from all sides—
arrows and great bows— all of them fixed their gaze upon the act of donning armor for battle.
Those best of kings went to the city of Dvāravatī.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then all the Yādavas, having seen that multitude of soldiers, [acted].
And when night had arrived, it was filled with great weapons.
Stirred up by great winds at the end of the eon, like the ocean,
it was inconceivable to all beings and resembled Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
Armed with weapons and eager for battle, they all stood ready in their armor; all those Yādavas, warriors skilled in arms, took up their torches.
Sātyaki, Balabhadra, Hārdikya, and Niśaṭha,
as well as the highly intelligent Uddhava and the very powerful Ugrasena.
And all the other Yādavas were intent on grasping their armor;
those vassals, skilled in battle, equipped themselves as warriors during the night.
Equipped with swords and weapons, all of them crowded with arms,
many powerful-armed warriors assembled for battle.
Chariot-warriors, elephant-riders, and likewise cavalrymen equipped with weapons—
these high-souled and supreme men among humans were ever-ready and skilled archers.
All the Sātvatas quickly emerged from the city in every direction with torches, crying out, "Where is Pauṇḍraka? (HV App. I, 31.1508–1509).
The region, illuminated by lamps, became free from darkness;
thereafter, the area was entirely cleared of gloom on all sides.
A terrible battle then ensued between the Vṛṣṇis and the Kṣatriyas.
Then there arose a great, hair-raising clamor;
horses were joined with horses, and elephants with the leaders of chariot-divisions.
Chariots were joined with chariots, and horsemen likewise with horsemen; O King, swordsmen fought with swordsmen, and mace-wielders with mace-wielders.
The mutual clash was most terrible, a battle like the agitation at the time of the great dissolution; such was the sound of those great-souled ones.
"Run forward! Strike! Rush about quickly!
Slay these kings!"—thus did the Vṛṣṇis cry out on all sides.
"Here is that mighty-armed, heroic one, falling with his sword;
here is that terrible shower of arrows proceeding against us most cruelly;
and this king of great prowess, armed with a mace, oppresses us all."
This charioteer, O Lord, is armed with arrows, a bow, a mace, and quivers; equipped with a sword, this powerful man moves everywhere with a spear in his hand.
Here stands this great trident facing every direction;
here on the path moves this elephant with its excellent tusks pointed all around.
O Lord of the World, Aśvin, who is all-pervading, heroic, swift, and like the wind,
strikes arrows with arrows and staffs with staffs.
They struck spears with spears, maces with maces,
and likewise iron clubs with iron clubs and pikes with pikes on all sides.
Thus, O Great King, as they engaged in that supreme battle,
there occurred a truly great conflict and a tremendous roar arose.
In that battle, thousands of musical instruments appeared, both very numerous and loud-sounding,
as did the resonant blasts of conch shells.
At night, during that great battle between the Vṛṣṇis and their enemies, a hair-raising sound arose in the conflict.
Some kings,
struck down, fell upon the earth; others, their brains crushed and their necks severed, those kings of great prowess fell to the ground with weapons still in their hands.
Some, however, with their armor shattered, rushed forward from here and there, striking one another while seeking each other's death.

Having laid down their weapons, those great-souled ones— some with bodies still smeared with flesh and blood— fell lifeless, increasing the population of Yama’s realm. Thus, O King, all those kings were indeed slain.
In the meantime, Śūra Ekalavya, the lord of the Niṣādas,
took up a most terrible bow that resembled Kāla, Antaka, and Yama.
He afflicted the Yādavas with many thousands of arrows,
indeed with more than a hundred sharp shafts that pierce the vital organs.
He crushed the entire army of the Vṛṣṇi heroes on all sides,
as well as the most heroic Kṣatriyas who were fighting with weapons in hand.
Having pierced Niśaṭha with twenty-five straight-knotted arrows,
Sāraṇa with ten, and the son of Hṛdika (Kṛtavarman) with five arrows;
He struck Ugrasena with eighty-nine arrows, Vasudeva with seven,
Uddhava with ten, and Akrūra with five shafts.
Having thus struck down everyone one by one with sharpened arrows,
the heroic one put the Yādava army to flight, proclaiming his own name.
The valiant and powerful Ekalavya said to the Yadus:
"Where will the heroic and mighty Sātyaki go now?"
"Intoxicated with wine, where is Halī, the wielder of the mace, going here in person?
Thus he spoke with a lion's roar, as if astonishing everyone.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
When the armies and the Vṛṣṇi heroes had indeed fled, HV App. I, 31.1562.
Then, O great king, when they were terrified and being slain on all sides in battle,
When the lamps had been extinguished and all was silent on every side, that supreme army of the Vṛṣṇis thought, "Victory! indeed.
Then the immensely powerful Pauṇḍra spoke to his own soldiers:
"O lords of men, go quickly with axes and spears to this city!"
O rulers of the earth, go forth in every direction with axes, spears, and stones, as well as with stones placed upon ploughs.
Let the rows of walls and the palaces be broken down on all sides;
let the women, the chief courtesans, and the elephants likewise be scattered in every direction.
Let the excellent horses and very great riches also be taken.
Let all the maidens and female slaves be seized from every side;
let the excellent horses and vast quantities of wealth also be taken.
"So be it," said all those high-souled kings;
and by the command of Pauṇḍraka, they all cut down the walls everywhere with axes,
as well as the palaces and the heaps of jewels.
Then, O Great King, a great clamor arose on all sides as the ramparts were being struck down with axes by those of mighty strength; at the eastern gate, the masses of the walls were shattered.
Hearing that most terrible sound, Sātyaki was overwhelmed with rage;
having entrusted everything to me, Keśava, the lord of the Yādavas,
departed for the peak of Kailāsa to behold the imperishable Lord.
"By all means, the city of Dvāravatī must certainly be protected by me," having thus reflected in his mind, he quickly took up his bow.
Having mounted the great chariot of the high-souled Dāruka,
which was formidable and had been prepared by his son, he himself indeed became the driver.
Taking up that great bow and arrows resembling venomous serpents,
he donned his formidable armor, which was unbearable under the impact of weapons.
Wearing armlets and earrings, equipped with quivers, arrows, a bow, a mace, and a sword, he rushed impetuously toward battle, calling to mind the words of Kaiśava.
In that region illuminated by lamps, the excellent Sātyaki proceeded.
And likewise, the heroic Baladeva, armed with a mace, arrows, and a sword, mounted his radiant chariot and set forth with the desire for battle.
Uttering a lion’s roar and letting out a terrifying cry,
the powerful Uddhava also swiftly mounted his elephant in person.
The exceedingly wise and mighty one, seeking the highest policy, entered that fierce battle of intoxicated and loudly roaring [warriors] while contemplating the supreme course of action.
All the other Vṛṣṇis as well, eager for battle, then set out,
having mounted their chariots and elephants, with the son of Hṛdika at their head.
And everywhere, O lords, with lamps held before them,
they let out lion-roars while remembering the words of Kaiśava.
Having arrived at the eastern gate, the Vṛṣṇis, eager for battle,
those of great strength, gathered together and took their positions there as was appropriate.
While the army stood there, formidable and terrifying, on a path illuminated by torches,
the hero Śini was equipped with arrows, a bow, a mace, and a quiver in his hand.
Having taken up the Vāyavya weapon and fixed the great arrow,
he drew back that most excellent and supreme bow until it reached his ear.
The powerful hero of the Śinis released [his weapons] among the enemy armies.
By the power of that Vāyavya weapon, all those best of kings stationed there were put to flight by the might of the missile to where Pauṇḍraka stood.
Having gone there, they all stood [there], but were swept away by the force of the wind;
where all those best of kings had previously stood, they were now driven away.
Standing there, that descendant of Śini quickly took up a sharp arrow resembling the hood of a serpent, and then Sātyaki spoke.
"Where now is that mighty-armed Pauṇḍraka, known as Rāja?
I stand here with resolve, O Śārṅga-wielder, and I too am possessed of great strength."
If you, O evil-souled one, are the witness, then you shall be the slayer of this lowest of kings;
for I am the servant of Keśava, standing here desiring to kill Pauṇḍraka.
But having severed his head while all the kṣatriyas look on,
I shall give [his flesh] to the vultures, crows, and dogs, O evil-minded one!
Who indeed would perform such an act, like a thief,
while all the high-souled Yādavas were sleeping everywhere in the night?
"This man is a thief in every respect; he is not a king, for a king endowed with power would not commit such theft if he were capable [of preventing it]. He is the lowest of men."
"Alas, how childish this king is as he performs the work of a thief!
In every way, I do not see his departure being possible at this moment."
Thus the heroic Sātyaki laughed aloud with a great sound;
having drawn his very firm bow, he fixed an arrow upon the bowstring.
Having heard those words of the wise Sātyaki,
the heroic Vāsudeva, possessed of great prowess, [spoke to] Pauṇḍraka, the best of kings.
Taking up a sharp arrow and approaching before the Yadu,
King Vāsudeva spoke, laughing in many ways.
"O Sātyaki, listen to my words if you are determined to fight:
Where indeed is Kṛṣṇa? Where is Gopāla? From where has he come to be here?"
The killer of women and the killer of cattle— he who was once called "Master"—
where could he be now, having taken that name of mine? He,
the slayer of his friend, the great hero Narakāsura of mighty power!
"Once that evil-minded one is slain, let that [victory] belong to me alone;
go as you wish, O hero, for you are not capable of fighting him."
Or rather, stay a moment; then you shall behold my strength.
I will strike down your head with terrible, unassailable arrows.
The earth shall drink the blood of you, a fallen hero;
likewise, that cowherd Gopa shall hear that Sātyaki has been slain.
That great pride which always exists in that cowherd will quickly perish once you have been slain, O best of the Yadus.
"O high-minded one, we have previously heard that the cowherd went to Mount Kailāsa after entrusting the protection [of the cows] to you."
"Take up a sharpened arrow if you are able to stand before me," he said;
having spoken thus, he took up his shaft and indeed resolved to fight.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O great king, the enraged Sātyaki, the bull among the Vṛṣṇis—
O King, he spoke these words to Vāsudeva, as if smiling.
O lowest of kings, do not speak such words to Vāsudeva! What man, desiring to live, would thus address the Lord of the worlds?
Death approaches you from every side as you speak such words;
may your tongue split into a hundred pieces for speaking such speech!
O Pauṇḍraka, I shall now strike off this head of yours from your body—
that name by which you are currently called "Vāsudeva."
"As long as the head remains upon the body, so long shall he endure;
for tomorrow that very one will become the Blessed Vāsudeva."
The Lord of the World alone is the creator of everything and is omnipresent;
O evil-souled one, there is no doubt that the God will exist in every way.
"O King, I shall cause this head of mine to fall from my body right now,
if that Blessed Viṣṇu does not arrive immediately."
Display now all your missiles, prowess, and strength;
O King, beyond this, no further power or valor remains in you.
Show me everything with effort; I stand here, resolute.
Armed with arrows, bow, mace, and sword, I am present in every way.
"I have come to this city from there; I tell you this in truth.
O Vāsudeva, having seen you, I am in every way one who has accomplished his purpose.
O King, having cut your body into pieces as small as sesame seeds, I shall give it to the dogs."
Having spoken thus, he took up an arrow and, drawing it back to his ear, pierced the mighty Vāsudeva with that sharpened shaft.
O best of kings, pierced by that Yadu, the powerful Vāsudeva vomited very hot blood from his limbs and his eyes.
Then that powerful King Vāsudeva became enraged;
laughing aloud in many ways, the king indeed pierced Sātyaki with nine and ten straight-knotted arrows.
Then, taking up a sharp iron arrow resembling Yama himself,
the powerful Vāsudeva, that best of kings, drew his bow and pierced Sātyaki once more in the night, gladdening his own men.
Pierced deeply in the forehead by that iron shaft, the hero Sātyaki,
who is true to his vow and the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis,
then sank down upon the seat of his chariot, O best of men, as if devoid of motion.
Then, at that very moment, the powerful hero of the Śini clan, his delusion gone and filled with rage, spoke these words while laughing:
"I shall strike down your prowess," he said, and took up his arrow.
Then King Pauṇḍraka, having pierced him with ten swift arrows,
firmly struck his charioteer with twenty-five and his four horses as well.
With their limbs smeared with blood, those horses and the charioteer became utterly overwhelmed on all sides while Vāsudeva looked on;
then Vāsudeva, the charioteer, let out a lion’s roar.
At that sound, Sātyaki then awoke;
seeing his horses thus pierced and his charioteer likewise fallen, he was roused.
Then the immensely heroic Śaineya, enraged, O best of kings, said, "Ah!
I shall see your prowess! and took up an arrow;
with that arrow, he pierced the chest of that mighty one.
Then, O King, struck by that arrow in battle, Vāsudeva wavered;
from his chest, he shed terrible, intensely hot blood.
O King, he quickly fell onto the floor of the chariot, sighing repeatedly;
he was no longer aware of what needed to be done and simply sat there.
Then Satyaki, having shattered the chariot with ten arrows,
cut down the standard of Vāsudeva with a broad-headed shaft;
the lord of the Vṛṣṇis then slew the four horses and the charioteer as well with his arrows.
Then, O king of kings, Yuyudhāna— that is, Sātyaki— struck with a sharpened broad-headed arrow and severed the charioteer’s head from his body.
He cut the chariot’s fastenings, and the horses fell lifeless;
having then slain the four horses with four feathered shafts, he struck them down.
Having easily cut the discus into pieces the size of sesame seeds with ten arrows,
O King, the mighty Vāsudeva laughed heartily.
And then, O King, Sātyaki, that best of the Yadus, quickly leaping down from his chariot and taking up a massive bow, stood upon the ground.
Then, with a sharp broad-headed arrow,
the hero Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth, swiftly severed the bowstring as if in the blink of an eye;
and with another broad-headed arrow, he cut through the bow, as if causing everyone to marvel.
Then, having cast aside his great bow in that great battle,
he took up another formidable bow and pierced [his opponent] with sharpened arrows.
Vāsudeva also, sighing, quickly took up his bow,
O King, as well as several arrows, his mace, and his sword with effort; then,
summoning all his strength, he stood upon the ground.
Standing on the ground, Vāsudeva quickly afflicted Satyaki, whose prowess is truth,
with many thousands of arrows.
At the head of the battle, he severed Sātyaki’s flagstaff and struck his chariot with ten sharp,
swift arrows.
Sātyaki [struck] that performer of cruel deeds, just as Indra [struck Vṛtra] during the slaying of Vṛtra.
And then, O best of kings, Yuyudhāna struck Vāsudeva with ten arrows, and again with ten, five, and likewise with five more.
With six, six, and likewise eight [arrows], he pierced him at the head of the battle,
O King, just as Bali’s enemy [Vāmana] pierced Bali in the war between the gods and the asuras.
O King, having quickly severed that most terrible bow of the bull of the Yadus into two pieces at the handle with ten arrows, Pauṇḍraka laughed loudly; but the mighty Vāsudeva simply smiled.
Then, while all the warriors looked on, the mighty Sātyaki, that bull among the Vṛṣṇis, strung his great bow and swiftly struck [his opponent] with seventy thousand arrows.
Then those arrows, resembling swarms of locusts, fell from all sides—
from above the head, from the flanks, from behind, and likewise from the front.
And in the mouth, O great king, as well as in the shanks and the buttocks,
those arrows striking his vital organs caused Vāsudeva extreme pain.
Agitated and mountain-like in form, he became motionless;
he was merely a mass of fortitude, like one afflicted by thirst with an arrow in his side.
Pauṇḍraka stood there just like a high-minded man who has been stripped of everything.
Then the powerful and majestic Vāsudeva became enraged;
taking up a crescent-shaped arrow (*ardhacandra*), he pierced Sātyaki in battle. Having struck him with seven arrows as he approached, he seemed to quiver with fury.
Then, pierced by him with five swift arrows,
Sātyaki cut the bow of Pauṇḍra and let out a lion’s roar.
O Lord, Vāsudeva, seizing his mace and whirling it from foot to foot,
swiftly brought it down upon the chest of Sātyaki.
Drawing it back with his left hand, Sātyaki, the joy of the Yadus,
took up an arrow and pierced Pauṇḍraka in battle.
Seizing him in the midst of that [conflict], the powerful Vāsudeva quickly struck Sātyaki with ten spears.
Pierced by them in battle, the hero Sātyaki, true to his promise,
struck Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, he who is faithful to his vow.
Casting aside that jewel of a bow and swiftly seizing a mace,
O King, the hero who is the leader of the Vṛṣṇis then struck him.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the enraged Sātyaki, the joy of the Vṛṣṇis, with mace in hand—
O King, he quickly struck Vāsudeva with a sharp mace;
but the powerful Vāsudeva, in turn, struck Sātyaki with his mace.
Then those two heroes, with maces raised, shone resplendent in battle like two proud lions in the forest, each seeking to slay the other.
Then Sātyaki, filled with rage, moved in a leftward circle;
O King, those two mace-wielders then struck each other with their clubs in that battle.
Struck on their chests, sides, and backs by the wielder of the mace,
both of them had their limbs smeared with blood, appearing like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
Uttering lion-roars like two great clouds in the rainy season, they cried out "Stay! Stay! while seeking to slay one another.
Vāsudeva struck him on the right side between the breasts,
and then the heroic Yuyudhāna struck him in the middle of the arms.
Struck forcefully, the hero fell to the ground on his knees;
then, rising up once more, he struck Yadu on the forehead.
Dejected and somewhat exhausted, the hero Sātyaki rose up quickly from there and struck Pauṇḍrasattama with his mace.
The powerful hero Vāsudeva, like another Death in person,
struck the Vṛṣṇi with his mace as if burning him with his very eye.
Struck by her with the mace released from her arm, Vṛṣṇi suddenly grasped the ground as if he had fallen into the lap of Death.
Furthermore,
O great king, having regained his composure and firmly grasping that mace with both hands by its handle, he seized it.
Having split his massive, auspicious mace made of black iron into two,
the hero suddenly let it go and uttered a lion’s roar.
Then the mighty King Vāsudeva, having leaped up,
seized Sātyaki with his left hand and [supported him] with his right hand.
Having formed a most terrible fist, O King, the powerful Vāsudeva struck Sātyaki in the middle of his chest.
But the hero of the Vṛṣṇis, the descendant of Śini, quickly casting aside his mace,
struck Vāsudeva with his palm on the field of battle.
Vāsudeva also struck Satyaki, who was true to his vow, with his palm;
thus, a most terrible battle of palms ensued between the two of them.
Striking with their knees, fists, arms, and likewise with their heads;
striking chest against chest, knee against knee, and likewise head against head;
and striking hand against hand, those two engaged in combat.
O Indra among kings, between those two closely situated *tāla* trees in the forest,
a most terrible fire arose, just like a fire that has broken out in a wood.
Those two celebrated heroes, Pauṇḍraka and Sātyaki,
both possessed of great strength, having cast aside their weapons during the night while all was still and silent,
fought in that great arena like two world-renowned wrestlers.
Then both armies, O Great King, fell into a state of uncertainty:
"Could it be that the heroic Sātyaki has been slain by this evil-minded one? Or rather, will Vāsudeva himself be killed by him?"
Or else, these two great heroes, seeking each other's death,
will slay one another and go to the heaven of heroes;
otherwise, these two renowned heroes will not cease from battle.
"Oh, what heroism! Oh, what fortitude in these two powerful ones!
These two are great warriors in the world; they are not considered ordinary men."
"Never before has there been such a most terrible battle even among the gods and asuras;
this kind of conflict has never been heard of or seen at any time."
Thus those soldiers of both armies would speak,
having witnessed that most terrible and fierce battle during the deep and dreadful night.
Then those two struck each other with force using their terrible arms.
Sātyaki struck the son of Pauṇḍra with ten fist-blows;
the mighty Pauṇḍra struck Sātyaki with five.
And between those two, a great crackling sound arose everywhere, shaking the very shell of the universe, as if to cause amazement to all.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: In the meantime, Ekalavya, the chief of the Niṣādas, became enraged.
Having looked toward Balabhadra and quickly taken up his bow,
that hero mounted his chariot and went to where the wielder of the plow was stationed.
Then, seeing the Niṣāda chief Ekalavya approaching,
the mighty Halin (Balarāma) stood before him, having become a charioteer, armed with a mace and arrows.
And he struck Baladeva with twenty garlands of arrows;
having struck the chariot with ten and the charioteer with ten swift shafts.
Then, letting out a lion’s roar,
he [Bali] cut the bowstring of Sīrin with ten arrows and let out a lion’s roar himself.
Having strung his bow,
Baladeva struck down the Niṣāda with ten iron arrows and ten sharp shafts;
while all the Kṣatriyas looked on, he severed that bow in half.
Having struck the charioteer with ten arrows and the chariot itself with thirty,
O Lord of the World, he cut down the Niṣāda’s banner with a broad-headed shaft.
Thereafter, the most heroic Niṣāda took up another great bow,
firm and strung with a sinew-cord, measuring ten palm-trees in length;
he swiftly struck Kāmapāla in the region of the chest with an arrow.
The mighty Baladeva, possessing great heroism, hissing like the serpent Śeṣa,
[struck back]; but the powerful Mādhava, the elder brother of Mādhava, cut that divine bow at the handle with ten arrows capable of enduring all force.
Ekalavya, the lord of the Niṣādas, quickly seizing a sharp sword of terrible form,
hurled it at Baladeva.
In that interval, the powerful hero of the Vṛṣṇis,
the bull of the Yadus and joy of the Yadu clan, cut him into pieces as small as sesame seeds with five arrows.
Then, after that, the charioteer, having observed the body of his driver, hurled another great sword, auspicious and made entirely of iron.
And in that great battle, the hero Mādhava, the bull among the Yadus, pierced those ten arrows as well with his own shafts in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Then, O King, having taken up his spear adorned with a garland of bells,
that mighty Niṣāda king, the exceedingly powerful one, dispatched it toward Baladeva and let out a most terrible lion’s roar.
That all-auspicious Śakti approached Baladeva.
Leaping up, the powerful Balabhadra seized that most terrible club,
as if to cause amazement to all the Niṣāda chiefs;
then that Mādhava swiftly struck him in the region of the chest with that very same weapon.
Struck by her with all his might, that heroic lord of the Niṣādas fell to the earth, overwhelmed in every limb;
the Niṣāda, struck by Rāma, had fallen into a state where his life was in peril.
O Indra among kings, his Niṣādas numbered in the hundreds and thousands;
eighty-eight thousand were Niṣādas who fought with weapons—
mighty bowmen of great strength, armed with maces and riding on horseback.
With many thousands of arrows, spears, and battle-axes;
with maces, pattisas, pikes, iron clubs, barbed darts, and javelins.
Then, O king of kings, with spears and axes they rushed with might toward Rāma,
like locusts toward a blazing fire. With their arrows, they struck down Rāma as if he were another Rāma.
Some struck him with axes, some with spears and battle-axes;
others approached with maces, and still others with javelins.
They suddenly assailed Rāma as he was quivering like a blazing fire.
Then the enraged wielder of the plow, having directly raised his plow,
quickly dragged them all [toward him] and crushed them with his mace.
Being slaughtered by Rāma, those Niṣādas who dwelt in the mountains fell upon the surface of the earth by the hundreds and by the thousands.
O Great King, having slain all those of great strength in an instant,
the immensely powerful Rāma stood there roaring like a lion.
Then at night, most terrible *piśācas* who feed on flesh drew away masses of meat and sat devouring them; they drank warm blood after tearing apart many corpses.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all the flesh-eating creatures quickly began devouring the corpse.
Laughing and making various terrible sounds that caused the earth to resound.
O King, the rākṣasas and flesh-eaters, drinking copious amounts of blood,
uttered benedictions over the corpse, those devourers of raw meat.
Then, O King, in that city, crows, vultures, eagles, hawks, and jackals— delighted by the battle— danced about, running here and there in a terrifying manner as they devoured [the corpses].
In the meantime, the heroic Niṣāda regained consciousness;
then, having observed that all the Niṣādas had been slain by the wielder of the plow (Balarāma).
Taking up his mace, the enraged leader of the Niṣādas went straight toward Rāma;
O King, he struck him on the collarbone with the mace.
Then, O King, the club-wielding Rāma,
Halāyudha, intoxicated with fierce pride, struck the powerful-armed Niṣāda with his mace.
And a tumultuous battle took place between the two of them with their clubs.
In the sky, during their battle, there was a great roar of sound,
like the noise of all the oceans coming together.
At the end of the eon, O Great King, that tumultuous sound arose;
the world of the nāgas was agitated, and the nāgas themselves fell into a state of great commotion.
Both the earth and the atmosphere appeared entirely filled with sound.
Then King Pauṇḍraka, skilled in battle, swiftly struck Sātyaki, the joy of the Vṛṣṇis, with his mace; O King,
the mighty Yuyudhāna likewise struck Vāsudeva.
And a tumultuous sound arose in that great battle between those two,
O King, as they fought with four others who were each seeking to slay one another;
the sound was most terrifying, O King, shaking the very shell of the universe.
Then dust appeared at the head of that battle;
the stars became lusterless as darkness thus reached its end.
When she awoke at dawn, the darkness vanished entirely;
the blessed sun rose, and the moon went to its setting.
Then, O King, when the sun had risen, a great battle broke out between those four mighty-armed warriors, resembling the conflict between the gods and the asuras.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then, at the clear dawn, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, [arose].
The Lord of the World desired to go from Badarikāśrama to the city.
Having paid homage to all the sages,
the Lord Viṣṇu, the master, mounted Garuḍa and went to Dvāravatī with great speed.
A very great sound was heard from them as they fought,
O King, while the God of gods was proceeding toward the city of Dvāravatī.
The Lord of the World reflected: "What indeed is this terrible sound that has arisen, born of battle and joined by the noble descendant of Śini?"
It is evident that Pauṇḍra has arrived at the city of Dvārakā;
a battle ensued with that evil-minded Pauṇḍraka.
This immense sound that has arisen from the Yadus and Vṛṣṇi heroes as they fight with one another is real; there is no need for hesitation here.
Having reflected thus, Hari himself blew his loud-sounding conch,
Pāñcajanya, gladdening the bulls among the Vṛṣṇis.
With that sound, Keśava filled the two worlds;
and the Yādavas and Vṛṣṇis, having heard that roar of the conch, [were moved].
"Clearly the Blessed One is approaching, for this is the sound of the Pāñcajanya," so thought those Vṛṣṇis and Yādavas, O King; and thus,
O monarch, the Vṛṣṇis and Yādavas became free from fear.
At that very moment, Tārkṣya, the best of birds, was seen;
and then the son of Devakī was seen by those lords of the Yādavas.
And the bards and panegyrists went before the Lord of the World to praise Hari, Viṣṇu, the Lotus-eyed One, with hymns of praise.
Then all the Yādavas surrounded Janārdana;
Kṛṣṇa, however, [said] to Garuḍa: "Go once more to the supreme Mount Meru."
Having spoken thus to Garuḍa and dismissed him, Viṣṇu, the bull among the Yadus, said this again to Dāruka: "O lord, bring my chariot."
Having promised "So be it," he quickly brought the chariot and said, "O Blessed One, O God, here is the chariot; what further task do you have for me?
Having spoken thus, he took the chariot, bowed before Hari, and stood at his side.
When Garuḍa had departed, Viṣṇu quickly mounted his chariot;
Keśava proceeded to the place where the battle was taking place.
Having gone there to the great arena, while the high-souled warriors were fighting,
that bull among the Yadus blew his great conch, Pāñcajanya.
Then Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva, seeing Kṛṣṇa eager for battle,
placed Sātyaki behind him and approached Vāsudeva.
Then, O King, the enraged Sātyaki checked Pauṇḍraka, saying:
"O King, you must not go from here; this is the eternal dharma."
"Having defeated me, O Indra among kings, go forth to fight another in this great battle;
for you are a Kṣatriya, O great hero, while I stand here eager for combat."
"I shall destroy all this pride of yours in battle," having said this, the Lord of the Yadavas stood before him as he was departing.
But the grandson of Śini, disregarding Pauṇḍraka even as he looked on, went instead to Keśava, the grandson of Śini.
Having rebuked him once more, Sātyaki, overwhelmed with rage,
suddenly struck Pauṇḍra with his mace while Vāsudeva looked on;
Sātyaki, whose valor is truth, fought according to his strength and as was appropriate.
Having seen this, the Blessed One then praised Sātyaki in this manner.
Having restrained Sātyaki, Kṛṣṇa said, "Let him do as he pleases. Thus forbidden by Kṛṣṇa, Sātyaki desisted according to what was appropriate.
Then King Pauṇḍraka said to Vāsudeva:
"O, O cowherd of the Yādavas, where have you gone now?"
"I am Vāsudeva, who has now arrived today specifically to see you."
"O Kṛṣṇa, having slain you along with your army and many followers,
once you have gone to the realm of Yama, O Keśava,
I alone shall become Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World."
O Govinda, that great and radiant discus of yours which is so renowned—
by this very discus of mine was he split asunder in battle.
"O Mādhava, whatever prowess you currently possess, thinking 'I have the discus,' I shall destroy it all while all the kṣatriyas look on."
"Know me as Śārṅgin; you are not called 'Śārṅgin.
I am the bearer of the conch, I am the bearer of the mace, and I am the bearer of the discus, O Janārdana.
Indeed, kings endowed with prowess should always address me thus."
In the beginning, you were an old cowherd who killed many women and children;
having now killed the cows, your great pride persists even today.
"I shall remove that for you, if you remain before me;
take up a weapon, O Govinda, if you are resolved to fight.
Having said this, he took up an arrow and stood at the side of the Lord of the World.
Having heard these words spoken by Vāsudeva,
Hari Kṛṣṇa smiled and addressed King Pauṇḍraka.
Speak your desire, O King, for I am indeed always a sinner, O King—
a slayer of cows, a slayer of children, and a killer of women in every way.
O King, always be the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the mace, and the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
O Lord, let my name Vāsudeva no longer be in vain.
"My being armed with the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the mace, and the conch—such things as these are useless to me.
However, I shall say something; listen, if you so desire."
"Those Kṣatriyas who are powerful while I, the Lord of the world, remain—
how is it that they speak thus to you, O Lord, even while I am still alive?"

That wheel of yours, which is most terrible, made entirely of great iron, and vast— its circular form is equal to my own wheel, but not its power. Furthermore, among all weapons, you possess a similarity to me only in sound.
O King, I am always a cowherd, forever the giver of life to living beings;
I am the protector in all worlds and the punisher of the wicked in every way.
"O King, the act of burning should always be performed after conquering one's enemies in battle;
why do you speak of it without having conquered them, while I stand here armed?"
"O Pauṇḍraka, O Indra among kings, kill me and speak [your challenge], if you are able;
for I stand here, equipped with a chariot, a bow, a mace, and a sword."
"Mount the chariot and prepare yourself for battle, O giver of honor!
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu let out a lion’s roar.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the powerful Vāsudeva, taking up an arrow, [acted].
He suddenly slew Pauṇḍra with a sharpened arrow.
Then Pauṇḍra Vāsudeva, with ten swift arrows,
quickly struck Vāsudeva, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi and the joy of the Vṛṣṇis.
The son of Vāsudeva struck Dāruka with twenty-five arrows, the horses with ten,
and the Yādava Vāsudeva with seventy.
Then Keśava, the slayer of Keśin and joy of the Yadus, laughed for a long time and, honoring him in his mind, thought, "He is indeed bold."
Drawing his Śārṅga bow and fixing it, the powerful Keśava, the crusher of enemies,
cut down the banner with an exceedingly sharp iron shaft.
And that bull among the Yadus, having severed the charioteer’s head from his body and having slain the four horses with four excellent arrows, [proceeded].
Having cut the chariot-thongs as well as both the outriders and the charioteer,
and having reduced the wheel to pieces like sesame seeds, he stood there smiling slightly.
But Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva, quickly leaping from his chariot and seizing a sharp sword, hurled it at Keśava.
Having cut that sword into a hundred pieces with ten arrows,
Keśava Hari stood there like a child, closing his eyes.
Then, taking up a sharp spear of terrible form,
he hurled it at the Vṛṣṇi hero and let out a lion’s roar.
And having reduced her to pieces as small as sesame seeds, that Keśava remained silent.
Then, having seized another most terrible iron club that resembled the Destroyer himself, the powerful Vāsudeva hurled it at Vāsudeva.
He hurled it at the Vṛṣṇi hero while all the kṣatriyas looked on;
the Lord of the worlds, the joy of the Yadus, split it in two.
Then, O great king, having taken up a most terrible wheel with a thousand spokes and great radiance, weighing thirty *bhāras* and made of iron, Keśava spoke these words.
"Behold this sharp and terrible discus, the destroyer of you!
O Govinda, best among the proud, by means of this I shall strip away your pride while all the kṣatriyas look on, O Vārṣṇeya!"
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, this most terrible and unassailable [weapon] has been aimed at you by me; if you are able, tear apart this great stronghold!"
Having said this,
the immensely powerful Pauṇḍraka, that best of kings and possessor of great heroism, whirled the discus a hundred times and then suddenly hurled it toward Hari while uttering a terrible roar.
Then, laughing, the Blessed One, Hari, seized that great and most terrible weapon as it came flying toward him and hurled it back with great force using that very same [weapon].
Seeing him approaching with great force, Pauṇḍraka, the best of kings and possessed of great strength, then leaped down from that place, abandoned it,
and let out a most terrible lion’s roar, O hero.
Then the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, was filled with wonder;
thinking, "Oh, what prowess! Oh, what fortitude! This Pauṇḍra’s strength is unbearable," the Lord of the World remained standing upon that excellent chariot.
Then, having taken up stones, he hurled them at Keśava;
the delighter of the Yādavas hurled those stones back at him.
After sporting with Pauṇḍra for a very long time, the Blessed Lord Hari then took up his sharp,
blood-drinking discus.
His limbs were smeared with the flesh of Daityas; he was the deliverer of women from the womb, resembling molten gold, formidable, and the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas.
The thousand-spoked, hundred-fathom, wondrous discus of Viṣṇu, which terrifies the Daityas and is eternally worshipped by the hosts of gods.
Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, the charioteer, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Hari who is ever-yoked and eternal—
by means of that [bow], Govinda slew Pauṇḍraka, the best of kings.
Then, having swiftly torn through his body, the flesh-eating discus returned once more to the hand of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of All. Thereupon, King Pauṇḍraka fell to the earth, deprived of life.
Having slain [the demons], the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign whose course is difficult to comprehend,
was honored by the Yādavas and entered the Sudharmā assembly hall.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Rāma, the best among the valiant, dispatched the Niṣāda with his spear.
He struck her at the pair of her breasts and let out a lion’s roar.
Then the world-renowned lord of the Niṣādas, enraged, struck the intoxicated and mighty Rāma on the chest between the breasts with his mace.
Struck swiftly by him, the exceedingly powerful Balabhadra,
that bull among the Vṛṣṇis, seized a most terrible mace with both hands and brought it down upon the Niṣāda.
Seeing that great, terrible, life-taking creature approaching,
the lord of the Niṣādas then fled toward the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters;
Rāma then pursued him as he ran toward the ocean, the home of makaras.
O King, while Ekalavya, the lord of the Niṣādas, was thus running away,
Rāma also ran after him wherever that Niṣāda leader had gone.
Having quickly entered the ocean and traveled five yojanas,
O King, Ekalavya, the chief of the Niṣādas, remained terrified; then,
O King, having entered a certain other island, he stood there like one who was senseless.
Then Rāma, the joy of the Yādavas, having conquered the lord of the Niṣādas,
entered that assembly hall rich with jewels and gems, he whose weapon is the plow.
Satyaki, inflamed with the passion for battle, entered that assembly hall,
O King, as did the other Yādavas, each arriving according to his rank.
When all the Vṛṣṇi heroes were seated on every side,
the blessed Keśava, the son of Devakī, having saluted all the elders as was appropriate, spoke these words at the proper time.
O best of the Yadus, Śaṅkara Nīlalohita was seen by me on the peak of Kailāsa; being pleased with me, he granted me a boon.
There, the gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism arrived;
having seen me and Śaṅkara, they approached, filled with joy and satisfaction.
O best of the Yādavas, I witnessed a most wonderful thing during the night:
two extremely terrible Piśācas were conversing about my own story.
The two of them went hunting, constantly thinking of me;
but upon seeing me, O Indra among kings, those two great-souled ascetics were filled with joy and, bowing low in devotion, then offered their salutations.
Then, seeing those two supreme heavens, I was entirely delighted;
having gratified Mahādeva, I departed from there at the end of the day.
Then all those Vṛṣṇis praised the God of gods;
in every way, those Vṛṣṇis had accomplished their purpose by taking refuge in Keśava.
All the Yādavas there then departed for their respective abodes.
Having entered the inner quarters, Hari, the Lord and Master of the World,
related to Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā exactly what had occurred.
When they were pleased and united with the joyful Keśava,
all this activity of Keśava has been narrated to you.
Having slain the wicked, the exceedingly powerful one ruled the entire earth;
[he subdued] Naraka of terrible deeds and Pauṇḍra, the best of kings.
The Lord of the Gods, worshipped by the best of sages, protected Hayagrīva, Niśumbha, as well as Sunda and Upasunda, and the brahmins and sages.
And Keśava gave wealth, cows, and jewels to the Brahmins,
while maintaining the *agnihotra* sacrifice and thoroughly satisfying the brahmins.
And by means of celibacy, Keśava always gratifies the sages; by sacrifice, the gods;
and by the offering of *svadhā*, all the ancestors.
While that lord of gods was ruling, the kingdom shone free from all thorns;
indeed, all the subjects lived in happiness, with the Brahmins at their head.
[Colophon] Janamejaya said: O best of the twice-born, [tell me] further concerning the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, I wish to hear his life-story in detail;
for there is no satiety for me here as I listen to the narrative concerning Kṛṣṇa."
Who indeed, upon hearing or even remembering the stories of Hari Viṣṇu, the god of gods and wielder of the discus, could ever reach satiety day and night?
This alone is the singular goal of human endeavor: the hearing of the stories of Hari.
How did the assembly of all beings between Haṃsa, the cause of the world, and Ḍibhaka come to be, always causing wonder?
How did the battle of the great-souled Dānava Vicakra come to pass?
We have heard this account of how he entered into friendship with those two.
Those two kings were endowed with heroism; they were disciples of the son of Bhṛgu, skilled in all weapons, heroic, and indeed said to have obtained boons from Hara.
"O Brahmin, you previously stated that there was a very great battle between those two kings and Keśava, the Lord of the World."
Whose two sons were they? What was their vigor and what was their prowess?
O best of the twice-born, O observer of noble vows, you ought to tell me all of this.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen, O mighty-armed King, to this story that destroys all sin,
concerning how the battle took place between those two and the wielder of the discus.
And how those two were born, and how that great conflict came to pass;
there were eighty-eight thousand high-souled Dānavas.
Moreover, O great king, the forces of the high-souled Dānava Vicakra in that battle were equipped with sharp spears.
Seeking an opening among the Yadus with a desire for battle,
Vicakra defeated the gods in the air during the great war between the gods and the asuras;
in that same manner, Keśava always exerted himself for the sake of Artha.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
O Indra among kings, there was among the Sālvas a king named Brahmadatta, the best of monarchs.
O King, that soul of all beings was known by the name Rājan, and he was devoted to compassion for all creatures.
Constantly devoted to the five sacrifices, having conquered his enemies and mastered his senses,
he was a knower of Brahman and a knower of the Vedas, always intent on sacrifice and auspicious.
O protector of the earth, O best of kings, he had two wives who were endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue, and were highly accomplished; yet they were childless.
With those two, the king rejoiced as Śakra with Śacī in the sky;
and he had a friend, the best of the twice-born, named Mitrasaha.
That king had a great yogi, a preeminent Brahmin who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
he was childless, just as the king himself was.
Accompanied by those two, that king worshipped Śaṅkara,
the trident-bearing Śarva, for ten years with undivided mind for the sake of a son;
that brahmin then performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrificial session for the sake of a son.

O Indra among kings, Śaṅkara Nīlalohita, being thus honored by him, revealed himself and spoke to the king in a dream: "I am pleased with you; may it be well with you. Choose a boon, O observer of noble vows."
Then the king spoke these words to the Lord of the World even as he slept:
"May I indeed have two sons. Having said, "So be it," Śambhu, whose banner is the bull, vanished; and the king was filled with joy.
That wise Mitrasaha also worshipped with devotion the imperishable god Keśava, the Lord of the World, who was then five years of age.
Honored by that brahmin, Janārdana, the God of gods,
Hari, granted him a single son who was his own equal.
Those two wives indeed conceived a fetus through the splendor of Śaṅkara;
O great king, the wife of the Brahmin received the splendor of Viṣṇu.
O protector of the earth, those two queens gave birth in due order to two sons of great heroism who were equal to Śaṅkara himself.
And for those two, O Great King, he performed all the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony according to the rules,
and he bestowed great wealth upon the Brahmins.
And that humble-minded brahmin begot a single son,
O King, who stood as the very Lord of the World incarnate in the form of his son.
He performed all the rites, beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman);
those two boys and he himself became three who were of equal age.
Having studied all the Vedas and likewise having heard the science of inquiry (anvīkṣikī),
they then became experts in the science of archery as well as in the use of missiles.
Haṃsa was the eldest son of the king, and Ḍibhaka was the next;
and he, O King, was the son of a Brahmin, known as Janārdana.
And all the young princes became friends with one another.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
The two high-minded ones, Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka, went forth to practice ascetic penance.
O best of kings, they both made their minds portions of Śaṅkara’s own self.
Having gone to the side of the Himalayas, they immediately performed austerities,
directed toward Śaṅkara, Śarva, the blue-throated Lord of Umā.
"Let us both possess the weapon of heroism (vīryāstra)," having thus resolved in their minds,
O King, they became single-minded and disciplined, subsisting only on air and water.
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, Śaṅkara!"—thus [he should call] day and night:
"Hara! Śarva! Śivānanda! Nīlagrīva! Umāpati!"
O Bull-bannered One, O Three-eyed One, O Tawny-eyed One, Lord of the worlds!
O Lover of your devotees, Lord of the Mountain, Sovereign, Vāmadeva, Śiva, Acyuta!
O Sadyojāta, Great God, God of gods, who dwells in the cave of the heart;
O Creator of beings, Lord of beings, you whose self is the *praṇava*, O Sadāśiva!
Constantly praising Śaṅkara Bhava with these and other names,
and keeping the Three-eyed Lord in their hearts, they performed penance with ease.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, established in a vow of silence,
O King, they then spent five years here with great vigor.
Then Śarva was pleased by those two and by their self-restraint;
Hara, clad in a tiger skin, revealed his own form—
Śaṅkara, the three-eyed Śarva, the wielder of the trident, the lord of Umā.
Seeing Śarva standing before them, adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
the two of them, their minds filled with joy, immediately offered their salutations.
The Blessed One said:
"O auspicious ones, choose a boon; let it be exactly as you desire."
Then they both said, "O King, O Blessed One, if you are pleased with us, [grant this]:
we two shall be invincible by the leaders of the hosts of gods and asuras, by rākṣasas, gandharvas, and dānavas, O Soul of All; this is our first boon."
The second was Virūpākṣa, who possessed a collection of fierce weapons,
including the Māheśvara, the Raudra, and the great Brahmaśiras weapon.
O Śarva, you have likewise always provided an impenetrable divine armor, an indestructible bow, and an axe, solely for the purpose of protection.
"O Mahādeva, two companions indeed accompany those who go into battle.
To this, Hara said to Bhṛṅgiriṭi, "So be it," O Lord of the Gods.
Kuṇḍodara and Virūpākṣa, who delight in the welfare of all living beings—
may you two, as lords of spirits, be my constant allies in battle.
"Let these two powerful ones go to the terrible battle.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Śarva vanished right there.
Then those two, Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka, endowed with heroism,
skilled in missiles, equipped with weapons, bearing bows, and exceedingly powerful, [set out].
Clad in armor, those two heroes were invincible even by the gods and dānavas;
they were utterly devoted to Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, who is blue-and-red in hue.
They constantly perform festivals for the God, beautified by the smearing of ashes;
they always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and have matted locks upon their necks;
all their limbs are adorned with rudrākṣa beads, and they are clothed in tiger skins.
"Salutation to Śiva, the peaceful, the wise Mahādeva"—
with such names as these, they constantly praised the auspicious God;
appearing like two great gods in person, the two wielders of the trident shone resplendent.
Then, having gone to their own abode, they grasped the feet of their father;
and at that time, being strong, they also grasped the feet of their father’s friend and their mother.
O King, after a long time, that righteous and highly intelligent Janārdana reached the further shore of learning through diligent effort.
And he, having conquered his senses and being eternally devoted to the reality of Brahman, worships Viṣṇu Hṛṣīkeśa, who is clothed in yellow silk.
Both Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka became householders,
and the righteous-souled Janārdana also indeed became a householder.
All of them were devoted to sacrifice and likewise dedicated to the five great sacrifices;
all were intent upon their own wives and devoted to the service of their gurus.
O King, they held that righteousness alone was the highest good.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
at one time, those two heroes went out on a hunt.
Together with Janārdana, they were accompanied by chariots, horses, and even elephants.
Having gone to the forest, O great king, those two heroes slew lions and tigers with sharp arrows,
as well as boars in every direction,
and other predatory beasts and deer, accompanied by their dogs, O monarch.
"Here comes a massive boar with long eyes;
cut him down with an arrow, for here goes the lord of beasts!
And here is another, a buffalo, with a serpent impaled upon his horn."
Indeed, these deer are running about in every direction with their fawns;
this great family of hares is wandering everywhere in fear.
This auspicious [object] must not be destroyed by the Śavanas along with their kinsmen;
all of this should be seized here after blocking it off from the packs of dogs.
"O King, best of monarchs, such a great clamor arose from the Kṣatriyas who were hunting and from the hunters as they ran about."
Having slain many deer, tigers, and lions, those two best of kings,
the heroes, became exhausted as the sun reached its midday course.
"Enough indeed with hunting for us; fatigue is arising," they said, O Great King, and they went to the Puṣkara lake.
Having approached the vicinity of a lake frequented by sages and perfected beings,
which possessed marshy banks fanned by gentle breezes, they rested there comfortably from their fatigue.
Then all those people, exhausted by fatigue, plunged into the lake and,
like those in distress, began to eat the lotus stalks, sprouts, and lotuses.
Together with Janārdana, Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka took refuge by a certain lake and remained there, casting off their fatigue.
Having plunged into that lake and drunk its sweet, cool water,
those two kings rested on the shore of the lake and sat there at ease.
O kings, those who did not hear the supreme Brahman proclaimed by the foremost of sages,
nor likewise the midday libation with its melodic chants, were all [excluded].
Then, having become joyful upon hearing the sound of the Vedas at that time, the two kings desired to behold the sacrifice performed by the sage.
Then, having stationed his entire army together with the deer,
and taking up his great bow and a few arrows, he departed.
Then the hero Janārdana, as well as Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka,
O great king, went on foot, it is said, to the hermitage.
Then, the great seer Kāśyapa was performing a sacrifice known as Vaiṣṇava,
together with sages devoted to the practice of recitation and burnt offerings.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: And Janārdana, the righteous-souled Haṃsa, and Ḍibhaka as well.
Having entered the sacrificial assembly, they then paid homage to the sages of the session.
When they had arrived, the high-souled sages, accompanied by their disciples,
diligently offered them water for the feet, seats, and other honors, performing a formal reception with great care.
Having accepted the hospitality, those two kings and that best of Brahmins,
being high-souled and delighted in spirit, sat down very comfortably, O King.
Then, O King, the swan spoke to those sages with restrained speech:
"O best of sages, our father indeed desired to perform a sacrifice with all its requirements.
O most excellent of munis, you must go there at the conclusion of the sacrificial session."
"O Brahmins, having performed a conquest of the quarters through the Rājasūya sacrifice,
we shall cause our righteous royal father to perform it. Let the best of Brahmins come there, together with their disciples and their retinues."
"Today itself, united, we shall surely conquer the quarters;
for we alone are capable of accomplishing this with our vast hosts of soldiers."
Neither gods nor dānavas are able to stand before us;
for we have diligently obtained this boon from the god whose abode is Kailāsa.
"Invincible against hosts of enemies and skilled in various weapons"—
having spoken thus, Haṃsa, filled with the pride of his strength, fell silent.
The sages said:
"O best of kings, if he were there, we would go;
otherwise, O King, we shall remain here. Thus indeed did those ascetics speak.
[Vaiśampāyana said: Then, O great king, with their minds resolved to go to those regions, [the two of them remained there].
On the northern shore of Puṣkara is where Durvāsas resides.
Having become ascetics,
those who devoted themselves to Brahman remained fixed upon the state of the *brahmasūtra*, intent on the illumination of its meaning.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, clothed only in a loincloth,
they [worship] that Self, the source of the world, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, the Auspicious One.
Śiva, who is of the nature of Brahman, peaceful, imperishable, and facing in all directions;
the unmanifest embodiment of the Vedānta, infinite, eternal, and auspicious.
Constantly disciplined, he meditated with his mind upon the god Virūpākṣa— the support of all beings, free from affliction, and facing in every direction— at all times.
Having constantly worshipped Durvāsas, their guru, whose sole essence was the Vedānta,
their minds were purified by the knowledge of the reality of the principles as determined through logic.
The two high-souled ones, Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa, disciples of the lord Durvāsas,
having gone there and seen those [ascetics] whose vital energy was drawn upward, [approached them].
While the highly intelligent Durvāsas was seeking the supreme state,
if that Durvāsas were to become angry, he would be capable of incinerating these worlds.
Even the gods are never able to look upon him when he is angry;
for he is the embodiment of wrath, the soul of the universe, who assumes every form.
Clad in a blood-red loincloth, he was a swan and indeed the Supreme Being himself.
O high-minded one, upon seeing him, this thought arose in those two: *HV_App.I,31.2290–2291*

Who indeed is this great being, clad in saffron robes and most excellent in knowledge of the colors? And what is this so-called stage of life (*āśrama*), having abandoned the householder's stage (*gṛhāśrama*)?
The householder alone is the soul of dharma; the householder is the best knower of dharma.
The householder is indeed the embodiment of dharma, and the householder is heaven itself.
The householder is always the mother of living beings and their constant source of life;
for he who exists without that [mother] in another form acts like a fool.
"He is mad, or he is deformed, or perhaps he is simply a fool;
or else he sits here as if constantly lost in thought, or even a deceiver."
"What are these people, possessing only ordinary knowledge, meditating as it were upon something?
We [must consider] these difficult-to-ascend stages that have been devised for other orders of life."
We shall forcibly establish all these dull-witted twice-born ones within our home— these fools who are intent on deluded knowledge,
seized by false attachments, childish, and of evil intellect.
Who among these is our teacher? We truly do not know in this matter.
Having established ourselves upon the path of Dharma, we shall both proceed toward final liberation.
Having reflected thus, O King, those two heroes, together with the Brahmin Janārdana,
[acted] out of delusion due to the exhaustion of their good fortune, O King.

O best of kings, having gone into the presence of that ascetic of rigid resolve, both kings spoke to Durvāsas, who had transcended the senses, as well as to the other self-restrained ascetics, being filled with anger.
[Colophon] Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka said:
"O twice-born one, you whose soul is devoid of even a fragment of knowledge, what is this resolve of yours?"
And what kind of hermitage is this, O Brahmin, which has been resorted to by you?
Having abandoned the life of a householder, what state have you attained?
I suspect you are clearly a hypocrite; I see no other reason for this.
O fool, you will always destroy these worlds while remaining at ease;
you will lead them all away and cast them into hell.
"O fool, having yourself perished, you strive to destroy others!
Alas, O dull-witted twice-born one, how can there be no teacher for you?"
In every way your teacher is free from sin; there is no doubt about this.
O Brahmin, having abandoned this hermitage, become a householder while remaining self-controlled.
"O Brahmin, always perform the five sacrifices and be diligent in them;
through that, you shall go to the highest heaven, for in heaven there is indeed great happiness. This is the path to the highest good, O Brahmin, if you have a desire to live."
Having heard what they had said, the righteous Brahmin Janārdana,
seeing the ascetic, spoke after bowing down like one who was very afraid.
"O dull-witted kings, do not speak such words;
such a terrible thing is unfit to be heard even by both worlds."
"Who, being dull-witted, would be able to speak [thus], even if he were to live with his kinsmen?
In every way, this is simply Time for you two of dull intellect;
the remainder of your lives has been exhausted, for you have both been struck down by the staff of Brahmā."
For these pure ascetics, whose minds are illumined by knowledge and whose karmas are burnt away by the fire of knowledge, offer their vital breaths into the vital breaths.
"Except for you two, who indeed would be capable of repeating such words?
In every way we have understood it: our lives here are now at an end."
O King, four stages of life were formerly ordained by the seers:
the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant.
Among them, this fourth stage of life, that of the mendicant, is considered the foremost;
in it dwells the one of great intelligence, for he is indeed remembered as the most meritorious.
Nor have you properly served the elders with humility;
therefore, you have not acquired knowledge from them—so who would speak in such a manner?
"O King, such a terrible thing as this should not have been heard by me, a living being.
O dull-witted one, what shall I do, since I am bound to you both by friendship, O kings?"
The knowledge that you have obtained from your teachers leads only to our sorrow in this matter;
for knowledge born of dharma should be applied according to one's purpose.
For by force, he indeed takes on the form of the ordainer of evil.
Either I shall depart leaving you both behind, or I shall fall upon a rocky surface;
or I shall drink terrible poison, or I shall throw myself into the great waves.
"O two kings, I shall here give up my very life while you all listen and watch!
Having said this, he lamented, constantly saying, "Do not speak thus!"
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Thereupon, Durvāsas became enraged, as if he would consume their very lives.
Then Durvāsas, with one eye that was always joined with fierce fire, [spoke].
Beholding those two evil-minded ones, his senses agitated by rage,
O King, he seemed at that time to reduce these worlds to ashes.
O King, looking at the Brahmin with a purely gentle eye, he spoke these words: "Perish! Perish! (HV App. I, 31.2356–2357).
"Go from here, O two kings; why do you delay? Do not tarry for long.
It is not possible for me to sustain the wrath born of your words."
Otherwise, I am capable of burning all you kings;
what rashness can anyone dare to speak before me?
The one renowned throughout the world, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, will remove your pride, O dull-witted ones! What more can I say now?
Then, having risen, the righteous lord of ascetics desired to depart;
thereupon, the swan strove to restrain that lord of ascetics.
Seizing his arm, Haṃsa, the best among the foremost of kings,
cruelly tore away his loincloth, O best of men, like Kṛtānta himself.
Other ascetics, losing their composure, fled in the ten directions.
Saying "Alas, what a tragedy!", the brahmin Janārdana, out of friendship,
restrained him to the best of his ability, saying, "What is this rash act?"
Then Durvāsas, though capable of slaying him even while he was devoted to truth and righteousness,
spoke these words very softly to Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka.
"Though I am capable of slaying these lowest of royal families by means of a curse, I shall not do so; for we are here ascetics."
For that god who is the Lord of the World, Keśava, the Sovereign of the Yādavas,
bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands, shall remove your pride.
While that best of the Yadus, the lord of the world, protects that realm,
it is my conviction that the life of both of you will be well-lived in every respect.
Jarāsaṃdha is also your kinsman, yet he does not wish to speak such words,
for he always remains on the path of dharma, which is loathed by the world.
To this extent he was your kinsman; he shall not be so hereafter.
Let there indeed be enmity between you two and that Magadhan lord of the earth.
If that kinsman, having heard this which is of such terrible form, should endure it, there would be a destruction of his merit; of this there is no need for deliberation.
Having said this, Durvāsas, the best of ascetics, spoke thus to Janārdana: "Go, go! he said repeatedly to the swan. Then he addressed Janārdana with these words.
May there be well-being for you, O chief of brahmins; may you have devotion to Janārdana.
May you have communion with Him who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Today, tomorrow, or the day after, may you always remain virtuous.
For there is no destruction of a virtuous person in either of the two worlds;
go and tell everything to your father, having learned the entire account exactly as it happened.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then those two, Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka, incited by Time, became enraged.
A carrying-net, a water-pot, and likewise a vessel made of split bamboo or wood.
Having cut and split apart all the staffs and various vessels in that region, O Great King, the hunters burned the flesh there; then,
having devoured it, the two of them departed from that place for their own city.
And the righteous Janārdana followed after the two of them out of affection;
thinking, "These two are lost," he was then exceedingly distressed.
When they had all departed, Durvāsas, the best of ascetics,
said this to all those lords of ascetics who were intent on fleeing:
Having departed from this land of Puṣkara, which is endowed with merit,
he proceeded very slowly, breathing deeply and resting here and there.
Having entered Dvārakā and seen the Lord who bears the conch, discus, and mace,
we, the best of ascetics, shall speak to that Sovereign.

For he, the primordial Viṣṇu, the teacher of the world, self-controlled and beloved by those who know reality, remained established on the path of dharma while protecting this universe; having uprooted all thorns, he ruled this earth.
May that Lord protect us all from all the most terrible sins committed by evildoers, we who are self-restrained in our knowledge;
O Brahmins, this is appropriate for today— let the departure be prepared now.
O best of men, whatever rash act was committed by those two, such as the breaking of the vessel and so forth—
all of this we shall show to Janārdana in its entirety.
"So be it," having thus promised, those ascetics possessed of the eye of knowledge took up the severed [limbs] from them, as well as the wooden carrying-frame.
Taking with them a split bamboo staff, a tattered cloth, a loincloth,
and bark garments, as well as a water-pot with a half-attached skull-cup, O King,
they set out to see Keśava.
And placing five thousand [attendants] before the great sage Durvāsas, who was born of austerity and was the self-born son of the Lord.
In a single day and night, all those high-souled ones— tamed, hairy, and devoid of hair— went to Dvārakā, which was protected by Kṛṣṇa.
Having entered the pond at dawn, O Indra among kings,
those lords of ascetics then bathed and sipped water, becoming pure through great effort.
Intent on seeing Viṣṇu, who was devoted to the extraction of the thorn [of the earth],
they assumed a single form and arrived at the gate of Sudharmā.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, whose eyes are like the filaments of a lotus—
Dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, glorious, with his robes and ornaments hanging down.
The diadem-wearer, the Lord of Śrī, Kṛṣṇa, with dark and curly hair;
the unmanifest, eternal God, both with parts and without parts, the auspicious one.
O King, Hari once went to a place for sporting and recreation together with other youths headed by Sātyaki.
In the midst of the Sudharmā hall, Keśava Kṛṣṇa, the best of the Yādavas and the doer of what is pleasing, engaged in a game of ball with Yuyudhāna.
"This ball is mine first;
yours shall come after," said Viṣṇu, the lotus-eyed one, to Sātyaki at that time.
O King, the Yādavas standing at his side, led by Vasudeva and headed by Uddhava, sat down somewhere there.
Free from all other activity, the soul of beings, the creator of beings,
wandered about, O King, just as Rāma did in former times with Sugrīva.
At midday, the infallible Mahāviṣṇu Kṛṣṇa, together with the descendant of Śini and the Yādavas, having sported for a very long time, came to rest.
Having been previously barred by the doorkeeper and remaining right at the entrance,
they entered that assembly hall, O King, thinking, "Now is the opportunity."
Placing the ascetic Durvāsas, whose wealth was his austerity, at their head, the self-controlled sages of long-standing penance, with joyful minds, beheld the Lord of the Yādavas.
Engaged in playing with a ball,
the Lord of the World held the ball in his hand and flicked it away with his big toe.
Hari gazed at Sātyaki with eyes as broad as lotus petals;
with one eye he gladdened him, while with the other he looked upon his eyeball.
And, O great king, ascetics were seen before that city;
as well as the Vṛṣṇis, the lotus-eyed one (Kṛṣṇa), Sātyaki, Balabhadra,
Vasudeva, Akrūra, and King Ugrasena.
And all the other Yādavas fell into a state of agitation; with their minds thus intensely preoccupied, they cried out, "What is this? What is this?"
Following even from behind, desiring to consume the three worlds,
[he saw] a certain twice-born man wearing only half a loincloth, who was reciting [the Vedas].
The ascetic was possessed by inner anguish, his staff broken;
blazing intensely with rage, he had incurred sin through his own actions.
The best of the Yādavas, filled with fear, beheld the lord of the Yādavas looking upon Durvāsas, who was like a great fire arising from his eyes.
"What will our lord do when he is angry, or what will he say to us?"—thinking thus, all the Yādavas approached him with palms joined in reverence;
and the Vṛṣṇis said something like this: "Here is a seat."
Then Hṛṣīkeśa Kṛṣṇa, leaping up slightly before him, said:
"This is your seat; please remain here at ease."
"O Brahmin, I am staying here; what shall I do? he said.
Then, sitting somewhat upon his seat, he whose form was like that of an ascetic—*yativigrahaḥ*—[remained there].
When that seat was prepared, the ascetics, free from envy and truly at peace,
took their places upon the seats according to their rank.
Kṛṣṇa, the wearer of the diadem, performed the customary rites of hospitality, beginning with the offering of water for the feet.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa spoke again to the lord Durvāsas, the ascetic:
"Tell me, O chief of brahmins, for what purpose have you all returned here?"
Or have you seen something, or do you have some great reason for this?
O best of the twice-born, you are renunciants free from all taint.
O best of the twice-born, you have always been free from desire toward us;
for there is nothing indeed to be desired, since you possess no longing whatsoever.
