Those of firm vows, whose actions are impelled by desire, go among the Kṣatriyas;
O Brahmin, nothing [of this] is seen by us even while being closely examined.
O Brahmin, I do not know the reason for your arrival;
yet, by this much, it can be inferred that there must be some cause. Therefore, tell us if one exists, for we shall learn it from you.
When Janārdana, the wielder of the discus and lord of the gods, had spoken thus,
O King, that brahmin’s great anger flared up once more;
his fury became even greater than before.
As if wishing to burn the three worlds and as if devouring those who were looking on, Durvāsas—
his eyes red with rage, furious, laughing as it were, and burning as it were—
spoke these words to Viṣṇu, overwhelmed by anger.
"Why do you say, 'I do not know,' O Lord of the Yadavas?
I know you, O God; you speak as if deceiving me.
We are ancient ones, O Viṣṇu, who know the events of former times."
For thus you are the God of gods, possessing a body that is illusory and human;
why then, O Lord of the world, do you conceal [your true nature] from us?
You are the very embodiment of those who know Brahman; this is that supreme state which is the unmanifest Supreme Brahman, and which we previously knew as the Knower.
That from which this entire world has come into being— that is this supreme state—
which they perceive as the gross reality through their minds according to its true nature.
O Lord of the Universe, those who know the past say that this is your supreme form,
which is attained through action, and by remembering which we have found peace.
O God, O Hari, even that form which humans do not perceive directly— we who are of dull intellect are certainly not like them.
"Why do you say 'I do not know'? Why such a reckless statement?
For those who truly understand the root, for them the discernment of the leaves is effortless."
O God, O slayer of Keśin, what is the fruit for one who performs [this]?
This splendor of yours, celebrated in the Vedānta, is now clearly perceived.
And that very form of the Lord which yogis, free from stain and satisfied with pure consciousness, behold within the lotus of the heart— this indeed is it.
O Lord, I recognize this very form of yours as the divine sovereignty which is celebrated in the Vedas as the splendor that is distinguished as Brahman.
"Vaiṣṇava is the supreme splendor," so it is recited in the Vedas;
O Viṣṇu, I understand that this very form of yours is that.
O Lord Viṣṇu, you are indeed that which is called the syllable *oṃ* and that whose speech is celebrated as the Veda; do not say that you do not know this.
If there were anything behind your back that you were being urged to say,
O Govinda, do not speak the rash words, "I did not know," O Hari.
From whom the universe emerged and into whom it is dissolved at the time of its end—
that divine splendor of yours, O Keśava, I recognize as this very one.
O Lord of the past and the future, you appear as the creator always within my heart;
whatever form I constantly remember, that very same one you are in my heart.
"Vāyu is indeed always Viṣṇu"—this is the conviction held in my mind. Therefore, O All-pervading Lord, you exist in that very form within the center of my heart.
Sometimes the mind is fixed on the thought that "Viṣṇu is space";
then, O All-pervading Lord, you abide right there within the center of the heart in that very form.
Sometimes the thought arises that you are Viṣṇu, the Earth;
at such times, you always appear to me in the form of the earthly king.
"O Lord, this is indeed the essence (rasa)," thus I sometimes think;
then, O Viṣṇu, O All-pervading One, you abide within the center of my heart as the very self of that essence.
O Supreme Person, when you shall be remembered by me as "Tejas" alone, and when you, endowed with that form, shall always appear within my heart; HV_App.I,31.2527–2528.
"Then, O Lord Keśava, beholding with my own eyes that lunar form as the Moon-god Hari, I was filled with joy."
O Lord of the World, when I am mindful that "this is the solar body," then,
through the application of that contemplation, you shine forth as the Sun himself.
Therefore, you alone are everything; such is my firm conviction.
Hence, O Janārdana, I am not able to say, "I do not know."
O Viṣṇu, established in this purpose, you do not even consider our suffering.
O Viṣṇu, we are exceedingly distressed, for we are entirely dependent upon you.
"O Keśava, you will not remember this state of ours; I think only that our good fortune has been lost. O Viṣṇu, we are of little merit, since you, O Lord, do not remember us."

"O Janārdana, two heirs of the Kṣatriyas named Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka, who pride themselves on being the best of mountain-dwellers, are harassing us. O Keśava, they constantly proclaim that the life of a householder is indeed the highest good."

holding the excellent conch with his hand and bearing the discus;
his limbs were adorned with refined gold.
He wore jewels illuminated by shimmering radiance.
I beheld him, together with the ancient Yadus and the immortals, as they duly discerned that which is to be known.
Its splendor was beautified by blossoming blue lotuses, and its interior shone with golden lotuses in full bloom.
I saw him at the head of the Yadus,
being attended by the foremost of the hosts of sages,
and being praised by masters, bards, and panegyrists.
Her lower lip was like a sprout, red as coral with a smile.
I beheld him, who is to be known through the ancient seers, having discerned him according to rule along with the immortals;
he whose splendor was graced by the beauty of full-blown blue lotuses.
Its interior was resplendent with full-blown golden lotuses.
Again I beheld the unborn Teacher of the World, propitiating the Yādavas with his words and performing the rites according to rule together with the lords of sages.
The ancient ones [established] the expanded injunctions for the meaning of the Vedas.
Again and again I beheld,
I beheld the Lord Hari, the sole benefactor of all the worlds,
dwelling here for the welfare of this universe.
Having overcome those enemies who pervade the world.
Furthermore, at the time of recreation, I saw him again sporting repeatedly with the lords of the Yādavas—
the praiseworthy one who delights the lords while he himself sports.
The best of the Yadus, the lord and chief of the Yādavas.
Once again, I beheld the lotus-eyed Hari,
the omnipresent Lord, reclining upon the ocean together with that daughter of Bhīṣma.
Hari, who is dear to his devotees and the refuge of those who are devoted.
"I saw, I saw him, being perfectly at ease,
drinking in his form again and again with my eyes alone, even as their lids were closed."
"At that time, I thought to myself: 'I alone am fortunate.'"
I beheld the Lord, the All-pervading One, the source of the existence and manifestation of all beings— the primordial, preeminent, vast, and radiant one— bearing a pair of lotuses.
Remembering him again and again, he became completely at peace.
I beheld Hari, the Lord of the worlds, adorned with the Kaustubha gem upon his chest,
and Kṛṣṇa, who was constantly being fanned by hundreds of chowries.
"Where are those two, or what are they doing—those who always remember Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Yādavas, with hearts filled with hatred? HV App I, 31.2930–2931.
"Where shall I see those two dull-witted ones, or where will they go before me?"—
as the Lord of Gods was thus reflecting, [the sound] was then heard from his hand.
I saw him laughing, speaking these words to Nārada, to Durvāsas, and to the Lord of Ascetics: "Give me a hand; this is my only request."
Seeing the god Hari again and again, causing the lords of sages to utter speech consisting of the words of the Brahma-sūtra, I reflected repeatedly.
"O best of kings, this which has been undertaken by those two is impossible to accomplish;
O protector of the earth, from this point forward, this task must not be undertaken."
O Haṃsa, that conversation regarding your taking my hand has ceased;
for this Sātyaki shall indeed tell you everything in its entirety.
Having heard these words, the swan, enraged, spoke these words:
"O base descendant of a Brahmin, what kind of speech is this from you,
to speak thus in our presence as we desire to conquer the three worlds?"
"By means of his illusory power (māyā), this Kṛṣṇa, who knows how to perform divine play, causes you to wander;
seeing him, this great delusion arises within you."
Adorned with the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and forest garland;
infused with the heroism of the Vṛṣṇis; and possessing uplifted glory.
It was proclaimed by bards and panegyrists, revealing the arms of heroes; it was a mass of most wonderful glory, where the circles of the world shone resplendently.
"The assembly of the Vṛṣṇis and Yādavas has been overcome by the power of the Four-Armed One;
oh, this was surely a delusion today, arising from the sight of that wielder of the discus!"
And now that great-souled Keśava is indeed making you whirl about, O dull-witted brahmin; for that was merely a feat of sorcery.
"O Brahmin, this very fickleness has arisen within you;
oh, how truly similar your behavior is to mine!"
"O Brahmin, I shall endure these words spoken by you here out of our friendship, O best of the twice-born; otherwise, who could endure this?"
Go now from here as you please, O dull-witted Brahmin!
Go, go wherever you wish; the earth is yours.
"Having conquered the heir of Gopāla and slain many Yādavas, this is our primary plan: 'We shall defeat the Yādavas. Go, O Brahmin; I do not wish to see you speaking such harsh words."
Having always eaten together with me while intent on praising the enemy faction,
I must not commit the slaughter of a Brahmin, even in the most dire calamity.
Having spoken thus to the brahmin, the swan spoke again to Sātyaki: "O descendant of the Yādavas, for what purpose have you come here? What did the son of Nanda say, or what command did he give me?"
Sātyaki said:
O Haṃsa, these are the words of Him who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace;
[he spoke them] as he gradually struck with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow, whetted on stone and tipped with sharp edges.
"I shall give you my entire hand,
or else with a sharp sword I will cut off your head, O Haṃsa, as a collection for the payment of tribute."
O dull-witted one, what is this audacity of yours, O lowest of kings?
That king who desires tribute from the God of gods, the Lord of the World—this is his summary punishment: the cutting off of his tongue, O lowest of men.
Having heard the words of Śārṅgarava and again those of Śaṅkha and Hari,
who indeed, desiring life, would now remain standing? O you who are proud of the boons granted by the Lord of the Mountains, you have spoken words that are utterly unworthy.
"We ourselves are these companions, led by Balabhadra;
he is the first, Balabhadra, the second is I, and that one is Sātyaki."
Kṛtavarman was the third, while the powerful Niśaṭha was the fourth;
then Babhru was the fifth, and Utkala is remembered as the sixth.
The seventh was the wise Sāraṇa, skilled in missiles and weapons;
the eighth was Sāraṅga, and the ninth was Vipṛthu;
and the tenth was the wise Uddhava—these are we, endowed with great strength.
These stand before that protector, the god of gods who wields the conch, discus, and mace, remaining there day and night throughout battles.
For those two heroes who are his sons, equal to him in their own strength—
endowed as they are with the pride of power— they alone are capable of slaying you both in battle.
That Lord of the Mountain remains on the mountain itself after having granted a boon;
for you two stand alone in battle, having taken up your bow and arrows,
prepared to wage war against your enemies.
When such servants as these are fighting with the enemies while he protects the three worlds, who would go to him seeking tribute?
"He will slay you both in battle with a single sharp arrow released from the Śārṅga bow— him who today protects the three worlds."
"Where shall our battle take place? the Lord of the World asked again:
"In Puṣkara, which is eternally merit-bestowing, or on Mount Govardhana?"
"May they display their powers to me in Mathurā or Prayāga—
those two gods who bear the conch and the discus and are intent upon the protection of the world."
Who would wish to perform the great sacrifice of the Rājasūya himself? Or what mortal, speaking with well-being, could travel happily without you?
"This is stupidity, this is folly; these are most extraordinary words!
If you desire this, O fool, you shall become an object of laughter on the face of the earth.
Having spoken thus, the hero Sātyaki stood as if laughing, O Lord.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Thereupon, O great king, Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka became enraged.
With eyes agitated by rage, they spoke these words.
Desiring to consume all the quarters and beholding all the best of kings,
they squeezed hand in hand while remembering those great words.
"Where indeed is the son of Nanda, or where is Rāma, so fierce in his strength?"—
thus they spoke reproachfully to Sātyaki, who was true to his vow.
"O heir of the Yādavas, why do you stand before us?
Depart from here, O dull-witted one; for now you are but a messenger."
Otherwise, you would surely deserve to be slain for uttering such harsh words;
you are truly shameless, since you speak such speech.
We two are kings who have restrained ourselves to rule over this entire world.
Who indeed in the world of mortals does not live as a tax-payer?
"Having slain Gopālaka in battle and captured many Yādavas, we shall seize their entire wealth from their hands; go hence, O lowest of men!"
"Being an inviolable messenger, you speak much that is nonsensical.
For he is the lord who can grant us boons, and indeed the master of all weapons."
"O you two great beings, protect us as we go to battle;
having slain the cowherds in the fray, we shall cause our father to perform a sacrifice."
All of these have been declared to be utterly cowardly in battle.
Having slain them along with their forces in combat, we shall once again conquer Keśava.
The great army must be prepared, always with bows grasped, spears and maces held, and armor donned.
It was crowded with thousands of mounted chariots and filled with maces and iron clubs;
it possessed abundant fuel and was strewn with plenty of fodder.
Endowed with abundant strength, accompanied by their wives and equipped with javelins; provided with umbrellas and banners, together with soldiers and excellent attendants.
"Let a formidable army be arrayed with commanders on all sides;
go forth as one truly invincible, for you have no fear of death."
"O King, our battle shall take place at Puṣkara tomorrow or perhaps the day after;
then we shall come to know the prowess of Keśava and Bala,
as well as the strength of those kings whom you mentioned for the conflict."
Sātyaki said:
"O kings, I shall go to slay you either tomorrow or the day after;
for today you must be slain by me, unless I become your messenger."
For neither tomorrow nor the day after will you two speak harshly;
indeed, the office of a messenger is always entirely painful for men.
"Otherwise, O lowest of kings, having slain you both, I shall attain peace;
meanwhile, display your own prowess and the pride of your arms."
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, bearing the Śārṅga bow and a diadem,
rich with dark, curly hair, long-armed, and endowed with splendor.
He is the source of all worlds, possessing universal form and beautiful appearance;
he is the slayer of Daityas and Dānavas, the ancient one to be meditated upon by yogis.
With a face like the filaments of a lotus, dark-complexioned, and possessing true valor,
he is the sole creator of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds, the Lord of the triple universe.
"With a sharpened arrow in battle, he shall strip away your pride," having said this, Sātyaki indeed mounted his chariot and set forth.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Having entered the city of Viṣṇu, Sātyaki, that bull among the Śinis, [proceeded].
Then he related to Kṛṣṇa exactly what had occurred between those two at that time.
Then, at the clear dawn, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin,
intent upon performing auspicious rites, spoke thus to the commanders of the forces:
Let the entire army, consisting of chariots, elephants, and horses, gird themselves for battle— an army crowded with many kettledrums and cymbals, and filled with spears, swords, and iron clubs.
"Provided with banners, flags, ornaments, and equipment"—
having assented with "So be it," all those army commanders did exactly that.
Taking up their very firm bows and mounting their chariots, clad in armor,
those best of men went far ahead of the army.

Wearing a forest garland, armed with a plow, clad in blue garments, and possessing a white radiance, O King, Rāma shone at the head of the army and marched forth with a splendor equal to that of Indra.
And likewise, O King, Sātyaki, having grasped his bow and filled with rage,
shone forth as he went at the head of the host, possessed of great strength.
And other heroic Yādavas, having grasped their great weapons,
uttered lion-like roars and proceeded with exceeding excellence.
Hari, however, having mounted the chariot which had been equipped by Dāruka,
took up the formidable Śārṅga bow, capable of bearing great weight, along with an arrow.
Then Janārdana, bearing the discus, conch, mace, trident, arrows, and sword,
had bound on his leathern finger-guards and wore yellow garments.
With a chest adorned by a garland of lotuses and dark, curly hair upon his head,
he proceeded in his chariot, praised with joy by the brahmins.
Being praised here and there by bards and sons of Magadha,
he led his entire army and then proceeded toward the northern direction.
Placing the Pāñcajanya conch to his mouth, Keśava blew it with all his might,
producing a great sound that increased the fear of his enemies.
Inflated by that monkey, O King, that king of conchs produced a sound;
from that conch, the roar filled both heaven and earth.
When that conch was thus blown, thousands of conchs resounded;
and kettledrums were struck, O King, as well as many clay drums. They roared exceedingly and beyond measure, like clouds at the end of the summer heat.
Then, O great king, those best of monarchs went to Puṣkara, which increases merit;
they went to that lake Puṣkara, O Indra among kings.
Having waited for Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka,
all the Yādavas, having arrived for battle,
O King, each established their own camp as they pleased, taking up their respective huts and tents.
The Blessed Govinda, too, having seen that most beautiful lake,
touched its waters and paid homage to those foremost among ascetics.
Desiring their arrival,
Viṣṇu sat at his ease upon the bank, listening on all sides to the sound of the Vedas recited by the Brāhmaṇas.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then those two, Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka, went toward Puṣkara.
O King, they held their great bows aloft, together with their chariots and banners.
With the great elements preceding them, as if violently withdrawing [the world],
they made a loud noise while enveloped in ashes.
With the three horizontal marks upon their foreheads and adorned with rudrākṣa beads,
those two were like two other Rudras, the agents of the destruction of the world.
Then, O best of kings, hundreds of armies followed them;
indeed, ten akṣauhiṇīs were assembled for those two.
But Vicakra, O great king, was a Dānava resembling a mountain;
he had previously been a friend to those two powerful ones,
before whom even Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, was not able to stand.
For that great hero, O Great King, in the encounter between the gods and the Daityas,
while slaying the gods in battle, then conquered the Lord of the Gods;
and in former times, he waged war against the powerful Viṣṇu.
O Great King, he who had previously harassed the leaders of the Yadus upon reaching Dvāravatī,
having now heard that war was at hand, has arrived there.
Surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of Dānavas armed with iron clubs, O best of kings, that Daitya became intent on providing assistance to Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka out of hatred for the Vṛṣṇis.
Then Hiḍimba, the lord of the Rākṣasas, became an exceedingly close friend to the Daitya Vicakra; he would even give up his own life for him in battle.
Together with other *rākṣasas* who held rocks, spears, and swords in their hands,
the man-eater Hiḍimba went for the sake of his assistance.
O great king, eighty-eight thousand Rākṣasas followed him,
carrying rocks and iron clubs in their hands.
As those two marched toward Keśava, their great army was joined on all sides by hosts of Daityas and Rākṣasas;
it was most wonderful, exceedingly fierce, and a source of terror to the three worlds.
Accompanied by that Daitya,
those two— Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka— went toward Puṣkara in order to kill Keśava directly.
Then, having heard that there was to be a conflict with the leaders of the Yadus, King Jarāsaṃdha did not provide assistance, thinking, "A curse will surely fall upon me."
O King, as the swan and Dambhaka proceeded toward their encounter,
they went with exceedingly swift strides to Puṣkara, O monarch.
Uttering lion-like roars and speaking to one another, they said:
"I alone shall fight with Hari first! 31.3125–3126.
Thus spoke the kings, O monarch, as they proceeded toward Keśava;
those best of men arrived at Puṣkara, the increaser of merit.
O King, the first Puṣkara is frequented by sages and inhabited by seers advanced in asceticism; it is exceedingly auspicious among all the worlds.
O Lord of the World, O King, both Puṣkara and Puṇḍarīkākṣa sever all sins through mere sight and touch.
O best of kings, Puṣkara and Puṇḍarīkākṣa—
these two alone were being served by the foremost sages and the high-souled hosts of gods.
For there are only two, O best of men, who are capable of destroying the flood of sin;
wherever those two are together, there your kings have taken their stand.
They beheld Hari, Viṣṇu, the supreme Viṣṭaraśravas,
at Puṣkara— the abode of merit, a sacred ford frequented by Brahman-sages.
O best of kings, offer them salutation with your mind;
O ruler of the earth, your sin has been entirely destroyed, of this there is no doubt.
And there the army arrived, teeming with Daityas and Rākṣasas;
it was filled with the clamor of many kettledrums, small drums, *jharjharīs*, and *ḍiṇḍimas*;
it resounded with *paṇavas* mingled with cymbals and was tumultuous with the roars of the Rākṣasas.
Having reached the shore of the Puṣkara lake, O lord of the people,
he showed him the god stationed there for battle.
[Colophon] O King, two armies met together, equipped with banners and their full accoutrements,
crowded with great iron bars and bristling with maces and spears.
Amidst the resonance of kettledrums and jharjharas, crowded with the sound of ḍiṇḍimas,
and while they grasped great weapons— spears, excellent swords,
and bows— the two, emboldened by one another, engaged in a supreme battle.
Released from their bows, O great king, those arrows pierced the bodies of the embodied beings and traveled far away by the thousands.
O King, the swords released from the arms of the warriors, having pierced through their chests and burst asunder,
then struck their heads and fell away.
Then, impelled by the arms of the kings,
the matchless iron clubs reduced the bodies of the royal demons to pieces as small as sesame seeds,
while the Daityas raised a roar, each desiring to slay the other.

O Indra among kings, the Daityas, Rākṣasas, and kings from all sides struck one another with iron clubs and great arrows released from bows; other mighty warriors struck each other fiercely with sharp shafts resembling the bodies of serpents.
O King, Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and others possessing the prowess of rutting elephants,
struck one another with great arrows released from their bows.
O Great King, the elephants were surrounded on all sides by elephants, and the horses by horses.
Chariots struck down chariots, and horsemen likewise struck down horsemen,
with volleys of swords, scimitars, and arrows, as well as with spears, shafts, and bolts.
In that battle, they struck one another with javelins, iron clubs, darts,
and battle-axes, as well as with most terrible slings.
O King, Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and Kṣatriyas from all sides ran hither and thither, uttering discordant cries; some, being slain by great swords, O Great King, fell upon the earth.
O great king, some of those most heroic warriors had their brains churned out by maces,
while others had their necks broken by iron clubs used as weapons.
Some went to the realm of Yama, while others ascended to heaven;
beholding their own bodies, they were joined by Apsarases.
Some, having slain both their own kin and those of others, became as if bewildered.
In the meantime, O King, thousands of conchs and kettledrums,
as well as many clay drums, resounded everywhere throughout the army;
while the sun had reached its zenith, they emitted a most terrible heat.
Then the hideous and formidable Piśācas with sunken bellies,
and the most terrible Rākṣasas, joyfully devoured flesh and hair-grass, drinking copious amounts of blood.
Heaps of corpses were gathered— headless trunks with swords in hand— who,
seeking the dead, had divided the battlefield into many sections.
Then hawks, cranes, herons, vultures, and others likewise,
having torn out corpses with their beaks, devoured them here and there.
O best of kings, eighty-seven thousand nāgas were slain;
thirty thousand and ten thousand (ayuta) of the finest horses were killed.
A hundred thousand chariots, O great king, were destroyed along with their warriors; thirty koṭis of horsemen, fully armed, were also violently slain there.
When the sun had reached the meridian, some who were slain emerged;
others, O King, being struck down, entered the Puṣkara lake.
Some, seizing the ground in fear, cried out thus in the battle;
some, with disheveled hair, fell down having abandoned their chariot.
Some, with their lips bitten together, were slain before their masters.
O best of kings, there was a most wonderful great battle at Puṣkara-tīrtha,
just like the battle between the gods and the asuras that occurred in former times.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
In the meantime, O King, single combats took place.
The wielder of the Śārṅga bow and the mace engaged Vicakra in battle.
Then Balabhadra fought with Haṃsa, Sātyaki with Ḍibhaka,
Hiḍimba the man-eater with Vāsudeva and Ugrasena,
and the remaining warriors, O king of kings, engaged in battle with their respective counterparts, undaunted in spirit.
Vāsudeva struck the Daitya on the chest with seventy-three arrows whose tips were sharpened and keen-edged, displaying his prowess in the battle.
Drawing his excellent bow back to his ear with a firm, sharpened arrow, the Dānava struck the Lord, the Sovereign of the Gods,
in the middle of his chest while the Lord of Śacī looked on.
Then, pierced in the region of the chest by him, Janārdana,
Viṣṇu, bled forth blood just as in the beginning of time the creatures [shed their blood].
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, filled with rage, struck down the standard with a razor-edged arrow;
having slain the four horses and the charioteer with three shafts,
he then blew his excellent conch, as he had done in the battle at Tārāmaya.
Suddenly leaping from his chariot, the Dānava, overwhelmed with rage,
seized a most terrible mace that was difficult to withstand and endowed with great prowess.
With that [mace], the lord of the Daityas struck Keśava on the crown of his head and again on the forehead; then Viṣṇu let out a lion’s roar.
Then, it is said, the Danuja seized a massive rock,
whirled it a hundred times, and struck it against Keshava’s chest.
Seeing it rushing toward him, Keśava seized it with his hand and struck the Daitya; hit by it, he fell to the ground as if his life-breath had departed, though he still lay there gasping.

Then, having regained consciousness, the Daitya blazed up with twice the intensity of his anger; seizing a terrible iron club, he spoke these words to Janārdana: [The Daitya said: "O you who are devoid of shame, O you who are cruel, O you who have abandoned dharma! You have struck me, who am innocent and unprovoked, while I was engaged in battle with another. Since you have struck me thus, you shall not escape from me alive today. Vāsudeva replied: "O wicked one, you are indeed speaking the truth. I have struck you because you were engaged with another. But now, having been struck by me, you shall not escape from me alive. Having spoken thus, the Lord of the world seized a mace made of gold and iron, adorned with a hundred bells, and decorated with a garland of flowers. With that mace, which was like a great meteor, he struck the Daitya on the chest. Struck by the mace, the Daitya fell to the ground, vomiting blood from his mouth. Then, regaining consciousness, the Daitya blazed up with twice the intensity of his anger; seizing a terrible iron club, he spoke these words to Janārdana.
"O Govinda, I shall destroy this pride that has arisen in you;
for you have always been a witness to my prowess in the battle between the gods and the asuras."
Those very same broad arms and that same person I am, O Janārdana;
nevertheless, O hero, you fight even while knowing my strength.
"O mighty-armed one, ward off this iron club hurled from his arm!
Having spoken thus to the Lord of the gods, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
the Daitya hurled [the weapon] at the Lord of the worlds while all the worlds looked on.
Seizing him by the arm and saying, "You are wicked!", Hari Kṛṣṇa caused him to be cut into pieces with a sharpened sword.
Uprooting a tree with a hundred branches and great top-knots, the lord of the Daityas struck the all-pervading Viṣṭaraśravas with it;
and seizing him as well with his sword, he cut him into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
After sporting for a very long time with that Daitya, Mādhava Kṛṣṇa then desired to kill the Daitya; taking up a sharp arrow and joining it with the Āgneya weapon, he struck him with it.
Having consumed the Daitya while all the world looked on,
that arrow quickly returned once more to the hand of the Blessed One, just as it was before.
Then the surviving Daityas fled in the ten directions;
even today they do not return, for they are indeed proceeding toward the great ocean.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
But the righteous-souled Baladeva, quickly taking up his bow, [set forth].
The best among wielders of arrows struck the swan with ten shafts;
the swan, in turn, pierced him back with five swift iron arrows.
In the meantime, the plow-wielder (Balarāma), having cut them with ten iron arrows,
swiftly pierced the swan on the forehead with a single iron shaft with great force.
Falling with great force, that iron arrow regained its consciousness;
having remained for a long time on the seat of the chariot, it took up the form of a pillar-eared bolt (sthūṇākarṇa).
Having regained consciousness after being struck by that best of the Yadus,
the swan roared like a lion in battle, causing the gods to marvel.
Then the plow-wielder Mādhava, pierced by that arrow, became enraged;
vomiting blood profusely, he sighed heavily upon the field of battle.
With his limbs suffused with red, he appeared as if moistened with saffron.
Clad in blue garments, the Yādava Halāyudha struck the heroic Haṃsa, who possessed the gait of a swan, with seven thousand iron arrows.
Those released, sharp, and terrible iron arrows with fine feathers,
O King, fell everywhere upon the chariot, the banner, the bow, the wheel, and the two quivers; they caused great pain and distress, O Monarch.
Then, O great king, the enraged Haṃsa, endowed with heroism and strength,
pierced the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) with an arrow and cut down his banner with another;
with four arrows, he struck down the horses and delivered the charioteer to the Lord of the Dead.
Then, enraged in that great battle, the mighty-armed wielder of the plow seized his mace and pounced upon Haṃsa, hissing like Śeṣa.
With that [mace], Halāyudha shattered the banner, the chariot, the wheel, the pole,
and the charioteer into pieces as small as sesame seeds, and he roared again and again.
Furthermore, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) indeed hurled a mace at Haṃsa;
that Haṃsa, seizing the mace, leaped down from that chariot.
Then those two, the swan and the boar— mighty chariot-warriors with great arms, whose splendor was renowned throughout the world— fought in that great battle.
Exceedingly wonderful and highly courageous, each desiring to slay the other,
they had exerted themselves in the great battle and moved with the stride of lions.
Just as in ancient times during the war between the gods and the asuras in the sky, Śakra and Vṛtra,
both with all their limbs drenched in blood in that great battle,
were utterly exhausted by each other’s strength in the fray.
Then, O king of kings, Balabhadra took hold of the right path,
while Haṃsa, true to his promise, took hold of the left.
Those two of elephant-like prowess struck each other with their maces in battle;
with all their might, the mighty-armed ones fought indeed for the sake of death.
They engaged in an exceedingly great battle, comparable to the war between the gods and the asuras,
upon the vast stage while the inhabitants of the triple heaven looked on.
Both the gods and the sages were filled with wonder:
"Aha! Indeed, such a battle as this has never been seen nor heard of before."
Thus spoke the gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras out of wonder;
filled with mutual enthusiasm, they waged a marvelous battle.
Then the swan, the most excellent of the right-footed, moved exceedingly well on the right side of the great arena; but the powerful and strong one moved on the left.
First bending their knees,
those two best among those skilled in combat fiercely struck each other with maces in that battle, while the inhabitants of the three heavens looked on.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Dhibhaka and Sātyaki fought an exceedingly fierce battle.
Both of them were indeed powerful heroes, renowned among the Kṣatriyas.
The two heroes, who had exerted themselves in great battles and were ever devoted to their elders—
Satyaki and the valiant Dhibhaka of true prowess—
pierced one another in the middle of the chest and on the breast with ten sharpened arrows.
Pierced by that powerful one, the best of Kṣatriyas, Ḍibhaka,
who was proud in battle, struck back with five thousand iron arrows.
Having checked them in their midst, the hero of the Vṛṣṇis roared in battle.
Then the enraged and excellent king, having pierced him with seven swift arrows,
struck Sātyaki again with a hundred thousand.
Then the valiant Yādava Sātyaki, with a sharp crescent-headed arrow, severed that bow of Dhibhaka.
Then, O King, taking up another bow, Ḍibhaka, the crusher of enemies,
struck Yuyudhāna, the best among warriors.
Then the valiant one [struck] with a fierce razor-edged arrow washed in oil.
Pierced by that arrow and vomiting blood, O King,
he shone exceedingly, O monarch, like a *kiṃśuka* tree in springtime.
But he cut asunder once more that great bow which had been taken up again.
Then, taking up another bow, Ḍibhaka struck the Lord of the Yādavas with sharp arrows while all the kṣatriyas looked on.
In that battle, Sātyaki again cut through the exceedingly fierce bow of the evil-minded Ḍibhaka with a sharp-pointed arrow.
Then, quickly taking up another bow, that best of kings,
O Indra among monarchs, pierced Sātyaki once again with that bow.
Having thus severed one hundred and ten bows, O Indra among kings,
the descendant of Śini let out a roar while all the kṣatriyas looked on.
Casting aside their bows, the two heroes, Ḍibhaka and Sātyaki,
took up extremely fierce swords and stood ready for battle.
For those two heroes, Dhiṃbhaka and Sātyaki, were the best among those skilled in the sword;
and likewise, O great king, were the son of Duḥśāsana and the son of Somadatta.
And the valiant Abhimanyu, and likewise Nakula—
these are proclaimed as the best among those skilled in the sword, the most excellent in battle.
For these two best of men, O king, were indeed preeminent among swordsmen;
eager for battle, those two engaged in combat with their swords.
Whirling, leaping upward, whirled around, cast forth, and darting out from his arms;
it was a source of destruction, a dispersal, a shattering—beyond all bounds and superhuman.
Contracted, expanded, with the left knee raised or lowered;
placed, variegated, cast down, gathered, hanging, and held.
With his left arm extended, then his right, and then his upper arm;
with three arms, tall arms, and arms raised and elevated on the left.
"Attacking from behind and likewise the celebrated 'warrior's strike'—
thus did those two swordsmen perform thirty-two modes of combat."
And as they continued to strike each other,
O Great King, those two, standing upon their lotuses and resolved for battle, did not experience any fatigue.
Then, O great king, the gods along with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis praised those two who had exerted themselves for victory:
"Oh, what prowess! Oh, what prowess! Of these two who possess such strength!"
These two alone are capable in battle, having reached the further shore of mastery in both sword and bow:
one is a disciple of Giriśa, and the other is indeed that of the wise Droṇa.
Arjuna, Sātyaki, and Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World—
these three, O great king, are always renowned in battle.
Ḍibhaka, Śaktibhṛt, and Charva—these three are great car-warriors;
all of them are renowned for their heroism and their strength.
Thus those gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and Mahoragas,
stationed in heaven, spoke in unison, longing to behold the battle.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Vasudeva and Ugrasena were both aged and weary of battles.
With all their limbs worn out by old age, their bodies and necks turned grey.
Endowed with both spiritual knowledge and worldly discernment, and skilled in the ways of the royal road,
they fought in that great arena against the evil-minded Rākṣasa.
In that battle, they afflicted the evil-minded man-eating Rākṣasa lord Hiḍimba with many thousands of arrows.
But Hiḍimba, the lord of the Rākṣasas, devouring men on all sides—
exceedingly powerful, evil-minded, with long arms and a large jaw— [remained there].
He had a protruding belly, deformed eyes, and tawny hair and eyes;
he had a nose like a hawk, was most fierce, with hair standing erect and mighty arms.
With limbs shaped like mountains, long fangs, and a face like a hare,
he had a protruding belly and long teeth, and was ever intent on devouring the world.
With a lofty face, a broad chest, and a long neck like that of an elephant,
he devoured heaps of flesh and drank pools of blood.
O best of kings, striking elephants with elephants, horses with horses,
having struck chariots with chariots, and likewise horsemen with horsemen;
Seeing men before him, he did not swallow them whole;
O Great King, having slain some of the Vṛṣṇi protectors on all sides, he devoured others.
The man-eating Hiḍimba suddenly devoured them;
assuming his hideous form, the Rākṣasa slew whichever he saw before him.
Devouring other Vṛṣṇi foot-soldiers, Hiḍimba, the lord of the Rākṣasas and man-eater,
suddenly hurled some of them away.
O King, at the time of their end, that Rākṣasa devoured all those living beings in a single moment, like the enraged Rudra.
Some of the heroic Vṛṣṇis, overcome with fear, fled in all directions;
others among those bulls of the Vṛṣṇi clan were devoured by that Rākṣasa.
O King, just as Kumbhakarṇa devoured the monkeys,
that man-eater likewise left the Vṛṣṇi army entirely without remainder.
The Vṛṣṇi army stood motionless, like figures in a painted canvas.
In the meantime, the two enraged elders, the best among the Yādavas,
took up a most formidable bow and stood before the Rākṣasa.
Like two rams most enraged at an angry lion,
those two Rākṣasas, having gaped their great mouths wide, saw him and then rushed toward him.
Then the Rākṣasa Virūpākṣa, resembling the depths of Pātāla and desiring to devour him, ran about, saying, "Eat! Eat the body!"
O King, those two heroes, the bulls of the Yadu clan,
filled with arrows the most terrible mouth of Hiḍimba, which was like that of Death with its jaws wide agape.
The enemy of the gods, assuming a hideous form, devoured them all;
then that terrifying Rākṣasa rushed forward with his mouth wide open.
Seizing their two bows,
the evil-minded Rākṣasa of deformed countenance quickly broke them in battle, stretching out his arms.
The foremost of the Rākṣasas strove to seize Vasudeva, the protector of the earth and king who honors the elderly, within the assembly of monarchs.
Hiḍimba said:
"O Vasudeva, O lowest of kings, I shall devour you both!
O Ugrasena, O wretch, why do you stand before me?"
"Come, enter my mouth;
you two have been created by fate as my food, O Vasudeva, father of Hari, grown old in age."
Hungry, afflicted by fatigue, and with your prowess quickened for battle,
do not enter through my mouth with such haste.
"Having drunk your blood, I shall attain satisfaction and be at peace;
and I shall eat your flesh as well, for the happiness of you two who have grown old."
Speaking thus, the enraged Hiḍimba, lord of the Rākṣasas, with his mouth wide open and large jaws,
then rushed forward swiftly.
O King, Vasudeva and Ugrasena, seeing [the danger] on all sides, became terrified;
those two bulls of the Vṛṣṇis, being unarmed, fled in all directions.
In the meantime, the powerful Balabhadra,
having seen Vasudeva and Ugrasena in such a state, looked upon them.
Having instructed Vāsudeva regarding the Lord Haṃsa who was fighting,
he emerged through the opening of that evil-minded Rākṣasa.
"O Rākṣasa, do not act rashly; release these two best of kings! I stand here, O Rākṣasa, desiring to slay my enemies—let us fight!"
"I myself shall slay you; what is this intimidation of yours?
Having spoken thus to the wielder of the plow, he released those two in the great battle.
"This one is large and well-fed; I shall devour him first!
Having torn open his mouth as before, he rushed toward Balabhadra.
Casting aside his bow and arrow, the powerful one stood before the Rākṣasa,
clenching his fist and flexing his mighty upper arm.
Then the evil-minded Hiḍimba, having clenched his fist and let out a great roar,
struck Rāma’s chest like Death with gaping jaws.
Then the enraged Balabhadra, struck by that fist,
the blameless Rāma struck the lord of the rākṣasas with his own fist.
A fist-fight took place between the hero among men and the hero among *rākṣasas*,
as those two lions among men and *rākṣasas* fought upon the fields of battle.
And a terrifying, crackling sound arose from the two of them.
Then, in the battle, the king of the Rākṣasas struck Rāma on the chest with his fist,
just as Purandara strikes with his thunderbolt.
Then the powerful Rāma, having diligently clenched his fist,
struck Hiḍimba— the enemy of the immortals— on the chest.
Then Rāma struck that Rākṣasa in the face with his two palms.
Struck by the blow of his palm, Hiḍimba, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
fell to the ground on his knees like a Rākṣasa whose life had departed.
Then Rāma, springing up and seizing the rākṣasa with both arms,
took him up and whirled him around from foot to foot by the force of his own arms.
Having whirled him around for a very long time, demonstrating his own strength,
Rāma lifted up that lord of the rākṣasas while all the world looked on.
Then Halāyudha hurled him a distance of one *gavyūti* from that place;
the Rākṣasa, as if lifeless, departed from that spot.
Whatever Rākṣasas remained there after the slaughter in that great battle,
they fled in the ten directions, terrified of Balabhadra.
Then the Blessed One, the sun-like Bhāskara, having withdrawn his splendors, the thousand-rayed one,
went to his setting, as did the sight of all living beings.
And he entered even slightly into the state of being most subtle.
When Prajāpati, the teacher of the world whose face is the universe, had entered the waters of the ocean,
the Lord of the Stars (the Moon) arrived.
Even the twilight darkness vanished, O best of kings.
At the time of dawn on Mount Govardhana, which resounded with the songs of *kiṃnaras*, those best of kings spoke thus in the battle.
Thus did those best of kings speak then.
O King, they ceased there that festival of battle.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Both Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka, during that very night, [reached] the great mountain.
Then, O King, they both went together to Govardhana, O monarch.
Then, when the dawn had become clear and the sun had risen,
Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, went quickly to Govardhana.
Śaineya, Balabhadra, and the Yādavas, Sāraṇa and the others, [were there];
the mountain resounded in many ways with the songs of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Then, O King, they both went together to Mount Govardhana;
the mountain resounded in many ways with the cattle-herds and the armies.
Having reached his northern flank, O best of kings,
the Yādavas drew near the Yamunā, O monarch, and then the battle commenced with Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka on one side and the Yādavas on all sides.
Ugrasena pierced Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka with seventy-three straight-knotted arrows, Vasudeva with seven,
Sāraṇa with twenty-five, and Kaṅka with ten.
O King, Niśaṭha struck him with thirty arrows, Sātyaki with seven,
Vipṛthu with eighty, and Uddhava with ten shafts.
O King, Pradyumna struck with thirty arrows, and Sāmba also with seven;
Anādhṛṣṭi, however, struck with sixty-one straight-knotted shafts.
Thus, O King, united together, all those Yādavas waged a battle that was most wonderful and exceedingly terrible, like those who are undaunted.
They waged a great battle against all those most powerful Yādavas, O Great King, while Vāsudeva looked on.
Both Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka pierced those kings in return;
having struck each one with ten well-aimed arrows,
they struck the lords of the Yādavas excessively with sharp shafts.
O King, all of them were distressed, vomiting much blood;
they appeared like *kiṃśuka* trees in bloom during the month of Mādhava.
And the Yādavas, O King, being terrified, were intent on flight;
in that interval, O King, the two sons of Vasudeva appeared, O monarch.
Vāsudeva and Halin, those two archers,
engaged in incomparable combat at the front of the battle, like Skanda and Śakra in the sky.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and great ṛṣis,
standing in their celestial chariots, beheld the battle which was like that between the gods and the Asuras.
Then those two beings appeared, sent by the wielder of the trident (Śiva) for the sake of protecting them in battle; they were indeed powerful.
Then the two lords, Haṃsa and Vāsudeva, engaged in battle,
as did Rāma and Ḍibhaka, both joined together in their desire for combat.
All of these were indeed valiant in weapons, missiles, and strength;
O King, standing each upon his own chariot, they all blew their conchs separately.
Then Kṛṣṇa Hṛṣīkeśa, whose eyes are like lotus petals, blew his great-sounding conch Pāñcajanya, as if to cause everyone to be struck with wonder.
Then, O great king, two most terrible spirits with pot-bellied bodies took up their spears and rushed toward Keśava;
they struck the Lord of the Yādavas with their spears, O king.
Struck by those two in the presence of the gods and gandharvas, the god Viṣṇu,
his lower lip slightly smiling, the lord of the world and best among the foremost of charioteers, quickly leaped up from his chariot and seized them both.
Having whirled it around a hundred times like a firebrand, Keśava,
the Hari, then hurled it toward Kailāsa.
Having reached the peak of Mount Kailāsa, O high-minded one,
they beheld that deed of the god and were filled with supreme wonder.
And Haṃsa, seeing that deed, his eyes copper-red with rage,
spoke these words to Viṣṇu while the inhabitants of heaven looked on.

"For what purpose, O Keśava, do you create an obstacle for the Rājasūya? King Brahmadatta is the performer of that great sacrifice. Pay tribute as is appropriate, if you desire to preserve your life."
"If you will wait for a moment, then, having understood the great task at hand, O son of Nanda, you shall give [the wealth]; then that sacrificer shall be my guru."
"I am always the lord of kings, like the wielder of the trident among the gods;
thus shall I destroy your power and majesty in battle."
Having spoken thus, O King, he drew his bow— adorned with arrows and resembling a *sāla* creeper—
as far as his strength allowed, and discharged a steel shaft at Keśava;
it struck him on the forehead and appeared like a crest-mark.
Kṛṣṇa said to Sātyaki, "O lord, drive my chariot";
having thus addressed Dāruka, who was holding the reins, Keśava, the Lord, spoke.
Then, commanded by him, Sātyaki, driving the chariot,
swiftly displayed many circular maneuvers in the battle.
Then, having been deeply pierced by that arrow, the Lord Hari, the Sovereign,
fixed the *āgneya* weapon upon a certain shaft;
O King of kings, he spoke to Haṃsa while dispatching Sātyaki toward the horses.
With this I shall burn you today; if you are able, then ward it off!
Enough of your much fighting, O ever-deceitful Kṣatriya!
If you desire a tribute from me, show your prowess today;
O swan, the ascetics dwelling in Puṣkara have been harassed by you.
"You are indeed the teacher of the Brahmins, O lowest of men, while I remain—
while I, the Lord of the World, remain after having struck down the thorns of the Kṣatriyas."
Furthermore, I am the punisher in this world of the wicked who hate the Veda;
O lowest of men, you have already been slain long ago by the curse of the foremost among ascetics.
"Having offered you today to Death, I shall protect the brahmins," saying this,
Keśava released that weapon in battle;
then the Haṃsa also neutralized that weapon with a Vāruṇa weapon.
Then Govinda released the Vāyavya weapon at Haṃsaka in battle;
O best of kings, he warded off that weapon with the Māhendra weapon.
Then, in the battle, Kṛṣṇa released the extremely fierce Māheśvara weapon;
at that very moment, Haṃsa warded it off with the Raudra weapon.
Then Keśava [employed] the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca;
then the Brahmāstra, as well as the Kaubera, the Āsura, and the Yāmya.
Having severed these, the swan quickly released them in battle for the sake of warding off those four weapons of Mādhava.
Then Keśava, overcome with rage, released the terrible weapon named Brahmaśiras, which destroys enemies, aiming it at Haṃsa.
He then directed that [missile] of most terrible prowess against the swan.
Then, seeing that most terrible weapon, the best of kings became afraid;
O Indra among kings, Haṃsa also warded off that arrow with it.

Having touched the waters of the Yamunā, Janārdana, the God of gods, Hari— the soul of all beings and the creator of the creator of beings— took up the Vaiṣṇava weapon and fixed it upon a well-sharpened arrow.
He employed that weapon, by which the gods had slain the Asuras and obtained sovereignty in ancient times,
for the purpose of slaying that king.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then, O best of kings, having seen that most terrible weapon, he was struck with fear.
King Haṃsa, O Great King, appeared as if motionless.
Leaping down from that chariot, he rushed toward the Yamunā,
where Kṛṣṇa Hṛṣīkeśa was subduing the powerful Kāliya.
And he crushed that most terrible [being] as far as the very foundations of the netherworld;
meanwhile, there appeared a vast, great dark-blue form, resembling black collyrium.
Then that swan fell into that most terrible lake. As the swan was falling, a great roar arose,
like the sound of mountains being cast down into the ocean by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Leaping from his chariot, Kṛṣṇa also fell upon him;
the God of gods, the Lord of the world, as if to cause the world to marvel,
Keśava then struck that mighty-armed one with his two feet.
Then, O best of kings, having received a kick from him, the swan died;
so indeed some say, O most excellent of monarchs.
Others say that he went to Pātāla and was devoured by serpents;
O Indra among kings, we have heard that even today he has not been seen at all.
Just as before, the Lord of the World approached the chariot.
When he had been slain, O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and your own forefather, performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
If that Haṃsa should live, who indeed would dare to challenge him in battle?
For he is a master of all weapons, O Lord, and has eternally received boons from Rudra.
In an instant, O Great King, this news spread throughout the land:
"The swan is slain! The swan is slain by Kṛṣṇa, the crusher of enemies!"
In the world of the gods, the lords of the Gandharvas sang day and night:
"By Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World, by Viṣṇu the Almighty—
by Kṛṣṇa [was this done] in the terrible pool of the Yamunā," thus they sang day and night.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that his exceedingly fierce brother, who was endowed with great heroism, had been slain...
Leaving Baladeva while he was fighting in the great battle.
The young boy, endowed with great vigor, followed along the Yamunā;
Balabhadra, whose weapon is the plow, pursued him with speed.
O great king, wherever the swan had fallen, there he himself plunged in,
having churned up the mass of waters in the Yamunā.
Then, O King, Ḍibhaka became exceedingly enraged; having churned the water violently,
he repeatedly emerged and submerged himself again and again,
yet he could not see his valiant brother.
Then, O King, having emerged and beheld Vāsudeva, the mighty-armed Dībhaka,
the most heroic of men, spoke these words:
"O scion of cowherds, where is that one who stands as a swan?"
"O King, ask Yamunā as well," said the righteous-souled Vāsudeva;
thus spoke the powerful Vāsudeva with a serene mind.
Having heard that, Dhibhaka— indeed, being devoted to his brother— entered the Yamunā once more and gazed upon his brother in many ways.
Then King Dribhaka, his mind bewildered, lamented:
"O Indra among kings, where indeed are you going, leaving me alone and without kin?"
"O brother, why would you go from here, abandoning me right here?"
Having lamented thus, O best of kings, Dhibhaka, who was devoted to his brother,
set his mind on self-surrender in the great pool of the Yamunā.
Diving in and emerging suddenly, having resolved upon death,
he pulled his tongue with his hand and lamented again and again.
Then, O King, having himself uprooted the tongue along with its roots,
that perpetrator of violence, Ḍibhaka, died within the water, destined indeed for hell.
When the lowest of men had departed and both Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka were slain,
the lotus-eyed one arrived, as if causing all beings to marvel.
Then, O great king, the powerful Vāsudeva, pleased and serene in soul,
having rested on Govardhana with Balabhadra as his companion,
dwelt there for some time in that place where he had previously stayed.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Yaśodā and Nanda the cowherd were both longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard that Vāsudeva, along with his elder brother, had gone to Govardhana.
Fresh butter, curd, milk-rice, and likewise rice mixed with sesame;
forest-grown flowers, O great king, and even the peacock's crest-ornament.
Together with other cowherds and gopīs on all sides,
O King, they both went quickly and joyfully to Govardhana.
In one place they beheld the long-armed Vāsudeva together with his elder brother, both dark-complexioned and with eyes like those of a black antelope, perched upon a tree.
Seeing him there, the two of great strength bowed down with great joy;
they presented the Lord with milk-rice and large quantities of food.
Upon seeing Nandagopa and Yaśodā, Hari was filled with joy;
then the powerful Vāsudeva spoke these words first to Nandagopa and the cowherds, and afterwards to his mother Yaśodā.
"Father, Mother, is all well in Vraja, in the cow-pen, and with our own cattle?
O father, are the cows full of milk, and are the calves and yearlings healthy?"
Or perhaps there is very pure milk, and the cows are very beautiful;
or perhaps, O mother, there are young calves, and O father, it is daytime.
"Are there many ropes, or even many stakes,
or various kinds of grasses always present here, O father?"
"O father, are there surely fragrant carts?
And have the cowherd women who possess sons given birth to boys?"
"O Mother, are there many jars here in the cow-pen that are all identical?
O Father, do the cows flow with incomparable milk day after day?"
What has produced the fresh butter from the previous night (*haiyaṅgavīna*), milk, or curd?
This entire wealth of cattle attains a state free from disease.
Nanda said:
"O best of the Yadus, O Lord, all this is free from disease;
O Keśava, the herds of cattle are likewise well in every respect at all times."
O Lord of Gods, because of your protection, we are always well-being;
O Keśava, together with our cattle and calves, we are indeed free from disease.
There will always be only sorrow, for we shall not see you again, O Keśava;
this thought that "this is pure suffering" is constantly held by my mind.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To him who was lamenting in this manner, Keśava said, "Go. He then spoke again to his mother: "Mother, go back toward the house."
And those who shall proclaim your praises shall attain heaven;
whoever bows down to you is always dearer to me.
"May my devotees always remain; go," Hari said to her.
Having spoken thus to his parents, the eternal Lord Vāsudeva departed.
Having embraced them both firmly, Keśava, filled with affection, sent them forth.
And having heard those words from Kṛṣṇa with devotion, [he spoke].
Yaśodā and Nandagopa indeed went to their own home.
Then Kṛṣṇa Hṛṣīkeśa, Viṣṇu, together with the Yādavas and Vṛṣṇis,
desired to go to the city of Dvāravatī.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or even read it with a concentrated mind,
shall possess sons and wealth, and in the end, attain liberation.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then Mahāviṣṇu, traveling along, reached Puṣkara together with the Yādavas.
But they did not see the chief sages who were staying at Puṣkara, O best of kings.
Having approached Mahādeva and performed the customary rites of hospitality, such as offering the *arghya*, those sages, free from envy,
addressed Viṣṇu— the Lord of All, the Master of the past, the future, and the present— as the foremost of the Yādavas.
O Viṣṇu, O Janārdana, this heroic power of yours is most wonderful,
by which Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka were both slain in battle.
O God, he who was wheel-less, invincible, and difficult even for the gods to withstand, has been slain in battle; it is our conviction that he was impossible to overcome.
May there be safety for us in all our undertakings as we practice supreme austerity;
O Lord of the World, by your grace, we perform this highest penance.
"O Hara, by remembering you we shall become free from all stain;
for you are the remover of all suffering for those who always meditate upon you."
O Lord, constant remembrance of you bestows merit upon every living being;
for you, O Hari, are our eternal sustainer and ordainer of ascetic power.
You are the syllable *oṃ*, you are the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*; you are the sacrifice, you are the Grandfather (Brahmā).
You are the light, the embodiment of Brahman; you are Brahmā and indeed Rudra as well.
"You are called the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the inner self (*antarātman*) of all beings;
O Lord of the World, you are to be worshipped by all beings with sacrifices and gifts."
Obeisance to the creator of the universe, O God; obeisance to you whose form is the universe. Protect this world, O God, by always slaying those who hate the Brahman.
Saying "So be it," Hari Viṣṇu went to the city of Dvāravatī;
he dwelt there together with the Vṛṣṇis, being praised by the Māgadhas.
This activity of the God of gods has indeed been told to you, O King Janamejaya, as you requested; what more do you wish to hear?

From that time forward, O Lord, that goddess fell under the delusion of passion;
remembering the words of the goddess and recollecting her husband at that time.
Finding no sleep at night nor food by day,
that princess, remembering her husband's state, lamented.
Censuring the moon in the sky and not resorting to sandalwood paste—
that young woman, O King, was deluded and tormented by desire.
Happy men attend upon her, though she is feverish even when free from fever;
her heart burns, even though it has been anointed with sandalwood.
Pallor on her cheeks was a sign, as were eyes filled with water;
likewise, yawning and sleep increased within her body.
Her friends repeatedly cast cool lotus-root powders upon her heart, which was tormented by the fire of love.
They fanned her and asked again and again:
"What is your distress? What is wrong with your body? What is this with you, O beautiful lady?"
"O goddess of beautiful countenance, tell me what pleases you;
O delightful one, why has this arisen which is so difficult to endure?"
"O lady with beautiful brows, these sarika birds speak words that follow your mind; indeed, these deep-blue parrots recite like men."
Why do you not speak today those words that produce joy?
Your father is a great hero, unconquerable even by the gods.
O woman of excellent complexion, no one at all stands before him on this earth;
for Bāṇa, the son of Bali, is a great hero who is difficult to overcome.
Having conquered the city called Śoṇita, which is like Amarāvatī,
where the god Maheśvara dwells with trident in hand.
"Know that this is my son," so said Hara to Bāṇa; O Uṣā, listen as Mahādeva spoke thus regarding your father.
"What is this pain? she asked, and her face shone with the tip of her nose;
dewdrops gleamed upon her lotus-like face like those that appear at the arrival of autumn.
Your face, resembling the full moon, has become lusterless like the moon behind thick clouds; tell me, what is the reason for this? Why do you not shine? (HV App. I, 32.29–30)
"You are sighing, O young girl, yet you find no delight in your heart;
accept this divine food, whatever it is that dwells in your mind."
"Tobacco was pleasing to you before; why is it not taken now? O Goddess, take these sweet things which are difficult for other people to obtain; arise and tell me of the pain born in your body."
Having heard this clamor arising from the palace, Uṣā heard it recounted there by her maidservants, each speaking separately in the presence of her mother.
O Queen, when the princess returned to the palace as a virtuous woman,
she appeared as if mute, having ceased her pastimes of sporting in the water.
Therefore, O Queen, we people, the servants, speak to you:
What is this delusion? What is this silence? What is this sleep, and how has this pallor come about?
O Queen, let physicians be consulted and directed toward the alleviation of this affliction.
O Goddess of lovely countenance, how does that body, so exceedingly delicate and resembling a *śirīṣa* flower, endure the burden of disease?
Having heard this, the goddess Uṣā, whose gait was like that of a swan, then quickly reached the place where [the body] lay and asked, "What is this thing of such miserable appearance?"
Then that noble lady, having touched his tender hand with her sprout-like hand,
effortlessly snapped his fingers.
"O auspicious lady, what is it? What affliction do you have?
These physicians have assembled and are indeed asking you about that."
The physicians said:
"The princess went there for water-sports with her circle of female companions;
we know that Pārvatī’s play there was born of exhaustion."
From exhaustion, lassitude has arisen, as well as frequent yawning;
sleep is born from that, so you should not be afraid.
The Goddess said:
"O physicians, you have applied sandalwood mixed with snow to my heart.
O ministers, what is this? Why does it so quickly form these bubbles?"
Excessive burning, profuse perspiration, thirst, and a lack of appetite for food—tell me with certainty according to the scriptures: what indeed is this state called? 32.59–60.
The physicians said:
"Women gathered for pleasure and recreation in the presence of the gods—
the goddesses who are peerless in beauty and the princess who is destined for greatness."
They cast their gaze upon her, and because of that, pain arose within the daughter.
Likewise, by means of protective mantras, yellow mustard seeds,
and water for sprinkling, that young girl shall attain supreme peace.
Having spoken thus, all the physicians departed from the king’s palace,
all of them hinting once more at the distress born of their desire for the king's pleasure.
Questioned by her mother, that illustrious woman of beautiful form, being bashful, spoke for a long time to her mother while weeping bitterly.
"Mother, neither conversation nor food ever pleases me; nor, O mother, does any festival. Always hear my heart's desire," having said this, Uṣā, that excellent woman, then fell silent.
All the women began gazing at one another’s faces, thinking,
"Indeed, youth in women should be characterized by a semblance of modesty."
"This princess is indeed worthy of a husband; what more need be said?
By the favor of her father and mother, she shall obtain a suitable bridegroom."

Standing there were the most excellent women, most wonderful in their variegated beauty.

having seen the mark of your skin upon the painted cloth given by me, she lives.

Whose life-breaths will you bewilder with the sounds of your conch, O Mādhava?
Who is this one who today, along with his retinue, shall go to the abode of Yama?
When these words had been spoken by the wise son of Vinatā, Vāsudeva spoke these words: "Listen, O best of birds!"
The unconquered son of Pradyumna was bound by Bāṇa, the son of Bali,
in the city named Śoṇita for the sake of Uṣā.
But Aniruddha, afflicted by desire, has been bound by serpents of virulent poison;
O Lord of Birds, you have been summoned by me for the sake of his liberation.
"There is no one equal to your speed; you are the foremost among birds.
O twice-born one, it would indeed be impossible for anyone else to travel that distance."
"Take me there quickly, where the son of Pradyumna resides."
"O hero, your daughter-in-law Vaidarbhī weeps, longing for her son;
by your grace, may she be reunited with her son."
"O hero, O destroyer of serpents, the nectar was indeed carried away by you.
At that time, O mighty-armed one, I approached you;
you are my banner, and all the Vṛṣṇis are devoted to you."
"Honor our friendship today, O Lord of Birds, and honor my devotion."
"There is no one equal to your speed among birds, nor is there anyone who is your peer;
O Suparṇa, destroyer of serpents, I swear this to you by my own good deeds."
In the past, you alone liberated your mother from slavery;
in the past, resorting to the fanning of your wings, you slew the warriors.
Having mounted all the hosts of gods upon your back by your prowess, you travel to regions that were inaccessible; indeed, your victory has spread far and wide.
In weight you are equal to Mount Meru; in lightness you are like the wind.
In prowess, there is no one equal to you in the past, the present, or the future.
O you who are true to your promise, O illustrious one, O Vainateya of great splendor!
Let assistance be rendered to Aniruddha in this moment.
Garuḍa said:
"O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, these words of yours are most wonderful!
O Keśava, by your grace, victory shall be mine everywhere."
"I am blessed, I am favored by your company, O Madhusūdana!
You are worthy of praise by me, O Kṛṣṇa; yet you yourself, O mighty-armed one, offer praise to me."
You are the overseer of the Vedas, the overseer of the gods, and the bestower of all desires. For you are one whose sight is never in vain, and you grant boons to those who seek them.
He has four arms and four forms; he is the originator of the fourfold sacrificial office (*cāturhotra*);
he is the officiant for the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*); he is the leader of the four [castes] and the great poet.
You are the wielder of the bow, the wielder of the discus, and the great wielder of the conch;
O Lord, in your previous bodies you were renowned as the upholder of the earth.
You are Lāṅgalin, Musalin, and Cakrin; you are the son of Devakī. You are the slayer of Cāṇūra, the beloved of the cowherds, and the destroyer of Kaṃsa.
He is the upholder of Govardhana, the enemy of the wrestlers, the one who brings prosperity to the wrestlers,
the lover of wrestlers, the great wrestler, and also the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa).

Beloved by the Brahmins, the benefactor of the Brahmins, the knower of the Brahmins, the one who causes the Brahmins to flourish; you are remembered as Dāmodara, the friend of the Brahmins and the most excellent.
The destroyer of Pralamba, the slayer of Keśin, the ender of the Dānavas,
the killer of Asiloman, and likewise the annihilator of Rāvaṇa.
The Blessed One is the giver of sovereignty to Vibhīṣaṇa and the slayer of Vālin; you are the bestower of the kingdom upon Sugrīva and the one who stripped Bali of his kingdom.
You are the stealer of jewels, the great jewel, and one born from the depths of the ocean;
you are renowned as Varuṇa, and you are the source of the rivers.
You are the wielder of the sword and the bow, a great and supreme archer;
renowned as Dāśārha, you are a mighty bowman for whom the bow is dear.
O you of excellent vows, you are the ocean renowned as Govinda;
you are both the sky and asceticism, and you are the churner of the ocean.
You are heaven, yielding manifold fruits; you are the great sustainer of heaven.
You alone are the great cloud, and you are the very ripening of the seed.
You are the crusher of the three worlds and the remover of anger, greed, and fear;
you are the granter of desires, Kāma himself, and the wielder of all bows.
Saṃvarta, Vartana, Pralaya, the great Nila,
Hiraṇyagarbha, the knower of forms, the possessor of form, and Madhusūdana.
"You are the Lord, O Mahādeva, endowed with innumerable virtues.
O God, you desire to praise me; yet you, O best of the Yadus, are the one worthy of praise."
Those terrible living beings who were gazed upon by you with your eyes have been slain by the staff of Yama; they are destined for rebirth as animals or for the hells.
Those living beings who have been looked upon by you with supreme affection—
both here and after death— they shall all be free from sin and go to heaven.
O mighty-armed one, here I am, remaining under your command and subject to your instruction.
"Command me, O mighty-armed one; I have accomplished my purpose in every way.
Then, having uttered a cry of victory, Garuḍa spoke to Keśava.
"Here I stand, O hero; ascend, O one of great strength!"
Then Mādhava, having embraced Garuḍa around the neck, said:
"O friend, for the destruction of the enemy, please accept this offering of honor."
Having offered the *arghya* with supreme affection, the mighty-armed Puruṣottama, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword, mounted upon Suparṇa.
