In the meantime, there in the battle, the attendants of Rudra [attacked];
thus, the wielder of the trident once again commenced the fight there.
Resorting to illusory warfare, they surrounded Pradyumna.
Having brought them all under the power of sleep, the heroic Makaraketu,
possessed of great strength, destroyed the Dānavas there with a net of arrows,
overwhelming the various hosts of Pramathas in every place.
Then, as the god of unwearied deeds yawned,
a flame burst forth from his mouth, as if burning the ten directions.
Then the goddess Earth, being oppressed by those high-souled ones,
approached the most noble Brahmā while trembling.
The Earth said:
"O God of gods, O mighty-armed one, I am being oppressed by your supreme splendor;
overwhelmed by the weight of Kṛṣṇa and Rudra, I shall once again become a single ocean."
"O Grandfather, consider this unbearable burden so that,
O Lord, having become lightened, I may sustain the world of moving and non-moving beings."
Then the Grandfather replied to Queen Kāśyapī:
"Restrain yourself for a moment; you shall soon become light."
Having seen this, the Blessed Brahmā spoke these words to Rudra:
"The destruction of the great Asuras has been accomplished; why do you still protect them further?"
O mighty-armed one, battle with Kṛṣṇa does not please you;
nor do you realize that Kṛṣṇa is indeed yourself divided in two.
Then, indeed, through connection with that body, the imperishable Lord, the Master,
having entered, beholds all the three worlds with their mobile and immobile beings.
Seeing himself thus expanded, equipped with both arrows and bow, [Ñ2.3 V B Ds D5.6 continue;
K1 D1-3 insert after 1375*]:
Having entered into *yoga*, with his soul absorbed in *yoga* and reflecting upon those boons,
and recollecting in their entirety everything that had been said at Dvāravatī,
he then offered no reply and simply withdrew.
He beheld his own self residing within Kṛṣṇa’s body, born from a single womb;
then, having emerged from it, Rudra ceased his speech in the battle.
And Rudra said to Brahmā, "O Blessed One, I shall not fight in battle with Kṛṣṇa; let the earth be lightened."
Then Kṛṣṇa and Rudra, having embraced one another and attained the highest joy, departed from the battlefield.
Regarding this matter, O King, in former times Nārada spoke to Mārkaṇḍeya:
"No one beheld those two yogins who had attained the state of yoga. (HV App. I, 37.27–28)
Having done so, the Grandfather of the worlds beheld that single Brahmā.
Having recognized that Mārkaṇḍeya was indeed far-sighted, he addressed this to him along with Nārada and questioned Pārśvatha.
O Brahmin, on the slope of Mount Mandara, in a lotus pond, I beheld Bhava and Keśava— Hara and Acyuta— in a dream during the night.
He saw Hari in the form of Hara, and Hara in the form of Hari;
Hara, with conch, discus, and mace in hand, wearing yellow garments.
[He saw] Hari holding a trident and a *paṭṭiśa* weapon and wearing a tiger skin;
and also Hara mounted upon Garuḍa, and Hari whose banner bears the bull.
O Brahmin, great is my wonder upon seeing that supreme marvel!
O Blessed One, observer of noble vows, explain this to me exactly as it is.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
To Śiva who has the form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu who has the form of Śiva—I offer salutations because I perceive no difference between them; by that, may they both grant me auspiciousness.
This imperishable and undecaying syllable is without beginning, middle, or end;
that very form of mine, consisting of both Hari and Hara, I shall now declare to you.
He who is Viṣṇu is indeed Rudra; he who is Rudra is the Grandfather (Brahmā). These three deities—Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha—are but a single form.
The givers of boons, the creators of the worlds, the lords of the world, and the self-existent ones— they,
as Ardhanārīśvaras, have undertaken this severe vow.
Just as water poured into water becomes that very water,
so too Viṣṇu, having entered Rudra, becomes identical with Rudra.
Just as fire that has entered into fire becomes fire itself,
so too Rudra, having entered into Viṣṇu, becomes identical with Viṣṇu.
One should know that Agni is of the nature of Rudra, while Viṣṇu is remembered as being of the nature of Soma;
indeed, the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of the essence of Agni and Soma.
Viṣṇu and Maheśvara are the lords who are the creators and the withdrawers of the world, both stationary and moving; they are the makers of the auspiciousness of the universe.
The agent and the instrument, the two agents who are the instruments;
the two gods, Nārāyaṇa and Maheśvara, who are the past, the future, and the present.
These two are those very speakers; these two are those very ones full of light.
These two are remembered as the protectors of the world and the creators of its manifestation;
they cause rain to fall, they shine, they blow, and they bring forth all things.
This supreme secret has been told to you, O Grandfather.
The man who recites this constantly and he who hears it attains the supreme abode born from the grace of Viṣṇu and Rudra.
I shall praise the two gods, Hari and Hara, who are united with Brahmā;
for these two supreme gods are the source of the origin and dissolution of the world.
Viṣṇu is the supreme of Rudra, and Śiva is the supreme of Viṣṇu;
being one alone, he moves eternally in the world, having become twofold.
Without Śaṅkara there is no Viṣṇu, and without Keśava there is no Śiva;
therefore, in ancient times, those two, Rudra and Upendra, attained oneness.

Homage to Rudra, the dark one; homage to him who moves in a compact host. Homage to the three-eyed one; indeed, homage to the two-eyed one. Homage to the tawny-eyed one; indeed, homage to the lotus-eyed one.
Homage to the teacher of Kumāra, homage to the teacher of Pradyumna;
homage indeed to the upholder of the earth, homage to the upholder of the Gaṅgā.
Homage to the one with peacock feathers; homage to the wearer of armlets. Homage to the one with a garland of skulls; indeed, homage to the one with a forest garland.

Salutations to the one who holds a trident in his hand; salutations indeed to the one who holds a discus in his hand. Salutations to the one with the golden staff; salutations to you, the bearer of the staff of vows.
Homage to the one clothed in skin; homage to you who wear yellow garments.
Homage be to the Lord of Lakṣmī; homage to the Lord of Umā.
Homage to the bearer of the skull-topped staff; homage to the wielder of the pestle.
Homage to him whose limbs are smeared with ashes; homage to the one who wears a dark-blue body.
Homage to the dweller in the cremation ground; homage to you who dwell in the hermitage.
Homage to the one whose vehicle is the bull; homage to the one whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
Homage be to you of manifold forms, indeed homage to you of many forms! Homage to the bringer of dissolution and homage to the creator of emanation!
Homage be to the one of many forms; homage to him who has the form of Bhairava.
Homage to the god Virūpākṣa, and homage also to the one with gentle eyes.
Salutations to the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and the subduer of Bali;
salutations to the dweller of the mountains and salutations to the dweller of the ocean.
Salutations to the slayer of the enemies of the gods; salutations indeed to the slayer of Tripura.
Homage be to the slayer of Naraka; homage to the destroyer of the body of Kāma.
Salutations to the destroyer of Puṣpadanta, the slayer of Madhu.
Homage be to the destroyer of Andhaka; homage to the slayer of Kaiṭabha!
Homage to the one with a thousand arms; homage to the one with innumerable arms!
Salutation to the thousand-headed one; indeed, salutation to the many-headed one.
Salutation to the divine Dāmodara, who wears a girdle of muñja grass.
Homage to you, O Blessed Viṣṇu; homage to you, O Blessed Śiva!
Homage to you, O Blessed God; homage to you, who are worshipped by the gods!
Homage to you, who are sung with the Sāman hymns; homage to you along with the Yajus formulas.
Homage to you, O slayer of the enemies of the gods; homage to you, who are worshipped by the Asuras.
Salutations to you, the action of those who act; salutations to you of immeasurable prowess!
O Hṛṣīkeśa, let there be salutation to you; O Svarṇakeśa, let there be salutation to you!
This hymn to Rudra and the high-souled Viṣṇu was composed after all the great-souled sages had gathered together and offered praise to those two.
By Vyāsa, the knower of the gods, and by the wise Nārada;
likewise by Bhāradvāja, Gārgya, and Viśvāmitra.
By Viśvāmitra, Vātsya, and likewise by Sumantu;
by Agastya, Pulastya, and the high-souled Dhaumya.

Whoever recites this hymn, which is essentially Hari and Hara, daily, becomes free from disease and endowed with strength; of this there is no doubt. He constantly attains prosperity and does not turn back from heaven.
A sonless man obtains a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband;
and a pregnant woman who hears this gives birth to an excellent son.
Rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas,
and vināyakas do not cause fear where this hymn is recited.

Then [he saw] the god Balabhadra, the illustrious one of great strength.
The high-minded Aniruddha, filled with joy, paid his respects.
Having saluted the high-souled Mādhava with palms joined in reverence,
he also paid homage to Suparṇa, the best of birds and one of great prowess.
Then, having approached his father, the lord Makaraketu, who bore variegated arrows, he paid homage to Pradyumna.
Surrounded by her circle of friends, Uṣā, the delight of her family,
[approached] Bala, Atibala, and the very invincible Vāsudeva.
Having saluted Asaṃkhyātagati and Suparṇa,
she, feeling bashful, paid her respects to the one who bears the flower-arrowed god.
Then, at the word of Śakra, Nārada, possessed of supreme splendor,
returned once more to the presence of Vāsudeva with a smile.
He congratulated that god Govinda, the slayer of enemies:
"By good fortune, O Govinda, you prosper through this reunion with Aniruddha."
Then, together with Aniruddha, they stood bowing before Nārada;
and after the celestial sage had honored them with blessings, he spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
"O Lord, let the marriage of Aniruddha, known as Vīrya, be performed;
for a desire has arisen in me to see Jambūlamālikā."
Then, everyone laughed upon hearing the words of Nārada;
the Blessed Kṛṣṇa said, "Let it be done quickly, without delay."
In the meantime, dear one, Kumbhāṇḍa arrived,
bringing the wedding requisites and bowing down to Kṛṣṇa.
The Kumbhāṇḍa said:
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, become the bestower of fearlessness!
O God, I have come to you for refuge; be gracious—here is my salutation with joined palms."
Having heard all of Nārada’s words beforehand,
that Acyuta granted freedom from fear to the high-souled Kumbhāṇḍa.
"O Kumbhāṇḍa, best of ministers, I am pleased with you, O observer of noble vows.
I recognize your good service; may you be the governor here."
May you, together with your kinsmen, be very happy and find peace here;
I grant the kingdom to you—live long through my protection.
Having thus bestowed the kingdom upon this high-souled Kumbhāṇḍa,
the wise [Bāṇa] then performed the marriage ceremony there for Aniruddha.
Then the blessed Fire-god himself appeared there;
for the marriage of Aniruddha took place under an auspicious constellation.
Then the throngs of Apsarases prepared to perform a spectacle there;
Aniruddha, having bathed and being well-adorned, was there with his wife.
Then the Gandharvas sang with affectionate and auspicious words,
and the Apsarases danced, adorning the wedding ceremony.
Then, having completed the marriage of Aniruddha, that wise destroyer of enemies was surrounded by all the hosts of gods.
Having addressed Rudra there, the giver of boons who is honored by the gods,
Kṛṣṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities, set his mind on departing.
Knowing that Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemies, was heading toward Dvārakā,
Kambhāṇḍa spoke these words to Madhusūdana with his palms joined in reverence.
Listen to my request, O lotus-eyed one, O Madhusūdana. **HV_App.I,38.44**1:1 /
The cows of Bāṇa indeed remain in the hand of Varuṇa;
from them flows milk that is like nectar, O Mādhava. Having drunk that, a man becomes exceedingly strong and invincible.
When Kumbhāṇḍa had spoken thus, Hari was then pleased in mind;
he set his heart on going, having resolved that he must depart.
Then the blessed Brahmā, having offered congratulations to Keśava,
departed for the world of Brahmā, surrounded by those whose abodes are their own celestial realms.
Indra, together with the hosts of Maruts, proceeded toward Dvārakā. Then Aniruddha, with a joyful heart, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence: **HV_App.I,38.53**2:1.
O God of gods, who indeed could conquer you, the most excellent being, in a great battle?
Even Śatakratu himself would not be able to stand before you;
mount Garuḍa quickly, let us go to the city of Dvārakā.
Wherever Kṛṣṇa went, there all followed, desiring victory.
Mounted upon her peacock vehicle and surrounded by her female companions, Uṣā,
having been sent forth by the goddess, set out toward Dvārakā.
Then Bala, Kṛṣṇa, the mighty Pradyumna,
and the heroic Aniruddha mounted Garuḍa.
And having set out, that radiant Garuḍa, the best of birds,
uprooted clusters of trees and made the earth tremble.
All the quarters became agitated and the sky appeared as if covered in dust;
when Garuḍa had set forth, the sun grew dim in its radiance.

Then the mighty-armed Āhuka, his eyes wide with joy, spoke to the highly effulgent Kṛṣṇa: "O delight of the Yadus, listen!"
"This being the case, let a great festival be held for Aniruddha;

A festival was being celebrated there in the house of Aniruddha,

In that city, women overcome by intoxication play musical instruments;
others there dance, and still others sing.
Some there were joyful, while others spoke to one another;
wearing garments of various colors, they sported here and there.

others, their eyes wide with joy, play at dice.
Having mounted a chariot drawn by peacocks and surrounded by her female companions, Uṣā was sent forth by the goddess Rudrāṇī with the words: "Let her be accepted!"
And this beautiful woman named Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, who brings honor to her family— accept this passionate lady as your bride.

she was led into the beautiful residence of Aniruddha.
Devakī, Revatī, Rukmiṇī, and the daughter of Vidarbha,
filled with affection and joy upon seeing Aniruddha, wept.
Revatī and Rukmiṇī likewise caused him to enter the principal residence.
O bride, you are increasing in prosperity by good fortune through the sight of Aniruddha.
Then, amidst the sounding of musical instruments, those noble women of beautiful countenances began to perform their rites, while Uṣā remained within her chamber.

Then, in due course, all those Yadu women, observing the conduct of the bride Ūṣā, chose it as their own custom.
All this has been related to you by me, O scion of the Kuru lineage:
how Bāṇa was conquered in battle and liberated while still alive by Viṣṇu.

Together with the lords of creatures, the gods, and the sages; with the ancestors, Gandharvas, and elemental spirits (bhūtas); with the Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
and with the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and birds.
The deeds of the Pāṇḍus and the Dhṛtarāṣṭras, as well as those of the Yadus together with the Vṛṣṇis,
and likewise the history of the kings of the Aila and Ikṣvāku lineages, have been recounted;
and the divine and human incarnations have been proclaimed.
The majesty of Viṣṇu, the god of gods and of immeasurable splendor;
his most wonderful deeds, his heroic strides, and his resolutions regarding dharma;
his diverse narrative episodes and his foremost, unsurpassed birth.
O Sūta, this narrative of ours being told by you in gentle words—
pleasing to the mind and ear— is like nectar and brings us delight.
By what ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is the *Mahābhārata* narrative to be heard?
"What is the fruit of this [Purāṇa], and that you ought to tell me?
[Sūta said:
The rule for listening to the sections and whatever fruit there is in the breaking of the fast."
That which was asked by Janamejaya at that concluding sacrificial bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the rite—
[Janamejaya said: "The highly meritorious [account] proclaimed by Vyāsa, adorned with the meaning of the Vedas— "
I have heard this entire narrative, which is endowed with many traditional accounts.
O best of the twice-born, having properly heard this purifying narrative,
I shall hereafter speak further of a most excellent and superior rite.
What is the fruit [of this], who are the gods to be worshipped here on the days of breaking the fast?
"O Blessed One, what should be given when [the recitation] is completed, and at every festival? What kind of reciter should be sought for this? Tell me that."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen, O King, to this procedure and also the fruit that arises from the Bhārata.
I have been rightly questioned by you, O Indra among kings, best of the wise.
I too have questioned the blessed Vyāsa, the foremost of those who know the Vedas;
and when questioned by me, that high-souled one declared this secret ritual.
I shall explain that to you correctly again and again with full concentration;
O Indra among kings, that which you ask me about arises from what has been heard.
O protector of the earth, the gods descended from heaven to the earth for the sake of sport;
having accomplished this very purpose, they have now returned to heaven.
Come now, listen with a concentrated mind to that which I shall declare to you:
the origin of the sages and the deities upon the surface of the earth.
The Vasus, the Rudras, as well as the Sādhyas and the eternal Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, and the two Aśvin deities, along with the world-protectors and the ṛṣis; HV App. I, 40.11–12.
The Guhyakas along with the Gandharvas, the Nāgas, and likewise the Vidyādharas;
the Siddhas, Dharma, the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), and the excellent sage Kātyāyana.
The mountains, the oceans, and the rivers, as well as the hosts of Apsarases;
the planets, the years, the solstices, and likewise the seasons.
O best of the Bharatas, the entire world— both the stationary and the moving, including gods and asuras— is seen here in the land of Bhārata as gathered in one place.
Having heard their foundation and the proclamation of their names and deeds,
a human being would be instantly liberated even after committing a terrible sin.
Having heard this history exactly and in its proper sequence,
one should restrain oneself, become pure within, and reach the further shore in this land of Bhārata.
O descendant of Bharata, having heard this account of the *Bhārata*, one should give the best of things to the Brahmins according to one's ability and with devotion, O bull among the Bharatas.
Great gifts should be given, as well as various kinds of jewels;
cows with bronze milking vessels, and maidens beautifully adorned.
There were various vehicles endowed with all the qualities of desire,
as well as diverse palaces, lands, garments, and gold.
Vehicles should also be given— horses, rutting elephants,
beds, palanquins, and well-adorned chariots.
One should present to the reciter fragrant garlands along with garments,
as well as bracelets, earrings, and likewise a sacred thread.
An umbrella, sandals, a turban, and especially a tunic—
one should worship these according to the prescribed rule and then bestow a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
He who performs the rite deficiently shall not obtain the full fruit.
O King, one should not act otherwise out of desire, greed, or delusion;
for by acting so, one goes to hell and obtains a contrary result.
Whatever is excellent in the house, whatever great wealth there may be— HV_App.I,40.31.
That and that should be given to the twice-born: one's self, one's wife, and one's sons.
With supreme faith, he gradually attained mastery over that [gift],
being capable, well-disposed, joyful, desirous of serving, and free from boastfulness.
Devoted to truth and uprightness, self-controlled, pure, endowed with ritual purity,
full of faith, and having conquered anger— listen to how such a person attains success.
O King, I shall relate briefly to you, the listener, the one who causes it to be heard.
And hear from me all the qualities that have been declared for the reciter:
he should be pure, endowed with virtuous conduct, dressed in white garments, and one who has conquered his senses;
he should be refined, a knower of all the scriptures, full of faith, and free from malice.
He knew the inclinations of others and was skilled in discerning their characteristics; he was a true poet and knew the proper seasons.
He was handsome, fortunate, self-controlled, truthful, and had conquered his senses.
And the reciter should be one who is motivated by gifts and honor.
One who is always angry, greedy, and has not conquered his senses;
who is dull-witted and discontented— such a reciter is to be abandoned.
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, accomplished, eloquent, logical, and most skilled in the knowledge of words—
[he approached] him who was unwavering in mind, not hasty, steadfast, and powerful.
With syllables and words unattached [to one another], it was endowed with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*).
Endowed with sixty-three phonemes and possessing eight locations,
the reciter— being healthy, seated comfortably, and well-concentrated— should perform the recitation.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory."
O King, descendant of Bharata, having heard such a *bhārata* from such a reciter,
a listener who is pure and established in self-restraint attains the fruit of hearing it.
The *Bhārata*, spoken in one hundred sections by the sage who perceives reality,
is traditionally held to have its completion through ten sets of ten sections each.
The first is said to end with the Sabhā; the second ends with the Vanavāsa;
the third ends with the Udyoga; and the fourth ends with the Bhīṣma.
The fifth ends with the Droṇaparvan; then the sixth ends with the Karṇaparvan;
the seventh ends with the Viśokaparvan, and the eighth ends with the Śāntiparvan.
The ninth [section] ends with the Svargaparvan; after that follows the Āścaryaparvan.
However, some maintain that because there is no mention of a specific number [of verses], the completion of ten thousand ślokas according to the rule of equality constitutes the *pāraṇa*.

Having first obtained the breaking of the fast, he should satisfy the twice-born with their desires;
that man indeed obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
He obtains a great celestial chariot crowded with hosts of Apsarases;
delighted and composed, he goes to heaven together with the gods.
Seated upon a celestial chariot drawn by swans, he, together with the deities, goes joyfully to heaven,
attended by hosts of immortals and composed in mind.
Having obtained the second breaking of the fast, one obtains the fruit of an Atirātra sacrifice;
being constantly attended by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, one dances.
He ascends a celestial chariot (vimāna) with golden railings, yoked to horses swift as thought and resembling the rays of the moon.
Having gone to heaven, filled with joy, he delights in the Nandana grove;
he ascends a divine celestial chariot composed of every kind of jewel.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
and always adorned with divine armlets, he is honored in the world of the gods.
He easily ascends to his well-constructed celestial palace, his dwelling,
adorned with a crown of fiery hue embellished with Jāmbūnada gold.
Surrounded by divine apsarases and attended by gods and gandharvas,
having reached the third fast-breaking meal, one obtains the fruit of twelve days.
Resembling an immortal, he dwells in heaven for tens of thousands of years.

O best among the foremost of men, on the fourth day one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, and on the fifth day one obtains double that fruit, provided there is a breaking of the fast at each stage.
Resembling the risen sun, blazing like a fire.
Having ascended a celestial chariot together with the gods, he travels through the sky;
for tens of thousands of years, he rejoices in the abode of Śakra in heaven.
In the sixth [level] it is twofold, and in the seventh the fruit is threefold;
it has the form of a peak of Mount Kailāsa and is furnished with an altar made of lapis lazuli.
Having ascended that celestial chariot, which was surrounded on all sides, adorned in many ways with jewels and coral,
capable of moving at will, and accompanied by throngs of Apsarases;
He wanders through all the worlds like a second sun.
On the eighth [day], at the conclusion of the Rājasūya sacrifice, one obtains the fruit;
one ascends a delightful celestial chariot (vimāna) resembling the rising moon.
Yoked with horses swift as thought, resembling the rays of the moon,
he was attended by excellent women whose faces were more beautiful than the moon.
Awakened from a pleasant sleep on the laps of exquisite women by the tinkling of their girdles and the sound of their anklets, he rises.
O Bhārata, that mortal obtains the fruit of the ninth sacrifice, the king of sacrifices, the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha), as well as a celestial chariot that moves at will.
It had turrets with pillars of gold and a terrace made of lapis lazuli;
it was surrounded on all sides by divine windows made of Jāmbūnada gold.
Attended by throngs of Apsarases and Gandharvas who roam the heavens,
he ascended his celestial chariot, blazing with supreme splendor.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial sandalwood paste,
he rejoices together with the deities in heaven like another god.
Having completed the tenth breaking of his fast and having paid homage to the twice-born,
[he mounted] that vehicle which resounded with the tinkling of networks of small bells and was adorned with banners and standards.
Resembling a diamond railing, with archways of lapis lazuli and jewels,
it was encircled by a golden net and featured eaves made of coral.
Adorned by Gandharvas skilled in song and by Apsarases,
he easily attains that celestial chariot, the abode of the gods.
Wearing a crown of fiery hue and adorned with ornaments of Jāmbūnada gold,
his limbs were anointed with divine sandalwood paste and he was decorated with celestial garlands.
Endowed with divine enjoyments, he wanders through the celestial worlds,
possessed of supreme splendor by the grace of the gods.
Then, for just that many years, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
thereafter, accompanied by Gandharvas, he remains there for twenty-one thousand years.
He shall dwell happily in those abodes;
then, for thousands of years,
he rejoices together with Śakra in the delightful city of Purandara.
Shining within celestial palaces and throughout various worlds,
surrounded by throngs of divine women, he dwells like an immortal.
Then, O King, he goes to dwell in the same world as Sūrya, likewise with Candra, with Śiva, and with Viṣṇu.
"It is so, O Great King; there is no need for deliberation here.
One must indeed be full of faith; thus did my guru speak."
To the scribe, however, whatever he desires in his mind should be given;
the manuscript of the *Harivaṃśa* should be presented along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should give a wrapping along with a cord according to one's available wealth;
and two auspicious small boxes for the sake of obtaining infinite fruit.
This should be given to the reciter by one who desires a son for oneself.

A bronze vessel filled with clarified butter should be given, as well as gold as a sacrificial fee; by this, one is liberated from all sins. Elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and especially mounts [should also be given].
As well as bracelets, earrings, and likewise the sacred thread.
One should worship him with variegated garments and especially with fragrances as if he were a god; thus one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
A pair of garments for the husband and wife should be given, as well as gold and wealth.
The ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers speak these words repeatedly:
"May someone in our lineage arise who listens to the *Harivaṃśa*;
surely by him we shall be delivered, for we are pleased with him and are granters of boons."
Upon hearing the *Harivaṃśa*, we indeed grant him a lineage of sons;
he shall surely possess sons for fifteen births.
He obtains sons who are pure and performers of sacrificial rites;
likewise, he obtains Vaiṣṇavas who are devotees of Viṣṇu and likewise devotees of the twice-born.
Indeed, the listener of the Harivaṃśa purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation.
Henceforth, O Bhārata, I shall declare those things which are to be given,
O King, when they are being recited to the brahmins at every sacred festival (parvan).
O bull among the Bharatas, O lord of men, having understood the birth, the country, the character, the greatness,
the duty, and the conduct of the Kṣatriyas.
Having first caused the twice-born to pronounce blessings, one should then proceed with the rite;
when the festival is concluded, one should then gratify the twice-born according to one's ability.
But first, O best of the Bharatas, [one should honor] the twice-born with perfumes and garlands;
and first indeed, the reciter, provided with garments and fragrances.
O best of the Bharatas, O King, at the Pauloma sacrifice, one should duly feed the twice-born, who are radiant with perfumes and garlands,
with excellent honeyed milk-rice (madhupāyasa).

Then, O King, one should feed an *āstika* with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) consisting mostly of roots and fruits, mixed with honey and clarified butter; and one should also give him rice with jaggery (*guḍaudana*).
Then, on the occasion of the Saṃbhava festival, food endowed with all excellent qualities was prepared,
consisting of *apūpas*, *pūpas*, and *modakas*.
O Indra among kings, in the *Sabhāparvan*, one should feed the twice-born with sacrificial food (*haviṣya*);
in the *Āraṇyakaparvan*, one should satisfy the best of the twice-born with roots and fruits.
Upon reaching the Āraṇyaparvan, one should cause a water-pitcher to be given,
as well as principal libations and forest roots and fruits.
One should cause food endowed with all desirable qualities to be given to the Brahmins,
as well as various garments, according to the Virāṭaparvan.

O best of the Bharatas, for the sake of the ritual purpose, one should cause cows with bronze milking vessels to be given away during the Udyoga, provided they are endowed with all desirable qualities.
Likewise, one should give gold when undertaking an enterprise or when hearing the Śruti;
one should feed the Brahmins with food, having adorned them with perfumes and garlands.
O king of kings, in the Bhīṣmaparvan, having provided an unsurpassed vehicle and delicious food,
one should cause eight gifts to be given.
Then one should give well-prepared food, endowed with all excellent qualities.
O Bhārata, at the Droṇaparvan, food endowed with all desirable qualities was offered to the brahmins with the highest honor.
And arrows should be given, O Indra among kings, as well as bows and excellent swords.
One should honor the best of the twice-born with armor, garments, and ornaments;
likewise, in the Karṇaparvan, one should provide food that fulfills all desires.
O King of kings, in the Śalyaparvan, one who has purified his mind should properly offer refined *saṃskṛta* food to the Brahmins, along with sweetmeats and rice mixed with jaggery.
One should cause all kinds of food to be offered with cakes and satiating drinks;
likewise, on the Gadā-parvan day, one should cause food mixed with mung beans to be offered.
Likewise,
in the *Sauptika-parvan*, one should provide food that fulfills all desires;
and in the *Strī-parvan*, one should satisfy the best of the twice-born with jewels.
And before the Aiṣīka rite, one should again cause rice cooked with ghee to be given.
Then one should give well-prepared food endowed with all excellent qualities.
Even when the Śāntiparvan has been completed, one should feed the twice-born with sacrificial food (haviṣya).
In the *Anuśāsana-parvan*, O King, one should feed the twice-born with refined food;

Likewise, while residing in a hermitage, one should feed the twice-born with sacrificial food (haviṣya).
In the Mausala-parvan, there was fragrance, garlands, and ointments possessing every excellence;
likewise, in the Mahāprasthānika-parvan, it was endowed with all the qualities of desired objects.
O best of the Bharatas, at the time of departure, one should give a pair of auspicious sandals;
likewise, on the day of departure, one should cause sweet foods to be given to the twice-born.
Likewise, during the Svargaparvan, one should feed the twice-born with sacrificial food (haviṣya).
In the *Svargārohaṇaka*, one should give food that fulfills all desires.
And one should present it, joined with gold, to the reciter.
At the conclusion of the *Harivaṃśa*, however, one should feed a thousand twice-born men.
Then follows the Harivaṃśa Parvan; there, milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is the food to be offered.
Indeed, in the Harivaṃśa, that which is most dear to him in his home should be given.
Likewise, in the Harivaṃśa Parvan, one should feed them milk-rice (*pāyasa*) there.
One should cause a book to be given with gold weighing just one *niṣka*;
by listening to it and by giving it as a gift, the attainment of a son occurs— of this there is no doubt.
One should present a single cow accompanied by a gold coin to a Brāhmaṇa;
O King, even a poor man should give at least half of that amount.
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are to be worshipped with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments.
The wise man should place an image of Umāmaheśvara before it;
having worshipped the book, adorned with garments, perfumes, and other offerings,
the recitation of the Harivaṃśa should be performed according to the prescribed rite.
He gave golden armlets, earrings, and other ornaments to the reciter,
as well as an image of Umā and Maheśvara for the couple, according to the prescribed rite.
One should cause the book of the Harivaṃśa to be given to the reciter,
and one should perform a fire sacrifice with a tenth part [of the offerings], using sesame seeds drenched in clarified butter.
And eleven gold coins of the finest quality should be given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
At the conclusion of each section, however, the wise man should indeed present the book,
adorned with gold, to the reciter.
O Prince, whoever should listen with a single-minded focus to even a single verse, or a quarter-verse, or even a single syllable, shall become beloved by Viṣṇu.
One should worship Vyāsa together with his wife according to the prescribed rite;
one should also worship that image of the divine Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa which has been consecrated.
Whoever honors the reciter with land, clothing, and an excellent cow,
by him Viṣṇu himself— the son of Devakī— is directly worshiped.
At every breaking of the fast, O King, O bull of the Bharatas, he did so according to the prescribed rule.
Having completed all the *saṃhitās*, being self-restrained and skilled in the scriptures,
he should then place them in an auspicious location, covered with linen cloths.
Having become pure, wearing white garments, adorned with garlands and well-ornamented,
one should worship [them] according to the rule, with various perfumes and garlands individually.
Having reverently honored the book with gold, jewels,
and fine silken cloths, he should then certainly pray for all his desired objects.
Then the couple, taking the *arghya* offering of *śrīphala* with both hands, [made this prayer]:
"Oṃ! O Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, grant me sinless sons."
O Brahmā, together with Sāvitrī; O Keśava, together with Lakṣmī;
O Lord Śiva, together with Pārvatī—grant us sons.
O Lord of Gods, by the gift of sons, make me possessed of sons.

Circumambulation and salutation should be directed toward Hari and the book itself.
Victory to you, O Lord of the lords of gods, abode of Lakṣmī; let there be homage to you!
Victory to you, O Lord of the worlds! Fulfill my desires.
Whatever desire one contemplates, that one certainly attains.
Victory is within the grasp of him by whom the *Harivaṃśa* has been heard.
Viṣṇu alone, the great yogin, is indeed praised through yoga;
he is praised by the ṛṣis together with Brahmā and by Śaṅkara;
he is praised by all the gods, whose strength and prowess are serene.
One should fashion an image of Nārāyaṇa with sixteen *karṣas* of gold,
O lord of men; an image of Nara with ten *karṣas* of gold.

Having adorned them with ornaments, one should perform their installation; indeed, one should perform the consecration with the Mahāpuruṣasūkta. Having worshipped them with perfumes and garlands, preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana).

One should offer oblations with sesame seeds one hundred and eight times using Vaiṣṇava mantras. At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, having become purified and with a faithful mind, one should worship the book of the Harivaṃśa together with the image of the deity.
Adorned with all ornaments, endowed with form and consciousness,
and accompanied by two painted figures of Puṣṭā, he should present it to the preceptor.
Then, O King, being self-restrained and pure in mind, he should [present] the Brahmins.
O King, being pure and well-composed, [one should worship] with Saṃhitā manuscripts,
with devoted offerings of meat, drinks, and various auspicious objects of desire.
Then one should cause gold and refined gold to be given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
In every case, three palas of gold should be given by one who is self-restrained.
Whether it be half of that or even a quarter, provided it is free from stinginess regarding one's wealth;
whatever is most desired by oneself, that very thing should be given to the twice-born. In every way, one should satisfy one’s own teacher, the reciter, with devotion.
One should proclaim all the deities, as well as Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having well-adorned the best of the twice-born with perfumes and garlands,
he should gratify them with two kinds of desires as well as with various gifts, both high and low.
A person obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice;
likewise, he shall obtain the fruit of the sacrifice on every single lunar festival (parvan).
O best of the Bharatas, he was a reciter whose syllables, words, and tones were clearly articulated.
O bull of the Bharatas, one should cause the Brahmins to hear the *Bhārata* concerning the future;
once the foremost of the twice-born have eaten, one should duly provide for them.
O best of the Bharatas, having fed the reciter and adorned him well, [one should honor him].
When the Brahmins are satisfied, all the gods are pleased.
Indeed, the man who listens to the *Harivaṃśa* according to this rite obtains the fruit of the *Atirātra* sacrifice. Furthermore,
he who performs this rite even while relying on stinginess regarding his wealth [attains the same].
As it has been said: "There is no doubt that he shall obtain the fruit here in this world.
Having heard this, the book should be given away, as well as an image, on a festival day.
One should diligently please the teacher as well as the Brāhmaṇa;
and when the reciter is fully satisfied, he bestows auspicious and unsurpassed joy.
When the reciter is fully satisfied, there arises a most excellent and auspicious joy;
therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, the invitation of the twice-born must be performed.
"With all desired objects according to rule, and with various kinds of virtuous people—thus has this procedure been described by me to you, O best of bipeds. (HV App. I, 40.155–156)
One must indeed possess faith regarding that which you ask me.
Janamejaya said:
O you of noble vows, by what ritual procedure is this meritorious *Harivaṃśa* to be heard?
A person should listen to this constantly and recite it with a self-controlled mind.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, I shall tell you all of that; listen with an undivided mind.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, the god Nārāyaṇa Hari,
as well as Vyāsa the son of Parāśara, and both me and you, O Lord of the World,
one should first worship the book with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having bathed, being pure and serene in soul, a man should take the book with his left hand;
having paid homage with his right hand according to the prescribed rite,
that man should always cause even a single chapter to be heard by the gods.
Having become restrained in speech and purified, one should recite a single chapter for the sake of the Gandharvas, Piśācas, and likewise the Guhyakas; thereafter,
with self-control, one should read as much as one is able.
A Brahmin should constantly and perpetually recite [this] to Hari, the Lord of Gods,
during times of happiness and sorrow, as well as in anger, and likewise during rites for the gods,
rites for the ancestors, on journeys, at weddings, and even at auspicious ceremonies.

Every evening and morning, O King, as well as whenever there is agitation of the mind; at the beginning of a study session, at its conclusion, and in the presence of receiving instruction— O Great King, one should have [the text] recited on each of these occasions for the sake of prosperity.
The deeds of the God of gods are indeed meritorious day and night;
therefore, O King, one should recite the lineage of Hari with every effort.
This should not be spoken to atheists, nor to the ungrateful, nor to the wicked.
Or even while reciting it, O Indra among kings, one should then remain silent and self-controlled;
otherwise, O King, one becomes a sinner—of this there is no doubt.
For the life-story of Keśava is eternal and bestows the fourfold aims of human existence.
Therefore, O Bhārata, this must always be guarded by you in all circumstances.
It should be spoken to one who is desirous of hearing it, after having paid homage to Janārdana.
The listener, established in self-restraint and pure, should hear it with a mind focused on nothing else.

And hear this other matter as well, O King; be diligent in it. This is the sequence for breaking the fast: one should gather *darbha* grass in a vessel, bring water-jars, and perform the breaking of the fast at the outset.
O King, when the breaking of the fast is completed, he should perform a ritual bath;
O Indra among kings, he should also give a pair of fine garments to the reciter,
and with great effort, he should also give rubies, gold, land, and cows.

By that, the delighted Hari-Viṣṇu shall lead [the devotee] to union with his own self. "This is meritorious! This is meritorious! the great sage said. The man who always causes this to be heard for Hari, according to his ability, [attains the highest goal].
One should constantly practice the recitation "Hareḥ vaṃśam, hareḥ vaṃśam.
O King, while the *Harivaṃśa* stands [as a refuge], who indeed would go to hell?
Even if one were wretched, whom do they say has fear of hell?
O King, O best of men, by hearing this and by performing its ritual conclusion (*pāraṇa*), one who is constantly diligent attains the highest welfare. {Sūta said:}

Thus, O Brahmin, I have declared to you this merit of the concluding ceremony (*pāraṇa*) and the procedure for the recitations (*śravaṇa*); these two have been proclaimed by me in the chanting of the *Mahābhārata*. It is a great book, of great meaning, and based upon a great war.
Because it is upheld by the great ones, it is called the *Mahābhārata*.
One should constantly listen to the *Bhārata* and one should recite the *Bhārata*.
