why is it that you lie in the midst of the single ocean, assuming the form of a child?
"O sinless one, by what name are you known in the world, and who are you, O Blessed One?
I conjecture that you are a great being; no ordinary being dwells here."
The Blessed One said: "I am Nārāyaṇa, I am Brahmā, the source of all embodied beings;
I am the cause of the origin of all creatures and the destroyer of all beings."
I am Brahmā and I am Rudra; I am the all-pervading one.
O Śakra, I am in the position of Indra, and I am also the year among the seasons.
I am the age, I am that which is called the age, and I am the revolution of the age.
I am all beings and all the deities without exception;
among the serpents I am Śeṣa, and among all birds I am Tārkṣya.
I am the thousand-headed heaven, who am encompassed by my strides;
I am the Āditya, the Person of Sacrifice, the divine sacrifice, and the ritual offering. I am Agni, the bearer of oblations, and the imperishable Lord of aquatic creatures.
On this earth, that Brahmin whose self has been purified through austerity over many births and whose soul is disciplined is called a *yati* among the best of the twice-born.
He is the possessor of knowledge who has seen the Self of the universe, the best among yogis in the knowledge of yoga;
he is the end-maker of all beings, known as Time for all things.
I am action, the agent, and the living soul; I am the seer of the dharma in all things.
I am devoid of action within all beings, the eternal light of the self.
I am the primordial God, the Primal Person (Puruṣa), unexhausted and immutable;
I am the Dharma and the austerity of those dwelling in all stages of life.
I am the horse-headed god in the great ocean of the Milky Sea;
I alone am the supreme Ṛta and Satya, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati).
I am Sāṃkhya, I am Yoga, and I am that supreme state;
I am Bhava, who is to be praised, and I am remembered as the Lord of Knowledge.
I am light, I am wind, I am earth, I am the sky;
I am the waters and the oceans, the stars, and the ten directions. I am the rain, I am Soma, I am Parjanya, and I am the sun.
I am the ocean Kṣīroda, the sea, and the submarine fire Vaḍavāmukha; becoming the fire of universal destruction, Saṃvartaka, I drink the oblation consisting of water.
I am the ancient and supreme, and likewise I am the ultimate refuge;
I am the source of what has been, what is to be, and what is present.
You are the future in every respect, the one who will come to be, and the source of all that exists. Whatever you see and whatever you hear— anything at all— [is you].
And whatever you experience in this world, all that is considered mine.
"The universe was created by me in the past, and behold me as I create it today;
and in age after age, O Mārkaṇḍeya, I shall create the entire world."
Therefore, Mārkaṇḍeya, comprehend all of this in its entirety.
Desiring to hear me and longing for dharma, move happily within my belly.
Brahmā resides within my body, as do the gods together with the ṛṣis.
Know me, the unconquered, as the manifest union with the unmanifest.
I am the mantra of one syllable and indeed of three syllables in every respect; I am the supreme three-word mantra, the manifestation of the purpose of the three aims of life.
Thus, in the ancient Purāṇas and in the Vedānta,
the Great Sage [Vyāsa] quickly extracted this clearly from the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
Then he who assumes the universal form caused him to enter his belly;
thereafter, that best of sages entered the belly of the Blessed One.
Having attained [this state], he rejoiced happily, desiring to hear about the imperishable Haṃsa.
Having resorted to that syllable in various ways,
the Lord known as Haṃsa moved slowly through the great ocean from which the moon and sun had vanished.
He creates the world and moves about it as time passes.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having become Āpava, that omnipresent Lord indeed performed ascetic penance.
Having covered his own body with himself, the one born from a jar [Agastya]—
Then the Great-Souled One, possessed of supreme power, being the source of the universe, reflected upon the creation of the world and the five great elements.
As he was thus reflecting there, his self purified by austerity,
[he perceived] the subtle and deep world consisting of water, which is without space.
Remaining within the water, he slightly agitated the ocean;
then, by that subsequent wave, a subtle opening appeared there.
There, having become the movement of sound and arising from the fluidity of the wind,
that unshakeable breath (samīraṇa) increased once it had found its opening.
Agitated by that powerful one as he moved about in various ways, the ocean was violently churned;
its waves, struck by one another’s force, dashed against each other.
When the great ocean was agitated and its waters churned,
the lord Vaiśvānara, the radiant one whose path is black, came into being.
Then the Fire-god dried up much water;
due to the depletion of the ocean, a vast opening appeared in the sky.
Due to the great depletion of the ocean, a hole was formed from which there issued forth holy waters resembling one's own vital energy,
like the taste of nectar.
Space arises from apertures; wind is born from space.
Seeing the clarified butter produced from friction and the fire born of that butter, the god, the creator of the great elements, was filled with joy.
Having seen the beings, the imperishable Blessed One, possessing many forms, reflected upon the purpose of the world's creation along with the birth of Brahmā.
When the cycle of a thousand yugas, numbering as many as the four ages,
has passed, [that which occurs] on earth for the best of the twice-born whose souls are purified by austerity—
A Brahmin who has suppressed the self through many births, an excellent ascetic,
possessed of knowledge, having perceived the Self of the universe, is the best among yogins, knowing the yoga of yogins.
Recognizing him as one possessed of yoga and endowed with complete sovereignty and prowess,
the Lord of the Universe, the knower of yoga, appoints him to the office of Brahmā.
Then, in those great waters, Hari Acyuta, this son of Pāvaka,
sleeps, plays, and rejoices in various ways.
Then he produced a single lotus arising from his navel,
with a thousand petals, stainless, radiant as the sun, and golden.
Then that lotus, possessing the luster of the blazing flames of a sacrificial fire,
fragrant and with the brilliance of the stainless autumn sun,
shone forth with noble splendor.
The body-hair of that great-souled one was beautiful to behold.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then he created one of great splendor, the best among those who know yoga.
The creator of all beings, Brahmā, whose face is turned in every direction.
Upon that golden lotus, extending for many *yojanas*,
composed of all qualities of splendor and endowed with the characteristics of the earth;
And those great seers who know the ancient lore declare that this lotus, the supreme tree of the earth, was born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
That goddess who is seated upon the lotus, they declare to be the Earth;
and those which are the essence of the sprouts from her womb, they know to be the divine mountains.
And Himavat and Meru, Nīla and Niṣadha as well,
Kailāsa and Muñjavant, and likewise the mountain Gandhamādana.
[He saw] Puṇya and Triśikhara, as well as the lovely Mandara;
the excellent mountain Udaya, Vindhya, and Mount Asta.
These are the hermitages of the hosts of gods, of the great-souled Siddhas, and of those of virtuous conduct— mountains endowed with all objects of desire.
The region between these is known as Jambūdvīpa;
it is there that the Yajñiyas performed the calculation of Jambūdvīpa.
The water that flows from the womb, which is like the nectar-essence of the gods,
is known as divine rivers, possessing the beauty of hundreds of celestial bathing places.
But those filaments of the lotus that extend all around are,
upon the earth, the innumerable mountains of all the elements.
O lord of men, those numerous petals of the lotus that point upwards are conceived as the inaccessible Mleccha lands, strewn with mountains.
Those lotus petals situated below, which served as dwellings, were divided respectively for the Daityas and the great-souled Uragas; that was Pātāla.
That which is situated below them is designated as "Water" (udaka),
where men who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka) sink down.
That great mass of water of the single ocean which exists intensely at the edge of the lotus is said to be the four collections of watery oceans situated in the cardinal directions.
This manifestation of the seer Nārāyaṇa originated from the great lotus;
therefore, it is designated by the name Puṣkara.
For this reason, the ancient supreme seers who were knowers of that [truth],
performers of sacrifice, and perceivers of the meaning revealed in the Vedas, have prescribed the lotus-rite in the sacrifice.
Thus was the supreme ordinance of the universe established by the Blessed One within the lotus,
fashioning the mountains, the rivers, and the lands.
O King, it is from this very source that the origin of all the gods, Gandharvas, and Rakshasas is derived; therefore, they are known as the Pauṣkarikas.
Vibhu, likewise of incomparable power,
the illustrious and great-souled Prabhākara,
the Self-born One himself, then created that upon his bed.
The lotus-ordinance pervading the world within the great ocean.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
At the transition of a thousand yugas, when the beginning of the four yugas has occurred...
In Tamas was born the great Asura named Madhu,
and his other companion, Kaiṭabha, was born in Rajas.
Possessed by *rajas* and *tamas*, those two were born able to assume any form at will;
both Madhu and Kaiṭabha arose as obstacles to his ascetic penance.
The two great asuras, wearing black and red garments, with white, blazing, and formidable fangs, agitated the entire waters of the single ocean.
Both were exceedingly fierce and formidable, radiant with armlets and bracelets;
they had large, distorted, copper-colored eyes, broad chests, and mighty arms.
With massive heads and firm frames, they were like two moving mountains;
resembling dark blue clouds and possessing faces like the sun.
With hands as copper-red as lightning and clouds, they were exceedingly terrifying;
with the force of their footsteps, they seemed to be tossing up the ocean.
As if shaking Hari, the slayer of enemies, as he lay there,
those two roamed about in that lotus which faces every direction.
As they beheld the one of radiant form, the foremost of yogins, the infallible Acyuta;
having approached that blazing one, the best among yogins, they then gazed upon him.
Commanded by Nārāyaṇa, he was creating all living beings,
as well as all the deities and the mental sons who were the sages.
Then those two best of asuras, arrogant, enraged with a desire to fight, and their eyes bloodshot with fury, spoke there to Brahmā.
Who are you, seated in the middle of the lotus, wearing a white turban and possessing four faces?
Disregarding us both out of delusion, you sit there free from all distress.
"Come, O Lotus-born One, give us battle!
It is not possible for us two, who are preeminent heroes, to remain standing in combat."
You are unable to remain in the ocean in the presence of us two supreme beings.
Who are you? What is your origin? By whom have you been impelled here?
Who is your creator and who is your protector? By what name are you designated?
Brahmā said:
"Who is he that is called 'Who' (ka) in the world, though unknown by the thousands? Why do you not understand me through the yoga of being born from him?"
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"O great sage, there is nothing superior to us in this world;
by us the entire universe is covered with darkness and passion."
We two, consisting of passion and darkness, are characterized by suffering for ascetics;
we are deceivers of those whose nature is righteousness and are difficult for all embodied beings to cross.
By us two, who are exalted, the world is deluded age after age;
we two are wealth and desire, as well as sacrifices and all forms of possession.
Where there is happiness, where there is joy, where there is prosperity, humility, and statesmanship—
whatever they desire, that very thing you two must consider.
Brahmā said:
"O best of those possessed of yoga, having concentrated that which is primordial and not born from a womb,
I, endowed with qualities, am established in the state of pure being (sattva)."
In that very God, the Lord of Yoga, from whom this entire universe has arisen during the transition of the ages, I have taken refuge age after age.
"O young women, having seen you, I have previously conquered [all others];
let not those two wicked ones trouble me, for I am established in this essence."
That which is the supreme for those disciplined in yoga, the imperishable and indeed the very essence (sattva);
he who is the creator of both passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), and the source of the individual soul (jīva).
He from whom all beings, whether characterized by goodness or otherwise, are born—
he alone, disciplined and self-controlled, shall subdue you both in battle.
Then, by means of his own creative power (*ātma-māyā*), Brahmā fashioned from the arm of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa— who was lying down and extended for many *yojanas*— the world.
Then, as those two mighty-armed ones were being dragged by his arm,
they were unable to move, like two birds being crushed.
Then, having gone there, those two bowed down to the eternal god Padmanābha Hṛṣīkeśa, and both of them spoke.
We know you to be the single source of the universe, the foremost among men;
this cause for our intellect has arisen for the purpose of worshipping you.
Since your vision is unfailing and true, O God who bestows all things upon the universe,
we therefore desire to behold you from every side.
Therefore, O subduer of enemies, we desire that a boon be granted by you;
O God of infallible vision, salutations be unto you, O unconquered conqueror!
The Blessed One said:
"Tell me quickly, O best of Asuras, what boons you desire; since I have granted you your lives once more, do you wish to live?"
"Therefore, O mighty ones, you shall obtain that for which you have exerted yourselves; however,
you two must become subject to death"— thus spoke Hari.
"So be it," said that god to us both; we requested that boon for our welfare. Both of us were high-souled, powerful, and devoted to the duties of the Kṣatriya.
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said: "O Lord,
O Sovereign of the Gods, we desire our death in a place where no one has ever died,
and we also wish to become your sons."
The Blessed Lord said:
"Indeed, my two sons, you shall become preeminent at the beginning of the new Kalpa; you will both come into being, of this there is no doubt. I tell you this truth."
Then, having granted a boon to the two great Asuras,
the eternal one, the all-pervading Lord who upholds the universe and is supreme over all,
[designated] those two as Bhava and Bhāvana through their qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*.
The enemy of the gods churned those two upon the surface of his thighs.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Having remained upon that lotus, Brahmā, the best among those who know Brahman, [proceeded].
Then the mighty-armed one, with arms raised high, resorted to severe asceticism.
Blazing as if with splendor, dispelling darkness with his own radiance,
that knower of all dharmas shone like the thousand-rayed sun with its beams.
Then, assuming another form, Śambhu, the imperishable Nārāyaṇa,
the eternal one of inconceivable nature, divided himself into two by means of his own self.
The highly illustrious teacher of yoga, possessed of great splendor, arrived;
and so did the wise Kapila, the preceptor of Sāṃkhya and the best among the knowers of Brahman.
These two, the best among the knowers of Brahman and Brahman itself, were praised by the celestial sages;
both were high-souled, powerful, and devoted to their sacred fields (kṣetra).
Having arrived there, those two of immeasurable luster— conversant with the distinctions between the higher and the lower, and honored by the supreme ṛṣis— spoke to Brahmā.
Because of your greatness and because of your state as Brahman, you are eternally Brahmā, O All-pervading Lord;
because of your multiplicity, you have many feet, and you are the soul of the universe and the support of the world.
He is the leader of all beings, Brahmā, the teacher of the world, and the most excellent.
Having heard those words of theirs, while muttering the three sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*),
he created these three worlds, just as the Vedic revelation (*brāhmaṇī śruti*) declares.
There the Lord procreated a son named Bhū;
then Brahmā went back and forth there to his imperishable mind-born [son].
But having arisen, the mind-born son spoke first to Brahmā:
"What assistance may I provide for you? Let the Blessed One speak."
Brahmā said:
"He who is named Kapila, as well as Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa—the granter of boons—speaks to you; therefore, O high-minded one, do as they say."
When Brahmā had spoken thus, and a further doubt had arisen, he, with palms joined in reverence, said: "I am desirous of hearing from you both: what should I do?"
The two Supreme Lords said:
"That which is the true, imperishable Brahman is indeed remembered as being of twenty-eight kinds;
remember that which is the true, the immortal, and the supreme."
Having heard these words, he then departed toward the northern direction;
and having gone there, he attained the state of Brahmā through the eye of knowledge.
Then the Lord Brahmā created a second [world] named Bhuvaḥ;
having fashioned it with his mind, that high-minded one did so by means of his mind alone.
Then he also spoke these words: "What shall we do? Having been commanded by the Grandfather, he approached Brahmā.
Then, accompanied by the two Brahmās, he went once more to the Blessed Lady;
having reached that supreme abode, he came into the presence of those two.
When that son had also departed, the Lord created a third;
they know him by the name Bhūrbhuva, who is skilled in the attainment of liberation.
Having attained that same dharma, he too went to the destination of those two alone.
Thus have these three sons of the high-souled Śambhu been described.
Having taken those sons of his, the Lord Nārāyaṇa and Kapila, the lord of ascetics, departed for the destination they themselves had earned.
At the very moment those two had departed and were liberated, Brahmā,
firm in his vows, once again resorted to even more rigorous asceticism.
Then Brahmā, the lord, performing austerities alone, did not find delight;
thereupon, he produced from half of his own body a beautiful wife.
By means of asceticism, splendor, radiance, and self-restraint,
he sought a wife worthy of himself and capable of creating the worlds.
Accompanied by her, Brahmā, who consists of ascetic power, took his delight there;
then [he created] all the lords of progeny (prajāpatis), as well as the oceans and the rivers.
Then he indeed created the three-footed Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas;
and he fashioned the four Vedas, which originated from the Gāyatrī.
For his own sake, the Grandsire, the creator of the worlds, produced the sons who are the lords of all creatures,
from whom the worlds have issued forth.
He first created his son, named Viśveśa, who was of great ascetic power;
he then created the holy abode of all stages of life (āśramas), known by the name Dharma.
Dakṣa, Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhṛgu, and the sage Aṅgiras.
These great seers, the sons of Brahmā, are known as the Atharvabhūtas;
now, listen to the lineages of these thirteen great seers.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Anāyuḥ, Siṃhikā, Muni,
Prādhā, Krodhā, Surasā, Vinatā, and Kadrū.
O descendant of Bharata, these twelve daughters were the offspring of Dakṣa;
may you be blessed, and the twenty-seven powerful stars were also his progeny.
Kaśyapa was the powerful son of Marīci, created through ascetic penance;
and daughters were given to Kaśyapa by Dakṣa, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
To him Dakṣa gave these twelve maidens, and he approved of them.
And the sage gave all the auspicious constellations, beginning with Rohiṇī, known as the *nakṣatras*, to Soma, the Vasu,
O Janamejaya.
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, as well as Sādhyā, the auspicious Viśvāvasuratā,
and the goddess Padmodbhavā were created of old by Brahmā.
O Bhārata, may you be blessed; these five most excellent women were given to Dharma, the best of the gods, by Brahmā, who perceives the true nature of dharma.
That wife of Brahmā, who consisted of half of his form and could assume any shape at will,
became the cow Surabhi and presented herself before Brahmā.
Then Brahmā,
who is honored by the worlds and who knows the cause for the creation of the world, approached her in sexual union for the sake of the cows, O Bhārata.
And he begot eleven sons of great stature, endowed with righteousness,
resembling the clouds of the crimson twilight, and possessing intense splendor.
Weeping and running toward the Blessed Grandfather,
they were known as the Rudras because of that weeping (rudana) and running (dravana).
Nirṛti, Sarpa, and the third, Aja Ekapāt;
Mṛgavyādha, Pinākin, Dahana, and indeed Īśvara.
The venerable Ahirbudhnya, Kapālī,
and the unconquered Senānī of great splendor— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
From that very Surabhī were born a bull,
as well as beans grown without cultivation, sand, speckled grains, and unhusked rice.
She-goats,
ewes, and buffaloes were likewise sprinkled with the urine of cows.
O Bhārata, you who know the cause of the creation of the world, for the sake of the cows...
Goats, single-hoofed animals, and likewise the supreme ambrosia,
as well as the most excellent medicinal herbs— all these arose from Surabhi.
From Dharma arose Kāma, the source of prosperity; from Sādhyā were born the Sādhyas, as well as Bhava, Prabhava, Īśāna, and Arati.
Araṇya, as well as the Maruts, Viśvāvasu, Baladhruva,
Mahiṣa, his own son Tanūja, and likewise Anagha and Vijñāna.
Matsara and Vibhūti, all the sons of Surabhi,
Suvarcas, Vṛṣa, and Nāga— these were the Sādhyas, who are honored by the worlds.
The goddess, followed by Vāsava, gave birth to a son;
the first was the god Dhara, and the second was the imperishable Dhruva.
Viśvāvasu as the third, and Soma the Lord as the fourth;
then Yogāyamāna, and immediately after him, Śama.
And then the fifth mountain, Yogendra, immediately after that.
The seventh was Vāyu, and the eighth was Nirṛti Vasu;
these were indeed the offspring of Dharma, born of Surabhi.
And the Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā from Dharma; such is the Vedic revelation.
And Dhanya, the mighty-armed, as well as Vivasvat likewise.
Dakṣa, the mighty-armed, and Vasu as his son;
Sudharmā, the mighty-armed, and Śaṅkhapād, the very powerful.
These two, Ananta and Mahīraṇa, were likewise the sons of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
Viśvāvasu, Suparvan, and the highly illustrious Viṣṭara;
and Ruru, the son of a seer, whose splendor was like that of the sun.
The Mother of the Gods gave birth to all the gods as her sons, the lords of all;
the beautiful Marutvatī gave birth to the radiant Maruts.
Agni, Cakṣus, Havis, Jyotis, Sāvitra, and Mitra; Amara, Śaravṛṣṭi, Saṃkṣaya, and Mahābhuja.
Viraja and Śukra, Viśvāvasu and Vibhāvasu; Aśmanta and Citrarasmi, as well as King Niṣṭhāvina; Kuyoni and Kṛti, Cāritra, and Bahupannaga.
And likewise, Marutvatī formerly gave birth from Dharma to the host of Maruts, including Bṛhant, Bṛhad-rūpa, and Tapanānana.
O King, from Kaśyapa and Aditi were then born the Ādityas:
Indra, Viṣṇu, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Aryaman, and Ravi.
Pūṣan, Mitra, Varada, Manu, and Parjanya—
these are the twelve Ādityas, the most excellent inhabitants of the third heaven.
To Āditya, by Sarasvatī, two auspicious sons were born,
most excellent in form and most excellent in body, the best among the embodied beings in the three heavens.
Vairaja, Babhru, and Viśvāvasu likewise;
Danu gave birth to the Dānavas, and Diti gave birth to the Daityas.
Kālā, however, [gave birth] to the Kālakeyas, the Asuras, and likewise the Rākṣasas.
Anāyuṣāyī’s daughters were Vyādhi and Adhi;
Siṃhikā was the mother of the grahas, and Muni was the mother of the gandharvas.
Prādhā, the most excellent of the Apsarases, gave birth to more Apsarases;
and Krodhā, O Bhārata, gave birth to all living beings as well as the Piśācas.
Likewise, O lord of the people, the flocks of birds, the Guhyakas,
and all four-footed creatures— except for the cows of the Surabhi lineage— [perished].
Aruṇa and Garuḍa were born of Vinatā;
the goddess Kadrū gave birth to all the Nāgas and the Mahīdharas.
In this way, O King, all the Viśvedevas increased in mutual prosperity at that time during the manifestation of the Great-Souled One on the lotus, in the Pauṣkaraka age.
I have heard from Dvaipāyana the ancient account of Puṣkara;
it has been narrated to you in its proper sequence and praised by the supreme ṛṣis.
And that high-souled person who, ever vigilant, recites this foremost, supreme, and ancient [work],
shall obtain all desires here and be freed from sorrow.
In the hereafter, he enjoys the fruits of heaven.
[Colophon] O Supreme Brahman, we have completed this wonderful account of Viṣṇu’s deeds. 44:1.574.44:1.
And also the account of the Boar incarnation, and thereafter that of the Man-Lion.
I have heard the account of Vāmana and likewise that of Pauṣkarika;
O Brahmin, I now wish to hear in truth about the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Once, on a peak of Mount Meru adorned with various jewels,
[Viṣṇu] was together with the gods, the sages, Hari, and Śaṅkara.
Dakṣa caused that unsurpassed sacrifice, Vājinegha,
to proceed. When that sacrifice had commenced, the sages of rigid vows performed various rites according to the injunctions of the scriptures.
Janamejaya said:
O Brahmin, we have heard this great account of our own lineage,
which is divine, produced through mutual succession, and honored by many virtues.
It is composed with meters born of rhythmic patterns, with very extensive compounds,
with concise and sweet-sounding expressions, and with the analysis of word-components (*padavigraha*).
It was endowed with the threefold aims of life— joined with dharma and artha—
and with desire in its many forms, residing within the body.
Through the power of the brahmins and the prowess of the warriors,
by means of the settling of enmities and by those who have fulfilled their vows;
When Ripuśravas was broken, no further pursuit was urged by the deer,
who had assumed the form of a brahmin, for the sake of destroying the lineage and its source.
And all the kingdoms of those kings who were slain in that most terrible battle were inherited by their sons.

The renowned Kaurava king was a follower of the Blessed One’s teaching; O bull among the twice-born, he proclaimed the Dharma in many ways for the excellence of the three castes, and it is celebrated as the cause of heaven even for heroes.
For the sake of favoring all beings, and never for the sake of arrogance,
[he taught] the various designations of the four castes in many distinct ways.
And as beings were falling into the womb, he was fully awakened;
he spoke to those who asked about the movement of the gods when merit is exhausted and karma is spent.
The union regarding the gift was also brought about in many ways;
by those two, a speech as sweet as honey was produced through their combined effort.
"O Brahmin, it is not possible for me to recount this great study of the *Bhārata* in a single day, even with divine vision."
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the detailed expansion and the concise summary of a day of Brahmā; for my curiosity is indeed great.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen with a single-minded focus, O King, having composed your five senses.
O King, as he was telling the story with an unwavering mind.
O King, it is connected with the lineage of Brahmā, yet unbound by karmas;
it was formerly perfected by Brahmā and was without sacrificial fees for Brahmā.
That which is the unmanifest cause is eternal, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent;
from that, the partless Puruṣa was born, originating from his own self.
The divine Lord of all beings, omnipresent, with a celestial body, is inconceivable and immutable; he is the inexhaustible source of the ages.
Unreal and unborn, having attained equality everywhere—
that which is beyond the unmanifest, those who know the ancient lore understand it to be so.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, possessing ears everywhere in the world, He stands encompassing all.
In that regard, the cause of both the non-existent and the existent must be understood:
though moving, the unmanifest is not seen even when it takes on a manifest form.
The unmanifest *vikārapuruṣa* is indeed formless, yet it assumes form;
inconceivable, it moves within all things, hidden like fire within wood.
The Lord is the source of the past and the future, the Supreme Being, the Lord of Creatures;
he is the Master of the entire world—such is his name in truth.
From the footless, however, a foot was born; from that, Nārāyaṇa came into being.
Though unmanifest, he attained manifestation through the yoga of Brahman by his own will.
Know him to be of the nature of Brahman; that Lord, the source of the entire world, both stationary and moving, obtained that sound.
"I, however," he said, "shall create progeny, O Bhārata—
I who am the source of all beings, whose thread these creatures are."
Everything arises from self-nature, and likewise it exists through self-nature;
and this entire world arises from the self-nature of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
All-pervading, without support, ungraspable, victorious, and eternal—
this light consisting of Brahman is designated by the word "Brahman."
Though unmanifest, he has attained manifestation through the five characteristics of ritual;
maintaining the manifestation of Brahman, he moves about extensively in manifold ways.
Then, having assumed a form by his own nature as impelled by Brahman,
Brahmā created the water by which all this is pervaded.
Then, having first beheld the wind, he who is the supreme among sustainers (dhātṛ) receives the designation "sustainer" (dhātṛ), which is known throughout the world, because of his act of sustaining.
In the beginning, this entire world was produced from Vāyu;
O Sarasvatī, even the gods themselves have long since transcended this.
One who desires the word "earth" perceives water as something distinct;
yet it is perceived in its entirety through both its solidity and its fluidity.
Because he was the source of water and because he was sinking in the water due to his own fruit,
the one born from the waters uttered auspicious words, as if filling the space on all sides.
"I truly wish to stand upright, yet I am sinking; lift me up!
[I am in] this deep-watered hole, its interior agitated by waves."
The goddess, bearing a form of radiant energy, causes all beings to flourish;
she has arisen according to her proper application, seeking her domain everywhere.
Having heard her speech and those well-spoken words,
he assumed the form of a boar and plunged into the great ocean.
Having lifted the earth from the waters and performed that most difficult task,
he entered into dissolution through meditative absorption (samādhi) and, being absorbed, was no longer seen.
That light consisting of Brahman which is designated as "space" (ākāśa)—
therein was born Brahmā, the grandfather of all beings.
Even now, he is sustained in his mind by the Creator, whose source is Brahman,
through subtle yoga of knowledge and out of a desire for the welfare of all beings.
Having pierced through the center of the earth, he goes toward his source;
meanwhile, the Sun stands above, as if scorching with his rays.
From the center of that mandala, however, a secondary mandala emerged;
from it was born the eternal Brahmā, who attained the gentle nature of Soma.
From the edge of the lunar mandala, the wind arose,
a light consisting of that syllable, increasing light upon light.
But from that knowledge consisting of yoga, which by its very nature arises from Brahman,
he creates the divine Puruṣa, the eternal source of Brahman.
That which was the liquid water became the solid earth;
the cavity therein is space (ākāśa), and that which is light is indeed the eye.
It vibrates by means of the wind, and from the conjunction [of elements] arises the manifestation of light;
from the Person (puruṣa) comes the Great Being (mahat), consisting of the five elements.
That eternal self of all beings is indeed my eternal body in each and every [form];
knowledge is hidden in the cave [of the heart], and through yoga, it is the eternal sacrifice.
That very form of the sun which is the fire dwelling within embodied beings,
is eternally joined and united with the bodily constituents within the body.
Through its own nature it goes to destruction, and through its own nature it goes to existence;
through its own nature it finds peace, and through its own nature it does not find [peace].
With his soul utterly deluded by the senses, he is bewildered regarding the state of Brahman;
through his actions, he undergoes both birth and death.
As long as one does not reach that sphere of Brahman here through knowledge,
so long does one undergo saṃsāra and births again and again.
When, indeed, through yoga he becomes distinct from the senses,
then, having attained the state of Brahman, he remains established at the beginning of the dissolution.
This world is forbidden to him, yet he becomes a possessor of Brahman;
he does not go by means of the exhaustion of passion, nor does he ever become attached.
Having attained supreme perfection, the omniscient one knows the coming and going, as well as the death and birth, of all living beings.
The destinies of the self, as well as the range of its objects, were previously brought about by karma; now he is established in the station of Brahmā.
One should restrain the knots of the mind with the intellect and the former torments as well;
being rent asunder by detachment, like the ocean agitated by the wind.
The heart, which was constricted, is ripened by the eye of knowledge through others;
here, indeed, the Self as proclaimed by Brahmā is liberated from the bondage of the body.
By means of his knowledge, he may even create another world or withdraw it;
like an embodiment of splendor, he may even emanate this world as if it were pierced [by his power].
Even those who have gone to the animal realm due to actions resembling those leading to hell shall be liberated from them by means of a mind united with Brahman.
Both the imperishable (*akṣara*) and the perishable (*kṣara*) are known through the practice of yoga;
yet the imperishable does not exist therein, for that Brahman is eternal and beyond all actions.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Whatever breach was made upon the earth by the expanding Tapaṇa, [it was filled].
Then Maināka was placed upon it, remaining immovable as ordained by his own nature.
Through its peaks it attains the state of being a mountain, designated by that name;
and because it is immovable, it possesses immovability by its very nature—it is indeed Meru itself.
On the very broad back of that mountain,
on that [place], dwells a manifest man of great supernatural power, born of light;
he has been ordained by that very Supreme Self through his own nature.
That splendor consisting of Brahman which is deposited within the head—
its form is composed of light, radiant, and having the shape of a person.
Emerging from his mouth, blazing as if with splendor,
he was endowed with four faces and four excellent arms.
From his mouth, Brahmā was born; Brahmā is the preeminent among Brahmins. That very same great being has now returned to the state of existence once more.
In former times, O lord of the earth, the goddess Earth was submerged in the depths of the waters;
she was fifty crores in extent here in the east.
Together with the shell of the cosmic egg, including its mountains, forests, and groves.
Having attained the state of Brahmā from the abode of Brahmā, he who was beyond the world entered into the world.
At the junction of the steps, the peak of Meru then became the world of Brahmā,
rising a hundred yojanas and indeed a hundred thousand yojanas high.
In this very way, its extent multiplied by the four qualities is such that it cannot be calculated by anyone at all,
even with many thousands of concise summaries or with a divine mind.
O King of kings, that mountain was surrounded on all four sides by stone walls extending for a hundred *yojanas* in width.
It has been multiplied by hundreds of millions upon millions of times by those who discourse on Brahman,
who are ever-yoked in yoga, eternally perfected, and constantly devoted to Brahman.
Together with the Maruts, the lords of the gods, the Rudras, and the Vasus,
as well as the Ādityas along with the Viśvedevas, he protected the rulers of the earth.
And the Blessed One, together with Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, and Vivasvat, protected the earth, O King, when it had been brought to a state of total destruction.
O Bhārata, by means of that Brahmin form attained through the realization of Brahman,
that splendor consisting of Viṣṇu has reached a state of equality everywhere.
That which is indeed called "Brahman" by the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas—
those who are devoted to the vow of truth and have attained it through many disciplines.
Thus these three worlds are gathered together during the day of Brahmā;
on that day, the unmanifest Brahman and the manifest are established in the vital breath.
The constant duty of Brahmā, impelled by his own power,
proceeds through his very being for those who always speak without deceit.
"This is the beneficial," so it was declared by the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas—
that which is designated as the one Brahman, the state that has attained universality.
That supreme splendor consisting of Viṣṇu, which has attained the state of being the universe (*viśvatva*),
is designated by the word "universe" (*viśva*) because of the multiplicity of its manifestations.
by Brahmins who have become one with Brahman and are devoted to the vow of truth;
Bringing about the state of being the form of the intellect— the form of Manu which is the universal form—
the Blessed One thus first created that pair, the primordial couple.
That very same eternal Lord Viśva, together with the Goddess,
having ordained vast enjoyments, moves about as Brahmā accompanied by his followers.
This very Blessed One, Brahmā, is eternally the foremost among those who know Brahman;
he is the guide for those traveling the path to Nirvāṇa and those seeking the way of possessing nothing.
From Soma, who took the form of the flowing water, Soma was born;
he was consecrated as the commander-in-chief of all beings by Maheśvara.
Having consecrated the Lord of Beings and performed his duties according to his own nature, he then uttered a roar; for that reason, she is called the River (Nadī).
Having surpassed the attainable world of Brahmā in a thousand ways,
that goddess descended from the sky to the earth and spread forth in seven streams.
O king of kings, manifesting this world and that world in a thousand ways and many ways again and again, he brings about their production from the perishable.
From that, living beings arose, as well as the fruits of the great elements;
from that, all undertakings of action proceeded for the wise.
From his lotus-like face, through his four mouths,
there issued forth that perfection consisting of syllables, which had attained the state of lordship.
His merit, consisting of knowledge, was eternal and possessed four quarters;
here, the god Brahmā, the Grandfather, became its Lord.
The Dharma has four feet by which this world is supported:
through manifest celibacy and through the purifying life of a householder.
Through the state of being a guru and through speech that follows the secret path—
these are the four steps of Dharma, proclaimed as the cause for attaining heaven.
Through justice, through dharma, and through the secret [teaching], Soma waxes in his orb;
Brahmā, together with those who practice sacred study, and the eternal Vedas continue to exist.
Then the ancestors are satisfied by the salutation of householders,
and the sages dwelling upon the summit of the mountain are likewise gratified through dharma.
Behold that mountain, the supreme peak of Meru;
having pressed his testicles with his feet, he is being deliberated upon by those sages.
Holding his neck and bending his back, as if laughing,
he placed both hands upon the region of the navel and drew all his limbs together.
Lifting Brahmā up to his head with his mind, that Grandfather,
through the yoga of the Lord of Yoga, mentally created Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu, with his senses distinct, was like one image raised from another;
the god, bearing a form of radiant light, was like the moon risen in the sky.
By means of the yoga of Brahman, that lord shone like another thousand-rayed sun,
illuminating the midst of the sky with incomparable splendors.
The deluded self does not perceive the eternal Brahman,
which stands manifest in the middle of the forehead, divided in two with respect to its functions.
Those who delight in the domain of the inner self first perceive with their intellect the luminous orb of the sun and the moon connected to the eyes.
Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and devoted to the vow of truth—none others ever perceive it; they do not understand the inner self (adhyātma).
O King, the Lord of Beings on earth, whose nature is disunion, was possessed by a mind fallen into delusion through practices involving violence toward all living creatures.
O Bhārata, having applied themselves through various despicable deeds to the slaughter of all living beings, men [suffer] within their own bodies.
Then Brahmā, with a concentrated mind, by reason of having attained liberation,
[beheld] that great light, a radiance shaped like the lunar disc.
Having quickly entered the heart between the eyes by means of the Gāyatrī,
[one perceives] the origin of the embryo, which consists of fourfold aspects of the Puruṣa.
Consisting of Brahman-splendor, unmanifest, eternal, stable, and imperishable,
he is not joined with the qualities of the senses, but is joined with the quality of light.
Resplendent, resembling the pure rays of the moon, and established in Brahman,
the Lord generated from his two eyes the Ṛgveda together with the Yajus.
The Sāmaveda from the tip of his tongue and the Atharvaveda from his head;
as soon as they were born, those Vedas truly found their field.
Because they find that state, they have attained the nature of the Vedas;
then those Vedas create the primordial, eternal Brahman.
A person possessing a divine form and luster through their respective dispositions and mental inclinations;
that which is the Atharvan portion is remembered as the head of the sacrifice.
Then the region between the neck and the arms became the portion of the *Ṛgveda*;
the heart and the sides were fashioned as the portion of the *Sāmaveda*;

Thus, this collection of Yajus portions, arranged as a sacrifice,
has become a Person (Puruṣa) possessing a divine splendor, born indeed from the immortal state.
For that sacrifice consists of the Veda and brings happiness to all beings;
O dear one, it is eternal and free from violence, pertaining to both worlds.
He who understands the undertaking of yoga, the eternal celibacy accomplished through action,
and the source of all beings— he is a knower of the Veda.
He is proclaimed a *siddha* in the world; there is no doubt that he is indeed perfection itself, [as recognized] by the sages who have transcended all actions and mastered the Vedas.
"‘This is a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice’— thus do those who have mastered the Vedas declare,
the Brāhmaṇas who are weary from their observances, regarding the state of the Vedic Upaniṣads."
Janamejaya said:
O great sage, I wish to hear according to the truth the cause for the perception of the mind, which is grasped by the mental faculty through desire.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Bhārata, there is indeed no external cause for this;
rather, O King, the cause is internal, pertaining to the body and the mind."
By which means mortals who are Brahmins of firm vows know that which is to be known.

O Lord of the Earth, even that which is unknowable becomes knowable, and that which cannot be known through ritual action can be known by a disciplined Brāhmaṇa who constantly devotes himself to the Brahman, who always knows the reality of things, and who seeks the cause of spiritual perfection.
And always remaining pure and disciplined in his sacred duties,
that twice-born man should attend upon his teacher with his hands joined in reverence.
In the evening and in the morning, the knower of reality, disciplined, with a concentrated mind and a sage-like disposition toward the Brahman, should perform the rites leading to liberation.
He should mentally attain the supreme station of Viṣṇu;
by meditating thus, the twice-born man of concentrated mind shall become serene.
He shall go to the supreme Brahman with an unchanging mind,
knowing the state of non-rebirth, free from the sense of "mine" due to being released from the bond of worldly existence.
They call that very thing the Imperishable (akṣara), which is that eternal Brahman;
for it is not revealed by the yoga of action, nor is it revealed by the yoga of knowledge.
Of those disciplined Brāhmaṇas who have gathered at the station of Viṣṇu,
who possess all material goods in abundance, and who censure the application of desire;
The worlds of those who do not return are established through the application of action,
O King, performed with a mind free from grasping in every deed.
Through grasping a living being is bound; through non-grasping one is liberated.
O lord of men, the attainment of ritual action by a living being comes from the Brahmins due to their previous birth.
Released from the bondage of the senses and having attained the supreme state,
he does not again assume a human bodily form.
[Colophon] Janamejaya said:
"Tell me of the obstacle, the application, and that state which is to be meditated upon."
I wish to hear, according to the truth, about the accomplishments (siddhi) and the qualities of those accomplishments.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen in detail to everything that you ask with your intelligence,
with a focused mind, concerning the various accounts of Brahmā and the others.
O King, for one who perceives Brahman with a mind disciplined by yoga, having abandoned the qualities of the five senses that dwell within those five senses, [he attains liberation].
Listen as I describe that manifold form of the eternal Brahmayajña, which Brahmā, while reflecting upon it, proclaimed due to his lack of sovereign power.
O Bhārata, [this is the state] of the village of the five senses with nine gates,
which is obstructed by desire and anger, yet firmly restrained by wisdom.
Having placed his splendor upon the head, a great smoke billowed forth,
possessing the luster of blue and red, along with yellow and white minerals.
With the luster of the color of madder-dye, as well as resembling the color of pigeons,
with the brilliance of pure vaidūrya gems, and with the radiance of lotus petals.

With [palaces] made of crystal, shining with the colors of excellent jewels, resembling the lords of serpents, possessing the hue of indragopaka insects, and radiant like moonbeams and water; HV_App.I,41.847–848.
With masses of smoke of many colors, possessing a splendor like that of Indra’s bow,

those dense masses, smoke-colored and bearing water,
discharged torrents of liquid and entered the depths of the earth.
And upon his head, the powerful mental fire was fanned,
joined with supreme yoga and enveloped by hundreds of flames.

blazing like the fires at the end of an eon.
As many as there were streams of rain,
so many rays of light from the fire converged upon the vast surface of the earth along with those torrents of water.
And when joined with the two syllables, the great wind vibrates intensely;
arising from the qualities of divine perfection, it is subtle and increases the vital breath.
Possessing speed, with a terrifying roar, powerful and within the range of vital breath;
he was joined together with those very masses of fire and the constituent elements.
Then, having assumed thousands and hundreds of diverse forms—
fire, wind, water, earth, and the elements— he was impelled by Brahmā.
O Lord of the Earth, having attained the state of inherence, they became the seed;
O King, the constituent elements were brought together by the power of Brahman.
That Brahman who is between the two eyes is the subtle Virāj Puruṣa;
from those two, the Supreme Person created many other subtle beings.
This very Lord Viṣṇu is both manifest and unmanifest, eternal;
he is the support of all beings and the one who brings about the end of dissolution at the time of universal destruction.
Impelled by Brahman, all those inner persons— who are the knowers of pleasure and pain— enter him who is bound at the crown of the head with the elements.
Then those forms, equal to Brahman, began to move;
having pierced through the goddess Earth, they proceeded toward the ten directions.
Thus all these kings, sages created by Brahmā,
have gone to dissolution right there and attain the state of the earth.
Through the exhaustion of karma, they are liberated from the elements and the bonds of karma;
through liberation from the exhaustion of karma and from the bondage of the senses,
they return to that very primordial nature (prakṛti) which is unknown through the spheres of action.
From the perishable comes the cessation of smoke; these [beings] have fire within them and consist of austerity.
By this, existence and non-existence proceed, veiled like a thread.
From smoke clouds are produced; from the cloud comes pure water.
From water the earth is produced, and upon the earth is whatever fruit there is.
From the fruit, the sap was produced; and from the sap, the vital breath of embodied beings arose.
The sap, however, was born as consisting of that which is the eternal Brahman.
Pradhāna has been designated as Brahman for many other reasons by the Brāhmaṇas who are exhausted by asceticism and devoted to the vow of truth.
O Bhārata, that which had attained manifestation from the unmanifest through its own nature,
moving within all beings together with knowledge.
O Indra among kings, though the agent of action exists manifoldly within the realm of objects,
it is not perceived by the eyes of those whose sins have been burnt away by austerity.
It is perceived by the wise who discourse upon Brahman with their two eyes;
having emerged from between his eyebrows, he is like the sun released from the clouds.
O Kauravya, by those who move through the world like birds— free from dualities and devoid of possessions— the certain fruit is attained through the practice of yoga.
Brahmā ordains the manifestation and the decay of beings, as well as their destruction; likewise, he exists during the period of dissolution.

The knower of the application of action [knows] that action [arises] from the elements; there is no doubt in this matter. It is for the non-destruction of the world and for the advancement of dharma as well.
Twelve thousand [years] constitute a yuga known as a thousand-yuga cycle;
this is called the Brahma-yuga, the first among the ages (yugas).
At the end of two thousand yugas, there is a dissolution that brings about the final end;
the worlds become subtle, changeless, and insentient.
Likewise, when the entire eternal world has reached dissolution,
it becomes merged into the subtle Brahman, which was fashioned by the causal qualities (guṇas).

O Brahmin, for one who has attained Brahman in its entirety during the first two ages, [there is no rebirth].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen in detail to everything that you ask me with your intelligence,
with a disciplined mind that accomplishes its purpose through faith in the divine.
But the Blessed One, whose self is yoga and who is born of Brahman, having attained supernatural power,
the Lord and Master brought about the abundance of living beings here on earth.
Seated upon the Brahmā-throne, the Lord Brahmā was suddenly distracted;
