And one is attached to the state consisting of omniscience regarding the object of liberation,
because thousands of such states come into being and cease to be.
Through yoga, he always performs the Brahma-sacrifice, which consists of the Vedas;
from this, vast knowledge and sovereignty arise for Brahman.
Then, desiring the welfare of all beings, Brahmā— who had become the Supreme Brahman— first set in motion that sovereignty while engaged in yoga.
But when the sovereignty of space proceeds for one who is engaged in yoga—
Brahmā, who has become Brahman through unchanging action— then [he attains it].
Then the stainless and imperishable Brahman reached the intermediate space;
it was the dissolution of all beings, both moving and stationary, as well as of those who discourse on Brahman.
Embodied beings attained a state of permanence through their connection with sovereign powers.
Through union with that which has become the sovereignty of space for the proponents of Brahman,
the sovereignty that is currently operating causes it to become like the wind,
accompanied by many transformations that have been attained, which are falling together and possess great power.
When these transformations have been fully realized and completely restrained on all sides,
the brahmin certainly attains sovereignty and becomes a perfected one (siddha).
Having emerged from the body, he runs through the sky;
then, being himself without support, he takes as his support those who are without support by means of the mind.
The elemental self (bhūtātman), having become sovereign, moves through the sky and is not seen even by many eyes in this world that are equal to those of Purandara.
Those best of Brahmins who, having withdrawn from all desires, study the syllable *oṃ* with their minds— those virtuous ones behold it.
For this is the supreme Brahman of the wise Brāhmaṇas;
know that it moves within all beings together with consciousness.
"This is the great sound, the ancient one born of Brahman;
having become wind and attained the imperishable, the twice-born speak thus."
Formless yet endowed with form, united with the elements,
he moves within living beings, acting according to his will as a master.
Then, having first meditated with their minds as if filling [the space],
those wise ones contemplated that sacrifice which consists of the Vedas.
The pure and self-controlled Brahmins of his lineage,
desiring the world of Brahmā and the supreme station of Viṣṇu, attained glory.
For this reason, O Bhārata, they perform all their activities free from feverish distress; indeed, these [sages] do not desire existence through procreation or acquisition.
O twice-born ones, with three kinds of offerings of garlands and with three types of inspired hymns,
they worship Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, whose prowess is truth.
O King, those who were preceded by Brahmā performed both the sacrifice and the heroic stride;
and Brahmā, with words declared in the Vedas, [addressed] the Vaiṣṇava splendor.
By Brahmins who were learned in the Vedas, knowers of Brahman, and exponents of Brahman;
by those who were pure, liberated from ritual action, and devoted to the vow of truth.
And at the time of liberation, that Great-Souled One is perceived through the elements;
He alone is the supreme Brahman, the most wonderful manifestation of Viṣṇu.
That sovereignty, which is of the nature of rasa, is seen at the end of the transformations;
those transformations of terrible form cause distress even to the Great-Souled One.
Being excessively covered by water, agitated and deprived of consciousness,
he is indeed overwhelmed by waves that manifest as both cold and hot.
Even when he has entered the great ocean, he is not burned and does not become stuck;
even when great rivers are broken [by him], he sinks in the water.
Sinking into cold water, he is forcibly cast down;
deprived of his senses, he is provided with neither food nor clothing.
And as he enters the abyss,
he is drenched with copious white-colored water from all sides upon his head by means of a stream.
Beholding the upward light, he is covered by white and yellow [clouds],
filled with water and very deep, shining as if with flashes of lightning.
When these transformations have been fully resolved and completely ceased,
the Brahmin attains eternal sovereignty and becomes perfected.
That sovereignty, consisting of nectar, issued forth from the tip of his tongue;
spread out in a thousand streams, it assumed the form of a cloud.
That perfected Lord creates various combinations of tastes for the sake of the bodily constituents of all beings, by means of the cause attained through yoga.
The form and sovereignty of his splendor increase along with its transformations;
remaining composed for the sake of the Brahmins, he brings no obstacle to himself.
He is struck by those of fierce form and violent transformations who carry staffs in their hands—
beings of terrible aspect, profound depth, tawny-eyed, and possessing human bodies.
Tearing out his terrible eye, he reaches the tip of his tongue;
yawning again and again, they simultaneously let out roars.
Then, having once again assumed many forms,
they began to dance, sing, and especially offer libations.
And all of them, having become women, hung on together while practicing their yoga;
and because of his many forms, he tempted them with obstacles at their throats.
They address him with sweet words, not out of fear;
bowing their heads, they all fall simultaneously at his feet.
Desiring serenity and fearing internal obstacles to yoga,
they speak in many ways and dance and take delight.
When these transformations have been fully realized and entirely restrained,
the Brahmin, having attained stable sovereignty, becomes perfected.
Like sparks from fire or rays from the sun,
drops of water were produced as manifestations of splendor and sovereign power.
The luminaries, enveloped by their qualities, have come together in the sky;
they move constantly in the world, following the course of the sun and the moon.
This divine, luminous, and supreme wealth, consisting of the moon and the sun,
shines in the world as the eternal wheel of time (kālacakra) moving through the firmament.
Half-months and months, as well as seasons and years; likewise, moments (kṣaṇas), lava-measures, muhūrtas, kalās, and kaṣṭhās.
The measure of day and night, as well as the opening and closing of the eyes,
and the movements of the stars and especially of the planets.
Furthermore, those engaged in yoga, when seized by the grasp of transformation, fall from their immovable seat once they have attained earthly sovereignty born of that very transformation.
Through non-attachment, he is instantly severed; trembling, he is proclaimed [in pain];
sinking into the midst of the earth, he is split open again and again.
Through various forms of spirits and other inhabitants of that place, he is quickly joined with sense objects; in short, he becomes completely deluded.
Then, while enjoying royal sovereignty in every respect,
he is struck down by many elemental beings (dhātu) in embodied forms.
With spears, javelins, swords, and maces as well, in great numbers.
He is struck down by thousands of swords with razor-sharp edges,
and he is pierced by the tips of arrows that are exceedingly sharp and capable of penetrating the vital organs.
When all these transformations have been completely restrained in every respect,
the Brahmin certainly attains sovereignty and becomes a perfected one (siddha).
Then, for one who is liberated from modification and whose absorption has reached dissolution, the sovereignty of a king manifests as he engages in meditative concentration.
He smells that divine fragrance and hears those divine sounds;
he is neither pierced nor cut by men of divine form.
Moving by his own nature as the infinite Pradhāna-self, he seems to flow along.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having attained another state of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) with his mind, that Grandfather (Pitāmaha) [proceeded].
With an inner self liberated, he undertook the performance of the Brahma-rite.
Having performed the retention of all his limbs, as if smiling within his mind,
the knower of yoga creates beings through his mind by means of the yoga of Brahman.
By his mind, the Lord creates Apsarases endowed with perfect beauty;
and from the tip of his nose, he creates Gandharvas dressed in most variegated garments.

Then the self-existent Lord, the blessed Master who knows yoga through the yoga of Brahman, [created] all those led by Tumburu— by the hundreds and thousands— skilled in dance and instrumental music, and skilled in the singing of the Sāmans.
She possessed beautiful eyes, lovely hair-ends, and fine eyebrows; her face was radiant with a charming luster.
She was resplendent like a beautiful hundred-petaled lotus—righteous, pure-spoken, worthy of service, the very embodiment of the goddess Śrī in the form of Brāhmī.
O King, the Brahman, the soul of all beings, created [the world] with his mind through a perfectly articulated consciousness and by means of the yoga of contemplation for all living creatures.
Creating from his eye Apsarases endowed with beauty, that Lord created from the tip of his nose Gandharvas who were eloquent and skilled in music.
He performed a discourse on singing, especially for the Gandharvas,
as well as for other Brahmins, concerning song as it is manifested by Brahmā.
From his two feet he creates beings that are both moving and stationary:
humans, kinnaras, yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
Elephants, lions, tigers, and deer by the thousands, as well as various kinds of grasses and four-footed creatures, [he created] for the sake of their existence.
But those who dig up their own hands due to the cause of their acquired karma—
just as one should consider karma to be produced from the hands, so too should it be considered to be produced from the mind.
Through the anus, he effects the emission for those beings who desire pleasure;
likewise, through the organ of generation, he brings about bliss by means of the concentration of the five senses.
From his heart he created cows, and from his arms likewise birds;
and other living beings as well, in their various and diverse forms.
[He saw] the seer Aṅgiras, a sage of blazing splendor,
divine, the progenitor of the lineage of Brahmā, whose six senses were transcended.
By means of yoga, the Lord, the master of yogis, produced within his two eyebrows the divine Bhṛgu,
a performer of the lineage of Brahmā and supremely righteous.
From the region of his forehead, the Great Yogin Pitāmaha created Nārada, whose form was beloved; and from his head, he created Sanatkumāra.
And the Grandfather consecrated Soma as the crown prince,
the eternal king of the Brahmins and the wanderer of the night.
Endowed with great ascetic power and preceded by the planets,
he moved through the midst of the sky, illuminating the world with his splendors.
Through his limbs and his mind, that Blessed One, having attained perfection through yoga,
created all beings, both stationary and moving.
There, Brahmā, the grandfather of all beings, established hundreds of abodes for living creatures and their various kinds of yogic powers.
This sacrifice consists of Brahman; it is, in truth, Yoga and Sāṃkhya.
It is also discernment, intrinsic nature, the field, and the knower of the field.
Oneness and separateness, as well as origination and destruction,
time and the exhaustion of time, and even discernment itself— these are to be known [as the objects of knowledge].
[Colophon] Janamejaya said: O Brahmin, I have heard about the Kṛta-yuga, the first of the ages.
O Brahmin, O Lord, I also wish to hear about the Yuga of the Kṣatriyas.
It is presented both concisely and in detail, filled with many restrictive rules,
proclaimed by those who know the means, and adorned with sacrificial rites.
Vaiśampāyana said:
I shall relate this to you— [the history] honored by sacrificial rites and graced by the people through various acts of charity and righteousness.
Those sages, the size of a thumb, were taken up by the rays of the sun through the method for attaining liberation and by unimpeded action.
Whether in active life or in renunciation, O lord of the earth, they are always devoted to Brahman;
having united with that supreme Brahman which is the ultimate refuge.
O lord of the earth, the Brāhmaṇas are adorned with prosperity, they are indeed purifiers,
they have practiced the vow of celibacy, and they are awakened by the knowledge of Brahman.
At the end of a full thousand yugas, those Brahmins who previously underwent dissolution— endowed with virtuous conduct, perfected in knowledge, and composed in mind— [reappear].
Viṣṇu, whose nature is yoga and who is born from Brahman,
having become Dakṣa Prajāpati, creates pure progeny with his transcendent senses.
From the imperishable [akṣara] come the gentle Brahmins; from the perishable [kṣara], the kinsmen of the Kṣatriyas;
from modification [vikāra], the Vaiśyas; and from the modification of smoke [dhūma-vikāra], the Śūdras.
O Brahmins, these castes were produced by Viṣṇu as he reflected upon them, with colors white, red, yellow, and blue.
Thereupon, O lord of the earth, the fourfold classes of beings appeared in the world according to their respective colors:
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Possessing single marks and distinct attributes, these two-legged beings are most wonderful;
they are endowed with the capacity for torment and possess knowledge of all karmic destinies.
The rites prescribed in the Vedas are traditionally held to belong to the three social classes;
or else, O lord of the earth, they are performed through that yoga of Brahmā or of Viṣṇu.
Through his union with wisdom and splendor,
that lord Prācetasa was none other than Viṣṇu himself, the great yogi, who had entered into the midst of ritual actions.
From that, the Śūdras were born through transformation; they are devoid of [Vedic] ritual action. Therefore, they do not deserve the sacraments, for the Veda does not exist among them.
Just as a mass of smoke arising from an araṇi wood being rubbed in a fire spreads forth, it is of no use for any practical purpose.
In this way, Śūdras spread throughout the earth by birth in its entirety;
they do not [attain status] through unrefined dharma or through action prescribed in the Vedas.
Then other sons of Dakṣa were born, whose source was Dharma;
they were powerful, possessed of great energy, great heroism, and great splendor.
Addressed by his father Dakṣa during the performance of the sacrifice, those great-souled ones said:
"I wish to hear the end of this matter, for I am but a weak child of the Earth;
then, O knower of truth, you shall ordain vast strength for all creatures."
For because the fields are vast, my offspring are also vast.
The goddess should not show her own form with her eyes to those sons of Prajāpati who desired her vast essence.
Then, during the Kṛta Yuga, when all existence was produced from the Self and was yet to be manifested,
she became the mother of all beings— both those born from eggs and those born from the earth.
Urged by the Mothers as the progenitor of consciousness and the nurse,
she [perceives] the minuteness and the subtlety of living beings who partake in the fruits of their karma.
[Colophon] Janamejaya said:
O best of Brahmins, I desire to hear properly concerning the Tretā age.
Knowing which, may I behold that supreme, imperishable state of all branches of knowledge.
Vaiśampāyana said: But Dakṣa, that best of men, having again assumed his female state through yoga,
sat down upon the mountain peak, he whose self is the Lord of Yoga.
With well-formed knees, full hips, beautiful eyebrows, and a face like a lotus, her eyes were red at the corners; she was lovely and enchanting to all beings.
The illustrious Manoramā reflected upon herself by means of her own mind.
Then the lord Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, begot [offspring] upon that maiden.
For from his body, by means of the yoga-rite, [he produced] maidens with faces like lotuses.
Dakṣa, having abandoned his female form and assumed the form of a man,
became more beloved than the most beloved to all beings upon being seen.
The lord Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, himself gave those maidens away according to the Brahma-rite,
O Bhārata, by means of the method obtained from Brahmā.
With a composed mind, he gave ten daughters to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to Soma for the sake of wives.
Then Dakṣa, having given those daughters away, approached the Brahman-kṣatra;
the sage, with a concentrated mind, went to that holy place inhabited by Brahmā.
Performing austerities together with the deer, O King, he wandered over the earth;
grown old in years and repeatedly aged by his asceticism, he subsisted on grass, roots, and fruits.
The deer rejoice in it, and the Brahmins rejoice in its fruit—
those who are consecrated, performers of meritorious deeds, whose sins have been burnt away by austerity.
At the time of battle, O dear one, the sage who knows the right moment and is the master of his own body perceives the characteristic perfection of those who perform the sacrifice of action.
Heroic in their generosity and honor, free from anxiety and devoid of worldly desire,
they grow old together with the deer, accompanied by their wives and their sons.
The Brahmins, perfected through their hymns of praise, dwell here at the first step of the progenitor;
and because it is inhabited by Brahmins, this place is called Brahmakṣetra.
By ascetics liberated from karma, who have conquered anger and subdued their senses—
by those brahmins wandering the earth seeking the path of those who possess nothing.
That progeny which was formerly ascended, mental and celibate—
that very same thing has now attained manifestation, its inherent nature being difficult to transcend.
The unmanifest has attained manifestation; its own nature is difficult to transcend.
And this movement of the manifest and the unmanifest, O lord of the earth, follows the laws of time.
O Bhārata, both the stationary and the moving, the gross and the subtle,
through the conjunction of time, come into being and cease to be, according to the knowledge of yoga.
All these various creatures were born here from the daughters of Dakṣa,
united with the imperishable Kaśyapa through the law of time.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and all the Viśvedevas together with the hosts of Maruts;
the many-headed Nāgas, as well as the Sādhyas and the Pannagas.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and Suparṇas, as well as others;
Garuḍa along with the Yakṣas, and the Kinnaras beautifully attired.

O lord of the earth, cows together with their herds of cattle, men, mountains, the earth itself, the creators, and the mountain ranges; likewise elephants, lions, tigers, horses, and winged creatures [were all present].
Swords, horned animals, bulls, and likewise deer;
The lords of the nāgas have four tusks; they are as radiant as lotuses and auspicious in color;
endowed with all the marks of excellence, these beings can assume any form at will.
With such forms, such limbs, such virtues, and such prowess,
sages have arisen again in the eternal field of Dharma.
In the world of men, there are knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) who are righteous and within the scope of the Vedas;
from them all the gods have arisen and are established in the heavenly world.
And those others, O lord of men, who were householders perfected through austerity, and those who attained perfection through celibacy by attending upon their guru; 1159–1160.

And those twice-born ones, O lord of the earth, who have attained the path of yoga for the sake of spiritual perfection, shall indeed obtain their livelihood through activities arising from karma that are intensified by afflictions.
Living by the practice of gleaning grains, patient, accompanied by their wives, and firm in their vows—
all these, having fulfilled their observances, become wanderers in the celestial realm.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having placed the Grandfather at their head, they remained composed on the summit of Mount Meru.
The Brahmins wear matted hair and deerskins; they have abandoned anger and have conquered their senses.
In a place situated between mountains, covered with many trees,
where the rocks were colored by minerals, level, and free from grass and thorns.
They were constantly devoted to the sacrifice of mantras and always delighted in the welfare of their vows, amidst the three Vedas of Brahmā resplendent with the five tones.
Having established but a single fire, all those bulls among Brahmins,
with their minds perfectly concentrated, divided it by means of the various Vedic mantras.
The sages who have mastered the Vedas have prepared the fire in three ways;
therefore, you have attained a state of threefoldness, since that which was one has been made threefold.
The great fire is indeed one alone;
it proceeds with the oblation through the utterance of *svadhā* by those who know the mantras, for the successful accomplishment of the mantras' purpose.
And Dakṣa himself arrived, the illustrious one, honored by all beings;
he is Brahmā, the creator of the Brahmins, the grandfather of all creatures.
Carrying a staff, a shield, arrows, and a sword, with a crest-lock and a face like a lotus,
he became free from all distress, having conquered anger and mastered his senses.
Brahmā, united with Medhā, performs sacrifice at Puṣkara;
the Sāmans proclaimed by Indra are sung there by the exponents of the Veda.
Clarified butter, milk, barley, and rice—all these are the supreme oblation;
as proclaimed in the Vedas, when offered in the sacrifice, they are ordained for the state of Brahman.
Having churned the fire-stick of the nature of Agni, which had arisen from the womb of the *śamī* tree,
that Brahmā first brought forth another fire within it.
For no other substance is prescribed for sacrificial rites in the same way as fire;
nor can it produce that power consisting of offered oblations through various divisions.
The fruits offered by them as oblations in the extended sacrifice are employed by the sages who know the ritual applications and proclaim the Veda.
Within six months, Bṛhaspati, the knower of Brahman, recited the four Vedas at the sacrifice of Brahmā with supreme excellence of articulation.
He speaks with Sarasvatī, who is endowed with the natural grace of training, sweet on all sides, and possessing a resonant passion for melody.
O Bhārata, by that word "Brāhmaṇa" uttered by Brahmā,
that sacrifice shone clearly like another world of Brahmā.
Makha, having emerged from the mouth of Brahmā,
grows as if speaking through the healthy sounds of the Veda when joined with ritual applications.
With sacrificial fuel-sticks, Soma-vessels, and ritual cups in full detail;
with barley, rice, clarified butter, and vessels filled with water.
With riches obtained in due order, with invincible deeds,
with milk-yielding cows, and with tender calves;
O Bhārata, he was advanced in sacred knowledge, advanced in age, and advanced in asceticism;
O Bhārata, those advanced in sacred knowledge, advanced in age, and advanced in asceticism— **[HV_App.I,41.1203]**.
The god, consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, is united with Vidyā.
O King, Brahmā, together with the Maruts, then offered oblations to those beings who consist of mental action and form, as well as those who are self-existent.
O King, he was not touched by that deed, either by his forms which bore a manifestation of splendor or by the ritual prescribed in the Vedas for all living beings.
Having churned the fire-drill made of *araṇi* wood produced from the womb of the *śamī* tree,
that lord first performed the sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma rite;
and with the members of the assembly, that sacrificial hall clearly shone during the performance of the ritual.
They utter sweet words accompanied by nasal resonances (*anusvāra*), and from those [words] proceed ritual actions.
O King, that great sacrifice shone with those who were devoted to their duties, endowed with asceticism, and masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; it gleamed like the sun and the moon,
and with its great sound of Vedic chanting, it was like another abode of Brahman.

He is honored in the heavenly world by all the inhabitants of heaven who have arrived there like the earth itself— by those disciplined exponents of the Veda who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and by those weary from ascetic toil who have traveled back and forth between this world and the next.
With those three blazing priests acting as the sacrificial fires at the rite,
that great sacrifice of Brahmā shone like the world of Brahmā itself.
The Sāman hymns proclaimed by Indra are sung by those who discourse on Brahman;
the Yajus formulas are uttered as speech during the extended sacrifice.
Exhausted by asceticism, devoted to the Veda, and concentrated in their vows of truth,
all the sages arrived with minds intent on hearing his words.
And there, O King, the Hotṛ was Bṛhaspati,
the ancient one born of Brahmā, the best among all knowers of dharma, who served in the office of the Brahman priest.
And at the conclusion of the sacrifice, O King, the sacrificer, having performed the worship of Viṣṇu,
[entered] into the western womb of Aditi, which was nurtured by ascetic fervor.
Viṣṇu is the unborn Brahmā, free from dualities and without possessions;
from him thousands of *padas* will come into being and arise.
Even the self of that [person] for whom sages become free from possessions is unfailing, immeasurable, and distinct from karmas.
O Lord of the Earth, objects of sense are acquisitions that bring about defects;
yet, by the power of the mind, they all simultaneously conceal those very defects.
Moving within the range of the collection of sense-faculties yet free from possessiveness,
O King, they regard even the "auspicious" grasping that is characterized by ignorance as [nothing more than] a possession.
O King, because of its connection with the characteristics of an instrument, the mind is not concealed [as a primary agent],
provided it is designated by the term "sage" (muni) by those who discourse on Brahman.
O best of the Kurus, by those who have bathed after completing their vows of Vedic knowledge and remain self-restrained,
the world of the virtuous in heaven is called the world of worlds.
O Bhārata, where the gods, nourished by oblations, never come to an end,
there the sacrificer, having attained the station raised by his own ritual acts through his respective shares,
rejoices with his wives, free from feverish distress, O lord of the earth.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the Lord gave the lord of mountains to the twice-born;
and with a stainless inner self, he bestowed it upon all living beings.
Although they exerted every effort, those [demons], whose limbs were distinguished from one another, were unable to break that mountain apart for the sake of division.
Then those groups of brahmins sat down upon the surface of the earth, O King;
all of them were overcome by exhaustion and their faces had turned pale.
Supārśva, the preeminent mountain, bowing with his head, spoke with sweet words to all those best of the twice-born.
For it is not possible for you, who are attached to the insubstantial and are mutually opposed, to break this apart by force, even in hundreds of divine years.
When you have all become one and are concentrated in meditative absorption,
you will simultaneously attain liberation through the absence of obstruction.
For power, O best of Brahmins, increases through passion and hatred;
but when freed from passion and defect, the eternal Brahman increases.
"When I shall shatter [him] with arrows whetted on stone that are distinct from those of heaven,
and with minerals spreading forth and mountain peaks falling down."
He was urged on by many serpents with shattered flanks and gaping sides who had fallen to the ground, and by those dwelling in caves who had assumed the forms of beasts of prey.
Having accepted those well-spoken words of the lord of mountains,
all those best of Brahmins then became silent.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, Bali’s offerings and oblations increased day by day.
Of the twice-born, rich in austerity and established in the duties of the householder.
O descendant of Bharata, from that time forward, the deities and others have been worshipped on earth by those who know Brahman and by the exponents of Brahman, O King.
Right there in the abode of Brahmā, on level ground free from grass and thorns,
in a holy place by a mountain slope where fuel and grass were abundant.
Where those highly fortunate ones, seeking to perform austerities and established in the vow of celibacy, take up residence after having witnessed the deeds of the Blessed One.
Devoted to the duties of a householder with a mind intent on giving,
even ascetics long for him through righteous conduct, desiring Hari.
Other eminent brahmins, devoted solely to the fruits of ritual action,
were purified by the vows of the *agnihotra*, had conquered their anger, and were composed in mind.
Endowed with actions joined by destiny, those best of Brahmins were clothed in rags and bark, self-restrained, and possessed of controlled senses.
Practicing the holy life and applying himself to rigorous effort,
O King, he followed this method in its entirety according to the proper sequence.
O King, they have gradually attained that eternal merit consisting of Vedic refinement,
which was practiced by the ancient sages who discoursed on Brahman.
One who does not know the Veda should not approach [the sacrificial fire], nor should he perform a fierce vow;
he should not depart by means of renunciation, nor should he abandon the duties of a householder.
Thus one should not depart without having attained the accumulation of the Vedas; first there is the collection of the Ṛgveda, O Bhārata, and then that of the Sāmaveda singers.
O Bhārata, he is both non-accumulation and accumulation, and he is the singing of the Sāman hymns.
And even those who have no sons shall obtain the fruit upon hearing it—
those Brahmins who are exhausted by asceticism and by the service of their preceptor.
O Brahmin, O lord of the people, if one has neither heard nor grasped this,
a righteous king may, at his pleasure, compel that person to perform the duties of a Śūdra.
Or rather, there would be no Brahman for the twice-born to revere, were it not so;
for first, the mind must be concentrated upon both [the ears] within the range of hearing.
Thus, a Brahmin endowed with prosperity who desires his own well-being should undertake all undertakings of the senses preceded by the Vedas.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
They, however, placed those cows and Brahmins at their head, with the moon and the sun before them.
O King, he honored the Brahmins with riches born of the Vasus.
O King, the Gandharvas and sages, headed by Nārada,
constantly worship the Grandfather with sacrifices performed according to the proper sequence.
With words of sweet speech, which dwell within the five senses,
which bring pleasure to all beings, and which seek the welfare of all beings.
And being praised at the conclusion of the sacrifice by those with their five senses composed, the Blessed One spoke, O Bhārata: "By good fortune! By good fortune! (diṣṭyā diṣṭyā).
Then, having addressed Kaśyapa, the Lord and Master said:
"You too, together with your sons, shall perform sacrifice upon the surface of the earth."
O Lord, through sacrifices performed with the highest attainment and complete sacrificial fees, all those yakṣas and gods attained their respective qualities according to their merit.
"We shall all sacrifice; we shall sacrifice first!"—thus, through mutual rivalry, those who were arrogant in their strength became divided.
Both the Daityas and the non-Daityas, desiring victory over one another,
set out for battle with their massive arms raised.
Though being restrained by sages whose sins had been burnt away by asceticism,
and by many other brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
they fought like bulls in a cow-pen even while being forbidden.
Enraged at the commencement of battle and desiring the victory over all living beings,
they entered the domain of Death while all creatures looked on.
Then, making a great noise, those of mighty strength,
filled with rage, blocked [the way] with their arms like winged birds with their wings.
The earth trembled, trodden down by those enraged ones,
just as a boat sinks when overwhelmed by men and their heavy burden;
and the mountains crumbled like bulls bellowing in rut.
And the great rivers were agitated, struck by the wind;
then, O Bhārata, a battle took place between Madhu and Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu crushed that army, which was terrible, capable of bringing about the end of an eon, and terrifying to all living beings, despite its full strength and prowess; just as one extinguishes a blazing fire with water.
In that manner, it was pacified by that Blessed One who had acted as an adversary. **[Colophon]** *Harivaṃśa*, Appendix I, 41.1324, 52:1.
Vaiśampāyana said: That powerful Daitya Madhu, of terrible prowess,
bound Mahendra with sharp nooses within the mountain.
O Bhārata, because of Prahrāda’s words, he who was skilled in the marks of royalty,
desiring the sovereignty of Indra, [fell] through the destruction of his intellect regarding the future.
He suddenly bound Indra in the midst with many iron nooses— variegated, powerful, rending, and yet not piercing his vital spots.
Skilled in battle, that leader, having come under the power of Time, challenged the fierce Viṣṇu himself in the midst of all his hosts.
Divided into two factions, the followers of Kāśyapa fell under the power of Madhu;
seizing their massive clubs, they rushed forward for battle.
The Gandharvas and Kinnaras, experts in instrumental music and song,
dance, sing, and laugh on all sides.
By means of their well-tuned strings, which are sweet by their very nature,
they agitate the mind of Madhu as he fights while still possessed by passion.
By the command of Brahmā, the lotus-born, the truth-speaking Gandharvas perform these transformations for the sake of Madhu’s strength.
For those attached to the Gandharvas fixed their minds upon that sound;
and the Dānavas and Asuras likewise went toward it visibly and roared.
Having captivated the mind of Madhu and beholding him with his yogic eye,
Viṣṇu reached Mount Mandara, hidden like fire within wood.
The sages, their minds radiant yet somewhat distressed,
placed the Grandfather at their head and vanished in an instant.
Enraged, Madhu, whose eyes were like honey, struck Viṣṇu with his arm upon the region of his temple;
yet he did not waver even a single step from his place.
And Viṣṇu struck the Daitya between the breasts with the tip of his hand;
he quickly fell to the earth on his knees, vomiting blood.
And Viṣṇu, skilled in battle and possessed of inconceivable prowess, did not slay him even when he had fallen, for he considered the agreement regarding a hand-to-hand struggle.
Rising from the surface of the earth on his knees like the banner of Indra,
Madhu, his soul overwhelmed with rage, seemed as if he were burning everything with his eyes.
Then, shouting at one another with harsh words,
they encountered each other in a wrestling match, each desiring to slay the other.
Both were strong of arm, both were skilled in battle;
both were exhausted by ascetic penance, and both possessed valor rooted in truth.
The two heroes, striking with firm blows,
dragged each other about like two lords of mountains fighting with wings as hard as stone.
Dragging each other and sporting upon the surface of the earth,
they moved about like two elephants with the tips of their tusks and the tips of their claws.
Then, from the openings of his wounds, much blood flowed forth,
like gold mixed with minerals streaming from mountains at the end of summer.
Drenched in streams of flowing blood and stained by the battle,
they then tore up the earth with their raised forefeet.
Having struck each other in many ways,
those two heroes fought like two moths greedy for flesh, using their wings against one another.
Then, in the sky above Puṣkara, all beings heard praises concerning Viṣṇu, uttered from the mouths of the Siddhas with supreme excellence of sound— truthful praises for him whose prowess is truth.
The body is joined with the elements and joined with consciousness;
that Brahman, endowed with the senses, is the eternal essence of light.
Those beings remain fixed when the subtle [element] has reached dissolution;
again, the subtle [element] arises in many forms and in manifold ways,
awakening the state of beings and granting their desires throughout the three worlds.
Possessing beautiful forms and many forms, he moves through those worlds as a master,
having assumed a mental body through many different means.
The Lord, whose self is yoga, upholds the vast earth; his self is like that of a serpent, increasing joy;
and as the Supreme Being who has become Brahman, he sustains himself through his subtle form.
He dwells among the Brahmins through the Brāhma [sacrifice], and among the Kṣatriyas through battle alone;
he dwells among the Vaiśyas through the act of giving, and among the Śūdras through service.
The cows [satisfy] by the giving of milk; the horses in sacrifices by sprinklings;
the ancestors here by the heat [of the offering]; and the deities by their share of the oblation.
With four limbs that are distinct, with three other elements,
and with the seven eternal ancestors, he protects the three worlds.
That form, consisting of the moon and the sun, is eternal and characterized by the destruction of the self;
it is hidden by its own splendor, both in light and in darkness.
The three Pitṛs always increase the Sun;
and by means of the four Pitṛs, the Moon increases in its orb.
Three groups of ancestors always eat the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) afterwards;
four other groups of ancestors are perfected ones, and I have accepted the fivefold [offering].
You alone are those five elements, and you alone are their non-fivefold state, O All-pervading Lord;
you are composed of the eternal, divine, and everlasting, born of Brahman.
Therefore, Agni and Vāyu withdraw that radiance from you in every way;
by virtue of that action, you have become the Āditya.
When the end of the age has arrived, you have attained supreme perfection, consuming the entire world as if with your rays.
On the new moon day at the junction of the fortnights, you wander through the world of men,
your true nature concealed by ṛṣis who possess a splendor like that of the sun, the moon, and the Vasus.
Performing fruitful action, let one sacrifice—that which increases prosperity;
let there be the proper application of causes, and may there be no perversion of karma.
You simultaneously undergo the states of forest trees and medicinal herbs;
for the sake of your childhood state, you assume the form of the earth, and in every fortnight, you undergo old age.
O Lord of Beings on earth, O Lord of all that shall be upon the surface of the world!
Whatever wealth exists anywhere on this earth, all that consists of you, O All-pervading One.
You alone [uphold] the twofold eternal Dharma upon the surface of the earth:
the sacrifice to the gods consisting of mantra-utterances, and the human-like sacrifice to the Self.
The path to heaven is twofold: the stainless sun and the moon;
the moon is the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*), and the sun is the path of the gods (*devayāna*).
United with the earth, you alone move through the universe by means of your power of illusion;
having unified all the hosts and withdrawn them from there, your manifestation occurs elsewhere.
You alone have arisen as the ancient, universal Puruṣa, the Virāj;
you are imperishable and immeasurable, the wielder of desires, and the self-controlled master.
Manifested from fire, the wind, moving through the sky,
remains eternally pervading it with seven forms and configurations.

He is the creator at the time of accomplishment and at the attainment of nirvāṇa; likewise, he is the sustainer during the period of maintenance and at the time of withdrawal and dissolution; he is the quarters of space when holding and the eye when gliding.
He was constantly attended by hosts of sages who were free from defilement,
who had attained truth through their actions, who possessed equal passion, and whose senses were conquered.
While being praised by the gods, the Siddhas, and the best of sages,
the great Hari, in the form of the horse-headed one, recalled his vast body.
Having assumed a form consisting of the Vedas and a body composed of all the gods,
Mahādeva was stationed in the middle of his head, while Brahmā resided in his heart.
The rays of the sun are his hairs; the moon and the sun are his two eyes;
the Vasus and the Sādhyas are the deities in his shanks and all his joints.
The god Vaiśvānara is indeed in the tongue; the goddess Sarasvatī is Truth;
and the Maruts and Varuṇa are stationed in the region of the knees.
Having thus assumed such a form, a great and wonderful one for the gods,
he, with eyes red at the corners from rage, tormented the Asura.
The earth appeared filled with honey, fat, and marrow,
like a woman dressed in red silk garments at the end of the rainy season.
O best of men, the very word "Medinī" was obtained from the earth;
the name of Dharaṇī was established by a thousand Asuras.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Having witnessed the slaying of Madhu at Puṣkara, all beings...
Exultant, they sing aloud and dance everywhere.
Supārśva, the foremost of mountains, shone as if scraping the sky with its many-colored peaks of gold,
variegated with various minerals.
And the mountains, too, shine, colored by their mineral ores;
with their lofty peaks, they resemble clouds charged with lightning.
The dust raised by the wind from its wings, along with powders of collyrium and sand,
covered the mountain peaks and shone like a great cloud.
With their peaks embraced by clouds and their trees scattered by the wind,
these mountains, abounding with outcroppings of gold, seem to stand suspended in the sky.
Winged and peaked, anointed with gold and minerals,
they— when tossed up by the wind— terrify the birds.
All the mountains are made of gold and are adorned with crystal gems,
as well as many stainless sun-stones and moon-stones.
And the great mountain Himavat was covered with white minerals and with golden peaks illuminated by the rays of the sun.
And with its shining jewels emerging from the flanks of its wings,
and with its peaks bearing copper-colored blossoms, it blazed with its own splendor.
And Mount Mandara, with its formidable peaks covered in crystal gems and diamond-filled,
supportless [caves], shone like heaven itself.
Kailāsa, adorned with its peaks and decorated with mineral ores,
was filled with dense, lofty gateways and towering trees.
With Gandharvas playing instruments and Kinnaras singing,
and with the graceful movements of celestial maidens, it appeared as if he were sporting in return.
With sweet instrumental music and songs, with dances rising through dramatic expression,
and with amorous gestures accompanied by graceful movements of the limbs, Mount Kailāsa acts like the god of love.
With its peaks shining like the sun and possessing the luster of a mass of crushed collyrium,
the Vindhya mountain— dark as a blue cloud— appeared like a rain-cloud torn asunder.
For the sake of nourishing all beings upon the mighty summit of Mount Meru,
they discharged pure water, like masses of excellent clouds.
With rocks of many variegated patterns and minerals of many forms,
water with the luster of crystal flowed forth from the openings of the caves.
Like clouds accompanied by lightning at the end of summer, bewildered by the wind,
the clusters of trees shone as if adorned with variegated flowers.
The nāgas were as if adorned with various ornaments made of gold;
and birds perched upon creepers that clung to the trees.
Hanging there with their flowers, they dance when struck by the wind;
tossed up by the great breeze on a day in the month of Mādhava.
They released a mass of flowers like the ocean releases water during the rains,
with their powerful, expansive branches and trunks covered in down-growth.
The earth is supported by trees with abundant foliage;
the honey-loving bees and birds, intoxicated by nectar,
seem to proclaim and sing of the arrival of the season of love.
And Viṣṇu, the slayer of Madhu, created the river Madhuvāhinī,
which issued from a spring, possessed excellent bathing-places, and abounded in water.
It had sands the color of glowing embers, a delightful honey-bank,
was filled with pure waters, and carried heaps of flowers.
Urged by the words of Brahmā, she entered Puṣkara,
accompanied by the sages who were devoted to the Vedic scriptures.
Dhātrī, having become a cow in the form of Kapilā,
yields sweet milk when the sacrifice is performed, impelled by the word of Brahmā.
Having reached the earth, he joined his head, which had become like the earth;
he then attained the pure, eternal, and most wonderful world.
Having passed beyond Marutīrtha— which arose from the Sarasvatī, dispels darkness, and is situated within the field of Brahmā— he proceeds to the Puṣkaras.
Possessing a most beautiful form and knowing the Dharma, he concealed his appearance— which was like that of one who had not grown old—
with a golden-hued luster born of the power of his asceticism.
Released by Ajagandha, that great mountain was produced;
it possesses the qualities of a heavy gateway, is eternal, and is frequented by the Siddhas.
It was resplendent with variegated golden railings;
its lotuses were fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, O giver of abundant sacrificial fees.
Just as the form of Mount Mahāmeru is enveloped by the five elements, so too was he endowed with consciousness,
his form wondrous to behold.
Then Mahādeva, desiring to favor the sacred fords, said:
"I too shall assume this manifold form in the world through my mind, like a conscious being embodied in earth, in order to follow the path of dharma."
May I enter the three worlds by means of the five elements;
and with the sixth, my mind, may I unite with her who walks the path of Dharma.
Beholding worldly prosperities as if through the delusion of attachment to possessions,
those who are liberated from all attachments nevertheless maintain their belongings.
And no one shall find me with the mind as one who takes form at will;
for those bound to the five elements are impelled by various utterances.
And those who study Viṣṇu in his various forms through the divisions of his quarters—
having their sins burnt away by austerity— they shall behold me in my unmanifest state.
And those men established on the path of dharma who should ascend me—
all of them, having conquered heaven and freed from fatigue, shall behold me.
And even if they were to ascend this lofty mountain established upon the summit of Meru,
those pure ones might fight there at the risk of their very lives.
Moving with the speed of thought, they would roam together with the Apsarases,
having reached the Nandana grove and the great Kāmyaka forest.
Having established themselves in this knowledge here at Puṣkara, my devotees,
emaciated by various kinds of vows, will cause their bodies to waste away.
Having attained success, those men may proceed with various kinds of desires;
they may move at their pleasure between this world and the next.
Gaurī became renowned throughout the three worlds by virtue of her knowledge as "Siddhā";
with minds composed, she displayed the power of her asceticism and her virtuous conduct.
Through the six intentions regarding knowledge and the gathering of hundreds of supernormal powers,
they would become free from exertion, their bonds released by the elements.
By giving even a thousandfold here, as if from the fruit of a gift,
through the vehicle of the Brahmins, by means of action with a pure mind,
they shall obtain an immeasurable and ultimate fruit everywhere.
In that world, those who know the ways of the world shall dwell together with all those born of noble lineage.
Those who are present here at this sacrifice crowded with Brahmins—
having consecrated them again and again, beginning with the patron of the sacrifice— [they shall attain their goal].
Likewise, O you whose wealth is asceticism, you consider that Gaurī, who practices righteousness, in your mind for the sake of favoring all beings and in my presence.
This supreme divine truth shall come to pass; there is no doubt in this matter.
No religious merit practiced by a celibate student is found to be fruitless.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Desiring to go to the divine northern quarter, he whose means are truth—
Likewise, he was on that heap of meritorious minerals upon the mountain slope.
Viṣṇu, whose nature is the supreme dharma, stands on one foot for ten thousand years upon Puṣkara, he whose eyes are like lotuses.
Having established the self within the self through austerity, he who is born of Brahman applies himself to fierce action for the sake of uplifting the world.
Having himself covered his radiant limbs with ashes, he remained thus.
Having covered his limbs with ashes,
he himself by means of his own self practiced asceticism for nine thousand years.
Having illuminated the luminaries with that splendor, that bull among Brahmins,
his soul absorbed in yoga, remained in the midst of them through ascetic power, sustaining the world.
Having withdrawn his senses from their objects and holding them with his mind, Soma—
steadfast, supremely righteous in soul— attained the perfection of Brahman.
He sees everything everywhere—in heaven, on earth, and in between;
luminous as he performs his actions, he appears in many forms through his perfection.
Maheśvara, his nature concealed, stands in the form of a bull;
with his right foot raised, he subsists on air, fully composed.
For eight thousand years, and a thousand and a hundred more,
Mahādeva, the great yogin born of Brahmā, remained in disciplined observance.
Then the wind, having become solidified, moved at the end of the Lord of Cows;
it emerged from his mouth as foam, exhaling the wind with great surges.
Having emerged from that mouth by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he who possessed the supreme self fell like exudation—
neither moist nor made of earth.
That foam, having entered the water, moved upon the surface of the earth;
it was neither wet nor dry in its form, having attained a solid mass like the wind.
At that time, the wind, together with the water, cast up foam;
being without support, he himself became the clouds in the supportless sky.
Struck by their own [weapons], they cast milk upon the ground;
appearing like dark clouds tinged with red, they are neither liquid nor earthly.
Assuming a Brahmanic form, the all-pervading and self-controlled Vāyu performed extensive ascetic penance for a full thousand years.
Having become a fire with many matted locks and wearing garments of rags and bark,
he performed austerities without food at Pauṣkara, having observed a vow of silence.
For four thousand years,
a great fire, produced from the gathered splendor of that Agni, proceeds with intensity.
He is the illuminator of heaven, a dweller in heaven, and the dispeller of darkness;
known as Bhūtaprakāśa in the celestial realm, he was born of Brahmā through ascetic penance.
The Brahman-fire, the creator of beings for the worlds, performs austerity;
that darkness, O king of kings, is established among men on earth. Therefore, O best of beings, it becomes the sun, the destroyer of radiance.
It exists by eclipsing the splendor of mortals and all living beings;
yet, O King, it cannot do so through the power of yoga, especially that of a Brāhmaṇa.
That darkness shall perish at night, and day shall come once again.
Puṣpamitra, a Yakṣa of great splendor, all-pervading and self-controlled,
practices austerities at Puṣkara, being righteous-souled and perfectly concentrated.
For as many years as it takes for the streams falling from the peak of Mount Mahendra to reach the earth,
he remains there, assuming his true form, for all those years.
Falling upon his knees on the ground, he beheld a light in the sky;
for a full thousand years, he gazed at the entire world with unblinking eyes.
When the sun had reached the meridian, his many eyes, like the sun with its rays and retinue, emitted light from their corners in manifold ways.
Those rays, through hundreds and thousands of eyes of light,
shone with the union of splendors like a fire amidst flashes of lightning.
With his eyes emitting sparks,
he follows after the sun at the end of his karma or at the end of the age, for the world possesses many forms.
Having manifested in many forms again, he sat upon the surface of the earth and performed most dreadful austerities for a full thousand years.
Having restrained his senses, he dallied with the Apsarases;
having reached the peak of Mount Meru, he discharged his desire through desire.
Desirous of performing penance, that Yakṣa Kubera, whose vehicle is man, is indeed Viṣṇu himself;
as the overseer of asceticism, he manifests at the conclusion of his splendor.
Indeed, O Indra among kings, there is no man whatsoever in the three worlds who could perform such austerity, except for the eternal Viṣṇu.
And Vāsuki, the many-headed lord of the Nāgas, having adopted silence,
practices penance correctly, fixing his mind within the mind.
The serpent Śeṣa, whose resolve is truth, who is powerful and born of Brahmā,
that righteous-souled one, having climbed a tree, hangs there with his head downwards.
Licking with his flickering tongues and emitting the venom born from his body,
that ascetic, devoid of food, remained thus for a full thousand years.
For that *kālakūṭa* poison became exceedingly great,
by which the world was overwhelmed, O King, and found no happiness.
O Lord of the Earth, the poison of serpents is sharp and pervasive;
indeed, their venom pervades everything, both the moving and the stationary.
O Bhārata, by means of that sharp [weapon] joined with lions and increased through mutual growth, he destroys his own limbs. O Bhārata!
Then, O King, the highly fortunate Brahmā, desiring the welfare of all beings,
uttered a mantra consisting of the imperishable syllable of Brahman, which is non-violent.
And then, by virtue of that yoga, the serpents were ordained as his food.
By the best of the twice-born, who were knowers of the Vedas and devoted to the vow of truth.
With his outspread wings, Garuḍa [covered] the water and the earth;
for a full thousand years, he hung with the tip of his crest hanging down.
With those wide-spread, blossoming loads of leaves upon the surface of the earth,
the ground shone, variegated by those many-colored leaves.
O Bhārata, O lord of men, by that conduct through which all beings may live in this world and in the world of the gods,
they shall be like the sky filled with uncounted stars spreading across the surface of the earth.
During the onset of the snowfall, Maghavat, the self-controlled one, wanders alone;
that righteous-souled one has his hair marked by fish upon the waters of Puṣkara.
Then, having ascended to Sutala,
the righteous-souled one performs austerities upon the earth with his tall body, raising his right arm.
O Suvrata, for a full thousand years and one hundred more,
he practiced austerities with a concentrated mind, subsisting on air alone through his disciplined application;
O Bhārata, this was achieved through the yoga of meditative absorption and the yoga of Brahman.
By whom, O King, this earth is supported— that which is born of Brahman,
without beginning or end, eternal, and seeking its domain everywhere.
He who is Viṣṇu, the unfathomable self, the supreme self, formless—
he sits during the day and indeed remains steady at night;
true to his promise and righteous in nature, he acts according to his own will.
That hand of his which is uplifted is equal to the earth upon the earth;
at night it becomes the sun, a vast orb in the sky.
O King, he brought the realm of the moon to rest,
as well as the movements of the planets and especially those of the stars.
Soma, the great yogin of lofty mind, cast that shadow upon the earth with his flowing orb, like a right hand.
This very shadow, having become the moon, entered the lunar orb;
though signless, it became the imperishable earth-sign in the sky through a wondrous transformation.
Embracing his limbs one by one, he practiced asceticism with firm resolve;
having sprinkled his feet along with his soles, the Earth addressed him.
Drawn up from the surface of the earth by the rays of the sun,
it is as if the earth, clothed in water, is being lifted at the end of the age by the splendor of Viṣṇu.
Intertwined with the rays of the sun, that great river shone like a beautiful crystal stream encased in golden minerals.
Seized by the Sun with rays produced from his fiery splendor,
the Goddess, situated within the solar orb, is not perceived by the eye.
Having emerged again by means of rays, she then flows forth through her yoga;
she has become the celestial Gaṅgā with her vast masses of water.
It shone with trees providing cool shade and fragrant creepers,
as well as various clusters of lotuses possessing divine scents.
Her hips were adorned with a golden girdle, her waist-belt was made of crystal,
she was yellowed by the pollen of lotuses, and she wore ruddy geese as her ear-ornaments.
With her dark-blue hair and beautiful locks, she was strewn with heaps of flowers;
spreading forth, she shone like an adorned young woman.
Through her friend Puṣkara, Gaṅgā obtained the fruit; she was composed in mind, well-disciplined, devoted to the maintenance of the worlds, and intent on great penance.
The eloquent Sarasvatī, who proclaims the Veda, recites with distinct accents;
having departed from the back of Mandara, the king of mountains, she flows slowly.
The four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, are encompassed by four quarters;
they are likewise strung together with the Yajus, the Sāmans, and the Śikṣā.
By sages who resembled blazing fires, whose sins had been burnt away by asceticism,
with most terrible curses at the foot of Mount Supārśva.
And listen to me with attention as all beings hear my sound as it spreads across the peak of Mount Mandara,
pervading the entire universe beyond the reach of the senses.
When the rule of cessation was reached, the goddess became silent;
because of her vow, the speaker of truth did not utter a word.
Then all beings became entirely silent;
they were unable to utter words by force from their mouths for the purpose of speaking.
Having analyzed with her mind the yoga of compassion toward all beings,
Sarasvatī, endowed with her own voice, uttered a great sound.
Embodied beings receive the science of phonetics (*śikṣā*) conjoined with Sarasvatī;
then, by means of that very science, they all sing songs in that [place].
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Maruts, together with the Aśvins,
[appeared] with matted hair, dressed in bark garments, and wearing girdles of muñja grass.
The Gandharvas and Kinnaras, along with the Nāgas and the aquatic beings;
the Gandharvas clothed in bark and the Kinnaras in their entirety.
The wise ones practice austerities together at Puṣkara.
Even with all the insects, moths, and crawling reptiles,
they diligently dry up their bodies through fierce asceticism.
Viṣṇu, having attained the state of Viṣṇu, cast off his former body;
that great yogi protects all those who move together with him.
Viṣṇu delights in Puṣkara; indeed, Viṣṇu himself has been divided into two, shining with his own splendors like a smokeless fire.
That fire, born from his mind, as if scorching the earth,
rushed along with him across the ten-yojana circle.
He was illuminated by the blazing rays of the king’s splendor, which hung down from behind like the spreading abundance of the leaves of a great tree.
They were unable to leap across the sparks of that fire,
which were scattered in many directions like the sun crossing its own boundary.
That fire, having blazed up and distributed its rays like a smokeless purifier,
was as if being sold at the sacrifice by the priests who resembled flames themselves.
Then that vast fire, having entered the smoke,
remains there until Viṣṇu, having reached his stride, completes the observance.
Even Viṣṇu, whose prowess is that of Viṣṇu, would not have recognized him after he had performed his protection;
having indeed assumed a hundred bodies, he became the serpent Bālāhaka.
The high-minded one [beheld] that fire, which was united with his own self, licking [the offerings],
greatly increased by its splendors out of a desire for the welfare of all beings.
Then the nāga Bālāhaka sprinkled water there upon the fire— water that was pleasantly cool and increased the life-force of living beings.
Then, attended by hosts of Siddhas at Puṣkara,
that great yogi of immense power performed austerities, having withdrawn his self into his mind.
Having withdrawn his limbs and feet and fixing his mind upon the crown of his head,
he attained an immovable posture and became silent.
For this is the true nature of all dharmas, not imagined through partiality;
it is beneficial for all beings both in this world and in the next.
Then the Daityas, having assembled there with their weapons raised,
were surrounded by various cities produced through their mastery of illusion.
O scorcher of enemies, the Daityas— of massive bodies, great strength, and resembling fire itself— assail the blazing Agni with mountain peaks.
Becoming clouds through their illusory powers, those who were arrogant in their strength rained down upon that very mass of fire, striking it with their own mass.
Those mountains, however, were consumed by his flames by the hundreds and thousands,
just as the Lord Sun desires to burn up all creatures at the end of a Yuga.
Those Daityas were unable [to withstand] Agni as he rose up toward their illusions,
blazing like the sun in the sky at the time of sunrise.
With all their efforts frustrated and their prowess broken,
the Daityas reached Mount Gandhamādana and sat down upon its summit.
And that fire, having entered the world of Viṣṇu like a mass of lightning,
moved through the sky, utterly consuming the Daityas who roamed the intermediate space.
And the Naga Bālāhaka, having come together with the clouds,
released water upon the earth like a rain-bearing Parjanya.
The Naga was urged by the mantras issuing from the mouths of the twice-born;
the Brahmins, impelled by the mantras, performed the oblation according to the ritual rules of the mantras.
Just as it is prescribed by the ritual rule, with an oblation purified by mantras.
He released a torrent of water, honoring the people born of the Brahmins.
[Colophon] Janamejaya said:
Having united with ascetic power, what did the gods do after that?
For indeed, there is nothing in this world that cannot be obtained through austerity.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having undertaken the initiation, all those hosts who were permeated by Viṣṇu drew forth the fire from Puṣkara and established it according to the prescribed ritual.
The Brahmins, impelled by the mantras, performed the oblation according to the ritual procedure for reciting mantras,
with an offering purified by mantras, exactly as prescribed by the rule.
And that fire increased there according to the prescribed rites through the power of Brahman;
having become multiplied by its splendors, it became a lord with the form of a person.
Known as Brahmadaṇḍa, he seemed to burn with his very form;
for he possessed divine weapons and carried a sword, a shield, and a bow.
He holds a mace, a plow, a discus, arrows, a shield, and an axe;
he bears a trident, a thunderbolt, a sword in his hand, a spear, and an excellent bow.
Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, the sword, the mace, and the plow;
and Nara, of great strength, grasping the plow and the mace.
Through the power of his asceticism, Indra seized the hundred-jointed thunderbolt;
the lord Rudra, for his part, mentally took up his trident and his bow, the Pināka.
Death took up a staff together with a noose, and Time seized a spear;
Tvaṣṭṛ grasped an axe, and Kubera a battle-axe.
Joined by hundreds and thousands of those who were free from transformation,
Viśvakarman and Tvaṣṭṛ indeed fashioned the weapons.
Agni gave a chariot to Indra and to the radiant Sūrya;
the Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, gave one to the high-souled Rudra.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, by means of the meters (*chandobhiḥ*), fashioned the army;
Viśvakarman constructed the celestial chariots (*vimānāni*) through many stages.
Extracting a portion of his own body, Viṣṇu, whose prowess is truth,
fashioned from his lotus-like navel a cloud on the full-moon day for the sake of the army.
He swiftly fashioned the sky, along with the sun and the stars,
by means of which, having employed it in battle, he pierced his enemy in the fray.
The Lord Brahmā, having become invisible, took up that appropriate staff according to the prescribed rite, remaining unchanging and composed.
And by his own powers, he [discharged] the fourfold collection of weapons in many ways—
the Aindra, Āgneya, Vāyavya, and Raudra— with fierce splendor.
Endowed with these transformations, the mighty sons of Diti were likewise distinguished by their asceticism,
their training, and their missiles and weapons.
Then, through their strength of the fourfold army and their concentrated valor,
they all became invincible in battle in an instant.
Leaving behind their chariot along with its equipment and implements in the middle of the cave,
they wandered upon the surface of the earth at the foot of Mount Mandara.
Having gathered his entire fourfold army,
Viṣṇu himself, the lord of darkness and great yogi, traversed the surface of the earth.
Furthermore, they practiced another austerity while wandering together with Brahmins,
as did all those hosts of gods who were clothed in skins and bark.
[Colophon] Janamejaya said: O Brahmin, while the Khila period prevails, when there is a lack of restraint and great distress, HV App. I, 41.1762.
And if beings were indestructible, how could there have been progeny at that time?
Vaiśampāyana said:
In ancient times, Prajāpati consecrated Pṛthu, the son of Vena, in the sovereignty.
Prajāpati,
together with the sages, consecrated Pṛthu, the son of Vena, as the protector of subjects for the sake of sovereignty— he who was devoted to the dharma of his subjects.
"This supreme king was born out of your mutual affection. When the Tretā age had fully commenced, they spoke thus to one another.

by means of action attained through truth, he is the creator of all beings.
In the meantime, the gods, exhausted by many observances, were seated upon the mountain ridges of Gandhamādana.
Then, having encountered that fragrance from all sides, the gods and dānavas,
when the month of Mādhava arrived, were intoxicated by that scent.
Whatever potency belonged to the mere flower was spread abroad by the wind;
it became every kind of captivating, pleasant, and supreme terrestrial fragrance.
Those Daityas, filled with a slight wonder by that fragrance,
became serene in mind and attained supreme happiness.
And they all spoke together, emboldened by that fragrance:
"If such is the power of the mere flower, what might its fruit be?"
The various activities and cognitions of embodied beings— both auspicious and inauspicious— are to be known through inference by means of the vital breath of the intellect.
Therefore, we churn the medicinal herbs from within the milk ocean,
using the vast, powerful Mandara mountain, which can assume any form at will.
We shall churn the ocean, whose waters are born of Soma, with our great fury;
and having drunk [the nectar], we shall all set forth together, able to assume any form at will.
The mighty Viṣṇu alone shall be their leader;
we shall enjoy both heaven and earth together with our enemies.
We seize all the planets upon the surface of the earth, along with their roots, leaves, branches, flowers, and foliage, as well as the nectar of immortality.
Having uprooted the peak of Gandhamādana from the foothills of the mountains,
the gods spoke these words as Mount Mandara trembled.
They rushed forward to rescue him, making the earth tremble;
with great heroism, they exerted themselves by stretching out their arms with determination.
Those born of the Danava lineage were unable to uproot that lord of mountains;
they fell upon their knees in the vast interior of the mountain.
Having composed themselves by concentrating the self within the self, their sins burnt away by austerity,

Nandī, born of Rudra and endowed with great strength, raised his *pināka* bow and,

Inconceivable, immeasurable, invincible, and the tamer of enemies,

Whoever, being pure and with a restrained mind, causes the wise to hear this divine narrative concerning Dakṣa’s sacrifice— having studied it— the one of immeasurable intelligence is glorified in the world of the gods, having mastered all of the inner self (adhyātma).
