Assuming a vast and immeasurable boar-form, with broad and elevated hips, honored by the marks of a bull,
Hari entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) for the purpose of lifting up the earth.
The Vedas are his feet, the sacrificial posts his tusks, the rituals his teeth, and the fire-altars his mouth;
Agni is his tongue, the *darbha* grass his hair, Brahman his head, and he is possessed of great ascetic power.
Day and night were his eyes; the Vedāṅgas were his ear-ornaments;
the clarified butter was his nose, and the sacrificial ladle was his snout; he was great, with the sound of the Sāmaveda as his roar.
Consisting of the truth of Dharma, glorious, honored by his successive strides,
with the great snout of the sacrificial rite (*kriyāsattra*), with knees like sacrificial animals, and of immense form.
The Udgātṛ is his limb; he is the Great Liṅga, whose seed is medicinal herbs and great fruit;
Vāyu is his inner self; the Mantras are his buttocks; he is the transformed one whose blood is Soma.
The altar was his shoulder, the fragrance of the oblation his scent, and he possessed great speed in carrying the offerings to the gods and ancestors;
the *prāgvaṃśa* hall was his body, and he was wise, adorned with various initiations (*dīkṣā*).
The yogin has the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as his heart; he is great, consisting of the great sacrifice (*mahāsatra*);
the *upākarma* rite is the luster of his lips, and the *pravargya* ceremony is the ornament of his whorls.
Following various meters and paths of movement, seated upon the secret Upanishads,
accompanied by his consort Chāyā, he— like a towering crest-jewel—
having become the Sacrificial Boar, that Guru instantly entered the depths.
Prajāpati reached that earth which was covered by the waters;
having gone down to the depths of the netherworld (rasātala),
the Lord, for the sake of the welfare of the world, lifted up the earth with the tip of his tusk.
Then the upholder of the earth,
the supporter of the world, having suddenly held her for a moment, brought her back to her own place and released her.
Then the earth attained liberation through its bearing of him,
and she offered salutation to that god Śambhu.
Thus, having become the Sacrificial Boar,
he who seeks the welfare of all beings raised up the goddess Earth out of a desire for the benefit of the worlds.
Then, having lifted up the earth with the desire to establish the world,
the lotus-eyed Lord set his mind upon the division of the earth;
thus did that best of gods reflect as it remained within the subterranean realm.
Then the Lord Vṛṣākapi, assuming the form of the most excellent boar, forcibly [tore her up] with his single tusk.
Thus, the supreme lord of gods, possessing inconceivable prowess and incomparable valor, assuming the form of the excellent boar,
lifted up the earth as it was sinking downward.
The one of great fame, the infallible one, for the sake of the welfare of the world.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Above that mass of water, she stood like a great ship.
But because the earth was spread out by his body, it did not undergo submersion.
Then that powerful lord reflected upon the division of the earth and the elevation of all the mountains on every side.
He reflected upon the carving out [of their beds], their dimensions, their courses, and their origins, as well as the majesty and the specific characteristics of the rivers.
Having fashioned the earth bounded by the four oceans and having likewise created the great ocean,
he made Mount Meru of gold in the center of the earth.
Then, having gone toward the eastern direction, he created the mountain Udaya,
which was one hundred yojanas in width and one thousand in height.
With peaks made of gold, resembling the rising sun,
composed of the quality of his own splendor, and fashioned with the expanse of sacrificial altars;
And there on that mountain, the lotus-eyed one created various great trunks and trees that were made of gold and always bore flowers and fruit.
Then that Mahādeva fashioned Mount Saumanasa, which was one hundred yojanas in width and three times that in height.
It was surrounded by breasts that yielded all desired fruits and were delightful with their essence;
having made there a magnificent accumulation of thousands of various jewels.
And he fashioned a multi-colored railing that had the luster of twilight clouds.
And he created the Sahasraśṛṅga mountain, which contains hundreds of dwellings made of various jewels,
and a dense forest of trees extending sixty yojanas in width.
There, Viśvakarman Prajāpati prepared for himself a supreme seat, honored by all beings, as his own dwelling place.
And he created the great mountain Śaiśira, which resembled a mass of snow,
difficult to penetrate, and adorned with the interiors of caves.
And it is heard that he created the river Vasudhārā, which originates from the Śiśira mountain, is crowded with flocks of birds,
and is endowed with sandy banks.
She beautifies the entire eastern quarter with her hundreds of faces,
which resemble nectar and are adorned with pearls and conchs, all made holy by her merits.
It was further adorned by lovely trees growing on the riverbanks, which were closely set together, endowed with flowers and fruit at all times, and provided excellent shade.
Having established the eastern division,
he then created a beautiful mountain in the southern direction, entirely composed of gold and silver.
Shining like the sun on one side and resembling the moon on the other,
that best of mountains, bearing these two colors, was exceedingly resplendent.
Simultaneously pervaded by splendor like the sun and the moon,
he beheld there that majestic and radiant great mountain.
It was surrounded by delightful and enchanting trees that bore the fruit of all desires;
and he likewise created an elephant, with a form resembling that of a great elephant.
On all sides is a golden cave extending for many yojanas;
and there is the mountain named Ṛṣabha, which resembles a bull.
He created Mahendra, the lord of mountains, rising a hundred yojanas high, rich with trees of gold and adorned with the laughter of flowers.
With its peaks made of gold and its great trees in full bloom,
the god fashioned upon the earth a mountain that seemed as if it were shaking the very world.

He made Mount Malaya strewn with various jewels and possessing a radiance like that of the sun and moon, with its trees in full and variegated bloom; and he likewise fashioned the great mountain Maināka, crowded with masses of rocks.
In the southern direction, he created a beautiful great mountain,
the Vindhya, which possessed a thousand peaks and was covered with various trees and creepers;
and he also created a river of vast whirlpools, adorned by its broad banks.
The sacred tradition says there is a stream of water resembling milk;
it flows toward the delightful southern quarter, which is thick with water and wonderful,
flooding it with its auspicious waters and the hundreds of divine bathing places as its side-glances.
Having established himself in the southern direction, he proceeded toward the western quarter;
there he fashioned a lord of mountains rising a hundred *yojanas* high,
adorned with various, well-grown, golden peaks.
It was adorned with golden rocks and caves,
and filled with radiant *sāla* and *tāla* trees that shone like the sun.
It shone with glorious altars made of gold and adorned with variegated platforms.
There he established sixty thousand mountains, which,
in both form and splendor, were equal to Mount Meru.
The Blessed One established a mountain resembling Mount Meru, possessing a thousand streams and endowed with the virtues of sacred fords;
it was sixty yojanas in width and just as high.
There, the Lord established a divine mountain of vaidūrya stone named Vārāha, after his own form;
there were divine mountain peaks made of silver and gold.
Right there, the Blessed One established a vast mountain resembling a wheel, possessing a wheel, endowed with great strength, and having a thousand peaks.
And he established a supreme silver mountain named Śaṅkha, which resembled a conch shell in form and was covered with white trees and creepers.
He established the great Pārijāta tree, born from the essence of gold and possessing a smile of blossoms,
upon the summit of a massive mountain.
The sacred tradition declares that the Lord Varāha created the auspicious and exceedingly flavorful river known as Ghṛtadhārā in the western direction.
Having arranged the mountains blazing with gold in the western direction,
he placed those of superior quality in the north, positioned at the front.
Then he made the gentle mountain gentle, equal in extent to the atmosphere,
covered with gold ore, and like unto the sun.
But that region, though devoid of the sun, is illuminated by his radiance.
He shone with exceeding splendor, like the sun shining intensely;
he was discernible by his subtle marks, appearing as radiant as the sun itself.
Furthermore, he created the mountain named Asta, which possesses a thousand peaks, is crowded with various sacred fords,
and is strewn with jewels.
[He saw] Mount Mandara, the best of mountains, endowed with enchanting qualities; and the mountain Gandhamādana, filled with the fragrance of unrestrained flowers.
Upon its peaks, he fashioned a Jambū tree made of Jāmbūnada gold,
produced from liquid gold, which was a sight of extreme wonder.
And likewise Mount Triśikhara and Mount Puṣkara,
as well as Kailāsa, the best of mountains, white and resembling a pale cloud.
And Hari, having assumed the form of a boar, established Himavat, the lord of mountains, adorned with divine minerals.
In the northern direction, the Lord created the divine river Madhudhārā, endowed with all excellent qualities and crowded with hundreds of mouths.
And all the mountains were made by the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, at that time to possess wings and to be able to assume any form at will.
Having thus divided the earth,
the creator of the worlds formed an inexhaustible resolve regarding the production of the hosts of gods and asuras.
In all directions, that Lord of the World, whose eyes were like blood, created various beautiful mountains for the welfare of the world.
And there are holy rivers enveloped in water.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
The primordial God, intending to create the world, reflected.
As he was thus reflecting, a man indeed emerged from his mouth.
Then that man approached the god, asking, "What shall I do?
The God of gods, the Lord of the world, smiled and said,
"Divide yourself," and having spoken thus, the Lord vanished.
Of that radiant god who has vanished yet remains embodied,
no trace is found, like that of a lamp that has been extinguished.
Then that Lord reflected upon those uttered words:
"The Blessed One who is heard of in the Veda as Hiraṇyagarbha."
This Prajāpati was formerly the lord of the world;
from that time forward, the first portion of the sacrifice was ordained for him.
Having seen the true nature of reality, he fashioned divine [seats] made of Jāmbūnada gold.
{Prajāpati said:}
"I have been told by that great-souled one, 'Divide yourself.
How can the self be divided? For I have a great doubt regarding this."
As he was thinking thus, the sound "Om" indeed arose;
it produced a resonance upon the earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven.
As he was thus practicing that very [mantra], the Lord delighted his mind;
from the heart of the God of gods, the *vaṣaṭkāra* arose.

The sacred Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), consisting of the essences of earth, the intermediate space, and heaven— namely *bhūr*, *bhuvas*, and *suvar*— and composed of great mindfulness, came into being.
The goddess who is the most excellent of meters became one consisting of twenty-four syllables;
recollecting that state, the Lord fashioned the divine Sāvitrī.
The blessed Lord, through an act joined with Brahman, composed all four Vedas— the Ṛg, Sāman, Atharvan, and Yajus.
Then from that very mind [were born] Sana, Sanaka,
and the venerable Sanātana, as well as the boon-granting Sanandana.
And there Sanatkumāra was born as the pervasive and eternal one;
these, beginning with Mānasa, are the six great seers (ṛṣis) of old.
Brahmā and Kapila— these six are the yogins whom the twice-born ascetics praise in the Yoga-tantras.
Then [he addressed] Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Manu the Prajāpati.
Śambhu created these eight mind-born [sons] as the ancestors of all beings, including the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas, as well as the great ṛṣis.
At the end of a thousand yugas, these beings and their offspring who have come into existence pass into final liberation when the kalpa has been completely dissolved.
Then, at the end of a thousand yugas, the kalpa is said to be complete;
once again, at the end of a thousand years, its re-origination is ordained.
Of these very gods, who were engaged in the practice of producing progeny.
However, due to the specific nature of their karma, the names and particular births of the deities change from age to age, as well as upon the reversal of the ages.
From his right thumb, the powerful and venerable sage Dakṣa was born;
from that very same [thumb], his wife was further born from the left thumb.
There, O lord of men, she had a daughter renowned as the Mothers of the World (Lokamātaraḥ),
by whose progeny the three worlds were pervaded.
Aditi, Diti, Kālā, Anāyu, Siṃhikā, Muni,
Prādhā, Krodhā, Surabhi, Vinatā, and likewise Surasā.
He gave thirteen daughters— Irā, Krodhavaśā, Surasā, Danu, and Kadrū— to Kaśyapa.
Having reflected upon the subjects with his mind and with his inner self that knows their destinies.
Arundhatī, Vasu, Yamī, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī,
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā, O descendant of Bharata.
Dakṣa gave ten daughters to Manu, the son of Brahmā;
and all those maidens were faultless-limbed and lotus-eyed.
Divine, fragrant, and enchanting, with faces like the full moon,
they are Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Buddhi, Medhā, and likewise Kriyā.
Dakṣa indeed gave Mati, Lañjā, and Vasu to Dharma.
Then from that [water] arose the lord Ātreya, whose essence was water;
he is the son who is the master of houses, the thousand-rayed one, the destroyer of darkness.
To him, Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave twenty-seven excellent daughters, headed by Rohiṇī, who were destined to be joined with the lunar mansions.
Now hear from me as I proclaim the sons and grandsons of these [wives],
as well as those of Kaśyapa, Manu, Dharma, and likewise Śaśin.
Aryaman, Varuṇa, Mitra, Pūṣan, Dhātṛ, Purandara,
Tvaṣṭṛ, Bhaga, Aṃśa, Savitṛ, and Parjanya— these are the renowned ones.
The gods were born from Aditi, the wife of the high-souled Kaśyapa;
we have heard that two sons were born to Kaśyapa from Diti.
Both Hiraṇyakaśipu and the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa were of immeasurable prowess; through their ascetic penance, they both became equal to Kaśyapa.
Four sons were born to Hiraṇyakaśipu;
they were perfected through austerity, perfected through yoga, and firmly established in celibacy.
Constantly devoted to the vow of truth, peaceful, and with their senses conquered,
they were endowed with supreme non-violence and were free from delusion and passion.
They were straightforward in their power, skillful, and heroic in their resolve for strategic deception;
all were radiant with energy and brave, and all were devoted to worldly existence.
For the sake of worldly existence, [they worship] the god Bhava, the supreme lord Śrīgarbha,
the flesh-eater, the lord of beings, the imperishable master of all creatures.
The inexhaustible, supreme god, the imperishable, the highest abode;
the god who is beyond the beyond, the supreme among both the high and the low.
The beginningless, unmanifest being, the Lord, the Supreme Person,
the teacher of gods and asuras, the divine one, the origin of all worlds, the most excellent.
The sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu sought refuge with the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose state is predominantly unmanifest and who is clothed in animal skins.
Hiraṇyakaśipu had exactly five sons of immense strength:
Prahlāda, Saṃhrāda, and likewise Anuhrāda.
And Hradavat was indeed the fifth, as well as Anuhrada.
Prahrāda was the eldest among them, and Anuhrāda was the one after him.
Saṃhrāda and Hrāda were his two younger brothers.
Prahrāda had three sons who were valiant and possessed of great strength.
And Virocana, the son of Prahrāda, became the highly illustrious lord of the Daityas.
Virocana, Jambha, and Sujambha were renowned; Virocana,
the son of Prahrāda, was invincible in battle.
Bali was the son of Virocana; Bāṇa was the sole son of Bali.
And the son of Bāṇa was Indradamana, a conqueror of enemy cities.
But Bala’s son was the powerful and majestic Bāṇa.
O Bhārata, those sons of Anuhlāda who are renowned everywhere were the many great Asuras famous in the lineage of Danu. Among them, Vipracitti was the first-born and became their king.
From Krodhā was born an endless multitude of sons and grandsons;
they were known as the Raudras and the Krodhavaśas, and they were indeed performers of cruel deeds.
Siṃhikā gave birth to Rāhu, the planet who torments the moon and sun,
the devourer of both the moon and the sun, and the destroyer.
The host belonging to Kālā was like Time itself, most terrible,
with eyes blazing like the sun and a luster equal to a dark cloud.
Śeṣa with a thousand heads, Vāsuki, and likewise Takṣaka—
these have attained preeminence among the many sons of Kadrū.
They are righteous souls, knowers of the Vedas, always devoted to the welfare of living beings;
they uphold the systems of the world, are bestowers of boons, and can assume any form at will.
Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, and the mighty Garuḍa,
as well as Aruṇa and Aruṇi, are remembered as the sons of Vinatā.
And Prādhā gave birth to these eight highly fortunate and auspicious Apsarases, who possess various meritorious marks and are honored by celestial sages.
Prādhā gave birth to women who were irreproachable, well-proportioned, flawless, beloved by their husbands, devoted, and fortunate.
Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, Puṇḍarīkā, Tilottamā,
Surūpā, Lakṣmaṇā, Kṣemā, as well as Rambhā and Manoramā.
Amitā and Subāhū, Suvṛttā and likewise Sumukhī,
Supriyā and Sugandhā, Surathā and Pramāthinī.
Kāśyā and Śāradvatī are known as the Apsarases of Mauneya;
Viśvāvasu and Bharaṇī are likewise renowned as Gandharvas.
Menakā, Sahajanyā, Parṇinī, Puñjikasthalā,
Ghṛtasthalā, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, and likewise Urvaśī.

Anumlocā is renowned, and Pramlocā is the tenth; these are remembered as the ten divine Apsarases, known as Manovatīs. Born from the creative resolve of Prajāpati, they are the very splendor of the world.
The nectar, the Brahmins, the cows, and the Rudras—these four are the offspring of Surabhi; such is the great certainty established in the Purāṇa.
This indeed is the offspring of Kaśyapa; now learn the lineage of Manu.
O sinless one, I shall proclaim all of that to you in brief.

The Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas. The Marutvats were born of Marutvatī, while the Vasus are recorded as being born of Vasu. O dear one, the Bhānus were born of Bhānu, and the Muhūrtas were born of Muhūrtā.
Then Lambā gave birth to Ghoṣa, and Nāgavīthī, the daughter of Jāmī;
the entire realm of the earth was born from Marutvatī.
From Saṃkalpa, O Kauravya, was born Saṃkalpa himself;
and from Dharma and Lakṣmī was born Kāma, the beloved of the world.
Yaśas and Harṣa are remembered as the two sons of Kāma born of Rati. Of Soma, the son Varcas was born of great splendor by Rohiṇī.
The Blessed One is indeed born radiant as he rises.
And the venerable Purūravas was united with Urvaśī;
in this manner, thousands of sons were born to women from one another.
This much, however, is the root of the world, wherein all worlds are established.
But the blessed Prajāpati, the knower of yoga, having observed embodied beings according to their qualities, appoints them to presiding offices for which they are suited.
The sages [saw] the ten directions, the earth, the oceans, the mountains, the trees,
the medicinal herbs, the serpents, the rivers, the gods, and the asuras; the lords of creatures, the creators of the world, the sky, and the earth.
Then he performed sacrifices and [ascended] the mountains.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, [this concerns] even the three worlds and the Ādityas.
He made Śakra king, possessing splendor equal to that of the sun.
That wielder of the thunderbolt, the armored victor, was born from Aditi;
accompanied by mindfulness, he was resplendent, just as he was praised by the *adhvaryu* priests.
Then, as soon as he was born, the Blessed One was covered by Aditi with *kuśa* grass;
from that time forward, the Lord of Gods attained the name Kauśika.
Having consecrated the thousand-eyed Purandara in the supreme sovereignty,
Brahmā proceeded to assign the kingdoms in due order.
He consecrated Soma in the sovereignty over sacrifices and austerities, as well as over the lunar mansions and the planets, the twice-born, and the medicinal herbs.
Dakṣa as the lord of the Prajāpatis, Varuṇa as the lord of the waters,
and Kāla, who has the brilliance of Vaiśvānara, as the universal destroyer of the Pitṛs.
And Mahādeva was made the lord of all the Gandharvas;
[he is the lord] of all the Gandharvas, of all beings, and of all embodied souls.
And at that time, Vāyu was made the lord of sound, time, and strength.
Of all spirits and piśācas, as well as of the Mothers and cows, and likewise of those afflicted by insanity and possession, of diseases and calamities; HV_App.I,42.434–435.
And Mahādeva was made the lord of all the pretas,
as well as of the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, the guhyakas, and of wealth.
Vaiśravaṇa was indeed made the lord of all jewels;
Śeṣa of all fanged creatures, and Vāsuki of the nāgas;
and Takṣaka was made the lord of all reptiles.
Parjanya,
the youngest of the Ādityas, was appointed as the sovereign lord over the oceans, the rivers, and the rain showered by the clouds.
He made Citraratha the lord and sovereign of the Gandharvas;
and Kāmadeva was made the lord of all the hosts of Apsarases.
Of all four-footed creatures and of all vehicles in every respect,
the glorious bull— the banner of Maheśvara— was made the sovereign.
And the one of great splendor, Hiraṇyākṣa, was made the lord of the Daityas and likewise of all the hosts of Dānavas.
Vipracitti, the first-born among them, was consecrated in the kingship;
and Hiraṇyakaśipu was likewise consecrated as the crown prince.
Mahākāla was appointed as the lord of the Kālakeya hosts;
then Vṛtra was made king over the sons of Anāyuṣā.
The son of the all-pervading Āditya was the highly illustrious Dharmarāja;
and he who was the son of Siṃhikā, the great planet known by the name Rāhu.
He was made the master of many inauspicious portents.
Furthermore, O Bhārata, [he knows] all the seasons, the yugas,
the fortnights, the nights, as well as the days, lunar dates, and the sacred festival days.
From the movement of the *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, and *muhūrtas*, as well as the two solstices (*ayana*),
the year was established by him as the king of yoga and calculation.
Then, the one of great strength, Suparṇa, was made the sovereign over all birds and over the Nāgas,
as well as the lord of the serpents.
Aruṇa, the brother of Garuḍa, possessing the luster of a cluster of *japā* flowers,
was made the lord of all yogas and of those who are to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
His son was named Viratha, the son of Kaśyapa Prajāpati.
He was appointed as the charioteer of the sun of immeasurable splendor;
likewise, the king was made the sovereign over the eastern quarter, as was Vāsava.
The son of the pervasive Āditya is the highly illustrious Dharmarāja;
Yama, honored by Mahendra, dwells in the southern quarter.
The legitimate son of Kaśyapa, likewise dwelling within the waters,
is known as Amburāja, the king in the western quarter, O monarch.
The son of Pulastya, the radiant lord named Ekākṣa Piṅgala, who resembles Mahendra,
is the king in the northern direction.
Having thus divided the kingdoms, the Self-Existent One,
the creator of the worlds, assigned the divine realms in the third heaven to each of them individually.
Some were like the sun, some resembled fire,
some were as radiant as lightning, and some were as pure as the moon.
He saw the worlds of the virtuous who have performed good deeds— worlds of manifold colors that move at will for many hundreds of yojanas, which are difficult for evildoers to attain.
And those regions which shine forth before them, gentle like clusters of stars—
these are the worlds of the virtuous who have been born as performers of meritorious deeds.
Those who sacrifice with meritorious offerings accompanied by excellent sacrificial fees;
those devoted to their own wives, patient, upright, and speakers of truth.
The Brāhmaṇas who bestow daily favors, free from greed,
having abandoned passion and being tranquil, go there, radiant with their ascetic penance.
Having thus instructed his sons, the Grandfather of the worlds,
Prajāpati himself, ascended to Puṣkara, the abode of Brahmā.
All the inhabitants of heaven, protected by Mahendra, took delight in their own worlds within the enclosures granted by the Self-Existent One.
The self-existent one appointed those gods, headed by Śakra,
to their respective duties of protection;
they attained auspicious fame and the celestial realm.
And those who partake of the sacrificial portions attained youth.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Once upon a time, those mountains, the upholders of the earth, possessed wings.
Having abandoned the earth, they have surely departed through his very power of illusion.
Then, having reached the western quarter, the abode of the Asuras protected by Hiraṇyākṣa, they plunged into the lake like elephants.
There, the gods proclaimed their sovereignty over the Asuras;
having heard that, all the Asuras then made a supreme effort.
Intent on seizing the earth, they formed a cruel and incomparable resolve;
and those of terrible prowess took up all their weapons.
Wheels, thunderbolts, as well as swords, *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, and bows; spears, nooses, javelins, maces, and likewise clubs.
Some, equipped with armor and mounted upon rutting elephants, were ready;
some had harnessed horse-chariots, while others were great chariot-warriors on horseback.
Some [mounted] camels, as well as rhinoceroses, buffaloes, and even donkeys;
others, relying on the strength of their own arms, were foot soldiers.
Surrounding Hiraṇyākṣa, all of them— armed with maces and bearing banners—
issued forth from here and there, joyful and eager for battle.
Thereafter, the hosts of gods, led by Purandara,
having learned of the exertions of the Daityas, made a supreme effort in return.
Well-ordered with a great fourfold army,
they were equipped with leather finger-guards for their bows, carrying quivers and arrows.
The gods, bearing formidable weapons, stationed themselves within their own ranks and followed behind Śakra, who was mounted upon Airāvata.
Then, amidst the sounding of trumpets and the great roar of kettledrums,
Hiraṇyākṣa rushed toward Purandara, the king of the gods.
With sharp axes, swords, maces, lances, spears,
clubs, and battle-axes, he covered Vāsava.
Then, by the force of the power of his weapon, showers of arrows— blazing, most terrible, fearsome in form, and possessing great velocity— fell down.
And the remaining powerful Daityas [attacked] with sharp-edged axes,
iron clubs, swords, missiles, and mallets.
And with massive boulders and rocks resembling mountains,
as well as heavy mallets and likewise with *śataghnī* weapons;
With yokes, machines, bolts, and rending weapons,
the Daityas struck down all the hosts of gods, including Vāsava himself.
With smoky hair and a tawny beard, bearing various weapons and missiles,
he resembled the clouds of the red twilight and wore an excellent diadem.
Wearing blue and yellow garments, with white, upturned, and formidable fangs,
with arms reaching to his knees, tawny-eyed, and radiant with ornaments of cat's-eye gems.

Within his body reside the gods, the oceans, and the rivers;

The Moon together with the constellations, the Ādityas along with Agni,

And you, accompanied by us and surrounded by all the hosts of Daityas,

And here are the high-souled Manu Prajāpati,

Passion, goodness, and darkness, as well as self-restraint.

Arrogance, delusion, and all the ancestors as well.

And the son of the lord of the Daityas,

"Protect me, O Great King, for Time itself is seen in its fierce form.
While her son was speaking thus, she was then overcome by both anger and fear.
He who is the vital breath of all beings, who is himself the sacrificial rite,

He who cannot be defined by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), yet is proclaimed as the very authority (*pramāṇa*);

Consisting of the *Ṛgveda*, this eternal soul of the Purāṇas has the form of sacrifice;

The giver of happiness, the giver of everything, eternal, the primordial creator, Janārdana—

[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having heard the words of Prahlāda, Hiraṇyakaśipu—

It is said that this Viṣṇu is indeed always to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation.

Then there is the staff-weapon (*daṇḍa*), the most excellent of all weapons and truly terrifying;

The wheel of dharma is the great wheel, known by the name Ajita;

With spears, nooses, tridents, maces, and clubs,

and with flowering *sāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *karṇikāra* trees.
And there is the vast mountain Ayomukha, adorned with minerals;
and the auspicious Malaya mountain, which possesses the fragrance of tamāla forests.
The Surāṣṭras, the excellent Bāhlikas, and likewise the Śūras and Ābhīras;
the Bhojas, the Pāṇḍyas, the Vaṅgas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Tāmraliptakas.
In the same way, the Andhras, the Pauṇḍras, the Vāmacūḍas, and the Keralas—

And there is the abode of Agastya, which was established by Agastya in ancient times;
it is frequented by hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas and is exceedingly beautiful.
It was filled with various kinds of colorful birds and trees and creepers in full bloom;
its peaks were made of gold and it was frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
And the mountain Puṣpitaka, endowed with beauty and pleasing to behold, rose up having pierced the ocean; he is the friend of the moon and the sun.
Surrounded by the waters of the ocean, it shone with its massive peaks as if scraping the sky, resembling the rays of the moon and the sun.
The glorious mountain Vidyutvān is extensive, stretching for a hundred yojanas;
it is there, upon that best of mountains, that the flashes of lightning are cast down.
There is the mountain Ṛṣabha, and the glorious Vṛṣabha, which is shaped like a bull;

The city of Bhogavatī, with its vast streets, difficult to assail, and the abode of serpents,
was also shaken by the lord of the Daityas.
Mahāmegha and Giri, as well as the mountain Pāriyātra;
Cakravān, the best of mountains, and the mountain Vārāha.
And there is the auspicious city of Prāgjyotiṣa, made of gold,

And there is Megha, the best of mountains, with a roar as deep as a thundercloud;
O lord of the people, sixty thousand mountains are located there.
Resembling the rising sun, the great mountain Meru is the auspicious and holy abode of the gods; it is the king of mountains, made of gold.
The great mountain Hemaśṛṅga, as well as the mountain Meghasakha,

And the great mountain Vindhya, filled with various trees and creepers,
was shaken by the lord of the Dānavas, that hero of mighty arms.
Its caves were constantly frequented by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and gandharvas;

By that [wind], the Vaikhānasa lake, covered with golden lotuses,

The mountain Triśṛṅga, the excellent river Kumārī,

And Uśīrabīja, the mountain Rudropastha, the king of mountains,

Devāvṛt and Parvata, as well as the mountain Āluka;
Krauñca, Saptarṣiśaila, and the mountain Dhūmavarṇa.
These and other mountains, regions, and likewise provinces,

And Kapila, the son of Mahī, as well as Vyāghrākṣa and Kampita;

Likewise, another fierce host appeared, armed with cloud-noises and goads;
the blessed wind did not blow, nor did the sun shine.
The entire cosmic egg, including the netherworld, became agitated on all sides;

Moving upward with terrifying speed, they were all trembling violently.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Therein were the Ādityas, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Maruts.
The Rudras, the gods, the high-souled Vasus, and those of great strength.
Having approached the presence of that lion among men, who possessed the splendor of the sun,
they spoke with terrified minds, afflicted by the destruction of the world of the gods.
O Lord, slay the son of Diti, the Dānava who destroys the worlds,
who is wicked in conduct and of evil behavior, together with all the great Asuras.
For you alone, O destroyer of Daityas, are the end of these Daityas and no other;
therefore, destroy them for the sake of our welfare and grant well-being to the worlds.
You are the teacher of all the worlds; you are Indra; you are the Grandfather.
Apart from you, there shall be no other refuge in the past nor in the future.
Having heard those words, the god who is the primordial source of the gods let out a very great roar with an exceedingly deep resonance.
The hearts and minds of the lords of the asuras were rent asunder by the great-souled lion with his mighty lion’s roar.
There was a host named Krodhavaśa, and another, the Kālakeya;
and there was also a host who was the son of Aṅga, as well as another, Bāhuśālin.
Vega, Vegaleya, and the heroic Saiṃhikeya.
Saṃhrādīya, Mahānādin, and another named Mahāvega; Kapila, the son of the Earth, Vyāghrākṣa, and Kṣitikampana;

Likewise, there was another fierce host led by Meghanāda, whose weapon was a goad;
they were Urdhvaga, Bhīmavega, Bhīmakarman, and Ārkalocana.
These and many others, with various weapons in their hands,
rushed toward the Man-Lion like moths toward a fire.
Then the Lord Nṛsiṃha, filled with rage, suddenly reduced all those foremost of Daityas to ashes by a mere *huṃ* sound.
Then, seeing them slain by the high-souled Man-lion,
he became enraged like the fire of universal destruction and resembled the Ender of Time at the end of an aeon.
Then there were Vajrī, Śūlī, Karāla, and Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Resembling a mass of clouds, possessing the speed of a mass of clouds,
having the roar of a mass of clouds, and possessing a luster like that of a cloud.
Pleased by the arrogant hosts of Daityas and by the high-souled king of beasts,
the proud enemy of the gods, the son of Diti, rushed toward Nṛsiṃha.
Possessing the prowess of a proud tiger,
he [encountered] the arrogant hosts of Daityas who were themselves fierce.
Then the enraged lord of the Daityas, quickly taking up his bow—
which was ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long— [acted].
Having fixed the Vaiṣṇava weapon upon that bow,
the one of great splendor stood before the lion, uttering a terrible and fearsome roar.
The lord of the Daityas discharged a weapon, and the lion swallowed it;
then, standing with his bow, he fixed the Nārāyaṇa weapon upon it.
Having witnessed that deed of the Daitya, Janārdana in his Nārasiṃha form rushed with speed toward that lord of the Daityas who stood before him.
The one of great splendor took up that jewel of a bow and that arrow;
having split the jewel of a bow in two, he let out a lion’s roar.
Then the mighty lord of the Daityas, seizing a mace, struck the lion in the chest; however, Acyuta shattered it.
In the battle, the Dānava seized the Nārasiṃha [form] with his arms;
a most tumultuous fight ensued between those two, the Dānava and the god.
With arms and fists, with teeth and blows to the head,
with arrows resembling thunderbolts, and likewise with strikes to the chest.
By the blow of his feet, the earth was pressed down;
then, as a man-lion, he crushed the son of Diti with his arms.
Having thus sported in many ways, the God of gods, the Lord of the world,
Hari, the Sovereign, set his mind upon the slaughter of the Daitya.

While all the world looked on, the lordly lion Hari seized him with his two arms; with his sharp claws, which were like the edges of swords, he tore open the heart of that great-souled lord of the Daityas.
Then, springing up, the king of beasts, aided by the syllable *Oṃ*, tore him apart with his sharp great claws and slew him in battle.
Seeing Hiraṇyakaśipu slain by the lord of beasts,
all the gods were thrilled and overjoyed; they honored the sovereign of the wild animals.
The earth and the world, the moon and the sky, the planets and the sun, and all the directions;
the rivers, the mountains, and the great oceans.
They have come into the light because of the destruction of the sons of Diti.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Thereupon, the gods were delighted, as were the sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
They praised the eternal primordial god with various hymns of praise.
O Lord, those who know the higher and the lower shall worship this very form of Narasimha which has been manifested by you.
And we too, O Lord, behold this body of yours as the Man-Lion (*nārasiṃha*) entered by you,
and your sovereignty as the King of Beasts among all creatures in the worlds.
Those of great fortune, their minds fixed upon your being, will worship you.
The deities have returned to their own abodes;
and the sages shall forever sing of you as "the Lion among Men," O King of Beasts.
"O Lord, through your grace, we have indeed returned to our own abodes."
Thus addressed by the hosts of gods, the high-minded lion among men and Brahmā, being supremely delighted, uttered a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu.
He praised him with verses recited from the four Vedas:
"You are the imperishable, unmanifest, inconceivable, supreme secret."
Unchanging, uncreated, the agent, eternal, and free from affliction.
The intellect established in the true meaning of both Sāṃkhya and Yoga [declares]:
"O Blessed One, the Lord is the self of knowledge, the eternal and immutable Puruṣa."
You are both the manifest and the unmanifest; from you this entire world proceeds.
You are my origin, O God; you are our origin, you are the Self, you are the Lord.
You are the one whose form is divided into four, the all-pervading Lord and Teacher of all the worlds;
you are the Master of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, the destroyer of the very end-maker of all worlds.
He who possesses the four Vedas, who is the four officiating priests (*caturhotṛ*), who is the eternal fourfold self;
he is the foundation of all beings, possessing infinite strength and manly prowess.
And it is the supreme goal of ascetics such as Kapila and others.
Without beginning, middle, or end, the Self of all, the Supreme Person;
you are the creator, you are the destroyer, and you alone are the sustainer of the world.
You are Brahmā and Rudra, Mahendra, Varuṇa, and Yama;
you are the creator and the transformer, the inexhaustible source of the worlds.
The supreme accomplishment and the supreme deity, the supreme mantra and the supreme austerity,
the supreme dharma and the supreme glory.
They call you the foremost, the ancient Puruṣa.
The supreme truth and the supreme oblation,
the supreme purifier and the supreme path,
the supreme sacrifice and the supreme priestly office.
They call you the foremost, the ancient Person.
The supreme beyond the supreme,
the supreme beyond even the supreme, the god who is the supreme beyond the supreme.
Beyond the highest, he also [attains] the supreme world; beyond the highest,
he also [attains] supreme liberation.
They call you the primordial, ancient Puruṣa, that supreme state which is even higher than the highest.
The supreme body and the highest abode; the supreme yoga and the supreme speech;
the supreme secret and the supreme goal.
He is the supreme one even beyond the supreme, and the sovereign lord; he is the supreme one even beyond the supreme,
and the highest glory.
And all the sages declare you to be the foremost.
The supreme beyond the supreme, and the supreme yoga; the supreme beyond the supreme, and the supreme liberation;
the supreme state, and the eternal Viṣṇu.
They call you the foremost, the ancient Puruṣa.
The supreme state even beyond the supreme; the god who is supreme even beyond the supreme;
the Lord who is supreme even beyond the supreme.
They call you the foremost, the ancient Puruṣa.
The supreme even beyond the supreme, the primary; the supreme even beyond the supreme, and the ultimate reality.
They call you the Supreme, even beyond the supreme, the Sustainer, the foremost, the ancient Puruṣa.
The supreme even beyond the supreme, the primary source;
the supreme secret and the most excellent mantra.
Through supreme yoga, they call you the ancient, foremost Person, who is most profoundly hidden.
The supreme secret even beyond the supreme;
that which is the highest even beyond the highest;
that asceticism which is the most supreme even beyond the supreme.
They call you the foremost, the ancient Puruṣa.
He who is higher than the highest, the supreme beyond even the supreme,
the all-pervading one who is higher than the highest.
They call you the foremost, ancient Person, whose gift is supreme even for the sake of another.
The supreme yoga, even higher than the supreme;
the supreme liberation, even higher than the supreme;
and the supreme sovereign power, even higher than the supreme.
They call you the foremost, the ancient Puruṣa.
The supreme beyond even the supreme, the ancient;
the supreme mantra and the most excellent mantra.
Through supreme yoga, they call you the most secret, the foremost, the ancient Puruṣa.
The supreme beyond the supreme, the ultimate refuge,
the supreme secret, and the highest mantra—
well-guarded by the supreme yoga.
They call you the foremost, the ancient Person.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus and having praised the divine Nārāyaṇa, the blessed Lord, the grandfather of all the worlds, departed for the world of Brahmā.
Having slain the lord of the Daityas and put the Asuras to flight in battle,
Viṣṇu then made Prahrāda, the king of the Daityas, the sovereign of the Dānavas.
Then the Blessed Lord Nṛsiṃha spoke this to Prahlāda:
"Meditate upon me constantly, O Daitya; thus shall there be purity of mind for you."
"So be it," the Daitya replied, bowing down to Hari, the Lord,
the primordial god, the master of the world, the imperishable one with lotus-eyes.
Then, while musical instruments resounded and the apsarases danced,
the Lord, the Sovereign, went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Having cast off his man-lion body and set that form aside,
he who has Garuḍa as his banner resumed his ancient form and departed.
By means of a splendid vehicle endowed with eight wheels and possessed of prosperity,
the Lord, the divine one whose nature is unmanifest, went to his own abode.
Thus, O King, in ancient times, that enemy of the gods, Hiraṇyakaśipu, was slain by that great-souled one in the form of a man-lion.
There, too, the wielder of the discus and mace made his bed for yoga;
the knower of yoga, whose self was absorbed in yoga, contemplated something that is beyond thought.
Devoted to the protection of the world, the Lord of the Universe reclines upon Śeṣa;
Hari, whose feet have red soles, likewise has his feet on the lap of another, the Goddess Śrī. With his mind absorbed in yoga, he sleeps peacefully indeed for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas.

Spoken by ancient poets, declared by Brahmā, and uttered by the Creator.

Then the Dānavas raised a cry of "Victory!
for Bali, who possessed incomparable heroism and was seated upon the lion-throne after his consecration.

then addressed him, bowing their heads to the ground.

Surrounded by thousands of hosts of Asuras, may you,
