The golden banner of that lord of the asuras, marked with the sign of a tiger,
shone in the middle of his chariot like the midday sun.
Possessing terrible speed and great strength,
he stood like the Himavat mountain, grasping his bow,
clad in blue garments and bound with golden bands.
Just like the elephant of the quarter, who possesses his flanks.
Resounding with the tinkling of networks of small bells, adorned with refined gold,
and equipped with banners and flags, it was like a rain cloud at twilight.
It was equipped with four wheels, with a distance of eight *nalvas* between them;
it was radiant, covered with a golden lattice, like the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra) arisen.
It bore various divine weapons, was adorned with tiger skins,
filled with herds of wild beasts, and resplendent with variegated patterns.
It was filled with hundreds of quivers, crowded with spears and javelins,
packed with clubs and mallets, and adorned with excellent bows.
It was graced by a thousand yoked bears, radiant with long manes,
and adorned with a silver lion-standard scattered about.
By that [chariot], the powerful Daitya Maya Viśvakarman shone resplendently,
standing upon that jewel of a chariot like the glorious sun situated on the mountain of sunrise.
His limbs were beautifully adorned with snow-white silver;
he was variegated with lovely patterns shining with jewels and gold;
and there were hundreds of thousands of myriads of his powerful [forms].
He follows after these chariots in the great battle.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Now,
the great Daitya Puloman was a cavern of darkness in appearance.
He ascended his terrible iron chariot, which crushes the chariots of enemies.
Resembling carved mountains with its interior lattice-work of iron,
it seemed to agitate the ocean with the great roar of its rims.
With maces, iron clubs, and swords, along with javelins and battle-axes,
it was strewn with spears and mallets like a rain-cloud laden with water.
Mounting a chariot yoked with a thousand camels, swift as the wind, Puloman,
intoxicated by battle, set out for war.
Sixty thousand chariots followed the great car-warrior Puloman;
they were sun-colored and seemed to blaze with splendor.
Standing in the middle of his chariot, he shone with his great sword-banner, which had the luster of molten gold, like the sun atop a mountain.
Grasping his great mace, which was bound with bands of beautiful gold and resembled Death itself, that one of great strength shone resplendent in the midst of the army.
Like a banner made of black iron raised upon the earth.
Hayagrīva, however, was powerful; Hayagrīva possessed great strength.
That best of chariot-warriors was surrounded by a hundred thousand chariots.
Mounting a formidable chariot that resembled a mountain and was capable of crushing the enemy host,
he stood facing the battle.
Resembling a white mountain and adorned with white earrings,
he shone as he stood in the middle of the chariot like a mountain with white peaks.
With a great, beautiful seven-headed serpent-banner,
variegated with lapis lazuli gems and adorned with sprouts of coral.
Hundreds of hosts of Asuras followed that powerful one, who possessed immeasurable strength, prowess, and splendor, and who was traveling in his excellent chariot.
like the hosts of the thirty gods following Vāsava as he departs.
But Prahrāda was possessed of great wisdom, learned in all the scriptures,
the master of all illusory powers, illustrious, and a performer of even hundreds of sacrifices.
The radiant one, possessing a splendor equal to the flame of fire,
equipped himself with a great array of chariots that roared like clouds during a storm.
Surrounded by a thousand Daityas, that hero of immeasurable valor, wearing golden earrings, appeared like the Grandfather [Brahmā] among the gods.
Through his own prowess, the leader was arrogant and possessed the stride of an elephant in rut;
he stood like a barrier against the entire army of the gods.
In steadfastness he was equal to the ocean; in physical form, he blazed like fire;
in splendor, he had the appearance of the sun; and in forbearance, he was equal to the earth.
With his blazing palm-tree bannered chariot shining intensely,
he went forth, and the Dānavas followed him in hundreds of groups.
All were clad in golden armor, all adorned with jewels,
wearing celestial unguents and ornaments, and never retreating in battles.
With their limbs variegated with gold from the Jambū river and their armlets fashioned from lapis lazuli,
they stood in the midst of divine chariots like great planets stationed in the sky.
Possessed of right conduct and having conquered his senses, devoted to dharma, intent on truth, and free from malice,
he stands like fire, water, cloud, and wind.
He was like the all-destroying Kṛtānta in bodily form.
Śambara, however, a master of great illusion and a leader of chariot-divisions among the Daityas,
skilled in every form of warfare, mounted his divine chariot.
Red-eyed and mighty-armed, wearing glowing, excellent earrings,
resembling a dense rain-cloud, and adorned with divine garlands and unguents.
With a crown radiant as the sun, flashing like lightning,
variegated with precious gems and beautiful with its interior of lapis lazuli.
Resplendent with his great golden armor shining like twilight clouds, the glorious one appeared like the majestic mountain of sunset shrouded by evening mists.
Then, three million Daityas, skilled in various modes of combat, powerful and like unto Death itself, followed Śambara.
He was mounted upon a silver chariot, yoked to a thousand white horses,
adorned with a flaming banner bearing the emblem of a curlew, and resplendent in battle.
It was covered with nets of gold and inlaid with lapis lazuli, variegated with various birds;
it possessed the brilliance of lightning, was fearsome to behold, and moved with great speed.
Having mounted his chariot, the Daitya shone resplendently.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, the Daitya Anuhrāda, who was exceedingly difficult to conquer, remained right there.
The son of Hiraṇyakaśipu set forth, eager for battle.
By means of a four-wheeled vehicle resembling three bundles of grass,
yoked with horses of great prowess that had lion-like faces and moved straight forward.
The heroic one [proceeded] with yoked horses having the faces of camels, covered with nets of gold,
and with the sound of their rims— a roar both terrifying and deep.
shaking the entire earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves.
Roaring, the hosts of Daityas went toward Anuhlāda;
roaring, the hosts of Daityas surrounded Anuhlāda.
A hundred times one hundred thousand chariots adorned with golden garlands.
With iron clubs, slings, crescent-headed arrows, spears, and battle-axes,
they held various weapons in their hands, with pikes and mallets in their grasp.
Adorned with diamonds set in golden lattices,
the great asuras prepared themselves with chariots, wheels, and armor.
Then, upon that chariot whose body was adorned with gold and which resembled a vast, towering mountain,
the lord of the Daityas shone, appearing in accordance with his entire army.
But he was established in a matchless and beautiful form.
And Virocana was powerful, possessing a splendor equal to Vaiśvānara;
he was skilled in all weapons, pure, and accompanied by a great multitude of chariots.
He was skilled in the deployment of battle arrays and knew the reality of both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom;
he was the foremost of the Asuras, the father of Bali, just as Vāsava is among the gods.
It was equipped with all the finest weapons, adorned with networks of tinkling bells,
and yoked to a thousand swift-moving, preeminent horses.
Having mounted the chariot, the lord of the Daityas shone like a second Mount Meru;
it was fringed with a network of small bells, adorned with the banner of a lordly elephant,
and decorated with pennants the color of twilight clouds.
Having mounted his chariot, which was variegated with patterns of coral and gold, whose inner rims produced the sound of bells, and which was adorned with a crown and garlands—
That great lord of the asuras went forth for battle.
And the Dānava named Kujambha, the younger brother of Virocana,
[advanced] with many thousands of chariots adorned with jewels and gold.
The enemy of the gods and crusher of foes was surrounded by those intoxicated with the pride of boons,
who were themselves enemies of the deities and swollen with the intoxication of their own power.
by the Dānavas, who longed for battle and held spears, nooses, and maces in their hands;
He had a form resembling a mountain, with the luster of a mass of split collyrium,
and was adorned with a great, radiant crown of exquisite brilliance.
Clad in armor variegated with every kind of jewel,
he was upon a great chariot of radiant form, like the moon with its rays.
With his great palm-tree banner made of gold,
he shone as he stood in the midst of the chariot like the sun atop Mount Meru.
Skilled in battle and possessed of great heroism, strength, and intelligence,
he proceeds swiftly toward the divine assembly.
Surrounded by hosts of Asuras, Kujambha was like the lord of the immortals, Vṛtra-slayer Indra, surrounded by the throngs of the thirty gods.
And there was the Dānava Asiloman, whose weapon was a mountain;
having assumed a terrible form, he was fierce and possessed a dreadful countenance.
Fierce, with eyes like the wheels of a cart, a great illusionist, and possessed of great strength;
clothed in black, with large tusks, red eyes, and a blood-red face.
He was surrounded by a flood of thousands of Daityas— those enemies of the gods who assumed various forms, were radiant, and resembled mountains, trees, and oceans.
Moving here and there in the sky with tridents in their hands,
making sounds like masses of clouds,
they covered the firmament like golden breastplates.
Like the dark clouds that arise at the onset of the rainy season.
The son of Anāyuṣā was the great asura named Vṛtra,
an enemy of the gods, possessed of a massive body, copper-colored face, and a sunken belly.
With a flaming tongue, a tawny beard, hair standing erect, and large jaws;
with a dark-blue body, a red neck, wearing a diadem, and adorned with red armlets.
With arms reaching down to his knees, deformed, with white fangs, and terrifying,
he was a master of great illusion, most fearsome, and adorned with golden armlets.
Well-encased in a great armor variegated with jewels,
wearing a golden garland, fierce, bearing the discus-banner, and impatient, he stood there.
Resounding with hundreds of small bells, adorned with refined gold,
it was yoked to a thousand horses and featured red banners and flags.
Mounting his divine chariot, the increaser of the Daityas' joy advanced toward the battle with a great array of chariots.
With eyes tawny like molten drops of gold,
the son of Diti was the leader of the asura army in battle;
his beautiful face possessed the splendor of a full-blown lotus.
With his white teeth, he shone as he sat upon the seat of the chariot.

But there, Ekacakra arose like the solar disc; fierce like the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), he stood with his weapon, the discus, raised as if it were the very embodiment of all weapons. Mounted upon that divine, radiant chariot composed of every kind of weapon, he shone forth.
He was surrounded by arrogant hosts of Daityas, who wielded weapons of black iron stone.
He had eighty thousand chariots with warriors who fought with diverse skills;
all were like Yama at the end of time, red-eyed, and possessed of great strength.
Clad in excellent armor made of both iron and gold,
those warriors shone in the sky like dark blue clouds.
With their lips bitten together, terrible, massive-bodied, and pot-bellied,
those of great strength armed themselves for the slaughter of the divine army.
All those heroes, resembling the Destroyer at the end of time, invincible in battle,
as deep as the belly of the ocean, with dark-blue faces and difficult to approach,
shone as they marched like the foremost of the Asuras, like oceans that have overstepped their shores.
Those masters of terrifying illusions, possessing perfectly formed bodies, wearing diadems and with limbs adorned with gold,
then proceeded with their weapons held aloft in their hands.
Like great winged mountains, they reached the sky.
Commanded by the son of Bali, the heroic and great Asura Vṛtra’s brother was told,
"Prepare yourself for the slaughter of the divine army."
Wearing a golden garland, possessing large tusks, adorned with a wreath and beautiful earrings,
wearing red garlands and garments, he was fierce and difficult to conquer in battle.
With large, wide-open eyes, wearing a diadem and wielding a bow,
he was like an elephant in rut, possessing the prowess of a tiger.
Drawing his bow, which resembled a great palm tree and was fitted with most beautiful arrows,
he exerted great force that produced a sound like the crash of a thunderbolt;
he rode in a chariot yoked with donkeys and bearing a banner marked by a serpent.
Seated upon his chariot, he shone like the sun at the time of twilight.
With many thousands of chariots adorned with bands of gold,
filled with spears and mallets like clouds filled with water.
With his lips bitten together, he was enraged and roaring most terrifyingly.
That lord of the Daityas advanced when that battle was at hand.
Moving with the speed of the wind, broad-chested,
and fair as the lovely interior of a blooming lotus,
he proceeded swiftly, mounted upon his excellent chariot.
His power was recognized by the hosts of the thirty gods.
And the son of Siṃhikā was the great Asura named Rāhu;
he was hideous, mountain-like in form, with a hundred heads and a hundred bellies.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, adorned with gold from the Jambū river, he resembles smooth lapis lazuli; his eyes are like the petals of a lotus.
It was entirely composed of gold, adorned with nets of jewels,
crowded with hundreds of banners, and yoked to excellent horses.
The Daitya of supreme valor ascended his divine chariot and let out a great roar, making the surface of the earth tremble.
Maya fashioned for him a divine, golden banner;
he also provided a peacock resplendent as the sun and armor with the luster of iron.
The one of great strength was attended by other divine chariots, brilliantly radiant, possessing terrifying speed and noise,
and strewn with various weapons.
The lord of the hosts of Asuras, moving with the gait of a great elephant,
became the refuge and the excellent path for the great Asuras;
the all-pervading one advanced toward the enemy host from every side.
He has departed like the sun to the setting mountain, the best of peaks.
Vipracitti, the increaser of Danu’s lineage, was born right there;
he was the illustrious son of Kaśyapa, equal to Brahmā in his splendor.
He was the performer of thousands of sacrifices, a knower of the Vedas, and endowed with ascetic power;
he had received boons from the Self-born Creator, was himself a granter of boons, and possessed independent sovereignty.
He held lordship, self-control, and greatness—belonging to that one of great splendor.
Endowed with the quality of sovereignty and as powerful as Brahmā himself,
that one of great strength donned his armor together with his sons and grandsons.
All were masters of illusion, heroic, skilled in weapons, and invincible in battle;
all possessed the luster of lotuses and were as tall as the peak of Mount Hemakūṭa.
All of them were like silver and resembled the peaks of Kailāsa;
all those chariots were fashioned by Maya and consisted of illusory power.
Wandering about, they shone like autumnal clouds;
all had white banners marked with swans and were raised upon white staffs.
The Daityas wore white garments and were adorned with white garlands;
they all possessed white parasols and were embellished with white earrings.

With chests encircled by pearl necklaces, they shine like the lords of the *nāgas*; their forms resemble great planets, causing the hair of their enemies to stand on end. They wear variegated garments of red silk and are adorned with diverse ornaments.
The valiant one, mounting the chariot named Trailokyavijaya,
which resembled the peak of Mount Kailāsa and measured eight *nalvas* in its interior width, [set forth].
It was yoked with a thousand white horses, radiant as the moon,
covered with hundreds of banners, and equipped with various weapons.
A large white parasol, resembling a swan, a lotus fiber, or a kunda flower, shone as it was held over the lord of the Danavas.
The moon has descended to the summit of the White Mountain.
Keśin, the chief of the Dānavas, was crooked and had copper-colored eyes;
he resembled a mass of dark clouds, black and possessing the form of a man.
Having a form resembling a great planet, he causes the hair of his enemies to stand on end;
he wears variegated garlands and garments, and is adorned with red ornaments.
He had a hundred eyes and a hundred arms, with a tawny beard and great strength;
he had spike-like ears, a loud roar, and was fierce to behold in his physical form.
Yoked with divine buffaloes, its sound produced by millions of bells,
he mounted that supreme chariot which had the form of a great rain-cloud.
It was adorned with a great banner featuring a camel of the hue of a blue filament,
and decorated with pennants variegated with many colors.
Fifty-two thousand chariots of fierce splendor followed that lord of the asuras as he set out against the gods.
As the Great-souled One departed, there shone forth [beings] resembling crushed collyrium,
with faces like half-moons and fangs, appearing like clouds accompanied by cranes.
That crown of the supreme asura, variegated with lapis lazuli and gold, radiant as lightning and equal to the rays of the sun, shines brilliantly.
Like a mountain peak ablaze with a forest fire.
And the glorious asura Vṛṣaparvan, the destroyer of the gods,
mounted his divine chariot like the sun ascending the peak of Mount Meru.
A great, noble chariot, capable of bearing heavy loads, adorned with coral and gold, its pole decorated with variegated designs,
beautifully ornamented, and featuring silver and golden wheels.
Resembling the rays of the sun, the stars, and lightning.
His arms were bound with armlets and bracelets,
and he was equipped with a shield marked by a thousand stars and various colorful ornaments for battle.
He became like the midday sun.
Possessing great strength, with his fingers and palms joined,
fierce in power, and with eyes as red as *kiṃśuka* flowers;
having seized [the bow] which was beautiful, variegated, and made of gold—
Standing with eyes that were round and wide, he held a bow.
While the armies were engaged in the process of donning their armor,
O Lord of the Earth, and the warriors were ready for battle;
The chariots had their poles made variegated with ornaments,
and the elephants were prepared for battle by the foot-soldiers.
Then Bali, the great lord of the asuras, surrounded by the great asuras,
ascended his vast chariot,
which was adorned with beryl and gold.
Vidyutprabha was sixteen cubits in height.
It was joined by a thousand sons of Diti,
with elephant-like faces and distorted countenances,
their broad chests adorned with gold.
And of the thundering clouds during the rainy season.
A great chariot, radiant like the chariot of a god, created by Maya through his thousandfold powers of illusion,
and variegated with the decorative patterns of sporting lions.
A divine chariot followed by heroic chariots.
It was filled with all kinds of missiles, possessed the speed of the wind,
was equipped with small bells, stainless, and very extensive.
Adorned with hundreds of golden lotuses,
Bali took up the Vaijayantī garland, made of various golden flowers, for the sake of victory.
Having fastened his variegated garland,
Bali then shone with his broad arms;
he gleamed with those limbs endowed with every perfection.
With great radiance, he stood in the sky like the sun.
Then Vairocana, endowed with all splendor, bound upon him a difficult-to-fasten garland that served as a necklace for all the Asuras.
He shines like the moon in autumn.
With its banks reddened by the glow of gold,
it was like a dark cloud touched by the sun;
and there were palaces and snares bound with gold.
Shields, swords, and battle-axes.
Bows possessing the splendor of the thunderbolt-weapon,
divine maces, and spears with diamond-tipped points;
divine swords and blazing arrows.
Various quivers filled with iron arrows were borne upon the chariot of that bull among the Daityas;
they shone like blazing torches.
And disciplined attendants, wearing crests of yak-tail fans, possessing fine tusks, and adorned with gold, pearls, gems, and gold,
fanned him with yak-tail whisks.
Well-adorned, they stood upon the platforms of their chariots.
Ayaḥśiras, Aśvaśiras, Durāpa, Śibi, Mataṅga, Vikaṭa, Śatākṣa,
Aja, Nikumbha, and the Dānava Kupatha.
These ten protected the lord of the Dānavas.
And thousands of Asuras marched as precursors, the foot-soldiers who protected the king of the Dānavas,
bearing in their hands *śataghnīs*, discuses, thunderbolts, and spears.
They went on ahead, possessing a speed equal to the wind.
Gongs with beautiful sounds, bound in gold; kettledrums, cymbals, and ḍiṇḍimas;
and great-sounding drums resounded.
At the departure of the chariot of the lord of the Daityas.
His great banner was raised high, rich with golden pedestals, made of gold, adorned with divine great flags, and bound with refined gold.
He shone like the sun, as it were, for that hero.
A raised golden parasol and a golden garland shine upon his chest;
and they attend upon him from all sides.
The sages among the Daityas worship with palms joined in reverence.
The family priests, intent upon the destruction of the enemy, as well as others who were advanced in learning and virtuous conduct,
[performed rites] with prayers, mantras, and medicinal herbs.
They performed a rite for the well-being of the Great-souled One.
There, the Daitya Bali gave to the Brahmins fine garments, auspicious cows, fruits, flowers, and likewise golden coins.
He shines forth exceedingly, like the Lord of Wealth.
It possessed a thousand suns and many small bells;
it was variegated with the finest Jāmbūnada gold;
and it bore a thousand moons and ten thousand stars.
The chariot of Bali shines like fire.
Mounted upon that chariot seized by the Dānavas,
the one of great strength, wielding his bow and arrows,
prepared to turn back the army of the lord of the thirty gods.
He bears an exceedingly fierce form.
That ocean of Daityas, possessing great speed and crowded with a multitude of heroic chariots, advanced toward the gods like a vast sea agitated by waves and billows.
Just as by the floods of water at the dissolution of the eon, so [was it].
With bodies that strike terror into the three worlds, those of great strength, with their bows raised high, marched ahead of Bala’s chariot.
O King, like forests together with their mountains.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: O Janamejaya, you have heard in detail the account of the Daitya army.
Furthermore, hear in detail from the beginning concerning the army of the thirty gods.
Then, having heard from the messenger about the armor-clad array of the Daityas, the lord of the gods—
The blessed lord of the gods, Vāsava, indeed commanded the deities—
the hosts of Maruts, the Ādityas, and the Viśvedevas.
[He subdued] all eight Vasus intensely, as well as the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and great serpents;
and he swiftly [subdued] the eight Vasus, the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kiṃnaras.
All the hosts of Vidyādharas and the Gandharvas of great power.
And the great oceans and mountains, as well as the Rudras of mighty power,
both Yama and Vaiśravaṇa, and Varuṇa, the lord of the waters.
But those who are perfected, the high-souled ones, the wise ancestors,
and likewise hundreds of royal seers who have attained perfection through yoga—
The powerful Śakra, the commander of the thirty gods, the lord, issues this command:
"O sirs, arm yourselves for the destruction of the Daityas!"
Having heard the words of Śakra, all those high-souled inhabitants of heaven, possessing prowess equal to that of Śakra, then equipped themselves for battle.
All were clad in various armor, with diverse armors and banners;
with hands raised holding various weapons, they were like great elephants in rut.
Some mounted tigers; some mounted elephants;
some mounted serpents; and some mounted bulls.
With tawny eyes and a tawny beard, he yoked his chariot— whose banner bore the elephant Airāvata—
with bay horses, and set forth toward the battlefield.
It was sun-colored, stainless, and well-polished; it had been fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ himself for the sake of the Lord,
and its lattices were variegated with inlaid designs of Jāmbūnada gold.
And it was adorned with golden garlands.
This vehicle of Indra, adorned with a beautiful seat and equipment,
made reddish-brown by the flashes of lightning,
resembles a peak of Mount Kailāsa.
A wheel with spokes that are exceedingly beautiful and lovely.
His entire body was honored with divine garlands by thousands of radiant, blazing stars;
he bore a raised banner of glory and possessed imperishable eyes.
blazing with his most excellent body.
Mounting that radiant chariot of swift speed,
Śacīpati, the lord of the worlds, the sovereign of the gods,
the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the protector of the universe—
The high-souled Lord Mahendra departed.
Then, having donned armor adorned with a thousand stars, possessing a splendor equal to fire and the sun,
he put on a diadem that shone like the sun.
And a garland made of Jāmbūnada gold, a Vaijayantī.
It was fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, blazing with radiant rays, possessing an exceedingly sharp, terrible, and stainless keen edge,
and fierce, drenched in the blood of the great Asuras.
Having grasped the vajra, the foremost of those with a hundred joints.
The great thunderbolt, the two [missiles] resembling great planets, the blazing and unerring spear of terrible power,
as well as the discus of Indra and the very great bow;
Having grasped it, Śakra set out for battle.
The thousand-eyed Lord of Beings, eternal,
he who is the eternal among the eternal,
the high-souled sovereign of the gods, departs.
And he took a variegated tiger skin.
These excellent ornaments, produced from the churning of the Ocean of Milk at the time of the ancient nectar,
were won by the gods and asuras through their exertion.
[They possess] the splendors of the moon, the sun, the stars, and lightning.
The jeweled earrings were given by Aditi to the Lord of the Gods as he set out for battle;
adorned with them, the Thousand-eyed One proceeds.
Illuminating indeed the intermediate directions and the cardinal quarters.
The Lord Hari, the sovereign of the gods, resplendent with his thousand eyes, shines as he faces the battle,
like a mass of white autumn clouds.
The vault of heaven, variegated with thousands of stars.
Then that great-souled one, having mounted Airāvata, the best of elephants, went forth for battle.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Jamadagni, and Aurva praised him with expansive words and blessings for victory as he departed, his strength and valor being exalted.
Bṛhaspati, Nārada, and Parvata.
The hosts of gods accompanied Mahendra as he set forth, possessing a splendor equal to the sun;
so too did all the Viśvedevas and all the Maruts.
Likewise, all the Sādhyas and the hosts of Ādityas.
And those horses of the king of the gods, Purandara, which were guided by Mātali,
proceeded along, carrying the lord of the gods.
As if they were kicking the surface of the sky with their feet.
And the brahmin seers, the divine seers,
and the royal seers, who possess worlds of inexhaustible merit.
They all followed Śakra, who was blazing, endowed with splendor, and the subduer of his enemies, moving with haste.
Grasping tridents and battle-axes, flaming bows and various thunderbolts,
and donning their golden armor.
They proceed with splendors equal to the rays of the sun.
Likewise, Kubera, having mounted a divine and highly precious chariot that was capable of enduring all things and yoked with a thousand horses, went forth for battle.
The Lord of Wealth, with a blazing mace held in his hand.
The night-stalkers, whose bodies were smoky with fire,
were bull-like Rākṣasas of that friend of Rudra,
their hands radiant with various broad weapons.
They go before King Vaiśravaṇa.
Those supreme Yakṣas, with eyes red as crushed collyrium powder, surround the god,
the Lord of Wealth, the Master of Yakṣas, and proceed along.
Indeed, they guard [it], with spears, clubs, and swords in their hands.
The meritorious lord, the master of living beings, self-restrained, son of Vivasvat, the most excellent among the upholders of dharma—
[he mounted] that chariot yoked with a hundred horses, which shone like lightning.
Mount the chariot that is like the sun.
The Pitṛs, purified of sin and blazing with glory, followed that guardian of the world;
and all the beings who are the foremost in the universe [did so as well].
With their hands occupied by various weapons, they were most terrifying.
Taking up the staff, that great weapon, the god [took] the world-goad, which has the purpose of determining the outcome of conflict;
[and he took] golden lotuses and water-lilies.
Having placed a beautiful garland around his neck.
Standing there, drenched in marrow, flesh, and blood,
he awaited the destruction of all the asuras,
wielding a fierce, radiant mallet of terrible form.
Dragging [him] along, his eyes were reddish-brown like smoke.
Endowed with many hundreds of diseases,
the lion-bearded one of noble spirit set his mind upon the destruction of the great asuras.
Then Kṛtānta, the lord of diseases, set it in motion.
Then the high-souled Lord of the Waters, mounting a chariot adorned with gold and yoked to massive three-headed serpents, which was as bright as a kunda flower or the moon, [proceeded].
The destroyer of the pride of the Asuras went forth to battle.
His body adorned with beryl, pearls, and jewels,
consisting of radiant energy and holding a noose in his hand,
the god appeared for the destruction of the great asuras.
He proceeds with his arms adorned by silver mines.
He was followed by water-deities and attended upon by aquatic creatures.
And he was being praised by throngs of great seers,
and honored by the great serpents.
Resembling a peak of Mount Kailāsa, immeasurable,
the lord of the ocean, the drinker of nectar, the great-souled one,
protected by his own great serpents and sons.
He departed on a chariot possessing a splendor equal to the sun.
As he of undaunted spirit proceeded toward battle,
all beings beheld that high-souled one, as radiant as the moon in the vault of heaven.
With their hair standing on end, they joined their palms in reverence.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Parjanya, Mitra, and the god Śaśin;
likewise Tvaṣṭṛ and the powerful Viśvakarman.
And Pūṣan was like the king of the gods himself in person.
With awnings provided with banners and small bells,
and adorned with neck-chains of lapis lazuli and gold;
Those gods mounted chariots yoked with excellent horses that shone like the horse of Śakra.
Some resembled the form of the sun; some were like the flames of a fire;
and some were like the rays of the moon.
Some [beings] resemble the brilliance of the flash of lightning.
Some [trees] resemble clouds with blue rays,
possessing the colors of flowers set upon copper-colored surfaces that have a blue luster.
Some resemble the appearance of black iron, while others shine with the luster of gold.
Divine armors of great splendor, fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, possessed of supreme radiance.
Wearing garlands of golden lotuses,
they proceed with a speed like that of water or wind;
and there are also the two Aśvins of great majesty.
They were supreme in form and the most excellent among the upholders of the Dharma.
Having mounted a chariot adorned with gold,
those two, whose complexion was like that of gold, went to the battlefield;
for they were all the sons of Manu and the Vasus.
The gods, fierce in their power, [set out] for the sake of slaying the Daityas.
Mounting chariots and elephants of immense size, they went forth with beautiful weapons in their hands;
and all the Rudras were of a reddish-brown hue.
They went forth with large, white bull-leaders.
Possessing great majesty and endowed with all virtues,
they blazed as if with splendors from their radiant selves;
with arms whose hands were occupied with various weapons, they [stood].
As if burning up all the worlds.
They went forth with their armies, adorned with gold,
like clouds accompanied by lightning;
and all the gods, blazing with ascetic power, followed.
They possess supreme vigor and are the color of sunbeams.
Accompanied by their armies, those who were irresistible in battle, fierce in their strength, and adorned with garlands of a thousand lotuses,
went forth on well-yoked chariots the color of refined gold.
Variegated with garlands of beryl, pearls, and jewels.
They were crowded with various forms of weapons and with fluttering white parasols.
With white umbrellas as lovely as the autumn moon,
consisting of radiant energy, beautiful and variegated with gold, and perfectly stainless like fire, they shone.
With breastplates adorned with banners and small bells,
with horses possessing a speed equal to the wind,
and with mighty elephants belonging to the quarters of the sky, they [advanced].
With great peaks resembling the summits of Mount Kailāsa.
With weapons raised and hands blazing, they advanced like flaming meteors at the end of the four ages;
so too did the Sādhyas and the gods of immense power.
With their wheels under their own control and their faces blazing,
they proceed through the sky with floods of troops along the paths of the Ganges' current, their limbs adorned with gold from Jambūnada.
Illuminating the intermediate and main directions,
those mighty ones, the best among victors,
possessed of excellent backs, lips, and arms, were exceedingly proud.
They possessed a splendor equal to that of Vaiśvānara and the sun.
They were being saluted by those who know Brahman and honored by the gods, together with Śakra.
Followed by hosts of Gandharvas for the sake of slaying those lords of the Asuras.
The appearance of those adorned with garments of gold and variegated cloths made of beryl, diamond, and the finest crystal, along with their magnificent ornaments, became truly resplendent.
For the destruction of the lords of the Daityas, they were adorned with ornaments.
And with the splendors of their own bodies, fierce in battle,
and with the splendors of their armor that dispel the darkness;
With the splendors of their own bodies, which are like excellent banners— possessing great radiance and intense brilliance— those foremost of gods, together with the Sādhyas, shine forth.
The sounds of blown conchs and lion-roars resounded.
Standing in great chariots, those dwellers of heaven,
possessed of great strength, advanced against the enemy force;
with great weapons in their hands, they went forth in fierce form.
The gods [struggled] for the destruction of the great asuras.
In that very manner, all the Maruts, possessed of extreme heroism,
fierce in their strength, and renowned for battle in the sky,
departed with a complexion like that of great clouds.
They possessed many weapons and roared with the sound of thunderclouds.
Resembling the standard of Mahendra, those of great strength,
fierce in battle and smeared with red sandalwood paste, took up their maces, which were the destroyers of all asuras.
Their limbs were adorned with golden garlands and garments.
Those heroes, skilled in battle, with strong arms and prowess,
fierce in their strength and eyes reddened with rage,
went forth wearing garlands of golden lotuses.
They assume various forms of desire according to their will.
With the surfaces of their shoulders darkened by the luster of their swords,
the gods indeed surrounded Purandara.
Having fastened upon their limbs great, radiant armors of beautiful form made of beryl and gold,
which ward off the weapons of the Daityas.
They go forth to battle, capable of enduring their rivals.
With those excellent banners, richly adorned with golden pedestals and possessing the hue of the sun’s rays,
that army of the gods, endowed with fierce energy, marched forth.
Uttering lion-like roars while shouting aloud in battle.
Thus was that fierce army of the Lord of the Thirty-three, possessed of great majesty,
as he set out to fight, bringing victory with him.
For the sake of the destruction of those lords of the Asuras.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Thereupon,
the conflict between the Asuras and the gods commenced.
Then the world, teeming with gods and asuras, appeared wondrous;
having transgressed their bounds like the great oceans at the end of a yuga, they seemed to support one another.
Their limbs were illuminated by the radiance of various uplifted weapons; they possessed great strength and drew their bows wide;
they were fierce with intoxication, and their hands were like the trunks of elephants.
The Sudurjayas have the roar of thundering clouds.
Suddenly drawing their bows,
they brandished wheels radiant as the sun and hurled terrible thunderbolts.
And they [wielded] swords, as well as thunderbolt-tipped spears.
They seized great maces bound with golden bands, as well as iron bows and clubs,
and flaming spears and trees.
Hundreds of heroes stationed on the battlefield roar aloud.
In the meantime, as they were striking one another,
dual combats took place between the gods and the dānavas.
Some with spears, others likewise with iron clubs,
and still others with swords and nooses, O lord of the earth.
Then some of those heroes of battle fought with bows, others with clubs, and some with spears in the fray.
Then other heroes there struck one another with wheels, axes, and swords, as well as with maces adorned with iron bands.
The great asuras and the best of gods, O King.
O King, spears struck against spears, and swords were struck evenly by swords;
and in the battle, heroic warriors struck lances with lances.
Now they have been struck down, yet they continue to shine.
Striking arrows with arrows, struck arrows [with arrows], and likewise striking shafts with shafts,
the chariot-warrior drove his chariot by force in that great battle.
The elephant-rider with spear in hand pursues the elephant;
the horseman with swift hand pursues the horse;
the rider with quivering lips pursues the foot-soldier.
And Khaḍgī, having slain that hero of battle in combat,
roared with his sword in hand; while Pāśī,
having bound him in the encounter with his noose, [roared].
Holding a noose, with his lower lip quivering.
Having slain only an elephant with his own elephant,
and when the lord of elephants had been struck down by that excellent sword,
he quickly pulled up two tusks and [attacked] another enemy.
He struck them with those two [weapons] and roared once more.
A certain warrior of fierce valor,
having slain a horseman with his own axes and spears,
swiftly struck down another of that man's followers.
The one of great strength took up his weapon in the battle.
And some elephants fell in the great battle; horses with their necks severed lay upon the earth;
and some chariots had fierce spears entangled within them.
And some of the soldiers had their axles and poles crushed.
Then, in the battle, hosts of Piśācas and the foremost of Rākṣasas moved about with nooses; likewise,
vultures, cranes, hawks, and pigeons [also moved].
Tearing at my flesh, they all cried out.
Tearing up and pulling out heaps of flesh,
they drink their fill of the blood of corpses;
having cut off many pieces of flesh in the battle, they devour them.
Then the hosts of Piśācas divided the locations.
Then, in that battle, many musical instruments produced a great and forceful sound; conchs,
kettledrums, cymbals, and ḍiṇḍimas [resounded].
Being struck repeatedly, they let out a great cry.
Suddenly the worlds fell into agitation, and all the masses of water were stirred up at the gathering of the Daityas and great Asuras.
Of the dwellers of heaven who were eager for battle.
When that great and most terrible battle between the gods and the great asuras had commenced,
single combats took place there in that supreme conflict.
O King, [this was said] by the gods and asuras who desired victory.
[Colophon] He who was the fifth of the Maruts fought with Bāṇa;
he was the mighty and excellent god whom they know as Sāvitra.
The son of Anāyuṣā was the great asura named Bala; he, being exceedingly fierce, fought in battle with Dhruva Vasu. And Namuci, the best of asuras, fought with Dhara.
Together with his entire army, he was like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
Viśvakarman, the best of the gods, fought with Maya;
they were both renowned as the foremost architects among the lords of the gods and the asuras.
The great Daitya Puloman fought with Vāyu;
armored and resembling a mountain, he fought in battle together with his army.
But Hayagrīva, the son of Diti, fought against Pūṣan.
By the hero of immeasurable valor, whose splendor was like the form of the sun.
Then Śambara, the great Asura of immense heroism and great power of illusion, who was intoxicated by battle, fought accompanied by Bhaga.
Śarabha and Śalabha, acting as the moon and sun for the Daityas,
fought together against Soma with the wise Śiśira weapon.
But the powerful Virocana, the father of the mighty Bali,
fought with the divine Viṣvaksena, who is to be accomplished.
Kujambha, possessed of great splendor and the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
then fought with a portion [of himself] using a spear as his weapon.
But Asiloman, O Lord, being equal in strength to Māruta,
fought then with a blazing face, deformed, and having mountains for weapons.
The son of Anāyuṣā, however, was the great asura named Vṛtra;
he fought in battle with the two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods.
But Ekacakra, the son of Diti, who was difficult to approach and held a discus in his hand,
fought with the divine Sādhya, the enemy of the sons of Diti.
But the powerful great asura Bala, honey-tawny-eyed and the brother of Vṛtra,
fought with Rudra in his form as the Deer-Hunter.
Rāhu, however, of deformed appearance, with a hundred heads and a hundred bellies,
fought in battle against Ajaikapāda, being himself clad in armor.
Keśin, the best of the Dānavas, who possessed the luster of a rain-cloud in the monsoon season,
fought in battle with the formidable Dhaneśvara.
But the powerful Vṛṣaparvan,
the lord of the Viśvedevas, fought in battle with the heroic Niṣkaṃbhu, who was accompanied by the Viśvedevas.
But Prahrāda, possessed of great heroism and surrounded by his own heroic sons,
fought against Kāla in battle, standing like Kāla himself.
In a great battle, Anuhrāda fought with Kubera, the giver of wealth,
who held a mace in his hand, while agitating the army of his enemies.
But Vipracitti, the son of Diti and the increaser of the joy of the Daityas, set out indeed to wage war against the high-souled Varuṇa.
But Bali, being powerful himself, fought in battle with Śakra, the high-souled lord of the gods and king of the deities, who was likewise mighty.
The remaining gods and Daityas struck one another in the battle,
uttering great roars, with spears, swords, arrows, and javelins.
The great portents that are said to appear at the destruction of the world were seen;
the seven winds became agitated and the mountains shattered.
Seven suns rose up, drying up the great oceans;
the earth was split in many places, as if churned by the wind.

And great clouds arose, their bellies marked by rainbows; all living beings cried out, and all the quarters of the sky were shrouded in gloom. A terrible defeat of the gods was seen, brought about by Time.
Brave enemies of the gods, created by Time, are seen.
[Note: T1.2 G1.3-5 M2.4 substitute for line 783; V3 B Ds D6 insert after line 783:]
Terrible portents arose as if at the time of the end of an eon;
for neither the atmosphere, nor the directions, nor the earth,
nor the sun could be seen due to the masses of dust.
Tumultuous winds accompanied by smoke blew forth,
and all the directions were shrouded in darkness.
These and many others, created by the gods, are seen everywhere—
terrible portents on the earth as well as in the atmosphere.
At the time of the end of the age, these and others likewise exist in reality.
The preceptor Brahmā, together with all the gods, beheld that battle between the gods and the Daityas, which was terrifying and fierce to behold.
The eternal, glorious one, born from the lotus, was surrounded by the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and branches of knowledge, as well as by the Siddhas and supreme ṛṣis.
Having ascended a vehicle variegated with thousands of pillars made of various jewels, the Self-Existent One beheld it—
resplendent and accompanied by thousands of living beings.
His body was blazing with supreme splendor.
Variegated and beautiful with well-refined gold, resounding with the beating of hundreds of drums of joy,
and radiant as the moon with its rays amidst the stars.
[With rays of light: His body was adorned with lapis lazuli, the moon, and the sun.
Then his own son Pulaha, as well as Pulastya, Marīci, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras,
praised him properly with the Ṛg and Sāman hymns.
They serve the boon-granting god in his celestial palace.
The Vedas with their auxiliary branches, the sacrificial deities, and the fires serve that self-existent Purifier, the Teacher of the World,
the God who is the Lord of the lords of the universe.
And other beings [honored] that one of great majesty.
These multitudes of men, as well as others—
the Vaikhānasas and those born from the sacrificial fire—
and all the priests of the gods, departed.
Eager for battle against all the gods and asuras,
they were six masters of yoga, radiant as the sun,
with their entire bodies adorned by ornaments of speech.
Janārdana is the Lord of the world, the Lord of the gods.
The Lord Mādhava himself— Śikhin, Cakrin, and the wielder of the arrow and the Śārṅga bow— having vanished from sight,
goes to witness the battle against the king of mountains.
Remaining in the sky, they indeed beheld Nārāyaṇa and the god Nara, who had become invisible.
With his four beautiful faces, which resembled the full moon and were the bearers of the four Vedas,
he made all directions free from darkness.
He was like the moon newly risen in the autumn sky.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, a battle then took place between those two armies.
Listen attentively, O King, to how the battle took place;
by the recitation of this account of that war, one is immediately liberated from sin.
Causing this imperishable triple world to tremble with his roar.
And the great sounds of *gomukha* trumpets, *āḍambara* drums, and kettledrums, together with clay drums, *jharjharī* cymbals, and *ḍiṇḍima* drums, were heard.
Then the tumultuous sacrifice of battle commenced, hair-raising and filled with great clamor upon the field; it was conducive to heaven and esteemed by the brave.
At the commencement of that sacrifice of war, Prahrāda, the best of the Daityas, was the Hotṛ;
likewise, Virocana was the Adhvaryu, the one who set the sacrifice of war in motion.
And there, Namuci Vṛtra was the Hotṛ priest,
while the Daityas were proclaimed as the formulators of the hymns (*stotra*) in that sacrificial rite.
He followed his father, or perhaps even excelled him in prowess;
there Bāṇa became a performer of sacrifices and stood ready in battle.
Indeed,
Bāṇa was the sacrificer there, and he remained perfectly established.
37:1 [On the other hand,]
That arrow was not desired there, for he remained standing in the battle;
[he discharged] the Aindra, Pāśupata, Brāhma, Sthūṇākarṇa, and Sudurjaya [weapons].
There, the mantras, properly applied and free from errors, came forth successfully.
And the Daityas were renowned there in the mantras and in the rites of the Yakṣas;
the illustrious Maya, the terrifier of all, stood there as the Udgātṛ priest.
Roaring aloud, the best of the Diti-born tore asunder the army of the gods.
But there was a radiant king named Bali, a great Asura who was eternally present there; indeed,
King Bali was powerful, with a splendor equal to that of Vaiśvānara.
Engaged in recitations and burnt offerings, the Lord performed the office of the Brahman priest.
The terrible fire of battle blazed forth, fanned by the fuel of enmity;
there, upon the altar of the chariot, the god Viṣṇu was consecrated by the gods.
With the tumultuous sounds of conchs and the great roar of kettledrums,
a vast proclamation was made, and the *subrahmaṇya* litany was chanted.
Bala, Balaka, and the great asura Puloman,
having assumed peaceful forms, properly invoked the mantra.
Rows of chariots, with their variegated poles, spotless and vast,
were fashioned like sacrificial posts for the great-yielding sacrifice of war.
Karṇis, nālīkas, nārācas, vatsadantas, and upabṛṃhakas;
tomara-spears, soma-vessels, and various kinds of bows.
In this sacrifice, the bones are the sacrificial vessels, the skulls are the *puroḍāśa* cakes, and the blood is the *ājya* clarified butter; these belong to Rudra and are offered therein.
There, the fuel-sticks were the sacrificial enclosures, and the spreading grass was massive maces;
Hayagrīva, Asiloman, Rāhu, and Keśin were the Dānavas.
Virocana, Jambha, the mighty Kujambha,
and the valiant Vipracitti were the officiating priests at that sacrifice.
In that great sacrifice, the arrows were the *sruva* ladles, beautiful and resembling the axles of chariots;
the tips of the bows and the bowstrings were the *sruva* ladles there.
Then Vṛṣaparvan performed the duties of the Pratiprasthātṛ priest;
Bali was initiated there, and Mahācamū was his wife.
There, Śambara, the son of Diti, performed the office of the *śamitṛ*;
there, the powerful Śambara then performed the office of the *āgnīdhra*.
During the Atirātra sacrifice, while the ritual was being performed, the mighty-armed one [acted].
The sacrificial fee for that sacrifice was the great Asura Kālanemi,
O Lord, who during the ritual of the fire-altar was renowned like the carrier of oblations (Agni) himself.
By means of the lifeless bodies of the thirty gods' army,
the sacrificial session (*savana*) established by the Daityas increased at that sacrifice.
In the sacrifice of battle, the fierce sons of Diti, roaring and exultant, drank the blood of the gods as if it were the soma-juice.
When the great Daitya Bali becomes the conqueror of the gods in battle, then indeed there will be the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) for the sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
The lords of the great asuras were performers of sacrifices who gave profuse sacrificial fees;
they were learned in the Vedas, possessed of good conduct, heroic, and all were ready to give up their lives.
Created for the abduction of the three worlds, they were consecrated for the sacrifice of battle;
all were observers of vows, wearing black antelope skins and bearing *muñja* grass.
Each person, according to their own capacity, engages in the work of battle as their respective duty.
Thus did that sacrifice of battle unfold among the high-souled ones,
as they struck one another with spears, double-edged swords, axes, and javelins.
Then those experts in the art of war each performed their respective duties as was fitting;
united in their resolve, they were intent on conquering the three worlds.
A great clamor arose from the armies of the gods and the Dānavas,
as they rushed forward in haste, bearing various weapons in their hands.
With the sounds of shouting and cries, with the trumpeting roars of elephants,
and with the terrible clatter of chariot wheels, a tumultuous din arose on all sides.
With the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and with the neighing of horses.
With the neighing of horses and the roaring of Dānavas,
along with the sounds of war-cries and shouts, as well as the noise of hands and feet.
The great, weapon-bearing [armies] of the Dānavas and their enemies seemed to split the very vault of the sky.
In that battle, the armies of the Daityas and the Suras, performing terrible deeds, shone forth.
Then the elephants and chariots, adorned with Jāmbūnada gold,
were seen shining brilliantly like clouds accompanied by lightning.
Sharp spears, swords, maces, tridents, javelins,
and battle-axes shone beautifully there, each in its own respective division within the ranks.
There were chariots of many forms by the hundreds and thousands,
their peaks covered in gold, blazing like fires.
The soldiers of both the Dānavas and the gods were seen,
all of them radiant with golden armor that possessed a brilliance equal to the blazing sun.
They appeared like luminous bodies arrayed in the sky;
with their various weapons raised, wearing hand-guards and carrying banners,
those bull-eyed hosts of gods shone as they took their positions at the head of the army.
In that battle, the wind blew away the multicolored banners and rows of standards belonging to those warriors who were intoxicated with the fray.
The radiant one caused the banners, ornaments, garments, shields,
and armor to shine with his rays, as they were colored by those very rays.
By the two immeasurable forces of those who travel on foot,
the dust covered everything, and the quarters of the sky became white like fine silk cloth.
All those gods and Dānavas then were bearers of divine weapons, with their arms and equipment blazing.
They engaged in a beautiful battle; the armies, arrayed against one another, stood firm against their opponents.
Then all those gods and dānavas, as tall as mountain peaks,
standing on the battlefield and fighting with diverse tactics, struck one another with sharp,
beautiful arrows, feathered and difficult to withstand.
With mallets, clubs, spears, iron-beaked hammers, and mortars;
with thunderbolts like lightning, as well as swords, trees, and the like.
Thus did that battle take place upon the summit of Mount Meru.
It was a great and terrible cause of destruction for the armies of both the gods and the dānavas.
When their clash had thus proceeded with marvelous prowess,
Bāṇa, seeking the slaughter of Sāvitra, took up his bow.
Covering the best of gods with a divine net of arrows,
he blazed forth with splendor through his power, like a flaming fire fed by oblations with mantras.
The bull among the Daityas dries up the great army of the gods with both oceans using floods of arrows, just as the sun dries up the sea with its rays.
That Māruta, possessing great velocity, hurled the supreme spear of Savitṛ at the son of Bali, just as Śakra hurls the thunderbolt at a mountain.
As that spear fell like a blazing great meteor,
it was split in two by a razor-edged arrow of wondrous power.
When the spear had been destroyed, Sāvitra, the best of gods,
[took up] a divine, very sharp weapon made by Viśvakarman, which was the destroyer of Dānavas.
He grasped a sharp sword that had a well-polished blade, vast, stainless, and radiant as the moon, like a venomous serpent.
Having seized that [bow] which was blazing with great luster at the front of the battle,
the one of great splendor stood with sword in hand near Bāṇa.
Then, observing that son of Savitṛ standing there—
red-eyed and of massive body— the delighter of Bala hurled [his weapon] at him and let out a roar.
Then the powerful one swiftly discharged a multitude of sharp arrows, which resembled the rays of the sun, were like thunderbolts, and were equal to venomous serpents.
He discharged on all sides fierce arrows that were gold-tufted, with blazing tips, of terrible velocity, beautifully adorned, and drawn back to his ear.
Those arrows, released from his firm bow and possessing the brilliance of fire,
covered Sāvitra just as clouds shroud Mount Kailāsa.
Being overwhelmed by the floods of weapons from Bāṇa, the son of Bali,
that best of gods turned his back and fled along with his chariot and banner.
Having defeated Sāvitra, Bāṇa, filled with supreme joy,
seized his formidable bow and advanced toward Śakra’s chariot.
And Bala, the best of the Asuras, seizing a massive club,
the Dānava hurled that terrible weapon at the head of Dhruva Vasu.
Then, in that battle, Dhruva’s body was shattered and his golden-decorated armor was indeed crushed by the terrible force of the mace.
And all the remaining Vasus covered the Daitya in battle with divine weapons of terrible appearance, just as clouds shroud the sun.
Then, provoked to anger by those arrows, Bala, the best of the Dānavas,
swiftly descended from that chariot, raising his mace with great force.
Having brandished it, the great asura brought down that supreme mace— which was made entirely of iron, divine, and adorned with gold—
upon his enemies.
Then he brought that mace down upon the heads of his enemies;
that great mace caused all the gods to flee in every direction.
Like Indra’s thunderbolt, they were increased by Indra and possessed a most great roar.
Then, agitated by that sound of Suvidyudghoṣā,
the chariot-warriors, having fallen from their chariots, fled in all directions.
That surging host of chariots, radiant as the sun and thundering like a cloud,
rained down upon the gods from all sides with showers of arrows—
kṣurapras, viśikhas, bhallas, vatsadantas, and śilīmukhas.
Again and again, the immensely powerful great Asura struck back;
Bala, mace in hand, was like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
Resembling lightning, a rainbow, and the sun, like another Vaiśvānara fire,
he seemed to drink up those showers of arrows rising from the celestial bow.
The lord of the Daityas rushed forward like another great ocean;
the Dānava, by his own prowess, made all the directions tremble.
The Daitya Sindhuvega crushed the gods like a torrent crushes mountains;
flourishing in his might, he overwhelmed the deities with his force as the wind overcomes trees with its power.
Then, subduing the great archers, he engaged in combat with the two Vasus.
And both subduers of enemies,
those scorchers of foes, rained down blazing showers of arrows like two clouds;
he [the opponent] cut down those flaming shafts as they were discharged in the sky.
They shattered various radiant palaces in the sky;
unable to endure that deed, Dhruva rushed toward him.
The two of them struck each other separately with showers of arrows.
Those two heroes of noble birth, who brought glory to the gods and the Daityas,
mangled one another with chariot-spears and arrows, like two tigers with their claws or two great elephants with their tusks.
Piercing each other’s limbs and scratching them with their arrows,
those two powerful warriors stood in battle, paralyzing one another and striking with their weapons;
they moved through various maneuvers and circular formations in their respective divisions.
Filled with pride and enraged, the two struck each other with mallets; then,
having cut down their divine shields and large bows with their swords, they who resembled mountains engaged in hand-to-hand combat.
Broad-chested, long-armed, and both skilled in wrestling,
they locked together with their arms like iron clubs.
Between the two of them there was a seizing and a restraining with blows of the arms;
it was exceedingly terrifying, like the crashing sound of a thunderbolt against a mountain.
Like two elephants with the tips of their tusks, or like two great bulls with their horns,
they seized one another in fury and dragged each other about for a moment.
Then, having been defeated by Balaka, the god Dhruva,
that Vasu, abandoned his chariot out of fear of him and fled toward the east.
And once again, a great and most terrible battle took place there between the enraged Namuci and the high-souled Dhara.
And those two mighty-armed, great archers, subduers of their enemies, being highly incensed,
gazed at one another as if burning each other with their eyes.
And having drawn his great bow, which was gold-backed and formidable from afar,
that best of the Vasus fought on, casting aside all regard for his life out of fury.
Surrounded by nets consisting of arrows, he covered the radiance of the sun with those brilliant shafts, polished on stone, as he advanced toward the chariot of the Daitya.
Then, laughing, Namuci discharged at Dhara blazing arrows, whetted on stone, possessing terrible velocity and difficult to withstand.
The Daitya, a great car-warrior (atiratha) of great splendor, mighty arms, and great speed,
pierced him with nine sharpened arrows.
Like an elephant being pierced by goads,
that best of Vasus, being struck by the feathered shafts, rushed furiously toward Namuci.
As he was rushing forward with speed and fury in the battle,
the Daitya Namuci charged against the god like one rutting elephant against another.
Then, having agitated that army— which resembled the surging ocean— he joyfully blew his conch shell, which resounded like a hundred kettledrums.
Mounting horses that had the hue of bears along with well-bred steeds the color of swans,
the Daitya overwhelmed Vasu in battle and covered him with arrows.
Then, seeing the two chariots of Vasu and Dānava closely locked together,
the great army of the gods trembled repeatedly.
Their eyes were copper-red, inflamed with anger, as they gazed at each other again and again.
Like two roaring tigers, or like two elephants in rut with temporal juice flowing.
The battlefield of those two was fierce, resembling a great cloud;
it was crowded with chariots, horses, and men, and thronged with rutting elephants.
Seeing those two great chariot-warriors looking on like a gathered assembly,
the warriors standing there in their respective groups hoped for victory from them both.
Desiring one another and relying upon one another,
they watched the imminent battle between those two great warriors.
Then the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Munis [were present], as were the Devas and Dānavas.
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Munis, and likewise Dānavas—
those two, covering each other in battle with sharpened arrows, [were watched by them].
Those two of great strength covered the sky with a mass of arrows.
Those two great chariot-warriors, desiring to slay one another, [assailed each other] with sharp arrows.
In that battle, those two struck one another with sharpened arrows.
They were even more beautiful to behold, like two rain-bearing clouds.
Discharging arrows fashioned of gold, those two subduers of enemies made the sky,
which was radiant like the sun, appear as if filled with meteors.
Then the arrows of those two, the god and the dānava,
shone like rows of intoxicated cranes in the autumn sky.
Indeed, in an instant, the earth was covered with the lifeless bodies of the gods, horses, and elephants, just as the sky is covered by clouds.
Then, in the battle, Namuci hurled at Vasu Dharāya a blazing discus, radiant as the orb of the sun.
By that falling wheel, the excellent chariot of Dhara [was destroyed].
With its banners and flags, it was consumed by fire, glowing with the brilliance of the sun's rays.
Abandoning his chariot, which was blazing with the splendor of his discus,
that god fled to his own excellent abode out of fear of that lord of the asuras.
Having defeated the gods, the Daitya Namuci, arrogant in his strength,
set out once more with his own army against the celestial host.
Those two who were renowned among the gods and Daityas as Maya and Tvaṣṭṛ—
the preeminent architects, experts in a hundred illusions— were there.
A fierce and most terrible combat ensued between the two; indeed,
the encounter between those two great-souled ones was life-threatening.
There, from long ago, they have been rivals to one another in combat.
For a long time, they had been rivals in battle out of mutual rivalry and fury;
then Tvaṣṭṛ, with sharpened arrows, struck the Daitya who was arrogant in his strength.
Having exerted his prowess, he struck him with thirty arrows.
But Maya pierced Tvaṣṭṛ in return with sharpened arrows—
well-polished, with bright points, and adorned with gold.
Maya, the best of the sons of Diti, roared as he was struck by Tvaṣṭṛ’s arrows.
Enraged, as if seeking to take the very life from the Daitya army,
the god seized a spear of great luster, adorned with gold, variegated eyes, and a decorated shaft;
and in the battle, he hurled it at the lord of the Daityas.
Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned it as a terrible weapon made entirely of iron, like the thunderbolt of Purandara.
Maya swiftly severed that [missile], which had been released from the arm of Tvaṣṭṛ and possessed the brilliance of the sun and Vaiśvānara,
with seven sharp-pointed, swift arrows.
Then, as if consuming Tvaṣṭṛ’s very life-force with his wrath, the great Asura,
filled with fury, discharged arrows feathered with peacock plumes.
Tvaṣṭṛ cut those arrows with his own blazing, straight-knotted shafts—
arrows of great velocity, adorned with gold, belonging to the Daitya.
Roaring like two bulls in the presence of a cow in heat, those two powerful men struck one another,
like two tigers locked in combat.
Piercing one another and each desiring the other's death,
they glared at one another like two enraged venomous serpents.
Like two great elephants attacking one another with the tips of their tusks,
they struck each other with arrows discharged from bows drawn to their full stretch.
Then the enraged Maya hurled at him in battle a massive, blazing mace adorned with golden bands, a weapon capable of taking the lives of all beings.
With that mace, the enraged Atiratha struck the supreme steed of Tvaṣṭṛ,
just as Indra strikes mountains with his thunderbolt.
Then, enraged in that battle, the great Daitya struck him with two razor-sharp blades;
furthermore, in that great conflict, he struck him again with two sharpened arrows.
Then, having cut down the banner of Tvaṣṭṛ, he sent the charioteer to the abode of Yama.
With his mace, he struck down the great horses, which were both powerful and swift.
Seeing the charioteer slain and struck down by two razor-sharp arrows, Tvaṣṭṛ—
Abandoning his chariot whose horses were slain and seeing his charioteer fallen upon the ground,
the immensely powerful one stood upon the earth, stretching his great bow.
Seeing his enemy standing there deprived of horses, charioteer, and chariot,
he was attended by the Goddess of Victory and shone like a mountain on fire.
Māya, resembling Kāla and Antaka, with a bow in his hand like Death himself,
scorched the divine armies as a forest fire consumes a woodland.
He discharged fourteen extremely fierce iron arrows of sharp brilliance,
polished on stone, and of various forms.
Adorned with golden ornaments, they drank the blood of that god like enraged venomous serpents impelled by Time.
They fell upon the earth and shone, drenched in blood;
as they lay falling on the surface of the ground, they were seen soaked in gore.
Half-entered and enraged, they were like great serpents within their holes.
Those iron arrows shone as they entered the earth,
like rays of light entering the sun as it goes to its setting.
But Tvaṣṭṛ pierced him in return with fourteen exceedingly fierce iron arrows (nārāca), adorned with gold, tearing him apart.
Having pierced that Daitya’s left arm,
those feathered arrows tore through it and entered the earth like swift-moving serpents.
Then Maya pierced Tvaṣṭṛ with three feathered arrows—
arrows that were winged, swift, deformed, flaming, and life-destroying.
The lord of the Daityas tormented him with blazing, blood-drinking arrows;
then the powerful Lord Tvaṣṭṛ was afflicted by the shafts released by Maya.
Having abandoned the battle and retreated, he was overcome with shame.
Seeing Tvaṣṭṛ there deprived of his chariot, with his charioteer and horses slain like a serpent whose venom has been neutralized, that Dānava was filled with joy.
Stretching his firm, beautiful bow adorned with golden armlets,
the lord of the Daityas stood in battle like a blazing fire.
But Puloma, the best of the Dānavas, proud and boasting of his strength,
appeared in battle on a chariot yoked with white horses.

He was joined by the powerful Vāyu, who was like Time itself.
There, Pavana, hearing the sound of the bowstring striking the palm,
could not endure it, just as an elephant in rut cannot bear the roar of a rival elephant.
The ten directions were covered by arrows discharged from the bows of the Daityas,
just as the world, including the sky, is pervaded by the mass of rays of the sun.
With copper-colored eyes, he was enraged like a hissing great serpent;

fletched with peacock feathers, shone like rows of swans formed into a flight.

tens of thousands of arrows were seen descending from the Daitya.

As he was rushing forward like the enraged God of Death,

Seeing his irresistible momentum, the eternal Wind-god,
assuming supreme speed, scattered the multitudes of arrows.
Then, having dispersed the nets of arrows like the wind,
the powerful one pierced him in the chest with sharp-pointed shafts and iron spears.
He pierced the Daitya with twenty straight-jointed arrows.
The ten foremost divine hosts of Maruts, possessed of great majesty, swiftly let out lion-like roars, crying, "Excellent! Excellent!"
When that tumultuous, hair-raising sound arose,
the sons of Diti, the Paulomas, rushed forward, overwhelmed with rage.
Having reached Pavana, they enveloped him with their finest arrows;
then they covered Pavana with showers of shafts.
Just as clouds in the rainy season drench a mountain with torrents of water.

Then, in the battle, Māruta raised his right hand— which was adorned with various jewels and shaped like an elephant's trunk— toward Akṣobhya.

seven great chariot-warriors were slain by him through the force of the wind.

yet the eternal Vāyu, seeing that [dart] of his was irresistible,
disregarded those flaming volleys of arrows from Pulomā.
Having pierced through the splendors of those high-souled Dānavas,
their crowns were drenched in blood, appearing like mountains wet with red chalk.
With their armor shattered and their bones and arms broken, those falling Dānavas shone like flowering trees crushed by a herd of elephants.
From the torn bodies of those high-souled Dānavas,
there then flowed forth a river of terrible form that struck fear into all.
Flowing with blood in battle, increasing the fear of the timid,
and drenched by the masses of gods and daityas in floods of gore,
the field of battle became fierce in every direction by the thousands.
It was filled with chariots that had their undercarriages, banners, quivers, and standards intact, and were occupied by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and sky-dwellers whose lives had departed.
With shattered jars, as well as with elephants beautifully adorned with bells,

With spears, javelins, and iron arrows; with pikes, swords, and battle-axes; with bows adorned with gold, maces, clubs, and sharp-edged spears—resembling venomous serpents unleashed by gods and demons.
With golden armlets, bracelets, jewels, and earrings;
With hundreds and thousands fallen and cast away,

Having cleared the path, that great chariot-warrior, the best of gods, proceeded onward.

Then, many swarms of sky-faring arrows with golden shafts and curved joints were seen in the sky.

Vulture-feathered arrows, polished on stone and adorned with gold;
vulture-feathered arrows, polished on stone and adorned with gold.

Those beings of deformed shapes appeared everywhere in the sky,
moving about on all sides like fireflies at the end of the summer heat.

mangled Pūṣan as clouds in the rainy season drench a mountain with torrents of water.
The Daitya covered Pūṣan with showers of arrows,
just as a rain-cloud covers a mountain with torrents of water.
The lord of the Daityas, possessed of terrible prowess, covered [him] in battle.

then Pūṣan also struck the Daitya with nine arrows.

having shattered the body of the son of Diti, those arrows,
their tips crimson with blood, entered the earth.

they seemed to have gone there swiftly to proclaim the prowess of the Infinite One.
Pūṣan, of terrible prowess, covered the lord of the Daityas.
Then the god of terrible prowess was shrouded in battle,
like the sun by masses of clouds when the time of dharma has passed.
Then the gods beheld the strength, heroism, prowess, resolve, and being of the divine Pūṣan, which were truly marvelous.
At that time, Pūṣan paid no heed to that shower of arrows rising up as if from the ocean, and he rushed against the Daityas in battle.
The great bow of Pūṣan had a golden back and a mighty sound;
it was curved and drawn into a circle like another thunderbolt of Śakra.
Then arrows appeared, as if filling the sky—
those gold-feathered shafts of Pūṣan, issuing forth from his bow.
Like a garland of gold-tufted arrows, a vast and most terrible mass of feathered shafts appeared, spread across the sky from the great bow of Pūṣan.
Then, those networks of arrows, distributed throughout the sky in every direction,
were struck and shattered by his straight-jointed shafts.
Then, as those gold-feathered arrows fletched with heron-plumes fell and were being struck down, the sky became completely covered by their swarms.
Pūṣan filled Hayagrīva with arrows whetted on stone,
engraved with his own name, resembling the sun, and adorned with divine gold.
