And while fighting in the battle with his chariot, that best of asuras vanished right there, appearing like a city of the Gandharvas.
Terrified, the thirty gods gazed upon Śambara, who possessed a thousand illusions and fought with diverse tactics, displaying fearsome prowess in battle.
Terrified by fear in the battle with the lord of the Dānavas,
that illustrious Bhaga abandoned his chariot and sought refuge with Mahendra.
Having defeated that god, the powerful lord of the Dānavas went to where the highly energetic Jātavedas of great splendor was located.
That powerful fire, enraged, threatened him with fierce words:
"I shall indeed become your death! Having said this, he vanished.
And in that very interval, the mighty Soma, the lord of Brahmins,
with his cool weapons, struck down the army of the Dānavas in battle.
Having the form of a peak of Mount Kailāsa and surrounded by radiant attendants,
he slew the arrogant Dānavas like Death himself with staff in hand.
Crushing multitudes of chariots and throngs of horses,
the illustrious conqueror roamed among the Daityas like the moon at the end of a yuga, acting as Time itself.
Dragging along masses of chariots with the speed of his thighs,
that moon-like one consumed all the Dānavas like a kindled forest fire.
He crushed chariot-warriors from their chariots, elephant-fighters from their elephants,
horsemen from the backs of their horses, and even foot-soldiers upon the ground.
With his cold, he scattered them all like a wind disperses trees by its might—
the Moon of immense splendor [scattered] the great army of the Dānavas.
That weapon of his became smeared with the blood of his enemies,
like the *pināka* of the enraged Rudra as he slaughters creatures;
glorious and powerful, resembling the end of an eon, he moved among the Daityas.
Having checked the great army as it charged again and again,
the warriors were struck with wonder upon seeing him approaching like Death himself, or like the moon.
Whithersoever the dispeller of darkness discharged his cold weapon,
in those very places the armies of the Daityas were shattered in the battle.
Surrounded by his own forces,
he tore through the armies like Death himself with gaping jaws devouring the ranks.
Seeing him of such terrible deeds, having seized his weapons in that great battle, the moon and the sun approached like a moon coming toward the Daityas.
Drawing bows as long as palm trees, those two of great strength covered the moon with their arrows, like two clouds at the end of the rainy season covering it with rain.
Then, as the bows were being drawn by the gods and the asuras,
there arose a truly great sound that seemed to make the very quarters of the sky resound.
With the trumpeting of great elephants, the neighing of horses,
and the blare of kettledrums and conchs, a tumultuous noise arose on all sides.
Desirous of battle, enraged, greedy for victory, and illustrious,
they bellowed at one another like great bulls in cow-pens.
As heads were being struck down in battle by sharp arrows,
there arose in the sky between those two armies what seemed like a rain of stones.
Adorned with earrings and turbans, and wearing garlands and garments of gold,
heads were seen fallen upon the front lines of the battle.
With limbs mangled by arrows, with arms still clutching bows,
and with other beautiful hands severed along with their thousands of ornaments;
With their limbs covered by armor and their thighs smeared with sandalwood paste,
and with faces resembling the moon adorned with earrings of refined gold;
In a mere moment, the entire earth became completely strewn on all sides with the limbs of elephants, horses, and men.
The vast clouds of bows flashed with the lightning of weapons,
and the roar of the mounts became like the thundering of rain-clouds.
That tumultuous and bitter battle, in which blood flowed like water,
broke out in the encounter between the gods and the dānavas.
In that great, fierce, tumultuous, and hair-raising battle,
that tumultuous clash increased the fear of cowards.
The enraged gods and dānavas rained down showers of arrows.
There, the elephants, tormented by the rain of arrows, trumpeted in distress;
and the horses, their riders slain, galloped in all ten directions.
Others, overwhelmed by the shower of shafts, leaped up and fell down.
In that battle between the gods and the Dānavas, where elephants, horses, and charioteers fought,
amidst those foremost and powerful heroes in the fray,
nothing at all could be discerned due to the sound of bowstrings and the slapping of palms.
With arrows, spears, maces, and swords, those of immeasurable splendor,
who were subduers of their enemies, struck down the great army of one another.
In that encounter between the gods and the daityas, heaps of arms, heads, and bows were seen there in the battle.
No end can be reached to the number of horses, elephants, and armored chariots that have been slain by the gods and asuras.
There, the warriors struck one another with maces, swords, spears, and straight-knotted arrows; likewise, there was a great slaughter of elephants and horses.
Then a terrible river began to flow through the midst of the armies, its waves consisting of floods of blood, with hair for its moss and grassy mats.
Then a great cry of "Alas!
Alas! arose among the warriors—the thirty gods—as they were being struck down by the Dānavas in that great battle.
A tumultuous sound arose like that of roaring clouds;
thus did that battle take place between the gods and the asuras.
Vibhīṣaṇa was most fierce, deformed, and terrifying to behold.
But Virocana, in that very great battle, struck Viṣvaksena— the Sādhya whose eyes were like blood— though he was the supreme archer among all bowmen.
Beholding him approaching, Viṣvaksena—
the immeasurable self, the best of gods, surrounded by the deities— pierced him back in the middle of the chest.
Struck by Bāṇa like an elephant tormented by a goad,
Virocana blazed with rage like the sacrificial fire at a ritual.
That best of Dānavas,
with seven blazing, swift arrows released from his bow, pierced Viṣvaksena in the battle.
Thus deeply pierced by the powerful Dānava, that best of gods, the Lord,
quickly fell into a swoon and leaned against his banner for support.
Then, having recovered his breath once more, Sādhya set his mind on battle;
stretching his great bow, he stood firm in the midst of the Daityas.
And the powerful Virocana fought on all sides,
agitating the celestial armies from every direction with his sharp arrows.
Then, as that lord of the Asuras was fighting in the encounter with sharp arrows,
while he was indeed engaged in combat in the fray—
A tumultuous sound is heard, like the roar of a thundercloud.
And he roared with a great sound, striking down the army of the gods;
like a fierce cloud accompanied by lightning and thunder, he rained down a shower of stones.
In that great battle, the Dānava, with his weapons raised, caused all the armies of the gods to flee in all directions with a rain of arrows.
Then, terrified, the chariot-warriors fled from their chariots,
the horsemen from the backs of their horses, and the foot-soldiers likewise to the ground.
Hearing the roar of the bow, which was like the crashing of a thunderbolt,
they became paralyzed, devoid of energy, and as if their life-force had departed.
He was constantly followed by his army wherever he entered a force.
All the troops, terrified, took cover in the battle.
Then, terrified by the fear of Virocana, the chariot-warriors fled from their chariots to where the hosts of foot-soldiers were,
where the god Śacīpati was.
That one of great strength struck down fourteen thousand foot-guards belonging to Viṣvaksena, the Sādhya, on every side.
The conqueror was seen striking down hosts of horses, elephants, and chariot divisions, as well as throngs of foot soldiers.
Spreading his wings like a hawk,
that mighty-armed one pierced through the army on all sides and, cutting it apart again and again, lopped off heads in the battle.
The surviving horsemen, foot soldiers, and chariot-warriors likewise,
together with Viṣvaksena, rushed toward Virocana.
With swords, maces, spears, iron clubs, darts, and lances,
they let out lion-roars as they rushed toward him who was alone.
Then that Dānava, raising his sword and exerting great speed,
cut off the heads and bows of the chariot-warriors in the battle.
The powerful Virocana, the slayer of enemies, moved through the throngs of chariots, elephants, and horses,
traversing twenty-one types of paths.
The Dānava displayed the maneuvers known as *bhrānta*, *udbhrānta*, *āviddha*, *āpluta*, *vipluta*, *pluta*, *saṃpāta*, and *samudīrṇa*.
Some, struck by the great-souled Dānava with his excellent sword,
shrieked with their armor shattered and fell down, deprived of life.
With their backs cut open and their riders slain by the high-souled Dānava,
the celestial elephants fled and slaughtered their own ranks.
Cut down from the sky by that firm bowman,
various *tomara* lances, bows,
and the heads of elephant-riders fell to the earth; [the arrows] struck back against the elephants and horses of firm prowess.
In the battle, he cut off the heads and the bows of the chariot-warriors.
Leaping up and seizing some of the chariot-warriors,
the mighty Dānava cut down their charioteers and even their chariots with his sword.
As the illustrious one repeatedly leaped up and ran in all directions,
the asuras were filled with wonder at the various paths he traversed.
He struck some with his foot, and having seized others, he crushed them;
with his sword he cut down others, and with his roar he terrified yet others.
Others, seized by stiffness of the thighs, fell to the ground;
others, beholding the Daitya, gave up their lives out of fear.
While that great and terrible battle was thus proceeding,
there occurred a massive destruction of the gods' multitudes of chariots, horses, and elephants.
On earth, it was like the end of an eon, causing trembling among the gods.
Kujumbha, the best of the Dānavas, fought against Aṃśa, the son of Āditya, in the encounter,
just as a bull fights another bull in battle.
Resembling a mountain and possessing the prowess of a rutting elephant, he struck him down.
In that great battle, thousands of divine armies, together with their chariots, were struck by many swift, sharp, and whirling arrows.
Having come within the range of his arrows, they did not turn back from any side.
All beings cried out, and the quarters of the sky became shrouded in darkness;
a cruel and terrible defeat of the gods ensued.
And Aṃśa, possessing supreme prowess,
struck down ten thousand swift elephants belonging to the army of the lord of the Dānavas.
Seeing the elephant division charging toward him, the Dānava Kujambha,
the subduer of enemies, descended from the seat of his chariot with mace in hand;
he grasped a massive, heavy mace made of the essence of stone.
He rushed toward the elephant division like Death with his mouth wide open.
Striking down elephants with his mace, that powerful one roamed through the battle;
Kujambha, the best of the Dānavas, was superior in strength, with mace in hand.
The powerful one, the best of Dānavas, repeatedly targeted those elephants, causing many of them to have their tusks shattered and their frontal globes split open.
With their tusks shattered and others with their frontal globes split open,
many elephants fled in the ten directions, tormented by Kujambha.
And as for those ministers of Kujambha, the Dānavas of terrible prowess,
he struck down those elephant-warriors with various sharp iron arrows.
With razors, crescent-headed arrows, broad-headed shafts, yellow-tipped missiles, and sharp *añjalika* weapons,
Kujambha, the foremost of the Dānavas, severed their heads.
The sky was filled with falling heads;
it appeared like a shower of stones along with arms still clutching elephant goads.
O Great King, elephant-warriors whose heads had been struck off were seen upon the necks of their elephants like headless palm trees.
As the great elephant charged toward him, Aṃśa, the best of the Asuras, struck it with a single arrow in his rage; thereupon, the elephant turned its face away.
Having thus plunged into the elephant division, Kujambha, the foremost of the Dānavas and the best among the strong,
struck down the elite soldiers with his mace.
All the gods beheld the great elephants struck down by Kujambha in a single watch, like mountains that had been toppled.
And upon the paths of Kujambha,
those great elephants were shattered like mountains split asunder by Indra with his thunderbolt.
All the thirty gods beheld him as if he were Death personified;
at his very scent, they were shattered like other animals before a lion.
Bearing that mace, which was sprinkled with the blood of elephants, he shone;
with mouth wide open, he roared in anger, terrible in form and fearsome.
Just as in the past, when the Blessed One was enraged at the destruction of living beings,
that great Asura sported with his mace in the midst of the battle.
Like a cowherd driving great elephants with a staff,
all the gods beheld Kujambha of terrifying prowess, who, like an enraged Death raised aloft his staff in the sky, was striking down the Dānavas.
But other excellent elephants there, with their riders slain and their temples flowing with rut,
were being struck by the mace and pierced deeply by arrows.
Unable to withstand the force of Kujambha’s mace in that great battle,
the mighty elephants fled, trampling their own ranks.
Scattering the elephants with his mace like a great wind dispersing the clouds,
he charged at the elephant division like Death with his mouth wide open.
The Daitya stood in battle like the all-consuming fire of universal destruction at the end of an aeon.
Then, by the command of the king of the gods, all the armies,
rejoicing and uttering terrible roars, rushed toward the sons of Diti.
Being struck by maces and their bodies wounded by arrows,
that boundless flood of the gods' forces was difficult even for the gods to approach.
It was surging forward like the shoreless ocean during a full moon tide,
thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, and resounding with the blare of conchs and kettledrums.
Like the shore against the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, she [stood firm] against that surging sea of an army— difficult to cross, shrouded on all sides by dust, and unshakeable.
Beholding that marvel, which was as if incredible and wonderful, they were struck with amazement.
That great army, teeming with chariots, elephants, and horses, was surging forward;
the entire host was raised up, complete with its steeds, chariots, and tuskers.
Having blocked [the way] in battle, the powerful Kujambha stood by his own might like the immovable Mount Meru obstructing the ocean; indeed, Kujambha held back the army of the gods with his mace.
Thus restrained, that army became overwhelmed and ceased its efforts.
While that most terrible battle was thus proceeding, [the following occurred].
Asiloman and Hari likewise struck each other down.
But the powerful Dānava Aśiloma, the lord of the Dānavas,
rose up like a comet over the entire army of the gods;
like the unfailing sun, he scorched the celestial hosts in battle.
Resembling the thousand-rayed sun, that powerful and excellent chariot of the Dānava rained down arrows upon the host of the gods like a cloud.
With blazing showers of arrows, he of terrible prowess scorched [the enemy];
fierce, cruel, invincible, and irresistible, he stood at the head of the army.
The lord fought with the gods as if devouring them,
possessing fierce arrows and a fierce countenance, even while being trampled by great elephants.
The exceedingly powerful one plucks off the heads of the gods;
the majestic one, with arrows for his fangs, devours the divine armies.
With a great bow like Indra’s rainbow, that Asura was like a massive cloud;
with a sword for his tongue and a discus in his hand, the Asura had his mouth wide open like a drawn bow.
The glorious one, whose nails were like axes, filled the air with the sound of mṛdaṅga drums.
That best of Dānavas stands in battle like a powerful tiger;
he is terrible, raining down a shower of arrows, with his bowstring for clouds and his roar for thunder.
Possessing both the bow of Śakra and the great bow, he was like a great cloud of the Asuras.
The sound of the bowstring was like thunder, and the great rain of arrows was renowned.
His bow was like another great cloud, swelling with the majesty of its lightning-string;
he was a formidable ocean of missiles and weapons, difficult to approach, with his arms as its grasping crocodiles.
The ocean of his training was fierce, with bows for its surging waves, arrows for its great whirlpools,
maces and swords for its sea-monsters, and the bowstring for its shoreline.
A vast ocean of infantry, roaring with the sound of shouts,
swiftly overwhelmed many horses, elephants, foot soldiers, and chariots.
In that battle, he submerged the enemy heroes, those great chariot-warriors;
that fierce lord of the Dānavas overwhelmed the hosts of gods.
The glorious one, the best in battle, standing firm in combat, crushed [his foes] in the fray;
all the thirty gods beheld him, radiant as pure gold.
Armed and fighting there like a blazing fire,
like the midday sun burning with its splendor,
all living beings were unable even to look upon that Dānava.
Just as at the end of the summer heat, a fire might consume a dry forest,
so did the Daitya burn the foremost of the gods with his strength and splendor.
The formidable strength of both the gods and the dānavas roared;
everything became utterly bewildered and thrown into confusion on all sides.
Then those heroes, fierce in their strength and mounted upon the necks of elephants, horses, and chariots,
having adopted noble resolve, did not abandon the great battle.
Then that tumultuous battle took place, causing the hair to stand on end;
in that conflict between the gods and the dānavas, there was a mire formed by the flowing blood.
Oppressed by the crocodiles of fear, they could no longer discern the directions.
Then, in that battle, struck by various weapons of the Dānavas, they became bewildered in mind; agitated, they slaughtered one another.
Confused and with weapons in hand, they could no longer distinguish their own kin from the enemy.
In the battle, one hero, seizing another by the hair,
cut off his head as he bit down upon his lips and mouth.
With arms and fists as formidable as thunderbolts and exceedingly cruel,
the heroes, having taken up their weapons, strike one another in battle.
In that fierce battle, which takes the lives of warriors, which strikes at the very gates of heaven, tumultuous and chaotic, and full of great terror;
In that great battle, horse rushed against horse, elephant against elephant, and hero against hero;
indeed, they charged at Asamañja in the conflict, desiring to slay him.
He rushed forward with speed and struck them down from close range;
both the Asuras and the Suras were great chariot-warriors, rich in prowess.
Sacrificing their lives in battle, they struck one another down.
With disheveled hair, stripped of armor, deprived of chariots, and with bows broken,
the Dānavas fought with the gods using only their hands and feet.
But Hari, in that battle, dispatched a sharp broad-headed arrow;
having severed the tip of his bow, it caused it to fall to the ground.
Furthermore, he [discharged] hundreds of straight-knotted arrows.
He suddenly hurled it at that lord of the Dānavas in the encounter.
Released from his body and impelled by the wind,
they entered him like serpents entering a mountain, with half their bodies submerged.
With those fallen limbs streaming with inexhaustible blood,
the mighty-armed Daitya shone like Mount Meru discharging its mineral ores.
Furthermore, [he discharged] hundreds of straight-knotted arrows;
then Asiloman, filled with rage, seized another great bow.
And he dispatched sharp arrows with golden shafts.
He pierced him in his vital spots with arrows resembling the venom of serpents and fire,
covering his body as clouds shroud a mountain.
Armed with all his limbs, the Dānava, arrogant in his strength, offered himself as a sacrifice to the gods;
then, aiming once more, he released an arrow resembling the God of Death.
Furthermore, he joined together another arrow that resembled the end of time,
well-feathered, radiant as the sun, and peerless in battle.
By that arrow-strike in battle from him of terrible deeds,
the god suddenly fainted and fell down upon the earth.
Then, when the god had descended to the earth, everyone raised a cry of "Alas!
Alas! Thereupon, struck in his vital organs, he fell down as if trembling.
The world, including the gods, was as agitated as if the sun had fallen.
Having slain his retinue in battle, that great Asura,
the foremost of the Dānavas, killed thirty-one thousand warriors.
Attended by the goddess of victory and shining like a mountain,
he grasped his formidable bow and advanced toward the chariot of Śakra.
In that very great battle, both the Aśvins,
together with their armies, engaged in combat against the powerful Vṛtra, the enemy of the gods.
With arrows, sword, and bow in hand, having renounced his life in battle,
that Daitya approached the two Aśvins and stood as immovable as a mountain.
Then, having blown his conch shell— which caused the hair of his enemies to stand on end—
he bewildered all living beings with the sound of his bowstring and the slapping of his palms.
Then, their hair standing on end with joy, the throngs of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and gods heard the sound of the conch and also the roar of Vṛtra.
Maces, javelins, swords, spears, tridents, and battle-axes,
grasped in the arms of yakṣas and rākṣasas, shone brilliantly.
Vṛtra likewise cut down with his own arrows of terrible speed and force the spears, javelins, and axes hurled by those of massive bodies;
he felled both those moving through the air and those standing upon the ground as they roared.
He of pleasing appearance pierced the limbs of the gods with arrows.

Only severed bodies and heads were seen.
Then a great rain of blood fell upon the earth,
originating from the limbs of the gods who had been shattered by maces and iron clubs.
All living beings beheld Vṛtra of terrible prowess as he covered [Indra] with floods of arrows, like the sun with its rays.
Like the sun with its scorching rays, he tormented all the gods;
enraged, he pierced those accompanied by their armies with arrows that split the vital organs.
Though tormented by arrows, the lord of the asuras uttered various cries;
yet in the battle, the gods did not see him fall into confusion.
Those great chariot-warriors rained down swords, maces, iron clubs, spears, javelins, battle-axes, and tridents.
Then Vṛtra, being violently provoked and oppressed by them with force,
the mighty Asura Vṛtra became enraged and acted with haste.
He of true valor rained down sharp arrows upon all of them.
Terrified by him, the gods, their great weapons scattered,
uttered a terrible cry of distress, afflicted by the fear of the asura Vṛtra.
Abandoning their maces, spears, tridents, barbed missiles, clubs, and thunderbolts,
they fled toward the northern direction, terrified by the wielder of the firm bow.
Then Vṛtra, with spear and mace in hand, broad-chested and mighty-armed, advanced in battle, terrifying all things moving and stationary.
There, a certain mighty-armed lord, bearing a sword and a spear,
rushed toward Vṛtra, the lord of the Daityas, who was peerless in battle.
Having taken up his bow with speed like an elephant in rut, he was seen rushing forward like a beast with temporal juice flowing from its temples.
Beholding him approaching like an elephant in rut, [he stood firm].
With three calf-toothed arrows, he pierced the best of the Asuras in the side.
Deeply pierced by those arrows, that great archer of immeasurable prowess,
the powerful hero skilled in mace-fighting, seized a mace.
Seizing that formidable, firm mace made of the essence of stone,
the valiant one suddenly approached Aśvin and struck him.
Then the horseman,
whose prowess was equal to that of Hara, hurled a massive, firm, and blazing trident at the Daitya Vṛtra.
Skilled in the art of mace-fighting, he shattered the spear with the tip of his mace,
suddenly threatening the son of Aśvin as Garuḍa threatens a serpent.
Leaping up from the air and brandishing his great mace,
the powerful one hurled it, resembling a mountain peak, at Nāsatya.
Struck by the mace, that horseman abandoned his unsurpassed spear and fled suddenly to where Vāsava was fighting.
Having defeated the Ashvin in battle,
Vṛtra, whose prowess was terrifying and who was attended by the Goddess of Victory, stood firm in the fight.
[Colophon] In that very great battle on the field of combat, the best of gods fought against the wise Daitya Ekacakra.
Having covered the path of the chariot while crying out with a great roar,
he overwhelmed that army of Ekacakra with showers of arrows.
The great asuras, possessed of great heroism and armed with great shields and spears,
hurled pikes and *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons in that great battle.
That immense rain of spears, crowded with maces and javelins,
was inauspicious, released by the sons of Diti, and difficult for all things moving and stationary to withstand.
In battle, the hosts of gods and asuras rained [weapons] upon one another—
those heroic and mighty beings who resembled the peaks of great mountains.
A hundred horses were yoked to his great chariot,
like those of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the foremost of the great asuras, in battle.
By the falling of those [weapons], by the sound of the rims of the wheels,
and by the descent of his arrows, hundreds of gods were indeed slain.
Then, enraged, he cut down weapons by the hundreds and thousands with swift, variegated, straight-knotted arrows.
Being struck by sharp arrows in battle, some of the Dānavas— chariots, elephants, and horses— were brought to destruction by the gods.
Then, observing that they were being destroyed,
the sons of Diti abandoned their lives and turned back, grasping their excellent weapons.
Blocking the cardinal and intermediate directions, those strikers,
the sons of Diti, assailed the gods with sharpened weapons in battle.
On the field of battle, the mighty-armed one released in the conflict a most terrible and fiercely blazing weapon called Mathana.
Then, by means of the great power of his weapons, the son of Diti cut down thousands of sharp spears and other missiles.
Having cut all those pikes, the great asura Ekacakra pierced that Sādhya with ten sharpened arrows.
Having thus neutralized the force of his weapon,
he quickly pierced his followers by the thousands with other blazing and swift missiles.
Their severed limbs shed blood like the peaks of mountains shedding torrents during the heavy rains of the monsoon.
Being driven away by the sons of Diti with arrows that were swift, straight-flying, and possessed a touch like Indra’s thunderbolt, those best of gods were struck with terror.
Standing in battle on his single wheel, Ekacakra beheld leaders of elephant herds,
resounding with the tinkling of excellent ornaments and possessing a roar like the ocean.
[Elephants] that are well-trained, spirited, supervised by great officers,
of noble breed, endowed with prowess, and capable of slaying rival elephants.
Like an asura among elephants, he struck down the elephants of the celestial army— elephants trained in the art of war and equal to Airāvata in combat.
They scattered great elephants of terrifying speed, discharging ichor in three ways, which,
with the thunderous roar of clouds, resembled great mountains that had suddenly risen up.
Numbering a thousand, they were divine, adorned with gold from the Jambu river,
spread over with golden nets, and possessed the brilliance of the rising sun.
Ekacakra, mace in hand, powerful and the best among wielders of clubs,
drove away the elephants as the wind disperses great clouds.
Having struck down all those elephants with his mace,
that great Asura, the crusher of elephants, once again beheld the powerful throngs of horses.
Those of parrot-like color, those of deer-like color, as well as those resembling peacocks;
those with the hue of pigeons, and likewise those with the hue of swans.

The mighty-armed one of incomparable prowess, powerful and of terrible valor, destroyed that cavalry force with his mace— the horses being Mallikākṣas, Virūpākṣas, and those the color of cranes, as swift as thought.
Seeing all those enemies of the asuras in battle, the glorious Raṇāja,
possessed of inconceivable prowess, advanced against the divine host.
Skilled in mace-fights, a leader of chariot-divisions,
with his army rejoicing, the mighty-armed one set forth in the presence of Śakra upon his chariot.
Having slain three million living beings in battle,
that lord of the Daityas stood there like a smokeless fire.
In that very battle, a great Asura, preeminent in strength,
fought in combat against the high-souled Mṛgavyādha, who remained unconquered.
Then, seeing that army, the great attendants of Rudra, the hunter of deer, who possessed a splendor equal to the blazing fire, sprang up.
With intoxicated elephants, divine chariots, and horses of great speed;
with sharp, whetted missiles and arrows resembling fire.
Then those heroes beheld the great asura blazing like the rising sun, garlanded with the rays of his own splendor.
Standing in the midst of battle, he was of great speed, a great being, and possessed of great strength;
he was of great intelligence, great energy, a great body, and a great asura.
Beholding that great warrior stationed in all directions,
they then assailed him from every side with terrible weapons.
Sharp, whetted arrows made entirely of iron and tipped with yellow poison were struck by the hunter upon his head, which resembled a mountain.
Pierced by those seven arrows fixed in his head,
he then leaped up into the sky, making the ten directions resound.
Then that heroic and mighty god, together with his chariot and his strung bow, followed him joyfully through the sky.
That powerful and mighty one, resembling a mountain, rained down with great force;
he covered that Asura in the sky with showers of arrows.
Like a rain-bearing cloud at the end of the summer heat, [he refreshed] the mountain.
Then, being tormented by that hunter of deer,
the Dānava let out a terrible roar in the sky like a rain-cloud.
Suddenly leaping a great distance toward the chariot of the hunter,
he descended with immense speed like a winged mountain.
Then the Daitya shattered the chariot whose pole and yoke were broken;
the mighty Mṛgavyādha, abandoning it, stood upon the ground.
Seeing Rudra deprived of his chariot, his auspicious attendants,
with terrible red eyes and mallets in their hands, rose up in the sky.
But he, having suddenly risen, stood in the clear sky,
struck by those terrible mallets like a tree struck by axes.
Having checked the momentum of those swift-moving ones, that great asura,
possessing prowess equal to Suparṇa, fell back down to the earth.
Uprooting a *sāla* tree with massive branches, that immensely powerful Dānava slaughtered all the attendants in the conflict.
With his body mangled by them and drenched in a flood of blood,
that best of Dānavas shone like the newly risen morning sun.
Then, having uprooted a mountain peak together with its deer, serpents, and trees,
the lord of the Dānavas struck those attendants in battle.
Then, when those great attendants had been struck down, that heroic one destroyed whatever force remained.
With horses against horses, elephants against elephants, warriors against warriors, and chariots against chariots,
the Dānava slaughtered them like Antaka destroying all creatures at the end of a Yuga.
With slain horses and elephants, and with great chariots whose axles were broken,
the earth had its paths blocked on all sides by the gods.
Thus endowed with such power was that lord of the Daityas, and the heroic hunter was likewise powerful;
when they fought in battle, those two strong men were like two elephants in rut.
Right there, Rudra fights a second battle with Rāhu;
he is renowned throughout the three worlds as the wrathful-souled Aja Ekapāt.
Then that great battle took place— tumultuous, hair-raising,
terrifying, and fierce— among the heroes who were desirous of victory.
With the bodies of gods and dānavas as its sands, difficult to cross, with hair for its grassy meadows,
this river of blood flows forth, carrying away the masses of corpses.
Then the powerful Lord Rudra, of fierce form, being enraged,
struck Rāhu— who possessed a hundred mouths and was the destroyer of enemy armies— in battle.
In that battle, the glorious and enraged [hero] struck down the Daitya’s chariot— its body variegated with gold, along with its horses and charioteer— with his arrows.

Then one of his attendants, possessed of great strength, joyfully pierced that Dānava in the middle of the chest with a chariot-spear in the battle. Thus, his limbs were mangled by Rudra as well as by the attendants.
As Rudra’s chariot was approaching, Rāhu, the foremost of the Dānavas,
frantic with rage, suddenly and swiftly struck it with his palm.
His limbs mangled by the sharp arrows of Rudra, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
he was like Mount Meru pierced by the rays of the sun.
But with the slain leaders of the Dānavas,
that great Asura struck down all the attendants of Rudra.
In that battle, Rudra pierced the Danava of fearsome appearance, who was discharging showers of arrows,
with his own straight-jointed shafts.
While that most terrible and hair-raising battle was raging,
great rivers with violent currents of blood flowed forth.
In the battle, the Dānava, resembling a mass of black collyrium,
pierced Rudra with sharp arrows, just as the sun pierces Mount Meru with its rays.
And by the slain leaders of the Dānavas with spears, tridents, and battle-axes, and by the fallen Dānavas who could assume any form at will, resembling mountains; ||| 1710–1711 ||
Then, having been struck by that fist in the battle, Rudra fell to the earth with his chariot and horses, like a city tower.
While that most terrible battle, the Lohamarṣaṇa,
was raging, those Daityas then shone like *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
Great rivers with violent currents, flowing with blood,
surged forth amidst the sounds of large kettledrums, clay drums, and small drums.
A wondrous sound arose, mingled with the tones of conchs and flutes; there,
a great clamor broke forth from the cries of the slain and the shouting Daityas, as well as from the gods and the Asuras.
The dust of the earth, kicked up by the hooves of horses and raised by the rims of chariot wheels,
blocked the path of the warriors and obscured their vision.
That battlefield, strewn with weapons as its floral offerings,
was terrifying and fierce for the heroes seeking victory.
With the bodies of gods and dānavas, the fierce river of battle became difficult to cross;
established in the endurance of physical forms, it flowed forth as a stream of blood.
Difficult to behold and difficult to fathom, it is a mire of flesh and blood.
With broken swords, maces, spears, javelins, and *paṭṭiśa* lances;
with broken swords, maces, spears, javelins, scimitars, and axes.
And with discarded and broken chariots, and those destroyed in the battle.
With slain rutting elephants as well as gods and dānavas,
and with wheels, axles, yokes, and weapons broken and fallen upon the earth,
the battlefield became terrible and swarming with flesh-eaters.
Eighty-eight thousand chariots were reportedly destroyed there;
O King, a hundred thousand elephants and three hundred thousand horses were slain, O Monarch.
And headless trunks rose up in all directions during the battle of the Daityas,
who were bound by mutual enmity and greedy for victory;
at that time, a most terrifying slaughter was taking place in the fight.
Of the armies arrayed for battle— of heroes who do not retreat—
and of Aja, Ekapāda, and the high-souled Rāhu.
As they fell there in their fury, a tremendous roar was heard,
like the upheaval of all living beings and the crashing of oceans.
There, the illustrious Rudra, the lord of sages, who was accompanied by Dhūmrākṣa and wielded a mace,
a sharp-edged spear, and a trident, pierced Keśin with a javelin.
Then the fierce and beloved attendants of Rudra— terrible to behold with fearsome eyes and wielding various weapons— rushed forward.
And having mounted his chariot, the illustrious Keśin, wearing earrings of refined gold,
fought in battle surrounded by Dānavas who were difficult to conquer.
From the mouth of that warrior intoxicated by battle, who possessed fierce valor and desired to fight at the front of the fray, flames indeed burst forth.
He, however, had shoulders as arched as a lion’s, a stride like that of a tiger,
resembled a great rain-cloud, and possessed a voice with the resonance of a mṛdaṅga drum.
As he was leaping forth, surrounded by the Dānavas, there arose a truly great roar that then agitated the triple heaven.
Terrified by that sound, the great army of the thirty gods,
using trees and rocks as weapons, advanced to do battle.
And the encounter of those gods and Daityas, who were eager to fight one another,
was exceedingly tumultuous, fierce, and brought fear to the world.
A most terrible battle, hair-raising to behold, broke out among those hosts of gods and dānavas as they cast away their lives in that great conflict.
For all were exceedingly powerful heroes, all resembling mountains;
all were experts in every weapon, and all had their various weapons raised for combat.
The thirty gods and the Dānavas were likewise intent on slaying one another.
As they roared in battle, their sound was like the thundering of clouds;
that exceedingly great noise was heard like the cry of a Garuḍa as it soars through the sky.
An exceedingly terrible sound was heard, causing both the moving and the stationary to tremble.
A dust, resembling the dawn, arose together with Bhīma;
raised up by the hosts of gods and Daityas, it obstructed the ten directions.
Enveloped by that dust, which was reddish-pale like silk and of many hues, they could not see anything at all.
Neither banner nor flag, nor armor nor even a horse was seen; neither weapon nor chariot, nor indeed a charioteer, was visible at all.
A tumultuous roar arose from them as they rushed at one another;
for flames issued forth from the mouth of that hero of fierce valor.
He, however, had the shoulders of a lion or a bull, the prowess of a tiger,
resembled a great rain-cloud, and possessed the roar of a great rain-cloud.
As he was rushing forth, surrounded by the Dānavas,
a tumultuous roar was heard, but their forms did not appear clearly.
There, the enraged Dānavas slew only the Dānavas themselves;
likewise, the gods then slaughtered only the gods in that tumultuous fray.
Striking down both their enemies and their own kin in battle,
those great Asuras and Suras likewise made the earth drenched in blood.
Then, drenched by a flood of blood, the dust was laid low;
strewn with hundreds of bodies, that great battle became [a scene of horror].
With spears, javelins, clubs, swords, iron maces, barbed missiles,
and lances, the gods and the Dānavas struck one another in the battle.
Then, striking with arms shaped like iron clubs and using mountains as weapons,
the Dānavas slaughtered all the attendants of Rudra.
And the attendants of Rudra, having advanced, tore him apart with great trees and massive rocks, and with weapons possessing the brilliance of the sun.
In the meantime, the enraged Keśī, the best of the Dānavas—
terrible and intolerant of battle— delighted his own armies;
then, filled with supreme fury, he discharged the Vajra weapon.
By means of the divine weapon Vajra and the great-souled blade,
all the invincible great attendants were slain in battle.
Afflicted by the vajra-weapon and bewildered in battle, the attendants of Rudra fell down like mountains struck by thunderbolts, with their trees scattered about.
Thus that tumultuous battle took place, causing the hair to stand on end;
the combat between Keśin and Rudra was like a marvel.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Vṛṣaparvan, the lord of the Daityas, beheld the entire universe as a wondrous sight.
He fought against Niṣkumbha, who possessed a luster equal to that of the red sun.
With his face overcome by rage and brandishing his supreme bow,
he beheld the enemy army and quickly spoke to his charioteer.
O charioteer, lead this chariot away from this very spot with all haste;
for these gods, united together, are destroying our army in battle.
I wish to slay these men, who boast in battle, in the midst of combat;
for by them this great army of the Dānavas has been torn apart.
Then, with his horses galloping, that best of chariot-warriors,
the great asura, being enraged, struck down his enemies with nets of arrows.
As that wise lord of the Dānavas displayed his prowess in battle,
the gods were not even able to stand their ground, much less fight him in combat.
Indeed,
those heroes who were exceedingly brave and never retreated in battles,
all fled when they were pierced by Vṛṣaparvan.
Pierced by Vṛṣaparvan, they all cried out there;
having fallen under the power of death, they had come under the sway of Vaivasvata.
Having observed that his kinsmen had been slain, the great asura stood firm.
Seeing Niṣkumbha there, all those best of the thirty gods gathered together and quickly surrounded him from all sides.
And seeing that Niṣkumbha standing firm, the best of the gods indeed became powerful through the strength and splendor of his weapon.
But Vṛṣaparvan, like Mount Mahendra with its torrents of rain, overwhelmed Niṣkumbha— who stood firm in battle like a mountain— with showers of arrows.
But disregarding the many arrows fallen upon his body,
that glorious and mighty one stood before him with his army.
Laughing, that one of great splendor rushed with speed toward Vṛṣaparvan in the battle, as if making the earth tremble.
As he was thus rushing forward, blazing with splendor,
his form became invincible, like that of a flaming fire.
Abandoning his chariot, that illustrious lotus-eyed one, filled with rage,
uprooted a massive, high-reaching tree with great branches;
he then hurled that tree at Niṣkumbha and Vṛṣaparvan.
Having seized that great tree with one hand,
the powerful Dānava let out a tremendous roar and whirled it around.
Then, with that tree, the Dānava struck the thirty gods along with their elephants and elephant-riders, as well as their chariots and chariot-warriors.
Having encountered Vṛṣaparvan— who was like the enraged God of Death himself and a taker of lives in battle— the gods fled in all directions.
Seeing him rushing forward, enraged and bringing fear to the thirty gods,
the archer Niṣkumbha grew angry and let out a roar.
There, the immensely powerful Niṣkumbha pierced the lord of the Dānavas with twenty sharp arrows that struck his vital organs.
With fierce arrows and spears, [he struck] the lord and sovereign of the Daityas.
Then Niṣkumbha, afflicted by the arrows and spears of the Daityas, [was struck].
Then the Daitya, the best of the Dānavas, became enraged at the head of the Dānava army;
with sharpened arrows, he pierced Niṣkumbha.
Pierced while standing in the midst of battle, he shed much blood.
Agitated, with disheveled hair, their pride shattered and defeated,
they all fled in fear of Vṛṣaparvan, gasping for breath.
Terrified by Vṛṣaparvan, they crushed one another;
agitated by fear from behind, they looked back again and again.
Then,
in that battle, Vṛṣaparvan, who was skilled in combat, caused all the soldiers of Niṣkuṃbha to be deprived of their weapons.
In that very battle, the highly valiant Prahlāda,
the red-eyed son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, fought against Kāla.
At the time of battle, the victorious deeds of that heroic Dānava took place while Hari Viṣṇu— the Lord of the worlds, accessible through knowledge, and identical with the universe— was present.
The actions of that king of the Dānavas were capable of enduring the time of battle.
The descendant of Bhṛgu, endowed with haste, performed those rites that bring about victory.
As he offered oblations into the fire and paid homage to the brahmins,
a fragrant breeze blew, carrying the scent of the clarified butter.
And for the sake of victory, Uśanas himself bound various and variegated garlands, consecrated with mantras,
upon the auspicious head of Prahlāda;
that great asura then went forth to battle against Kāla.
That descendant of Bhṛgu brought peace to the exceedingly powerful Prahlāda.
The high-souled Bhārgava had ten thousand disciples,
and they recited the unsurpassed peace-mantra for the sake of the Dānava heroes.
Then the Atharvan, divine, and impelled by the praise of Brahman.
The Dānavas gradually performed the rites for his safe entry into battle;
indeed, they performed a victorious act worthy of entering the fray.
Then those who were skilled in all weapons, never retreating in battles,
endowed with knowledge and asceticism, and having performed the rites for auspiciousness—
With bows in hand and clad in armor, the Dānavas leaped forward with great speed;
having honored King Bali, they surrounded Prahrāda.
Having mounted a vast, divine chariot that crushes the chariots of enemies— a mountain-like vehicle equipped with wheels and strewn with various weapons— [he set forth].
In a moment, that peak of Mount Meru became filled with the sounds of shouting and the slapping of arms, like the sky at the onset of the rainy season when it is crowded with clouds.
Having donned garlands of lotus petals and being well-adorned,
those who delight in battle fall down after completely abandoning their kinsmen.
The glorious lord, wielding great weapons and wearing auspicious armor, was equipped with a helmet and body-protector; armed with a bow, he was supremely invincible.
Thousands of Daityas, possessing the pride of lions and tigers and adorned with tinkling bells, went before him in that great battle as he roared.
Seventy thousand chariots, exceedingly difficult to conquer, were slain on his side by the army, and the elephants were exactly that many as well.
But in the center, within the belly of the formation, stood the great asura Kālanemi;
stretching his terrible bow, he roared and laughed aloud.
Hundreds of thousands of powerful Dānavas, whose splendor was equal to that of Śakra, marched in front of that one of great luster.
But that great array of Dānavas, standing level and expanded on both flanks, became impenetrable by all the gods.
There were sixty thousand chariots of the bow-wielding Dānavas,
and there was no measure to the number of those bearing various weapons.
Grasping maces, iron clubs, swords, spears, mallets,
and axes, the Dānavas, resembling mountains, shone resplendently.
Roaring, shrieking, and crying out again and again,
those of great heroism, who never retreat in battles, fought on.
There arose a great clamor from thousands of musical instruments,
and from the neighing of horses and the trumpeting of elephants as they roared with intense vigor.
The roar of kettledrums, resembling the thundering of rain-clouds,
was heard, along with the sound of conchs and the resonance of drums.
By that blare of conchs, the sound of kettledrums and musical instruments,
and the roar of the chariots, the expanse of the sky seemed as if it were crying out.
Surrounded by a vast army resembling the ocean in its surge,
the enraged Prahrāda fought like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
At that fierce and terrible roar of him, who possessed incomparable prowess,
all living beings shrieked out with sounds that spread through the three worlds.
A meteor fell from the sky and a harsh wind blew;
jackals howled dreadfully while vomiting forth fierce fire.
But the illustrious Prahrāda, of great heroism and intoxicated by battle, smiling,
spoke these excellent words appropriate for the occasion:
"Today I shall demonstrate the mighty strength of my own arms."
Today in battle you shall behold the gods struck down by my arrows.
Those Dānavas whose kinsmen were slain here in battle by the gods shall today offer the flesh of their enemies as an oblation.
Today, I shall settle this dust that has arisen at the head of the battle with the flowing blood of my enemies.
My arrows shall fall like fireflies upon the sky, which has its sun obscured by a flood of darkness and turned crimson by the dust of my army.
Rejoice and be filled with joy; let fear of the gods be cast aside.
Today, in battle, I shall slay Kāla-indra with my bow.
I shall gratify King Bali, the best among the powerful,
after slaying in battle the thirty gods along with their hosts, who resemble the God of Death himself.
My quivers are inexhaustible, and my arrows are like venomous serpents;
who, desiring to live, would be able to stand before me in battle?
By slaying hosts of enemies, one gains contentment and the affection of kings;
for one who has been slain, there is residence in the third heaven—there is no destiny equal to that of battle.
Having cast fear behind them in battle, O best of Dānavas,
slay all these enemies and rejoice in the Nandana grove!
Having spoken thus, Prahrāda, the best of the Dānavas,
forcefully crushed that great and most fierce army of Kāla with his own vast host.
He was an expert in all weapons, a hero, and always undefeated;
he constantly faced his enemies in battles, confident in the strength of his own arms.
There were sixty thousand chariots carrying various weapons,
belonging to that exceedingly powerful Prahlāda and his own biological sons.
They have performed hundreds of such extensive sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
they are ever patient, devoted to the Dharma, and dedicated to the vow of truth.
They were givers and pleasant speakers, eloquent in matters of the sacred scriptures;
they were always devoted to their own wives, devoted to Brahman, and true to their promises.
They were constant performers of sacrifices with various rites, ever devoted to the study of the Vedas,
all skilled in archery and weaponry, and many times proven in their prowess.
Possessing the prowess of rutting elephants, they were the crushers of enemy armies;
with the stamping of their feet, they tore asunder the most terrible whirlwinds.
With minds ever eager for battle, their eyes reddened with rage,
and their lips bitten together, the Daityas of terrifying prowess let out a roar.
They gladdened one another with the sounds of shouting and the slapping of arms,
as well as with the sounds of flutes and conchs, and with abundant lion-roars.
Diving again and again into the battle with sudden force,
those of immense strength repeatedly surrounded him from all sides, drawing their bows which were as long as palm trees.
Unable to endure him, the Dānavas, with arrows in hand, suddenly engaged Antaka in battle—
even though he was unconquered by the great Asuras.
All those proud Dānavas wore ornaments of refined gold and were clad in white garments; all of them were desirous of attaining heaven.
All the heroes were seekers of victory, all intent on the slaughter of their enemies;
that radiant army, garlanded with banners and standards, shone brilliantly.
Crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, it was intent upon the path to heaven.
Then Kāla emerged, terrible and of fearsome prowess,
roaring with a massive body and surrounded by many diseases.
He beheld a vast army of powerful Dānavas,
filled with joy and roaring loudly toward him as if toward the very hour of destruction.
Then Antaka, accompanied by the Diseases, quickly turned back that onrushing host of the powerful Dānavas.
Having entered their army, the valiant one,
surrounded by his own division, caused them to be slain like Time himself with blood-red eyes.
In the battle, Kāla struck the exceedingly fierce Bala and the mighty Prahrāda with his staff, mallet, and sharp-edged spear.
Arrows, spears, double-edged swords, and scimitars; spikes, maces, clubs, iron bludgeons, and various kinds of battle-axes.
And various bows and iron *śataghnīs* were hurled by diseases at the front of the Dānavas' army in the battle.
Diarrhea, fevers, consumption, diseases born of phlegm,
ailments of the head, diseases of the eyes, and those disorders of the stomach— [all these were cured].
In that battle, many diseases slew many of the foremost Asuras;
likewise, many hosts of Daityas also slew numerous diseases.
Some were crushed by spears, some were cut down by battle-axes,
some were struck by iron clubs, and others by supreme weapons.
Some, split in two by swords, fell quivering upon the earth;
thus were the Vyādhas torn apart by the Dānavas with various weapons.
And all those Dānavas were pierced by various excellent weapons—
by broad and sharp swords, spears, lances, and mallets—
and were cut to pieces with pikes and axes.
In that great battle, they were wounded by mallets and spears, by diseases of immense power,
by many weapons, and by fists.
With their teeth and eyes fixed in a stare, they vomited unshakeable blood.
There arose a tumultuous sound in that battle, hair-raising and terrifying, from those crying out in piteous tones and roaring with lion-like roars.
Their heads were repeatedly struck by fists and their limbs by palms;
even as they stood in the midst of battle, they fell to the earth.

It was filled with *astraphenā* (foam of missiles) and *dhvajāvarta* (whirlpools of banners), with great serpents whose arms were severed, and it teemed with *śūla* (spears) and *śakti* (javelins) as its great fish, and was crowded with *cāpa* (bows) as its crocodiles.
Crowded with chariots as its boulders, covered by the trees that were banners,
and spreading with a terrible roar, that river became one whose waters were blood.
With their bows like Indra’s rainbow and their golden armlets like flashes of lightning,
those two Daityas, who were like clouds at the end of time, released a torrent of arrows.
Then those two, resembling great clouds and mounted upon their chariots and elephants,
became exceedingly enraged like two rain-bearing clouds.
Clad in armor of refined gold and adorned with divine necklaces,
those two, exerting themselves, shone like the sun and the fire.
Resembling two great mountains, those two struck each other at the head of their armies in battle with arrows whose touch was like the thunderbolt.
Having encountered one another in that battle which was difficult to withstand,
the warriors then did not even hope for their own lives in that conflict.
With all their limbs pierced by arrows and their lives exhausted in battle,
the foremost warriors fell down, their chests drenched in blood.
With warriors whose lives had departed— some already fallen, some falling, and others being struck down in the battle— the earth became strewn with them.
In that battle, despite their utmost effort, no one could perceive any interval between those two as they were taking up their terrible arrows nor as they were fixing them to the bowstrings.
And because of their lightness of hand, O mighty-armed one, those two of great strength, who were skilled in battle,
simultaneously drew their bows into circles.
And by the floods of arrows from Prahrāda, the army of Antaka fled,
being struck by that powerful one like a mass of clouds driven by the wind.
Then Prahlāda, the best of the Dānavas, seizing a mallet,
hurled it at Antaka; by that blow, Antaka was shattered.
Having fallen into a state where his life was in danger, he collapsed upon the surface of the earth.
Perceiving that his pride had been humbled, Prahlāda understood that it was the right time for battle;
and having observed that his enemy had retreated from the conflict, he reflected upon him.
Thinking that the one named Tṛṇānana was terrified because he was the son of Śārṅgin,
and perceiving him to be under his control, Prahrāda, who was fierce in battle, [laughed].
Right there, that great asura once again crushed another army.
The battle that took place between Kāla, Prahlāda,
and the others was such as had never occurred before in all the worlds, nor will it ever happen again.
Thus Prahrāda, possessed of such marvelous vigor and strength, bore the scars of many great battles; yet as he grew older, Time itself withdrew from the field of combat.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Anuhrāda, the powerful younger brother of Prahrāda, [became] the lord of wealth.
Accompanied by his army, he fought, agitating the host of yakṣas.
And with a great flood of troops, the powerful and preeminent asura Anuhrāda,
filled with rage, began to harass the Lord of Wealth.
Unable to endure the thirty gods standing in battle with weapons raised,
the great asura, bow in hand, wrought a terrible slaughter.
A great whirlpool, as it were, arose from that vast army;
it was like the overflowing of the immeasurable ocean when it is agitated.
The earth became covered with the bodies of the thirty gods and the Dānavas—
terrible beings like mountains at the time of universal dissolution.
In the month of Mādhava, the summit of Mount Meru shines, dyed red on all sides as if by *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
A great river began to flow, with slain heroes, elephants, and horses;
it had a vast current of blood for its water and increased the population of Yama’s realm.
It had excrement and fat for its great mud, scattered entrails for its moss,
severed trunks and heads for its fish, and limbs and members for its grassy weeds.
Crowded with vultures and swans, resounding with the cries of herons and cranes,
strewn with the foam of fat, it was filled with the sounds of shrieks and thundering roars.
That great river on the battlefield, difficult for cowards to cross,
was like a river at the end of the dry season, adorned by flocks of swans.
The thirty gods and the Dānavas crossed that river so difficult to traverse,
just as leaders of elephant herds cross a lotus pond covered with the pollen of lotuses.
Then the god beheld Anuhrāda standing upon his chariot, swiftly discharging floods of arrows and slaughtering the Yakṣa host.
Then, enraged, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) destroyed the army of the Daityas,
just as the wind in the sky forcibly scatters a vast mass of great clouds.
Having observed that tumultuous battle,
King Anuhrāda pursued Kubera on a chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
That best of archers, having drawn his bow at the forefront of the battle,
discharged sharp arrows at the high-souled Lord of Wealth.
Having reached Kubera, those well-aimed arrows, having pierced through him,
struck other Yakṣas and Rākṣasas who were stationed behind him.
Struck by arrows resembling blazing fire,
the enraged god advanced against Anuhrāda in that great battle.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa, full of wrath along with his hosts of yakṣas,
the powerful one, rained down showers of arrows upon the Dānava.
Just as a bull, unable to resist the onset of the autumnal rain that has arrived so swiftly,
closes its eyes while receiving it.
In this very way, the great Asura Daitya, with eyes suddenly closed, endured the terrible shower of arrows from Kubera.
Enraged by the shower of arrows from the Lord of Wealth,
the mighty one swiftly leapt from his chariot and reached the ground on foot.
He beheld on all sides a tree resembling the banner of Indra.
Enraged, the Daitya uprooted a tree complete with fruit, its branches and boughs fully grown, and its young shoots and sprouts; he then struck down the excellent,
high-speed horses of Kubera.
Seeing his most terrible deed, all the great Asuras,
thrilled by the joy of Anuhrāda, uttered lion-like roars.
Then a tumultuous battle broke out between those two, the god and the Daitya.
For the sake of conquering Bali and Indra, and for the sake of conquering the three worlds,
those two, their eyes red with rage and each desiring to slay the other, [then set out].
They struck each other with various terrible weapons in the battle.
Then the thirty gods, having crushed the Dānavas in battle, gave up their lives;
and the thirty gods were also struck down upon the earth by the enraged Dānavas.
Then the Dānavas, filled with rage, pierced the gods with sharp,
straight-flying arrows resembling fire, fletched with heron feathers.
Though being torn apart by the hosts of Daityas, the exceedingly powerful gods,
becoming even more indignant, performed their deeds fearlessly once again.
The Dānavas were tormented by the gods with most terrifying maces, sharp-edged spears, tridents, clubs, and iron bars with extremely keen points.
With their limbs pierced by arrows and their chests mangled by swords,
those foremost of Asuras seized rocks and trees as well.
Those sons of Diti, possessing terrible speed, roaring again and again,
crushed the heroic gods by the hundreds and thousands.
Then a most tumultuous battle ensued between them,
fought with massive rocks, trees with a hundred branches,
iron clubs, spears, crescent-headed arrows, slings, and battle-axes.
Some had their heads severed, some were split asunder,
and some gods and asuras lay struck down upon the ground, drenched in blood.
Some were routed and perished, tormented by one another’s slaughter; some lay there with their hearts pierced and their feet severed; and some, mangled by tridents, had lost their lives on the spot.
That most terrifying great battle, crowded with gods and dānavas,
became tumultuous with weapons and thick with rocks and trees.

The battle shone like a Gandharva performance, with the bowstrings serving as sweet lutes, the gasping for breath providing the rhythm, and the sounds of the distressed warriors' cries enriching the melody.
With bow in hand, that Kubera, enraged at the forefront of the battle, put the Dānavas to flight in all directions with showers of arrows.
Seeing the army afflicted by Kubera and fleeing in retreat,
the Dānava Anuhrāda seized a massive boulder and rushed forward.
With eyes twice as red from rage and possessing prowess equal to his father,
he caused that rock to fall upon Kubera’s excellent chariot.
Seeing the rock falling upon him, the Lord of Wealth, mace in hand,
leaped from his chariot with speed and stood firmly upon the earth.
Having shattered his excellent chariot— complete with wheels, pole, flagstaff, and bow— the rock fell to the earth.
Having crushed the chariot of Kubera, the younger brother of Prahlāda wrought havoc among the gods with trees possessing trunks and branches.
With their heads severed and broken, drenched in blood, and their limbs crushed by trees, the gods fell upon the surface of the earth.
Having put the vast army to flight, Anuhrāda, the best of asuras,
seized a great mountain peak and rushed toward Kubera.
As he was rushing forward, the valiant Dhanada,
raising his mace and roaring aloud, challenged the mighty lord of the Dānavas.
Enraged at him, the lord of wealth, the powerful master, hurled that mace bristling with many spikes onto the chest of the Dānava.
But the Daitya, his eyes copper-red with rage, disregarding that blow,
then hurled a mountain peak upon the Lord of Wealth.
With all his limbs overwhelmed, struck by the mountain peak,
he suddenly fell to the ground like a shattered mountain.
Seeing the Lord of Wealth overwhelmed, all those Yakṣas and Rākṣasas of terrible prowess surrounded that high-souled one and protected him.
For a moment the lord, the son of Viśravas, became overwhelmed;
fallen upon the ground, he shone like a mountain whose wings had been clipped.
Then that mighty, tawny-eyed one suddenly rose up once more.
And he let out a great roar, making the three worlds resound;
it was as if he were generating a thunderous din and shattering the mountains.
Realizing that he was invulnerable, and seeing him rise up again after being struck down,
the Dānavas fled in all directions as the tawny-eyed one approached.
Seeing them fleeing, the asura Anuhrāda spoke to Kālanemi, Nemi, and the Dānava Mahānemi:
Having forgotten yourselves, your valor, and your noble lineage at that time,
where are you going, terrified with fear like common Dānavas?
"Turn back, O you of great prowess! Why do you seek to protect your lives?
This yakṣa is no match for battle; this is merely a great intimidation."
Today, by exerting my prowess, I shall dispel this terror that has arisen among the Dānavas; turn back, O great Asuras!
Then those great asuras, having turned back like elephants in rut,
being exceedingly enraged, struck down the army of the gods.
Some, their weapons exhausted, possessing voices like the roar of great clouds and fierce with pride, engaged in combat using only their arms.
With dust, wood, and stones, those of great strength,
acting with speed, likewise hurled one another with their arms.
With their fists, palms, and blows from their nails,
and with trees possessing great branches, those of mighty strength fought upon the field of battle.
But Anuhrāda, filled with rage, crushed the great army of the gods,
like a fire that has arisen consuming the forests, being most intensely provoked.
Many of the best of warriors lie there drenched in blood;
severed and fallen upon the ground, they resemble trees with copper-colored blossoms.
But the valiant Anuhrāda discharged sharpened arrows at the gods, who resembled venomous serpents as they fought in the battle.
When Anuhrāda was pierced by the Lord of Wealth in battle,
flames mixed with glowing coals issued from the mouth of the enraged one.
Then, in that battle, the enraged and foremost of Dānavas pierced the Lord of Wealth with a thousand arrows, like Antaka himself bearing his staff.
But Kubera, pierced on all sides by arrows and drenched in blood,
flowed with gore like a mountain with its waterfalls.
And for a moment, the god who is the lord of the Giver of Wealth became utterly distraught.
Having regained consciousness, that god, his eyes red with rage,
possessed of terrible prowess and overwhelmed by fury, seized a fearsome mace and hurled it with force toward the Daitya.
Then, before that mace could reach him, the Asura, roaring in rage, shattered it with his own mace; that was a marvel at that time. But seizing his mace once more, he rushed toward the Dānava.
Seeing him rushing toward him,
the exceedingly powerful Anuhrāda then uprooted a mountain peak resembling Mount Kailāsa and charged at the Lord of Wealth like Death with his mouth wide open.
He was approaching like Death himself, unconquerable by all the gods;
that Daitya seemed to be swallowing the entire triple world in his fury.
Beholding him in such a state, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), out of fear,
abandoned the battle and went to where Śakra, the lord of the gods, was.
Then, having witnessed his great feat, the Lord of Wealth,
the master of riches, thought, "I am not capable of fighting him in battle," and thus reflected.
Terrified with fear, he went to where the god Śacīpati was.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
Vipracitti, however, was the first of the Daityas, the imperishable Varuṇa.
Enraged, he struck with multitudes of arrows that were like blazing great serpents.
Being scorched by the Daitya with the blazing rays of his arrows,
that lord of the waters did not know what ought to be done in the battle.
Just as Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati is to the Lord of all the worlds,
so is he to Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor.
The powerful Lord of the Waters was unable to stand before Nārāyaṇa, O Vipracitti.
The great array named Vajra is fearless and faces in all directions;
having formed that array, the Dānavas fought back against the divine host.
There, the face of the great-souled Daitya Vipracitti shone like a flame of fire and resembled the orb of the sun.
But Varuṇa, of great splendor, desiring victory, gazed upon the great asura Vipracitti as if burning him with his own energies.
Having prepared a space just wide enough for a chariot, with an interval of five finger-breadths left between them,
the Daitya— adorned with garlands, wreaths, and ornaments, and beautified by armlets and bracelets—
seized a mace that resembled the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
Bound with golden bands and adorned with a golden garland, it was made of iron;
terrible like the staff of Yama, it brought destruction to the fear of the Daityas.
Brandishing that [mace], which resembled the great banner of Śakra,
the immensely powerful and great asura Vipracitti, with his mouth wide open, let out a roar;
he was adorned with a golden necklace upon his neck and armlets upon his arms.
With two variegated earrings and a most wonderful garland.
The Dānava shone with his ornaments and his iron club,
like a thundering cloud accompanied by lightning and an Indra’s bow.
Brandishing that iron club, he tore through the vault of the sky;
with the tip of the iron club, he of great roar shattered the masses of wind.
It blazed forth with smoky flames, like a fire produced by friction.
Together with the hosts of Vidyādharas, he [beheld] even the cities of the Gandharvas,
along with Amarāvatī and likewise the worlds of the Siddhas.
Adorned with the sun and moon, and graced by the movements of the planets and constellations,
the vault of heaven seemed to whirl, shaken by the iron club of the lord of the Daityas.
That lord, difficult to approach, appeared wearing a mace as his ornament;
he was like the fire of the end of the eon, with the lord of the gods as its fuel and the lord of the asuras as its flame.
The thirty gods and Varuṇa themselves were unable to move for fear;
there, however, the lord Kauśika Vāsava alone remained fearless.
He brought down upon the army of the high-souled Lord of Waters a terrible iron club, resembling the sun and fierce to behold.
As he fell in battle, ten thousand beings belonging to the great-souled Lord of Waters were struck down by his iron club.
He fell once more swiftly upon the chest of Varuṇa, as if onto the breast of Varuṇa himself;
having struck his body, he shattered into a thousand pieces.
Having struck their limbs, it shattered into thousands of pieces;
as it broke apart, it appeared like hundreds of meteors in the sky.
Then, having whirled him around once more, he cast him down before Varuṇa.

Then, as that body was being struck down, Varuṇa’s terrible iron club shattered against the god’s limb and fell apart; as it broke,
its fragments scattered through the sky like fireflies.
But by that blow, the lord of the waters trembled,
like a mountain struck by a club during an earthquake in battle.
Then, when his armies had been broken and their bodies mangled in battle,
the impatient Lord of Waters fell into agitation for a moment.
Overcome by indignation, Varuṇa of immeasurable prowess,
the crusher of his enemies, brought about the total destruction of his own side.
Surrounded by the four blazing oceans together with their serpents,
he bears this body which, like a conch, pearl, or gem, consists of water.
Clad in white, fluttering garments, with his arms adorned with various jewels,
the glorious Varuṇa holds his noose and is surrounded by tortoises and fish.
Then Varuṇa, having looked at his own soldiers with anger, spoke to them joyfully: "Fight with the desire to slay the Dānavas!"
"Cast aside your fear and fight; I shall slay him.
Then all those serpents, who had their refuge in the waters of the great ocean, [acted accordingly].
Roaring at the front of the battle, those eager for victory struck down the Daityas.
But those followers of Varuṇa, filled with joy, struck down the arrogant Dānavas with hollow arrows, iron shafts, maces, and even iron clubs.
But Vipracitti, enraged and possessed of great strength and prowess,
struck down the bodies of the serpents at the forefront of the battle.
With the Gāruḍa weapon,
that best of Dānavas caused the serpents to be slain in battle by Garuḍas, the devourers of snakes.
In that battle, the hero, difficult to conquer, crushed the serpents with arrows resembling the sun and adorned with gold.
With their limbs mangled in battle and tormented by arrows,
those serpents fell with all their bodies crushed, like elephants struck down by great elephants.
Enraged in battle, the lord Varuṇa rushed toward him who was blazing like the sun with the rays of his flaming arrows.
Seeing him approaching in a rage as the slayer of many Dānavas,
the Dānavas there were then slain by the thousands with their bodies mangled.
Distraught and bewildered, they fled in the ten directions;
for the sake of Indra, Varuṇa exerted his prowess and, casting aside his life,
that best of wielders of the noose fought in battle with a roar.
The Vāruṇas and the Pannagas, fierce in battle,
assailed the great Asura Vipracitti in the fray with their fists.
Then, striking with missiles and rocks,
that exceedingly powerful and highly energetic great Asura Vipracitti drove them away.
Then, with well-aimed, swift-moving arrows resembling fire,
he pierced Varuṇa’s horses of great speed in the battle.
By that great deed of the high-souled Vipracitti,
his splendor increased like that of a fire into which clarified butter has been offered as an oblation.
With well-aimed, swift-moving arrows resembling the sun,
that great asura crushed that vast army of Varuṇa.
He rendered her, whose weapons were exhausted, overwhelmed by arrows, and stupefied by a web of shafts, pierced by pikes,
spears, and double-edged swords, and drenched in blood.
Pierced by spears, javelins, and double-edged swords, obstructed by arrows, and wounded by shafts.
