With well-aimed, straight-knotted arrows resembling fire,
he pierced Varuṇa’s horses of great speed in the battle.
Then the Lord of the Waters, along with his army, was assailed by the Daitya.
Afflicted by fear of Vipracitti, he sought refuge with Mahendra.
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said: Having witnessed the defeat of the gods, Agni, the best of the thirty deities, [acted].
Praised by the Brahman-sages, he set his mind upon the slaughter of the Daityas.
The son of Svayaṃprabhā and Śāṇḍilī was Havyavāhana;
he was Hiraṇyaretas, Piṅgākṣa, Devadūta, and Hutāśana.
Red-hued, with a red neck, the taker, the giver, the oblation, the sage;
the purifier, the consumer of all, the god whose mouth is all the gods, the Lord.
He whose self is the supreme Brahman, who possesses excellent luster, who has a thousand rays, the source of light;
he whose path is black, who has variegated radiance, the foremost of the gods, the multiform, the sole sovereign.
The witness of the world, offered by the twice-born, fond of the *vaṣaṭ* call, radiant,
the consumer of oblations, born from the *śamī* tree, self-originated, and the performer of all rites.
The purifier of all beings, the treasury of asceticism for the thirty gods,
the subduer of all evils, the licking flame composed of austerity.
His crest curls to the right; his hair is pure; he has the form of a sacrificial fire.
He is the consumer of oblations, the Lord of the past and the future, the carrier of the sacrificial portions, and Hari.
The drinker of Soma, possessed of great splendor, the Lord of Beings, the destroyer of all beings,
the invincible, the purifier, the source of existence, the soul of all beings, and indeed the sovereign of the Svadhā offerings.
Lord of the *svāhā* invocation, sung by the Sāma-chanters, whose food is purified by the *soma*, and who upholds the mountains;
the God of gods, the Great Wrath, whose self is Rudra, born from Brahmā.
Mounting a chariot with red horses and wheels of wind, the creator of beings—
the best of gods, whose banner is smoke and whose crest is smoke, clad in blue garments— [proceeded].
Raising his great divine Āgneya weapon in battle, the god [slew] thousands,
millions, and hundreds of millions of Dānavas.
The Blessed One, the Fire-god,
whose charioteer is the Wind, desiring victory in battle, consumed them like the enraged fire at the time of universal dissolution.
The vital breath (prāṇa) which dwells within the hearts of all beings in fivefold ways.
He who is the driver of the sacrificial fire, the friend, the master, and the Lord;
he who is the shatterer of the worlds and the destroyer of all at the end of the age.
He whose source is extolled in songs consisting of the seven notes;
he who is the god dwelling in space, far-reaching, and the origin of sound.
He who is the creator and the transformer, the goal and the lord of those who have a goal,
the maker of the gods, who is equal in the world to the eternal Brahmā.
That wind which they call formless, the great element, the most mighty—
he, the wind, stirred up the fire within the womb of the *śamī* tree.
Expanding in all ten directions with flames that ascended to the third heaven,
he arose like the fire at the end of an eon for the destruction of the Dānavas.

Seeing in the battle that river of combat, whose great mud was fat and marrow, whose moss and grass were hair, which carried away the stones of warriors' heads, whose fierce banks were dead elephants, and whose water was blood— the Lord [beheld it].
The fire-god, increasing the terror of the Daityas, caused them to flee;
for the powerful Agni then defeated all the sons of Diti,
led by Prahlāda, as they cried out in the great battle.
Some had flaming crowns; some had blazing hair;
some had burning garments; and some had glowing arms and faces.
Some were seen there with blazing words, some with umbrellas, banners, and chariots;
the Asuras appeared there enveloped by a flaming fire.
And others [placed] banners upon their crowns and on their armlets.
And those soldiers of yours did not shine in battle, struck down by the fire;
the asuras, terrified with fear, fled in the ten directions.
Having abandoned all their weapons along with their excellent chariots and banners,
their limbs scorched in battle, they were terrified and defeated by the fire.
And none of them saw the embodied one at the head of the banner-bearing host;
instead, the Dānavas beheld the quarters, the sky, the earth, and the clouds all ablaze.
"Surely Dhruva was created by the Self-Existent One at the end of the age from the waters"—
thus did all the Dānavas think, their minds filled with terror.
Then Maya and Śambara, both masters of great illusion,
employed the illusions of Parjanya and Varuṇa, which caused a downpour of water.
Then that fire, having arisen, was extinguished by those two illusory powers;
at that time, that fire was quelled.
The wondrous fire was extinguished by the two Daityas of terrible form.
Then, with thick clouds raining down torrents of water in great abundance,
the fire was brought to a state of peace by Maya and Śambara;
with those mountain-like floods of water, the flames became mild in the battle.
While the fire that destroys the Daityas was being extinguished in the battle,
Bṛhaspati, of great fame and great splendor, spoke to Vahni.
O golden-seeded one, with beautiful crests, eternal flame, consumer of all! O seven-tongued one, with mouths emaciated, licking, and possessed of great power!
O All-pervading Lord, the wind is your self and the plants are your body;
the waters are your womb, and you are the womb of the waters.
O illustrious one, your rays go upward and downward, move across the sides,
and emanate in every direction.
O Agni, you alone are everything; this entire world is within you.
You sustain all beings, and you support the universe.
O Agni, you alone are the carrier of oblations; you alone are the supreme oblation.
And the virtuous always worship you alone at the highest sacrifice.
O All-pervading Lord, you consume the food of living beings— whether chewed, drunk, or eaten; O Master, you also lick and drink it.
O Lord, you consume living beings at their end;
you were within living beings as the consumer of what was burnt and drunk.
Victory is centered in you; the worlds are established in you.
O Bearer of Oblations, when the time arrives, you, being fully kindled, cook all these three worlds;
O Jātavedas, you alone are born for the sake of austerity.

"Welcome to you, O best of gods, who have come into my presence. Whom shall I favor, and what boon shall I grant? I stand here as the giver of boons."
Then Kaśyapa and Aditi,
having bowed their heads at his feet, received that boon from him, the soul of yoga.
"May the Blessed One himself become our son; of this there is no doubt. Having been addressed with such supreme devotion, he will say, "So be it."
"May all the gods say to you, 'You shall be our brother,' and that glorious creator of all the worlds will reply, 'So be it.'"
Therefore, having thus received this boon, O best of the thirty gods,
all of you, having accomplished your purpose, may now return to your respective abodes.
"So be it," said all the gods, as well as Kaśyapa and Aditi;
having paid homage at the feet of Brahmā, they departed toward the northern direction.
They reached the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk without delay,
exactly as it had been pointed out by the blessed Brahmā, the teacher of the Veda.
Having crossed all the oceans and many mountains in an instant,
those best of gods traversed various divine rivers upon the earth.
And they behold a most terrible region, utterly devoid of all living beings,
sunless, without boundaries, and shrouded in darkness.
Having reached the abode of immortality together with Kaśyapa and the gods,
they were initiated into a divine vow that grants all desires for a thousand years.
For the sake of propitiating that Lord of the Gods, the wise one of Yoga,
for the divine Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-eyed one, for the sake of prosperity.
Through celibacy, through silence, through the hero’s posture, and through self-restraint,
all these heroes have undertaken difficult ascetic penance.
There, for the sake of inspiring faith in that Great-Souled One, the Blessed Kaśyapa uttered that hymn declared in the Vedas, which they call the supreme praise.
And Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana declared that it is indeed endowed with all objects of desire.
Having joined his palms in reverence and uttered the *praṇava* once,
becoming single-minded and self-restrained, he praised the Lord of the World.
[Colophon]

Kaśyapa said: Homage be to You, O God of gods, the One-Horned One, the Boar, whose radiance is like a bull, the Bull of the Ocean, Vṛṣākapi, the Bull among the Suras, created by the Suras, the Uncreated, the Auspicious One, Kapila, Viṣvaksena, the Eternal Dharma, King of Dharma, Vaikuṇṭha, the Hundred-Fold Revolving One!
O you who are without beginning, middle, or end; O Dhanañjaya; O you of pure renown; O fire-born; O Vṛṣṇi-born; O unborn; O unconquerable; O Lord of immortality; O eternal one;
O Ordainer; O you whose desires are threefold; O you whose abode is threefold; O Trikakuṭ; O Kukuḍmin; O Dundubhi; O Mahānābha; O Lokanābha; O Padmanābha;
O Viriñci; O most excellent one; O you of many forms; O Virūpa; O Viśvarūpa; O imperishable; O immutable; O truly immutable; O Haṃsākṣara; O consumer of oblations.
O Khaṇḍaparaśu, Śukra, Muñjakeśa, Haṃsa, Mahad-akṣara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Sūkṣma, Paramasūkṣma, Turāṣāṭ,
Viśvamūrti, Surāgraja, Nīla, Nistama, Viraja, Tamorajaḥ-sattvadhāman, Sarvalokapratiṣṭha,
Śipiviṣṭa, Sutapas, Tapogra, Agra, Agraja, Dharmanābha, Gabhastinābha, Dharmanemi, Satyadhāman!
O you whose syllables are truth, O you whose rim is radiant, O sinless one, O you whose chariot is the moon, you alone are the dweller in the ocean; O unborn, O single-footed one, O thousand-headed,
O measured by a thousand, O great-headed, O thousand-eyed, O thousand-footed, O downward-faced, O large-mouthed, O Great Person, O Supreme Person,
O thousand-armed, O thousand-formed, O thousand-faced, O thousand-eyed, O thousand-shouldered, O thousand-fold origin, [salutations] a thousand times!
The Vedas call you [the Supreme].

O Viśvadeva, source of all, you are the auspiciousness of all the gods and their primary refuge from the beginning; you are the nourisher of the universe; they call you the universe; you alone are the supreme granter of boons, O Puṣpahāsa;
you alone are Vauṣaṭ.
They say that you alone are the syllable Oṃ and the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, the foremost recipient of the sacrificial portions.

O hundred-streamed, thousand-streamed! Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ! You alone are the past, you are the world, you are the self-sovereignty (svadhā). You alone are the one who lies within Brahman, you are composed of Brahman, you are the source of Brahmā and all else.
You alone are this.

*//* You are heaven; you are earth; you are Pūṣan; you are Mātariśvan; you are Dharma; you are Maghavan; you are the Hotṛ, the Potṛ, the leader, the slayer, the thinker, the Hotṛ of the oblation, the Hotṛ beyond the beyond—you alone are the Hotṛ of the oblation.*//*

You are the waters, you are all-voiced; by the supreme measure of the Creator, you alone are the ladle from the quarters, the sacrificial vessel, the one to be sacrificed to, and the one to be praised. You are Tvaṣṭṛ; you alone are the kindled fire; you alone are the goal of those who possess a goal. You are liberation, you are yoga, you are the secret, you are the perfected, you are the auspicious, you are the sustainer, you are the supreme, you are the sacrifice, you are Soma, and you are the sacrificial post.
You are the sacrificial fee; you are the consecration; you are the universe.

O most ancient one, O elder, O conqueror of all, O Golden Embryo, O Golden Navel, O Golden Nārāyaṇa, O Inner Soul of Nārāyaṇa, O Refuge of men, O Sun-colored One, O Splendor of the Sun, O Great Person, O Best of Gods, O Primordial God, O Lotus-navelled One,
O Sleeper on the Lotus, O Lotus-eyed One, O Womb of the Lotus, O One with golden-tipped hair, O Pure One, O Universal God, O One whose face is everywhere, O All-seeing One.
O source of the universe, O consumer of the universe, you alone are [all this].

O you of vast prowess, whose stride is the wheel, who possess great valor in the three worlds; O self-valiant one, who traverse the heavens, the tawny-hued one, the all-pervading lord, the maker of light, Śambhu, the self-born, the source of all beings, the soul of all beings, the great element, the consumer of the universe—you alone are the protector of the world, O sustainer of the universe! You are the purifier, the wise one, the sacrificial oblation, the performer of the rite of oblation, whose fuel is nectar, and the teacher of gods and asuras.

"O Great Primordial God, god among men, whose deeds are exalted, whose soul is purified, Lord of the Immortal, who touches the heavens; O Lord of the Universe, you are the one from whom the *ghṛtācī* [goddess] proceeds.
You, whose actions are infinite, belong to the lineage of Druhiṇa and your own lineage; you are the universal noose. You alone sustain the universe; protect us who seek your favor."
[Colophon] Vaiśampāyana said:
But the blessed Nārāyaṇa, having heard this supreme hymn of praise...
It was spoken by Kaśyapa, the best of the twice-born, who is a knower of Brahman.
With a mind filled with joy, he [heard] the smooth and deep resonance, sounding like the roar of a thundercloud, of the high-souled gods.
He spoke these words properly, with joyful and well-articulated syllables:
"The gods heard [the voice] from the sky, but no form was perceived.
Then the glorious, pleased-minded Lord, the Sovereign Master, spoke."
"I am pleased with you all, O best of gods; choose a boon from me, for I am the giver of boons. May it be well with you, O supreme gods."
Kaśyapa said:
O best of immortals, as soon as the Blessed One is pleased with us all, at that very moment we have accomplished our purpose; for you are our supreme refuge.
"If the Blessed One is pleased, or if another [gift] is to be given— may the illustrious Blessed One,
the younger brother of Vāsava, the increaser of the joy of his kinsmen,
truly become my son born of Aditi."
Ishampayana said: Aditi, the mother of the gods, seeking boons and desiring sons, spoke to the Blessed One, the granter of boons, regarding this very same supreme matter.
Desiring a son, she indeed entreated him, saying, "May you become our son.
For the sake of the ultimate welfare of all the great-souled gods,
please be our brother, our sustainer, our creator, and our refuge.
When you have attained the status of being the son of Aditi, the gods, together with Indra, will bear the title of "Deva" [as your descendants];
therefore, become the son of Kaśyapa.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Viṣṇu spoke to those gods and to Kaśyapa.
"So be it; may it be well with you. May you obtain your desired wish.
All those who shall be your enemies shall not stand before me for even a moment."
And I shall also diligently perform that which brings happiness to others for my own sake.
I am well-pleased with you, O gods, by this vow of mine.
Having received the boons from the Grandfather and likewise the boons from Maheśvara,
I shall slay the wicked Dānavas, the enemies of the immortals.
Having slain all the hosts of Asuras and whoever else are enemies of the gods,
I shall make all the deities enjoyers of the first portions of sacrificial offerings;
I shall make all the gods eaters of the *havya* and the ancestors eaters of the *kavya*.
"O best of the wise, I shall perform the duty pertaining to the supreme state;
O foremost of the gods, return by the path you came."
"O mother of the gods, Aditi, and Kaśyapa of immeasurable soul, you shall do as you desire; you may now go to your own abode."
When these words had been spoken by the powerful Viṣṇu,
the gods, with delighted minds, honored him in every way;
as did the high-souled Viśvedevas, Kaśyapa, and Aditi.
The Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, and the mighty Śakra,
having paid homage to that god, the lord of the gods, the impetuous one (Raṃhas), [proceeded].
They set out toward the eastern direction for the vast, divine hermitage of Kaśyapa.
Having gone to that hermitage frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages, they dwelt there,
devoted to the study of the Vedas, desiring the womb of Aditi.
And Aditi, the mother of the gods, conceived a fetus of exceeding splendor—
the Great-Souled One who is the self of all beings, divine, and destined for a thousand years.
When the abode of the worlds had entered the womb of the mother of the lord of gods— she who is worshipped by the world of the gods— [the following occurred].
And all the mighty Daityas were agitated;
they fell into a state of turmoil when Hari, the teacher of the world, was provoked.
The wives of the Daityas and Dānavas suffer miscarriages;
the forces of the powerful Daityas undergo sudden agitation as the Teacher of the World, the Lord of the past and the future, grows in power.
When a full thousand years had passed, she gave birth to an excellent embryo—
the god who is the refuge of the gods and the destroyer of the asuras.
Then the gods were protected by the Great-Souled Lord while he was still in the womb, as he was absorbing the splendors of the three worlds.
When that Lord of Gods was born— one who brings happiness to the three worlds,
who causes fear to the hosts of Daityas, and who increases the joy of the gods—
All the gods, together with Indra, were free from sorrow and joyful in their minds.
**[Colophon]**
Vaiśampāyana said:
The seven lords of creatures and the seven great seers paid homage to that god who had been born.
Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, Gautama, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha,
and the Sun-god who was impelled when all was lost.
The venerable Atri also arrived there.
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
and the progenitor Dakṣa likewise offered their salutations.
Aurva, the son of Vasiṣṭha, Stamba, Kaśyapa,
Kapīvān, Akapīvān, Datta, and Niścyavana.
The seven sons of Vasiṣṭha were renowned as the Vāsiṣṭhas;
they were the sons of Hiraṇyagarbha, born of Aurva, and possessed of great splendor.
Gārgya, Pṛthu, and likewise Agrya; Yāmya, Vāmana, Devabāhu, Yadudhra, and Parjanya, who was born of Soma.
Hiraṇyaroman, Vedaśiras, Satyanetra, as well as Viśva, Ativiśva, Cyavana, Sudhāman, Virajas,
Atināman, and Sahiṣṇu likewise offered their salutations.
Radiant in their forms and adorned with every ornament,
the most excellent of the Apsarases danced before Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods.
Then, while the musical instruments of the Gandharvas resounded in the sky,
Tumburu sang along with many Gandharvas.
Mahāśruti, Citraśiras, Ūrṇāyu, Anagha,
Gomāyu, Sūryavarcas, and Somavarcas as the seventh.
Simultaneously, Tṛṇapa, Kārṣṇi, Nandi, and Citraratha;
the thirteenth was Śāliśiras, and Parjanya was the fourteenth.
Kali was the fifteenth here, and Nārada was the sixteenth;
these fifty-six were proclaimed in that very place, O lord of the earth.
The two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, and the immensely radiant Haṃsa,
as well as Parvata, who was a great orator and skilled in the rhythm of stringed instruments.
All those gods and gandharvas sang in accompaniment to Keśava.
In the same way, the Apsarases were joyful, adorned with every ornament;
they were beautiful of form, possessed of shapely hips, and lovely to behold in all their limbs.
And the illustrious, large-eyed women danced and sang—
those with slender waists and beautiful midsections, the foremost of beloveds with lovely faces.
Anūkā, as well as Jāmī, Miśrakeśī, Alambuṣā,
Marīci, Śucikā, Vidyutparṇā, Tilottamā,
Adrikā, Lakṣmaṇā, Rambhā, and likewise Manoramā.
Asitā and Subāhu, Supriyā and likewise Subhagā,
Urvaśī, Citralekhā, Sugrīvā, and Sulocanā.
Raktāṅgā, Sugārā, Surathā, Pramādinī,
Nandā, Sarasvatī, and likewise other prosperities were present there.
Puṇḍarīkā, Sugandhā, Surathā, Pramāthinī,
Nandā, Sārasvatī, and likewise others there in great numbers.
Menakā, Sahajanyā, Parṇikā, and Puñjikasthalā—
these and thousands of other Apsarases were dancing there.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga;
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Savitṛ—
these are declared to be the group of sons of Kaśyapa known as the Viṣṇus.
Thus these twelve Ādityas, blazing and possessing the splendor of the sun,
paid homage to that high-souled lord of the gods.
Mṛgavyādha, Sarpa, and the highly renowned Nirṛti;
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita.
O lord of the people, Dahana, Īśvara, Kapālī,
Sthāṇu, Bhaga, and the blessed Rudra were present there.
And the blessed Lord Rudra, as well as the other eleven,
the two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, and the Maruts of great strength.
The Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas stood before him with palms joined in reverence;
likewise did the highly fortunate Śeṣa and his younger brothers, headed by Vāsuki,
as well as Kacchapa, Apahantā, and the mighty Takṣaka.
They were fierce with poison, possessed of great heroism, powerful, and renowned;
they were unassailable, endowed with splendor, exceedingly wrathful, and mighty in strength.
These high-souled Nāgas stood before him with their palms joined in reverence.
These and many other nāgas stood with palms joined in reverence before that great-souled one; they all offered their salutations.
Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, and the mighty Garuḍa,
as well as Aruṇa and Aruṇi— the sons of Vinatā— presented themselves there.
They all stood with palms joined in reverence and offered their salutations; likewise,
the deities dwelling in heaven, led by Śacīpati, did the same.
The ṛṣis and the ancestors—both those who drink soma and those who drink water.

He burned the entire triple world and those Sādhyas who were rich in asceticism; they offered salutations to that high-souled Lord of the Gods. And the blessed Grandfather himself, the creator of the worlds, arrived there in person.
The illustrious preceptor of the gods, together with all the high-souled ones, performed the birth rites and other ceremonies according to the rules and with affection, and then spoke.
Since from him the eternal and powerful world is produced,
let this glorious Viṣṇu alone be the Lord of the World.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the master, together with the celestial rishis,
paid homage to the Lord of the Gods and returned once more to heaven.
But he was born as the lord of the gods, the powerful son of Kaśyapa;
he had the luster of a cloud during a fresh storm, red eyes, and a dwarf-like form.
Then all the apsarases, their eyes wide with wonder, beheld the glorious one upon whose chest the Śrīvatsa mark shone, formed by a cluster of hair.
If the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth simultaneously in the sky,
it might be similar to the radiance of that Great-Souled One.
Resembling a celestial sage, glorious, the source of the earth and the atmosphere, the creator of all beings,
with pure hair, great shoulders, consisting entirely of splendor, he is the Lord.
He who is the goal of those with meritorious fame and the non-goal of evildoers;
whom they know as the Great-Souled One perfected in yoga, the supreme yoga itself.
He who possesses eightfold sovereignty, whom they call the best of gods,
having attained whom the disciplined Brahmins seeking liberation reach the eternal state.
They enter the Great-Souled One, the eternal one perfected in yoga.
That which they call the eternal and divine—let it be sung for those who desire liberation;
by it, those who fear worldly existence are released from both birth and death.
That which those dwelling in all the hermitages call "austerity"— that difficult vow which they observe, established in it and restricted in their food.
He who is known as Ananta among the Nāgas, served by all the serpent-beings—
Sahasramūrdhan, Raktākṣa, Śeṣa, and others who are unsurpassed.
He who is worshipped as the Sacrifice by the lords of sages desiring heaven,
he who dwells in various places, the glorious, the one, the supreme seer.
The Vedas sing of him as the Knower who bestows shares in the sacrifice—
the God whose rays are like a bull, whose eyes are the moon and sun, and whose form is space.
The all-pervading Lord, possessed of great splendor, spoke to all the gods with supreme speech;
though he already knew [the truth], he had through yoga assumed the state of a child.
"What shall I do, O best of gods, and what boon shall I grant you?
Tell me with joy what is desired by all of you."
Having heard those words of the high-souled Vāmana,
all those gods, the sons of Kaśyapa, were delighted in heart;
with palms joined in reverence, the deities led by Śakra spoke to Viṣṇu.
By the granting of a boon from Brahmā, our entire world has been seized,
despite our great asceticism, valor, and self-restraint.
"O best of gods, that son of the chief Daitya Bali, who is all-knowing and high-souled, is indeed said to be incapable of being slain by anyone at all, including us."
"O you of noble vows, no one else has the power over that;
therefore, seeking refuge, we all approach you—
the god who is worthy of refuge, the giver of boons, and the remover of fear from all the gods."
And for the benefit of the sages and of the worlds, O Lord of the Gods.
And likewise for the sake of Priyā, as well as for Āditya and Kaśyapa.
O best of beings, for the sake of our welfare and that of the three worlds, you have offered what is appropriate for the ancestors as *kavya* and the supreme oblation for the gods as *havya*.
O mighty-armed one, O best of gods, let it proceed as it did before.
For the sake of pleasing Aditi and likewise Kaśyapa,
and for the purpose of discharging his debt to the high-souled Vāsava, the lord of the gods.
Bring back this imperishable triple world of Mahendra.
He, the giver, performs sacrifice with the Vājimedha rite,
according to the ritual prescribed by rule, employing a ceremony endowed with the qualities of all seasons.
O Lord, since you have come to this place together with the inhabitants of the three worlds,
reflect upon what is appropriate for the restoration of these people.
Thus addressed by the gods, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a dwarf,
then spoke these words to all the gods, gladdening them:
"Let the great seer Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras, who has mastered the Vedas and possesses vast splendor, lead me into the presence of that sacrifice."
O best of gods, I have arrived at his sacrificial enclosure;
I shall move about as is fitting for the purpose of seizing the three worlds.
Then the illustrious Bṛhaspati, possessed of great splendor, led the Lord Vāmana to the sacrificial enclosure of the wise lord of the Dānavas.
Wearing a girdle of muñja grass and the sacred thread, bearing an umbrella, a staff, and likewise a banner;
the Blessed One, assuming the form of a dwarf, had smoke-colored and reddish eyes.
Having gone to that sacrificial enclosure frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages,
that glorious lord of the gods entered the sacrificial arena itself.
The Blessed One described that sacrifice as being none other than himself.
The glorious Lord of the lords of the world, the Blessed One, though not aged, was then attended by the gods led by Brahmā as if he were an elder.
The best of gods, whose nature is inconceivable, went to the sacrificial enclosure of that lord of the Dānavas, Bala Vairocana.
For Pālita, though surrounded by the Daityas with their battle equipment at the gate crowded with Dānavas, entered all of a sudden.
Surrounded on all sides by officiating priests with mantras and other rituals,
the powerful Bali approached the king of the lords of Daityas and Dānavas.
O best of immortals, having described the eternal sacrifice according to the rule,
as well as its various applications in detail, the sacrifice itself [spoke].
He also took charge of Śukra and the other priests who were experts in sacrificial rites;
he surpassed them all and rendered them speechless.
Then, from afar, as well as from all sides among his forces and the officiating priests,
that omnipresent Lord [established] the sacrifice itself as his own self through various reasons and causes.
Furthermore, O Bhārata,
Citragu described it once more with Vedic and secret hymns in the presence of the hosts of ṛṣis.
Then, seeing those sages along with their preceptors— who were unsurpassed, venerable,
and possessed of great majesty— he, though not yet old and being a dwarf, [beheld them].
And the powerful son of Virocana considered it a marvel;
with his head bowed and palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words with confidence.
"From where have you come? Who are you? To whom do you belong? And what is your purpose here?
Never before have I seen a twice-born man such as you."
The boy was the best among the wise, skilled in both theoretical knowledge and practical realization;
he was refined in speech, endowed with beauty, charming, and pleasing to behold.
There are no such [beings] among the sons of the gods, nor even among the ṛṣis;
there are none among the nāgas, nor the yakṣas, nor the asuras, nor the rākṣasas.
"You belong neither to the ancestors, nor to the Siddhas, nor likewise to the Gandharvas.
Who you are, that you are; homage be to you! Tell me, what shall I do for you?"
Thus addressed, the Vāmana of inconceivable nature, who was powerful and knew the truth of expedients, spoke these words with a smile:
"Aha! The sacrifice of the lord of the Asuras is well-prepared and provides much food."
Just as in ancient times when the Grandfather Parameṣṭhin was performing a sacrifice.
O mighty lord of the Dānavas, you have distinguished the sacrifices of Sureśvara Śakra, Yama, and Varuṇa.
Perform the Vājimedha sacrifice, the most excellent of rituals,
which destroys all sins and reveals the path to heaven.
For this is considered by the exponents of Brahman to consist of all desires;
it is remembered as the glorious Aśvamedha, the most excellent of sacrifices.
For he is the great-souled Suvarṇaśṛṅga,
the lord of the world, composed of wind, the high-minded one;
he has eyes like heaven and is as fair as gold within.
He is the source of all, for he is the supreme object of sacrifice.
Having mounted the horse of the Aśvamedha sacrifice and performed the rite, men cross over their evil deeds—
him whom the foremost of the twice-born, learned in the Vedas, indeed call [the sacrificial horse].
Vaiśvānara, the prize-winner of the horse sacrifice.
Just as the householder’s stage of life is the most excellent among the stages of life, and just as the Brāhmaṇas are the most excellent among men,
so are you the most excellent here among the Asuras.
Likewise, among sacrifices, the horse sacrifice is the most excellent.
Having heard this spoken by Vāmana,
Bali, the lord of the Daityas and master of the Daityas, filled with supreme joy, spoke.
"Whose son are you, O best of brahmins? What do you desire? I shall give it to you.
Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—and obtain whatever wish you desire."
Vāmana said:
"I do not desire a kingdom, nor vehicles, nor jewels, nor women—
if you are pleased with me, and if your mind is set upon dharma."
"O Dānava, grant me three steps for the sake of my preceptor;
this is my supreme boon for the purpose of providing a shelter for the fire."
Having heard the words of Vāmana, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, spoke.
Thus addressed by the best of the gods, O Bhārata, Bali, the best of the Asuras,
became free from fear and then spoke these words to the host of the gods.
Bali said:
"O best of Brahmins, O foremost of speakers, what need have you for three words?
You are seeking hundreds of thousands of verses."
Śukra said:
"Do not give him away, O mighty-armed one! You do not know him, O great Asura;
this is the Lord Hari, the most excellent, concealed by his illusory power."
"Assuming the form of a dwarf and wearing the guise of a young brahmin boy, the all-pervading Lord came here out of a desire for the welfare and benefit of Śakra, in order to deceive you."
Thus addressed by Śukra, Bali, the king of the Dānavas, reflected for a long time; then, disregarding those words, he spoke.
Filled with great joy, what more than this could be desired as a worthy recipient?
Taking the golden pitcher in his hand, undisturbed, Bali said:
"O best of Brahmins, stand facing the east; you are standing there, O lotus-eyed one."
"Accept it! Give it! What land? How much, sir? Three paces!
It has been given to you; pour the water, so that the preceptor’s word may not be false."
Śukra said:
"O Daitya, why should this not be given? For it is certainly known how this [Viṣṇu] is truly constant.
Who is this Viṣṇu? Oh, what joy! You have been deceived; you were not deceived."
Bali said:
"How is it that this Lord Viṣṇu himself has appeared at my sacrifice? Whatever this Lord, the God of gods, desires, that I shall give."
"Who else could be a more worthy recipient than this Viṣṇu?
Having spoken thus, Bali quickly poured out the water."
Vāmana said:
"O sinless lord of the Daityas, three steps are sufficient for me.
For that which was previously spoken by me is indeed so; it cannot be otherwise."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of the immensely powerful Vāmana, [the gods spoke].
Then Vairocani, having made a black antelope skin his upper garment, [proceeded].

and he gave the northern direction to Kubera, the lord of the Yakṣas;

Having thus divided the three worlds, Viṣṇu, the best among the powerful,
established Vāsava as the great sovereign of the three worlds.
The unconquered Lord brought about the removal of the grief of the gods.
The monkey Hari bestowed upon Jāmbavat both imperishability and immortality;
having granted this removal of grief to the gods, the deity, honored by the celestials,
departed for the third heaven while being worshipped by the great seers.
Praised by Nārada and worshipped by the gods, Vāmana, the Lord of the World,
established Vāsava among all beings.
And having established that superiority toward all beings, Keśava— **HV_App.I,44B.2967**231:1.
Thus I have told you everything regarding how the dwarf-form was attained;
how Hari, Viṣṇu, the Lord of all, reached heaven along with the gods;
and when that invincible Vāmana of immeasurable splendor had departed.
All the gods rejoiced, placing Śatakratu at their head.
When Kṛṣṇa had bound Bali, the son of Virocana, and departed for the third heaven,
he was accompanied by the seven-headed nāgas, beginning with Kambala and Aśvatara.
Then that celestial seer Nārada approached Bali, the son of Virocana, who was afflicted by the suffering of being bound as a *nāga*, and questioned him.
Seeing him fallen into such distress, he was overwhelmed with compassion and said to that best of Dānavas, "I shall grant you a means of liberation."
This is the hymn of praise to the wise Vāsudeva, the God of gods,
who is without beginning or end, imperishable and immutable.
Study that, O Lord of Daityas, with a pure inner self;
having become intent upon it and focused on it, you will swiftly attain liberation.
Then the son of Virocana, self-restrained, pure, and composed, with palms joined in reverence,
studied the *Mokṣaviṃśaka* from Nārada.
Having studied that divine hymn uttered by Nārada, the great asura recited it— that very hymn by which the earth had been uplifted.
Oṃ, homage be to the Lord of infinite dominion, the imperishable Great Self,
the god who reclines upon the waters, the lotus-navelled Viṣṇu.
Having assumed the form of seven suns, you have traversed the three worlds;
O Blessed One, you are the death of Death—by that truth, deliver us!
When the sky is devoid of sun and moon, and the performance of sacrifices and austerities has perished, you shall again contemplate the worlds; by that truth, deliver us!
Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Vāyu, Agni, the rivers, the serpents, and the mountains—all these are seen by you as abiding within you; by that truth, set me free!
In a former kalpa, Mārkaṇḍeya entered your belly and beheld all that is moving and unmoving; by that truth, set me free!
You are alone, with knowledge as your companion; you are a yogi who has attained yoga.
By that truth, having once again renounced the three worlds, grant me liberation.
Sitting upon your bed, you have entered into yogic sleep;
by that truth, deliver the worlds once more.
Assuming the form of a boar and placing the Vedas and sacrifices before you,
by that truth through which the earth was raised up from the waters, deliver us!
O Hari, having lifted up the sacrifices with your tusk,
you made them into three lumps for the ancestors; by that truth, set us free!
All the gods fled, afflicted by the fear of Hiraṇyākṣa;
O Lord, you have protected us—by that truth, deliver us!
By that truth, [by which] with his long-faced form he severed the head of Hiraṇyākṣa in battle with his discus, deliver me!
In ancient times, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu had his head, bones, and brain shattered; he was slain by a mere roar (*huṃkāra*). By that truth, deliver [him].
In the past, while Brahmā looked on, the Vedas were stolen by two Dānavas; they were rescued by you, O Lord. By that truth, set me free!
Having assumed the form of Hayashiras and slain Madhu and Kaiṭabha, you restored the Vedas to Brahmā; by that truth, grant me liberation!
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, siddhas, and great serpents do not see your end; by that truth, set me free!
He who was born as the son of the God, known by the name Apāntaratamas, has indeed established the meaning of the Vedas; by that truth, grant me liberation.
The Vedas, the sacrifices, the *agnihotra* oblations, the ancestral rites, the sacrificial offerings, and the secret doctrine of the God—all these are yours; by that truth, set me free!
The sage named Dīrghatamas was born blind due to his teacher’s curse;
by your grace he has regained his sight—by that truth, set me free!
For you indeed liberated that lordly elephant who was seized by a crocodile, wretched and fallen under the power of death; by that truth, deliver me!
You are imperishable and undecaying, devoted to Brahman, and affectionate toward your devotees;
you are the restrainer of those who are arrogant—by that truth, deliver us!
I propitiate with my head the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the Śārṅga bow, and Garuḍa; may they release me from these bonds.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, quiver, and the Śārṅga bow, Garuḍa and the others propitiated Hari, saying, "Release Bali from his bonds."
Then the blessed Lord, being pleased, commanded Garuḍa, the lord of birds and slayer of serpents: "Release Bali from his bonds."
Then, having spread his wings, Garuḍa, possessed of incomparable prowess,
went to the base of the earth where Bali remained bound.
Having learned of his arrival, the Nāgas released the great Asura and,
tormented by the fear of Vainateya, went to the city of Bhogavatī.
To him who had been released by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, who was reflecting with his face cast down,
whose splendor had vanished, and from whom the serpent had departed, Garuḍa spoke these words.
"O mighty-armed lord of the Dānavas, the Lord Viṣṇu has spoken to you:
'Released, dwell in Pātāla together with your sons, people, and kinsmen.'"
"O Dānava, you must not go from here even for the distance of two krośas;
if you should break this agreement, your head shall shatter into a hundred pieces."
Having heard the words of the lord of birds, the lord of the Dānavas said this:
"I abide by the agreement with that infinite, great-souled one."
"O Lord of Birds, may that Blessed One provide some means of livelihood for me; remaining here, seated in comfort, may I be nourished by him."
Having heard Bala’s words, Garuḍa spoke this:
"A means of livelihood has already been secured by that high-souled one."
Those sacrifices which will be performed— devoid of ritual rules, lacking officiating priests,
and ignorant of the rites of atonement— the sacrificial portion from them shall be yours.
The deities do not accept their share of the sacrifice;
having had your strength nourished by this, you shall dwell here in happiness.
"O mighty-armed lord of the Dānavas, the Blessed One, the son of Kaśyapa, Viṣṇu, the creator of the three worlds, has given this message."
The man who recites with devotion this hymn to the Infinite One, which liberates one from all sins, his transgression is destroyed.
One who has killed a cow shall be liberated from that sin; a slayer of a Brahmin shall be freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
A sonless man obtains a son, and a maiden obtains a desired husband. A woman with a dead fetus shall be delivered from it, and a pregnant woman shall give birth to a son.

And those seekers of liberation in the world who are yogins or followers of Sāṃkhya and Kapila— by means of this hymn, they go to Śvetadvīpa, freed from all taint. For this hymn to the Infinite One is proclaimed as the bestower of all desires.
The man who, having risen at dawn, recites this while pure and with a restrained mind, shall obtain all his desires; of this there is no doubt.
This manifestation of the Great-Souled One, known as Vāmana,
is indeed recited by the twice-born who are learned in the Vedas as the glory of Viṣṇu.
But he who, being self-restrained and full of devotion, always listens to this divine manifestation of the Great-Souled One as Vāmana on every sacred festival day—
The king conquers his enemies just as the mighty Viṣṇu does;
he attains vast fame and acquires abundant wealth.
He becomes beloved by all beings, just as Vāmana was;
and he obtains virtuous sons endowed with the qualities of clouds.
Dharma, lifespan, wealth, health, and the excellence of virtues increase.
By constantly reciting this entire life-story of Vāmana with devotion,
one becomes free from sin and shall attain a long life.
One who desires to obtain prosperity should constantly meditate upon Vāmana;
one should cause this divine narrative to be heard by Brāhmaṇas day after day.
And their sons and grandsons increase in the perfection of health and virtuous qualities.
Janārdana, the God of gods, is pleased with one who recites this;
and Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana has declared that such a person shall indeed possess all their desires.
A woman who is frequently pregnant, upon hearing this and bowing to Vāmana,
will certainly give birth to a son by the glorification of the God of gods.
But he who shall read this entire compendium of the *Harivaṃśa*, at the end of his life he will indeed go to the world of Brahmā; there is no doubt about this.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather;
the great-grandfather, the father, and even Viṣṇu himself—of these there is no doubt. One must not engage in censure of Viṣṇu, Rudra, or the Self-born (Svayambhū).
Having become a worm because of slander, one revolves in that very same place.
One should avoid hatred toward these [beings] in thought, deed, or speech;
there is no doubt that one enjoys the infinite fruit both after death and in this very world.
Know Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa to be the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
for who else but the Lotus-eyed One could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
Who else but that Lord could speak of the past and future states of all things?
Let your great sacrifice proceed exactly as you have intended.
Having resolved upon the horse sacrifice and having heard the eternal dharmas,
O lord of men, you shall go [to heaven] at the end of your life after performing ascetic penance.
Having heard this great narrative of yours, O best of kings,
you should then commence all the rites for the purpose of completing the sacrifice.
This manifestation of Vāmana has been narrated by me to you in the presence of the royal sages,
the ṛṣis, and Nārada.
This Vaiṣṇava conduct has been proclaimed by me to you in its entirety,
O dear Janamejaya, as you asked while this sacrifice was being concluded.
The man who hears this entire section on the marvels shall not encounter anything inauspicious and shall attain a long life.
And that Brāhmaṇa who, having become pure and eternal, studies this,
being devoted to the god Nārāyaṇa, full of faith, and with his senses conquered;
Together with the four Vedas— along with their *sakhilas*, *sakalpas*, and *sapādās*, as well as their sequential recitations— he shall become a partaker of their fruits.
O best of kings, your fame and renown shall undoubtedly extend even unto the abode of Brahmā; I tell you this as the truth.
Having heard this account of the Harivaṃśa from the bull among the twice-born, as spoken by Vaiśampāyana, King Pārikṣita became free from all taint.
Indeed, that *Harivaṃśa* which was proclaimed by those from Śaunaka both in brief and likewise in detail—
what else shall I tell you?
[Colophon]

Janamejaya said:
O Brahmin, I wish to hear in truth,
in brief, about the slaughter by Tryakṣa of those three who were known as the cities and who moved through the sky.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen in detail to all that you ask me regarding the destruction of the Daityas, who were mighty in their arms and hostile toward all living beings.
O King, in the past, Śaṃkara brought about the slaughter of the lords of the asuras— who sought the destruction of all beings— by means of three straight-flying spears.
O tiger among men, Tripura, impelled by the great element,
strides through the midst of the sky like a mass of clouds that has arisen.
It was resplendent with a lofty rampart of gold,
and with archways adorned with shining jewels and every kind of gem.
Blazing with supreme splendor,
it shone in the midst of the sky like the towering city of the Gandharvas, accomplished through their own deeds.
The steeds, endowed with wings and arrogant in their strength,
carry [him] to the most excellent city of Prabhākara, moving at will through thought alone.
Running and neighing with strides sustained by their vital strength,
they seemed to challenge the very sky with their hooves, which shone like dark green leaves.
With speeds equal to the force of the wind, as if shaking the very sky,
they were seen everywhere by those whose eyes were fixed upon them.
It was filled with the sounds of singing and instrumental music by sages who resembled blazing fires, their sins consumed by asceticism; it was like a city of the Gandharvas.
It was adorned with many-colored, lofty mansions, filled with variegated weapons and possessing the luster of refined gold.
That place of great splendor shone with the forms of the palaces of the lord of gods,
and with lofty mansions possessing the luster of the peaks of Kailāsa.
The city of the Daityas shone like the sky filled with many suns,
endowed with ramparts and watchtowers, and possessing the luster of molten gold.
Then,
O great lord, it shone as if ablaze with splendors;
it was filled with many shouts and roars and resounded with lion-like cries.
It shone like the Caitraratha forest, crowded with beautiful people.
With its banners raised high and resplendent with swords,
O King, that great Tripura shone like the sky filled with lightning.
And Sūryanābha, O Bhārata, and Candranābha, the lord of the Daityas,
as well as other Dānavas of great heroism, arrogant in their strength.
Bewildered by the Supreme Lord,
O Bhārata, they both crushed and broke down the path for the gods and the path for the ancestors.

O tiger among men, O best of the Bharatas, when that great path of the gods— frequented by the ancestors and the fire-god— was seized by those foremost of Asuras and Dānavas with their bows drawn, the sacrifice was carried away.
Then all the hosts of gods, their faces pale and dejected, now that their power of movement was severed, rushed toward Brahmā.
Standing before him, they spoke with voices resonant with distress:
"We are being struck down by hosts of enemies because our shares have been cut off, O Lord of Shares!"
And tell us, O best of speakers, the means for their slaughter;
knowing which, we may slay our enemies in battle, even though they are strong of arm.
Then, having consoled them, Brahmā, the giver of boons, spoke to the deities:
"Go now, all you immortals, to propitiate Rudra on earth."
He alone is capable of subduing the Daityas; there is no doubt in this matter.
Through the asceticism of that god, one indeed becomes capable;
for the sake of propitiating Rudra, the eternal God of gods.
"O best of the thirty gods, worship Mahādeva Virūpākṣa!
He alone, having slain them all, will provide for your welfare."
Listen, all you deities, to this supreme counter-measure against the enemy:
all the Dānavas are invincible, with the exception of the imperishable Śaṅkara.
Having accepted those words with both their minds and their speech,
O Bhārata, they all descended to the earth together with the Rudras.
At the foot of the Vindhya, on Mount Meru, and in the middle of the earth’s surface,
all those sages became knowers of yoga through fierce asceticism;
as descendants of Kaśyapa, they reached Hara while chanting the *Brahmasaṃhitā*.
Upon the fire for those most excellent women,
there were copper and iron ornaments placed upon a heap of *darbha* grass.
O best of the Kurus, there were soft and beautiful skins for clothing, taken from black deer that had died of themselves,
which had been stripped from the bodies of forest-dwellers.
Then, having reached the intermediate space, those gods, enveloped by their illusory power (māyā),
all entered the abode of Hara, clad in tiger skins.
Then, having prostrated before the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, those wretched ones addressed Hara with clearly articulated speech.
Like an oblation offered in ignorance into fires covered by ashes,
O Blessed One, the granting of a boon to us is in vain when you have turned away from us.
Let the word of Brahmā be carried out according to the place and according to the time,
as it was spoken by the God of gods in the presence of the sky-dwellers.
Thus propitiated by the gods,
the Blessed One, the God of gods whose banner is the bull and who is worshipped by both gods and asuras, became gracious in heart.
He vowed the destruction of the Asuras, along with their servants, forces, and vehicles.
Then the Blessed One spoke to those led by Purandara:
"Let all of you follow me with the intent to destroy Tripura."
Thus, by the words of the gods and by the power of the destined event,
Mahādeva equipped himself together with the gods, including Indra.
Having mounted their chariot, the Ādityas— fully armored and well-adorned—
all shone with a golden luster like blazing fires.
Accompanied by Rudra, those Rudras were as if burning with their splendor;
armored and wearing beautiful crowns, they were tall like mountains.
All of them, possessing universal forms, powerful, and able to assume any shape at will,
those high-souled ones equipped themselves, desiring to bring about the end of the Dānavas.
Surrounded on all sides by these commanders of the forces,
the Three-eyed Lord, grasping his bow with an arrow, fought against Tripura.
Then the Daityas, their bodies shattered like those trapped in the upper stories of a city,
fell to the earth with their limbs broken like mountains.
Pierced and struck down, O King,
the hosts of Daityas fell like mountains shattered by the thunderbolt as they were driven into the hollows of the *ṭāla* trees.
Struck by the gods with swords, spears, discuses, and axes,
and their vital organs pierced by arrows in the field of battle, the lords of the Daityas fell together upon the earth like mountains whose wings had been clipped.
There, they lost their sense of perception because of that blazing radiance;
thus, in their mutual collision, they were destroyed by the process of destruction.
Even with divine vision, they could not perceive one another.
When the sun had set at the beginning of the night, those leaders of the gods,
their mouths mangled, pierced, and wounded, fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then the Daityas, having achieved victory at night with their sharpened arrows,
roared with loud cries like thundering clouds of great sound.
Upon attaining victory, those Asuras spoke to one another:
"All the gods have been terrified in battle by us, who are endowed with strength and armed with spears, swords, and javelins, and who desire victory."
Having achieved victory and being roused by the invocation of Uśanas,
those best of Daityas, endowed with strength and equipped with weapons, shone resplendent in battle.
Accompanied by all the gods, Śaṅkara mounted his chariot and,
as if splitting the very quarters of the sky, he struck down the arrogant Daityas.
At the end of the age, like the sun spreading its rays,
that foremost of beings burns all creatures when the time of dissolution has arrived.
Carried by swift horses fleet as thought, that chariot shone in the midst of the sky like a rain-cloud accompanied by lightning.
O Bhārata, with the bull upon its banner-top bellowing,
O King, that chariot shone like a cloud accompanied by Indra’s bow.
Then the perfected ones (siddhas) situated in the sky praised the bull-bannered Lord Tryambaka,
the first-born of former times, for his pure deeds.
And the ṛṣis, exhausted by their austerities and devoted to the vow of truth;
and the hosts of gods by the thousands, who consume the nectar of immortality.
And the Gandharvas,
with joyful faces and gentle countenances, sang with the celestial voice of the Gandharvas in that other region of the Pitṛs, O King.
In that city of the Daityas, which was filled with watchtowers and crowded with hundreds of *śataghnī* weapons, there was terror for all living beings.
Then the Daityas and Dānavas, the enemies of the gods, released showers of sharp-pointed arrows from all sides in the midst of the deities.
Striking with *śataghnī* weapons, with broad-headed arrows (*bhallas*), and with spears (*śūlas*), O Bhārata,
those Dānavas, skilled in battle, performed a great feat.
With maces they struck maces, and with broad-headed arrows they cut down broad-headed arrows;
they countered weapons with weapons, and illusions with illusions themselves.
Then others, raising up arrows, spears, axes,
and most terrible thunderbolts, joined them by the hundreds of thousands.
Being struck by swords fashioned through illusion, which fell within the range of death,
those gods stood firm despite the showers of arrows.
That chariot, together with its horses, began to sink like a city of the Gandharvas,
being struck by the hosts of Asuras with spears, swords, and javelins.
With those heavy Daitya weapons, such as maces and clubs,
and with many various other missiles, the Lord of Śacī stood his ground.
Then, O lord of the earth, a divine voice manifested from the midst [of the assembly],
O Bhārata, even among the great seers who were the sons of Brahmā.
This very chariot, which was established upon the earth before Śaṅkara,
has become invincible and yet has attained conquerability while all the world looks on.
When that preeminent chariot among chariots had fallen, O King,
lord of the earth, all living beings fell to the ground.
The mountain peaks trembled and the great trees shook;
the oceans were agitated and the ten directions lost their luster.
And there the aged Brahmins chanted that supreme mantra,
which is the splendor consisting of Brahman for those who desire victory everywhere.
For the sake of the peace of all beings in this world and in the next,
having composed the self by means of the self through the cause that is the attainment of yoga.
Then, O Bhārata, with the *rathantara* chant having become the sacred *brahman*,
he blazed with the splendor of Viṣṇu and the high-souled Three-eyed One.
And of all the gods, powerful and able to assume any form at will,
and of the sages rich in asceticism dwelling in the lonely forest.
Then Viṣṇu, the great yogin, having perceived the reality of all things from every side,
assumed the form of a bull and lifted up that excellent chariot,
which had been overwhelmed by the hosts of gods endowed with complete strength and prowess.
Having weighed it with his two horns, the exceedingly powerful and mighty one roared with all his strength,
like the ocean being churned.
Having ascended to the third realm, the domain of the wind,
Viṣāṇavat let out a powerful roar like the ocean during the change of the moon.
Then, terrified by that roar, the Daityas,
who were fierce in battle and possessed of great strength, donned their armor once more and fought again.
All of them indeed possess the strength of arms and are endowed with capable power and prowess;
grasping their bows, they crush the army of the gods.

Having fixed that well-aimed arrow upon his bow and joined it with the Brahmāstra, the imperishable one released it toward the city of the Daityas like the staff of Brahmā, accompanied by a sound that resounded in three ways.
O Bhārata, the Lord, having mentally aimed that threefold arrow through his prowess— with truth, the yoga of Brahman, and supreme austerity— [discharged it].
In the city of the Daityas, he released arrows that snatch away the lives of all beings—
blazing, with the luster of gold, resembling Garuḍas, and perfectly pure.
Having released terrible, excellent arrows like venomous serpents,
that [object] was split asunder by three well-blazing, swift shafts.
O Bhārata, like the peaks of the Vindhya mountains ablaze from the falling of arrows,
the gate-towers, being consumed along with the asuras, O Bhārata,
appear as if they are crumbling away, O lord of men, like great mountains.
Blazing with fire and containing fire within them, O Bhārata,
those cities descended upon the earth, O lord of the earth.
But those [weapons] of his, resembling lapis lazuli, were indeed consumed;
they fell like the burning peaks of a mountain,
O King, as they were utterly burnt by Śaṅkara with the Brahmā-weapon.
Then the victorious Rudra, being attended by the great seers,
proceeded toward the mountain while worshipping Viṣṇu in his form as the bull.
Whoever should constantly hear this victory of Śaṃkara shall attain victory everywhere and obtain long life.
When Tripura was being destroyed by the gods, words were indeed uttered by them out of joy:
"O Supreme Person, slay all these enemies who have grown so great!"
Viṣṇu himself, the great yogin, as if smiling through his yoga,
was praised by the ṛṣis who were like Brahmā, and by Śaṃkara,
together with the gods endowed with strength and prowess, including Brahmā.
[Colophon] [h:

In this *Harivaṃśa*, these accounts are here related in their proper sequence.
Therein, first is the primary creation, followed by the creation of the elements;
then the narrative of Pṛthu Vainya, as well as the enumeration of the Manus.
The origin of the family of Vaivasvata, as well as the story of Dhundhumāra;
the birth of Gālava and the proclamation of the lineage of Ikṣvāku.
The account of the birth of Pitṛkalpa, as well as that of Soma and Budha,
and the glorification of the lineage of Amāvasu, which increases one’s fame.
The departure and the establishment of Śakra, the birth of Kṣatravṛddha, the life-story of Yayāti, and the proclamation of the lineage of Pūru.
The establishment of Divodāsa and of the Kṣatriya Triśaṅku;
the narration of the birth of Kṛṣṇa, as well as that of the Syamantaka jewel.
Thus, the manifestations of Viṣṇu have been briefly recounted; hereafter [follows] more.
The battle with the Tārakas and the description of the world of Brahmā;
the emergence of Viṣṇu from his yogic sleep and the speech of the Creator (Brahmā).
The speech of Pṛthvī, as well as the descent of the portions of the gods,
the slaying of Pralamba, and likewise the description of autumn.
The commencement of the mountain-sacrifice during the lifting of Govardhana,
as well as the words of Nārada and the procedure for the conception in a dream.
Furthermore, the *Āryāstava*, the detailed account of the birth of Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu’s journey to Govraja, and the overturning of the cart; HV App. I, 44.16–17.
The slaying of Pūtanā, the breaking of the twin Arjuna trees,
the appearance of the wolf, and the settling in Vṛndāvana.
Also the description of the rainy season, the sight of the Yamunā lake,
the subduing of Kāliya, and likewise the slaying of Dhenuka.
The death of Pralamba and the description of autumn;
the commencement of the mountain sacrifice and the lifting of Govardhana.
The consecration of Govinda, as well as the sporting of the gopīs,
the slaying of the demon Riṣṭa, and likewise the dispatching of Akrūra;
The words of Andhaka, the death of Keśin, the arrival of Akrūra, and the vision of the world of the Nāgas; HV App. I, 44.26–27.
The journey along the royal highway, the request for clothes from the washerman,
the solicitation of garlands from the florist, and indeed the granting of a boon to him.
Herein is the sight of Kubjā and her request for unguent;
here is the arrangement made for Kubjā and the non-injury of Akṣata;
thereafter follows the account of the breaking of the bow and the words of Kaṃsa.
Then the wrestler’s instruction and the report to the Great Minister;
the slaying of Kuvalayāpīḍa and likewise the slaying of Cāṇūra.
Also the death of Kaṃsa, the lamentation of Kaṃsa’s women,
the performance of the funeral honors for Kaṃsa, and the consecration of Ugrasena.
The consecration of Ugrasena, as well as the consolation of the Yādavas;
then the return of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa from the preceptor’s house is described.
The siege of Mathurā and the turning back of Jarāsaṃdha.
The speech of Vikadru, the sight of Rāma, and likewise his conversation; also the ascent of Mount Gomanta, and the arrival of Jarāsaṃdha.
The burning of Mount Gomanta, his journey to Karavīrapura,
the slaying of Śṛgāla there, and thereafter his arrival at Mathurā.
The dragging of the Yamunā, as well as the departure from Mathurā,
and the slaying of Kālayavana by means of a stratagem have thus been proclaimed.
The manifestation at Dvāravatī, as well as the abduction of Rukmiṇī;
the marriage with Rukmiṇī, and likewise the death of Rukmin.
The meritorious daily observance (*āhnika*) of Baladeva and the majesty of Bala;
likewise, the slaying of Naraka and the seizing of Pārijāta.
The slaying of Naraka and likewise the seizing of the Pārijāta tree.
In this [chapter], there is the slaying of Naraka and the seizing of the Pārijāta tree; specifically,
the description of the reconstruction of Dvāravatī,
the entry into Dvārakā, and the entry into the assembly hall.
The words of Nārada, the glorification of the Vṛṣṇi lineage,
the narrative of the slaying of Ṣaṭpura, and the destruction of Andhaka.
The sea voyage of Kṛṣṇa, his curiosity for water-sports,
and likewise the indulgence in drinking wine by the heroic sons of Bhīma.
Then follows the example of Hari’s abduction of Chālikyagāndharvā; the fame of his carrying off Bhānu, the daughter of the Sun;
and the narrative of the slaying of Nikumbha is proclaimed in full detail.
Then, in Vajrapura, through many diverse contrivances of skillful means,
the slaying of Vajranābha was displayed there by means of an elaborate narrative.
The slaying of Śambara, as well as the episode of Dhanya,
the majesty of Vāsudeva, and the detailed account of the battle with Bāṇa are [described].
And herein the future burning of Tripura is proclaimed; likewise,
the future Puṣkara is celebrated in full detail.
The Vārāha, the Nārasiṃha, and the extensive Vāmana;
the journey to Kailāsa by Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the slaying of Pauṇḍraka.
And the slaughter of the young swan is likewise proclaimed.
By means of the Sudarśana, the rites of driving away and burning [the enemies] are likewise performed.

The burning of Tripura, the greatness of the fruit of hearing the *Bhārata*, the rules regarding the magnitude of the reward, and the worship of the reciter— thus has this summary of the narrative of the *Harivaṃśa* been proclaimed.
Whatever merit there is in a hundred horse-sacrifices, and that of four thousand sacrifices of Śatakratu,
shall become infinite through the gift of the Harivaṃśa.
And it was proclaimed by the great seer Vyāsa.
Whatever fruit is seen from the Vājapeya sacrifice, and whatever other [fruit] from the Rājasūya and the elephant-chariot [sacrifice], that is obtained;
the word of Vyāsa is the authority.
And it was sung by the great seer Vālmīki.
The stainless lotus of the words of Pārāśarya, intense with the fragrance of the meaning of the Gītā,
its filaments being various narratives awakened by the awakening of the stories of Hari—
this is drunk with joy day after day by the bees that are the virtuous in this world.
May the lotus of the *Bhārata*, which destroys the impurities of the Kali age, lead us toward our supreme welfare.
Eighteen thousand verses have indeed been proclaimed;
along with eighty-four verses, the Harivaṃśa is thus celebrated.
In the *Khilas* and here in the *Harivaṃśa*, these have been enumerated by the Great-souled One. All this has been fully recounted from the original compendium of the *Bhārata*.

Thus ends the section known as the *Khila* (Supplement), containing the complete life-story of Hari, within the *Pārijāta* [Parvan] of the glorious *Mahābhārata*, the compilation of one hundred thousand verses composed by Vyāsa.
//* **HV_App.I,44.58** 10:22: May there be the offering to Śrī Prayāgamādhava //*
And the burning of Tripura—this is the summary of the account.
By hearing the *Harivaṃśa*, one is indeed liberated from all sins. He who hears the *Harivaṃśa* here in this world—[his... // 59 //
... ... ... should cause [it] to be recited. **HV_App.I,44.59**11:3 / [k: follows postscriptum in prose -- not transliterated.
:k] [k: V1 inserts *12 = lines 160-173 of Appendix I, No. 40. :k]
O tiger among kings, this has been narrated, which destroys all sins.
O best of the Kurus, he who listens to this account with a concentrated mind every morning and evening shall attain his desires and go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
This collection of all scriptures is auspicious, conducive to fame and longevity, and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Thus [he spoke].
Whoever should recite it once a day, twice a day, or even three times a day.
In a temple of the gods, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), and especially here at the abode of Viṣṇu;
likewise in a shrine of Śiva, in the holy field of Naimiṣa, and similarly at Puṣkara.
Having become pure, the wise couple should worship the reciter with a single-minded focus,
[offering] even a single string of mantras from the *Khila*.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu,
the All-pervading One, becomes pleased by the recitation of the *Harivaṃśa* Saṃhitā as well as its auspicious table of contents (*anukramaṇī*).
And having heard it, one obtains fortune and a lineage desired by the mind;
one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this auspicious summary, he is as one who has bathed in all sacred fords.
From him who was self-controlled, whose hands were adorned, who had the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, who wore yellow garments, whose lower lip was like the fruit of the red bimba,
whose face was as beautiful as the full moon, and whose eyes were like lotuses.
I know of no reality whatsoever that is superior to Kṛṣṇa.
The wise man who should recite this in its entirety, or even half of it,
or a quarter, or half of that, or even a single excellent episode;
He is always to be honored with effort for the complete gratification of Viṣṇu.

... having honored him as one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), one should always offer [this] to him with diligence for the complete satisfaction of Viṣṇu. Whoever, having had this beautiful book copied, offers it...
By him all the Purāṇas were given, and not otherwise. Herein, however many narratives there are, as many indeed as the verses,
likewise as many as the quarters (pādas), and as many as the syllables...
However many measures [of ink] there may be, however many rows of leaves,
however many threads in the cord, however many warp-threads in the cloth, and whatever beautiful and variegated forms are in the book—
For as many thousands of ages as there are syllables, the donor is glorified in heaven.
Even one who is childless, if he listens with faith after having bathed well,
shall indeed obtain sons through the power of Nārāyaṇa.

From hearing this, men shall achieve victory everywhere; moreover, one whose heart is pure shall obtain good fortune in all places. For him with whom Viśveśvara is pleased, the inclination to hear this [text] arises.
It arises for one endowed with merit and a greatly pure mind. A person desiring the supreme state should listen to that;
this is the supreme purifier, this is the manifestation of Dharma.
This [work], endowed with all virtues, should be heard by one desiring the highest good;
one obtains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—of this there is no doubt.
[Colophon and Postscripts — not transliterated] [h: HV (CE) Appendix I, No. 45, transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus, proofread by Horst Brinkhaus]

Janamejaya said: [The manuscripts Dn D3.5.6 continue after App. I, No. 44: {Janamejaya said:}
O best of eminent sages, when the Harivaṃśa Purāṇa is heard, what is the fruit and what indeed is the gift [to be given]? Tell me that in my presence.
Vaiśampāyana said: O best of the Bharatas, when the Harivaṃśa Purāṇa has been heard,
whatever [sin] has been accumulated through body, speech, or even mind— [is all purified].
All that goes to destruction, like snow at the rising of the sun.
Whatever fruit one may obtain from hearing the eighteen Purāṇas, a Vaiṣṇava attains that same fruit; there is no doubt about this.
Both women and men shall attain the station of Viṣṇu by reciting even half a verse or a single quarter-verse originating from the *Harivaṃśa*.
Listening with faith, they shall attain the station of Viṣṇu.
Relying upon Jambūdvīpa, O King, those who will listen in the Kali age will be rare; I tell you the truth, the absolute truth.

And women desiring sons should indeed listen to this glory of Viṣṇu. In this matter, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of three *niṣkas* of gold should be given to the reciter according to one's ability by one who desires the fruit as it has been described.
Desiring his own welfare, he should indeed give to the reciter a tawny cow with golden horns, accompanied by her calf and covered with a cloth.
And one should indeed give ornaments for the hands, O bull of the Bharatas;
one should give an earring as an ornament and especially a vehicle.
O lord of men, one should bestow the gift of land upon a Brāhmaṇa;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to the gift of land.
Such a man who either hears or causes others to hear the *Harivaṃśa* should give a swift horse and a bull yoked to the pole. (HV App. I, 45.20–21)
Freed from all evil, he shall attain the station of Viṣṇu.
A pair of earrings and likewise a woolen garment should be given;
at the conclusion, according to the rules, a linen cloth should be given to the twice-born.
O bull of the Bharatas, he delivers all his ancestors born of the eleven origins, as well as himself, his sons, and his wife. O lord of men,
a fire-oblation here should indeed be performed by a learned man using a tenth part [of the materials].
All this has been told by me before you, O bull among men;
by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
One who is childless obtains a son, and one who is destitute shall obtain wealth.
Whatever fruit is obtained by men through the human sacrifice and the horse sacrifice,
that fruit one certainly obtains from hearing the Purāṇa of Hari.

The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of an embryo, the killer of a cow, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the guru’s bed—by hearing this Purāṇa even once, one becomes purified; it is not otherwise.
This great, boundless, and wonderful majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa has been proclaimed by me to you. By hearing or reciting it, one shall quickly attain the fruit.
And that which is also very difficult to obtain in the worlds, the great [truth].
[Colophon and Postscripts]
